title: American Alliance of Museums Survey: One-Third of US Museums Report Lost Federal Funding
institution: National Endowment for the Arts; National Endowment for the Humanities; Institute of Museum and Library Services (cross-agency museum funding, per the American Alliance of Museums' nationwide survey)
status: Survey findings published November 11, 2025, documenting cumulative funding losses since January 2025; the underlying agency actions this survey measures the combined effect of are separately tracked in this database (see cross-references below), several of which remain ongoing or only partially reversed.
date_of_action: 2025-11-11 (survey publication date; documents cumulative funding losses since January 2025)
what_changed: On November 11, 2025, the American Alliance of Museums (AAM) published a survey of 511 museum directors nationwide finding that roughly one-third had lost federal grants or contracts since Trump took office, with a median loss of $30,000 among affected museums. The most commonly cancelled grants came from the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS), the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH), and the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) -- the three federal grantmakers whose own agency-level actions this database already documents separately: NEA's mass May 2025 grant terminations (see nea-grant-terminations-trump2.json), NEH's grant terminations and staff cuts (see neh-grants-staff-cuts-trump2.json), and IMLS's executive-order dismantlement, later permanently blocked by a federal court (see imls-dismantlement-reversed-trump2.json). Those entries document each agency's own action; this survey is the first sector-wide measurement of the combined real-world effect on museums specifically -- a grantee category none of the three agency-specific entries isolates. Two-thirds of affected museums reported the lost funding had not been replaced by foundations, sponsors, or donors. **About a quarter of museums that lost federal funding had cancelled or reduced programming serving students, people with disabilities, rural communities, or the elderly**, and 28% had cancelled or reduced general-public programming. The survey landed alongside a parallel, separately-tracked pressure campaign over museum content: in August 2025, Trump said he wanted to expand the ideological content-review process already applied to the Smithsonian (see smithsonian-content-review.json) to the nation's roughly 22,000 museums broadly; AAM President and CEO Marilyn Jackson publicly pushed back, saying the vast majority of U.S. museums are independent nonprofits guided by professional standards, not subject to federal review of their exhibitions.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Directed the FY2026 budget proposals and agency actions eliminating or restructuring NEA, NEH, and IMLS funding to museums that this survey measures the cumulative effect of, and separately proposed expanding ideological content review from the Smithsonian to museums nationwide.

estimated_impact.summary: One-third of surveyed U.S. museums lost federal grants or contracts since January 2025, with a median loss of $30,000 per affected museum and most of that funding unreplaced -- forcing cuts to programming for students, people with disabilities, rural communities, and the elderly.

The August 2025 pushback from AAM President and CEO Marilyn Jackson on Trump's proposal to expand ideological content review from the Smithsonian to museums nationwide is independently corroborated by NPR and Al Jazeera.

title: 2.6 Million Fewer Americans Have ACA Coverage After Enhanced Subsidies Expire; HHS Blames "Phantom" Enrollment
institution: ACA Health Insurance Marketplace (HHS/CMS)
status: Ongoing -- enhanced subsidies lapsed Jan. 1, 2026 and Congress has not restored them; enrollment was ~2.6M lower by Feb. 2026. On Sept. 22, 2026 CMS said it had canceled ~315,000 enrollments (~760,000 people) as alleged fraud, with at least 419,000 more people under review.
date_of_action: 2025-12 (enhanced ACA subsidies expire) through 2026-02 (enrollment data showing the decline)
what_changed:
Before the subsidy fight, a Trump-backed Republican policy bill enacted by mid-2025 narrowed ACA access through rule changes rather than repeal -- shortening sign-up periods, adding paperwork burdens, and cutting subsidy eligibility for many legal immigrants; the CBO projected 4 million people would lose coverage from that bill alone, with millions more at risk if the temporary enhanced subsidies also lapsed (New York Times, June 2025). Within a day of the bill's July 4, 2025 enactment, Massachusetts illustrated the mechanism concretely -- AP News reported the law's tighter documentation/redetermination rules and cuts to ACA tax credits and Medicaid funding could strip coverage from up to 100,000 of the roughly 400,000 people enrolled in the state's Health Connector marketplace, the exchange Massachusetts pioneered in 2006 as the model for the ACA itself. Sen. Elizabeth Warren's office had already estimated on June 10, 2025 that the bill would cost roughly 300,000-plus Massachusetts residents their coverage overall, combining the marketplace losses with new Medicaid work requirements and more frequent redeterminations; about 37,000 lawfully-present noncitizens were separately set to lose access to subsidized ConnectorCare plans starting January 2026 under the law's immigrant-eligibility provision. State estimates put the average Marketplace premium increase at $1,300 a year, with some enrollees facing increases of $10,000 to $25,000.

The subsidy expiration was preceded by a months-long legislative fight. By September 2025, CMS had already moved to expand access to 'catastrophic' ACA plans carrying deductibles above $10,000, shifting risk onto patients ahead of the subsidy cliff, while a federal court temporarily blocked a separate Trump-administration verification rule that could have stripped up to 1.8 million people of coverage (CBS News, September 2025). Contemporaneous reporting warned that without an extension, premiums for more than 20 million enrollees could spike over 75% and roughly 2 million people would lose coverage outright, hitting GOP-led states like Florida and Texas hardest (New York Times, September 2025); a KFF analysis the same week projected average annual premiums for subsidized enrollees rising from $888 to $1,906 absent action -- the steepest one-year jump since 2018 (CNBC, September 2025). The fight became entangled with the fall 2025 government shutdown: the administration cut ACA-navigator funding and refused to negotiate even as families faced roughly $2,000 more per year (NBC News, October 2025), and by November reported premium increases had reached 26% or more, with some families citing monthly premiums above $1,500 (CNN, November 2025). Trump escalated: he refused to discuss extending the subsidies until the shutdown ended, called instead for redirecting subsidy funds away from insurers, and Senate Republicans rejected a one-year extension Democrats proposed (New York Times, November 2025). Within weeks Trump made the alternative explicit, telling Republicans he would not support extending the subsidies and insisting the roughly $35 billion in annual subsidy funding instead be redirected as 'direct payments' to individuals -- GOP leadership adopted this framing in rejecting a simple extension even as 22 million enrollees faced the looming cliff (NBC News, November 2025). Senate Democrats kept pushing through late November, but GOP demands for concessions weakening the law made a 60-vote deal unlikely (Semafor, November 2025), and in late November Speaker Mike Johnson told the White House that most House Republicans had little interest in extending the subsidies, as Trump's advisers were drafting a two-year extension plan (CBS News, November 2025).

Bipartisan talks collapsed by early December, with GOP senators tying a deal to unrelated abortion-restriction riders (AP News, December 2025). On Dec. 11, the Senate rejected, 51-48, a motion to advance Democrats' three-year extension bill (the Lower Health Care Costs Act, S.3385), short of the 60 votes needed, with four Republicans voting yes; a competing Republican health-savings-account proposal also failed (Senate roll call vote 644; NPR, December 2025). Reporting through mid-December detailed who stood to lose most as the deadline approached -- contractors, freelancers, and chronically ill workers disproportionately reliant on marketplace coverage (Mother Jones, December 2025) -- and the shape of the coming cost shift, with out-of-pocket caps rising above $10,000 and some premiums more than doubling amid simultaneous medical-cost inflation (New York Times, December 2025). By mid-December, with open enrollment still underway, marketplaces were preparing contingency plans and first-time sign-ups were falling as Congress remained deadlocked (NPR, December 2025). On Dec. 16, Johnson said a moderate-Republican effort to secure a floor vote on an extension had failed for lack of GOP consensus, reversing earlier signals he would allow one (New York Times; USA Today, December 2025). Before the House left town, four swing-district Republicans -- Brian Fitzpatrick, Rob Bresnahan and Ryan Mackenzie of Pennsylvania and Mike Lawler of New York -- joined all 214 Democrats on a discharge petition forcing a January vote on a three-year extension, and Congress then adjourned for the year without acting (NBC News, December 2025). The subsidies formally lapsed on Jan. 1, 2026, with KFF estimating that premium payments for the more than 20 million subsidized enrollees would rise 114% on average (CBS News, January 2026). On Jan. 8, the House passed the discharge-petition bill reviving the credits for three years, 230-196, with 17 Republicans joining all Democrats, but many GOP senators had no interest in reviving the funds and a bipartisan Senate group seeking a scaled-back version had no agreement (NBC News, January 2026). Two early-2026 federal data snapshots, both reported in the same window and not clearly sequenced relative to each other, showed the decline already underway before the ~2.6 million year-over-year figure below was tallied: one showed enrollment down more than 800,000 from the prior year, with states reporting rising terminations and a shift toward high-deductible bronze plans (NBC News, January 2026), and another showed enrollment down roughly 1.4 million year-over-year, with experts expecting further declines once auto-renewal enrollees saw their higher bills (New York Times, January 2026).

In February 2026, Trump officials proposed new ACA plan options featuring lower monthly premiums but deductibles exceeding $15,000 for individuals and $31,000 for families -- a structural shift officials framed as expanding choice, which critics say would leave enrollees exposed to catastrophic out-of-pocket costs before coverage meaningfully applies. A KFF poll reported in March 2026 found roughly 8 in 10 Americans with ACA marketplace plans were already paying higher health care costs following the subsidy expiration, with **many enrollees cutting back on essentials like food and gas to afford coverage, while others reported reducing medication use or dropping coverage entirely** as premiums and out-of-pocket costs rose. The coverage loss also threatens hospitals, not just enrollees: an analysis by Premier Inc., a healthcare performance-improvement company, projected that U.S. hospitals would lose more than $68.6 billion in revenue across 2026-2027 from rising uninsurance tied to the premium-subsidy and Medicaid-eligibility changes combined, with Florida hospitals facing the largest average hit, about $51.8 million per hospital. Florida -- one of ten states that never expanded Medicaid, leaving its hospitals with no expanded state safety net to absorb the loss -- was hit hardest: federal data later showed the state lost about 443,000 marketplace enrollees in 2026, more than any other state (AP, July 2026), and Bloomberg reported between 750,000 and 1 million Floridians at risk of losing coverage overall given the state's above-average reliance on the enhanced subsidies; Florida, Georgia, and Texas together accounted for over 43% of national marketplace enrollment for the 2026 plan year. Individual Florida-serving hospital systems quantified their own exposure: HCA Healthcare, whose largest market is Florida, raised its companywide 2026 estimate of the ACA hit to $1-1.2 billion by July, and AdventHealth projected roughly $1.5 billion in lost annual gross patient revenue from combined Medicaid and marketplace cuts. Federal data released in mid-2026 then showed the fuller national scope: roughly 2.6 million fewer Americans had ACA marketplace coverage in February 2026 than a year earlier, with Ohio and Oklahoma each losing nearly a third of their enrollees -- steeper drops than any other state (AP, July 2026). HHS, under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., attributed a significant share of the enrollment decline to a federal crackdown on 'phantom' or fraudulent enrollments: a June 26, 2026 issue brief from its Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation said anti-fraud efforts had removed or blocked about 2.9 million improperly subsidized enrollees through February 2026, estimated that 2.6 million improper or phantom enrollments still remained -- including more than 1 million without a Social Security number -- and said nearly half of ACA enrollment growth from 2021-2024 was suspected to be improper, phantom or fraudulent. Experts noted that many lawfully present immigrants legitimately lack Social Security numbers and that a missing number can reflect data or broker errors rather than fraud (CNBC, July 2026). Independent analysts and state officials disputed that framing, saying the enrollment collapse was more directly attributable to the subsidy expiration itself, sharply higher post-expiration premiums, and separately tightened eligibility rules restricting which immigrants can access subsidized coverage. CNBC reported that about 22 million people -- more than 90% of marketplace enrollees -- had received the enhanced credits, and that KFF estimated the lapse more than doubled premiums for the average recipient.

Congress did not restore the enhanced subsidies: the Senate's S.3385 had fallen short of 60 votes in December 2025, the House-passed three-year extension (H.R. 1834) was never taken up by the Senate, where bipartisan talks on a scaled-back two-year version stalled by mid-January, and no extension had been enacted as of September 2026. Separately, KFF's analysis of 2027 marketplace rate filings from 276 insurers found a proposed median premium increase of 15% for 2027 -- a second consecutive year of double-digit marketplace premium increases (2026's finalized median increase was 20%) -- in line with analysts' warnings that a smaller, sicker risk pool would drive further increases, though these are proposed rather than final rates (KFF, August 2026). That 2026 median increase traces in part to early insurer rate requests: as insurers began filing 2026 rate requests in July 2025, Centene (the largest ACA marketplace insurer) pulled and refiled its bids to raise premiums, while Elevance and Molina also filed significant increases; Blue Cross Blue Shield's Illinois and Texas affiliate (HCSC) specifically requested +27% in Illinois and +21% in Texas, among the steeper state-level requests reported at the time, with insurers citing both rising medical costs/utilization and the anticipated expiration of the enhanced federal subsidies.

The administration's 'phantom enrollment' claim moved from estimate to action. On Sept. 22, 2026, CMS said that in August it had canceled roughly 315,000 ACA marketplace enrollments covering about 760,000 people, in an action led by Vice President JD Vance's White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, alleging they were improperly enrolled or did not exist; the task force estimated the action would save roughly $2.2 billion in subsidies. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz said CMS flagged enrollees who had been signed up through a broker or agent, had never filed a claim, had their entire premium covered by federal tax credits, and lacked a Social Security number or immigration documents CMS could verify in real time; the administration did not give details of how they were notified (NBC News, September 2026), though Oz said officials had been "writing them, telexing them, walking to them, FedExing" to reach them (HFMA, September 2026). KFF's Cynthia Cox, who NPR reported had heard about the effort from insurance-industry contacts, said the administration sent a list of about a million people to insurers and asked them to try to reach those enrollees, and that plans were ultimately canceled when people did not respond within 30 days; she said there is fraud in the marketplace but that qualified people may also have lost coverage -- someone who filed no claims may simply have been healthy, and someone who moved may have missed the notice. CMS did not answer NPR's questions by airtime about its process or what happens to people canceled in error (NPR, September 2026). Ellen Montz, who oversaw the marketplaces at CMS under President Biden, said the announcement lacked detail on how the administration chose whom to cut and predicted that some consumers would ask why their enrollment was canceled (AP, carried by NPR, September 2026). Vance said a further 419,000 to 450,000 people would face additional verification of legal residency and income (Reuters, September 2026). Oz said the enrollees facing verification had "something about their story that was a little bit different than what we expected from the 100 percent fraud story," adding "we're giving them another chance." The administration separately imposed, by interim final rule effective Sept. 22, 2026, a moratorium through Feb. 1, 2027 (which Oz called six months) on registering new agents and brokers -- those without a 2026 agreement -- to sell 2027 coverage on the federally facilitated exchanges, with Oz saying most of the fraud was concentrated among such agents (Federal Register; Reuters, September 2026).

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: HHS under Kennedy publicly attributed the enrollment decline primarily to a fraud/'phantom enrollment' crackdown rather than to the enhanced-subsidy expiration or premium increases that independent analysts identified as the more direct cause.

estimated_impact.summary: About 2.6 million fewer Americans had ACA marketplace coverage in February 2026 than a year earlier after the enhanced subsidies lapsed, with Ohio and Oklahoma each losing nearly a third of enrollees and Florida losing about 443,000. About 9% of 2025 enrollees had become uninsured by early 2026, 8 in 10 returning enrollees reported higher health costs, and 55% said they had cut or planned to cut spending on food and other household basics. In September 2026 CMS said it had canceled coverage for about 760,000 more people over alleged fraud, with at least 419,000 others under review. KFF had estimated the lapse would more than double premium payments for the ~22 million subsidized enrollees, and hospitals face a projected $68.6 billion revenue loss over 2026-2027 as uninsurance rises. HHS attributes much of the decline to removing improper enrollments; independent analysts point to the subsidy lapse and higher premiums.

estimated_impact.caveat: The 2.6 million enrollment drop is measured federal data; HHS's separate 2.6 million figure is its own estimate of improper enrollments still remaining in 2026 (it says a further 2.9 million improper enrollments were removed or blocked), and independent analysts dispute its fraud framing, noting many lawfully present immigrants lack Social Security numbers. It is unknown how many of the ~760,000 people whose coverage was canceled were actually ineligible; KFF's Cynthia Cox said cancellations followed 30 days without a response to insurer outreach, so some eligible enrollees may be among them. The 114% figure is KFF's pre-lapse estimate, not a measured average, and the 2027 increase is proposed, not final. The hospital figure is Premier's projection and combines subsidy and Medicaid effects. The entry documents no direct health or mortality estimates; beyond KFF's survey estimate that about 9% of 2025 enrollees became uninsured, the health effects of lost coverage and delayed care are not captured.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core enrollment-decline figures and state-level breakdowns, sourced to federal effectuated-enrollment data analyzed by AP (carried by PBS and the Washington Times) and corroborated by CNBC and HHS's own ASPE report. MODERATE confidence on attributing primary causation to either explanation (subsidy expiration/premiums vs. fraud crackdown) -- a genuinely disputed empirical question between HHS and independent analysts. HHS's 2.6 million figure is its own estimate of improper enrollments still remaining in 2026, not a count of those who left. The 114% premium figure is KFF's pre-lapse estimate for subsidized enrollees, not a measured outcome. The hospital revenue-loss figure ($68.6B, 2026-2027) is Premier Inc.'s projection. The 2027 figure (median 15%) is KFF's analysis of proposed, not final, rates. The legislative timeline (Senate cloture vote Dec. 11, 2025; House passage Jan. 8, 2026) is HIGH confidence, confirmed by the Senate roll call and NBC News. The Sept. 2026 cancellations and broker moratorium are HIGH confidence, from CMS statements reported by CNBC, NBC News and Reuters and the Federal Register interim final rule; how many canceled enrollees were actually ineligible is unknown. The Massachusetts figures (AP; Sen. Warren's office) measure overlapping but not identical populations and are presented separately. Florida's at-risk range and the AdventHealth figure rest on Bloomberg's reporting. Update 2026-10-03 (how the cancellations were carried out): The account that insurers were asked to reach about a million flagged enrollees and plans were canceled after 30 days without a response is HIGH confidence: KFF's Cynthia Cox gave it on NPR, and HFMA and Morgan Lewis (citing CMS officials, who put the list at nearly 1.2 million) reported the same 30-day insurer-outreach window. How many canceled enrollees were actually eligible is unknown.
pull_quote: Roughly 2.6 million fewer Americans had ACA marketplace coverage in February 2026 than a year earlier.

section_summaries.what_changed: Enhanced ACA subsidies lapsed at the end of 2025; 2.6 million fewer Americans had marketplace coverage by February 2026, and CMS later canceled coverage for ~760,000 people over alleged fraud.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: About 2.6 million fewer people had ACA coverage and ~760,000 more lost it in fraud cancellations; enrollees' premium payments rose 58% on average (KFF).
section_summaries.confidence_note: Enrollment figures are federally sourced and well-corroborated; the competing causal explanations (fraud vs. subsidy expiration) remain disputed between HHS and independent analysts.

title: Only National Research Center for Parents With Disabilities Loses Federal Funding After ACL Pulls Its Grant Competition, One of 36 Disability Research Awards Withdrawn
institution: Administration for Community Living (HHS)
status: Federal grant ended August 31, 2026 with no renewal competition issued; on August 27 the center said it had no clear path to federal funding and would finish work underway while seeking other support. No restoration reported as of September 28, 2026.
date_of_action: 2026-07-07 (funding opportunity found removed from Grants.gov)
what_changed: The Administration for Community Living (ACL), the $2.5 billion HHS agency that funds disability and aging services and research nationally, removed from Grants.gov, before applications could open, the forecasted funding opportunity for the competitive five-year, roughly $5 million grant from its National Institute on Disability, Independent Living, and Rehabilitation Research (NIDILRR) that has funded Brandeis University's National Research Center for Parents with Disabilities since 2016 -- **the only federally funded research center in the country dedicated to the needs and experiences of parents with disabilities and their families**. The opportunity had appeared on the Grants.gov forecast in September 2025 and was expected to open for applications in February 2026; the center's principal investigator, Monika Mitra, found on July 7, 2026 that it had been removed. The center's grant was due to run out August 31, 2026, and in mid-July researchers said the center's work (research, training, and translating findings into resources for parents, professionals, advocates, and policymakers) would end abruptly unless the funding opportunity was restored within weeks. Mother Jones reported that the opportunity was one of 36 expected NIDILRR awards, together worth more than $6.5 million, removed from the federal grants database so far in 2026, and that Mitra was told by a NIDILRR contact it would not be reposted; The Imprint called it one of dozens announced and then withdrawn by the agency in recent weeks. HHS did not respond to questions from Mother Jones, The Imprint or GBH and has given no public explanation, even as other NIDILRR competitions (rehabilitation engineering, knowledge translation, field-initiated research) stayed open with deadlines in late July and early August 2026 -- a detail suggesting this was a selective withdrawal rather than part of an across-the-board NIDILRR funding action. On August 27, 2026, the center said it had no clear path to continued federal funding and no assurances about future funding, and that it would finish projects already underway while pursuing other ways to sustain the work. Its NIDILRR grant ended August 31, 2026, the day WBUR's Here & Now reported that the center was set to close. No restoration of the funding opportunity had been reported as of September 28, 2026.

title: HHS Dismantled the Administration for Community Living -- Closed All 10 Regional Offices, Fired Half Its Staff, Threatening Meals on Wheels and Services for Older and Disabled Americans
institution: Administration for Community Living (ACL), HHS
status: Completed -- ACL's regional office network eliminated and roughly half its staff terminated as of late April 2025; its functions nominally absorbed into other HHS components (ACF, ASPE, CMS) with no detailed transition plan identified in reporting reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-03-27 (restructuring announced) through 2025-04-25 (dismantlement substantially complete, reported by NYT)
what_changed: On March 27, 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a department-wide reorganization eliminating 10,000 positions and consolidating 28 divisions into 15, including dissolving the Administration for Community Living (ACL) -- the roughly 200-person HHS agency responsible for aging and disability policy, including oversight of Older Americans Act programs like Meals on Wheels, home and community-based services, adult protective services, and caregiver support -- entirely, with its functions nominally redistributed to the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE), and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS). On April 1, 2025, roughly half of ACL's approximately 200 employees were terminated, including most of the agency's leadership, policy staff, and budget staff, and all 10 of ACL's regional-office administrator positions were eliminated, closing the regional office network that coordinated directly with state and local aging/disability service organizations nationwide. By April 24-25, 2025, the New York Times reported the dismantlement substantially complete, with no detailed public plan for how the absorbing HHS components would carry out ACL's former functions. Sixty-three House Democrats, led by Reps. Schakowsky, Matsui, and Bonamici, sent HHS a formal letter demanding answers on the disbandment. **Advocacy groups including Justice in Aging and USAging warned the cuts put home and community-based services, Adult Day Programs, senior-center and medical transportation, and elder-abuse/exploitation legal services at risk.** This dismantlement is the same underlying event referenced by an April 2 NPR report ('HHS layoffs put seniors, disabled and LIHEAP recipients at risk') describing the elimination of entire ACL teams days into the broader HHS purge, and is distinct from this tracker's separate LIHEAP-staff-elimination entry (liheap-staff-elimination-funding-delay-trump2.json), which documents the same-week firing of the ~10-person LIHEAP energy-assistance office within a different HHS component (ACF's Office of Community Services).

title: AFRICOM's Commander Warned Trump's Foreign-Aid Cuts Were Undermining African Counterterrorism Partnerships as China Filled the Gap
institution: U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM), Department of Defense; State Department (absorbing USAID functions)
status: Ongoing as of last verification -- aid programs remained under review with no full restoration reported, even as U.S. airstrikes against al-Shabaab in Somalia nearly doubled
date_of_action: 2025-05 (Langley's warning and Defense One/Breaking Defense reporting)
what_changed: **AFRICOM Commander Gen. Michael Langley warned in testimony and public remarks in May 2025 that the Trump administration's foreign-aid cuts -- including the dismantling of USAID and reduced security-assistance funding to partner nations -- were undermining U.S. counterterrorism capacity in Africa, allowing al-Shabaab (Somalia) and ISIS-affiliated groups in the Sahel to gain ground**, with the Sahel described as the global 'epicenter' of terrorism. Langley specifically noted China was moving to 'replicate' U.S. security-assistance activities as Washington pulled back, training and arming African militaries in the resulting vacuum, even as China continued to vastly outspend AFRICOM's own budget militarily on the continent. The State Department, having absorbed USAID's functions, was still determining which aid programs to preserve, acknowledging some cut programs had been 'really helpful' to U.S. military stability operations. Notably, even as security-assistance funding was cut, the administration simultaneously escalated direct military action, nearly doubling airstrikes against al-Shabaab in Somalia compared to 2024 -- pairing reduced long-term partnership investment with increased short-term kinetic operations.

title: DOGE-Driven Cuts Terminated $400 Million in AmeriCorps Grants and Sidelined Tens of Thousands of Volunteers Before Courts and a 2026 Settlement Intervened
institution: AmeriCorps (Corporation for National and Community Service), including its National Civilian Community Corps (NCCC) program
status: Partially reversed through litigation and a September 2026 settlement -- courts ordered funding and members restored in roughly two dozen states plus D.C. in June 2025, OMB released $184 million in withheld funds in August 2025, and a September 2026 settlement with a 23-state coalition now bars AmeriCorps from repeating mass grant terminations, mass layoffs, or mass service-member dismissals without 30 days' advance notice through the end of FY2026
date_of_action: 2025-04-08 (agency unveils internal workforce-reduction plan) through 2025-04-25 (DOGE-driven grant terminations and staff administrative leave across all 50 states), with litigation and a further settlement continuing into 2026-09-10
what_changed: On April 8, 2025, AmeriCorps' own leadership unveiled an internal plan to cut the agency's workforce by "up to 50 percent or more." Days later, the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) arrived at the agency and moved far beyond that plan: on April 17, AmeriCorps National Civilian Community Corps (NCCC) members were informed by email that their service was ending early, citing "programmatic circumstances" tied to Trump's government-efficiency executive order -- volunteers who perform disaster response, education, and conservation work were sent home just before hurricane season. By April 25, DOGE had terminated roughly $400 million in AmeriCorps grants -- about 41 percent of the agency's total grant funding -- affecting 1,031 grantee organizations and 32,465 AmeriCorps members and senior volunteers nationwide, while placing approximately 85 percent of the agency's own employees on administrative leave. The cuts, notified to grantees late on a Friday with instructions to shut down projects immediately and without the notice-and-comment process required for terminating congressionally appropriated grants, **disrupted disaster-response teams, food-security programs, and tutoring/mentoring services supplied to schools nationwide**. Roughly two dozen states and the District of Columbia sued, arguing the abrupt cancellations violated the Administrative Procedure Act. On June 5, 2025, U.S. District Judge Deborah L. Boardman (D. Md.) ruled for the states, finding the cuts likely violated the APA, and ordered the administration to stop enforcing the terminations and restore grant funding and AmeriCorps members in the roughly two dozen plaintiff states and D.C. On August 29, 2025, the Office of Management and Budget released $184 million in previously withheld AmeriCorps funding nationwide. The underlying dispute was not fully resolved until September 10, 2026, when AmeriCorps reached a settlement with a coalition of 23 state attorneys general and two governors: the agency committed not to conduct mass grant terminations, mass reductions in force, or mass service-member dismissals during FY2026 without giving the coalition states 30 days' written notice and identifying its legal authority for any such action, and agreed to commit substantially all of its FY2026 funding by September 30, 2026, and to operate NCCC and AmeriCorps VISTA in accordance with their governing statutes. The settlement pauses the litigation through February 1, 2027, when the coalition will voluntarily dismiss the case if AmeriCorps has complied.

primary_proponent.note: No single named DOGE staffer was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing the AmeriCorps-specific cuts, distinct from other entries in this tracker (e.g. the NEH grant-screening entry) where individual DOGE staffers were named and deposed.

estimated_impact.summary: DOGE's April 2025 action cut off roughly 41 percent of AmeriCorps' total grant funding overnight, disrupting disaster-response, food-security, and school tutoring/mentoring programs run through more than a thousand grantee organizations and sidelining tens of thousands of volunteers and staff -- without the legally required notice-and-comment process. Courts restored funding and members in about half the states within two months, but full nationwide resolution took a September 2026 settlement more than 16 months later.

title: Arizona SNAP Enrollment Cut in Half as State Adds Paperwork, Cuts Caseworkers to Avoid Federal Penalties Under Trump's Benefits Law
institution: Arizona Department of Economic Security (implementing federal SNAP rules under HR1/OBBBA)
status: Ongoing -- enrollment stabilized and ticked up slightly in June 2026 after nearly a year of decline (471,871, up from 451,762 in May), though still roughly half the pre-HR1 level; steeper federal error-rate penalties phase in starting October 2027
date_of_action: 2025-07 (HR1/OBBBA enacted) through 2026-05 (enrollment data)
what_changed: Following passage of Trump's HR1 ('One Big Beautiful Bill') tax and spending law, which imposes steep financial penalties on states with high SNAP payment error rates (Arizona's 2025 error rate was 10.8%, putting the state at risk of up to $300 million in penalties by fiscal year 2028 if the rate continues) and shifts more administrative costs onto states, Arizona increased the paperwork required of SNAP applicants while simultaneously cutting the caseworker staff available to process it. The number of Department of Economic Security staff reviewing SNAP eligibility fell from 1,370 in July 2024 to 880 by mid-2026. As a direct result, Arizona's SNAP enrollment collapsed from approximately 910,000 people in June 2025 to about 452,000 by May 2026 -- roughly a 50% decline in under a year. Applicants have described being unable to reach a caseworker despite placing up to 100 phone calls to the program. Food bank visits in the state now exceed SNAP enrollment for the first time, as many people who remain legally eligible for benefits are unable to navigate the increased paperwork burden with reduced staff support to process it. Update 2026-07-28: HR1 cuts SNAP by an estimated $187 billion nationally over the next decade, per NBC News reporting -- Arizona's enrollment collapse documented in this entry (**roughly 200,000 children among those losing benefits**) is one state-level instance of that broader national reduction, with food banks nationally reporting record demand as a result. Update 2026-08-17: USDA's official FY2025 SNAP payment error rate for Arizona, released June 24, 2026, confirmed the 10.8% figure already in this entry (up from 8.84% in FY2024). Reporting on the resulting penalty exposure varies by outlet -- figures of $208 million, roughly $200 million, and up to $280 million have all been reported, in addition to this entry's existing $300 million figure -- reflecting different assumptions/timing rather than a single authoritative number; treat the penalty size as a reported range (~$200-300 million), not a fixed figure. On the underlying penalty structure: the cost-share penalty HR1 created does not take effect until fiscal year 2028 (starting October 1, 2027); states with an error rate under 6% in either FY2025 or FY2026 owe no cost share. Arizona's stated goal is to bring its FY2026 error rate (the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026) under 6%, but that official rate will not be published until June 2027 -- meaning whether Arizona's paperwork/staffing response actually achieves its stated goal will not be independently verifiable for many months yet. Update 2026-08-30: after nearly a year of straight-line decline, Arizona's SNAP caseload ticked up for the first time -- from 451,762 in May 2026 to 471,871 in June 2026, a gain of roughly 20,000 people -- per DES's own monthly enrollment data reported by AZPM; state officials attribute this to clearing application backlogs rather than a policy reversal, and the underlying error-rate penalty question remains unresolved (the FY2026 rate that determines whether Arizona avoids the FY2028 cost-share penalty won't be published until June 2027). This is a real, if modest, correction to this entry's prior 'decline continuing' framing -- the collapse has not reversed, but it has stopped worsening month-over-month for the first time since the collapse began. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 51): a dollar-denominated version of this same collapse, not previously in this entry alongside its enrollment-count and staffing figures, corroborates the same July 2025-to-June 2026 window -- statewide monthly SNAP issuance fell from $162.5 million to $79.1 million, roughly a 51% reduction, tracking closely with the ~48% enrollment decline already documented here. No July 2026 caseload or issuance data had been published in sourcing reviewed as of this recheck.

what_changed.base: Following passage of Trump's HR1 ('One Big Beautiful Bill') tax and spending law, which imposes steep financial penalties on states with high SNAP payment error rates (Arizona's 2025 error rate was 10.8%, putting the state at risk of up to $300 million in penalties by fiscal year 2028 if the rate continues) and shifts more administrative costs onto states, Arizona increased the paperwork required of SNAP applicants while simultaneously cutting the caseworker staff available to process it. The number of Department of Economic Security staff reviewing SNAP eligibility fell from 1,370 in July 2024 to 880 by mid-2026. As a direct result, Arizona's SNAP enrollment collapsed from approximately 910,000 people in June 2025 to about 452,000 by May 2026 -- roughly a 50% decline in under a year. Applicants have described being unable to reach a caseworker despite placing up to 100 phone calls to the program. Food bank visits in the state now exceed SNAP enrollment for the first time, as many people who remain legally eligible for benefits are unable to navigate the increased paperwork burden with reduced staff support to process it.

updates.text: Update 2026-07-28: HR1 cuts SNAP by an estimated $187 billion nationally over the next decade, per NBC News reporting -- Arizona's enrollment collapse documented in this entry (**roughly 200,000 children among those losing benefits**) is one state-level instance of that broader national reduction, with food banks nationally reporting record demand as a result.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-17: USDA's official FY2025 SNAP payment error rate for Arizona, released June 24, 2026, confirmed the 10.8% figure already in this entry (up from 8.84% in FY2024). Reporting on the resulting penalty exposure varies by outlet -- figures of $208 million, roughly $200 million, and up to $280 million have all been reported, in addition to this entry's existing $300 million figure -- reflecting different assumptions/timing rather than a single authoritative number; treat the penalty size as a reported range (~$200-300 million), not a fixed figure. On the underlying penalty structure: the cost-share penalty HR1 created does not take effect until fiscal year 2028 (starting October 1, 2027); states with an error rate under 6% in either FY2025 or FY2026 owe no cost share. Arizona's stated goal is to bring its FY2026 error rate (the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026) under 6%, but that official rate will not be published until June 2027 -- meaning whether Arizona's paperwork/staffing response actually achieves its stated goal will not be independently verifiable for many months yet.

updates.text: Update 2026-08-30: after nearly a year of straight-line decline, Arizona's SNAP caseload ticked up for the first time -- from 451,762 in May 2026 to 471,871 in June 2026, a gain of roughly 20,000 people -- per DES's own monthly enrollment data reported by AZPM; state officials attribute this to clearing application backlogs rather than a policy reversal, and the underlying error-rate penalty question remains unresolved (the FY2026 rate that determines whether Arizona avoids the FY2028 cost-share penalty won't be published until June 2027). title: Pentagon Watchdog Found Border-Mission Soldiers Housed in Sewage-Leaking, Overcrowded, Fire-Risk Barracks
institution: Department of War (Defense) Office of Inspector General; U.S. Army, Joint Task Force-Southern Border
status: Soldiers were relocated from the Doña Ana Range Complex in November 2025, before the report's public release; no source reviewed confirmed comparable relocation or remediation at Fort Bliss itself, and no named Army or Pentagon official's corrective-action statement was identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-03 (roughly 2,400 soldiers deployed) through 2025-12-18 (DoW Inspector General management advisory publicly released)
what_changed: Roughly 2,400 soldiers of the 2nd Stryker Brigade Combat Team, 4th Infantry Division (based at Fort Carson, Colorado) deployed in March 2025 to support Joint Task Force-Southern Border operations, housed at Fort Bliss, Texas and the Doña Ana Range Complex in New Mexico. The brigade's own preventative medicine team documented health concerns between May and August 2025, and the Department of War Inspector General conducted site inspections in late July 2025, finding conditions that did not comply with Army housing requirements, in some cases for extended periods without documentation: **leaking raw sewage, non-functional toilets, and general facility disrepair; air conditioning units causing respiratory symptoms among soldiers**; standing water from AC condensation and rain that fueled a large increase in insects and mosquitoes; and electrical systems Fort Bliss officials themselves said risked tripping circuit breakers and creating a fire hazard in the aging buildings if soldiers exceeded the housing areas' electrical capacity. Living space fell well below standard: as little as 45 square feet per soldier at Fort Bliss and 69 square feet at the Doña Ana Range Complex. Soldiers were relocated out of the Doña Ana Range Complex in November 2025, before the Inspector General publicly released its management advisory on December 18, 2025, which the watchdog framed as urgent enough to warrant a rare advisory-level warning to commanders about immediate health and safety risks rather than waiting for its standard full-report process.

title: Staffing Cuts Forced the Army Corps of Engineers to Close or Curtail Hours at 30+ Federal Lake/Reservoir Recreation Sites Across Six States
institution: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
status: Closures/curtailments took effect starting May 1, 2025; no reported reversal identified as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-04-28 (reporting) through 2025-05-01 (closures effective)
what_changed: **The Associated Press reported April 28, 2025 that campgrounds, boat ramps, visitor centers, and other recreation facilities at federal lakes and reservoirs managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers would close or have hours curtailed at more than 30 locations across six states -- South Dakota, North Dakota, Montana, Nebraska, Kansas, and Washington -- starting in mid-May 2025, as the administration's broader federal workforce reduction left the Corps facing staffing shortages and budgetary restrictions.** The Corps' Omaha district announced it would close six campgrounds in the Dakotas on May 1, plus three visitor centers in South Dakota and Montana, and would suspend or limit tours of four South Dakota dam powerhouses and reduce tours at Montana's Fort Peck Dam. The Corps' Walla Walla, Washington district separately announced closure of two visitor centers and eight camping/recreation areas. Pennsylvania's Raystown Lake and additional Washington-state facilities were also slated for scaled-back operations. Corps spokesman Douglas Garman said the agency was concentrating remaining staff at fewer sites so those sites could keep a 'full range of services' for visitors, rather than spreading thinned staff across every location.

title: Army cancels training courses, cuts pilot flight hours amid $4-6 billion budget shortfall tied to Iran war and border deployments
institution: U.S. Army
status: Ongoing -- shortfall and resulting cuts were still in effect as of May 2026 reporting
date_of_action: 2025-08 (National Guard deployment to Washington, D.C. begins) through 2026-05 (reporting of internal Army budget documents)
what_changed: The Army faced a budget shortfall of some $4-6 billion, according to a U.S. official cited by ABC News, and internal Army documents showed the resulting cancellation of training courses, cuts to pilot flight hours, and warnings of reduced overall readiness. The Army's premier combat-engineering school, the Sapper Course, was canceled, as was an artillery course set to begin at Fort Campbell, Kentucky. Aviation readiness was hit particularly hard, with pilots limited to minimum required flight hours. III Armored Corps, the Texas-based headquarters overseeing roughly 70,000 troops and hundreds of tanks, saw its training budget cut by nearly $292 million in late April 2026. Officials linked the shortfall to costs from the Iran war, an expanded southern-border military mission, rising personnel and fuel costs, and an ongoing National Guard deployment to Washington, D.C. that the Congressional Budget Office estimated at about $55 million a month -- money originally budgeted for training and readiness effectively redirected to cover these other mission costs. On August 20, 2025, just after 6 a.m., an armored National Guard vehicle (a Mine-Resistant Ambush Protected All-Terrain Vehicle) collided with a civilian car at 8th Street SE and North Carolina Avenue SE on Capitol Hill after the Guardsman driving it ran a red light; **the civilian driver was extracted by DC Fire and transported to a hospital with minor injuries, including a head laceration** (NPR, NBC4 Washington, The Hill, August 2025) -- a concrete early illustration of the deployment's on-the-ground risk to residents, as opposed to just its budgetary cost. That D.C. deployment traces to a broader Trump 'crime crackdown' begun in August 2025 (the Pentagon's 'D.C. Safe and Beautiful' mission): as reported by the New York Times on September 1, 2025, Republican governors had sent additional Guard troops to Washington even as cities in their own states -- including Memphis, Houston, and Cleveland -- recorded comparable or worse violent-crime rates, while Trump declined to deploy troops to those cities and falsely claimed they lacked serious crime problems. By September 11, 2025, per further New York Times reporting, over 2,300 Guard troops were stationed in D.C. despite the city's falling crime rate, with most tasked with picking up trash, mulching parks, and patrolling Metro stops rather than conventional law-enforcement duties -- the deployment whose ongoing cost is now cited as a contributing driver of the Army's training shortfall. Update 2026-08-02: Surging fuel prices tied to the Iran war are a specifically quantified driver of the shortfall -- the average price the Pentagon paid per barrel of fuel climbed from $154.14 in October 2025 to $195.72 in April 2026, a nearly 27% increase in six months, which ABC News reported could saddle the Pentagon with more than $1 billion in unplanned costs this year to power jets, tanks, and other equipment. The Air Force alone is burning through roughly 10% more fuel than it had projected amid the ongoing Iran war. Update 2026-09-23: ABC News reported on May 13, 2026, citing internal documents and multiple U.S. officials, that the Army was cutting training to cover a shortfall of some $4 billion to $6 billion, a figure it attributed to one of those officials. CNN reported on May 27, 2026, citing an internal document it reviewed, that III Armored Corps' training budget was cut by nearly $292 million, noting that ABC News was first to report the cuts. The Congressional Budget Office's Jan. 28, 2026 letter to Sen. Merkley estimated that continuing the ongoing domestic troop deployments at their end-of-2025 size would cost $93 million per month in total, with per-city costs ranging from about $6 million a month in New Orleans to about $55 million a month for 2,950 personnel in Washington, D.C.; CNN reported on Jan. 29, 2026 that the $93 million monthly figure, which CNN said covers deployments to Los Angeles, Washington, Memphis, Portland, and Chicago, would amount to more than $1.1 billion in 2026. ABC News's May 13 report attributed the roughly $1.1 billion figure to the D.C. deployment alone. President Trump authorized the D.C. National Guard deployment in an August 11, 2025 memorandum, and troops began appearing in the city the next day, according to the Congressional Budget Office and contemporaneous reporting.

Safe and Beautiful' mission): as reported by the New York Times on September 1, 2025, Republican governors had sent additional Guard troops to Washington even as cities in their own states -- including Memphis, Houston, and Cleveland -- recorded comparable or worse violent-crime rates, while Trump declined to deploy troops to those cities and falsely claimed they lacked serious crime problems. title: DHS Proposed Extending Asylum Seekers' Work-Permit Wait From 180 Days to a Year and Disqualifying Most Who Crossed Illegally
institution: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Department of Homeland Security
status: Formal proposed rule (NPRM) published February 23, 2026; comment period closed April 24, 2026, with final-rule status not yet confirmed as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-06 (draft/plans first reported) through 2026-02-23 (formal NPRM published)
what_changed: CBS News reported June 5, 2025 that Trump administration officials were drafting a rule to sharply restrict work-permit access for asylum seekers, extending the existing 180-day waiting period (before which asylum applicants may apply for work authorization) to one year, and requiring asylum cases to be resolved within an unrealistic 180-day window as a condition. The plan was formalized on February 23, 2026, when USCIS published a proposed rule, 'Employment Authorization Reform for Asylum Applicants,' that would: **extend the work-permit eligibility wait from 180 to 365 days; extend USCIS's own permit-processing deadline from 30 to 180 days**; pause new work-permit applications entirely whenever average asylum-case processing times exceed 180 days; and disqualify migrants who crossed the border illegally from work-permit eligibility unless they affirmatively told immigration officials within 48 hours of entry that they were fleeing persecution. The public comment period ran through April 24, 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Kristi Noem
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Homeland Security
primary_proponent.note: DHS/USCIS is the issuing agency for the proposed rule; reporting attributes it to the department generally rather than to Noem's specific personal direction of this rule's drafting.

estimated_impact.summary: Extending the work-permit wait to a full year, while simultaneously giving the agency itself up to 180 days just to process applications, would leave many asylum seekers without any lawful way to support themselves for well over a year after applying -- pushing them, as advocates warned, toward informal/underground economic activity -- while the illegal-entry disqualification would categorically bar most border-crossing asylum seekers from work authorization regardless of the merit of their underlying claim.

title: DOJ Cut Two-Thirds of ATF's Gun-Dealer Inspectors and Proposed Merging ATF Into DEA, Then Quietly Abandoned the Merger
institution: Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), Department of Justice
status: Inspector cuts implemented; the ATF/DEA merger plan was quietly abandoned by January 2026 after bipartisan pushback
date_of_action: 2025-06-19 (inspector cuts reported) through 2026-01-17 (merger plan abandoned)
what_changed: In June 2025, DOJ eliminated 541 of ATF's roughly 800 Industry Operations Investigators (IOIs) -- the inspectors responsible for scrutinizing federally licensed gun dealers and identifying businesses suspected of selling firearms to prohibited buyers or straw purchasers. The cut, roughly two-thirds of the inspector workforce, was reported to **reduce ATF's overall capacity to regulate the firearms and explosives industries by about 40%**, with DOJ claiming roughly $82 million in savings. The cuts accompanied a broader proposal, first floated in March 2025, to merge ATF into the Drug Enforcement Administration, with DEA absorbing select ATF functions related to violent crime, drug enforcement, and firearms crimes; Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly defended the proposal. The plan drew opposition from both gun-rights and gun-control advocacy groups, and by January 17, 2026, the Trump administration had quietly abandoned the ATF/DEA merger plan after months of bipartisan pressure -- though the inspector-workforce cuts themselves were not reported as reversed.

primary_proponent.role: Attorney General
primary_proponent.note: Bondi publicly defended DOJ's proposal to end ATF as a standalone agency and oversaw the inspector cuts; the merger itself was later abandoned, but reporting does not indicate the inspector-workforce reduction was similarly reversed.

estimated_impact.summary: Cutting roughly two-thirds of the inspectors responsible for policing federally licensed gun dealers for illegal sales and trafficking reduced the agency's regulatory capacity by an estimated 40%, raising concerns from advocacy groups and reporting (including from New York state enforcement contexts) that reduced dealer oversight could enable more illegal firearms sales and trafficking to reach criminal buyers.

title: Atlanta Forfeited $37.5M in FAA Airport Grants After Refusing to Certify Against DEI Programs
institution: FAA -- Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport infrastructure grants
status: Final for the 2025 funds -- the city confirmed the forfeited money is not recoverable, though the airport remains eligible to apply for future FAA grants; Atlanta later joined litigation challenging the anti-DEI grant terms generally
date_of_action: 2025-07-29 (Atlanta declines FAA certification terms) through 2025-09-26 (forfeiture publicly reported)
what_changed: The FAA required grant recipients to certify they do not 'operate any programs promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that violate any applicable Federal anti-discrimination laws' as a condition of receiving airport infrastructure funding, per Trump's executive orders targeting DEI programs. title: Bird Flu Surged Through 66 Poultry Flocks in a Month as Federal Surveillance and Genetic Sequencing Capacity Collapsed
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA); Department of Health and Human Services / CDC
status: Ongoing and freshly re-illustrated -- Congress publicly demanded restoration of surveillance capacity in late November 2025 and again in 2026, with no confirmation in sourcing reviewed that USDA had done so; in August 2026, USDA's own APHIS livestock-detection tracker, which states it updates each weekday, went nearly 30 days without posting new H5N1 detections before a batch of new poultry and dairy-cattle infections appeared all at once
date_of_action: 2025-04-23 (HHS directs NAS to cancel its bird-flu PPE-training workshop) through 2025-11-06 (NPR reporting), with a congressional letter following 2025-11-late
what_changed: Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0285: Reuters reported that HHS informed the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine on April 23, 2025 that it should terminate all work on a workshop scheduled for June 26-27, 2025 on best practices for personal protective equipment among farmworkers and veterinarians at heightened risk of bird flu -- no final product was released. At the time, **bird flu had infected 70 people over the preceding year, most of them farmworkers**, and farmworker advocates said PPE training and communication were critical to prevention; CDC itself had said suboptimal PPE use contributed to farmworker cases during an earlier Colorado outbreak. This is the earliest documented instance of the training/communication-capacity loss this entry's later 2025-2026 updates document at larger scale. NPR reported on November 6, 2025 that H5N1 avian influenza had struck 66 poultry flocks in the preceding 30 days, killing more than 3.5 million turkeys, chickens, and ducks -- a sharp increase over the summer months, with states in the central U.S. hit hardest as migrating wild birds spread the virus. Scientists tracking the outbreak told NPR they lacked good visibility into what was happening in both animal and human populations because the federal government had scaled back surveillance, genetic sequencing, research coordination, and public communication -- a combination of staffing purges (this database separately documents a related but distinct February 2025 episode in which USDA accidentally fired bird-flu response staff, see usda-bird-flu-response-staff-accidental-firing-2025), disruption from the October-November 2025 government shutdown, and new restrictions on public-facing communication about the outbreak. Compounding the surveillance gap, NPR and a related Stateline report found that immigration enforcement fears were deterring the largely undocumented farmworker population from participating in testing or long-term research: a survey of several hundred farmworkers across three states found roughly 20% reported symptoms coinciding with sick animals on their farms, but most said they were never tested, and California farmworkers interviewed described being too afraid to even leave their homes. In late November 2025, a bipartisan group of members of Congress, led by Reps. Sarah McBride and Jim Costa, sent USDA a letter demanding it immediately restore full avian-influenza surveillance and coordination capacity, warning that reduced federal coordination -- caused by the shutdown and broader reductions-in-force -- was undermining farmers' ability to detect and contain outbreaks quickly. Update 2026-08-17: No confirmation of USDA restoring full surveillance capacity was found in sourcing reviewed as of this recheck; a follow-up congressional letter again urged USDA to fully restore avian-influenza surveillance and coordination as HPAI outbreaks returned 'in full force' into 2026, again citing furloughs, staffing cuts, and reductions-in-force at USDA and CDC as limiting real-time reporting capacity and farmers' ability to respond to outbreaks. Update 2026-08-30: A fresh, concrete example of the surveillance gap this entry documents surfaced in trade-press reporting: APHIS's livestock H5N1 detection map -- which states on its own page that it is updated every weekday -- went nearly 30 days in mid-to-late summer 2026 without posting new confirmed detections, only for a cluster of new dairy-cattle and poultry infections to appear all at once once updates resumed (three dairy herds in Texas and Utah; a 29,700-bird outbreak in Edmunds County, SD, plus smaller outbreaks in Brule County, SD and Ada/Canyon counties, ID). During the reporting gap, anyone checking the tracker -- a reporter, a farmer, a local health official -- would have seen stale numbers with no on-page indication they were stale. CDC's own bird-flu situation-summary page separately carried a last-updated date from early March 2026 as of this recheck; CDC stopped publishing USDA's animal-detection data on its own site in mid-2025, directing readers to USDA's page instead, the same page found to have gone dark for nearly a month. CDC's human-surveillance systems continued to show no indicators of unusual human influenza activity as of this update -- this is a data-reporting and transparency gap on the animal-surveillance side, not a confirmed undetected human outbreak. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0721): a ProPublica investigation published November 28, 2025 found USDA rejected genomic and wind-pattern evidence that a December 2024-February 2025 H5N1 outbreak spread through the air, not just via 'shared people and equipment' as USDA's official explanation maintained. Tracing a unique genetic signature back to Howe's Hens in Ohio, ProPublica simulated dust-dispersion patterns using December 22-31 weather data and found farms downwind of the initial outbreak were roughly 20 times more likely to become infected within three weeks; 16 of 17 farms testing positive in that window fell within the predicted wind plume. Indiana's avian health director Maria Cooper independently described the same pattern anecdotally: hard wind on an outbreak day reliably preceded news of another farm's dead hens five to seven days later. A USDA spokesperson said 'there is no compelling evidence that indicates aerial transmission poses a greater risk than other known transmission routes' and the agency declined to investigate wind patterns, citing an inability to rule out other mechanisms -- even as USDA's own former chief epidemiologist, Brian McCluskey, told ProPublica 'it just seems so likely to me that this was an airborne thing,' and poultry researcher Erica Spackman acknowledged feathers readily become airborne during culling operations. The underlying outbreak killed more than 20 million egg-laying chickens (about 5% of the U.S. flock) across 83 farms in six Ohio and Indiana counties over three months. A proven poultry vaccine has existed since July 2023, and France's 2023 duck-vaccination campaign achieved a near-total case reduction, but USDA has not authorized U.S. use, citing trade concerns that other countries might restrict American poultry imports over fears vaccination could mask infections -- leaving the country reliant on biosecurity protocols ProPublica's analysis found failed to prevent an estimated 73% of the recent farm-to-farm spread. Infectious-disease researcher Erin Sorrell warned of the pandemic stakes if an infected farmworker simultaneously contracts seasonal flu, enabling a human-transmissible reassortment: 'the minute it transmits in humans, it's done.'

updates.text: Update 2026-08-17: No confirmation of USDA restoring full surveillance capacity was found in sourcing reviewed as of this recheck; a follow-up congressional letter again urged USDA to fully restore avian-influenza surveillance and coordination as HPAI outbreaks returned 'in full force' into 2026, again citing furloughs, staffing cuts, and reductions-in-force at USDA and CDC as limiting real-time reporting capacity and farmers' ability to respond to outbreaks.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-30: A fresh, concrete example of the surveillance gap this entry documents surfaced in trade-press reporting: APHIS's livestock H5N1 detection map -- which states on its own page that it is updated every weekday -- went nearly 30 days in mid-to-late summer 2026 without posting new confirmed detections, only for a cluster of new dairy-cattle and poultry infections to appear all at once once updates resumed (three dairy herds in Texas and Utah; a 29,700-bird outbreak in Edmunds County, SD, plus smaller outbreaks in Brule County, SD and Ada/Canyon counties, ID). During the reporting gap, anyone checking the tracker -- a reporter, a farmer, a local health official -- would have seen stale numbers with no on-page indication they were stale. CDC's own bird-flu situation-summary page separately carried a last-updated date from early March 2026 as of this recheck; CDC stopped publishing USDA's animal-detection data on its own site in mid-2025, directing readers to USDA's page instead, the same page found to have gone dark for nearly a month. CDC's human-surveillance systems continued to show no indicators of unusual human influenza activity as of this update -- this is a data-reporting and transparency gap on the animal-surveillance side, not a confirmed undetected human outbreak.

updates.label: Added
updates.text: Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0721): a ProPublica investigation published November 28, 2025 found USDA rejected genomic and wind-pattern evidence that a December 2024-February 2025 H5N1 outbreak spread through the air, not just via 'shared people and equipment' as USDA's official explanation maintained. Tracing a unique genetic signature back to Howe's Hens in Ohio, ProPublica simulated dust-dispersion patterns using December 22-31 weather data and found farms downwind of the initial outbreak were roughly 20 times more likely to become infected within three weeks; 16 of 17 farms testing positive in that window fell within the predicted wind plume. Indiana's avian health director Maria Cooper independently described the same pattern anecdotally: hard wind on an outbreak day reliably preceded news of another farm's dead hens five to seven days later. A USDA spokesperson said 'there is no compelling evidence that indicates aerial transmission poses a greater risk than other known transmission routes' and the agency declined to investigate wind patterns, citing an inability to rule out other mechanisms -- even as USDA's own former chief epidemiologist, Brian McCluskey, told ProPublica 'it just seems so likely to me that this was an airborne thing,' and poultry researcher Erica Spackman acknowledged feathers readily become airborne during culling operations. The underlying outbreak killed more than 20 million egg-laying chickens (about 5% of the U.S. flock) across 83 farms in six Ohio and Indiana counties over three months. A proven poultry vaccine has existed since July 2023, and France's 2023 duck-vaccination campaign achieved a near-total case reduction, but USDA has not authorized U.S. use, citing trade concerns that other countries might restrict American poultry imports over fears vaccination could mask infections -- leaving the country reliant on biosecurity protocols ProPublica's analysis found failed to prevent an estimated 73% of the recent farm-to-farm spread. Infectious-disease researcher Erin Sorrell warned of the pandemic stakes if an infected farmworker simultaneously contracts seasonal flu, enabling a human-transmissible reassortment: 'the minute it transmits in humans, it's done.'

confidence_note.base: HIGH confidence on the outbreak figures (66 flocks, 3.5 million birds), independently corroborated across NPR's national broadcast and numerous NPR-member-station syndications (NHPR, KUNC, Houston Public Media, OPB, and others) all citing the same underlying reporting. HIGH confidence on the farmworker-testing findings and immigration-fear dynamic, corroborated by the same NPR reporting and a related Stateline article. The late-November 2025 congressional letter demanding restored surveillance is corroborated by Rep. McBride's own press release. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no USDA response confirming restored surveillance capacity was found; a follow-up 2026 congressional letter repeated the same restoration demand, consistent with this entry's 'ongoing, no confirmation of reversal' status. Real correction, GSR recheck batch 28 (2026-08-30): the nearly-30-day APHIS tracker reporting gap and the specific detections that appeared afterward are corroborated across The Poultry Site and Medical Daily trade-press coverage, both published in August 2026; the 2026 year-to-date herd-outbreak comparison (85 in 2026 vs. 171 in all of 2025 vs. 917 in 2024) comes from the same coverage citing APHIS's own published totals and should not be read as evidence surveillance itself improved, since the entry's concern is reporting-cadence/transparency, not raw case totals. Re-verified 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 49): no material change -- CIDRAP's coverage of the same August 2026 detection cluster and reporting gap corroborates, without adding to, what this entry already documents; no confirmation found that USDA restored full surveillance capacity or responded to Congress's restoration demands. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0285: the April 23, 2025 HHS-directed NAS workshop cancellation is HIGH confidence, corroborated by Reuters' original reporting and wide wire pickup (US News, Yahoo, AOL, trade press including The Poultry Site and The Cattle Site).

updates.text: Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0721): the airborne-transmission evidence, USDA's rejection of it, and the named officials/scientists (McCluskey, Spackman, Cooper) are HIGH confidence, sourced directly to ProPublica's original data-driven investigation, which independently modeled wind-dispersion patterns against confirmed outbreak sites rather than relying solely on official statements; single-source as of this entry, worth rechecking for independent corroboration or a USDA response to the specific wind-modeling findings.

title: Interior/BLM Reversed Approvals for Two Major Public-Lands Renewable Projects, Idaho's Lava Ridge Wind Farm and Nevada's Esmeralda 7 Solar Complex
institution: Department of the Interior (Bureau of Land Management)
status: Lava Ridge: approval formally canceled, Aug. 7, 2025. Esmeralda 7: Interior canceled the project's combined environmental review and disputes that this means the project itself is dead, saying each of its seven sub-projects will now be reviewed individually -- contested characterization, not a confirmed full cancellation
date_of_action: 2025-08-07 (Lava Ridge cancellation) through 2025-10-16 (Esmeralda 7 review cancellation)
what_changed: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order suspending the already-approved Lava Ridge Wind Project in south-central Idaho pending an Interior Department review. **On August 7, 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum formally reversed the Biden-era approval and canceled the 1,000-megawatt, 241-turbine project outright, framing the move as 'protecting tens of thousands of acres from harmful wind policy' and citing local opposition over turbine height (up to 660 feet) and visual impacts on the nearby Minidoka National Historic Site, where thousands of Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II.** Environmental and clean-energy advocates called the reversal politically motivated obstruction of a five-years-in-development project. Two months later, on October 16, 2025, BLM updated its public planning website to mark its environmental review 'cancelled' for Esmeralda 7, a proposed 6.2-gigawatt solar-and-battery complex on federal land in Nevada that would have been the largest solar project in the U.S. by capacity, enough to power an estimated 1.8-2 million homes. The Department of Interior subsequently disputed characterizations that it had killed the project outright, saying BLM and the project's applicants had instead agreed to abandon the combined, programmatic environmental review covering all seven sub-projects in favor of reviewing each of the seven individually -- a change Interior described as a shift in review approach rather than a cancellation, while independent reporting (Canary Media, Heatmap News) characterized the change as a new procedural obstacle that increases uncertainty and cost for the overall complex regardless of how it is formally labeled.

primary_proponent.name: Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of the Interior
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the Lava Ridge cancellation on August 7, 2025; BLM, the sub-agency he oversees, separately updated its Esmeralda 7 review status two months later.

estimated_impact.summary: Two major renewable-energy projects on federal land -- a 1,000 MW wind farm already fully approved, and what would be the largest solar project in the country by capacity -- had their federal approvals reversed or their review process disrupted within the same several-month span, adding to the pattern of federal renewable-project rollbacks this tracker documents elsewhere.

figures.value: 6.2 gigawatts -- enough for an estimated 1.8-2 million homes

estimated_impact.caveat: Interior disputes that Esmeralda 7 itself was canceled, only its combined environmental-review process; whether the project ultimately proceeds via individual sub-project reviews, and on what timeline, was not resolved as of this entry's addition, so this entry documents a disrupted review process for Esmeralda 7, not a confirmed project cancellation on the same footing as Lava Ridge. A separate discovery-record claim that oil-industry lobbyist Kathleen Sgamma had been 'installed' to lead BLM by October 2025 was checked and found incorrect -- her nomination for BLM director was withdrawn in April 2025, and no confirmed director was in place as of the Esmeralda 7 review change -- so that claim was not included in this entry.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the Lava Ridge cancellation, its date, and its stated rationale, corroborated across the Interior Department's own press release, Idaho Business Review, Capital Press, Utah News Dispatch, KUER, U.S. News, and Renewable Energy World. HIGH confidence on the Esmeralda 7 environmental-review cancellation and Interior's dispute of the 'project killed' characterization, corroborated across E&E News/POLITICO, Utility Dive, ESG Dive, Heatmap News, and Canary Media. One specific discovery-record claim (that Kathleen Sgamma had been installed as BLM director) was checked against primary sources and found factually incorrect -- her nomination was withdrawn months earlier -- and was deliberately omitted rather than propagated; see the caveat above. Record dates for both events matched their primary-sourced dates closely (within a few days), unlike several other clusters processed this session.
