title: Trump Fired the BLS Commissioner for 'Rigged' Data — His Own First-Term BLS Commissioner Called the Firing 'Totally Groundless'
institution: Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Department of Labor
status: Complete: McEntarfer fired Aug. 1, 2025; Antoni nomination withdrawn; career BLS economist Brett Matsumoto confirmed 51-47, took office Aug. 11, 2026. As of March 2026, BLS had lost ~25% of staff since Feb. 2025; Labor IG review of data collection opened Sept. 2025.
what_changed: On August 1, 2025, hours after BLS reported that job growth had slowed to just 73,000 for July -- below expectations -- and revised the two prior months' job gains down sharply by a combined 258,000 (the biggest two-month downward revision since April 2020, at the start of the COVID crisis), **Trump fired BLS Commissioner Erika McEntarfer via a Truth Social post, writing: 'I have directed my Team to fire this Biden Political Appointee, IMMEDIATELY. She will be replaced with someone much more competent and qualified.' Trump provided no evidence that McEntarfer, a Biden appointee confirmed to a fixed term in 2024, had manipulated the data**, and Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer publicly supported the firing the same day, naming Deputy Commissioner William Wiatrowski as acting director. This was the first time in the Bureau's history a commissioner had been fired, rather than completing or being reappointed past their term. Trump nominated Heritage Foundation economist E.J. Antoni to permanently lead BLS in August 2025. Antoni had been filmed on Capitol grounds during the January 6, 2021 insurrection (though not shown entering the building or facing charges), had publicly echoed Trump's 'rigged data' claims and pushed for suspending monthly jobs reports, and, unlike McEntarfer, had no prior government experience, per CNN. CNN's KFile reported September 5, 2025 that Antoni had operated a now-deleted Twitter account containing sexually degrading attacks on Kamala Harris, homophobic slurs, election and COVID conspiracy theories, and insults directed at Trump critics. Facing that reporting -- with Republican Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski having declined to meet with him, according to a person familiar with the matter cited by CNN, and his confirmation hearing never formally noticed -- the White House withdrew Antoni's nomination on September 30, 2025, before any Senate confirmation vote occurred. Trump's own budget proposal for the year had already called for an 8% staff reduction at BLS (per CNBC), and the Urban Institute separately documented a broader pattern across federal statistical agencies of data being removed from government websites or having fields altered in connection with executive orders targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion programming. On September 9, 2025, BLS's routine preliminary annual benchmark estimate found the economy had added 911,000 fewer jobs in the year through March 2025 than initially reported; Labor Secretary Chavez-DeRemer said it gave the public "even more reason to doubt the integrity of data" published by BLS. The next day, the Labor Department's Office of Inspector General notified acting commissioner Wiatrowski that it was opening a review of BLS's challenges in collecting and reporting CPI, PPI, and employment data, after BLS had curtailed some CPI and PPI data collection for lack of resources. In January 2026, Trump announced his pick of Brett Matsumoto, a BLS research economist since 2015 specializing in inflation measurement who was serving as a senior economist on the White House Council of Economic Advisers, to lead the agency; the formal nomination followed on May 11, 2026. Congress did not enact the proposed 8% staff cut: the final FY2026 appropriations bill gave BLS $708.5 million, a modest increase. The final benchmark, published February 11, 2026, revised March 2025 employment down by 862,000 not seasonally adjusted (898,000 seasonally adjusted) -- a large revision, but one BLS and outside economists (EPI) describe as a normal, transparent statistical process using more complete data, not a correction of an error or evidence of the manipulation Trump alleged in firing McEntarfer. By March 2026, the Friends of BLS -- co-chaired by former commissioners Erica Groshen and William Beach -- reported that BLS had lost approximately 25% of its staff through early separations since February 2025, with nearly 40% of leadership posts vacant; Bloomberg Law attributed the losses to early retirements and buyouts since January 2025 and a hiring freeze that kept the posts from being filled. In April 2026, a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper by economists Nicholas Bloom, Erica Groshen, Duncan Hobbs, and Michael Strain estimated that the spike in economic policy uncertainty following the firing reduced U.S. output by roughly $20 billion -- about $25 for every $1 of BLS's budget -- while noting that markets and businesses kept relying on BLS data. The Senate confirmed Matsumoto 51-47 on August 7, 2026, and he became the 17th Commissioner of Labor Statistics on August 11, 2026, ending Wiatrowski's year as acting commissioner.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Directly ordered the firing via social media, framing the weak jobs numbers themselves as evidence of manipulation. Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer publicly endorsed the move, stating she supported ensuring 'the American People can trust the important and influential data coming from BLS.' Notably, William Beach -- who served as BLS Commissioner during Trump's own first term -- publicly and specifically rejected the firing on the record: 'The totally groundless firing of Dr. Erika McEntarfer, my successor as Commissioner of Labor Statistics at BLS, sets a dangerous precedent and undermines the statistical mission of the Bureau... This escalates the President's unprecedented attacks on the independence and integrity of the federal statistical system. The President seeks to blame someone for unwelcome economic news.'

estimated_impact.summary: Firing the commissioner over an unwelcome jobs report, with no evidence of manipulation, damaged trust in the federal government's core labor and inflation data. Economists Bloom, Groshen, Hobbs, and Strain estimate that the resulting spike in economic policy uncertainty cost roughly $20 billion in lost U.S. output and about 31,000 payroll jobs in their baseline scenario. The firing also came as BLS was losing capacity: it had already curtailed some CPI and PPI data collection for lack of resources, and by March 2026 it had lost about a quarter of its staff since February 2025, with nearly 40% of leadership posts vacant. Trump's own first-term commissioner, William Beach, explained that the commissioner has no access to the data while it is collected and summed, and that the May-June downward revisions reflected new information (including state and local education reporting), not interference. The Urban Institute warned the firing 'undermines the integrity of the federal statistical agency data ecosystem' that governments, businesses, and households rely on.

estimated_impact.caveat: The $20 billion and 31,000-job figures are the authors' own back-of-the-envelope baseline from an unreviewed NBER working paper; they map a one-week rise in a news-based uncertainty index onto output using earlier research, and the authors call the figure imprecise and likely conservative, noting that markets and businesses never stopped relying on BLS data. BLS's staff and leadership losses stem mainly from the 2025 hiring freeze, buyouts and early retirements, not from the firing itself. Beach's rebuttal addresses the narrower question of whether a commissioner could manipulate the data; the Urban Institute's broader data-integrity concern also draws on separate incidents (website data removal, DEI-related field changes) and should not be conflated with the firing. Harm to health or mortality is not documented.

confidence_note: Exceptionally strong sourcing specifically because the most substantive rebuttal comes from within Trump's own political circle -- his first-term BLS Commissioner, not an opposition figure -- giving both a credibility advantage and a specific technical explanation (rather than just political disagreement) for why the manipulation claim doesn't hold up mechanically. Core facts (the jobs numbers, the firing, the public statements) are corroborated across CNBC, PBS News, and the Urban Institute with no factual dispute about what happened, only about whether it was justified. No reversal or vindication of the firing has occurred; the data-integrity concern broadened institutionally (IG review, staff and leadership attrition) before a career BLS economist was confirmed as commissioner in August 2026. The 911,000-job preliminary benchmark revision (finalized at 862,000 not seasonally adjusted; 898,000 seasonally adjusted) needs context -- it is a much larger number than the original 258,000 two-month revision that preceded the firing, but EPI and BLS's own methodology describe annual benchmark revisions as routine, not as further evidence of manipulation either way; the two figures are different kinds of revision and should not be conflated, and the larger number is not by itself evidence of scandal. The Antoni nomination and its withdrawal are HIGH confidence, corroborated across NBC News, CNN (including CNN's own KFile investigative report), and Fox Business's independent confirmation of the withdrawal -- the last of which strengthens confidence this isn't a one-sided characterization, since Fox Business covered the same withdrawal without disputing its cause; the report that Sens. Collins and Murkowski declined to meet Antoni rests on a single anonymous source cited by CNN. The $20 billion output-loss estimate is MODERATE confidence: a back-of-the-envelope figure from an unreviewed NBER working paper whose authors call it imprecise.
pull_quote: William Beach, Trump's own first-term BLS Commissioner: “The totally groundless firing of Dr. Erika McEntarfer, my successor as Commissioner of Labor Statistics at BLS, sets a dangerous precedent and undermines the statistical mission of the Bureau.”

section_summaries.what_changed: Trump publicly fired BLS's commissioner over social media hours after a weak jobs report, alleging data manipulation without offering proof.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: Economists estimate the post-firing uncertainty spike cost ~$20 billion in output and ~31,000 jobs; BLS separately lost a quarter of its staff; Trump's own ex-BLS chief rebutted the rigging claim.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Very strong sourcing, notably from Trump's own former BLS chief; no reversal since, a later benchmark revision is routine, and the $20 billion cost estimate is a rough working-paper figure.

title: DOGE Targeted Offshore Drilling Safety Offices for Closure in 2025, Then Interior Recombined the Post-Deepwater-Horizon Safety/Leasing Split Entirely -- With a Proposed 20% Staff Cut -- as Democrats Sought a GAO Probe
institution: Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) and Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE), Department of the Interior
status: Secretarial Order No. 3451, signed July 10, 2026, established the Marine Minerals Administration, merging BOEM and BSEE effective immediately, with operations phased in. Democrats' July 8, 2026 request for a GAO review had no publicly reported GAO decision as of late September 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-03-11 (regional office leases reported as slated for termination) through 2026-07-10 (Secretarial Order No. 3451 establishes the Marine Minerals Administration); merger plan announced 2026-04-03; GAO review requested 2026-07-08
what_changed: In March 2025, DOGE and GSA listed the leases for BOEM's and BSEE's regional offices in Camarillo, California (Pacific offshore region) and New Orleans, Louisiana (Gulf region, whose outer continental shelf is home to about 97% of U.S. offshore oil and gas production, according to BOEM) among federal office leases slated for early termination, as part of the administration's broader real-estate cost-cutting push. These offices **field emergency oil-spill and drilling-incident reports, review offshore energy permit applications, inspect drilling rigs and production platforms, and enforce environmental compliance**; a BOEM spokesperson said only that the bureau was 'working with GSA to ensure facilities or alternative options will be available for the continued delivery of Interior services,' with no public detail on where displaced staff -- geologists, engineers, biologists, environmental specialists -- would relocate. The bureaus' workforce kept shrinking: BOEM and BSEE together employed about 1,500 full-time staff under the Biden administration but about 1,000 in 2026, according to Office of Personnel Management data reported by POLITICO's E&E News, after hundreds of offshore employees left through buyouts and early-retirement offers; the administration has proposed reducing the staff further, to 874 people. In fall 2025, BSEE's top offshore safety regulator in Alaska wrote in a public comment that cuts during the Trump administration had left his office at 'below sustainable levels' to manage current leasing, even as the 2025 budget law required five more Alaska offshore lease sales through 2032; days after his warning was reported, he went on leave -- at first it was unclear whether he was placed on leave or stepped away, but E&E News reported in April that the administration had put him on leave. On April 3, 2026, Interior announced the start of a phased plan to combine BOEM (offshore leasing, planning and environmental review) and BSEE (safety enforcement and inspections) into a single new bureau, the Marine Minerals Administration, a plan also laid out in the president's FY2027 budget proposal, and said internal alignment activities would begin soon and all existing regulatory protections and safety standards would remain in place. Interior's FY2027 request paired the merger with a 42 percent funding cut and a 20 percent staff cut for the combined bureaus, including a 37 percent cut to oil spill research, while expanding the new bureau's scope to include offshore critical-mineral leasing. At a May 2026 hearing, Secretary Doug Burgum said the aim was 'to get more people that are actually in the jobs that actually matter,' adding that he wants more inspectors. On July 8, 2026, House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman and Senate Energy and Natural Resources ranking member Martin Heinrich, joined by Sen. Alex Padilla and Rep. Luz Rivas, asked the Government Accountability Office to examine the plan, writing that it 'raises serious concerns about whether Interior is collapsing the firewall between resource development and independent safety oversight that was established after Deepwater Horizon.' The House's FY2027 Interior-Environment spending bill did not mention the merger but proposed cutting BOEM spending by 20 percent and BSEE by 11 percent. A GAO spokesperson confirmed receipt and said GAO has a process to determine whether and when to do work, 'which we are working through right now'; no GAO decision to take up the review had been publicly reported as of late September 2026. On July 10, 2026, two days after the letter, Burgum signed Secretarial Order No. 3451, establishing the Marine Minerals Administration 'effective immediately' and vesting all of BOEM's and BSEE's functions, personnel, assets and authorities in it. The order phases in the new bureau's operations, lets BOEM and BSEE keep their operating authority during the transition, and gives the MMA director nine months to finalize its structure; as of late July 2026, BOEM's acting director, Matthew Giacona, was also acting MMA director. The merger reverses the split Interior itself made after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster, which killed 11 workers: Secretary Ken Salazar ordered the old Minerals Management Service divided on May 19, 2010, and it was dissolved in October 2011, replaced by BOEM, BSEE and a separate revenue office. The presidential commission that investigated the spill found that combining leasing and safety duties in one agency 'led inevitably to internal tensions and a confusion of goals that weakened the agency's effectiveness and made it more susceptible to outside pressures.'

primary_proponent.note: Announced the plan on April 3, 2026 and signed Secretarial Order No. 3451 on July 10, 2026, establishing the Marine Minerals Administration by combining BOEM and BSEE, effective immediately. The merger reverses the 2010-2011 split of the former Minerals Management Service, whose combined leasing and safety roles the Deepwater Horizon commission found had left it 'more susceptible to outside pressures.'

estimated_impact.summary: Offshore drilling's independent safety enforcer, split off from the leasing agency after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout killed 11 workers and a presidential commission found the combined agency 'more susceptible to outside pressures,' was folded back into one bureau in July 2026. The merger came as the bureaus' staff had already fallen by about a third since the Biden administration and BSEE's Alaska safety chief warned his office was 'below sustainable levels' for current leasing, and Interior's FY2027 request proposes a further 20% staff cut, a 42% funding cut and a 37% cut to oil spill research while the new bureau takes on expanded oil and gas leasing and a new offshore mining program. The regional offices listed for closure in 2025 field spill and incident reports, including for the region producing about 97% of U.S. offshore oil and gas.

title: Federal Prisons Losing Corrections Officers to ICE en Masse After BOP Wage Cuts and a Canceled Union Contract
institution: Federal Bureau of Prisons
status: BOP plans to close six facilities (announced July 1, 2026), citing 'extreme staffing challenges' and a $4B+ maintenance backlog. The union's suit over the canceled contract survived dismissal April 28, 2026; its injunction motion was undecided as of the latest public docket entry (Aug. 10).
what_changed:
The Federal Bureau of Prisons entered 2025 with at least 4,000 vacant positions, by its own February 2025 testimony to Congress, and then cut its own pay and hiring. Effective March 23, 2025, BOP halved retention-incentive pay at most facilities that used it and ended it at seven, cutting the paychecks of about 23,000 employees by as much as 25%; BOP blamed a budget shortfall under a continuing resolution. In May 2025, newly appointed Director William K. Marshall III halted some hiring; union officials called it a hiring freeze, while BOP denied that and said it would still fill critical posts such as correctional officers. On September 25, 2025, Marshall terminated the collective bargaining agreement covering more than 30,000 BOP employees, citing Executive Order 14,251. AFGE's National Council of Prison Locals sued on November 13, 2025 (National Council of Prison Locals v. Federal Bureau of Prisons, 3:25-cv-01907, D. Conn.), alleging First Amendment retaliation and an Administrative Procedure Act violation.

At the same time, ICE ran a monthslong recruiting blitz offering $50,000 signing bonuses; DHS said in January 2026 that ICE had more than doubled its officers and agents, from 10,000 to more than 22,000. A ProPublica investigation published November 21, 2025 found corrections officers leaving federal lockups from Florida to Minnesota to California for ICE, and internal prison data showed that, after retirements and other attrition, BOP had lost at least 1,400 more staff than it hired in 2025 through the start of November. ProPublica's reporting described **federal prisons running low on basic supplies including food and toilet paper amid the staffing collapse**, along with more lockdowns, fewer health services, and, according to staff complaints at the Victorville complex in California, ailing prisoners missing hospital procedures because too few officers were assigned to hospital visits. 'We're broken and we're being poached by ICE,' an official with the prison workers union told ProPublica.

On February 20, 2026, four House Judiciary Democrats (Reps. Jamie Raskin, Lucy McBath, Jasmine Crockett, and Joe Neguse) sent Marshall a six-page letter demanding he address the 'persistent, unsafe conditions' and 'pervasive shortage of critical staff' (the letter attributes the 'poached by ICE' quote to a BOP official; ProPublica attributed it to a union official).

On April 28, 2026, U.S. District Judge Vernon D. Oliver denied the government's motions to dismiss, stay, or transfer the union's lawsuit, holding that the union had made out a prima facie case of First Amendment retaliation and declining to decide the APA claims' merits before the administrative record was produced; he heard the union's preliminary-injunction motion on April 30. The government produced an 11-document administrative record on May 13, which the union called 'meager' in a May 27 motion for extra-record discovery, and answered the complaint on July 8.

On July 1, 2026, BOP announced it will close six low- and minimum-security facilities -- Beaumont FCI Low, Big Spring FCI and its satellite camp, La Tuna FCI and its satellite facilities, Lexington FMC's satellite camp, Petersburg FCI Low, and Taft FCI, in Texas, Kentucky, Virginia, and California -- citing 'extreme staffing challenges' and a deferred-maintenance backlog exceeding $4 billion, which Prison Legal News put at nearly 25% of the $20 billion in BOP repair needs estimated two years earlier. The closures affect about 500 BOP employees: staff at Beaumont, Lexington, and Petersburg will transfer to nearby BOP units, a reduction-in-force will take effect at Big Spring and La Tuna, and La Tuna's satellite low and Taft were already non-operational. AFGE urged Congress to stop the closures, noting that BOP had received nearly $5 billion under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including about $3 billion for staffing and training. As of the lawsuit docket's latest public entry (August 10, 2026), no ruling on the preliminary-injunction or discovery motions had appeared.

estimated_impact.summary: Federal prisons that already had at least 4,000 vacant positions lost more staff than they hired in 2025, which ProPublica linked to more lockdowns and fewer health services, amid shortages of food and hygiene supplies; staff complaints at one California complex alleged that ailing prisoners missed hospital procedures for lack of officer escorts. BOP's own cuts to retention pay (up to 25% of pay for about 23,000 employees), hiring curbs, and cancellation of a 30,000-employee union contract compounded ICE's higher-paying recruiting drive. By July 2026 the bureau was closing six facilities, affecting about 500 employees, rather than restaffing them.

title: Pentagon Allowed CBP to Test an Anti-Drone Laser Near Fort Bliss Without FAA Coordination, Forcing an Abrupt El Paso Airspace Closure
institution: Department of Defense / Customs and Border Protection / FAA
status: El Paso airspace reopened Feb. 11, 2026 after about eight hours; a Feb. 26 incident (a military laser downed a CBP drone) led to a smaller Fort Hancock restriction that was scheduled to run until June 24. DoD and FAA ran a joint laser safety test in March; a joint IG probe was requested March 13.
date_of_action: 2026-02-10 to 2026-02-11 (El Paso closure); 2026-02-26 (second incident, Fort Hancock)
what_changed: **The Pentagon allowed CBP to use an anti-drone laser near Fort Bliss, Texas without coordinating in advance with the FAA**. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had signed off in recent weeks on loaning CBP the Defense Department-developed laser, CNN reported; CBP physically operated it, with Defense personnel present, and fired it earlier that week at what sources described as Mylar balloons (AP later reported that firing hit no target; the administration said the targets were Mexican cartel drones). FAA and Pentagon officials had been scheduled to meet on February 20 to review the risks and mitigation measures for a test of the system, but the Defense Department sought to use it sooner around El Paso. Late on February 10, 2026, the FAA issued a 10-day temporary flight restriction grounding all flights up to 18,000 feet in a 10-mile radius around El Paso -- set to expire February 21, a day after the planned meeting -- effectively shutting El Paso International Airport without first telling the White House, the city, or the area's congressional representative. The restriction was lifted about eight hours later, on the morning of February 11, after seven arrivals and seven departures were canceled and some medical evacuation flights were rerouted; Reuters and other outlets reported the FAA agreed to lift it if the Pentagon delayed further testing pending an FAA safety review. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the closure to a cartel drone incursion and said 'the threat has been neutralized.' Sen. Tammy Duckworth called the episode the latest example of 'the lack of coordination that's endemic in this Trump administration'; Senate Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) said he would request an FAA briefing; and Rep. Veronica Escobar, whose district includes El Paso, said neither her office nor local officials received any advance notice. On February 13, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem called it 'a joint agency task force mission' and said the government was 'continuing to work on the communication through that.' On February 26, 2026, the military used a laser to shoot down a CBP drone that had been launched near Fort Hancock, Texas, about 50 miles southeast of El Paso, without notifying the military task force assigned to the border; the FAA then imposed a smaller flight restriction around Fort Hancock, set to run until June 24, that did not affect commercial flights. A joint DoD-FAA-CBP statement described the target as 'a seemingly threatening unmanned aerial system operating within military airspace' and said the agencies 'will continue to work on increased cooperation and communication to prevent such incidents in the future.' After a closed-door briefing in early March, Cruz said that 'coordination fell far below what should have happened'; the Pentagon's counter-drone task force and the FAA ran a joint high-energy laser safety test at White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico, on March 7-8; and on March 13 Duckworth asked the inspectors general of the Departments of Transportation, Defense and Homeland Security to investigate both incidents jointly.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Defense / Customs and Border Protection
primary_proponent.role: Federal agencies whose uncoordinated laser deployment triggered the FAA's emergency airspace closure
primary_proponent.note: Critics, including Rep. Escobar, questioned the administration's cartel-drone explanation, but the accountability concern here is the lack of interagency coordination before deployment, not the underlying counter-drone objective.

estimated_impact.summary: The uncoordinated use of a Pentagon-loaned anti-drone laser led the FAA to ground all flights over El Paso, a city of nearly 700,000, for about eight hours: 14 passenger flights were canceled, travelers were stranded and some medical evacuation flights had to be rerouted, with no advance notice to the city, its congressional representative or the White House. Sixteen days later a military laser shot down a CBP drone near Fort Hancock, forcing a second, smaller closure that spared commercial flights but showed the Pentagon, DHS and FAA still lacked working coordination on counter-drone operations; a joint safety test followed only in March 2026.

Whether the laser posed a real risk to civil aircraft is disputed: a Pentagon-run March 2026 test reported no structural damage to a grounded airliner fuselage, but results were not released. Duckworth, Rep. Escobar, Sen. Cruz and DHS Secretary Noem, and a joint DoD-FAA-CBP statement confirming the Fort Hancock engagement. MEDIUM on what the El Paso laser hit: sources described Mylar balloons, AP later reported the firing hit no target, and the administration cited cartel drones.

title: CBP Mail-Entry Rule Threatens to Cut Off Lower-Cost Prescriptions Mailed From Canada and Abroad Starting Oct. 22
institution: U.S. Customs and Border Protection / Food and Drug Administration
status: Rule mostly in effect since July 24, 2026; from Oct. 22, FDA-regulated mail, including prescriptions, needs formal entry or a bonded electronic entry test. Pharmacy groups expect most personal shipments to stop. Lawmakers of both parties have asked for a delay or assurances; no change announced.
date_of_action: 2026-06-24 (interim final rule published) through 2026-10-22 (compliance date for FDA-regulated mail shipments)
what_changed:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) published an interim final rule in the Federal Register on June 24, 2026, signed by CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott, that indefinitely suspends the de minimis exemption for international mail shipments valued at $800 or less and creates a new postal informal entry process, backed by an entry bond, for mail shipments valued at $2,500 or less. It builds on President Trump's July 30, 2025 executive order suspending duty-free de minimis treatment; Newsmax, in a story summarizing Wall Street Journal reporting, said mail-order patients began paying customs fees for the first time in August 2025 on shipments that had always crossed duty-free. Most of the rule took effect July 24, 2026 (the de minimis suspension itself took effect on publication), but merchandise subject to other federal agencies' import requirements, a category that includes FDA-regulated drugs, has a compliance date of October 22, 2026, after which it is shut out of the new postal process and must use formal entry or a voluntary electronic informal entry (Entry Type 13) that CBP began testing September 22; both require an importer of record and an entry bond. The rule text does not specifically address prescription drugs or personal-use medicines, MedicalDaily noted. CBP has said the change protects tariff revenue and blocks traffickers from using low-value packages to smuggle fentanyl and counterfeit goods.

In practice, according to The Wall Street Journal as summarized by Newsmax, mailed prescriptions would have to go through a customs process requiring a licensed broker and a financial guarantee that few mail-order prescriptions have ever had to clear. Pharmacy groups predict that most shipments will stop, which The Timberjay called a de facto ban. The Canadian International Pharmacy Association said that unless those arrangements change, "Americans should expect that virtually all routine personal prescription orders mailed from licensed Canadian and international pharmacies will be unable to reach them" (MedicalDaily stresses this is the group's prediction, not a CBP finding). The Timberjay reported that pharmacy representatives expect shipments to be rejected when the medication is already sold in the United States, because the FDA's long-standing discretion to let some personal imports through does not extend to drugs marketed to Americans. The association says the customs firm Zonos serves as broker of record for nearly all major international postal systems, so if no broker takes responsibility for pharmaceutical parcels, many may have no practical route through customs. CIPA says the Entry Type 13 option does not change that, because the FDA's conditions for admitting the medicine still apply. A Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson said the FDA will continue to review imports case by case under guidance that allows a limited supply of unapproved foreign drugs when no U.S. treatment exists and there is no unreasonable safety risk. British Columbia-based Northwest Pharmacy told customers it would accept orders only "on a case-by-case basis for a short period of time" after October 9.

A 2020 study in JAMA Network Open, based on 2015-2017 survey data, estimated that about 2.3 million U.S. adults bought prescription drugs from other countries to save money. **Many patients say they will be forced to cut their doses, skip pills or go without their medicine, Newsmax reported from the Journal's story, and one Medicare patient on the blood thinner Eliquis, quoted by The People's Pharmacy, said the only other option would be to stop taking it, which the patient's doctor advises against.** A Dallas patient who orders the gut-disorder drug Xifaxan from a Canadian pharmacy said she pays about $10 a week for it and expects to pay $1,100 a week once the exemption expires, since her insurer will not cover it.

The change runs opposite to Trump's first-term stance. The Timberjay notes that he promoted Canadian drug importation in his 2016 campaign and in July 2020 signed an executive order directing HHS to facilitate waivers letting individuals import lower-cost prescription drugs when doing so posed no additional safety risk and saved patients money. The separate, government-supervised state importation programs authorized in his first term are not necessarily ended by the customs change, the paper added.

Members of Congress from both parties have pushed back. On September 24, Republican Reps. Aaron Bean, Gus Bilirakis and C. Scott Franklin of Florida wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commissioner Scott and Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas that the rule "will inadvertently impact our constituents and millions of other Americans' access to safe, affordable medications sourced through Canadian and International pharmacies," and asked for answers by October 2, according to the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation. On October 1, 71 members of Congress led by Reps. Jan Schakowsky and Mark Pocan wrote to the same officials: "We urge HHS, FDA, DHS, and CBP to delay any implementation of new procedures with respect to prescription medicines unless you can provide clear assurances that your agencies will not prevent genuine prescription medicines clearly intended for personal use and not appearing to present an unreasonable risk from entering the United States." Neither CBP nor the FDA had announced a delay or a personal-use exemption ahead of the October 22 date.

estimated_impact.summary: The rule could end a mail-order channel that has let uninsured, underinsured and fixed-income Americans buy brand-name medicines at a fraction of U.S. prices. Patients who lose it face much higher costs or rationing and going without drugs such as blood thinners, though no one has quantified the health effect.

title: RFK Jr. Removes All 17 Members of CDC Vaccine Advisory Committee, Installs Replacements
institution: Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
status: Complete (new panel seated and has already voted on policy changes)
date_of_action: 2025-06-09 (removal); 2025-06-11 (replacements announced); first new-panel meeting 2025-06-25
what_changed: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 sitting members of ACIP -- the CDC's expert panel that recommends the vaccine schedule guiding clinical practice and insurance coverage nationwide -- announcing the move via a Wall Street Journal op-ed rather than through the committee's standard process. He cited industry conflicts of interest as justification, calling the prior panel a 'rubber stamp for industry profit-taking agendas.' Two days later, Kennedy named 8 hand-picked replacements, several with documented public records of vaccine skepticism, affiliations with anti-vaccine advocacy organizations (e.g. the National Vaccine Information Center), or ties to lawsuits against vaccine makers -- notable given that Kennedy himself had collected referral fees from such litigation before becoming HHS Secretary. Former CDC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Debra Houry later cited this purge, alongside Kennedy's handling of the 2025 measles outbreak, as a reason for her own resignation in protest (see the related entry on RFK Jr.'s measles-outbreak conduct in this database for her fuller account). Committee members are ordinarily not political appointees and typically serve staggered four-year terms specifically to prevent any single administration from controlling a majority of the panel; removing the entire sitting panel let the administration seat a full majority immediately rather than waiting until 2028, as Kennedy himself acknowledged in his op-ed. **The reconstituted panel has since voted to remove thimerosal from flu vaccines and end the universal newborn Hepatitis B birth-dose recommendation.** The CDC canceled its scheduled February 2026 ACIP meeting entirely, with no new date set, as RFK Jr. continued reshaping federal vaccine policy -- a further disruption to the committee's normal operating cadence beyond the original member purge. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0259): the purge produced a second protest resignation beyond Houry's. On June 16, 2025, Dr. Fiona Havers, who led CDC surveillance on COVID-19 and RSV hospitalizations, resigned ahead of a key vaccine meeting, citing concern that surveillance data would no longer be used with scientific rigor under the reconstituted panel. Separately, the reconstituted panel's credibility took a direct hit on June 24, 2025: slides posted online for its first meeting cited a non-existent study, misattributed to a UC Davis professor, to support claims about the vaccine preservative thimerosal. Reuters flagged the error and the CDC removed the slide before the presenter, Lyn Redwood, gave her thimerosal presentation to the panel on June 26. Redwood, the former president of Children's Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group Kennedy founded, was not an ACIP member; in a June 27, 2025 letter, Sen. Patty Murray objected to Kennedy's reported decision to appoint her to oversee vaccine safety at CDC and asked him to reverse it. Update 2026-09-23: A peer-reviewed research letter published in JAMA on August 18, 2025, by Genevieve Kanter and Toni Mankowitz of USC and Peter Lurie of the Center for Science in the Public Interest examined reported conflicts of interest on ACIP from 2000 to 2024. It found that an average of 6.2% of ACIP members reported a financial conflict of interest at any given meeting from 2016 to 2024, and that conflicts tied to personal income (consulting, stock, royalties or ownership), which the USC Schaeffer Center described as personal income from vaccine makers, had a prevalence under 1%. The Schaeffer Center said reported conflicts on ACIP 'had been at historic lows for years before Kennedy's abrupt dismissal,' and that income from vaccine makers, the type of conflict usually considered most concerning, 'had been virtually eliminated' among members. The JAMA letter noted that Kennedy's claim that '97% of the people on [ACIP] had conflicts' cited a 2000 congressional report on a single vaccine; the study itself used a database of CDC disclosures created by HHS. The American Medical Association and the Infectious Diseases Society of America publicly condemned the removals, CNN reported, and the 17 dismissed members spoke out as a group in a June 16, 2025 JAMA Viewpoint. One dismissed ACIP member, speaking to CNN without being named, said: 'This will fundamentally destabilize vaccination in America.' FactCheck.org reported on July 10, 2025, that when Redwood's slides were first posted to the CDC website, they included two references to animal studies that do not exist.

title: CDC Fired Nearly Half the Staff -- and the Entire Leadership Team -- of Its Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities Center, Likely Halting Sickle Cell Data Collection and Cutting Newborn Hearing-Screening and Adult Disability Tracking Work
institution: National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities (NCBDDD), CDC/HHS
status: Ongoing -- no confirmation of NCBDDD staff/program reinstatement specifically, though the underlying litigation (New York v. Kennedy, D.R.I.) survived an April 7, 2026 motion-to-dismiss ruling and has produced reinstatements at other HHS divisions (NIOSH, FDA/CTP, ASPE/DDTA) covered by the same restructuring plan
date_of_action: 2025-04 (RIF notices delivered; reported April 10, 2025)
what_changed: In April 2025, as part of the Trump administration's broader HHS restructuring under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., nearly half of CDC staff working on birth defects and developmental disabilities were laid off, along with the entire leadership team of the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities (NCBDDD). **Work likely to be halted by the cuts, CBS News reported, included data collection for studying Americans with sickle cell disease, a painful blood disorder that predominantly affects Black families.** The cuts also hit the Disability and Health Promotion Branch, which had been responsible for a federal database tracking state-level rates of adults with disabilities, and stalled a pending data release that had been expected to help shed light on a recent increase in cognitive disability among younger adults. The cuts also ended CDC work on the congressionally mandated Early Hearing Detection and Intervention (EHDI) programs, which fund state efforts to screen and diagnose hearing issues in newborns and infants. They also eliminated CDC staff who partnered with Special Olympics on athlete health screenings and data collection. An HHS spokesperson, Vianca Rodriguez Feliciano, said the department was 'taking a careful look at all divisions to see where there is overlap.' Update 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): the April 2025 cuts occurred amid a broader HHS reorganization proposal, announced March 27, 2025, to fold NCBDDD and other CDC centers into a new 'Administration for a Healthy America' (AHA) -- but Congress rejected creating AHA, which remains an unenacted budget proposal requiring authorizing legislation Congress has not passed. Separately, Congress's FY2026 Labor-HHS-Education appropriations act (Division H of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, P.L. 119-75, signed February 3, 2026) funded NCBDDD's child health, disability health, and blood disorders programs at $205.06 million, essentially flat versus FY2025 (about $1 million, or 0.5%, below). This shows Congress did not adopt the administration's broader plan to eliminate or consolidate the center, though continued topline funding does not by itself indicate the specific staff and programs cut in April 2025 (leadership team, sickle cell data collection, the adult disability database, hearing-screening support) were reinstated -- no reporting reviewed confirms staff reinstatement or program restoration at the operational level. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 34): identified the specific litigation underlying the AHA/reorganization plan's stalled status, which this entry's prior updates referenced only in general terms. Nineteen states and D.C. sued HHS Secretary Kennedy in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island (New York v. Kennedy, D.R.I. No. 1:25-cv-00196, Judge Melissa R. DuBose) over the broader ~10,000-position HHS RIF and reorganization plan that included the April 2025 NCBDDD cuts. The court granted a preliminary injunction (revised/clarified August 12, 2025) enjoining HHS from further implementing its RIF and restructuring plans, finding the states were likely to succeed on their claim that the plan was arbitrary and capricious under the APA; the First Circuit denied the administration's emergency motion for a stay pending appeal on September 17, 2025. As of a July 2026 case-tracker snapshot, briefing in the district court remained ongoing, with defendants filing a factual-developments notice as recently as February 9, 2026 (in an unrelated NIOSH context) and further filings into July 2026. Two important scope caveats: this injunction blocks further implementation of the RIF/restructuring plan -- it does not, by itself, establish that the specific April 2025 NCBDDD staff cuts (which predate the injunction) were reversed or that laid-off staff were reinstated; and no reporting reviewed ties this case specifically to NCBDDD by name, only to the broader HHS reorganization NCBDDD's cuts were part of. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 48): on April 7, 2026, the court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the operative complaint, finding plaintiff states had adequately alleged standing through 'tangible harms, such as missed vaccine deadlines and disruption of critical public health services' -- a procedural advance past this entry's prior update, which stopped at the case's July 2026 filing activity without noting this ruling. The litigation has also produced concrete reinstatements at other HHS divisions swept into the same RIF/restructuring plan: HHS rescinded all remaining NIOSH RIF notices on January 13, 2026 (reinstating hundreds of employees), and rescinded remaining RIF notices for FDA's Center for Tobacco Products (CTP) and ASPE's Division of Data and Technical Analysis (DDTA) on March 27, 2026. No reporting reviewed documents a parallel reinstatement action specific to NCBDDD -- meaning the injunction's real-world remedial effect has been uneven across the HHS divisions it covers, with NCBDDD's April 2025 cuts still not confirmed reversed even as sibling divisions caught up in the same restructuring plan were restored. Update 2026-09-23: CBS News, which cited multiple officials for the 'nearly half' figure, gave no numerical headcount, and reported that only a handful of researchers remained on the job in the center. The American Society of Hematology's president, Dr. Belinda Avalos, warned that if the sickle cell work was not restored it would 'increase preventable hospitalizations, complications, and deaths,' and a current CDC official told CBS News the disability branch's loss was 'a step back,' saying the branch 'provided key public health expertise for disability in adulthood, where people spend most of their lives.' CBS News reported that nearly all U.S. newborns are now screened for hearing loss thanks in part to the Early Hearing Detection and Intervention programs, up from less than half of newborns 25 years earlier; CDC describes its support for state and territorial EHDI programs as tracking infants to ensure they receive diagnostic services and are enrolled in early intervention.

estimated_impact.summary: A CDC center dedicated to birth defects, developmental disabilities, and related health data lost nearly half its staff and its entire leadership. CBS News reported that sickle cell disease data collection (a condition that predominantly affects Black families) was likely to be halted, that the branch responsible for a federal database tracking state-level rates of adults with disabilities was cut and a planned data release stalled, and that CDC work on the congressionally mandated Early Hearing Detection and Intervention programs for newborns and infants ended -- concrete staff and program cuts affecting some of the country's most vulnerable populations, not merely a projected risk. title: CDC Stripped Seven Childhood Vaccines of Universal Recommendation, Triggering a 15-State Lawsuit
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
status: Blocked by court order since March 16, 2026, when Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) stayed the January 5, 2026 schedule changes in AAP v. Kennedy; the government's appeal is set for First Circuit argument October 6, 2026. A separate 15-state suit (N.D. Cal.) remains pending.
date_of_action: 2026-01-05 (CDC Decision Memo; stayed by federal court 2026-03-16)
what_changed:
The Jan. 5, 2026 Decision Memo below did not emerge without warning. On June 30, 2025, RFK Jr.'s reconstituted ACIP announced it would review the full childhood and adolescent vaccine schedule -- including hepatitis B and MMR -- forming new workgroups to study cumulative vaccine effects and dosing timing, consistent with Kennedy's own vaccine skepticism. By August 3, 2025, federal agencies under Kennedy had already weakened flu, RSV, and COVID-19 vaccine guidance; outside medical organizations and the independent Vaccine Integrity Project began issuing their own evidence-based recommendations to fill the resulting gap.

The hepatitis B birth-dose shot -- one of the seven vaccines the Decision Memo ultimately downgrades -- became the specific flashpoint that fall: NPR reported on September 16, 2025 that RFK Jr.'s panel was expected to vote at its September 18-19 meeting to recommend delaying the shot from birth to age 4, reversing more than 30 years of CDC advice during which the disease was 'virtually eradicated among American children'; instead, the panel voted 11 to 1 on September 19 to table the birth-dose question. On September 22, Trump said at a White House press conference that 'there's no reason to give a baby that's almost just born hepatitis B,' adding, 'I would say wait till the baby is 12 years old,' advice Dr. Andrew Pavia told NPR was 'extremely dangerous,' noting that about half of childhood infections before universal newborn vaccination came from mother-to-child transmission.

The panel's December 4, 2025 session grew chaotic -- committee members voiced confusion over the proposal's voting language, and anti-vaccine presenters offered a barrage of misleading, cherry-picked claims, including one activist's scientifically baseless suggestion that vaccine side effects could be linked to brain swelling, rejected on the spot by a physician panelist -- forcing the vote to be pushed to the next morning; even so, **a major independent review of 400+ studies found the newborn hepatitis B vaccine reduces infection by more than 95%, directly contradicting the delay push, given that infant infection carries a 90% risk of becoming chronic, lifelong disease**.

The panel voted 8-3 on December 5, 2025 to end the universal birth-dose recommendation and back individual-based decision-making for infants born to mothers who test negative for the virus, delaying the shot to two months of age in that group; CDC formalized the birth-dose portion of that rollback on December 16, 2025, allowing delay for infants whose parents test negative, over pediatric and infectious-disease experts' objections.

The Jan. 5, 2026 Decision Memo below extended this same shift to six additional vaccines. Then-acting CDC Director Jim O'Neill signed a January 5, 2026 'Decision Memo' demoting seven childhood vaccines -- protecting against rotavirus, several forms of meningitis, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, influenza, COVID-19, and RSV -- from 'universally recommended' status. As the states' later complaint describes the memo, the rotavirus, influenza, COVID-19, hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal shots moved to 'shared clinical decision-making,' given case-by-case after a discussion between a provider and the parent, while RSV (along with hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal shots) moved to a tier recommended only for certain high-risk groups, rather than remaining standard guidance for all children.

On January 13, 2026, days after the Decision Memo took effect, Trump falsely claimed the U.S. had been 'requiring 72 jabs for our beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children,' sharing a misleading graphic comparing U.S. requirements to a single 'European country' requiring 11 injections; AP's fact-check found no state requires anywhere close to 72 doses, and that Trump's count appeared to include every individual vaccine dose (including oral and combination doses, and non-required annual flu/COVID shots) through age 18 to reach that number.

A Stanford-backed epidemiological model, published by ProPublica, projected the long-term consequences if childhood vaccination rates continued declining toward disappearance: researchers estimated a measles resurgence alone could kill roughly 290,000 people over subsequent decades, with tens of thousands more deaths and disabilities from the return of polio, rubella, and diphtheria -- diseases effectively eliminated in the U.S. for decades. This is a projected, modeled long-term scenario, not an observed outcome, but it quantifies the stakes of the schedule-recommendation changes and related vaccine-policy shifts documented in this entry and elsewhere in this tracker.

The rollback's fallout continued through early 2026: on January 8, 2026, Merck said it is 'critical that changes are informed by comprehensive data and guided by experts,' and Reuters reported that Bernstein analysts estimated a potential $2 billion impact on Merck's annual revenue from the schedule changes, citing its RotaTeq rotavirus and Gardasil HPV vaccines (the new schedule calls for a single HPV dose); amid a severe flu season, the Guardian reported on January 16, 2026 that, with children's flu-shot recommendations changed in early January to 'shared clinical decision-making,' officials had 'stopped fully recommending the flu shot,' that CDC press statements said 'the decision to vaccinate is a personal one,' and that a flu-vaccination campaign called 'Wild to Mild' had been halted and not resumed, as New York logged its most flu hospitalizations ever in the week ending December 27 and mortality among children was rising; and on February 3, 2026, the American Academy of Pediatrics broke publicly with CDC, recommending children continue to be vaccinated against all 18 diseases in its own schedule rather than the pared-down 11-disease federal schedule, saying the CDC's changes reflected ideology rather than science.

A coalition of 15 states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin), with Pennsylvania represented by Gov. Josh Shapiro rather than its attorney general, sued the federal government in the Northern District of California on February 24, 2026, arguing the Decision Memo's change put children's lives at risk, was made without adequate scientific basis, and 'will reduce vaccination rates for the diseases against which the Demoted Vaccines protect.'

On March 16, 2026, U.S. District Judge Brian E. Murphy in Boston, ruling in a separate suit by the American Academy of Pediatrics and other medical groups, stayed the January 5 schedule changes, the appointments of 13 members Kennedy had named to ACIP, and the reconstituted panel's votes, including its December 2025 vote downgrading the hepatitis B birth-dose recommendation; Reuters reported that Murphy found the CDC lacked authority to change the schedule without consulting ACIP; he wrote that vaccine decisions had followed 'a method scientific in nature and codified into law through procedural requirements,' and that the government 'has disregarded those methods and thereby undermined the integrity of its actions.' HHS spokesman Andrew Nixon said HHS 'looks forward to this judge's decision being overturned,' and the government filed its appeal to the First Circuit on April 29, 2026.

On September 8, 2026, the court in the states' suit granted in part and denied in part the government's motion to dismiss, per the Oregon Department of Justice's litigation tracker, leaving that case pending; on September 11, Judge Murphy paused further proceedings in the AAP case until the First Circuit rules on the government's appeal, which the appeals court is scheduled to hear October 6, 2026.

Bernstein analysts estimated a potential $2 billion impact on Merck's annual revenue from the schedule changes, citing its RotaTeq rotavirus and Gardasil HPV vaccines (the new schedule calls for a single HPV dose), Reuters reported.

title: Acting CDC director blocks COVID vaccine effectiveness study; researchers publish it outside the agency
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
status: Complete -- study ultimately published outside CDC's own journal
date_of_action: 2026-03 (scheduled MMWR publication blocked) - 2026-06-01 (published in JAMA Network Open)
what_changed: **A CDC-authored COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness study, led by Ruth Link-Gelles of the agency's National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, had already cleared scientific review and been approved by editors for publication in the CDC's flagship scientific bulletin, the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR), when Acting CDC Director Jay Bhattacharya intervened and blocked its release in March 2026**, citing objections to the study's 'test-negative design' methodology -- a standard epidemiological approach that compares vaccination status between people who test positive versus negative for a disease. With the CDC's own channel closed off, the study's authors published their findings independently in JAMA Network Open on June 1, 2026, without CDC's imprimatur.

primary_proponent.name: Jay Bhattacharya
primary_proponent.role: Acting Director, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
primary_proponent.note: Personally raised methodological objections and blocked the study's release in MMWR after it had already passed scientific review and been approved by MMWR's own editors.

estimated_impact.summary: A completed, peer-reviewed federal study documenting substantial vaccine effectiveness was kept out of the CDC's own public-health bulletin -- the channel clinicians and health departments most directly rely on -- and only reached the public because its authors found an outside publisher, delaying dissemination of findings relevant to real-time public health guidance.

estimated_impact.caveat: Bhattacharya's stated objection -- to the test-negative design -- is a genuine, widely-used epidemiological method, not a fringe technique; reporting does not establish whether his methodological concern was raised in good faith or as a pretext, since the study had already passed MMWR's own scientific review process before he intervened. This entry describes the suppression and republication, not a definitive finding on Bhattacharya's motive.

confidence_note: Extensively corroborated by independent outlets (Washington Post, NBC News, ABC News, Deseret News), plus the study's own eventual publication record in JAMA Network Open confirming both its content and the CDC-to-outside-journal path. No formal GAO or Inspector General finding on the suppression decision itself has been identified.

title: CDC Suspended Diagnostic Testing for Rabies, Pox Viruses, and Dozens of Other Infectious Diseases as Staffing Collapsed Under Kennedy
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
status: Ongoing as of July 2026 reporting -- a government spokesperson called the pause temporary in April 2026 and said some tests would resume within weeks, but that timeline was not met; as of July 2026 there was no full public accounting of what testing capacity has been restored, remains reduced, or has been permanently discontinued
date_of_action: 2026 (staffing decline through early 2026, testing pause announced ~April 1-2, 2026)
what_changed: The CDC suspended diagnostic testing for rabies, a group of pox viruses that includes smallpox and mpox, Epstein-Barr virus, and roughly 30 other infectious diseases, after mass layoffs, hiring freezes, and resignations under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. depleted the specialized laboratory teams responsible for the testing. **The New Republic reported that by July 2026, the rabies team would be down to just one person with the clinical expertise needed to advise state and local health officials, and the pox virus team would have zero such specialists remaining.** Overall staffing in the affected testing programs fell by an estimated 20-25%, with the pox virus and rabies labs specifically losing about half their prior staff. State and local health departments, which rely on CDC's specialized testing and expertise when they cannot perform certain diagnostic work themselves, lost access to that support as the suspension took effect. A CDC/HHS spokesperson described the suspension as part of 'a routine review to uphold our commitment to high quality laboratory testing' and said some paused tests would resume within weeks; as of a July 2026 status check, that restoration had not been publicly confirmed, and New York and California state public health labs had stepped in to provide some backup testing capacity for services CDC paused.

title: Trump Budget Proposal Zeroes Out CDC's Global Health Center, Cuts Gavi Vaccine Funding as U.S. Exits WHO
institution: CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) / HHS
status: Proposed and largely implemented for FY2026 -- the administration's FY2026 budget request eliminated CDC's standalone Global Health Center line item and zeroed out Gavi funding; later FY2027 budget materials describe successor global-health funding as held level with FY2026, suggesting the final FY2026 structure was less severe than the original zero-out proposal (see caveat)
date_of_action: 2025-05 (FY2026 budget request released) through 2025-09 (reporting characterizing the Global Health Center as shut down, alongside the ongoing WHO withdrawal)
what_changed: The administration's FY2026 budget request, released in May 2025 and detailed further that summer, eliminated CDC's Global Health Center as a standalone budget line -- funded at $693 million in FY2025 and $711 million in FY2024 -- folding a reduced successor ($239 million under 'CDC-Wide Activities') into a new consolidated Administration for a Healthy America (AHA), an HHS reorganization championed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that also absorbed CDC's chronic-disease programs and some NIH institutes. The New York Times reported in June 2025 that the proposal specifically cut $230 million from CDC vaccine programs, including U.S. contributions supporting polio and measles vaccination and funding for the Gavi vaccine alliance; KFF's budget tracking confirmed the FY2026 request eliminated Gavi funding entirely and cut the broader Global Health Programs Account from $10.0 billion (FY2025) to $3.8 billion. By September 2025, Time reported the CDC's Global Health Center had effectively been shut down and global health funding cut by 67%, framing this alongside the administration's separate, ongoing withdrawal from the World Health Organization (announced by executive order in January 2025, taking formal effect January 2026) and warning from public-health experts that the combined cuts weaken the U.S.'s ability to detect and contain outbreaks before they reach American soil, citing estimates that another pandemic as severe as COVID-19 carries roughly a 50% chance of occurring within the next 20-25 years. The Gavi funding line item became a concrete diplomatic act around June 25-26, 2025, when HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced at Gavi's own pledging summit that the U.S. was withdrawing the roughly $1.2 billion pledge the Biden administration had made to the vaccine alliance, saying Gavi had 'ignored the science' on vaccine safety and 'lost the public trust,' and citing a 2017 observational study of infants in Guinea-Bissau as evidence -- a study public-health researchers have specifically disputed as unrepresentative of Gavi's broader immunization record (Gavi says its programs have vaccinated more than 1.1 billion children in low-income countries over 25 years). The withdrawal contributed to Gavi's pledging summit falling short of its $11.9 billion replenishment target. A December 4, 2025 Gates Foundation Goalkeepers report gave the first concrete real-world read on the cumulative effect of these cuts: **global under-5 child deaths, which had fallen every year for decades, were projected to rise in 2025 for the first time this century, from 4.6 million in 2024 to an estimated 4.8 million** -- an increase of just over 200,000 -- as global health aid fell 26.9% below 2024 funding levels; Bill Gates said Trump administration cuts were 'part of that picture,' given the U.S.'s historic role as the largest single global-health donor, and warned that up to 16 million additional children could die by 2045 if the funding cuts persist.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Publicly championed the Administration for a Healthy America reorganization that absorbed CDC's Global Health Center, describing it as eliminating 'an alphabet soup' of departments by merging them into AHA; defended the broader HHS budget cuts, including CDC restructuring, in congressional testimony.

estimated_impact.summary: Sharply reduced dedicated federal funding for global vaccine and disease-prevention programs, compounding the separate loss of WHO-coordinated surveillance access, at a moment public-health experts warn U.S. outbreak-detection capacity is already strained.

Precise enacted (as opposed to proposed) FY2026 dollar figures were not independently confirmed in sourcing reviewed.

title: CDC orders federally funded health programs to accept priorities deprioritizing harm reduction and backing 'parental authority' on short deadline
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
status: Notice sent June 24, 2026 with a July 1 compliance deadline, which has passed. As of Sept. 28, 2026, no reporting found of funding canceled under it; separately, an April 2026 SAMHSA guidance letter already bars HHS funds for drug-test strips given to people who use drugs.
date_of_action: 2026-06-24 (notice sent) - 2026-07-01 (compliance deadline)
what_changed: On Wednesday, June 24, 2026, the CDC informed state, territorial, tribal, and local health programs receiving federal funding that they must agree to a list of CDC priorities within five business days, or by July 1, 2026, according to a copy of the memo obtained by the Guardian. Programs focused on immunization, HIV, hepatitis, and tobacco received the notice; the Guardian said it was not clear whether all state, territorial, tribal, and local programs did. The priorities **deprioritize 'housing first,' harm reduction, and safe consumption approaches to substance use (strategies proven to help reduce drug overdoses)** in favor of 'parental authority' and policies giving parents 'greater control over their children's education,' along with programs to reduce homelessness, drug use, and 'public disorder,' a term the memo did not define. Matching harm-reduction and housing-first language appears in CDC's published agency priorities, dated Sept. 17, 2025, which say CDC grants will deprioritize so-called harm reduction and safe consumption efforts and housing-first policies and, where law allows, favor grantees in states and cities that enforce bans on open drug use and urban camping. The requirement was not explicitly tied to funding, but the grant note referenced an earlier CDC statement that funding may be canceled if programs do not comply with the agency's terms. A source familiar with the memo told the Guardian that the notice did not come from CDC program staff, who were unaware of the new requirement; reporting has not named who issued it. After the Guardian's story ran, HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard said grantees 'were directed to review their work plans and ensure their activities align with the Department's priorities and produce meaningful public health outcomes.' Street-drug researcher Nabarun Dasgupta of the University of North Carolina warned that moving away from harm reduction and housing first while the adulterant medetomidine spreads would fill ICUs and emergency rooms with people in severe withdrawal. The notice capped more than a year of moves against harm reduction. A preliminary FY2026 budget document obtained by the Washington Post and reported in late April 2025 proposed eliminating the roughly $56 million-a-year First Responders-Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (FR-CARA) naloxone grant program, which in fiscal 2023 distributed more than 101,000 overdose-reversal kits and trained nearly 77,000 people to use them, according to a SAMHSA budget document cited by CNN. The administration's FY2026 budget request kept the termination, and some congressional Republicans told NOTUS they would not take up that cut; the FY2026 Labor-HHS spending law Trump signed on February 3, 2026 instead funded SAMHSA's CARA first-responder overdose-reversal training line at about $59 million, per an Addiction Policy Forum tally of the final bill. Trump's July 24, 2025 executive order 'Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets' directed that SAMHSA discretionary grants not fund so-called 'harm reduction' and 'safe consumption' efforts, saying they 'only facilitate illegal drug use and its attendant harm,' and a July 29, 2025 SAMHSA letter to grantees shifted the agency away from harm reduction while still allowing its funds for naloxone, fentanyl test strips, and HIV and hepatitis prevention services, according to the National Association of Counties. In Alaska, Anchorage police chief Sean Case and other police chiefs warned in December 2025 that an expected 35% cut to the state's High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area (HIDTA) funding, proposed in the White House's 2026 budget, could increase the flow of fentanyl into a state that, a Guardian analysis found, had yet to see a sustained decline in overdose deaths, while a Brookings Institution researcher warned that Medicaid work requirements enacted in the 2025 'big, beautiful bill' could cut people with addiction off treatment; the fate of the HIDTA funding was unknown at the time. In January 2026, CDC officials told Overdose Data to Action (OD2A) grant recipients in a compliance meeting that anything that could be construed as encouraging drug use was now prohibited; asked whether health departments could keep promoting the message to 'never use alone' (so that someone is present to give naloxone or call for help in an overdose), the officials called it a gray area and would not give a clear answer, while saying naloxone and fentanyl test strips would remain permitted. An HHS spokesperson told the Guardian only that 'HHS is committed to implementing the President's Executive Orders across the Department.' On February 2, 2026, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a $100 million plan to carry out Trump's executive order on the 'Great American Recovery'; the HHS press release faulted prior policies for backing 'non-effective interventions such as harm reduction, supporting housing first.' On April 24, 2026, SAMHSA issued an updated letter barring any HHS funding for fentanyl or other drug test strips intended for people who use drugs, for syringes and safer-smoking supplies, and for 'overdose hotlines' that give people a virtual companion while they use drugs; naloxone purchase and distribution remained fundable.

primary_proponent.role: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
primary_proponent.note: Issued the notice and its priorities; a source told the Guardian it did not come from CDC program staff, and reporting has not named the issuer. HHS, under Secretary Robert F. estimated_impact.summary: State, territorial, tribal, and local programs funded for immunization, HIV, hepatitis, and tobacco work were given five business days to accept CDC priorities that deprioritize harm reduction and housing first, strategies proven to help reduce drug overdoses, under a funding-cancellation warning the memo referenced but did not state outright. Researchers warned the shift will worsen the overdose crisis, especially as the medetomidine adulterant spreads and people in severe withdrawal end up in ICUs and emergency rooms. The notice sits on top of an April 2026 HHS-wide bar on federal funds for drug-test strips given to people who use drugs and for overdose companion hotlines. A separate proposal to end the roughly $56 million FR-CARA naloxone grant, which distributed more than 101,000 kits in fiscal 2023, was not adopted by Congress.

estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar figure, program count, or reported funding cancellation has surfaced for the June 2026 notice itself as of Sept. 28, 2026, and its funding consequence was referenced from an earlier CDC statement rather than stated outright. The health harm is projected by researchers quoted by the Guardian, not modeled. The FR-CARA figures describe a program Congress kept funding, so they measure what the proposed cut would have put at risk, not a realized loss. The count of affected programs is unknown; the Guardian could not confirm whether every program received the notice.

The compliance deadline is firmer than the funding consequence, which the memo referenced rather than stated. CDC's published priorities page and SAMHSA's April 24, 2026 letter are primary documents; the FY2026 funding level for the CARA first-responder line comes from an Addiction Policy Forum tally of the final bill, and the law's February 3, 2026 signing from a Brownstein client alert. The FR-CARA program figures come from a SAMHSA budget document as reported by CNN; the proposed cut is corroborated by The Independent (via Yahoo, citing the Washington Post), CNN, and NOTUS. The January 2026 'never use alone' meeting account rests on the Guardian alone, which reviewed a grant note and meeting details. The Alaska HIDTA and Medicaid warnings rest on the Guardian's on-record local interviews and were not cross-checked against a second outlet.

title: CDC Disbanded Its 34-Year-Old Hospital Infection-Control Advisory Committee Without Telling Committee Members for a Month
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Disbanded since March 31, 2025; as of the most recent reporting reviewed, no confirmation was found that the committee has been reinstated despite repeated calls from professional infection-prevention societies (APIC, SHEA, IDSA, and others) urging CDC/HHS to restore it.
date_of_action: 2025-03-31 (termination effective) through 2025-05-02 (CDC disclosed the termination; committee members were not notified until a virtual meeting in early May, over a month after the effective date)
what_changed: **CDC disbanded the Healthcare Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee (HICPAC), established in 1991 to issue national, science-based guidance on preventing healthcare-associated infections and antimicrobial resistance in U.S. hospitals, effective March 31, 2025.** HHS characterized HICPAC as one of the 'unnecessary government entities and federal advisory committees' identified for termination under a Trump executive order directing agencies to eliminate such bodies. CDC did not disclose the termination publicly until May 2, 2025, and did not inform HICPAC's own committee members until a virtual meeting in early May -- more than a month after the committee had already ceased to exist. At the time of its termination, HICPAC was actively working to update federal guidance on two active issues: return-to-work recommendations for healthcare personnel following COVID-19 infection, and isolation precautions in healthcare settings generally -- both left without a resolution because the committee that would have issued the updated guidance no longer existed. Infection-prevention professional societies -- including APIC (Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology), SHEA (Society for Healthcare Epidemiology of America), and IDSA (Infectious Diseases Society of America) -- publicly characterized HICPAC as 'a critical asset to the nation's public health infrastructure' and called for its reinstatement.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.role: Federal health department implementing the executive order directing elimination of 'unnecessary' federal advisory committees
primary_proponent.note: No single named HHS or CDC official was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally responsible for identifying HICPAC specifically as an 'unnecessary' committee for elimination under the broader executive order.

estimated_impact.summary: HICPAC's elimination removed the federal government's dedicated science-advisory body for hospital infection-control standards -- guidance hospitals nationwide rely on to prevent healthcare-associated infections and slow antimicrobial resistance -- leaving two active guidance updates (COVID return-to-work recommendations, general isolation precautions) unresolved with no committee remaining to complete them. Professional societies warn that without an ongoing federal advisory body, infection-control standards risk becoming outdated as clinical evidence evolves, a risk with direct patient-safety implications given how directly hospital infection-control practice depends on this kind of centralized, science-based guidance.

figures.source: APIC, SHEA, and multiple other professional-society statements

estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar-cost or quantified health-outcome figure specific to HICPAC's elimination was found in sourcing reviewed -- the impact documented here is the loss of an ongoing federal guidance-setting function and the stalling of two specific in-progress guidance updates, not a modeled or measured infection-rate increase attributable to the committee's absence.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- corroborated across NBC News, Healio, LeadingAge, the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Society, and multiple infection-prevention professional societies' own public statements (APIC, SHEA, IDSA), all describing the same March 31, 2025 effective date, the delayed May 2025 notification, and the committee's 1991 founding and role. No sourcing reviewed disputes the basic facts of the termination; the characterization of HICPAC as 'unnecessary' is HHS's own stated rationale under the executive order, not an independent finding.

section_summaries.what_changed: CDC disbanded its 34-year-old hospital infection-control advisory committee (HICPAC) effective March 31, 2025 under an executive order targeting 'unnecessary' federal advisory bodies, but didn't tell committee members until early May -- over a month later -- leaving in-progress COVID return-to-work and isolation-precaution guidance updates unresolved.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: Hospitals lose the federal government's dedicated science-advisory body for infection-control standards, with professional societies warning guidance will grow outdated as clinical evidence evolves without an ongoing committee to update it.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Well-corroborated across NBC News, Healio, and multiple infection-prevention professional societies; HHS's 'unnecessary' characterization is its own stated rationale, not an independently verified finding.
