title: CDC Injury Center Lost 200+ Staff in April 2025, Eliminating Its Drowning-, Motor-Vehicle-, and Child-Maltreatment-Prevention Teams
institution: CDC National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (Injury Center)
status: Ongoing -- whether the April 2025 staff terminations were reversed remains unconfirmed in sourcing reviewed. A January 2026 appropriations bill restored level funding to the Injury Center's parent unit after a proposed outright elimination (see cdc-injury-center-funding-freeze-2025.json), but no sourcing confirms the specific specialist teams named here -- drowning, motor vehicle, child maltreatment, rape prevention, traumatic brain injury, falls -- were rehired or reconstituted. Restored unit funding is not the same as restored team staffing.
date_of_action: 2025-04 (mass layoffs directed by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) through 2025-08-27 (NPR follow-up confirming the drowning team remained eliminated and its FY2026 elimination was proposed in the federal budget)
what_changed: In April 2025, as part of the broader HHS workforce purge directed by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., entire specialist teams at the CDC's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (the Injury Center) were eliminated: units focused on motor vehicle crashes, child maltreatment, rape prevention and education, drowning prevention, traumatic brain injury, and falls among the elderly, along with the center's data-analysis branch, a key database-maintenance team, and staff supporting the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (the CDC's emergency-room-based injury-tracking system). The loss of that CDC support staff had an immediate downstream effect at the Consumer Product Safety Commission, which co-administers NEISS's broader All Injury Program: an internal CPSC email dated April 11, 2025 stated that 'due to the recent reductions-in-force and budget cuts across CDC's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control, the [All Injury Program] supported portion of NEISS is coming to an end very quickly,' and Reuters reported the 47-year-old program -- which draws from a representative sample of 100 hospital emergency departments and tracks injuries from motor vehicle crashes, alcohol, adverse drug effects, aircraft incidents, and work-related injuries -- would stop collecting that data effective the same week, cutting the program's overall data collection by as much as 65%. Safe States Alliance director Sharon Gilmartin identified more than 200 positions eliminated at the Injury Center in the cuts. A CDC senior health scientist told OPB/member station reporting, 'A lot of the work we do will not be picked up by anyone else.' Christen Rexing of the Society for Advancement of Violence and Injury Research warned, 'We will not know what is killing us and that's very scary.' Beth Moracco of UNC's Injury Prevention Research Center called the work 'critical...done at such a low cost with such a high return,' and Mark Rosenberg, the Injury Center's former director, said, 'There's nothing partisan about injuries.' Injuries are the leading cause of death for Americans under 45, and car crashes are the second-leading cause of death for children ages 1-12. Among the eliminated units, the drowning-prevention team drew particular attention: Politico reported May 26, 2025 that the team -- which tracked national drowning data, issued safety alerts, and partnered with groups including the YMCA to fund swim lessons for at-risk children -- was cut even as drowning remains the leading cause of death for children ages 1-4. NPR reported August 27, 2025 that the drowning-prevention unit, staffed by just three scientists on a roughly $2 million annual budget, had also partnered with the American Red Cross and specifically served autistic children, who face dramatically elevated drowning risk; the Trump administration's FY2026 budget request separately proposed eliminating the drowning-prevention program altogether, on top of the staff terminations already carried out. **Drowning kills more than 4,000 Americans annually and is the leading cause of death for children ages 1-4 and among the leading causes for ages 5-14.** This entry documents the staff-elimination action specifically; a related but mechanically distinct action -- OMB's freeze of Injury Center program funding, and a separate FY2026 proposal to eliminate the center's parent unit entirely that was defeated by a bipartisan appropriations campaign -- is documented in this tracker's cdc-injury-center-funding-freeze-2025.json entry; that entry's January 2026 'reversed' resolution restored level funding to the Injury Center as a whole but no sourcing reviewed confirms whether the specific specialist teams named here, terminated months earlier in the April 2025 RIF, were ever rehired.

estimated_impact.summary: More than 200 CDC Injury Center positions were eliminated, ending federal data collection, safety-alert issuance, and prevention-program funding (including swim-lesson partnerships for at-risk and autistic children) across six injury-prevention specialties, at a moment when injuries are the leading cause of death for Americans under 45.

title: OMB Froze CDC Injury Center Funding for Youth Violence, Gun Injury, Diabetes, and Tobacco Programs
institution: CDC Injury Center / Office of Management and Budget
status: Reversed (partial), plus a separate elimination threat that was also reversed -- CDC staffers confirmed delayed FY2025 funds began being disbursed as of August 2025 following press and congressional pressure; a subsequent White House FY2026 budget request to eliminate the Injury Center's parent unit entirely was defeated by a bipartisan appropriations campaign, with Congress fully funding the center through the rest of FY2026 in a bill signed into law by January 2026
date_of_action: 2025 (freeze in place through mid-2025) through 2025-08-05 (WSJ report and NPR follow-up on disbursement); separately, 2025-05 (FY2026 budget request proposing elimination) through 2026-01 (appropriations bill signed, fully funding the center)
what_changed: Earlier, on April 4, 2025, Trump ordered CDC to cut $2.9 billion in contracts -- about 35% of its contracting budget -- by April 18, 2025, as part of a broader HHS-wide DOGE contract-cutting directive. The CDC-specific directive followed an earlier firing of roughly 2,400 CDC employees, including scientists who had worked on asthma, lead poisoning, violence prevention, and climate-related public health research -- overlapping directly with the Injury Center's youth-violence and firearm-injury-prevention portfolio described below. The Wall Street Journal reported that the White House Office of Management and Budget had **frozen funding for at least five CDC Injury Center programs -- youth violence prevention, adverse childhood experiences, firearm injury prevention, injury control research centers, and general injury-prevention activities** -- alongside broader CDC chronic-disease funding covering diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and tobacco use, with the amount withheld estimated at up to $200 million. This followed a months-long pattern in which CDC did not receive the roughly $9 billion Congress had appropriated for fiscal year 2025 in full, instead receiving disbursements in small increments approximately every 30 days, sufficient only to cover payroll and other limited expenses. Following the WSJ report and subsequent public and congressional pressure, NPR reported on August 5, 2025 that CDC staffers said the agency had begun disbursing previously delayed funds, including money for overdose-prevention programs; separately, funding previously frozen for rape and domestic-violence prevention programs was also reported as being released around the same time. ABC News and the Trust for America's Health's 2025 public-health-infrastructure report characterized this episode as part of a broader, ongoing pattern of 'red tape and budget constraints' delaying CDC program funding beyond this specific freeze. Update 2026-08-30: beyond the funding-freeze episode above, a separate and more severe threat emerged and was later reversed -- the White House's FY2026 budget request, released May 2025, proposed eliminating the CDC's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (the Injury Center's formal parent unit) entirely, not merely delaying its funding. A coalition of over 50 national organizations, philanthropies, universities, and health agencies, organized as the 'Keep America Safe Coalition' by the Safe States Alliance, campaigned against the proposal by highlighting local program outcomes (suicide-prevention work in Louisiana, infant-mortality reduction in Washington state, trauma-center initiatives in Chicago) to Congress and the public. Bipartisan appropriations leaders -- Reps. Tom Cole (R-OK) and Rosa DeLauro (D-CT), and Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) and Tammy Baldwin (D-WI) -- championed retaining the center's funding. title: CDC's Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Team Was Cut Entirely, Then Denied Milwaukee's Request for Help With a School Lead Crisis
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Center for Environmental Health / Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry
status: Not restored as of last verification -- Milwaukee ultimately completed its own lead-abatement work in the affected schools by December 2025 without direct CDC field support
date_of_action: 2025-04 (staff cuts confirmed; Milwaukee's request denied 2025-04-03)
what_changed: In January 2025, a Milwaukee Public Schools (MPS) student was diagnosed with elevated blood lead levels, traced to flaking lead paint in a school basement bathroom; **a subsequent citywide inspection found lead hazards present in 99 MPS schools built before 1978, when lead paint was still legal**. On March 26, 2025, MPS and the Milwaukee Health Department formally requested CDC assistance -- an EpiAid deployment, the CDC's standard mechanism for sending expert field support to a local health emergency. On April 3, 2025, Dr. Aaron Bernstein, director of CDC's National Center for Environmental Health/Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, wrote to Milwaukee officials that the agency could not help: 'I sincerely regret to inform you that due to the complete loss of our Lead Program, we will be unable to support you with this EpiAid request.' Milwaukee Health Department Commissioner Dr. Michael Totoraitis said the city had only learned of the program's elimination via that email, with no advance notice. The CDC's lead poisoning prevention program had been eliminated as part of the broader HHS restructuring and reduction-in-force actions of early 2025 (see hhs-early-2025-workforce-purge-hiv-office-elimination for the department-wide purge this program's staff were caught up in). Wisconsin Rep. Gwen Moore sent a formal letter to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over the denial. Milwaukee proceeded to manage the lead-abatement effort using city and state resources without direct federal expert support, completing lead-hazard remediation across the affected schools by late December 2025, roughly ten months after the crisis began. Milwaukee was not the only community left without help: CDC's lead branch was also in the early stages of coordinating with a state health department and tribal officials on an American Indian reservation over child lead-poisoning concerns when the elimination brought that collaboration to a standstill too. Kennedy himself later called eliminating the Lead Poisoning Prevention and Surveillance Branch a mistake, before walking the remark back; HHS subsequently said it intended to continue lead-poisoning prevention work under the planned Administration for a Healthy America.

primary_proponent.note: No single official is named in reporting as personally ordering the Lead Program's elimination specifically; attributed institutionally to Kennedy as HHS Secretary, under whose broader restructuring the program's staff were let go. Dr. Aaron Bernstein, the CDC official who denied Milwaukee's request, was communicating an existing staffing reality rather than making the underlying policy decision.

estimated_impact.summary: A functioning, standing federal expert-response capacity for childhood lead poisoning -- the kind of local public health emergency it existed specifically to support -- was eliminated and then unavailable at the exact moment a mid-size American city needed it, during an active child-health crisis affecting dozens of schools.

title: CDC Had a Senate-Confirmed Director for Less Than a Month in Trump's First 18 Months, Missing the Vacancies Act Deadline
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
status: Vacancy resolved: the Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz (nominated April 2026) as CDC director, 51-44, on August 5, 2026, nearly a year after Monarez's August 2025 firing. The missed 210-day Vacancies Act deadline and ~80% center-director turnover during the gap are not undone.
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2026-08-05 (vacancy ended with Schwartz's confirmation), with an early wave of five center/office-head departures on March 25, 2025
what_changed: In the first 18 months of Trump's second term, CDC had a Senate-confirmed director for less than a month -- Susan Monarez, who was fired in August 2025, 29 days into the job, following a clash with HHS Secretary RFK Jr. over vaccination policy. The center-director exodus the WSJ later reported at ~80% had visible early markers well before that March 2026 report: on March 25, 2025 -- the day after the White House announced it would nominate Susan Monarez as CDC director -- five center and office heads departed at once (Leslie Ann Dauphin of the Public Health Infrastructure Center, Dr. Karen Remley of the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, Sam Posner of the Office of Science, Debra Lubar of the Office of Policy, Performance and Evaluation, and Leandris Liburd of the Office of Health Equity), on top of three other recent departures -- close to a third of the agency's top management at that point, per the Associated Press (whose report STAT News carried); CNN separately reported the five departures. The departures, described as retirements, were announced at a meeting of senior agency leaders but not publicly; the AP confirmed them with two CDC officials who were not authorized to discuss them. After Monarez's firing, HHS Deputy Secretary Jim O'Neill served as acting CDC director. On November 26, 2025, CBS News reported that Louisiana Surgeon General Ralph Abraham -- who in February 2025 had ordered his state health department to stop promoting mass vaccination -- had been named CDC's principal deputy director; he formally started there on January 5, 2026, per Reuters, though CDC's internal directory listed him in the post from late November. In February 2026 the churn accelerated: O'Neill left the acting director post on February 13; on February 18, NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya was named to run CDC temporarily while keeping his NIH job; and on February 23, Abraham resigned effective immediately, citing unforeseen family obligations, about seven weeks after his January start -- the second top CDC official to leave that month. In early March 2026, **The Wall Street Journal reported that roughly 80% of CDC's center directors -- the agency's division-level leadership -- had resigned or been forced out since January 2025**, citing the CDC Data Project, an independent tracker of staffing and funding reductions, while the agency's overall workforce had shrunk by about a quarter; current and former employees described staff left without supervisors to approve travel, manage grants or coordinate cross-team work. The Journal reported the administration intended to nominate a permanent CDC director in the coming weeks. It had not done so by the deadline: by late March 2026, the White House had missed the deadline under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, which limits how long an acting officer may serve in place of a Senate-confirmed official to 210 days, without nominating a permanent replacement; HHS said Bhattacharya would continue overseeing CDC by performing the 'delegable duties' of the director role. This leadership vacuum coincided with the nationwide measles outbreak, at its highest level in three decades, and other public-health developments this tracker separately documents. The White House nominated Dr. Erica Schwartz -- a retired rear admiral in the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps and former deputy surgeon general who had served as the U.S. Coast Guard's chief medical officer -- in April 2026; the Senate confirmed her 51-44 on August 5, 2026, making her the first Senate-confirmed CDC director since Monarez and the first Black woman to hold the post. Her confirmation ends the specific vacancy this entry tracks, roughly a year after Monarez's firing and well after the missed 210-day Vacancies Act deadline; it does not reverse the center-director attrition (~80% turnover) or the other leadership churn documented above, which remain part of the historical record regardless of the vacancy's resolution.

estimated_impact.summary: For nearly a year -- from Monarez's August 2025 firing to Dr. Erica Schwartz's August 5, 2026 confirmation -- the agency responsible for the national response to U.S. measles cases at a three-decade high and other disease threats ran without a confirmed, accountable director, under a string of acting and part-time leaders (O'Neill, then NIH Director Bhattacharya alongside his NIH job), and past the 210-day limit Congress set for acting service. The gap came alongside the loss of roughly 80% of CDC's center directors and about a quarter of its workforce since January 2025. Schwartz's confirmation ends the vacancy but does not restore that lost leadership.

title: CDC Shut Down Its 30-Year Maternal-Mortality Data System and Eliminated the Team That Ran It
institution: CDC Division of Reproductive Health, Department of Health and Human Services
status: Data collection remains disrupted as of the most recent reporting reviewed (early 2026); no restoration of the Division of Reproductive Health's staff or the PRAMS data system to pre-cut levels has been identified in sourcing reviewed.
date_of_action: 2025-01 (PRAMS data-collection software abruptly shut down) through 2025-04 (Division of Reproductive Health workforce cut by roughly two-thirds, PRAMS team eliminated)
what_changed: In January 2025, for the first time in three decades, CDC abruptly shut down the software system used to collect data for the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) -- a CDC/state-health-department partnership survey that is the country's most comprehensive source of data on health behaviors and outcomes before, during, and after pregnancy, widely used by researchers to study maternal mortality and its racial/geographic disparities. In late March and early April 2025, HHS workforce reductions cut the CDC's Division of Reproductive Health staff by roughly two-thirds, eliminating the entire team responsible for running PRAMS -- about 20 people, per AP's reporting. Rep. title: 38 of 82 Regularly Updated CDC Public Health Databases Stopped Updating Within Months of RFK Jr.'s Confirmation, Nearly All Vaccine-Related
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
status: Confirmed via peer-reviewed research published January 26, 2026; no restoration of the stalled databases identified in sourcing reviewed.

what_changed: A study published January 26, 2026 in Annals of Internal Medicine examined 82 CDC databases that had been updated monthly as of early 2025 and found that by late October 2025, 38 of them had stalled, including 34 with no new entries at all in the prior six months. The paused databases tracked vaccination coverage (including COVID-19 vaccination rates among pregnant women and the general adult population), respiratory illness activity in emergency departments, and RSV preventive-drug usage; some, including COVID vaccination databases, had last been updated in late April 2025. Kennedy Jr. was confirmed as HHS Secretary. **Nearly 90% of the paused databases specifically concerned vaccination.** Study researcher Noel Brewer said, 'it's curious that all these changes are primarily, and almost exclusively, in the area of vaccination.'

title: CDC Laid Off Its Entire Full-Time Cruise Ship Health Inspection Team During a Record Norovirus Year
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Vessel Sanitation Program
status: Not restored as of last verification -- program continued operating with a skeleton staff of Public Health Service officers

what_changed: In April 2025, all full-time CDC employees working for the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) -- which inspects large cruise ships for sanitation hazards and investigates onboard disease outbreaks -- were laid off, part of the broader April 2025 HHS reduction-in-force that cut roughly 2,400 CDC positions overall (see hhs-early-2025-workforce-purge-hiv-office-elimination.json for the department-wide purge). Doris Matsui sent letters to CDC demanding answers about the program's ability to continue meeting its inspection and outbreak-response mandate with the reduced staff.

title: CDC Holds Up Free COVID Vaccines for Children in the Vaccines for Children Program for Nearly Four Weeks
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Vaccines for Children (VFC) program and Section 317 immunization program, Department of Health and Human Services
status: CDC opened Vaccines for Children ordering for the 2026-27 COVID shots on Sept. 23, 2026, nearly four weeks after FDA approval; doses reach clinics on state-by-state timelines. Sens. Markey, Schumer and Sanders asked CDC and HHS to explain the delay by Oct. 9; no public answer found yet.
date_of_action: 2026-08-27 to 2026-09-23 (FDA approval of the 2026-27 vaccines to CDC opening VFC ordering)
what_changed: The Food and Drug Administration approved updated COVID-19 vaccines for the 2026-27 season on August 27, 2026, and retail pharmacies began stocking them within weeks; CVS told CNN on September 17 that pediatric doses had begun arriving at some of its stores the week before and that a pediatric shot would cost $149.99 without insurance coverage. The CDC, however, did not open ordering for the same vaccines through the Vaccines for Children program, which buys vaccines and provides them at no cost to children who are uninsured, underinsured, eligible for Medicaid, or American Indian or Alaska Native. CNN reported that about half of U.S. children are eligible for the program; the Guardian put the eligible share at 52%. California's health department said it also could not order COVID shots through the separate Section 317 immunization grant program. The Wall Street Journal first reported the delay on September 16, noting that government orders are typically placed within two weeks of vaccines becoming commercially available. Public health officials in California, Georgia, New York, Pennsylvania and South Carolina told CIDRAP News that the shots were not yet available to their VFC programs; New York told providers they could vaccinate VFC-eligible children with privately bought doses and replace them later. The Guardian reported on September 23 that the holdup cut off COVID vaccines for all children, insured or not, in at least 11 states and one U.S. territory that buy vaccines for every child through the program: Alaska, Connecticut, Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wyoming and American Samoa. HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard told CIDRAP News the CDC was "finalizing decisions regarding COVID-19 vaccine procurement through the Vaccines for Children and Section 317 programs," that "an arbitrary September date should not be treated as a public-health deadline for COVID-19 vaccine procurement," and that "HHS and CDC have a responsibility to ensure responsible stewardship of taxpayer resources and that vaccines procured through federally funded programs are appropriate for the populations those programs serve." Michelle Fiscus, chief medical officer of the Association of Immunization Managers, said the gap creates a two-tiered system that leaves low-income children vulnerable longer than wealthier children, and that last year COVID shots did not reach the program until October 6, 40 days after approval. The usual route for adding a vaccine to the program, a vote by the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, was unavailable: a federal judge found in March that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. likely violated federal law in replacing the committee's members, and the panel has not met since December 2025. American Academy of Pediatrics president Andrew Racine said the administration "promised that changes to the federal vaccine process would not interfere with families' ability to access recommended vaccines, yet that is exactly what is occurring." Kennedy, speaking at a Children's Health Defense conference in mid-September, said, "We have not taken vaccines away from anyone." On the evening of September 23, the CDC notified states that the VFC ordering portal was open and released its clinical guidance, nearly four weeks after FDA approval; that guidance recommends the vaccine for children 6 months through 17 years with moderate to severe immunocompromise and leaves other children to shared clinical decision-making. Opening ordering did not put doses in clinics the same day: Drug Topics reported that availability depends on how fast each state sets up ordering, how large initial supplies are and how quickly states ship doses to clinicians, so it will vary by state. This was the second year in a row that COVID shots reached the program late. On September 29, Sens. Edward Markey, Chuck Schumer and Bernie Sanders wrote to CDC Director Erica Schwartz and Kennedy that the delay left **millions of low-income and uninsured children waiting for vaccines heading into the fall respiratory illness season** while commercially insured families could already get them. They asked why ordering took nearly four weeks, whether any political appointee at HHS or CDC delayed or intervened in VFC procurement or ordering, and how the CDC told states about the delay, and requested written answers by October 9, 2026. Their letter also cited Kennedy's May 2025 decision to stop recommending COVID vaccines for healthy children and President Trump's August 2026 executive order directing that the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine be split into separate shots.

title: Census Bureau to Test a Citizenship Question Ahead of the 2030 Census, Breaking 75 Years of Practice
institution: U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce
status: Field test underway as of this entry's addition (2026) -- conducted in Huntsville, AL and Spartanburg, SC, pared down from an originally-planned six locations to two

what_changed: The Census Bureau plans to include a citizenship question -- drawn from American Community Survey (ACS) question wording never before used in a census field test -- as part of its 2026 practice test ahead of the 2030 census. title: OMB Moves to Eliminate 2030 Census Race/Ethnicity and Sexual-Orientation Questions
institution: Office of Management and Budget; U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce
status: Formal Federal Register proposal published September 10, 2026, with a public comment period running through October 13, 2026, ahead of a final rule; not yet finalized.
date_of_action: 2025-12-05 (OMB signals review reopened) through 2026-09-10 (formal Federal Register proposal)
what_changed: On December 5, 2025, Mark Calabria, OMB's chief statistician, told the Council of Professional Associations on Federal Statistics that the administration had reopened review of the 2024 Biden-era update to federal race/ethnicity data standards -- including new checkboxes for 'Middle Eastern or North African' and a reformatted combined 'What is your race and/or ethnicity?' question -- saying 'we just wanted to be able to take a look at the process and decide where we wanted to end up on a number of these questions,' while cautioning the review was not prejudging any outcome. That review produced a formal proposal: **on September 10, 2026, the administration published a Federal Register notice proposing to eliminate the census race and ethnicity question entirely, citing its 'sensitive nature' and a 'reduced need for or usefulness of this information,' and to ban a sexual-orientation question -- reversing the approach used on the 2020 census, which asked same-sex and opposite-sex couples to identify as such**. The same proposal formalizes a separate, previously-tested change: excluding non-U.S. citizens without a green card from the census count used for congressional apportionment and Electoral College allocation, a practice never before used in U.S. census history (this apportionment-exclusion piece was already tracked, at its earlier field-test stage, in census-2026-test-citizenship-question-2030.json; that entry's 'separate legal dispute' framing is now superseded by this formal proposal). The public comment period runs through October 13, 2026, ahead of a final rule; a congressional report on the proposed 2030 census questions is due by April 1.

primary_proponent.role: Chief Statistician, Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.note: Publicly announced the reopened review of the 2024 race/ethnicity standards on December 5, 2025; the review he described led to OMB's September 10, 2026 formal proposal to eliminate the race/ethnicity question.

estimated_impact.summary: Civil rights advocates and demographers warn eliminating the race/ethnicity and sexual-orientation questions, combined with the non-citizen apportionment exclusion, would degrade the federal data used to draw voting districts, enforce the Voting Rights Act, and target anti-discrimination and civil-rights enforcement -- while also shifting congressional apportionment and Electoral College weight toward states and districts with fewer non-citizen residents. NPR Illinois's reporting separately names 'federal funding allocation' among the areas the proposal would affect: Census Bureau data of the kind this proposal would stop collecting or would undercount guides several hundred billion to (per the Bureau's own FY2021 accounting) roughly $2.8 trillion annually in federal program funding distributed by formulas that rely in part on race/ethnicity and population-count data, so degrading that data's granularity or accuracy plausibly misdirects some share of that money away from the communities it's meant to reach -- though no single figure isolates the dollar effect of eliminating the race/ethnicity question specifically, as distinct from the broader census-accuracy question.

title: Commerce Department ban on Census Bureau statistical-noise privacy protections
institution: U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Economic Analysis (Department of Commerce)
status: Ongoing (order in effect as of Sept. 2026, no reversal identified; Census Bureau implementing it, full ACS transition by 2029; could be revoked before the 2030 census; related suit dismissed with prejudice July 7, 2026; Supreme Court appeal No. 26-205 docketed Aug. 18, 2026, responses due Oct. 14)
date_of_action: 2026-06 (order issued; effects unfolding through 2030 census preparation)
what_changed:
**The Commerce Department, which oversees the Census Bureau, issued Department Administrative Order (DAO) 216-26, 'Disclosure Avoidance for Statistical Products,' on June 4, 2026, banning 'noise infusion' -- the whole category of methods that add random values, or noise, to data, which covers differential privacy and other noise techniques, though the order names no specific method. Noise infusion was one of the bureau's core techniques for anonymizing survey and administrative-record data before public release and one way it met federal law's requirement (13 U.S.C. §§8, 9) to protect respondents' confidentiality.** Noise infusion has been used for decades, and more recently through a differential-privacy system built under former chief scientist John Abowd, to make it mathematically much harder to re-identify individuals in small-area statistics.

The order leaves the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis two remaining options: 'coarsening' data (releasing broader, less-detailed categories) as the preferred method, or, as a last resort, suppression (not publishing some statistics at all). Data experts warn this could make data for many rural counties and small communities unpublishable, and that 2030 census redistricting data preparation - already underway - will need to be redesigned from scratch. The order followed, and is intertwined with, a separate 2025 lawsuit, later led by America First Legal (co-founded by White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller), challenging the bureau's differential-privacy system, and came after a broader thinning of the bureau's statistical expertise amid Trump administration workforce cuts. It was issued with no public technical rationale, no advance opportunity for outside statisticians to review or comment, and no response from Commerce to a reporter's request for specific examples of the harm it claims to be fixing.

Commerce spokesperson Kristen Eichamer told NPR that 'indiscriminate use of noise infusion—even when not mandated by law—ultimately undermined confidence in the department's products and cast doubt on their integrity,' and that the order made coarsening the preferred technique to 'maintain public confidence in our data while upholding our duty to safeguard the privacy of those who provide information'; asked by NPR for specific examples, Eichamer did not respond. Beth Jarosz, a senior fellow at Georgetown University's Massive Data Institute and vice president of the Association of Public Data Users, told NPR that 'rural communities' data may be not publishable' and that the order 'takes the public out of the process. It takes the experts out of the process.' Former Census chief scientist John Abowd, who led the bureau's adoption of differential privacy, told NPR that under the order 'the only confidentiality protection available is coarsening,' which 'is guaranteed to reduce the level of detail drastically.' A current Census Bureau employee, speaking anonymously to NPR, said 'it would not be a major overreaction to say that this is cataclysmic' and that if the policy stays in effect 'it's the end of a lot of our data production.'

NPR and Georgetown CCF reported that Republican state officials in Alabama sued in March 2021 to block differential privacy in 2020 census redistricting data; a court denied their request that June and the state dropped the suit. Georgetown's Center for Children and Families reported that the Census Bureau's own simulation found only 10% of currently published Quarterly Workforce Indicators data could be released using the remaining methods, and warned in July and August 2026 that the ban, alongside other administration actions, could mean less detailed race and ethnicity data from Census Bureau sources such as the American Community Survey. On August 17, 2026, George M. Cook, performing the duties of the Census Bureau director, wrote that the bureau 'will rely solely on coarsening and suppression methods,' that the American Community Survey's move to compliant methods 'will occur gradually, with a full transition by 2029,' and that the bureau plans a 2030 census demonstration data product in mid-2027.

Separately, the lawsuit referenced above, University of South Florida College Republicans v. Lutnick (M.D. Fla. No. 8:25-cv-02486), was filed on September 15, 2025 by two Florida Republican groups, the University of South Florida College Republicans and the Pinellas County Young Republicans, and their presidents, against Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and acting Census Director Ron Jarmin, challenging the 2020 census's use of group quarters imputation and differential privacy. America First Legal announced on October 8, 2025 that it was 'leading' the suit in partnership with the St. Petersburg, Florida firm Weber, Crabb & Wein, and a Second Amended Complaint in November 2025 added Rep. Byron Donalds as a plaintiff. The suit was dismissed on February 3, 2026 by a three-judge federal court as time-barred (plaintiffs waited too long to sue), without prejudice and with leave to amend; the court also rejected Donalds's 'delegation-strength' injury theory, finding that injury was Florida's, not his, and time-barred in any event. On February 17, 2026, plaintiffs filed a Third Amended Complaint in the same case that dropped the differential-privacy challenge entirely and focused solely on a different technique, statistical imputation (used to fill in missing population data) -- meaning the June 2026 noise-infusion ban was not compelled by any court ruling; it was a standalone Commerce Department policy action, issued independent of and after the litigation's core privacy claim had already been abandoned by its own plaintiffs. On July 7, 2026, the same three-judge court dismissed the case with prejudice, finding that plaintiffs lacked Article III standing and that their claims were untimely, and on July 8, 2026 plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal to the Supreme Court. On July 17, 2026 the Eleventh Circuit dismissed an appeal the district court clerk had 'erroneously transmitted' to it, and on August 18, 2026 the Supreme Court docketed the direct appeal as No. 26-205; it later extended the time for responses to October 14, 2026.

estimated_impact.summary: Data experts warn that banning noise infusion, a category of techniques (including differential privacy) the bureau used to meet its legal confidentiality obligations, leaves only coarsening or suppression, which they say would drastically reduce the detail the bureau can publish - the bureau's own simulation, reported by Georgetown's Center for Children and Families, found only 10% of currently published Quarterly Workforce Indicators data could be released using the remaining methods. They warn the ban could shrink or eliminate published statistics for small counties and rural areas, reduce detailed race and ethnicity data, and force 2030 census redistricting-data preparation already underway to be redesigned from scratch.

title: CFPB Ordered to Stop All Work, Nearly Defunded — Federal Judge Called It 'Hanging by a Thread'
institution: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
status: Ongoing litigation. Mark Paoletta has served as Acting Director since Vought's FVRA-based authority expired August 1, 2026, with Vought reported remaining at CFPB in a senior-adviser capacity; the Senate Banking Committee had not scheduled a vote on nominee Brian Johnson through late August 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02-10 (stop-work order issued) through 2025-12-30 (federal judge's 'hanging by a thread' ruling)
what_changed:
Before the dismantlement began, in CFPB v. Community Financial Services Association (May 16, 2024), the Supreme Court held that CFPB's Federal Reserve-based funding mechanism satisfies the Constitution's Appropriations Clause. As of January 30, 2025, the agency reported it had returned $19.7 billion to consumers since its creation, NPR later reported. On February 10, 2025, newly installed Acting Director Russell Vought (who simultaneously serves as OMB Director) ordered all CFPB staff and contractors to stop working entirely and not return to agency offices. DOGE personnel were given access to CFPB's HR, payroll, and enforcement-records systems around the same time; Elon Musk posted 'CFPB RIP' on social media. A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order on February 14, 2025 blocking further firings, data destruction, or funding cuts, but by then CFPB's website had already been taken down and staff locked out of buildings and systems. Vought separately moved to cut off the agency's Federal Reserve funding entirely and canceled roughly $100 million in CFPB contracts. Court filings from CFPB leadership itself, filed in March 2025, proposed shrinking authorized staff from 1,174 to 556, sparing only the legal division (which defends the agency in the litigation over its own dismantling) from cuts.

CFPB's top enforcement official, Eric Halperin, resigned in February 2025 as the dismantlement began. Lisa Rosenthal, a CFPB attorney for 13 years who had helped victims of predatory payday loans and supervised teams working on markets from student loans to auto financing, also resigned after the stop-work order, telling NPR: 'This work that I had carried out for these decades and that I cared so deeply about -- this was no longer that work.' Halperin's principal deputy, Cara Petersen, served as de facto acting enforcement director for the next four months before she too resigned, on June 10, 2025, telling staff it had been 'devastating to see the Bureau's enforcement function being dismantled through thoughtless reductions in staff, inexplicable dismissals of cases, and terminations of negotiated settlements that let wrongdoers off the hook' -- citing the dismissal of major cases against Capital One and Walmart among the terminated actions.

The Associated Press detailed several of those dismissed cases on July 15, 2025. CFPB dismissed its lawsuit against Walmart and workforce company Branch Messenger, which had accused the companies of deceptively steering delivery drivers into high-fee Branch accounts and sought $10 million in restitution for harmed drivers -- dropped within the administration's first weeks. Navy Federal Credit Union, which had already settled CFPB's unfair/deceptive-overdraft-fee accusations by agreeing to refund members $80 million, saw that consent order dismissed at the credit union's own request after the administration took over, with CFPB giving no public reason. **The bureau also abandoned its suit against Zelle's parent company (Early Warning Services) and several of the nation's largest partner banks, which had accused them of failing to protect customers from what the lawsuit itself claimed was approximately $870 million in fraud losses accumulated over seven years.**

On the layoffs themselves, D.C. Circuit rulings moved back and forth over several months: an April 11, 2025 panel order granted a partial stay allowing some layoffs to proceed, and it was under that narrow window, around April 17-18, 2025, that about 1,400 employees who had chosen to remain received reduction-in-force notices -- a reduction that would have left only about 200 of the agency's original ~1,700 staff; NTEU, the union representing CFPB employees, argued the 24-hour, no-notice process made a legally required 'particularized assessment' of each position implausible. The D.C. Circuit reinstated the full preliminary injunction on April 28, 2025, blocking further reductions pending appeal (oral argument was set for May 16, 2025), before a different D.C. Circuit panel lifted that injunction again on August 15, 2025, allowing the RIF to proceed toward the ~200-staff target. In December 2025, that panel decision was itself vacated, leaving the layoffs blocked, NPR reported.

Separately, on July 4, 2025, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut the statutory cap on CFPB's annual funding request from the Federal Reserve by roughly half (from 12% to 6.5% of the Federal Reserve's total 2009 operating expenses, adjusted for inflation -- about $823 million to $446 million) -- a cut CFPB told employees by September 2025 could force it to cut jobs just to make payroll. ProPublica reported August 12, 2025 that many of the same Republican lawmakers who voted for that funding cut had themselves routed thousands of constituent complaints to CFPB for help -- Sen. John Cornyn's office had referred more than 800 constituents to the agency, the most of any current lawmaker from either party, while Reps. Darrell Issa and Rob Wittman's offices had each referred more than 100; Issa's spokesperson said most referrals 'occurred several years ago' and reflected 'a conventional way' to handle constituents' consumer issues.

CFPB also rolled back two Biden-era consumer protections in this period: on July 11, 2025, a federal court in Texas vacated CFPB's rule barring medical debt from credit reports, at the Bureau's own joint request with industry plaintiffs in Cornerstone Credit Union League v. CFPB; and effective October 29, 2025, CFPB formally rescinded a separate Biden-era rule that would have required nonbank financial companies with a history of breaking consumer-protection laws to register in a public 'repeat offender' database, followed in early November 2025 by an interpretive rule declaring that state laws in 15 states banning medical-debt credit reporting are preempted by the Fair Credit Reporting Act -- 'salt in the wound,' one consumer advocate said, on top of the rule vacatur three months earlier. By December 2025, more than 30% of CFPB's authorized staff had departed.

On December 22, 2025 -- a separate legal track from the NTEU v. Vought litigation below -- attorneys general from 21 states and the District of Columbia filed State of New York v. Vought (D. Or.), arguing Vought's administration was reading the statutory term 'combined earnings' too narrowly (limiting CFPB's funding requests to the Federal Reserve's net profits, which were negative) when Congress intended the broader 'combined revenues,' and asking the court to compel Vought to request continued Fed funding before the Bureau exhausted its operating funds in January 2026; per Consumer Finance Monitor's December 31, 2025 reporting, it remained pending on a summary-judgment briefing schedule, with no ruling yet issued in that case specifically. On December 30, 2025, the same federal judge overseeing the [NTEU] case -- Judge Amy Berman Jackson, D.D.C. -- separately rejected the administration's argument that Vought could lawfully withhold the agency's funding, ordering him to request continued Federal Reserve funding, which he did -- keeping CFPB funded through at least March 2026. In her order, Jackson wrote that the administration was 'actively and unabashedly trying to shut the agency down again, through different means' -- this time through funding cuts rather than layoffs, NPR noted -- and that 'the agency is hanging by a thread.'

A February 2026 report from Sen. Elizabeth Warren's office estimated that changes imposed after Vought took control of CFPB had cost Americans at least $19 billion in lost financial relief -- $15 billion from two rescinded rules (an overdraft-fee cap projected to save $5 billion/year, and a credit-card late-fee cap projected to save roughly $10 billion) plus nearly $4 billion from dropped enforcement actions and unfulfilled consent orders.

In May 2026, CFPB removed roughly 1,700 web pages of consumer advisories, press releases, and testimony predating February 2025 from its public website (The Guardian's later, more precise count -- comparing the current site against Internet Archive Wayback Machine snapshots and a mirror site maintained by a former CFPB employee -- found at least 2,200 pages deleted as of early June 2026; the two figures describe the same underlying deletion campaign rather than separate events, with the most common deleted-page topics being enforcement, mortgages, banking, and rulemaking; CFPB also deleted its blog entirely and removed all press releases predating February 2025).

Also in May 2026, acting CFPB Director Russell Vought ordered all remaining CFPB staff -- including roughly 450 workers previously based out-of-state -- to relocate to a new, smaller Washington, D.C. headquarters, ending remote work entirely; the bureau terminated leases on all four of its regional offices (San Francisco, Atlanta, Chicago, and New York). The new headquarters space, at 445 12th Street SW, has capacity for only about 550 workers -- roughly half the bureau's remaining headcount of approximately 1,100 -- a mismatch reporting characterized as designed to drive further attrition beyond the office's stated capacity limit alone. Relocation began June 1, 2026 with a hard compliance deadline of August 31 or termination.

In June 2026, Trump nominated Brian Johnson -- a former CFPB deputy director under Kathy Kraninger and current Capital One executive -- to be permanent CFPB Director. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, said: 'Starting in August, Russ Vought can no longer legally serve as Donald Trump's hatchet man at the CFPB. So here comes the next hatchet man to try to finish the job.' Also in June 2026, CFPB removed all prior public reports describing its own supervisory activity. On June 22, 2026, Senate Banking Committee Democrats sent a formal letter to Acting Director Vought demanding an accounting of the deleted content and its legal basis.

Senior leadership reported to the new headquarters starting July 6, 2026, with full D.C.-area staff required back five days a week by July 13. The Senate Banking Committee held Brian Johnson's confirmation hearing on July 23, 2026; Johnson declined to endorse eliminating the CFPB and said he keeps an 'open mind' about staffing levels, while deflecting questions about the agency reportedly dropping 42 enforcement cases against presidential donors.

Separately, the D.C. Circuit remanded NTEU v. Vought (the litigation over the Bureau's proposed 2026 reduction-in-force) back to the district court and held the appeal in abeyance, after CFPB and NTEU jointly asked for a stay pending Johnson's confirmation so he could decide whether to proceed with, modify, or abandon the RIF plan.

Committee advancement is expected before the August recess, with a full Senate vote anticipated in September 2026 -- meaning Johnson is very unlikely to be confirmed before Vought's August 1 FVRA deadline, raising the practical likelihood that Deputy Director Mark Paoletta becomes acting director in the interim (if Johnson is not confirmed by August 1, 2026, Paoletta would become acting director in Vought's place).

Ahead of a Vought oversight hearing, a July 2026 follow-up report from Sen. Warren's office found an additional $7.5 billion in costs in the first half of 2026 -- ~$15 billion cumulative from abandoning the credit-card late-fee cap, ~$7.5 billion from repealing the overdraft-fee cap, and ~$4 billion from dropped enforcement actions and abandoned settlements/consent orders (including the 42 dropped enforcement cases against presidential donors) -- bringing the cumulative total Warren's office attributes to the CFPB rollbacks to up to $26.5 billion.

Vought's FVRA-based authority to run CFPB expired August 1, 2026, and Deputy Director Mark Paoletta -- CFPB's chief legal officer -- became Acting Director that day. Reporting indicates Vought is expected to remain involved at CFPB in a senior-adviser role even after formally leaving the acting-director post, pending Johnson's confirmation. The Senate Banking Committee had not scheduled a vote on Johnson's nomination following his July 23, 2026 hearing, meaning the expected 'before the August recess' committee-vote timeline slipped; reporting through late August 2026 showed it still had not been scheduled. Mark Paoletta continues serving as Acting Director since his August 1, 2026 transition, with Russell Vought reported remaining at CFPB in a senior-adviser capacity.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Acting Director of CFPB (concurrently Director of the Office of Management and Budget)
primary_proponent.note: Vought was one of the architects of Project 2025, which explicitly called for Congress to abolish the CFPB (p. 837 of the document). He has publicly criticized CFPB staff in interviews, telling The Charlie Kirk Show that 'all they want to do is weaponize the tools of financial law against basically small mom-and-pop lenders and other small financial institutions.' This is the same official whose separate impoundment-related actions (NIH funding, broader OMB spending disputes) are covered in other entries across this project's Government Services Redirected and Cabinet-Level Legal Exposure trackers.

estimated_impact.summary: Sen. Elizabeth Warren's office attributes up to $26.5 billion in costs to Americans to the CFPB rollbacks, from abandoning the credit-card late-fee cap, repealing the overdraft-fee cap, and dropping enforcement actions and abandoning settlements; the agency's own reporting states it had returned $19.7 billion to consumers since its 2010 creation as of January 2025 -- the scale of consumer-facing enforcement work now substantially curtailed. The presiding federal judge's own characterization is unusually direct for a legal ruling: she wrote that the administration was 'actively and unabashedly trying to shut the agency down' through funding cuts after being blocked from doing so through layoffs, and that CFPB 'is hanging by a thread.' Former 13-year CFPB attorney Lisa Rosenthal, who resigned after the stop-work order, described the halted work (protecting victims of predatory payday loans, supervising student loan and auto-financing practices) in terms of what it no longer was: 'This work that I had carried out for these decades and that I cared so deeply about -- this was no longer that work.'

estimated_impact.caveat: CFPB was created by Congress (via Dodd-Frank), and in May 2024 the Supreme Court upheld its funding mechanism as constitutional (CFPB v. Community Financial Services Association) -- meaning the core legal dispute is whether the executive branch can functionally dismantle a congressionally-created independent agency through funding and staffing actions alone, without Congress formally eliminating it. This litigation (NTEU v. Vought and the related Baltimore case) remains ongoing and unresolved: the D.C. Circuit remanded the reduction-in-force litigation to the district court and held the appeal in abeyance after CFPB and NTEU jointly asked for a stay pending permanent-director nominee Brian Johnson's confirmation. A separate 21-state/D.C. suit (State of New York v. Vought, D. Or.) was pending with no ruling as of Consumer Finance Monitor's December 31, 2025 reporting. Judge Amy Berman Jackson's December 30, 2025 ruling addressed only the funding question, not the broader dismantlement question.

title: CFTC Lost Over a Fifth of Its Staff in a Year, Including Its Entire Chicago Enforcement Team
institution: U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)
status: Ongoing -- staff down about 21.5% in fiscal 2025 (CFTC IG) and roughly 24-25% since January 2025; Chicago enforcement office emptied by Feb. 2026; buyouts still offered June 2026; Sen. Warren's July 21, 2026 GAO review request had no published findings as of late July 2026
date_of_action: 2025-07-16 (initial post-ruling layoffs begin) through 2026-06 (buyouts and early retirement still offered)
what_changed: On July 16, 2025, eight days after the Supreme Court's July 8, 2025 order in Trump v. AFGE cleared the way for agency-wide federal reductions in force, the CFTC -- the independent agency that regulates derivatives and commodity futures and has become a front-line crypto-market enforcer -- began layoffs expected to affect more than two dozen employees across its enforcement, market oversight, administration, and data divisions, Reuters reported. Reuters put the agency at 636 full-time staff as of fiscal 2025, already reduced by voluntary exits, under acting Chair Caroline Pham. Headcount kept falling through layoffs, buyouts, and early and deferred retirements: the CFTC's own Inspector General, in a December 3, 2025 report, put full-time-equivalent staff on payroll at about 708 at the end of fiscal 2024 and about 556 at the end of fiscal 2025 -- a 21.5% one-year drop. A CFTC spokesperson said voluntary separations accounted for the vast majority of the headcount change. The CFTC's Chicago regional enforcement office -- historically its lead litigation hub for complex fraud cases, including the Binance and FTX matters -- went from 20 enforcement attorneys to none through reductions, retirements, and transfers; Barron's reported that the last remaining enforcement lawyer there resigned on February 9, 2026. On February 26, 2026, Sen. Dick Durbin and four other Senate Agriculture Committee Democrats wrote to Chairman Michael Selig about the Chicago losses and an enforcement-division decline of at least 25%, noting the CFTC brought 13 enforcement actions obtaining less than $10 million in relief in fiscal 2025. By February 2026 the agency had 535 employees, Cryptopolitan reported in April 2026, adding that the CFTC had lost 24% of its staff since Trump returned to office, leaving it at its lowest staffing level in 15 years; Selig's budget request asked Congress to fund 108 enforcement positions, down from 140 filled in 2025 (a 23% drop). **Enforcement output has fallen sharply alongside the staffing losses: the CFTC brought 58 enforcement actions and obtained over $17.1 billion in monetary relief in fiscal 2024, versus 11 enforcement actions and less than $1 billion in the 12 months after the change in administration** -- less than $10 million of it from actions filed by the current administration, according to a January 2026 Reuters analysis. Selig has publicly defended the smaller staff, telling the House Agriculture Committee in April 2026 that the agency is "running more efficiently and effectively" and leaning on AI and automation. Politico reported on June 1, 2026 that the CFTC was offering buyouts and early retirement packages; Selig, meanwhile, had said the agency was hiring. On July 21, 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren asked the Government Accountability Office to review the CFTC's workforce reductions -- which she put at 25% since January 2025 -- including whether the cuts and buyouts complied with federal law and civil service protections, how they affected the agency's mandate and the enforcement decline, and whether they contributed to, detracted from, or had no impact on fraud, waste, and abuse at the CFTC. GAO confirmed receiving the letter and said it was working through its process for deciding whether to take on the work; no GAO findings had been published as of late July 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Caroline Pham (then acting CFTC Chair), under the Trump administration's federal workforce-reduction initiative
primary_proponent.role: Acting CFTC Chairman during the 2025 cuts, carried out under the government-wide RIF and reorganization policy (Executive Order 14210)
primary_proponent.note: The cuts took place mainly in 2025 under acting Chair Caroline Pham, whom Decrypt described as chiefly responsible for reducing agency staff by over 21% that year; her successor, Chairman Michael Selig, has defended the smaller staff. The reductions are part of the same court-cleared, government-wide RIF and separation wave documented at other agencies elsewhere in this database.

estimated_impact.summary: The CFTC, the main federal cop for commodity, derivatives, and much of the crypto and prediction-market trading that ordinary investors now reach, lost roughly a fifth to a quarter of its staff in about a year and emptied its Chicago enforcement office, its lead fraud-litigation hub. Enforcement collapsed alongside: from 58 actions and over $17.1 billion in relief in fiscal 2024 to 11 actions and less than $1 billion in the 12 months after the change in administration, less than $10 million of it from newly filed cases -- meaning far less money recovered for defrauded customers and fewer fraud and manipulation cases pursued as the agency's mandate grows.

title: CIA Offers Buyouts Agency-Wide and Freezes Hiring to Realign Workforce with New Priorities
institution: Central Intelligence Agency
status: Implemented -- buyouts (Feb 2025) and probationary firings done; ~1,200-job cut plan reported May 2025. By Aug 2026 new CIA retirees faced 9+ month waits for full pensions amid a historic exodus; OPM's claims backlog fell to 15,427 that month from a Feb 2026 peak of 65,237.
date_of_action: 2025-02-04 (buyout offer announced) through at least 2025-05 (multi-year reduction plan reported)
what_changed: On February 4, 2025, the CIA under newly confirmed Director John Ratcliffe offered buyouts to its entire workforce: eight months of pay and benefits for employees who chose to resign. A CIA spokesperson declined to say whether employees faced a deadline to decide. The agency simultaneously imposed a hiring freeze and began reviewing already-extended conditional job offers to new recruits, indicating offers not aligned with the agency's new focus were likely to be rescinded. A CIA spokesperson said Ratcliffe was "moving swiftly to ensure the CIA workforce is responsive to the Administration's national security priorities." An aide to Ratcliffe told the Wall Street Journal the agency would put a greater focus on the Western Hemisphere, targeting countries not traditionally considered U.S. adversaries, take a significant role against Mexican drug cartels, and support Trump's trade war and efforts to undermine China; at his confirmation hearing Ratcliffe had promised more hard-edge spying operations and covert action. By March 6, 2025, the CIA had begun terminating some probationary employees after reviewing personnel within their first two years of service; the agency did not say how many. The firings came a week after a federal judge, ruling on a separate action against officers assigned to diversity, equity and inclusion roles, permitted Ratcliffe to fire employees at his discretion. They were a distinct, involuntary action layered on top of the earlier voluntary buyout program. The cuts came days after CNN reported on February 28, 2025 that an NCIS document said the intelligence community assessed with "high confidence" that foreign adversaries were trying to recruit federal employees, and that Russia and China were targeting recently fired or at-risk employees with security clearances, including through LinkedIn, raising concern that thinning the intelligence workforce during a period of active foreign recruitment efforts compounded the risk. On May 2, 2025, the Washington Post reported (and the AP confirmed with a person familiar with the plan) that administration officials had told Congress of a multi-year plan to cut the CIA's workforce by about 1,200 positions, alongside thousands of cuts at the NSA and other intelligence agencies. The CIA reduction included several hundred people who had already opted for early retirement; the rest was to come partly through reduced hiring and was not expected to require layoffs. OPM, which processes retirement claims government-wide (including CIA retirees'), was meanwhile shrinking: its workforce fell by roughly a third, from just over 3,000 employees in FY2024 to about 1,980 in FY2026. Government Executive reported that OPM's pending retirement claims reached 34,587 in October 2025, the most since a roughly 36,000-claim peak in March 2022, against OPM's steady-state goal of about 13,000. The backlog kept climbing to an all-time high of 65,237 in February 2026, and average processing time reached 109 days in July 2026, the slowest since OPM began tracking it in 2018. The Washington Post reported August 20, 2026 that a historic wave of CIA retirements and resignations, together with OPM's cutbacks, was swamping the retirement system. CIA headcounts are classified, but a former official estimated that perhaps more than 1,000 of the agency's roughly 22,000 employees had left; some former officials called it the largest downsizing since the early 1990s. New CIA retirees were told their first full pension check could take nine months or longer; OPM's interim payments, typically 60-80% of the eventual benefit, begin only after the CIA's Retirement Branch finishes a case, and a CIA note to alumni gave retirees toll-free numbers to call if more than six months had passed since their final paycheck. **Some CIA officers pulled back their retirement requests because they could not afford to go months without pay, one former official said.** Others drew down savings or took second mortgages. The CIA surged personnel to its Retirement Branch, and a spokesperson said it had recently hired its largest class of operations officers in two decades. OPM's backlog then fell sharply: by the end of August 2026 it stood at 15,427 pending claims, and average processing time dropped back to 79 days. Whether CIA retirees' waits have shortened is not reported.

title: CISA Lost Roughly One-Third of Its Workforce, Including Election Security and Threat-Sharing Capacity
institution: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing: CISA has lost about a third of its staff and has had no Senate-confirmed director since January 2025 (Nick Andersen acting since Feb. 26, 2026); as of Sept. 9, 2026, about 250 prospective hires held tentative offers pending clearance, vs. the ~600 hires Mullin says are needed.
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2026-06 (rolling cuts across multiple rounds: buyouts, layoffs, forced reassignments)
what_changed:
Since January 2025, CISA -- the nation's primary civilian cyber-defense agency, created in 2018 specifically to coordinate federal response to critical infrastructure attacks -- lost roughly 1,000 employees, about one-third of its workforce, through a combination of buyout offers, early retirements, formal layoffs (reduction-in-force notices), and Management Directed Reassignments transferring CISA staff to ICE, CBP, and the Federal Protective Service (refusing a reassignment could be grounds for termination). In March 2025, under DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, the administration partially defunded the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC), which provided free and low-cost threat-sharing and incident-response services to more than 17,000 state, local, tribal and territorial entities: it revoked $10 million for MS-ISAC work it called redundant, a cut StateScoop reported affected about $8.3 million of the $15.7 million left in the center's 2025 budget. In August 2025, DHS barred state and local cyber grant recipients from spending that money on MS-ISAC memberships, and CISA's cooperative agreement with the Center for Internet Security, which runs MS-ISAC, expired on September 30, 2025. The cuts disproportionately hit CISA's election security and disinformation-monitoring functions, which had drawn Republican criticism as politically biased 'censorship' under the prior administration. The administration's FY2026 budget request, detailed in documents released May 30, 2025, proposed cutting CISA's total funding by about $495 million, eliminating its 14-position, $39.6 million Election Security Program, and projected CISA's workforce falling from 3,292 to 2,324 employees. The agency has operated without a permanent, Senate-confirmed director since January 2025.

The early 2025 cuts had specific, named costs: on March 3, 2025, NOTUS reported CISA had laid off more than 100 people the previous month, including agents tracking Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon, the Chinese state-sponsored hacking campaigns that had already infiltrated U.S. telecom networks and critical infrastructure; on March 7, 2025, CBS News reported that about 130 probationary CISA workers had been fired over the mid-February holiday weekend, among them top recruits including the former manager of **CyberSentry, a program built specifically to detect cyberattacks against the U.S. power grid, pipelines, and water systems**. On March 5, 2025, former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce testified to Congress that the mass federal layoffs -- more than 100,000 federal workers had taken early retirement or been laid off by that point, and more than 130 CISA positions had been cut -- would set back U.S. cyber defenses against China.

Joyce continued sounding this warning publicly: at the Black Hat security conference in August 2025, Marci McCarthy, who oversees CISA's public affairs, defended the staffing purges as a return to the agency's 'core mission,' while Joyce countered that the U.S. had 'backslid' and lost critical national-defense capability, with nearly a third of CISA's workforce gone by that point. The October 2025 government shutdown compounded the damage months before the separate February 2026 DHS funding lapse described below: the Washington Post reported only about 35% of CISA staff remained active during the October shutdown even as ransomware and Chinese cyberattacks intensified, and Politico reported the 2015 Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act -- the law providing legal liability protection for companies that voluntarily share cyber-threat data with the government -- lapsed during the same shutdown, prompting some companies to halt that cooperation entirely.

Nextgov/FCW reported the reassignment wave itself on October 9, 2025 -- hundreds of DHS employees drawn not just from CISA but also FEMA, TSA, and the Coast Guard had been directed to transfer to ICE, CBP, or the Federal Protective Service, with one week to accept (the notice said a non-response would be treated as a declination) and 60 days to relocate; declining, or accepting and failing to report, could lead to removal from federal service. On October 20, 2025, House Democrats led by Rep. James Walkinshaw wrote to Noem alleging that DHS violated the Antideficiency Act by conducting a reduction in force during the shutdown, including termination notices to CISA's Stakeholder Engagement and Infrastructure divisions, and urging her to move CISA staff reassigned to ICE, CBP, and the Federal Protective Service back into cyber-defense roles; a separate New York Times report the same week noted the cuts had also reached the State Department's cyber-diplomacy function. During the shutdown, the Congressional Budget Office disclosed on November 6, 2025 that it had been hacked, by a suspected foreign actor according to the Washington Post; WIRED, reporting the breach the next day, cited experts warning that shutdown gaps in routine patching, monitoring, and device management could expose federal systems, though CBO did not say whether the shutdown had affected its security work. In December 2025, Bloomberg reported the administration was ending CISA's Cybersecurity Retention Incentive program -- a tool used to keep cyber defenders from leaving for better-paying private-sector jobs, covering nearly half of the agency's employees -- even though CISA had already lost about a third of its staff; the incentives ran from 10% to 25% of salary, and Cybersecurity Dive reported it was unclear what would happen to recipients, some of whom might be moved into CISA's separate Cybersecurity Talent Management System. At a January 21, 2026 House Homeland Security Committee hearing, acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala defended the cuts ('we have the staff that we need') and said CISA had in 2025 helped more than 4,000 cyberattack victims and triaged more than 30,000 incidents; an internal agency report entered into the record by ranking member Bennie Thompson counted at least 998 CISA employees who had quit, been laid off or been transferred since the administration began, 65 of them through forced reassignments.

The February 2026 DHS funding lapse compounded this attrition: The New York Times reported CISA furloughed more than half of its remaining workforce during the shutdown, leaving fewer than 1,000 employees on duty at the nation's primary civilian cyber-defense agency during the funding gap; ABC News reported on March 31, 2026, 45 days into the lapse, that Senate appropriators put the share of CISA employees furloughed at about 60%, forcing the agency to cancel vulnerability assessments and further weakening federal cyber defenses at a time when officials were warning of rising Iran-linked cyber threats to critical infrastructure, including power, water, and federal civilian networks. The lapse, which began February 14, would become the longest agency shutdown on record, ending when President Trump signed a DHS funding bill on April 30, 2026. Also in February 2026, acting CISA Director Madhu Gottumukkala moved to reassign two senior career officials -- CIO Bob Costello (CISA's CIO for over four years) and acting Chief Human Capital Officer Kevin Diana -- giving them seven days to accept new roles elsewhere in DHS or resign, following an earlier unsuccessful attempt to oust Costello over a contracting-decision dispute that other political appointees had previously intervened to stop. On February 26, DHS moved Gottumukkala to a strategic-implementation role at the department and named Nick Andersen, CISA's executive assistant director for cybersecurity, acting director. Kristi Noem was replaced as DHS Secretary by Markwayne Mullin, confirmed by the Senate 54-45 on March 23, 2026 and sworn in March 24. In April 2026, Sean Plankey, Trump's first nominee to lead CISA, withdrew his own nomination, writing 'After thirteen months since my initial nomination, it has become clear the Senate will not confirm me' -- the nomination had been held up by a mix of Democratic senators (Ron Wyden, over a withheld telecom-security report) and Republican senators (Rick Scott, over an unrelated Coast Guard shipbuilding dispute), plus broader holds affecting all DHS nominees. Andersen had told staff on March 23 that DHS approved a 'critical hire list' of 329 'mission critical hires,' and in June he said CISA expected to make about 180 tentative job offers by the end of that month -- the first concrete numbers behind the agency's 2026 hiring push, which acting director Gottumukkala had laid out in a November 2025 memo warning that 'the recent reduction in personnel has limited CISA's ability to fully support national security imperatives' as China continued to target U.S. critical infrastructure. On June 16, 2026, Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA), vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, wrote to Andersen that CISA's efforts to restore staffing, including the roughly 200 job offers it was extending, 'appear insufficient given the scale of threats facing our nation's cybersecurity and critical infrastructure, particularly at the state level'; he noted that five of CISA's ten regional directors -- the primary points of contact for state and local governments seeking federal cybersecurity help -- were serving only in an acting capacity, and faulted a proposed FY2027 budget that would cut more than $700 million from CISA. At a June 25 House Appropriations subcommittee hearing, Mullin said the president had met with a likely CISA director nominee, whom he did not name, and that CISA needs about 600 new hires, a rebuild he said can't proceed in earnest until a director is confirmed. On September 9, 2026, Andersen said roughly 250 prospective hires had received tentative job offers and were awaiting security clearance to start, with operational and regional roles prioritized over reaching the larger headcount goal.

State election officials from both parties told USA Today that, ahead of the 2026 midterms, they no longer expect federal agencies to reliably share election-threat intelligence with them -- a concern USA Today tied to officials' broader loss of confidence following staffing cuts, funding reductions and organizational changes at CISA, since 2018 a primary conduit for election-security briefings and cyber assistance. States say they're increasingly relying on private technology companies and nonprofits to fill the gap in federal threat-sharing coordination.

primary_proponent.note: Noem's DHS partially defunded MS-ISAC in March 2025 and later barred grant funds from paying for memberships (Warner's June 4, 2026 letter to Mullin called it 'Secretary Noem's abrupt cancelation of MS-ISAC funding'), and she set the 'smaller, more nimble' policy direction the cuts followed. Mullin replaced her as DHS Secretary in March 2026 and has said CISA needs a Senate-confirmed director before a full rebuild can proceed, and that the president has met with a likely nominee.

estimated_impact.summary: CISA, the civilian agency that defends federal networks and helps protect power, water, hospitals and elections, has lost about a third of its staff since January 2025. The cuts removed people tracking Chinese state hacking campaigns and running the CyberSentry grid-and-water monitoring program; ended federal funding for MS-ISAC, which had given more than 17,000 state and local entities free or low-cost threat-sharing and incident-response help; left half of CISA's regional director posts, the main contacts for state and local governments, filled only on an acting basis; and pulled back election-security support ahead of the 2026 midterms. Two shutdowns then furloughed most of the remaining staff, cancelling vulnerability assessments while Iran-linked cyber threats were rising. Rehiring has begun (about 250 tentative offers awaiting clearance as of September 2026), short of the roughly 600 hires DHS itself says are needed.

title: Federal Indigent-Defense Funding Ran Out for Nearly Three Months, Leaving 12,000+ Court-Appointed Lawyers Unpaid
institution: Federal Judiciary -- Defender Services (Criminal Justice Act panel attorney program)
status: Resolved for FY2025 arrears by a later appropriation, but the underlying funding mechanism (annual Defender Services appropriation) remains subject to future continuing-resolution risk
date_of_action: 2025-03 (continuing resolution freezes judicial-branch funding at FY2024 levels) through 2025-10-01 (payments resume) and into 2026 (arrears repayment sought)
what_changed: A continuing resolution Congress passed in March 2025 to fund the government for FY2025 froze all Judicial Branch funding at FY2024 levels. Because Defender Services funding needs grow year-over-year with caseload, that freeze meant the Criminal Justice Act (CJA) panel-attorney program -- which pays private attorneys, investigators, paralegals, expert witnesses, and interpreters appointed to represent criminal defendants who cannot afford counsel -- ran roughly $130 million short of what the judiciary had requested. The program's funds were depleted on July 3, 2025, and payments to CJA panel attorneys and support staff stopped; the Judiciary told them they would be paid once Congress passed a new budget. The lapse dragged on nearly three months -- the longest such pause on record -- worsened by the fall 2025 government shutdown, which delayed the appropriations process that would have restored funding. During the gap, some CJA attorneys **refused new indigent-defendant cases or took out loans to stay afloat, straining already-overworked federal public defenders forced to absorb the difference, and delaying some trials**. The Judiciary requested $116 million in supplemental funding specifically to cover the missed FY2025 payments, folding that figure into its $1.77 billion total FY2026 Defender Services funding request. Payments resumed October 1, 2025 with the start of the new fiscal year, though some CJA attorneys reported continuing to wait for full back-payment into 2026.

title: NOAA Fired Climate.gov's Entire Content Team; the Site Was Later Shut Down Entirely, Then Resurrected by Former Staff
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)
status: Climate.gov was shut down and its URL redirected to NOAA.gov/climate; former staff separately relaunched an independent replacement site in 2026
