what_changed: On May 31, 2025, NOAA fired the roughly 10-person contract team responsible for producing and publishing new content on Climate.gov, a public-facing NOAA website providing science-based climate information and education to the public for over a decade. title: Administration Strips 'Climate' From Federal Research Funding, Websites, and Course Materials
institution: Multiple federal science and research-funding agencies, government-wide
status: Ongoing -- as of Grist's March 27, 2026 analysis, NSF grants mentioning 'climate change' were down 77% from 2023 and USDA researchers were still avoiding the ARS memo's banned terms; no rescission of the memo was found. A related OMB grant rule was proposed May 29, 2026.
what_changed: The Guardian reported on February 21, 2025 that the administration was withdrawing grants and other support for research that referenced 'climate,' both in the US and overseas. One environmental scientist kept a previously awarded Department of Transportation climate-adaptation grant only after retitling it to remove the word 'climate'; course materials at the University of Hawaii's National Disaster Preparedness Training Center were revised at the administration's behest to delete references to 'climate change'; Fulbright grant descriptions were altered to remove 'climate change,' and at least one Fulbright grant to the University of Helsinki was withdrawn; and mentions of climate change had already been stripped from government websites. On March 20, 2025, Sharon Strickland, an Agricultural Research Service (ARS) administrator in USDA's Northeast Area, sent ARS staff a list of 110 banned words and phrases, instructing that when agreements are evaluated, "those entries that include these terms or similar terms cannot be submitted." Roughly a third of the terms were climate-related (including "climate change," "global warming," "climate science," and "carbon sequestration"), and the list reached well beyond climate to terms such as "clean water," "safe drinking water," "microplastics," "affordable housing," "equity," and "DEI." The outlet More Perfect Union published the memo on March 30, 2025, and Investigate Midwest detailed the full list on April 7, 2025. On April 11, 2025, Sen. Ron Wyden and Reps. Chellie Pingree, Andrea Salinas, and Jill Tokuda, joined by seven other senators and 16 other House members, wrote USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins warning that the list would harm rural communities facing wildfires, drought, and food insecurity, and calling the exclusion of the terms from funding consideration "an intentional effort to hinder, distort, and improperly steer federal scientific work in the name of political expediency." USA Today's July 10, 2025 reporting found the pattern at NOAA: former NOAA employees, including a former Climate.gov editor, said staff had been told verbally to avoid the word 'climate' and use 'environmental change' instead. The same reporting described setbacks that meteorologists warned could make hurricane and extreme-weather forecasts less accurate, including a fleet of Saildrone ocean drones that went undeployed that summer after a contracting issue, amid the broader staffing and budget cuts documented elsewhere in this database. **Grist reported on March 27, 2026 that the number of NSF grants whose titles or abstracts mentioned "climate change" fell from 889 in 2023 to 148 in 2025, a 77% drop -- partly because NSF approved fewer climate-related grants, while researchers self-censoring also appears to play a role, Grist said, evidenced by a corresponding rise in the substitute term "extreme weather."** The same analysis found "DEI" mentions had vanished from NSF grants entirely, with "clean energy" and "pollution" also declining, though less sharply than "climate change"; Government Executive republished the Grist article on March 31, 2026. Ethan Roberts, union president at USDA's National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research, told Grist that after the ARS memo his union concluded the best course was to avoid the banned terms and work around them, with "climate change" swapped for softer synonyms across the agency; Trent Ford, Illinois's state climatologist, said he now frames grant proposals around terms like "weather extremes" and uses "climate change" only when absolutely necessary. A broader, separately tracked mechanism -- an OMB proposed rule published May 29, 2026 that would give political appointees authority over individual federal grant decisions -- could turn this self-censorship pattern into direct political control of funding. American Meteorological Society executive director Amanda Staudt warned that the rule's bar on federal-fund recipients' "issue advocacy or public messaging" that promotes a particular policy could give weather professionals pause before warning the public about an oncoming hurricane or heat wave, especially given the politicization of climate change. That rule's status is tracked in this database's separate white-house-200b-research-funding-overhaul-2026 entry.

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration
primary_proponent.role: Directed the cross-agency effort to remove climate-related language and funding eligibility
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing this cross-agency language and funding policy; it is documented as a coordinated, government-wide pattern rather than one agency's isolated decision, distinct from (though related to) the agency-specific climate-research funding cuts documented in this database's separate NOAA entry. The USDA ARS banned-term memo itself was sent by Sharon Strickland, an ARS Northeast Area administrator, who wrote that the review would ensure compliance with the administration's executive orders.

estimated_impact.summary: Research on climate change is being dropped, retitled or disguised to stay fundable, and a USDA research memo barred agreements using terms such as 'clean water,' 'safe drinking water' and 'microplastics.' Lawmakers warned the USDA list would undercut research that rural communities rely on for wildfires, drought and food insecurity. The measurable result so far is a sharp fall in federally funded work that names climate change.

title: CMS Rescinded Guidance That Encouraged States to Use Medicaid Funds for Housing, Food, and Other Health-Related Social Needs
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
status: Rescission in effect since March 4, 2025. States' existing approved Section 1115 waivers are not immediately eliminated, but face uncertain odds at renewal; new waiver applications are now evaluated case-by-case without the prior encouraging framework, which multiple outlets reported will likely make them harder to obtain.
what_changed: On March 4, 2025, CMS issued an informational bulletin rescinding Biden-era guidance -- a November 2023 bulletin, a December 2024 bulletin, and an accompanying 2023 Health-Related Social Needs (HRSN) coverage framework -- that had outlined and encouraged states' use of Medicaid Section 1115 demonstration waivers to cover housing assistance, nutrition supports, and other non-traditional "health-related social needs." CMS spokesperson Catherine Howden said the prior guidance "distracted the Medicaid program from its core mission: providing excellent health outcomes," and that ending it would prevent "draining of resources" from services CMS characterized as duplicative of other federal programs such as SNAP and HUD housing vouchers. North Carolina pioneered the HRSN waiver model during Trump's first term, using Medicaid funds to cover security deposits, first month's rent, transportation to medical appointments, wheelchair ramps, and fresh-produce prescriptions; at least 24 additional states had gone on to launch similar programs, with California's CalAIM program (launched 2022) the largest, committing $12 billion over five years and generating approximately 577,000 referrals for benefits, and Oregon's program covering home-delivered meals, rental assistance, and climate-control devices. As of the March 2025 rescission, 18 states had CMS-approved Section 1115 waivers specifically addressing HRSN. CMS's new policy does not immediately terminate those 18 states' existing approved waivers, but reporting at the time noted they could face challenges at renewal, while new state applications are now considered on a rolling, case-by-case basis without reference to the rescinded framework -- **a standard multiple outlets reported will likely make approval harder to obtain going forward**.

title: Trump Unilaterally Withdrew From the Biden-Era Columbia Basin Salmon Agreement With Northwest Tribes, Reviving Two Decades of Dam Litigation
institution: Multiple federal agencies (via White House memorandum) -- Army Corps of Engineers, Bonneville Power Administration, Bureau of Reclamation
status: Withdrawn -- litigation the agreement had paused for over 20 years was reactivated
what_changed: On June 12, 2025, the Trump administration issued a memorandum directing federal agencies to withdraw from the Resilient Columbia Basin Agreement (RCBA), a 2023 Biden-era agreement with the four lower Columbia River treaty tribes (Nez Perce, Yakama, Umatilla, and Warm Springs), the states of Washington and Oregon, and environmental groups including Sierra Club and Columbia Riverkeeper. The RCBA had committed more than $1 billion toward salmon and steelhead restoration and clean-energy investment in the Columbia and Snake River basins, and critically, had paused decades of litigation over federal dam operations that harm fish migration -- litigation in which courts had repeatedly ruled against the federal government's hydropower management, ordering it to spill more water through dam floodgates to protect fish rather than maximize electricity generation. **By unilaterally withdrawing, the administration reactivated that paused litigation, reopening a legal fight the government had been losing for more than 20 years.** The administration's public framing characterized the underlying dam-breaching debate as driven by climate-change ideology rather than legitimate ecological or treaty concerns. Tribes and environmental groups condemned the withdrawal as a broken federal promise and a betrayal of treaty obligations.

title: Commerce's Export-License Bureau Hit Its Worst Backlog in 30+ Years, Costing Nvidia $8B in a Single Quarter
institution: Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security
status: Reported ongoing as of August 2025; Nvidia subsequently reported receiving some H20 export licenses in mid-August 2025, though the broader backlog's resolution status for other applicants was not confirmed in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-08 (Reuters investigation published; backlog and understaffing conditions accumulated over the preceding months)
what_changed: Reuters reported August 1, 2025 that thousands of export-license applications were stalled at the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) -- described by officials as the worst such backlog in more than three decades -- leaving billions of dollars' worth of goods and technology in limbo. Sources said the bureau under Secretary Howard Lutnick had failed to issue expected new export-control rules, stifled routine communication with industry representatives seeking guidance, pushed out experienced career experts, and lost additional staff to buyouts and resignations, including DOGE-driven cuts that left vacancies in China-focused export-control offices. **The highest-profile example was Nvidia, whose stalled licenses to ship AI chips to China were part of curbs the company said would cut roughly $8 billion from its July-quarter sales**; the backlog was not limited to China-related technology, however -- Reuters cited Compliance Assurance, a Florida-based company, reporting delayed license approvals for sensors, radar, and sonar equipment destined for Latin America, unrelated to any China-specific policy dispute. This dysfunction followed the administration's February 21, 2025 removal of Matthew Borman, the bureau's principal deputy assistant secretary for export administration and a career official with direct responsibility for enforcing China-related export controls (documented separately in this database's commerce-china-export-official-forced-out-2025.json), which this entry's sourcing connects as a contributing loss of institutional expertise ahead of the backlog reported six months later. Nvidia subsequently reported in mid-August 2025 that it had begun receiving some H20 chip export licenses, though the broader bureau-wide backlog's resolution for other applicants, including the Latin America-bound equipment cited by Reuters, was not confirmed in sourcing reviewed as of this entry's last-verified date.

title: Commerce Pushed Out the Executive Director of Its China Tech-Threat Office Days Before Moving to Approve Nvidia AI Chip Sales to China
institution: U.S. Department of Commerce, Office of Information and Communications Technology and Services (OICTS)
status: Ongoing -- leadership vacancy at OICTS as of this writing; Senators Warner and Warren's Feb. 12, 2026 letter to Secretary Lutnick set a March 4, 2026 response deadline
date_of_action: 2026-02 (Cannon's ouster and deputy's administrative leave, reported early Feb. 2026)
what_changed: The Wall Street Journal reported that **senior Trump administration officials pushed out Elizabeth Cannon, executive director of the Commerce Department's Office of Information and Communications Technology and Services (OICTS, created in 2022), along with an unnamed deputy who was separately placed on administrative leave. OICTS investigates and can restrict or ban foreign-linked technologies -- particularly from China and Russia -- that pose espionage or critical-infrastructure risks**; the office and its staff were integral to a 2025 rule widely restricting the import and sale of internet-connected passenger vehicles and related hardware/software with China/Russia links. The departures came as the administration moved closer to approving Nvidia H200 AI chip sales to China and amid a broader retreat from export-control enforcement during ongoing US-China trade talks -- a sequencing WSJ's sourcing connected directly to the ouster. This entry is a companion to commerce-china-export-official-forced-out-2025.json, which documents a separate February 2025 ouster (export-licensing official Matthew Borman, roughly one year earlier) -- together the two entries show a sustained, year-long pattern of Commerce pushing out career China-tech-security personnel across different offices (export licensing vs. supply-chain/ICTS investigations) rather than a single isolated departure. Sens. Mark Warner and Elizabeth Warren sent a February 12, 2026 letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick demanding to know who ordered the dismissals, who currently leads OICTS, and whether any investigations or rulemakings (including on connected trucks/buses and Chinese-made drones) were delayed as a result, writing that 'diminishing OICTS, and now pushing out its leadership, sends a clear signal that truly standing up to China is not a priority of this Administration.' The senators set a March 4, 2026 response deadline.

title: Commerce Voided a $7.4 Billion CHIPS Act Grant to the Semiconductor R&D Nonprofit Natcast, Canceling Two of Three Planned Facilities
institution: U.S. Department of Commerce / National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) -- National Semiconductor Technology Center (NSTC)
status: NIST assumed direct operational control of NSTC as of August 25, 2025. Two of the program's three planned facilities -- a Design and Collaboration Facility in California and an Advanced Packaging Piloting Facility in Arizona -- will not move forward; work continues on the Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) Accelerator facility, for which up to $825 million had already been committed. No litigation or reversal identified as of this entry's sourcing.
date_of_action: 2025-08-25 (Commerce Department announcement voiding Natcast's grant agreement and transferring NSTC operations to NIST)
what_changed: Natcast was a nonprofit created in 2023 under the CHIPS and Science Act to operate the National Semiconductor Technology Center (NSTC), a public-private semiconductor R&D consortium. In January 2025, days before Trump's inauguration, the outgoing Biden administration finalized an agreement granting Natcast up to $7.4 billion in federal funding to run NSTC over the following decade. **On August 25, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced Commerce had determined Natcast was unlawfully established -- the department's Office of General Counsel found its creation violated the Government Corporation Control Act, which requires explicit congressional authorization to establish a government-backed corporation -- and voided the $7.4 billion grant agreement as a result.** Lutnick publicly called Natcast a 'semiconductor slush fund' for Biden administration allies and said the arrangement lacked adequate transparency and statutory compliance. NIST assumed direct operational control of NSTC in Natcast's place, with Commerce saying NSTC's operations would be reformed to align with statutory requirements and increase transparency. Of NSTC's three originally planned facilities, only the Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) Accelerator facility -- for which up to $825 million had already been committed to stand it up -- continues; a Design and Collaboration Facility planned for California and an Advanced Packaging Piloting Facility planned for Arizona will not move forward. A subsequent Harvard Kennedy School analysis warned, as an interpretive assessment rather than a confirmed outcome, that the resulting uncertainty and asset liquidation ('fire sale') risk driving semiconductor research talent and intellectual property toward foreign competitors -- citing UK and EU universities already recruiting displaced researchers and PhD students, and noting China's history of acquiring semiconductor IP both legally and illegally -- though no source reviewed confirms this brain-drain effect has concretely occurred as of this entry's sourcing.

title: Community Health Centers Serving 32-34 Million Patients Faced a Grant Freeze, a Lapsed Federal Fund, and OBBBA Medicaid Cuts All at Once
institution: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA); federally qualified community health centers nationwide
status: Ongoing -- Community Health Center Fund runs only through Dec. 31, 2026 (Feb. 3, 2026 appropriations act); discretionary health-center funding rides a stopgap to Dec. 11, 2026; no multi-year reauthorization; OBBBA Medicaid-revenue pressure continues
date_of_action: 2025-01 (grant freeze first delays health-center payments) through 2026-02 (short-term Community Health Center Fund extension)
what_changed: Community health centers -- federally qualified clinics serving roughly 32-34 million patients nationally, 90% of them at or below 200% of the federal poverty level -- faced four compounding federal funding and administrative threats across 2025-2026. First, beginning in late January 2025, after an administration memo froze federal grant funding (the memo was rescinded and the freeze blocked by federal judges), health centers in at least 10 states were at least temporarily unable to draw down already-approved grant money, and a Richmond, Virginia center temporarily closed three of its sites, PBS News reported in early February 2025. The same freeze plunged Medicaid and other funds into chaos, Mother Jones reported, and advocates warned that proposed Medicaid cuts could force closures or service reductions; centers received $4.4 billion in federal grants in early 2024 (versus the $5.8 billion a year advocates say is needed) plus Medicaid, which made up 43% of the $46.7 billion in 2023 health-center revenue nationally. Second, HRSA itself -- the $12-billion-a-year HHS agency that administers this and other grant programs to clinics, rural hospitals, and workforce initiatives -- lost about a quarter of its roughly 2,700-person workforce between February and early July 2025, per a KFF Health News analysis of the HHS staff directory, including analysts, auditors, grant managers, and nursing consultants. The losses included a firing of about 7% of HRSA staff on February 14, 2025 and the HHS reduction in force announced March 27, 2025 under the DOGE workforce order; an April 2025 letter from Democratic senators said DOGE had reportedly fired 40% of HRSA's Bureau of Primary Health Care, the office that oversees the Health Center Program. Virginia's health-center association told KFF Health News that HRSA grants had been harder to obtain since February 2025, with clinics now required to file itemized spending lists after grants were approved. Third, the Community Health Center Fund -- which provides about 70% of centers' federal funding -- was extended in March 2025 only to September 30, 2025, and then lapsed when Congress failed to pass renewal legislation before the government shutdown began; a temporary extension to January 30, 2026 was included in the continuing resolution that ended the 43-day shutdown in November 2025, and a further extension through December 31, 2026 ($4.6 billion for fiscal 2026, a modest increase, plus about $1.16 billion for October-December 2026) came via the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, signed February 3, 2026 -- short-term stopgaps rather than the multi-year reauthorization advocates had sought. Fourth, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's Medicaid provisions layered a projected $32 billion five-year revenue loss onto the sector, per a Commonwealth Fund estimate that also projects 5.6 million health-center patients will lose Medicaid coverage over the next decade as states enact work requirements, compounding the funding and staffing uncertainty. Trump's proposed FY2026 budget separately called for eliminating HRSA entirely, along with specific programs including rural hospital grants, workforce training, Ryan White HIV/AIDS programs, and emergency medical services for children. The National Association of Community Health Centers warned in May 2025 that one in four centers may close or reduce services over the next two years without increased funding, and **concrete harm followed: in October 2025 Ammonoosuc Community Health Services closed its Franconia, New Hampshire site, whose roughly 1,400 patients, almost half of them older, must now drive at least 10 miles for care, with officials blaming Medicaid cuts.** Beyond health centers, Virginia's Augusta Medical Group closed three rural clinics in September 2025 as part of what it called its "ongoing response to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act," and in early 2026 Iowa hospital system MercyOne closed an Ottumwa clinic and laid off 67 workers at its Des Moines medical center, moves CNN reported the providers tied in part to the law. Health centers also rely on a separate discretionary Section 330 appropriation, about 30% of their federal funding, that was set to expire September 30, 2026. A stopgap signed September 2, 2026 (the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027) carries it at largely fiscal 2026 levels only to December 11, 2026, and does not touch the Community Health Center Fund, which still expires December 31, 2026 -- two cliffs twenty days apart, both in the post-election lame-duck session, with no multi-year reauthorization enacted.

primary_proponent.role: The administration implemented the funding freeze/delays; Congress's failure to pass timely Community Health Center Fund reauthorization and its OBBBA Medicaid cuts drove the funding gap
primary_proponent.note: No single named official was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally directing the grant-payment delays; the Community Health Center Fund lapse and OBBBA cuts are legislative/administrative in origin rather than tied to one individual's decision.

estimated_impact.summary: A primary-care safety net for 32.7 million mostly low-income patients is losing capacity: at least one health-center site has closed (a Franconia, N.H. clinic whose ~1,400 patients, many elderly, now travel 10+ miles), the Commonwealth Fund projects 5.6 million health-center patients will lose Medicaid over the next decade, and the national association warns one in four centers may close or cut services. Financially, OBBBA is projected to cost centers $32 billion over five years, while the fund that supplies ~70% of their federal funding has been renewed only in short stopgaps and now expires Dec. 31, 2026, and HRSA, the agency that awards those grants, lost about a quarter of its staff.

title: Trump Fires Librarian of Congress and Register of Copyrights; Appeals Court Orders Reinstatement Amid Unsigned-Certificate Chaos
institution: Library of Congress / U.S. Copyright Office
status: Ongoing -- Perlmutter reinstated pending appeal since Sept. 10, 2025; Supreme Court deferred ruling on the administration's stay application as of Nov. 2025
date_of_action: 2025-05-08 (Hayden fired) through 2025-05-10 (Perlmutter fired); litigation ongoing into 2026
what_changed: On the evening of May 8, 2025, Deputy Director of Presidential Personnel Trent Morse emailed Dr. Carla Hayden, the first woman and first African American Librarian of Congress, a two-sentence notice terminating her effective immediately (CBS News, Library Journal, May 2025). Hayden had been targeted since February 2025 by the American Accountability Foundation's 'DEI Watch List,' which also named Register of Copyrights Shira Perlmutter (NPR, June 2025). Trump then named Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche acting Librarian of Congress; on May 10, Blanche executed the removal of Perlmutter and sought to install Paul Perkins, an Associate Deputy Attorney General, as Acting Register of Copyrights, with Brian Nieves as acting deputy librarian (Publishers Weekly, May 2025). **On May 12, Perkins and Nieves went to the Library of Congress carrying a White House letter asserting their new roles, but Library General Counsel Meg Williams and staff denied them building-badge access to the Copyright Office; staff called U.S. Capitol Police, and the two officials left voluntarily after being asked to** (The Daily Beast, Publishers Weekly, May 2025) -- a more concrete confrontation than some contemporaneous coverage's looser framing that the replacements simply 'never showed up to work.' Perlmutter sued in Perlmutter v. Blanche (filed May 22, 2025), arguing the President has no authority to remove the Register directly and that Blanche, himself installed without the Librarian-appointment process the statute requires, had no authority to remove her either (Authors Alliance, NPR, May 2025). With no Senate-unaffected Register in place, the Copyright Office continued issuing registration certificates but without the Register's signature, prompting law-firm client alerts warning of downstream validity questions for registrants relying on those certificates in infringement litigation (Venable LLP, Copyright Lately, June 2025); the vacancy also left the office's pending AI-related policy guidance -- including its copyright-and-AI report released just before Perlmutter's firing -- without a confirmed Register to see it through (Wired, Deadline, May-June 2025). A district court initially declined to block the removal (IPWatchdog, July 2025), but on September 10, 2025 the D.C. Circuit granted Perlmutter an injunction pending appeal, reinstating her as Register while the case proceeds on the merits (NISO, Patently-O, Roll Call, September 2025). The administration asked the Supreme Court to stay that reinstatement; in November 2025 the Court declined to act on the request, holding it alongside similar administration removal-power fights over an FTC commissioner and a Federal Reserve governor rather than ruling on Perlmutter's case on its own timeline (SCOTUSblog, November 2025).

primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Directed both firings by email through aide Trent Morse, then named Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche acting Librarian of Congress; Blanche in turn executed Perlmutter's removal and attempted to install Paul Perkins as Acting Register of Copyrights.

estimated_impact.summary: Two senior Library of Congress officials -- the Librarian of Congress and the Register of Copyrights -- were removed without the statutory process their removal requires, leaving the Copyright Office issuing unsigned registration certificates for roughly four months and its pending AI-copyright policy work without confirmed leadership, until a federal appeals court ordered the Register reinstated pending a still-unresolved legal fight over the President's removal authority.

The scope of actual harm from unsigned certificates (e.g. how many registrants have faced litigation complications) was not quantified in the sourcing reviewed.

Circuit's reinstatement order -- corroborated across CBS News, NPR, Library Journal, The Daily Beast, Publishers Weekly, Authors Alliance, NISO, and Patently-O. MODERATE confidence on the unsigned-certificate legal-risk framing, sourced mainly to law-firm client alerts (Venable, Copyright Lately) rather than independent news reporting -- real but a narrower professional-audience concern than the headline firings. Note: initial reporting (Wired) described the replacement officials as 'loyalists who never showed up to work'; independent verification found a more specific and better-documented event -- Perkins and Nieves did show up on May 12, 2025 but were denied badge access and left after Library staff called Capitol Police -- which this entry uses instead of the vaguer original framing. As of this writing (Sept. 2026 index period) the Supreme Court has not ruled on the administration's stay application; the underlying removal-authority question remains unresolved.

section_summaries.what_changed: Trump fired Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden and Register of Copyrights Shira Perlmutter in May 2025; his attempted replacements were physically denied access to the Copyright Office, Perlmutter sued, and a federal appeals court ordered her reinstated in September 2025 pending an unresolved legal fight over presidential removal authority.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: The Copyright Office issued registration certificates without a signed Register for roughly four months, and its AI-copyright policy work went without confirmed leadership during the vacancy; no dollar or health figure applies to this institutional-independence story.

title: Congress Rescinded $1.1B From Public Broadcasting; CPB Dissolved After 58 Years
institution: Corporation for Public Broadcasting (CPB)
status: Complete: CPB's board voted December 10, 2025 to dissolve (announced January 5, 2026) after Congress rescinded its $1.1B through FY2027; related lawsuits were dismissed in January and February 2026. Congress gave FEMA's NGWS $48M for FY2026 but no money to CPB.
date_of_action: 2025-04 (Trump moves to fire board members) through 2026-01-05 (CPB announces board's December 2025 vote to dissolve)
what_changed: In March 2025, CPB sued FEMA in federal court, alleging the Trump administration was withholding reimbursement funding CPB needed to pay back public media stations for equipment investments already made under the Next Generation Warning System (NGWS) grant program -- a FEMA program Congress created in 2022, and funded with $136 million between 2022 and 2024, to help rural, tribal, and other underserved public media stations replace and upgrade their emergency-alert equipment, administered by CPB under a FEMA contract. A federal judge denied CPB's request for a temporary restraining order; FEMA released its hold on the funds in April 2025, but cut the funding off again in May. In April 2025, Trump moved to fire three members of CPB's board of directors (Laura Ross, Tom Rothman, and Diane Kaplan); CPB and the directors sued, arguing the dismissal was governmental overreach targeting an entity whose congressional charter guarantees its independence from political control. On June 8, 2025, U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss denied a preliminary injunction but wrote that Congress intended to bar the President from directing or controlling the corporation, and CPB affirmed that the three remained directors under bylaws it had amended in May; in July the administration filed its own suit to oust them. In July 2025, Congress passed a $9 billion rescissions package (canceling previously appropriated funds) requested by the White House, including $1.1 billion earmarked for CPB through fiscal year 2027 -- which CPB's Patricia Harrison called the first time in nearly 60 years Congress had refused to fund CPB. The House vote was 216-213, with all but two Republicans (Brian Fitzpatrick and Mike Turner) in favor; in the Senate, only Republicans Susan Collins (R-ME) and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) broke with their party to vote against the package. After both chambers passed the bill, Trump wrote on Truth Social: 'REPUBLICANS HAVE TRIED DOING THIS FOR 40 YEARS, AND FAILED....BUT NO MORE.' Trump signed it into law, and on July 31, 2025, the Senate Appropriations Committee declined to restore any CPB funding for the following budget year. CPB announced August 1, 2025 that it would begin winding down, eliminating most staff positions by the September 30 fiscal year-end and retaining a small transition team through January 2026 to handle compliance and music-rights obligations. The same day, Rothman left the board and moved to dismiss his claims; Ross had resigned in July. NPR reported (Aug. 28, 2025) that the NGWS reimbursement delays and stop-work orders were compounding the effect of CPB's own defunding and wind-down: rural broadcasters that had already been awarded NGWS funding were still waiting to be reimbursed for equipment upgrades, even as CPB -- the program's administering entity -- itself faced dissolution; the Office of Management and Budget told NPR the program would continue, and FEMA posted a new $40 million funding announcement that same August inviting states and tribes to apply, but station executives said the delays and CPB's own uncertain future **left completed and in-progress emergency-alert upgrades in limbo**. Reps. Nanette Barragán, Robert Menendez, and April McClain Delaney led a September 9, 2025 letter, signed by 59 House Democrats in all, urging FEMA to take over disbursing the NGWS funds and brief Congress on a plan within 14 days. PBS itself -- a distinct entity from CPB -- announced on September 4, 2025 that it was cutting approximately 15% of its own staff, more than 100 positions including 34 immediate layoffs, as PBS CEO Paula Kerger said the system was taking a 21% hit in revenues from the loss of federal funding; NPR CEO Katherine Maher separately said on CBS's Late Show that an estimated 70 to 80 of NPR's 246 member stations could have to shut down. By the September 30 fiscal year-end, CPB decided to distribute its final $7.1 million across its TV and radio stations, and one of its final acts was awarding up to $57.9 million to a new nonprofit to handle interconnection between stations, a role NPR had long controlled. NPR sued; a federal judge declined a restraining order but later had CPB set aside $36 million pending trial, and in November 2025 NPR and CPB settled, with CPB funding NPR's Public Radio Satellite System with nearly $36 million over five years and the new nonprofit, Public Media Infrastructure, receiving $47 million. On December 10, 2025, CPB's board voted unanimously to dissolve the organization entirely rather than continue to exist in a defunded, vulnerable state, and CPB announced the decision on January 5, 2026; CPB President and CEO Patricia Harrison said its final act would be 'to protect the integrity of the public media system' by dissolving. Director Diane Kaplan had resigned from the board effective January 4, 2026. On January 14, 2026, Judge Moss dismissed both board-removal lawsuits as moot. FEMA, which by then had taken over the NGWS program, reimbursed CPB for all expenses it sought under the grant (some stations were reimbursed for costs incurred before their grants were frozen), and CPB and FEMA stipulated to dismiss the NGWS lawsuit in late February 2026. Congress's fiscal 2026 Labor-HHS appropriation (Public Law 119-75, enacted February 3, 2026) included no money for CPB, while a separate Homeland Security law (Public Law 119-86, enacted April 30, 2026) appropriated $48 million for the Next Generation Warning System.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Personally pushed the rescission package and has called CPB a 'monstrosity' and has long said public broadcasting -- particularly NPR -- displays an extreme liberal bias. OMB Director Russell Vought, who requested the rescissions package on the administration's behalf, told reporters afterward the administration would 'likely' send additional rescissions packages, saying 'there is still a great enthusiasm for these rescissions bills, because Congress wants to be a part of voting for these cuts and making them permanent.'

estimated_impact.summary: CPB funded more than 1,500 local public radio and TV stations; roughly 70% of its money went directly to 330 PBS and 246 NPR member stations. The heaviest human cost falls on rural, tribal and remote communities, where public stations are often the only reliable source of emergency alerts: rescission-driven wind-down plus FEMA's freezes stalled or killed Next Generation Warning System upgrades (backup generators, transmitters), and as of August 2025 CPB said about $96 million appropriated for FY2023-24 would go undistributed unless FEMA took over. Stations in remote areas also lost the largest shares of their budgets (KSTK in Wrangell, Alaska lost more than half its annual revenue) and could not replace the money. Financially, PBS cut about 15% of its jobs, NPR's CEO estimated 70 to 80 of NPR's 246 member stations could have to shut down, and stations from Seattle (KCTS) to Charlotte (WFAE) to State College, Pennsylvania (WPSU, weighing closing its radio station) cut journalism, facilities or programs, while local shows such as 'South Dakota Focus' were cancelled. NPR's CEO has estimated about 96% of U.S. classical music broadcasting airs on public radio. Sen. Susan Collins, who voted against the cut while criticizing NPR's bias, cited Maine's emergency alert network and local high school coverage as what the money supported.

estimated_impact.caveat: There is no single estimate of total harm; figures are from CPB, PBS, NPR and news reporting, and station-closure numbers are NPR leadership's projection, not a count of closures. The entry does not document deaths or injuries from missed alerts; the emergency-alert harm is lost resilience in areas with poor cell and broadband service. FEMA later reimbursed CPB for expenses it sought and some stations for costs already incurred, but what became of the rest of the FY2023-24 NGWS money is not established here; FEMA now runs NGWS, and Congress appropriated $48 million more for it for FY2026 (P.L. 119-86), while the FY2026 Labor-HHS law (P.L. 119-75) restored no CPB funding. Donations offset losses at some larger stations, not remote ones. The policy dispute is contested: Sens. Collins and Murkowski backed bias concerns about NPR while opposing the scale of the cut.

confidence_note: Extremely well-documented: a formal recorded congressional vote (not just an executive action), consistent figures across NPR, NBC News, CNN, AP (via PBS News), and Time, and specific named station-level impacts rather than general claims. The court history (board-removal suits, the NGWS suit against FEMA) is confirmed by Current's docket-based reporting and the CourtListener docket. PBS's September 2025 layoffs rest on NPR's reporting; the GPB, OPB and WYPR versions are syndicated copies of that story, not independent corroboration. The NGWS reimbursement-delay details come from NPR's national desk and an AP story (run by KJZZ) that reached them separately. An April 2025 draft-budget proposal to eliminate CPB funding is tracked in its own entry as an antecedent of this rescission.

section_summaries.estimated_impact: Rural stations lost the federal money they relied on most, and emergency-alert upgrades stalled; stations cut jobs and local shows, and NPR's CEO warned 70-80 member stations could close.

title: CPSC's Three Democratic Commissioners Fired, Battery-Safety Rule Delayed a Year, Seats Refilled Only With Administration Picks
institution: Consumer Product Safety Commission
status: Complete: on a joint motion by both sides after Trump v. Slaughter, the Fourth Circuit reversed the commissioners' reinstatement in September 2026; the commission regained a quorum August 7, 2026 with two Trump nominees, so all three sitting members are administration-aligned, with two seats vacant
date_of_action: 2025-05-08 (firings) through 2026-09-22 (Fourth Circuit reversal)
what_changed: On May 8, 2025, President Trump fired three of the CPSC's five commissioners -- Alexander Hoehn-Saric, Mary Boyle, and Richard Trumka Jr., all Biden appointees -- citing 'neglect of duty or malfeasance in office' without further detail, hours after the three had voted to block DOGE representatives from entering CPSC headquarters to fire staff employees. The CPSC's founding statute allows removal only for 'neglect of duty or malfeasance in office' and requires no more than three of five commissioners share a political party, structural protections designed to preserve a bipartisan agency that regulates the safety of thousands of consumer products. The fired commissioners sued; a federal judge in Maryland ruled the firings unlawful and ordered reinstatement, and the Fourth Circuit declined to stay that order, but the Supreme Court granted an emergency stay on July 23, 2025, allowing the firings to proceed while the appeal continued. During the roughly five weeks the three commissioners were absent, the two remaining Republican-aligned commissioners -- Acting Chairman Peter Feldman and Douglas Dziak -- withdrew a previously approved (3-2 vote) **e-bike and lithium-ion battery safety testing standard** from public comment; lithium-ion battery fires from e-bikes and similar devices have been a rising home-fire and fatality concern nationally. The same two commissioners released a CPSC FY2026 budget request proposing to cut the agency's funding and staffing and to transfer CPSC's functions to the Department of Health and Human Services, led by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court's ruling in Trump v. Slaughter -- which held FTC commissioners' for-cause removal protections unconstitutional -- prompted CPSC Acting Chairman Feldman to state publicly that the fired commissioners' 'claims should now fail as a matter of law.' On September 22, 2026, at the joint request of the administration and the fired commissioners, the Fourth Circuit reversed the district court's reinstatement ruling in light of Slaughter and sent the case back to the district court. In the meantime the commission had shrunk further: Commissioner Dziak resigned in August 2025, leaving Feldman as the sole commissioner, running the agency under delegations of authority that he and Dziak approved before Dziak left, until the Senate confirmed two Trump nominees, Karen Sessions and Brien Lorenze, on a 51-47 vote on August 7, 2026, restoring a three-member quorum with two seats still vacant. The lithium-ion battery standard was finally published as a proposed rule on June 24, 2026; Covington & Burling wrote that the administration's review had delayed public comment 'for the better part of a year' without substantive changes to the rule.

estimated_impact.summary: A statutorily bipartisan, five-member consumer-safety commission ran as a two-member, single-party body after the May 2025 firings and then, from August 2025 until August 2026, as a one-commissioner agency acting under delegated authority, while a pending battery-fire safety standard was held back for about a year and a budget proposal to shrink and fold the agency into HHS was released. Its restored quorum is made up entirely of administration-aligned members.

Slaughter decision confirms 'officials who exercise executive power are accountable to the President' and that the prior for-cause removal protections were themselves unconstitutional -- i.e., that the firings were lawful all along, not merely permitted going forward. The e-bike/lithium-battery standard was not abandoned: after its withdrawal from public comment and interagency review it was published as a proposed rule on June 24, 2026 (written comments closed August 24, 2026; an oral-comment hearing is set for October 21, 2026), so the harm is a delay of about a year rather than a reversal of CPSC safety findings. Consumer-safety groups (Consumer Federation of America, National Consumers League, Public Citizen, which represented the fired commissioners) and the fired commissioners themselves argue the firings undermine the bipartisan design Congress built into the agency; the HHS-transfer budget proposal has seen no visible congressional movement as of mid-2026 per Covington & Burling's analysis, so its practical effect remains prospective rather than realized.

title: CVE Vulnerability-Tracking Program Nearly Shut Down When CISA Let Its MITRE Contract Lapse
institution: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Averted -- 11-month contract extension executed April 16, 2025, through March 16, 2026; CVE board told in January 2026 there would be no funding cliff at that deadline, and a more durable arrangement has since replaced the stopgap, though the underlying contract's terms remain undisclosed even to CVE board members
date_of_action: 2025-04-15 (MITRE warning letter) through 2025-04-16 (CISA contract extension)
what_changed: MITRE, the nonprofit that has run the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) program -- the foundational database used worldwide to catalog and cross-reference software security flaws -- and the related Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) program under contract with CISA since 2018, disclosed on April 15, 2025 that the government did not plan to renew its contract, set to expire the next day. Yosry Barsoum, MITRE vice president and director of its Center for Securing the Homeland, warned in a letter to the CVE board that a lapse would cause 'multiple impacts to CVE, including deterioration of national vulnerability databases and advisories, tool vendors, incident response operations, and all manner of critical infrastructure.' The warning came less than a month after MITRE had marked the CVE program's 25th anniversary. On April 16, 2025, with hours to spare, a CISA spokesperson announced the agency had exercised the contract's option period to 'ensure there will be no lapse in critical CVE services,' extending **the $57.8 million agreement for 11 months, through March 16, 2026**. Barsoum said on LinkedIn that CISA had 'identified incremental funding to keep the programs operational.' The near-lapse triggered the founding of the independent CVE Foundation, formed to explore alternative governance models less dependent on a single, opaque federal contract. The CVE board was told at its January 21, 2026 meeting there would be 'no funding cliff in March,' and reporting since indicates the stopgap has been replaced by a more durable funding arrangement -- though a source close to the program described the underlying contract as still 'a mystery contract with a mystery number,' opaque even to CVE board members.

status: Ongoing -- disputed between DoD implementation and a congressional reversal effort

what_changed: Starting in early 2025, the Defense Health Agency began a facility-by-facility review of military treatment facilities (MTFs) across the U.S. military medical system to determine whether each should be closed or downgraded from a full hospital to a clinic. title: DHS Tied Counterterrorism/Homeland-Security Grants to Immigration-Enforcement Cooperation; Courts Blocked It Twice, DHS Kept Trying
institution: U.S. Department of Homeland Security (FEMA Homeland Security Grant Program / State Homeland Security Program)
status: Ongoing litigation -- a federal judge ruled against DHS in September 2025, and again after DHS disabled states' ability to formally accept their already-approved grant awards; DHS then imposed new population-estimate and shortened-spending-deadline conditions on all states. A coalition of 26 states plus two governors filed a further suit July 23, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island, challenging both the immigration-cooperation condition and new voter-data-sharing/election-practice conditions.
date_of_action: 2025 (conditions first imposed) through 2026-07-23 (latest multi-state suit filed)
what_changed: **DHS's FEMA-administered Homeland Security Grant Program -- post-9/11 funding used by states for items like bomb detectors, security-analyst salaries, and emergency-preparedness capacity -- was conditioned on states cooperating with the administration's immigration-enforcement crackdown**. Oregon and 19 other states (a coalition including California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Washington, Wisconsin, and Vermont) sued, arguing DHS was holding emergency-preparedness funding hostage in violation of the Constitution and the Administrative Procedure Act. A federal judge ruled in September 2025 that DHS could not attach immigration-cooperation strings to the grants. After that ruling, Oregon officials found the button to formally accept their already-approved award had been disabled on the federal grant website; states went back to court and won again, treating the disabled button as a defiance of the original order. Nearly $18 million was at stake for Oregon alone in the 2025 round; Portland had received an average of $5 million a year in homeland security grants over the prior two decades. DHS subsequently imposed two new conditions applying to all states regardless of the immigration dispute: states must estimate their populations net of people who had been deported, and the spending deadline for awarded funds was cut from three years to ten months. Separately, in September 2025, Trump ordered National Guard troops deployed to Portland, citing 'violent radical left terrorism' -- a characterization the city disputed -- adding a second front to the same underlying dispute over whether Oregon and similarly-positioned jurisdictions would be treated as partners or adversaries in federal counterterrorism/homeland-security funding. The dispute escalated further in 2026: on July 23, 2026, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield led a coalition of 26 states plus the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania in a new suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island, challenging DHS grant conditions requiring states to assist with federal immigration enforcement, alter election practices, and provide DHS with personal information on registered voters, as well as challenging FEMA's asserted authority to cancel grants at any time -- again on Administrative Procedure Act and Spending Clause grounds. Oregon alone receives roughly $10 million annually through the Homeland Security Grant Program; the 2026 suit put the nationwide funding at issue above $1 billion. Rayfield's office noted it had already won two similar cases in Rhode Island federal court in 2025.

primary_proponent.name: Kristi Noem
primary_proponent.role: DHS Secretary (through March 31, 2026)
primary_proponent.note: DHS, under Noem's leadership during the period these conditions were first imposed and initially litigated (2025), tied Homeland Security Grant Program funding to state cooperation with federal immigration enforcement; no more specific named individual within DHS was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally authoring the specific conditions. Noem left DHS in March 2026 (see doj-dhs-public-safety-grant-cancellations-2025.json for her successor's confirmation); no reporting reviewed here confirms whether the department's position changed under her successor, Markwayne Mullin, ahead of the July 2026 suit.

estimated_impact.summary: Direct dollar figures are well-documented (Oregon-specific and nationwide), but the litigation remains unresolved as of this entry's last verification, so no final dollar amount has been definitively withheld or restored long-term -- this documents an ongoing coercion/conditioning dispute over emergency-preparedness and counterterrorism funding, not a finalized cut.

title: DHS Halved Its Office of Intelligence and Analysis Workforce Through Buyouts After Public Backlash Blocked a Direct 73% Cut
institution: Department of Homeland Security, Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A)
status: Ongoing as of this entry -- the second deferred resignation round's September 14, 2025 deadline has passed, with approved participants receiving pay through early December 2025; I&A's overall headcount reduction (roughly halved since January 2025) was reported as effectively achieved through voluntary means despite the direct-layoff plan's earlier withdrawal.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (73%-cut plan proposed, then halted within days after backlash) through 2025-09-14 (second deferred resignation program deadline)
what_changed: In July 2025, DHS proposed cutting its Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A) -- one of the 18 formal elements of the U.S. Intelligence Community, and the primary channel for sharing federal intelligence with state, local, and tribal law enforcement -- from roughly 1,000 employees to just 275, a roughly 73% reduction. The plan drew significant public opposition from law-enforcement organizations and Jewish advocacy groups that rely on I&A's threat-warning intelligence, with **one organization privately warning Congress the cuts would create 'dangerous intelligence gaps'**; DHS put the plan on hold within days of the backlash. Rather than abandon the restructuring, I&A pursued the same reduction gradually: it sent deferred resignation program (DRP) offers -- modeled on OPM's 'fork in the road' buyout template -- to staff twice since July, offering voluntary early retirement and separation incentives. By October 2025, Defense One reported roughly 300 employees had already departed through early retirement and the first DRP round, with another 200 expected to leave through the second round (deadline September 14, 2025; approved participants continued receiving pay through early December 2025). The combined effect was reported as essentially halving I&A's workforce since January 2025 -- achieving through voluntary attrition close to the same magnitude of cut the direct 73% layoff plan had proposed, after that plan itself was withdrawn in the face of public opposition.

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration / DHS leadership
primary_proponent.role: Executive branch decision to pursue I&A workforce reduction via voluntary buyouts after a direct layoff plan was withdrawn under public pressure
primary_proponent.note: No single named DHS official was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally directing the buyout strategy; the pattern -- proposing a direct cut, withdrawing it after backlash, then achieving a comparable reduction through voluntary separation incentives -- matches this administration's broader approach to other agencies' workforce reductions documented elsewhere in this tracker.

estimated_impact.summary: I&A is the Intelligence Community's primary conduit for sharing federal threat intelligence -- including on domestic extremism and foreign interference -- with state, local, and tribal law enforcement; law-enforcement and Jewish advocacy groups warned the cuts create 'dangerous intelligence gaps' at exactly the analytical capacity meant to support frontline threat detection.

title: DHS Rescinded Its Decade-Old 'Sensitive Locations' Policy, and Nearly Half of Undocumented Adults Report Avoiding Medical Care Out of Fear
institution: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) / Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)
status: In effect since January 21, 2025; no reported reversal as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (policy rescinded) through 2025-01-21 (ICE directive announced)
what_changed: Within hours of Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, DHS rescinded the decade-old 'Sensitive Locations' policy that had directed immigration enforcement to generally avoid arrests, searches, surveillance, and questioning at hospitals, health clinics, doctors' offices, schools, and places of worship. ICE announced a new directive on January 21, 2025 eliminating those restrictions on enforcement at what the prior policy termed sensitive or 'protected areas.' Health care providers and researchers subsequently documented a measurable chilling effect: surveys found nearly half of likely undocumented adults in the U.S. had avoided seeking medical care since the rescission, providers reported patients delaying or avoiding hospital emergency-room visits (including for conditions like gunshot wounds, diabetes complications, and high-risk pregnancies) out of fear of encountering immigration enforcement, and clinics reported drops in patient visits and interpreter usage. **Health workers documented downstream effects including delayed diagnoses of life-threatening illnesses, children presenting at emergency rooms unaccompanied, and young children showing anxiety symptoms tied to fear of family separation**.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Homeland Security
primary_proponent.note: DHS/ICE rescinded the policy and issued the new enforcement directive; reporting attributes the January 20-21, 2025 rescission to the administration broadly at the moment of inauguration, before Noem's own Senate confirmation (January 25, 2025), so the initial rescission is more directly attributable to DHS/ICE career and transition leadership acting on the incoming administration's direction than to Noem personally.

estimated_impact.summary: Removing the decades-old buffer that kept immigration enforcement out of hospitals and clinics produced a documented, measured chilling effect on healthcare-seeking behavior among undocumented immigrants, with clinicians and researchers linking the fear directly to delayed care for serious and life-threatening conditions.

title: Trump Budget Proposals Sought to Zero Out Federal Disability-Rights 'Protection & Advocacy' Funding -- and State Agencies Already Cut Services in 2025, Before Any Cut Was Enacted
institution: Health and Human Services (Administration for Community Living); the nationwide network of state Protection and Advocacy (P&A) systems
status: Proposed -- Congress had not enacted the FY2026 cuts as of the sources reviewed; several state P&A agencies had already curtailed services in 2025 due to funding-release delays tied to the broader federal funding freeze, independent of the final appropriations outcome
date_of_action: 2025-04 (leaked HHS budget draft and first state-level service pauses) through 2025-07-31 (formal FY2026 budget proposal)
what_changed: A leaked HHS budget draft reported in April 2025 revealed plans to zero out federal funding for the nationwide network of Protection and Advocacy (P&A) systems -- federally mandated, legally independent disability-rights agencies in every state and territory that investigate abuse and neglect, including in group homes and institutions, and provide free legal representation to people with disabilities -- alongside state councils on developmental disabilities, the lifespan respite program, and University Centers for Excellence in Developmental Disabilities. Even before any budget was enacted, funding-release delays tied to the broader administration funding freeze **forced P&A agencies in New Jersey, Mississippi, and Arkansas to pause or limit services in April 2025, including halting intake of new clients**. By July 2025, the administration's formal FY2026 budget request confirmed the leaked draft's direction in a more concrete form: it proposed eliminating three of the four major federal grant streams that fund the P&A network outright and cutting the fourth by roughly 60%. The National Disability Rights Network, which represents the state-based P&A agencies, calculated the proposal would cut the system's total federal funding from $148 million to about $69 million -- a roughly 53% reduction -- for a network of 57 agencies nationwide.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: HHS is the department that drafted and proposed the cuts; reporting ties the plan to RFK Jr.'s department and to Project 2025 architects, though no single named HHS official's signature on the leaked draft was identified in sourcing reviewed -- the formal FY2026 budget request came from the administration as a whole via OMB.

estimated_impact.summary: A 53% proposed federal funding cut (from $148M to ~$69M) threatens the free legal-advocacy and abuse-investigation function of the only federally mandated, legally independent disability-rights infrastructure in the country, present in every state; real service reductions -- new-client intake halts in at least three states -- had already occurred by April 2025, months before any final budget action, because of funding-release delays alone.

title: Federal Disease Surveillance Cuts Coincide With Emergence of Flesh-Eating Bacteria, Screwworm, and Malaria-Reintroduction Risk
institution: HHS/CDC and USDA disease-surveillance programs
status: Ongoing -- FoodNet reporting on 6 of 8 pathogens remained optional as of late July 2026; the ocean-instrument removal was reversed. CDC declared the 12,883-case Cyclospora outbreak over Sept. 11, 2026; screwworm cases reached 50 by Sept. 21.
date_of_action: 2025 (surveillance program cuts begin) through 2026-07 (reporting on emerging health threats)
what_changed: The Trump administration reduced or eliminated multiple federal disease-surveillance programs beginning in 2025. As of July 1, 2025, CDC's FoodNet (the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, a CDC/USDA/FDA partnership with 10 state health departments covering about 16% of the U.S. population) stopped requiring reporting on six of the eight pathogens it was built to track -- Campylobacter, Cyclospora, Listeria, Shigella, Vibrio, and Yersinia all became optional, leaving only Salmonella and STEC (E. coli) mandatory; Cyclospora had been part of FoodNet's surveillance since 1997. The change was not publicly announced; NBC News first reported it on August 26, 2025, citing CDC talking points that said funding 'has not kept pace' with the resources needed to keep all eight pathogens under surveillance. A CDC spokesperson said other CDC systems, including the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System and the Listeria Initiative, still track the six pathogens, but food-safety experts noted those systems are passive, while FoodNet actively audits clinical laboratories. The administration also began removing hundreds of deep-sea instruments that monitor ocean waters and yield data used to predict conditions in which bacteria such as Vibrio flourish; it reversed that plan after bipartisan opposition in Congress. USDA lost 18% of its workforce in the first six months of 2025, according to a USDA Office of Inspector General report, and more than 20,000 employees have left the department amid the administration's cost-cutting. The dismantling of USAID in 2025 stripped more than $300 million from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, which monitors zoonotic diseases such as screwworm; about 80% of USAID grants for global malaria programs were targeted for termination, according to KFF; and work was disrupted on the President's Malaria Initiative, in which USAID had invested more than $9 billion since 2005. CDC's Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria was reported dissolved in 2025 (by Politico, as cited by Newsweek, and by KFF Health News), with its staff reassigned; a former CDC enteric-laboratory official told Food Safety Magazine in July 2026 that only the division's USAID-funded operations were cut, and that Cyclospora is now overseen jointly by CDC's foodborne-disease division and the parasitic-diseases division. These reductions coincided with the emergence or resurgence of multiple disease threats in 2026. Vibrio vulnificus ('flesh-eating bacteria') had infected eight people in Florida by early July and was detected in coastal waters on New York's Long Island; CDC estimates about 80,000 Vibrio infections a year, and **about 1 in 5 people infected with Vibrio vulnificus die, sometimes within a day or two of becoming ill**. On June 3, 2026, USDA confirmed the first new U.S. case of New World screwworm, in Zavala County, Texas; confirmed cases totaled 30 in June (29 in Texas, 1 in New Mexico), 14 in July (all Texas), and 3 in August (two sheep and a goat in Texas's Big Bend area, with no cattle cases), according to Oklahoma Farm Report, and reached 50 (48 in Texas, 2 in New Mexico) by September 21, according to Houston Public Media's tracker, with federal officials saying the parasite's northward spread had slowed but the threat remained. In May 2026, CDC guidance warned that 'the country remains susceptible to malaria reintroduction,' although malaria was eradicated from the U.S. in 1951. The same summer brought the largest known Cyclospora outbreak in U.S. history. Michigan, which is not a FoodNet state, detected an unusual rise in cases and notified CDC on June 25, 2026; CDC issued a Health Alert Network advisory on July 14, and FDA and CDC traced the outbreak to iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, which was recalled on July 17. When CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, 2026, it counted 12,883 laboratory-confirmed illnesses from 21 states, at least 570 hospitalizations, and two deaths in Michigan, and said the true number was likely higher; Michigan alone had confirmed 14,510 cyclosporiasis cases by August 27, not all of them tied to the lettuce. FDA was also investigating separate Cyclospora outbreaks whose food source had not been identified as of late July. Food-safety commentators, including Food Safety News publisher Bill Marler and eFoodAlert, argue that the FoodNet downgrade left the country slower to see and characterize the outbreak, while other food-safety experts say FoodNet was built to track disease trends rather than detect outbreaks and that its cuts did not cause this one -- see caveat.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Oversees the HHS restructuring that included the FoodNet reporting changes and broader public-health surveillance reductions; HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard defended the reforms in response to press inquiries. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins separately denied that USDA staffing cuts caused the screwworm's return.

estimated_impact.summary: The entry documents weakened early-warning capacity at the moment several serious threats arrived. FoodNet's 10 active-surveillance sites stopped being required to track six of eight foodborne pathogens -- including Listeria, Vibrio and Cyclospora -- ahead of the largest known U.S. Cyclospora outbreak (12,883 confirmed illnesses, at least 570 hospitalizations, two deaths), rising Vibrio vulnificus infections that kill about 1 in 5 people infected, the return of screwworm to U.S. livestock (50 cases by Sept. 21, 2026), and a CDC warning that malaria could be reintroduced. Global disease programs lost U.S. money: about 80% of USAID malaria grants were targeted for termination and more than $300 million was stripped from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, while USDA, which helps lead the screwworm response, lost 18% of its staff in the first half of 2025. Public health experts, including former CDC director Tom Frieden, say the country is less able to catch such threats early.

estimated_impact.caveat: The harms here are documented threats and outbreaks that coincided with the cuts, not a proven causal chain for any single case. Federal officials say CDC still tracks the six downgraded pathogens through other national systems, HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard defended the reforms generally, and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins denied that USDA cuts caused the screwworm's return. On the Cyclospora outbreak, experts at a July 16, 2026 George Washington University briefing (including CSPI and GWU researchers) said FoodNet tracks trends rather than detecting outbreaks and its cuts did not cause the outbreak, a view echoed by a Will Campbell for Texas campaign fact-check; Michigan, the epicenter, is not a FoodNet site and caught the rise itself. Food Safety News and eFoodAlert argue the weakened system still slowed detection and characterization. CDC's case counts cover laboratory-confirmed illnesses only, and CDC says the true number was likely higher. The global figures (USAID, FAO) measure lost money and program capacity abroad, not a counted U.S. health toll.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the surveillance-program changes: the FoodNet downgrade is reported by CIDRAP, Food Safety Magazine, Food Safety News, and KFF Health News (republished by CBS News), all tracing to CDC and HHS statements first obtained by NBC News. The USDA workforce figure comes from a USDA Inspector General report and the malaria-grant figure from KFF, both as reported by KFF Health News. HIGH confidence on the Cyclospora outbreak's final scale, from CDC's and FDA's own outbreak pages. MODERATE confidence on the screwworm monthly counts, which come from trade press (Oklahoma Farm Report) and are consistent with Houston Public Media's cumulative tracker but were not checked against USDA's own case page. The dissolution of CDC's Division of Parasitic Diseases and Malaria is disputed: KFF Health News and Newsweek (citing Politico) report it dissolved, while a former CDC official told Food Safety Magazine only its USAID-funded work was cut. MODERATE confidence at most on any causal link between the cuts and a specific outbreak: administration officials and several food-safety experts dispute it, while other food-safety commentators argue the opposite.
pull_quote: The 2026 Cyclospora outbreak, the largest known in U.S. history, sickened at least 12,883 people in 21 states -- a year after CDC stopped requiring FoodNet sites to track the parasite.

section_summaries.what_changed: CDC made 6 of 8 FoodNet pathogens optional, USDA lost 18% of staff and 80% of USAID malaria grants were targeted for termination, as a record Cyclospora outbreak, screwworm and Vibrio hit in 2026.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: Experts say weaker surveillance leaves threats harder to catch early; the 2026 Cyclospora outbreak alone had 12,883 confirmed cases and 2 deaths, though its link to the cuts is disputed.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Surveillance cuts are well documented by KFF Health News, CIDRAP and CDC/FDA outbreak pages; a causal link to any specific outbreak is disputed by officials and some food-safety experts.

title: U.S. Physicians Sought Canadian Medical Licenses at Sharply Higher Rates, Citing the Trump Administration
institution: N/A -- workforce/institutional-trust effect, not a specific federal agency action
status: Ongoing trend as of last verification, based on Q1 2025 licensing data
date_of_action: 2025-05-29 (NPR reporting on Q1 2025 licensing data)
what_changed: NPR and multiple other outlets reported in late May/early June 2025 that Canadian provinces saw a measurable increase in U.S.-trained physicians seeking to relocate since Trump's return to office, with doctors citing moral concerns about the administration's policies and fear of professional or political reprisal. **The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario registered 116 U.S.-trained doctors in the first quarter of 2025 -- at least a 50% increase over the prior two quarters -- and received roughly 260 license applications from U.S.-trained doctors in that same quarter.** British Columbia licensed 28 U.S.-trained doctors in the fiscal year ending February 2025, triple the prior year's total. The recruitment firm CanAm reported a 65% increase in American doctors seeking Canadian jobs from January to April 2025, with as many as 15 inquiries per day. Some applicants told reporters they were seeking Canadian licensure specifically because of the current U.S. administration.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Physicians cited the administration's broader policy direction and climate generally as their reason for relocating, rather than any single named official's specific action; this entry documents an institutional-trust/workforce-migration effect rather than a discrete agency action.

estimated_impact.summary: A measurable rise in U.S.-trained physicians seeking Canadian licensure represents a potential loss of medical workforce capacity and expertise from the U.S. health system, driven by physicians' stated loss of trust in the administration's direction on health policy and broader governance.

title: DOE Proposed ~$19-20 Billion in Budget Cuts, Deemed 43% of Its Workforce Non-Essential, and Targeted 47 Energy-Efficiency Regulations for Elimination
institution: Department of Energy (DOE)
status: Ongoing -- FY2026 budget cuts proposed, not yet fully enacted; the 47-regulation deregulatory push formally announced and underway
date_of_action: 2025-01 (first deferred-resignation round) through 2025-05-12 (47-regulation deregulatory announcement)
what_changed: In April 2025, DOE extended an agency-wide hiring freeze and, in an internal reorganization plan, classified 43% of its workforce as non-'essential.' The hiring freeze and reorganization ran alongside a separate voluntary-departure mechanism: more than 2,600 DOE staffers accepted the administration's second round of deferred-resignation offers by April 10, 2025, more than double the 1,217 who took the first round in January 2025, with the Grid Deployment Office (responsible for power-grid maintenance) and the Loan Programs Office (low-interest financing for high-tech energy, nuclear, and transmission projects) among the hardest-hit, alongside the Policy Office and the offices of Manufacturing and Energy Supply Chains and Clean Energy Deployment. At least 114 employees were laid off from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) on May 5, 2025, part of a broader wave of departures and forced exits across the department's clean-energy and research functions. The administration's FY2026 budget proposal sought to cut DOE's budget by roughly $19.3-20.3 billion compared to FY2025 levels, with deep cuts concentrated in the offices funding renewable-energy research and demonstration projects, including NREL's parent office. Separately, on May 12, 2025, DOE announced it would pursue the elimination or reduction of 47 regulations -- what the department itself called the first milestone in 'America's biggest deregulatory effort' -- the large majority targeting consumer-appliance and building energy-efficiency standards (covering products such as refrigerators, water heaters, and furnaces), alongside some administrative/testing-process rules and DOE's own diversity-related grant-recipient requirements. DOE workers and outside experts warned the combination of budget cuts, workforce losses, and the efficiency-standard rollbacks would **raise household energy costs, slow clean-energy innovation, and dismantle energy-efficiency programs that had historically saved consumers money on utility bills**.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Energy leadership
primary_proponent.role: Directed the FY2026 budget proposal, the workforce reorganization/layoffs, and the 47-regulation deregulatory announcement
primary_proponent.note: Reporting reviewed did not identify a single named DOE official as personally directing every element of this rollback; this entry names the department consistent with this tracker's convention when sourcing does not clearly identify a more specific individual for the combined action.

estimated_impact.summary: The combination of workforce cuts and the rollback of consumer-appliance energy-efficiency standards threatens both DOE's research and grant-administration capacity and the cost savings the efficiency standards had provided consumers, according to DOE's own workers and independent energy-policy analysts.

title: DOE Cancels $4.9 Billion Loan Guarantee for the Largest Planned U.S. Transmission Line, Days After a Senator's Personal Appeal to Trump
institution: U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), Loan Programs Office
status: Cancelled -- DOE formally withdrew the conditional loan guarantee July 23, 2025
what_changed: The Department of Energy announced July 23, 2025 that it was **cancelling a $4.9 billion conditional loan guarantee for the first phase of the Grain Belt Express**, a planned 578-mile, 2,500-megawatt transmission line intended to carry wind and solar power from Ford County, Kansas to Callaway County, Missouri and onward toward eastern markets -- widely described as the largest transmission-line project in active development in the United States. The Biden administration had issued the conditional guarantee in November 2024. DOE said a review of the project's financials found the conditions necessary to issue the guarantee were unlikely to be met and that federal support was not critical to the project. The cancellation came one week after Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley told the New York Times he had personally appealed to President Trump to halt the project, and that Trump had promised to instruct DOE to do so -- establishing a direct, on-the-record line between a senator's personal lobbying and the federal funding decision that followed. The project had drawn opposition from some Missouri and Kansas landowners over eminent-domain use for the transmission corridor, a concern Hawley and other opponents cited publicly, separate from DOE's own stated financial-risk rationale.

primary_proponent.name: Chris Wright
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Energy
primary_proponent.note: DOE under Wright issued the formal cancellation; Sen. Josh Hawley's on-the-record account credits his personal appeal to Trump, who then directed DOE to act, as the proximate political trigger.

estimated_impact.summary: The cancellation removes federal financial backing from the largest active U.S. transmission-line project, one intended to carry wind and solar power from the Great Plains to eastern markets at a time of rising electricity demand and costs; the project's developer retains the option to proceed without the federal guarantee, but on less favorable financing terms.
