title: DOE's nuclear waste cleanup office loses nearly half its workforce, GAO finds
institution: Department of Energy, Office of Environmental Management
status: Ongoing -- 45% vacancy rate at end of FY2025 per GAO, with site-level rates as high as 100%; DOE plans to hire 174 workers in FY2026
date_of_action: 2025-03-04 (first Carlsbad Field Office lease-termination attempt) through 2026-05 (GAO report)
what_changed: The Carlsbad Field Office's eventual collapse to 100% vacancy had an earlier warning sign than the GAO report alone shows: on March 4, 2025, DOGE included the Carlsbad Field Office's 90,000-square-foot Skeen-Whitlock Building lease on a spreadsheet of more than 7,000 federal leases marked for termination, citing roughly $810,000 in annual savings. The office, staffed by about 200 workers, directly manages the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant (WIPP) -- the only U.S. site licensed to permanently dispose of transuranic nuclear waste, including plutonium-contaminated material, stored in a deep salt formation -- and includes an emergency response center for handling nuclear-material accidents. Following bipartisan New Mexico congressional pushback (Rep. Gabe Vasquez among others) over the national-security and public-safety risk of disrupting the only facility of its kind, GSA reinstated the lease within days, confirming by March 6, 2025 the office was no longer slated for termination. That reversal, however, did not stop the underlying workforce attrition documented below: a Government Accountability Office report found the Department of Energy's Office of Environmental Management -- responsible for cleaning up nuclear contamination from World War II- and Cold War-era weapons programs at sites across the country -- ended FY2025 with a 45% vacancy rate, roughly half its needed workforce. Of 409 staff who left in 2025, 76% (312) departed through the White House's deferred resignation program; nearly half of those departures (180) were in positions GAO classified as mission-critical, spanning engineering, contracting, physical sciences, and IT management. Vacancy rates varied sharply by site: 62% at Los Alamos National Laboratory, and **100% -- every position empty -- at the Carlsbad Field Office**, the same office whose building lease had been targeted, then spared, a year earlier. GAO further warned that 35% of DOE-EM's remaining 856 employees will be eligible to retire by the end of 2030, meaning attrition is likely to continue independent of any further resignation programs. DOE has said it plans to hire 174 workers in FY2026, which GAO's analysis indicates would still leave significant workforce gaps.

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration (White House deferred resignation program)
primary_proponent.role: Government-wide policy driving the departures
primary_proponent.note: The deferred resignation program offered government-wide accounted for more than three-quarters of DOE-EM's 2025 departures; no single named DOE or EM official was identified in reporting reviewed as personally directing this specific office's staffing reduction, distinguishing this from entries with an individually accountable official.

estimated_impact.summary: The federal office responsible for overseeing radioactive waste disposal and contamination cleanup at some of the nation's most hazardous nuclear sites lost nearly half its workforce, with some sites left entirely unstaffed, per the government's own independent watchdog.

title: DOE Dismantles Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, Cancels $3.7B+ in Awarded Projects
institution: Department of Energy (Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations)
status: Complete (office wound down; zero FY2026 funding provided by Congress)
date_of_action: 2025-05-30 (first project terminations announced) through 2026 appropriations (OCED zeroed out)
what_changed: The Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (OCED) was created in 2021 to manage roughly $27 billion in funding for large-scale clean energy demonstration projects -- hydrogen hubs, direct air capture hubs, long-duration energy storage, and industrial decarbonization -- and had committed over $18 billion to about 100 projects by November 2025. On May 30, 2025, Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced **the termination of 24 OCED projects worth more than $3.7 billion in financial assistance**, citing lack of economic viability and misalignment with administration priorities. Internal documents reviewed by Latitude Media showed a broader target list of nearly $24 billion in awards for cancellation across six DOE offices. Staffing followed funding: OCED's roughly 250-person staff was cut to a planned temporary staff of 35, a reduction of about 86%. On November 20, 2025, DOE announced its updated agency-wide organization chart, removing OCED entirely and folding remaining functions into the newly created Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation alongside similarly eliminated offices (Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy, Grid Deployment Office, Office of Fossil Energy and Carbon Management); reporting at the time put the value of clean-energy awards canceled as part of this specific reorganization at more than $7 billion, on top of the May 2025 $3.7 billion figure above and distinct from the broader ~$24 billion cross-office target list. As part of the same reorganization, DOE's Loan Programs Office was rebranded the Office of Energy Dominance Financing, a change trade press described as centering the office around fossil and nuclear energy financing and de-emphasizing its prior broader mandate supporting clean-energy technologies from any source. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0507): on December 1, 2025, DOE renamed the National Renewable Energy Laboratory the National Laboratory of the Rockies, with Assistant Secretary Audrey Robertson stating the agency was 'no longer picking and choosing energy sources' -- a symbolic rebranding in the same November-December 2025 window as the organizational changes above. On January 22, 2026, the Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced it was de-obligating roughly $29.9 billion of the $83.6 billion in Biden-era loan principal referenced below and revising the remaining $53.6 billion, with $9.5 billion of the total specifically tied to wind and solar energy projects; DOE framed the review as covering $104 billion in Biden-era obligations, including roughly $85 billion the department said was 'rushed out the door' in the final months after the 2024 election. Congress's FY2026 appropriations bill, passed in early 2026, formalized the outcome by providing zero new funding to OCED and directing DOE to report quarterly on the redistribution of the office's remaining obligated and unobligated funds.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Energy
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the May 30, 2025 termination of the 24 OCED projects and oversaw the November 2025 reorganization that removed OCED from DOE's organizational structure entirely.

estimated_impact.summary: An $18-billion-plus federal clean energy demonstration portfolio lost the office that managed it, with over $3.7 billion in already-awarded projects formally cancelled and total targeted cancellations across DOE clean energy offices approaching $24 billion.

estimated_impact.caveat: DOE's stated rationale, per Secretary Wright, was that the terminated projects lacked economic viability and did not align with the administration's energy priorities, which the department has reoriented toward nuclear, fossil fuels, and critical minerals over renewable and demonstration-stage decarbonization technologies -- a shift DOE frames as 'restoring commonsense to energy policy' and lowering costs. Critics, including the nonprofit Clean Tomorrow and various clean-energy industry voices, argue the cancellations forfeit federal investments specifically designed to de-risk early-stage technology for private capital, citing lost private co-investment (for example, more than $14 billion in private capital tied to the $6 billion Industrial Demonstrations Program alone) and pointing to Project 2025's explicit call to shut OCED down as evidence the outcome was predetermined rather than a case-by-case economic viability review. Some project cancellations and workforce reductions elsewhere in DOE's energy programs (e.g., power marketing administrations) were later partially reversed when operational risks became apparent, suggesting the cuts were not uniformly implemented without pushback internally.

confidence_note: High confidence on the dollar figures, staffing cut, and organizational elimination, which are corroborated across multiple independent trade outlets (Latitude Media, pv magazine USA, Holland & Knight, Politico's E&E News) citing DOE's own announcements and budget documents. The $24 billion cross-office target-list figure is sourced to internal documents obtained by one outlet (Latitude Media) rather than a public DOE statement, and is presented as a reported figure rather than an officially confirmed total. Added 2026-09-09: the exact November 20, 2025 reorg date and the Office of Energy Dominance Financing rebranding (Holland & Knight, ProjectFinance.law, energy.gov's own EDF page), the December 1, 2025 NREL rename with Assistant Secretary Robertson's quote (DOE's own press release), and the January 22, 2026 loan-action breakdown ($29.9B de-obligated / $53.6B revised / $9.5B wind-solar-specific), independently corroborated across pv magazine, Solar Power World, and PV Tech and more precise than this entry's existing single $83.6B total. The '$7 billion' November-2025-specific award-cancellation figure is presented cautiously -- it is close to, but not confirmed identical to, the existing $24B cross-office target-list figure or the $3.7B May 2025 figure, and may represent partial overlap with either; preserved as reported rather than reconciled.

section_summaries.what_changed: DOE canceled dozens of clean-energy demonstration project awards worth over $3.7 billion, cut the managing office's staff by about 86%, then erased it from the org chart in a Nov. 2025 reorg that also rebranded its loan office around fossil/nuclear financing and, weeks later, renamed the National Renewable Energy Laboratory.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: Clean-energy awards worth roughly $3.7 billion are gone for good, the office managing a program worth well over $18 billion no longer exists, DOE's wider target list reportedly runs toward $24 billion, and a January 2026 loan review de-obligated/revised $83.6 billion more, $9.5B of it wind/solar-specific.

title: DOGE Built an AI Tool to Draft Deletion of Half of All Federal Regulations, Already Used to Write 100% of CFPB's Deregulatory Actions
institution: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), deployed at CFPB and HUD
status: Tool deployed and in active use at CFPB and HUD as of July 2025; White House would not confirm any government-wide plan as formally approved
date_of_action: 2025-07 (reporting on internal July 1, 2025 DOGE presentation)
what_changed: A DOGE-built 'AI Deregulation Decision Tool' is being used to review the roughly 200,000 active federal regulations and generate draft deregulatory actions with minimal human oversight, according to internal documents including a July 1, 2025 PowerPoint presentation reported by the Guardian and independently reviewed by TechCrunch. The tool's stated goal, per that presentation, is to place 100,000 regulations -- half of the total -- on a 'delete list' for elimination, targeting regulations DOGE's analysis determines are 'not required by law.' **As of the reporting, the tool had already been used at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to draft 100% of that agency's deregulatory actions, and at HUD to make determinations on 1,083 regulatory sections.** A White House spokesperson said 'no single plan has been approved or greenlit' while praising the DOGE team as 'the best and brightest in the business,' but did not dispute that the tool was being piloted at the two agencies. The reporting noted DOGE had previously deployed a separate AI tool, reported as error-prone, that 'hallucinated' the size of Department of Veterans Affairs contracts -- raising accuracy concerns about applying a similarly automated, low-human-review process to drafting federal deregulatory actions with legal force.

primary_proponent.role: Built and is deploying the AI tool across agencies; led in its early months by Elon Musk
primary_proponent.note: No individual DOGE official was named in reporting as personally responsible for the tool's design or deployment decisions at CFPB and HUD.

estimated_impact.summary: If deployed as described, the tool would let an AI system with a documented prior history of factual errors draft the elimination of roughly half of all active federal regulations across every agency, with reporting indicating minimal human review at the two agencies where it has already been used -- a scale and speed of deregulatory drafting far beyond what traditional agency rulemaking review processes could produce.

title: DOGE Quietly Dissolved Eight Months Ahead of Schedule, Scattering Its Personnel and Technology Into Permanent Agency Roles
institution: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE); Office of Personnel Management
status: Dissolved as a centralized entity as of November 2025; its personnel, technology tools, and some functions absorbed into OPM and other individual agencies rather than eliminated outright, with several accountability questions (data-retention, surveillance-tool status) left unresolved as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-01 (DOGE established by executive order, 18-month charter through July 2026) through 2025-11-23 (dissolution publicly confirmed)
what_changed: DOGE was established by executive order in January 2025 with an 18-month charter running through July 2026. On November 23, 2025 -- eight months ahead of that schedule -- Reuters reported OPM Director Scott Kupor told the outlet DOGE 'doesn't exist' as a centralized entity; Kupor subsequently pushed back on that framing, saying he meant DOGE might no longer exist as a distinct organizational unit while its underlying mission remained 'alive and well,' with OPM having absorbed many of its functions, particularly workforce-management and efficiency mandates. **Rather than being eliminated, DOGE's personnel and technology were dispersed into permanent roles across multiple agencies: Joe Gebbia (Airbnb co-founder) took a leadership role at the National Design Studio; Zachary Terrell became Chief Technology Officer at HHS; Rachel Riley became Chief of the Office of Naval Research; Jeremy Lewin moved to the State Department overseeing foreign assistance; and Scott Langmack moved to OMB to develop AI deregulation applications.** The government-wide hiring freeze DOGE had helped impose was lifted around the same time, which the administration characterized as DOGE completing rather than abandoning its mandate. Unresolved as of this entry: the operational status and data-retention practices of DOGE's AI-driven monitoring tools -- including capabilities reportedly used to scan federal employee communications for signs of 'disloyalty' -- and whether previously reported security vulnerabilities in DOGE-built or DOGE-accessed systems (including the unauthorized SSA server documented in this tracker's doge-ssa-fraud-review-data-access-2025-2026.json entry) were remediated before personnel and access were transferred to their new agency homes.

primary_proponent.role: Director, Office of Personnel Management
primary_proponent.note: Confirmed DOGE's dissolution as a centralized entity to Reuters, then publicly disputed the news agency's exact quotation while confirming OPM had absorbed many of DOGE's functions.

estimated_impact.summary: Rather than winding down DOGE's activities, the dissolution redistributed its personnel and technology into permanent positions across at least five federal agencies without public confirmation that its data-access practices, surveillance tools, or previously documented security vulnerabilities were reviewed or remediated in the process -- extending DOGE's operational reach and personnel network past its original centralized, time-limited charter rather than ending it.

title: DOGE/GSA Targeted 793 Federal Office Leases for Termination Government-Wide -- Then Repeatedly Cut Back the List as Agencies Were Blindsided
institution: General Services Administration (GSA), coordinating with DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) across dozens of federal agencies including IRS, Social Security Administration, and U.S. Geological Survey
status: Target list repeatedly reduced -- from 793 leases (mid-March 2025) to 485 (June 2025) to 384 (August 2025); GSA had finalized only about 30% of the roughly 900 government-wide lease terminations it had sent to landlords by February 2026
date_of_action: 2025-03-15 (793-lease list first reported) through 2026-02 (finalization rate reported at ~30%)
what_changed: CBS News reported on March 15, 2025 that DOGE/GSA had listed 793 federal office leases for termination government-wide, covering roughly nine million square feet and targeting a claimed ~$500 million in savings. Agencies including the IRS, Social Security Administration, and U.S. Geological Survey were among those affected, with reporting describing agencies as blindsided by the cancellations and left scrambling to relocate staff and operations with little notice; some cancellations were reported as made in error and later reversed. The rollout proved chaotic and the target list did not hold: E&E News/POLITICO and other outlets tracked DOGE continuing to add and drop leases (including further EPA and Interior Department terminations) through the spring, while the overall government-wide list was cut back from 793 in mid-March to 485 by June 2025, and to 384 by August 20, 2025. Individual agencies saw partial rollbacks under political pressure -- for example, USDA cut its own office-closure list roughly in half. **By February 2026, Federal News Network reported GSA had finalized only about 30% of the approximately 900 government-wide lease terminations it had sent to landlords earlier in 2025, indicating the bulk of the originally announced list was never actually executed.** This entry documents the government-wide program as a whole; individual high-profile instances within it -- including the National Park Service's 34 targeted buildings and the Alaska/Hawaii volcano observatories -- are tracked in their own separate entries (national-park-service-lease-terminations-2025, doge-volcano-observatory-lease-terminations-2025) cross-referenced here as specific examples of this broader push.

primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally responsible for the specific agencies or leases selected; GSA and DOGE described the effort in general cost-savings terms.

estimated_impact.summary: A government-wide list of nearly 800 office leases was targeted for termination with agencies reporting they were given little advance notice, creating relocation and continuity-of-operations disruption across the federal government -- but the list itself proved highly unstable, shrinking by more than half within five months and only about 30% of the total was actually finalized within a year, indicating much of the initial disruption stemmed from an unreliable, repeatedly-revised list rather than a stable, fully-executed cost-cutting plan.

title: DOGE Imposes a $1 Spending Cap on Government Credit Cards at GSA and the Pentagon
institution: General Services Administration (GSA) and Department of Defense (Department of War), following a governmentwide Trump executive order
status: Implemented as of February-March 2025 reporting
date_of_action: 2025-02-21 (GSA implementation) through 2025-03-05 (Pentagon/DoD implementation)
what_changed: DOGE imposed a $1 spending cap on SmartPay government credit cards used by General Services Administration employees and contractors, effectively freezing routine purchasing on those cards. Wired reported similar spending limits had already been put in place at several other federal agencies as part of the same broader cost-control push -- one of those agencies was the Pentagon: following a February 26, 2025 executive order from President Trump outlining governmentwide cost-saving initiatives, Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Darin Selnick signed a March 5, 2025 memorandum (with acting acquisition/sustainment head Steven Morani separately confirming the policy) **reducing the spending limit on all DoD civilian government purchase and travel cards to $1 and ordering cancellation of non-exempted official travel, with employees already traveling directed to return to their duty stations as soon as feasible**. Travel directly supporting military operations or a permanent change of station was exempted. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the Pentagon, in coordination with DOGE, had identified an initial $80 million in wasteful spending.

title: NLRB Deleted DOGE System-Access Records Before GAO Investigators Could Examine Them
institution: National Labor Relations Board (NLRB)
status: Complete -- GAO report published; the underlying account-access records cannot be recovered
date_of_action: 2025-04-16 (DOGE detail begins) through 2025-08 (access records deleted, after DOGE detail ended and before GAO could examine them)
what_changed: Two DOGE staffers were formally detailed to the National Labor Relations Board beginning April 16, 2025, under agreements running through July 25, 2025, and requested access to seven internal HR systems covering personnel records, payroll, and hiring databases -- a request that prompted an NLRB IT staffer to file a whistleblower disclosure with Congress and the agency's inspector general to open an investigation into a potential data breach. A Government Accountability Office report -- titled 'National Labor Relations Board Detailees Did Not Access IT Systems Between April 16 and July 25, 2025' -- found no evidence the DOGE detailees accessed those systems during that specific window. However, GAO also found that **in August 2025, after the DOGE detail had ended but before GAO investigators requested to observe the systems, NLRB deleted the team members' system-access accounts and associated audit-trail records -- eliminating the digital evidence needed to independently verify what access, if any, occurred, and undercutting confidence in the agency's own account**. Access logs for sensitive systems are generally subject to a six-year retention requirement under the General Records Schedule; the deleted records were only months old.

title: DOGE's SSA 'Fraud Review' Found Almost No Fraud, Slowed Claims 25%; Whistleblower Says DOGE Copied 300M+ Americans' Data to a Vulnerable Cloud
institution: Social Security Administration (SSA); DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
status: Ongoing litigation, now proceeding to discovery -- the Fourth Circuit vacated the injunction limiting DOGE's SSA data access and remanded (April 2026); on remand, the district court granted discovery (April 14, 2026), then denied the government's motion to rescind that order (June 26, 2026), holding that defendants' own January 2026 disclosures justified continued discovery and declining to cap its scope. A June 2026 sworn whistleblower declaration separately alleges a DOGE official proposed marking 2.7 million living recipients as dead to pressure self-deportation or expose them to ICE, which SSA disputes as ever implemented.
date_of_action: 2025-03-08 (review publicly reported) through 2026-04-10 (Fourth Circuit ruling); data-access disclosures continuing into 2026
what_changed:
Starting in mid-February 2025, Elon Musk publicly laid the political groundwork for DOGE's Social Security fraud review with two separate, since-debunked claims: that 20 million people 'definitely dead' were still marked alive in SSA's Numident database, and, in a March 11, 2025 Fox Business interview, that $500-700 billion in Social Security 'waste' needed to be eliminated. Fact-checkers and SSA's own then-acting commissioner rejected both claims -- SSA data traces the '150-year-olds' figure to a database-structure quirk (SSA's own inspector general found improper payments of all kinds, fraud included, totaled less than 1% of the $8.6 trillion paid out from FY2015-2022), and experts told ABC News Trump and Musk were falsely implying millions of dead Americans were actively receiving benefits rather than merely still appearing as unremoved records.

In March 2025, ABC News and other outlets reported that DOGE was searching through $8.6 trillion in Social Security payment records as part of the same stated anti-fraud effort, with DOGE engineer Aram Moghaddassi and Musk separately claiming that up to 40% of phone calls to SSA requesting direct-deposit changes came from fraudsters -- a narrower claim used to justify new anti-fraud identity checks on phone-based claims starting in early April 2025. Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek later confirmed the review's scope in a letter to Congress. The actual results, revealed in internal SSA documents reported by Nextgov/FCW and cited by Sen. Elizabeth Warren in a May 15, 2025 release, contradicted the fraud claims: of more than 110,000 phone claims examined under the new checks, only 2 were found to have a high probability of fraud, and fewer than 1% were flagged as even potentially fraudulent at all -- consistent with SSA's own data showing fraud is a negligible share (a fraction of the already-small 0.3%) of the program's improper payments.

The new checks themselves caused documented harm: an internal SSA document from May 2025 found they **slowed retirement claim processing by 25% and caused a 'degradation of public service,'** prompting SSA to consider walking the policy back. Separately, Nextgov/FCW reported on May 15, 2025, amid an influx of retirement claims described in an internal SSA email, that **SSA had over 140,000 unprocessed retirement claims more than 60 days old**, a figure Sen. Warren repeated in her May 15, 2025 release.

A federal court had issued a temporary restraining order in March 2025 limiting DOGE's SSA data access -- U.S. District Judge Ellen Hollander's order barring DOGE affiliates from accessing SSA's sensitive personal data -- and Acting Commissioner Dudek initially told reporters the order applied so broadly it would force him to shut down the agency; Hollander responded in two same-day letters to counsel calling that characterization 'inaccurate' and then 'patently incorrect,' clarifying the order applied only to SSA staff working on the DOGE data-access effort specifically, and Dudek reversed himself hours later, saying the agency would remain open and continue operating under the TRO. Reporting found DOGE associates continued accessing sensitive data even after that order.

The allegation that DOGE had copied Americans' Social Security data to a cloud environment came from SSA's own Chief Data Officer, Charles Borges, not from the January 2026 court filing described below. Borges filed a protected whistleblower disclosure with the Office of Special Counsel and congressional committees on August 26, 2025, alleging DOGE staff had created a live copy of the nation's Social Security data in a cloud environment that circumvented oversight (a 'vulnerable cloud environment,' in his complaint's words as reported by CBS News), putting more than 300 million Americans' records at risk. He resigned August 29, 2025, days after filing, writing in his resignation letter that retaliatory actions against him made it impossible to do his job 'legally and ethically'; he separately filed a Prohibited Personnel Practices retaliation complaint. SSA spokesperson Nick Perrine said the data referenced in the complaint 'is stored in a long-standing environment used by SSA and walled off from the internet' and that SSA was 'not aware of any compromise to this environment' (CNN, Aug. 26, 2025).

Separately, and more seriously, court filings beginning in January 2026 revealed that DOGE staff had improperly accessed and shared SSA data well beyond the stated fraud-review purpose: a January 16, 2026 DOJ court filing (SSA's Notice of Corrections) corrected prior sworn agency testimony and admitted that, beginning March 7, 2025 and continuing until March 17, members of SSA's DOGE Team 'were using links to share data through the third-party server "Cloudflare,"' which it said 'is not approved for storing SSA data.' SSA told the court it had 'not been able to determine exactly what data were shared to Cloudflare or whether the data still exist on the server,' that, for a call-center profile a DOGE Team member could use to reach PII from April 9 to June 11, 2025, 'it is unknown at this time whether any PII was accessed,' and that its review of the DOGE Team's actions 'is ongoing.' The filing gave no count of people whose data passed through Cloudflare; the 300 million figure comes from Borges's disclosure. The filing also disclosed that on March 3, 2025, an SSA DOGE Team member emailed DHS, copying Steve Davis, then a senior advisor to the U.S. DOGE Temporary Organization, and a DOGE-affiliated Department of Labor employee, attaching an encrypted file SSA believes contained PII, including names and addresses, of approximately 1,000 people. The same filing revealed a DOGE Team member had signed a 'Voter Data Agreement,' in his capacity as an SSA employee, with an outside political advocacy group seeking to find evidence of voter fraud and 'overturn election results in certain States,' prompting SSA, in late December 2025, to make two Hatch Act referrals to the U.S. Office of Special Counsel; SSA told the court that DOGE Team members 'could have been asked to assist the advocacy group by accessing SSA data to match to the voter rolls, but SSA has not yet seen evidence that SSA data were shared with the advocacy group.'

The district court's June 26, 2026 opinion (see below) later detailed further specifics of the Voter Data Agreement beyond what was previously known: SSA says it first learned of the agreement during an unrelated November 2025 review, and plaintiffs say documents produced in a related FOIA suit (Democracy Forward Found. v. SSA, ABA-26-1188, D. Md.) include an email from a member of the SSA DOGE Team to DOGE personnel at the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Labor attaching a password-protected Excel workbook containing personally identifiable information on 971 beneficiaries.

A further whistleblower complaint reported in March 2026 alleged a former DOGE associate planned to take sensitive citizen data to a subsequent government-contractor job. That complaint is plaintiffs' March 10, 2026 'First Factual Notice' (ECF 208), which the June 26 opinion clarifies specifically alleged the departing DOGE associate took restricted SSA databases to a private-sector employer potentially on a thumb drive.

On April 10, 2026, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals, sitting en banc, vacated the district court's preliminary injunction restricting DOGE's SSA data access. Its lead opinion held that plaintiffs did not show, 'based on the record before the district court' when it entered the injunction, that they were likely to suffer irreparable harm, and vacated the injunction 'without addressing whether plaintiffs satisfy the remaining three Winter factors'; it also called the government's recent acknowledgments 'alarming.' Judge King, joined by five judges in an opinion dissenting from the judgment, wrote that given the January 2026 corrections, the prior rulings -- the preliminary injunction, the Fourth Circuit's denial of a stay, and the Supreme Court's grant of a stay -- 'were rendered on a materially erroneous record.' On remand, the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland lifted its stay of the case on April 14, 2026 and granted plaintiffs' motion for discovery -- meaning the case is now proceeding to fact-finding on the scope of DOGE's SSA data access, rather than simply sitting dormant after the Fourth Circuit's ruling.

Defendants then moved to rescind the April 14 discovery order (ECF 215), arguing discovery was improper and citing the DOGE Temporary Organization's then-upcoming July 4, 2026 expiration date. Separately, plaintiffs' June 5, 2026 'Second Factual Notice' (ECF 233) attached a sworn declaration from former SSA senior executive Jeremiah Schofield, who says he was present when a DOGE official, Jon Koval, laid out a plan to mark roughly 2.7 million living Social Security recipients as dead in SSA's Death Master File -- with the stated purpose, per Schofield, of forcing those individuals to either self-deport or go to a local SSA office to prove they were alive, where ICE could then detain and deport them. Sens. Warren and Blumenthal made the declaration public and sought records and answers from SSA Commissioner Bisignano and the named DOGE-affiliated staff. SSA publicly disputes the account, saying it 'did not add a list of 2.7 million names to the Death Master File' and that the plan, as alleged, was never implemented.

On June 26, 2026, Judge Ellen Lipton Hollander (D. Md.) denied the Motion to Rescind in a 39-page opinion, holding that defendants' own January 16, 2026 Notice of Corrections -- which disclosed that SSA had falsely assured the court of TRO compliance, concealed the DOGE Team's full systems access, and misrepresented that DOGE work was confined to fraud detection -- itself justified the discovery, and declined defendants' request to cap it at five requests for production, five interrogatories, five requests for admission, and zero depositions. The opinion found SSA and DOGE had made 'serious if not egregious misrepresentations' to the court. The opinion quotes Judge King's concurring and dissenting opinion within the Fourth Circuit's en banc ruling (AFSCME VI, 172 F.4th 361) -- not the court's own holding -- in which he wrote that, given the corrected record, 'we should not accord the defendants any benefit of the doubt or readily trust in anything they say.'

As of the entry's last litigation recheck, defendants' separate May 1, 2026 Motion to Dismiss for Lack of Jurisdiction remains pending and undecided; no ruling on it, and no outcome of the now-authorized discovery itself, has been identified.

title: DOGE Canceled 585 VA Contracts After Backlash Forced It Down From an Initial 875 -- Officials Gave Congress Inconsistent Figures
institution: Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), with DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
status: Implemented, with ongoing congressional oversight pressure over transparency and inconsistent figures
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial ~875-contract cancellation list) through 2025-05-16 (Collins gives Congress a differing figure)
what_changed: DOGE, under Elon Musk, moved to cancel roughly 875 VA contracts as part of its cost-cutting campaign. Reporting and VA employees flagged that many targeted contracts covered essential services, including cancer-registry maintenance, sterility certification for medical equipment, air-quality testing, suicide-prevention support, physician recruitment and retention, and safety inspections at VA medical facilities. **Frontline Veterans Health Administration employees warned the cuts would imperil safety at the VA's nearly 1,400 hospitals and clinics.** Facing that backlash, the VA paused its planned cuts, then announced the termination list had fallen by about a third, to 585 contracts, with an alleged combined value of $1.8 billion; the VA said the reductions would let it redirect more than $900 million to health care, benefits, and services for VA beneficiaries. The VA declined to disclose the full list of canceled contracts despite congressional requests, drawing criticism from senators including Richard Blumenthal and Angus King over the lack of transparency and consultation. VA Secretary Doug Collins subsequently gave Congress inconsistent figures on the scope of the cuts -- telling lawmakers on May 16, 2025 that the VA had canceled more than 440 contracts worth $120 billion, a figure sharply at odds with the earlier 585-contract/$1.8 billion accounting, without a public reconciliation of the discrepancy identified in sourcing reviewed. Update 2026-08-30: identified the specific mechanism behind the cancellation list -- an AI review tool built and operated by a DOGE software engineer with no prior healthcare or government experience, which ProPublica reported was error-prone and, per Government Executive/Nextgov reporting on a June 11, 2025 forum, appeared to select contracts for termination by matching keywords rather than individualized review. House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee Democrats raised the AI tool's use directly at that forum. A concrete example of the tool's effect: Task Order 169, a contract held by Aptive Resources (a veteran-owned and woman-owned small business) supporting VA's Electronic Health Record Modernization program by resolving identity-record anomalies in the VA's master person index, was terminated abruptly and without a transition plan despite having resolved 13,400 such anomalies -- inaccuracies that can otherwise block veterans from receiving medical care, disability compensation, or other earned benefits. At least six contracts directly supporting the EHR-modernization rollout, all held by service-disabled or veteran-owned small businesses, were similarly terminated. Separately, DOGE's broader public accounting of its savings claims, including the VA figures described above, was reported to have quietly removed some previously touted savings figures from its own public tracking website after they were found to be inflated or erroneous, though no source reviewed specifically confirms whether the VA contract figures in this entry were among those quietly revised.

title: DOGE/GSA Moved to Cancel Leases for the Alaska and Hawaii Volcano-Monitoring Observatories, Then Backed Off Under Congressional Pressure
institution: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) -- Alaska Volcano Observatory and Hawaiian Volcano Observatory; General Services Administration (GSA)
status: Alaska lease reversed after congressional intervention; Hawaii's temporary Hilo lease threat was overtaken by a previously-planned, congressionally-funded permanent relocation
date_of_action: 2025-03-06 (leases publicly reported as targeted) through 2026-04 (new permanent Hawaii facility opened)
what_changed: In early March 2025, NOTUS and the Washington Post reported that DOGE/GSA had listed the leases for the Anchorage office housing the USGS Alaska Volcano Observatory and the Hilo, Hawaii office housing the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (which monitors Kilauea) among hundreds of federal office leases slated for termination as part of the administration's real-estate cost-cutting push, with GSA claiming roughly $2.2 million in savings from the Anchorage lease alone. Scientists and local officials warned that ending these leases -- on top of concurrent GSA staffing cuts complicating any relocation of specialized monitoring equipment and servers -- **risked degrading real-time eruption-warning capability near active volcanoes in both states**; a former observatory scientist specifically flagged the difficulty of moving a recently purchased $500,000 backup generator and critical monitoring servers without risking data loss or monitoring gaps. In Alaska, Rep. Nick Begich's office intervened with the Department of the Interior and GSA, and the Anchorage lease was reinstated by March 18, 2025, according to the Anchorage Daily News and Begich's own office -- though GSA itself did not confirm the reversal on the record to the Anchorage Daily News, leaving the reinstatement independently reported but not agency-confirmed. In Hawaii, the Hilo Ironworks Building lease -- always a temporary arrangement dating to 2018, when the observatory's original Kilauea-summit headquarters was damaged beyond repair by earthquakes -- was listed for termination effective September 30, 2025; that threat did not require a comparable reversal because a new, permanent, non-leased Hawaiian Volcano Observatory headquarters (funded separately through congressional disaster-recovery appropriations after the 2018 damage, shared with the Pacific Island Ecosystems Research Center) opened in Hilo in April 2026, mooting the lease question for that observatory's long-term housing.

primary_proponent.note: No named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally responsible for including the two observatory leases; GSA described itself only as 'reviewing all options to optimize our footprint' when asked for comment.

estimated_impact.summary: Two of the nation's volcano-hazard monitoring facilities were briefly slated for lease termination with no documented relocation plan for specialized, hard-to-move monitoring equipment, at a time when both regions had active volcanic activity (Kilauea eruptions in Hawaii) -- an example of a blanket cost-cutting process moving without an apparent case-by-case safety review.

Correction (2026-08-11): this entry's Hilo savings figure previously ran a $44,391-$150,692 range sourced to "multiple outlets" -- the $150,692 figure actually belongs to a separate DOGE-targeted Hilo facility, NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory support office (a different agency and mission, atmospheric CO2 monitoring rather than volcanic-hazard monitoring), documented in its own entry. The correct, single figure for this entry's USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory Ironworks Building lease is $164,391. The Hawaii outcome should not be read as GSA/DOGE standing down on the merits -- the permanent facility that resolved the housing question was already funded and under construction for unrelated reasons (2018 earthquake damage) before the 2025 lease-termination push began.

title: DOJ Civil Rights Division Lost About 75% of Its Attorneys — Voting Section Down From 30 to 3
institution: Civil Rights Division, U.S. Department of Justice
status: Ongoing: departures still counted at roughly 75%, with 100+ new hires sworn in July 2026; Voting Section led on an acting basis by a former Public Interest Legal Foundation attorney; an August 2026 whistleblower disclosure alleges predetermined outcomes in at least three antisemitism investigations.
date_of_action: 2025-01 (initial departures begin) through 2025-10 (Justice Connection's most recent departure count)
what_changed:
Since President Trump's January 2025 inauguration, an estimated 250-260 attorneys -- roughly 70% of the division's approximately 365-person attorney roster -- have resigned, accepted the administration's deferred-resignation offer, or been reassigned elsewhere within DOJ. Stacey Young, founder of Justice Connection (a support network founded by former division attorneys), had spent 18 years as a Justice Department litigator -- first in the Civil Division and later in the Civil Rights Division -- before leaving in January 2025, according to her Jan. 31, 2025 statement at a House Judiciary Committee briefing; in April 2025 she told NBC News that she didn't think there was 'any precedent for an administration almost completely refocusing the civil rights division's enforcement priorities the way this one has.' ABC News reported more than 100 attorneys had already left the division by April 29, 2025, tying the departures directly to a priority shift away from voting-rights and policing-reform enforcement toward pursuing culture-war priorities including transgender-athlete policy and 'anti-Christian bias' claims. The Voting Section specifically -- responsible for enforcing the Voting Rights Act -- fell from an estimated 30 attorneys in January to just 3 by May 2025. Democracy Docket reported in May 2025 that Joseph Rich, chief of the Voting Section from 1999 to 2005, asked what would happen when the reduced section started 'bringing voting fraud suits right in the middle of an election, or even close to an election.' The section devoted to ensuring nondiscrimination by recipients of federal funds was left with no attorneys whatsoever, per the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights. By July 23, 2025, Reuters put the cumulative departure count at 368 staff, a dated data point between the January-May ~250-260-attorney figure and the October 2025 ~400-person/75% estimate. By October 2025, Justice Connection estimated the departure count had grown to nearly 400 people, about 75% of attorneys. Departures across the division have since continued to be counted at roughly 75%, consistent with Justice Connection's October 2025 estimate, rather than climbing further.

Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, confirmed in April 2025, sent new mission statements to each of the division's 11 sections shortly after taking office, redirecting the Voting Section's focus from protecting against discrimination toward pursuing voter fraud, and telling the Educational Opportunities Section that its work required 'the full dedication of this section's resources, attention and energy to the priorities of the president.' Separately, the division's priority shift also reached environmental-justice enforcement: on April 11, 2025, the Civil Rights Division terminated a March 2023 interim resolution agreement with the Alabama Department of Public Health covering Lowndes County -- a rural, majority-Black area with a **longstanding raw-sewage exposure crisis from inadequate septic infrastructure** -- that had required ADPH to prioritize septic and wastewater fixes there based on residents' sewage-exposure risk; DOJ's own press release framed the termination as advancing Executive Order 14151's ban on 'illegal DEI and environmental justice policies.' The agreement had been the first-ever use of federal civil rights law to address an environmental-justice claim, making its termination a specific, named instance of the division abandoning a novel enforcement theory rather than merely reassigning staff away from existing casework.

Career section-chief managers -- in some cases with decades of institutional tenure spanning multiple administrations of both parties -- were removed from leadership roles and reassigned to processing public records requests or complaint intake, which several described as a deliberate push to induce their resignation. By August 2025, DOJ was actively soliciting permanent internal transfers from other CRT sections to refill the most depleted offices (Voting, Employment Litigation, Educational Opportunities), some of which were themselves already down more than 75% of their attorneys. The Voting Section is now led in an acting capacity by Maureen Riordan, previously an attorney at the Public Interest Legal Foundation, a conservative legal group whose stated mission is to 'fight against lawlessness in American elections' -- a notable leadership choice for a section redirected toward pursuing voter fraud rather than voting-rights enforcement.

Reuters reporting (Feb. 2026) found the division's unit prosecuting police and federal-agent misconduct lost roughly two-thirds of its attorneys, from about 40 down to as few as 13, with charges under the civil rights statute most commonly used in federal excessive-force cases falling about 36% to 54 total in 2025 -- the lowest since 2020. Section supervisors reportedly instructed staff early in the administration that law-enforcement-misconduct investigations would proceed only in egregious circumstances (e.g. a death in custody or sexual assault), with state and local authorities expected to lead most other cases. Former DOJ lawyers cited in the reporting expressed doubt the diminished section could conduct thorough investigations of recent incidents, including the fatal shootings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis.

An earlier, concrete instance of the same leniency-toward-police pattern predates the Reuters staffing report. On July 17, 2025, career prosecutors' successor DOJ leadership recommended a one-day sentence and three years of supervised release for Brett Hankison, the former Louisville officer convicted in November 2024 of violating Breonna Taylor's civil rights by firing blindly into her apartment during the 2020 raid that killed her -- an about-face after DOJ had spent years prosecuting the case through two trials. U.S. District Judge Rebecca Grady Jennings rejected the recommendation on July 21, 2025 as treating the offense as 'an inconsequential crime' and sentenced Hankison to 33 months. DOJ's involvement did not end with sentencing: in November 2025 the department asked the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals to release Hankison from prison pending his appeal, and the court granted the request December 19, 2025, ordering him released on his own recognizance.

As of March 2026, the White House was reportedly considering ending funding for a separate, longstanding DOJ election-observer program aimed at protecting minority voting rights, according to CBS News sources. A DOJ spokesperson has since gone on the record denying the reported consideration of ending the election-observer program's funding, stating the Department 'has no plans to end its monitorship program which is integral to assessing compliance with federal voting rights laws across the country.' This answers the reported defunding consideration with an explicit denial, though it does not address or retract the underlying reporting that such defunding had been discussed internally.

In July 2026, Dhillon swore in more than 100 new attorneys and staff to the Civil Rights Division, beginning to refill the roster hollowed out by departures. The division's new composition drew public scrutiny after DOJ published a group photo of the incoming class; commentators (Atlanta Black Star) highlighted the demographic makeup of the new hires as a marker of the division's redirected priorities. Coverage citing DOJ deputy leadership (Jeffrey Morrison, elevated to Deputy Assistant Attorney General by May 2026 and now counsel on the department's Title VI suit against the University of California; Eric Sell, who followed Dhillon from the Center for American Liberty) describes a division now oriented toward Second Amendment cases, litigation against transgender-related policies, and alleged campus antisemitism -- confirming that the redirected mission is now staffed with new personnel aligned to it, rather than remaining merely depleted.

A whistleblower disclosure from former Civil Rights Division attorney Haley Van Erem, filed through the Government Accountability Project and forwarded to four congressional committees including the House Judiciary Committee (reported Aug. 18-19, 2026), alleges that DOJ and HHS officials departed from longstanding investigative practices in at least three high-profile antisemitism investigations -- Harvard, Brown, and Columbia -- conducted under the administration's Task Force to Combat Antisemitism (led by DOJ official Leo Terrell), claiming the investigations' outcomes were 'predetermined, without regard to the evidence' and that for at least some of them there was 'little to no factual predicate justifying opening them.' Van Erem, who spent nearly a decade in the Special Litigation Section before being reassigned off five active ADA cases onto Title VI investigations on March 21, 2025, left DOJ May 30, 2025, citing unwillingness to continue in what she described as politically motivated investigations. Per Above the Law's coverage, her disclosure separately provides 'the first direct acknowledgment' that some departing Civil Rights Division attorneys' exits were driven by concern that continued participation in the division's current work -- including alleged use of 'poison pill' settlement language designed to force litigation rather than resolution, and opening at least one investigation based on a single news article -- could expose them to state bar discipline.

At a Federalist Society event, she likened the division's work under Democratic administrations to a 'speeding train' and, addressing the departing attorneys directly, said 'we wish them well in their future endeavors and their passions. They need to pursue them elsewhere. That's not going to be happening at the DOJ.'

estimated_impact.summary: Most of the Civil Rights Division's attorneys have left, and its enforcement has moved away from voting rights, police misconduct and environmental justice: the Voting Section fell from an estimated 30 attorneys to 3, the unit prosecuting police and federal-agent misconduct lost roughly two-thirds of its attorneys, and the division ended an agreement that was the first-ever use of federal civil rights law to address an environmental-justice claim, which had required the Alabama Department of Public Health to prioritize septic and wastewater fixes for Lowndes County residents exposed to raw sewage. More than 100 new attorneys and staff sworn in during July 2026 began refilling the roster, aligned with the redirected priorities. Stacey Young, an 18-year Justice Department attorney who spent the later part of her career in the Civil Rights Division and founded Justice Connection, told NBC News she doesn't think there's 'any precedent for an administration almost completely refocusing the civil rights division's enforcement priorities the way this one has.' Joseph Rich, who led the Voting Section from 1999-2005, warned the reduced section could bring voter-fraud suits 'right in the middle of an election.'

title: Mass Reassignment of Federal Agents to Immigration Enforcement Collapsed Drug, Trafficking, Child-Exploitation, and Counterterrorism Casework
institution: Department of Justice (DOJ/OCDETF); Department of Homeland Security (Homeland Security Investigations); FBI; ATF
status: Ongoing -- reassignments continued through the reporting reviewed, with no announced reversal
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OCDETF case-transfer order) through 2025-11 (Senate disclosure of reassignment percentages)
what_changed: Starting in mid-2025, the Trump administration redirected thousands of federal law-enforcement agents and prosecutors from their existing casework to immigration enforcement and mass-deportation operations. On July 23, 2025, the Deputy Attorney General ordered the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Force (OCDETF) -- described by former officials as the nation's largest and most effective anti-crime task force -- to transfer all of its 5,000-plus active cases to a newly created Homeland Security Task Force structure that placed far greater emphasis on immigration offenses and human smuggling than on joint law-enforcement efforts against organized crime and drug trafficking. A Reuters analysis of nearly 2 million federal court records found that, as a direct result, federal drug prosecutions fell roughly 10% compared to the same period in 2024 (about 1,200 fewer cases), the slowest pace since at least the late 1990s, while federal money-laundering prosecutions fell 24%. For the first time in decades, nearly half of all people charged with federal crimes in 2025 were accused of immigration violations, and roughly 700 additional federal prosecutors -- more than one in ten nationwide -- were assigned to at least some immigration casework. Reuters quoted federal officials describing high-priority cases stalling as a direct result, including one supervising prosecutor who said a fentanyl-trafficking investigation was at a standstill because the agents leading it had been ordered to focus on deportations instead. The Wall Street Journal and New York Times separately reported the reassignment extended well beyond DOJ: at Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) -- one of the primary federal agencies combating child exploitation, human trafficking, and fentanyl smuggling -- personnel warned the reassignments were **dismantling one of the country's most effective child-protection and national-security forces, with key trafficking routes left unstaffed**. NYT reported the same pattern hit counterterrorism and sanctions-enforcement work: investigations into the black-market Iranian oil trade used to finance terrorism were delayed by months, and highly trained specialized personnel were reassigned to routine traffic stops and immigrant roundups. Sen. Mark Warner disclosed in November 2025 that 25% to 45% of FBI agents working counterterrorism, cyber, espionage, and child-exploitation cases had been reassigned to immigration enforcement; separate reporting put the reassignment rate at roughly 25% of FBI agents overall and as high as 80% of ATF agents. A subsequent Reuters/NYT analysis of federal data found drug arrests and gun seizures had dropped sharply nationwide as HSI and other agencies pulled agents off narcotics and firearms casework to staff deportation operations, with former officials describing key investigations as stalled or abandoned outright.

title: DOJ and DHS Canceled Hundreds of Millions in Public-Safety and Violence-Prevention Grants in 2025, With Most Recipients Still Unreimbursed Months Later
institution: U.S. Department of Justice (Office of Justice Programs) and U.S. Department of Homeland Security (Center for Prevention Programs and Partnerships / FEMA)
status: Ongoing -- a May 2026 retrospective found the DOJ cuts' damage unreversed; the Vera v. DOJ appeal is pending; an injunction barring re-obligation of the funds was extended through Sept. 1, 2026, no later extension identified. Bondi's and Noem's successors are not reported to have revisited the cuts.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (CP3 cuts and workforce reductions begin) through 2025-11 (NPR follow-up documenting unreimbursed DOJ grantees)
what_changed:
Two parallel cancellation waves hit federal public-safety and violence-prevention grantmaking in 2025. At DHS, in a single week in mid-March 2025, the department cut roughly $20 million from more than two dozen programs in a DHS wing outside its Center for Prevention Programs and Partnerships (CP3), the office responsible for terrorism and targeted-violence-prevention grants; the cut programs included counterterrorism and school-shooter-prevention initiatives; the roughly $90 million CP3 had awarded to community groups and law enforcement since 2020 was placed in jeopardy. ProPublica cited grant-reliant prevention work such as a Boston Children's Hospital intervention team for young patients showing signs of violent behavior and the Eradicate Hate prevention umbrella group; projects ProPublica described as at risk included research into far-right-extremist disengagement, a national compilation of threats to public officials, and a law-enforcement threat-assessment database, and at DOJ, hate-crimes training grant programs were in jeopardy; one recipient told ProPublica that programs based in 'sanctuary states' resisting deportation cooperation were specifically targeted. FEMA's separate Nonprofit Security Grant Program, which funds physical security upgrades at religious institutions including synagogues, was also frozen amid the same review.

On March 3, 2025, CP3 dismissed roughly 20% of its workforce through probationary-employee terminations; Director William Braniff resigned the same night, calling the terminations 'wrongful.' DHS's own framing, in a July 2025 press release, characterized $18.5 million in canceled CP3 grants as eliminating 'wasteful, misdirected spending' rather than shutting the office down, and DHS materials indicate CP3 continued operating afterward in a reduced form -- a more precise characterization than some contemporaneous reporting describing the office as fully 'shut down.'

A ProPublica investigation published June 4, 2025 found DHS had installed Thomas Fugate, a 22-year-old with a one-year-old undergraduate degree and no counterterrorism background, to lead CP3's remaining work. The same report said at least five high-profile targeted attacks had unfolded across the U.S. in the prior seven weeks, including a car bombing in California and the gunning down of two Israeli Embassy aides in Washington, and that analysts feared the spring's burst of extremist violence could extend into the summer given inflamed political tensions and the disarray of the federal agencies tasked with monitoring threats. On June 27, 2025, House Homeland Security Committee ranking members Bennie Thompson and Seth Magaziner sent a letter demanding Fugate be called to testify on current threats to the homeland. The Daily Beast then reported (published on or around July 8, 2025) that police had investigated Fugate in 2020, at age 18, over threatening text messages he allegedly sent a romantic rival in a teenage love triangle; DHS denied any police investigation occurred, calling it a parental matter, but the Cedar Park (TX) City Attorney's Office told Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in a letter that an investigation involving Fugate over 'alleged injury to a child' had in fact taken place -- Fugate was not charged either way.

By July 22, 2025, DHS itself walked back Fugate's public profile, telling reporters he was only a 'Special Assistant' who never held CP3's director role or exercised operational control over it, contradicting DHS's own earlier framing (and much contemporaneous reporting) of him as the office's head; Fugate gave an interview describing himself as 'low-level' staff.

Separately at DOJ, the Office of Justice Programs (OJP) abruptly canceled roughly 350-373 grants worth more than $800 million on April 22, 2025, terminating funding mid-cycle for programs supporting crime victims, opioid-abuse and trauma recovery, rural law enforcement, disability services, and legally mandated functions including prison-rape-elimination-act audits. Among that April 22 wave, 69 of 145 community violence intervention (CVI) grants -- worth $158 million of more than $300 million DOJ had awarded to CVI programs -- were abruptly terminated, hitting groups in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Washington D.C., and Baltimore that trained outreach workers to de-escalate conflict, connected at-risk people to social services and employment, and ran hospital-based programs for gun-violence victims; a Council on Criminal Justice analysis found more than 550 organizations affected, almost all nonprofits. That analysis, published May 27, 2025, also counted 373 terminated OJP grants originally valued at about $819.7 million, and estimated the rescinded remaining balances at about $500 million.

Five organizations -- the Vera Institute of Justice, the Center for Children and Youth Justice, Chinese for Affirmative Action, FORCE Detroit, and Health Resources in Action -- sought a preliminary injunction and reversal in a lawsuit filed May 2025; in July 2025, U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta denied the injunction and dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction and failure to state a constitutional claim, while separately calling DOJ's conduct 'shameful' and likely to harm vulnerable communities. Plaintiffs appealed to the D.C. Circuit the next day (case no. 25-5248); the appeal was argued October 14, 2025, and no ruling had been issued as of the docket's last update (June 22, 2026) -- the case remains open on appeal, not finally resolved.

Six months after the cancellations, NPR reported in November 2025 that most affected organizations still had not been reimbursed for money already spent under the canceled grants, forcing layoffs, draws on reserve funds, and reduced services; organizations that appealed the cancellations reported no response, and several had filed additional lawsuits. DOJ told NPR the government shutdown then underway -- which began roughly five months after the cancellations -- was hindering its ability to process appeals and reimbursements, though the cancellations themselves predated the shutdown by months.

A May 1, 2026 Vera Institute one-year retrospective found the damage from the DOJ cancellations had not been reversed by the pending appeal -- affected organizations remained, in the piece's own framing, 'on life support,' many having rolled back programs and reduced services, and at least one **20-year-old community-violence-intervention nonprofit, Equal Justice USA, had closed entirely as a result of the funding loss**. The piece noted that restoring funding, if it happens, would not undo harm already done to organizations that folded.

Neither of the two officials who directed the original 2025 cuts remains in office. Attorney General Pam Bondi, under whom DOJ's Office of Justice Programs implemented the April 2025 grant cancellations, was removed by President Trump on April 2, 2026 (reporting cited frustration over her handling of the Epstein files) and replaced on an acting basis by Todd Blanche, who was then confirmed by the Senate in a narrow 50-49 vote on August 8, 2026 as permanent Attorney General. DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, under whom the parallel CP3 cuts were carried out, was separately pushed out amid criticism including over her handling of two fatal shootings by federal agents during the Minneapolis immigration crackdown and over how efficiently disaster relief was distributed: President Trump announced on March 5, 2026 that she would leave, naming Sen. Markwayne Mullin to succeed her effective March 31, 2026, but the Senate confirmed Mullin 54-45 on March 23, 2026, and he was sworn in March 24, 2026; Noem moved to a newly created role as special envoy for a security initiative called the Shield of the Americas. No reporting identified at last check indicates either successor has revisited the CP3 cuts or the DOJ grant cancellations themselves.

Separately, the stipulated injunction in Vera Institute v. DOJ barring DOJ from re-obligating or further diminishing the terminated grant funds -- entered July 21, 2025 and extended to May 5, 2026 by a February 25, 2026 status report -- has been extended multiple additional times since, most recently (per an April 30, 2026 joint status report) to July 10, 2026 and (per a July 8, 2026 joint status report) currently through September 1, 2026; the parties' next joint status report, due August 28, 2026, was to determine whether the injunction is extended further, but no report content or ruling had been identified at last check. The D.C. Circuit appeal (No. 25-5248) itself remains pending with no opinion issued. A companion entry covers a distinct legal dispute in the same department and overlapping 2025 timeframe: DHS conditioning FEMA's separate state-formula Homeland Security Grant Program on states' cooperation with immigration enforcement -- courts blocked it twice in 2025, and a 26-state coalition sued again in July 2026.

title: DOJ Career-Staff Purge Guts Environment Division Enforcement Capacity
institution: U.S. Department of Justice — Environment and Natural Resources Division (ENRD), with related reassignments touching the Civil Rights and National Security Divisions
status: Ongoing and formalized — the attorney exodus continued into mid-2026, the division was renamed in June 2026 with its mission reoriented toward 'U.S. energy dominance,' and July 2026 pardons unwound Clean Air Act cases ENRD attorneys had prosecuted, leaving remaining staff to absorb the fallout
date_of_action: 2025-01-24 (initial reassignments first reported) through 2025-03-25 (formal DOJ-wide reorganization memo), with effects documented into 2026
what_changed:
In the days immediately following Trump's January 20, 2025 inauguration, DOJ began reassigning senior career officials across multiple divisions -- national security, civil rights, and public corruption staff were transferred into a newly created Sanctuary Cities Enforcement Working Group, often into roles outside their expertise. At the Environment and Natural Resources Division (ENRD), at least four section chiefs -- Tom Mariani (Environmental Enforcement, chief since 2016), Deborah Harris (Environmental Crimes), Jennifer Neumann (Appellate) and James Gette (Natural Resources), E&E News reported on January 24, 2025 -- were told they were being involuntarily transferred to the working group; Mariani chose retirement instead, leaving in February 2025. The division's civil-rights-focused work was also frozen -- DOJ reportedly halted all Civil Rights Division cases pending review.

Separately, career staff working on environmental-justice and diversity initiatives were placed on administrative leave, incoming Honors Program job offers to new attorneys were rescinded, and DOJ requested a list of probationary employees from the White House, raising concerns about a broader mass-firing push. On March 25, 2025, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a formal memorandum cementing a sweeping DOJ-wide reorganization, including further ENRD reassignments to the Office of Sanctuary Cities.

Bloomberg Law reported on October 9, 2025 that the administration's FY2026 budget request **sought $90 million for ENRD, a 22.5% drop from FY2025, and proposed cutting division staffing from 641 to 449 positions, including 79 attorney positions**; DOJ's own FY2027 budget submission later showed the $90 million level was enacted for FY2026, down from $116.2 million in FY2025. The same Bloomberg Law report said former Environmental Enforcement Section chief Tom Mariani told an American Bar Association conference in September 2025 that the section had gone from about 120 lawyers in February to between 65 and 70 (Bloomberg's article calls it the 'environmental defense section,' but Mariani led the Environmental Enforcement Section). Mariani wrote in a December 19, 2025 Justice Connection essay that the section 'has fallen from approximately 125 lawyers to fewer than 70 today.'

A January 22, 2026 memo from Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche ordered federal prosecutors to halt criminal prosecutions and dismiss all pending cases targeting 'defeat devices' used to tamper with vehicle emissions controls -- affecting more than a dozen pending criminal cases across multiple federal districts (including two separate cases indicted in Pennsylvania during 2025) and more than 20 ongoing investigations. The memo rests on an untested legal theory, championed by ENRD Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General Adam Gustafson, that defeat-device software tampering can only constitute a civil Clean Air Act violation, never a criminal one; EPA's Office of Enforcement and Compliance Assurance, under Jeffrey Hall, was separately directed to cease its own criminal investigations into the same conduct. Blanche's stated rationale was 'to ensure consistent and fair prosecution under the law, as well as to ensure the best use of Department resources.' Former DOJ appellate official Andy Mergen called the memo 'essentially a confession of error,' questioning whether the department had applied the correct legal standard in the cases it was now abandoning, and career EPA lawyers separately argued the civil-only theory contradicts the Clean Air Act's own intent.

E&E News reported on February 3, 2026 that at least 140 lawyers, at least a third of the lawyers on staff, had left ENRD in the administration's first year, according to interviews with 11 former attorneys and its own analysis; the division had employed about 400 attorneys at the start of 2025, and the 11 senior attorneys and managers interviewed alone accounted for more than 260 years of legal expertise lost. E&E reported that the enforcement sections were 'among the hardest hit': the Environmental Enforcement Section 'lost about 54, or roughly half, of its lawyers,' and the Environmental Crimes Section 'lost about 13, or 35 percent, of its attorneys.' ENRD declined to comment and did not refute the departure count. On February 5, 2026, the Environmental Integrity Project reported that DOJ had filed only 16 civil complaints in EPA-referred cases in the year after January 20, 2025, a 76 percent decline from the Biden administration's first year, according to its review of federal court records.

In June 2026, DOJ formally renamed ENRD to the Energy and Natural Resources Division, per the department's own press release, explicitly reorienting its stated mission toward 'advancing U.S. energy dominance' rather than environmental protection -- confirmed directly against justice.gov, whose ENRD landing page now carries the new name. On July 3, 2026, Trump pardoned nine people convicted of Clean Air Act violations for installing 'defeat devices' that bypass diesel-engine emissions controls (part of a larger 11-person pardon batch that included non-CAA cases), calling the recipients victims of Biden-era 'persecution' for 'fixing their car' -- which, with the January 22, 2026 memo, means the division's remaining attorneys are now unwinding cases their own predecessors built rather than only losing capacity to bring new ones. Inside Climate News reported on July 28, 2026 that, according to Mariani, the Environmental Enforcement Section was now down to less than half the size it had been on the day he left, and that former Environmental Crimes Section chief Deborah Harris said her section had 42 attorneys at its peak and was now down to half that size; Mariani wrote in Justice Connection the next day that the enforcement section 'now has less than half the lawyers that it had at the start of this administration.' Gustafson, now the division's head, told Inside Climate News that 'this attrition does not prevent us from fulfilling our mission, but it forces us to focus our affirmative litigation on cases that will achieve the greatest practical benefit for the American people,' and said in an emailed statement that the division is 'hiring in our defensive and enforcement sections, and we continue to attract great lawyers who are proud to represent the United States.' DOJ spokesperson Matthew Nies pointed to 'significant environmental enforcement and defense work,' including a $100 million air pollution penalty won at trial against a coke plant near Detroit -- a case, Inside Climate News noted, filed in 2022 by the prior administration. Separately, Law360 reported August 19, 2026, citing court filings, that a top deputy in the renamed division left the agency; the deputy's identity and reason for departure were not accessible in sourcing reviewed (Law360's full report sits behind a paywall), so this is noted as an unconfirmed-detail data point rather than asserted as fact.

title: DOJ and FBI National-Security Ranks Gutted by Departures Just as U.S. Braced for Iranian Retaliation; DHS Dissolved Its WMD-Countering Office the Same Month
institution: Department of Justice (National Security Division), Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Homeland Security
status: Reported as a completed set of departures/reorganizations as of mid-2025 reporting; sourcing reviewed for this entry did not identify a walk-back or reversal of the DOJ/FBI departures or the CWMD dissolution
date_of_action: 2025-01 through 2025-06, surfacing publicly in reporting dated 2025-06-16 (CWMD dissolution) and 2025-06-24 (DOJ/FBI staffing losses)
what_changed: As the U.S. braced for possible Iranian retaliation following the June 22, 2025 U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear sites, NBC News reported that political departures and forced-outs had hollowed out the national-security ranks of both DOJ and the FBI. DOJ's National Security Division -- the division responsible for nationwide visibility into terrorism and counterintelligence threats -- had its Law and Policy section's staff drop by as much as two-thirds, while its Counterintelligence and Export Control section lost roughly one-third of its workforce. At least 20 FBI national-security personnel departed in the three months preceding the report. Robert Wells, head of the FBI's National Security Branch, was forced out shortly after Trump took office in January 2025; David Scott, the FBI's counterterrorism chief, left in May 2025. Four ousted National Security Division officials alone represented close to 100 years of combined institutional experience, according to a former senior DOJ official who said 'the senior ranks of the FBI and DOJ's national security teams have been decimated.' Former DOJ counterintelligence chief David Laufman said the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran 'heightened the risk of Iranian retaliation in the homeland' and warned the losses could 'adversely impact' the FBI's ability to prevent Iranian attempts within the United States, given the National Security Division's role providing nationwide visibility into the threat landscape during exactly this kind of crisis. Separately, the New York Times reported the same week that DHS and the FBI had redirected national-security and counterterrorism resources toward immigration enforcement even as Iran-retaliation risk rose. DHS's FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification, published June 16, 2025, formalized the complete dissolution of the **Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction (CWMD) office -- the DHS component responsible for coordinating federal defense against chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and high-yield-explosive threats, including biosurveillance and detection-equipment procurement -- eliminating all 286 of its positions** and redistributing its $409.4 million budget across other DHS components: policy functions to the DHS Office of Strategy, Policy, and Plans; the National Biosurveillance Integration Center to the Office of Health Security; operational programs including BioWatch to CISA's Infrastructure Security Division; R&D to the U.S. Coast Guard; and $142.9 million in federal assistance programs to CISA. This dissolution is a distinct action from, and predates, the roughly one-third CISA workforce reduction documented separately in this tracker (see cisa-cyber-workforce-cuts-trump2.json) -- CWMD was a standalone DHS office with its own chemical/biological/radiological/nuclear mission, not a CISA program, though CISA absorbed some of its functions and budget in the dissolution.

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration (DOJ, FBI, and DHS leadership)
primary_proponent.role: Directed or oversaw the personnel departures and the CWMD office's budget-driven dissolution
primary_proponent.note: No single named official was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally ordering the DOJ/FBI national-security departures described here, which are attributed institutionally across DOJ and FBI leadership under the administration; the CWMD dissolution is a formal DHS budget-request decision documented in DHS's own FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification.

estimated_impact.summary: At the exact moment U.S. officials were warning of heightened Iranian retaliation risk following the June 2025 strikes on Iran's nuclear sites, DOJ's National Security Division and the FBI's national-security ranks had already lost a large share of experienced staff, and DHS had formally dissolved its dedicated office for countering chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear threats -- a convergence former officials say directly weakened the government's capacity to detect and respond to exactly this kind of crisis.
