title: Two-Thirds of the DOJ Unit That Defends Trump's Policies in Court Have Quit
institution: U.S. Department of Justice — Civil Division, Federal Programs Branch
status: Ongoing as of July 2025 reporting -- no reversal, staffing-restoration effort, or updated attrition figure identified in later sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2024-11 (post-election departures begin) through 2025-07-14 (Reuters' cumulative reporting)
what_changed: Reuters reported July 14, 2025 that **roughly 69 of the 110 attorneys who staffed DOJ's Federal Programs Branch -- the Civil Division unit responsible for defending nearly every federal policy and executive action against legal challenge, including the bulk of the lawsuits filed against the second Trump administration -- had left since the November 2024 election, a roughly two-thirds attrition rate**. The departures included at least 10 of the branch's 23 supervisors, experienced litigators who in many cases had served across multiple presidential administrations regardless of party; former officials described this level of turnover mid-administration as unprecedented for the unit. Departing attorneys gave two overlapping reasons: at least three said they left specifically over fear of being sanctioned for refusing department pressure to skew facts in court filings or otherwise violate professional ethics rules, while others described broader demoralization and exhaustion from continuously defending an unusually large volume of litigation against the administration's own policies -- work several described as being asked to defend actions they personally viewed as unconstitutional. This is a distinct, narrower thread from the department-wide attorney attrition already documented in doj-workforce-collapse-trump2.json (which separately cross-references the Civil Rights Division and ENRD exoduses); the Federal Programs Branch's specific role -- as DOJ's primary in-court defender of the administration's own actions -- makes its attrition rate a direct measure of institutional strain on the government's litigation capacity precisely where that capacity is most tested by legal challenges to the administration itself.

title: DOJ Fired More Than 100 Immigration Judges Starting in 2025, Even After Congress Funded Hiring More to Cut a Nearly 4-Million-Case Backlog
institution: Department of Justice, Executive Office for Immigration Review
status: No reinstatements reported. UN experts said information indicates at least 113 immigration judges were terminated from January 2025 to July 2026. MSPB upheld two February 2025 firings under Article II (March 2026); the Federal Circuit granted en banc review in June 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02 onward: first immigration judge fired February 5, 2025; 17 judges fired July 11-14, 2025, days after the July 4 law funding more judges; further rounds in September, November and December 2025
what_changed: Beginning in February 2025, the Justice Department's Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) fired immigration judges in successive rounds, most without a stated cause. On February 4, 2025, the day before the first firing, the corps of permanent immigration judges numbered 726 (683 immigration judges and 43 assistant chief immigration judges), according to data obtained by NPR. The first judge fired, Tania Nemer of the Cleveland Immigration Court, was dismissed in the middle of a hearing and escorted out of the building; she has since sued over her termination. On Friday, February 14, 2025, five assistant chief immigration judges and 13 incoming judges received termination notices, according to the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers (IFPTE), the union representing immigration judges. On July 4, 2025, the reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21) appropriated $3.33 billion to the Justice Department, with hiring immigration judges and support staff 'to address the backlog' as its first listed purpose, and capped the immigration judge corps at 800 effective November 2028; the backlog then stood at nearly 4 million cases. Days later, 15 immigration judges learned on Friday, July 11, that they would be placed on leave with termination effective July 22, and two more judges, in Chicago and Houston, learned on Monday, July 14, that they were being fired; IFPTE said the 17 worked in courts in California, Illinois, Louisiana, Maryland, Massachusetts, New York, Ohio, Texas, Utah, and Virginia. The termination email NPR reviewed stated: 'Pursuant to Article II of the Constitution, the Attorney General has decided not to extend your term or convert it to a permanent appointment.' IFPTE president Matt Biggs said, 'It's outrageous and against the public interest that at a time when the Congress has authorized 800 immigration judges, we are firing large numbers of immigration judges without cause,' adding, 'you can't enforce immigration laws when you fire the enforcers.' On July 17, 2025, Ila Deiss, an immigration judge on the San Francisco court since 2017, was fired by email with no advance notice and no stated reason; she told NPR she had only excellent reviews and was on track to resolve about 1,000 cases that year (NPR could not independently verify her productivity statistics), and she was three months short of 25 years of federal service, when her pension would vest. The next day DOJ fired Carolyn Feinstein, a forensic accountant in Austin who had worked seven years for DOJ's U.S. Trustee Program policing bankruptcy fraud and whose husband developed the ICEBlock app for tracking immigration agents; DOJ said she had an interest in the company holding the app's intellectual property, and a DOJ spokeswoman said the app endangers ICE officers. DOJ cited the president's Article II power to dismiss both Deiss and Feinstein. NPR reported that more than 200 career DOJ civil servants had lost their jobs in 2025 by then, according to the group Justice Connection. On August 27, 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth approved sending up to 600 military and civilian Defense Department lawyers to serve as temporary immigration judges, in groups of 150 on details of up to 179 days, according to a memo reviewed by the AP. On August 28, 2025, DOJ published a final rule in the Federal Register allowing any attorney to be designated a temporary immigration judge; previously, eligibility was limited to former immigration judges, administrative law judges, and DOJ attorneys with at least 10 years of immigration-law experience. DOJ said the change was needed to address the backlog, which the rule said peaked at about 4.1 million cases in January 2025. In September 2025, nearly 20 more judges were fired, the largest monthly total since February, and NPR reported that EOIR had lost more than 125 judges to firings and voluntary resignations in nine months, with some cases delayed as far out as 2029. By year's end the firings reached tenured judges and court supervisors, including judges in New York and San Francisco in November and December; **NPR's independent tally counted nearly 100 immigration judges fired in 2025**. In November 2025 DOJ launched a public hiring campaign for 'deportation judges'; by February 2026 it had hired 17 permanent judges, most from ICE and other DHS backgrounds, and 52 temporary judges who are military lawyers. As of February 23, 2026, there were 520 permanent immigration judges and 33 assistant chief immigration judges, and 202 judges who had been working in early 2025 were gone; EOIR had also lost over 400 legal assistants, attorney advisers and legal administrative specialists, 14 courts were operating with two or fewer permanent judges, and the San Francisco court, which lost 16 judges in 2025, was set to close with its roughly 120,000 cases moving to Concord. On March 20, 2026, the Merit Systems Protection Board's two members ruled that DOJ lawfully fired two assistant chief immigration judges dismissed in February 2025, Megan Jackler and Brandon Jaroch, under Article II, reversing an administrative judge's August 2025 ruling that ordered their reinstatement; in June 2026 the Federal Circuit granted initial en banc review of their appeal. On July 16, 2026, two UN special rapporteurs said information indicated that at least 135 judges, including at least 113 immigration judges, 13 assistant chief immigration judges and nine appellate immigration judges, had been terminated since January 2025, and that 65 of 78 removed immigration judges with public data had asylum grant rates above the national or court average.

primary_proponent.name: Pam Bondi
primary_proponent.role: Attorney General
primary_proponent.note: The termination emails stated that 'the Attorney General has decided not to extend your term or convert it to a permanent appointment,' and DOJ cited Article II authority for the dismissals; EOIR, which carries out the firings, operates under Bondi's authority.

estimated_impact.summary: People facing deportation, including asylum seekers whose cases decide whether they are sent back to possible persecution or torture, have lost experienced judges: the permanent immigration judge corps shrank by about a quarter in a year, some cases were pushed out as far as 2029, and 14 courts were left with two or fewer permanent judges. UN experts warn that the removals, in which 65 of 78 removed judges with public data had above-average asylum grant rates, can deprive people of a meaningful opportunity to present their claims, with potentially irreversible consequences. NPR reported that the replacements include 'deportation judge' hires, mostly from ICE and other DHS backgrounds, and military lawyers serving as temporary judges. The losses came while Congress was spending $3.33 billion to hire more judges to cut a backlog of nearly 4 million cases.

title: DOJ Sued 21 States to End In-State College Tuition for Undocumented Students, Winning 5 and Losing at Least 1
institution: Department of Justice / state higher-education tuition policy nationwide
status: Ongoing, mixed outcomes -- 5 states (Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois) resolved on terms favorable to DOJ; a Minnesota federal judge ruled in March 2026 that state's Dream Act may stand; litigation against additional states continued through at least September 2026
date_of_action: 2025-04-28 (EO 14287 signed) through 2026-09 (litigation ongoing against additional states)
what_changed: Following Trump's April 28, 2025 executive order 'Protecting American Communities from Criminal Aliens' (and the related EO 14218, 'Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Open Borders'), the Department of Justice began a sustained litigation campaign against states that let undocumented students pay in-state college tuition rates or receive state financial aid, arguing the practice unlawfully discriminates against U.S. citizens from other states who pay higher out-of-state rates. DOJ filed its first suit against Texas on June 4, 2025; Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Trump-aligned Republican, signed a consent agreement the same day the suit was filed, immediately ending the state's 24-year-old law -- a turnaround fast enough that the Texas Tribune and other observers raised questions about coordinated state-federal collusion rather than adversarial litigation. DOJ then expanded the campaign through the rest of 2025 and 2026, ultimately suing 21 states including Minnesota, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Illinois, California, Virginia, Nebraska, New Jersey, Kansas, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maryland, Colorado, New York, Connecticut, Vermont, Arizona, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington. Five states -- Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, and Illinois -- resolved on terms favorable to DOJ, ending their programs. The campaign was not uniformly successful: a federal judge in Minnesota ruled in March 2026 that the state's Dream Act could stand, rejecting DOJ's challenge. As one documented financial-scale example, DOJ's own complaint against Arizona stated that 432 people without legal immigration status received in-state tuition at Arizona State University in fall 2025 alone, totaling $10.5 million in reduced tuition at that single school in a single semester. Advocacy groups estimated **roughly 500,000 undocumented students nationally could lose access to affordable in-state tuition if the campaign succeeds everywhere it has been filed**.

title: DOJ Cuts Over 4,000 Jobs at FBI, ATF, DEA, and National Security Division While Immigration Enforcement Gets More Funding

what_changed: Justice Department management-unit records obtained by Reuters under the Freedom of Information Act show the Trump administration cut more than 4,000 employees from several of the DOJ's top law-enforcement components even as the administration publicly vowed to get tough on crime. status: OCDETF remains closed. DOJ reinstated 31 staff in early 2026 (9 returning CRS, 6 ATJ, 16 OCDETF), all detailed within EOUSA; by June 2026, 5 of the 9 were expected to stay detailed to Sept. 30 and 22 others no longer CRS staff. Feb. 2026: CRS restart plans 'not yet set.' No ruling reported.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OCDETF case-transfer order) through 2026-06 (reinstated CRS staff still on detail; summary-judgment briefing)
what_changed:
In September 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi approved the most sweeping Justice Department reorganization in two decades, which, according to DOJ documents reported by Reuters, would cut about 275 positions department-wide and eliminate or involuntarily reassign about 140 employees. The plan closed the Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETF) and eliminated the Community Relations Service (CRS) and the Office for Access to Justice as standalone units; it also merged the Tax Division into the Criminal and Civil divisions and folded other offices together, including moving DOJ's INTERPOL liaison office into the U.S. Marshals Service. The reorganization built on an order the Deputy Attorney General had issued July 23, 2025, directing OCDETF -- established under President Reagan in 1982 as the Attorney General's centerpiece program for coordinating multi-agency drug-cartel and organized-crime investigations -- to transfer all of its 5,000-plus active cases to newly created Homeland Security Task Forces, a structure created by a Trump executive order on his first day in office that did not become fully operational until September 2025.

DOJ ordered OCDETF operations shut down by September 30, 2025, and its last employees departed through a Reduction in Force on October 31, 2025, ending a 43-year program that, per its own final report, had conducted more than 37,200 investigations, dismantled or significantly disrupted over 21,100 criminal enterprises, convicted more than 321,000 defendants, and seized $13.4 billion in cash and property and over 870,000 weapons -- including the investigation that led to the conviction of Sinaloa Cartel leader Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzman.

In a notification signed July 9, 2025, DOJ told Congress it 'plans to eliminate OCDETF as a standalone $547 million appropriation,' and the administration wanted $500 million to go directly to other DOJ components instead, Roll Call reported. Congress had directed $547 million annually to OCDETF for the two prior fiscal years and included that funding rate in the continuing resolution then in effect; the Republican-led Senate Appropriations Committee's report said eliminating OCDETF's appropriations account was 'infeasible without further consultations between the Committee and the Department,' and veteran House appropriator Harold Rogers told a September markup that 'our commitment to the work of the task forces can't be underestimated or understated,' but DOJ disbanded it regardless, characterizing the move as a reorganization rather than a closure. Thomas Padden, OCDETF's acting director during the closure, wrote that **the replacement structure -- which places more emphasis on immigration offenses and human smuggling than on joint law enforcement efforts against organized crime and drug trafficking, and deprioritizes financial investigations -- leaves America 'more vulnerable to organized crime threats'**; former Rep. Matt Cartwright, D-Pa., who had chaired the House Appropriations subcommittee overseeing DOJ funding, called the unilateral fund repurposing illegal under the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, saying he 'could not imagine DOJ taking this kind of unilateral action' in his 12 years on the subcommittee.

The Community Relations Service (CRS) -- a DOJ agency created by Title X of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, nicknamed 'America's Peacemaker,' that mediates racial and ethnic conflict and had deployed to incidents including the unrest following George Floyd's 2020 killing -- was slated in DOJ's FY2026 budget summary to close all offices by the end of FY2025 with no FY2026 funding. On September 29, 2025, DOJ sent Reduction-in-Force notices, effective October 31, to 14 of CRS's 15 remaining active employees, according to the court's later order. On October 30, 2025, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani (Boston) declined to issue a temporary restraining order blocking the terminations, sought by plaintiffs including the Ethical Society of Police and two NAACP branches, who alleged the dismantling violated the Civil Rights Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, and separation of powers. Talwani found the plaintiffs 'have made a strong showing that they are likely to succeed on the merits, where Defendants concede that only Congress, and not the executive branch, may eliminate a Congressionally created agency,' but held they had not shown irreparable harm sufficient for injunctive relief while the case proceeded.

The Office for Access to Justice -- established in 2010 to expand legal aid and promote fairness in the criminal justice system -- was hit the same way, with RIF notices issued September 29, 2025. On November 2, 2025, DOJ realigned CRS, its functions and its one remaining employee from a stand-alone component into a unit within the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys (EOUSA), DOJ later told the court. The layoffs at both offices were reversed in January 2026: on January 9, DOJ's human resources office sent letters to former CRS and Access to Justice employees rescinding their RIF notices, Bloomberg Law reported. In a January 13 court filing, DOJ said it had rescinded the CRS notices 'as a matter of administrative discretion,' sending them to the 13 employees who had been separated by RIF, resignation or retirement; the fourteenth, DOJ said in a later filing, had been reassigned to another DOJ position before the layoffs took effect. The January 13 filing did not say whether the employees would resume CRS duties, and the plaintiffs asked the court to assess the impact; Talwani had not yet ruled on their preliminary-injunction motion. Bloomberg Law noted that the letters went out less than a week after congressional spending leaders reached a bipartisan deal that would fund CRS in fiscal 2026 -- funding that, as Reuters reported, the administration's budget proposal 'contained no money for' -- and that a short-term spending extension passed in 2025 also barred federal worker layoffs during the lapse in government funding; the plaintiffs argued in court that the November continuing resolution required the rescission and reinstatement.

The fiscal 2026 spending law signed January 23, 2026 appropriated $20 million for CRS. It also gave $300 million, down from $547 million, to OCDETF's former account, renamed 'Interagency Crime and Drug Enforcement,' limited to the purposes for which the money was obligated in fiscal 2024; the accompanying joint explanatory statement said the money was provided 'to continue the inter-governmental drug interdiction work' of OCDETF and, because DOJ was 'instead participating in a new task force co-led by the Department of Homeland Security,' directed DOJ to report quarterly on how it is used. On February 11, 2026, DOJ told the court that 12 CRS employees had been reinstated retroactive to November 1, 2025 (one employee's rescission was withdrawn at the employee's request) and that nine of them reported for work on February 9. It counted 31 reinstated employees at CRS -- the nine returning CRS staff, six reassigned from the Office for Access to Justice and 16 from OCDETF -- but said all 31 were on detail within EOUSA for developmental training, with salaries not charged to CRS, and that specific 'plans for resumption of operations of CRS' were 'not yet set'; the plaintiffs said CRS personnel were not performing CRS functions. By June 2026, DOJ said five of the nine CRS returnees were expected to remain on detail through September 30, 2026, and that the other 22 reinstated employees 'are no longer considered CRS employees.' The plaintiffs moved for summary judgment on March 30, 2026 and DOJ cross-moved on May 8; briefing ran into June 2026, and no ruling has been reported. No reversal has been reported for OCDETF, whose closure and case transfer to the Homeland Security Task Force structure remain in effect.

title: DOJ withholds $88 million in appropriated anti-trafficking victim services funding
institution: DOJ Office for Victims of Crime (OVC), Office of Justice Programs
status: Ongoing (as of Nov. 2025 letter; funds not yet released)
what_changed: On October 1, 2025, DOJ's Office for Victims of Crime **allowed grants funding more than 100 anti-trafficking victim service providers to lapse without issuing new grants, cutting off services for at least 5,000 trafficking survivors nationwide**; the lapse coincided with that day's federal government shutdown, which separately affected services for over 17,000 survivors. As of a November 14, 2025 letter, OVC had still not released any notice of funding opportunity for the $88 million Congress appropriated to these programs (authorized under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act) in FY25 -- 45 days after the lapse. A coalition of 45 national anti-trafficking and anti-violence organizations plus 22 state and local organizations (Freedom Network USA, Polaris, International Rescue Committee, Kids in Need of Defense, and others) wrote directly to Attorney General Pam Bondi, Deputy Assistant Attorney General Maureen Henneberg (Office of Justice Programs), and Acting OVC Director Katherine D. Schmitt, urging DOJ to release the FY25 funds and, in the interim, offer non-competitive one-year awards to existing FY22 grantees so survivors don't lose access while a new funding-opportunity process runs (which the letter itself estimates can take multiple months). An earlier, separate letter -- signed by 74 advocacy and faith-based groups and reported October 3, 2025 -- had already warned lawmakers that the freeze would strip survivors of housing, counseling, and legal support.

title: DOJ Lost Over a Quarter of Its Attorneys in a Year, With Its Entry-Level Recruitment Pipeline Frozen and a Growing Public Archive of Resignation Letters
institution: U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) -- department-wide attrition, distinct from this tracker's Civil Rights Division- and Environment Division-specific entries
status: Ongoing: Justice Connection's April 2026 count puts attorney departures at 3,402 through January 2026; the one-year experience-requirement waiver for new prosecutors remains in effect through February 28, 2027, and AUSAs face a 25-open-matters caseload floor reported in July 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-01 (hiring freeze, Honors Program cancellation) through 2025-11 (Justice Connection's ~5,500-departure estimate, farewell-letters archive reporting)
what_changed:
President Trump's January 20, 2025 government-wide federal hiring freeze immediately triggered cancellation of the Attorney General's Honors Program -- DOJ's 'premier' entry-level attorney recruitment pipeline, in place since 1953 and typically responsible for more than 100 hires per year from top law schools. Accepted job offers were revoked, with rescission emails citing the freeze directly; the program was later reopened for the 2025-26 recruiting cycle, but the initial cancellation disrupted a full incoming class and, per legal-trade reporting, left the program with diminished appeal to law students and law-school career offices. The freeze also paused support-staff hiring in at least some U.S. Attorneys' offices: the Southern District of New York's support-staff employment page, updated January 30, 2025, said that, 'due to the current federal hiring freeze,' the office was 'not currently accepting applications for support staff positions.' By June 21, 2025, Trump himself stated that more than 4,000 DOJ employees had accepted voluntary-departure packages under the department-wide 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation program, with officials signaling further rounds of workforce reductions were expected -- a documented mid-year checkpoint between the initial January 2025 hiring freeze and the fuller attrition below.

Departures continued over the following months. The Washington Post reported on November 10, 2025 that in 2024 'roughly 10,000 attorneys worked across the Justice Department and its components, including the FBI,' and that 'the department did not provide a breakdown of attorney departures, but officials did not deny that widespread vacancies exist.' Replacement hiring filled only a fraction of the resulting vacancies, with the process snarled, per the Post, by 'a lack of qualified candidates, bureaucratic delays and hiring freezes,' and reporting found new hires skewed toward candidates with more overtly political or ideological alignment with the administration, including hires drawn from Republican congressional offices and conservative advocacy groups rather than DOJ's traditional recruitment channels. The understaffing forced DOJ attorneys to repeatedly seek case-schedule delays across multiple active litigation matters, per the ABA Journal.

Justice Connection, a support network for departed DOJ staff founded by former DOJ Civil Division attorney Stacey Young, estimated, according to the Post's November 10, 2025 report (which called it 'an advocacy group that has been tracking departures'), that roughly 5,500 people -- not exclusively attorneys -- had left the department via resignation, transfer, buyout, or termination since January 2025; by November 23, 2025, Young said the cumulative purge had 'eclipsed 5,000 employees.' Justice Connection also maintains a public 'farewell messages' page (thejusticeconnection.org/farewell-messages) that had grown, by that point, into a chronicled archive of DOJ resignation letters, including from senior officials, describing political interference, retaliation, and pressure to pursue cases some departing attorneys viewed as targeting the administration's perceived critics rather than legitimate law-enforcement priorities.

This entry documents DOJ's department-wide attorney attrition and recruitment-pipeline collapse; narrower threads already tracked in this database document specific divisions in more depth: the Civil Rights Division's roughly 75% attorney exodus, the Environment and Natural Resources Division's career-staff purge, and the Civil Division's Federal Programs Branch, which lost roughly two-thirds of its attorneys defending the administration's own policies in court by July 2025.

A November 26, 2025 Washington Post analysis found the department-wide pattern extending to DOJ's ability to secure indictments at all -- federal grand juries had begun declining to return charges prosecutors sought, and judges had admonished DOJ prosecutors for misconduct at least three times since November 2025, a marked departure from historical norms (as a baseline, DOJ secured indictments in all but six of roughly 130,000 federal cases charged in 2016). Lindsey Halligan's installation as interim U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia and grand juries' partial rejection of her case against James Comey were the Post's lead example of this broader trend, not an isolated incident.

A December 17, 2025 Reuters analysis, citing Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, found **the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia's criminal-complaint dismissal rate had risen to 21% over an eight-week span in mid-2025, compared to a 0.5% rate over the prior decade**, and tied the pattern to more than 2,900 DOJ attorney departures from January through November 2025, a total that public records show is 'triple the number of those who left in each of the previous four years,' per Reuters -- a separate count, on a different measurement window, from the Washington Post and Justice Connection figures already documented above. Reuters also documented a dismissed gun case after an unlawful backpack search lacking probable cause, improper public statements by FBI Director Kash Patel and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche that courts cited in vindictive-prosecution rulings, and federal courts quashing DOJ subpoenas for bad faith. Former federal prosecutors quoted by Reuters attributed the pattern to institutional-knowledge loss from the mass departures documented above, combined with political pressure to bring cases before they were ready.

A DOJ attorney wrote in a February 19, 2026 court filing in a civil lawsuit against the IRS, surfaced by journalist Scott MacFarlane and reported by The New Republic in May 2026, that 'the Appellate Section has lost over 40 percent of its attorneys since February 2025, due to retirement, resignation, or temporary transfer'; the ABA Journal repeated the figure. DOJ later made a formal, dated policy response to the recruitment-pipeline collapse. On March 13, 2026, DOJ headquarters sent U.S. Attorneys' offices nationwide a memo titled "Suspension of Attorney One Year Experience Requirement," waiving the department's longstanding requirement that newly hired federal prosecutors have at least one year of legal practice experience -- permitting hiring directly from law school with only a law degree and active state bar membership. The suspension, which cites an "exigent hiring need for attorneys across the department," remains in effect through February 28, 2027. Job postings reflecting the change appeared in multiple U.S. Attorneys' offices with documented attrition, including Minnesota, Southern Florida, Montana, Alaska, and Louisiana. Harvard Law School affiliates and former federal prosecutors quoted in press coverage said the policy could expand access to public-service legal careers but risks oversight and mentorship gaps for prosecutors trying cases without prior practice experience.

Justice Connection published its own detailed "By the Numbers" accounting on April 7, 2026, covering the full period from January 2025 through January 2026 -- a later, more granular count than the earlier estimates above. Drawing on Office of Personnel Management data, Justice Connection's count puts DOJ's attorney corps at 12,955 as of December 31, 2024 (a larger baseline than the Post's ~10,000, which included the FBI) and documents 3,402 attorney departures between January 2025 and January 2026 -- about 26%, or "over a quarter of its legal machinery in a year," per the group's own framing.

The breakdown: 1,421 departures from DOJ headquarters (including 338 in leadership roles), 1,356 from U.S. Attorneys' Offices (including 260 leaders), and 370 from the Executive Office for Immigration Review. The average departing employee had 16.6 years of federal service (over 22 years among departing leaders), and 2,069 of the 3,402 resigned before becoming eligible for retirement -- consistent with departures driven by working conditions rather than planned retirements. This is a later, more precise count from the same organization whose earlier ~5,500 estimate appears above; that estimate covered all staff, not only attorneys, as reported in November 2025, while this count covers attorneys over the full January 2025-January 2026 year. In May 2026, The New Republic (May 4) and the ABA Journal (May 5, citing The New Republic) set the ~5,500 all-staff estimate against a ~10,000 attorney baseline (the same number the Post had reported for 2024); the two numbers cover different groups, so that comparison does not measure attorney attrition.

DOJ leadership imposed a new caseload floor on the prosecutors it has retained -- in the weeks before a July 14, 2026 Bloomberg Law report, the deputy attorney general's office told all 93 U.S. Attorney's offices that Assistant U.S. Attorneys must maintain at least 25 open matters at all times, with DOJ leadership monitoring case-management databases to flag prosecutors falling below that line for possible transfer. DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels defended the floor as 'the bare minimum' -- noting hundreds of AUSAs already juggle 100+ open matters -- and framed it as a tool to push out 'low productivity AUSAs.' Former DOJ official Mark Yancey and other critics warned the quota risks pressuring prosecutors, especially those handling long-running white-collar, corruption, or national-security matters that can occupy a full docket for months, into bringing weak or premature charges to hit the number. This is a direct operational consequence of the attorney-corps attrition documented above -- a formal productivity mandate imposed on the shrunken remaining workforce rather than a new departure or hiring datapoint.

title: Trump Halted Labor Department Contractor Civil-Rights Enforcement in His First Week, Killing a Near-Complete BAE Systems Sexual-Harassment Case
institution: Department of Labor / Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs (OFCCP)
status: Complete -- EO 11246 revoked Jan. 21, 2025; all EO 11246 cases, incl. the near-complete BAE probe, closed without resolution. DOL's final rule rescinding the EO 11246 regulations takes effect Oct. 26, 2026; CWIT's injunction against the DEI certification mandate is on appeal (as of Sept. 2026).
date_of_action: 2025-01-21 (Executive Order 14173 revoking EO 11246) through 2025-01-24 (DOL acting secretary's cease-and-desist order)
what_changed: On January 21, 2025 -- the day after his inauguration -- Trump signed Executive Order 14173, which revoked Executive Order 11246, the 1965 order requiring federal contractors to comply with anti-discrimination and affirmative-action obligations, and ordered the Department of Labor office enforcing it to immediately cease holding contractors responsible for affirmative action. Acting Labor Secretary Vincent Micone followed on January 24 with an order directing DOL staff to 'immediately cease and desist all investigative and enforcement activity under the rescinded Executive Order 11246,' including all pending cases, conciliation agreements, investigations and complaints, and putting the office's disability (Section 503) and veterans (VEVRAA) reviews in abeyance. This effectively shut down the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs' active enforcement docket, including a nearly-complete two-year investigation into BAE Systems -- a defense contractor holding roughly $8 billion in annual federal contracts for weapons, vehicles, and cybersecurity tools -- over findings that **male managers at a Norfolk, Virginia Navy shipyard had demanded oral sex and other sexual contact from female employees in exchange for promotions and overtime pay, and that Black women had been paid and promoted at lower rates than men**. Investigators had been preparing to propose a resolution requiring BAE to make seven-figure payouts to affected workers and adopt reforms, or risk losing its federal contracts; that resolution was never presented as a result of the halt. In July 2025 the office announced it would administratively close all of its pending compliance reviews and resume processing the disability and veterans complaints it had held in abeyance. On August 21, 2026, the Labor Department published a final rule rescinding the EO 11246 implementing regulations, effective October 26, 2026. The EO 11246 revocation's downstream effects reached beyond individual enforcement cases to the organizations that had grown up around it. Chicago Women in Trades (CWIT), a nonprofit founded in 1981 in direct response to Johnson's original executive order and the resulting Labor Department requirement that federal contractors make good-faith efforts to place women on construction sites, sued the Trump administration in February 2025 (Chicago Women in Trades v. Trump, N.D. Ill.) over Trump's anti-DEI executive orders, including a certification provision requiring federal contractors and grantees to certify they do not operate DEI programs 'promoting DEI that violate any applicable Federal anti-discrimination laws' -- with knowing false certifications exposed to civil and criminal penalties. U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly granted CWIT a temporary restraining order in March 2025 and, on April 14, 2025, a preliminary injunction barring DOL from terminating one of CWIT's grants and from enforcing the certification requirement against any grantee or contractor nationwide; in May 2025 he declined to extend the grant protection to CWIT's other federal funding. CWIT -- whose participants are roughly 70% Black and Latina, and which as of January 2025 drew about 40% of its annual budget from Labor Department grants across five federal programs -- was still in limbo as the case went on, NPR reported in November 2025, with Executive Director Jayne Vellinga saying, 'There's a lot of threats out there but no clarity on what is illegal DEI.' The government appealed the injunction to the Seventh Circuit in July 2025, after the Supreme Court's Trump v. CASA ruling limited injunctions that cover nonparties; on October 30, 2025, Kennelly refused to narrow it, finding that blocking enforcement of the certification requirement against all recipients of federal funds was necessary to give CWIT complete relief. The Seventh Circuit heard argument on January 30, 2026, and had not ruled as of mid-September 2026.

estimated_impact.summary: Women workers at BAE Systems' Norfolk, Virginia Navy shipyard, who federal investigators found had been pressed for sex in exchange for promotions and overtime and, for Black women, paid and promoted less than men, lost a nearly finished two-year case before any payout or reform could be imposed. Investigators had been preparing to propose seven-figure payouts to workers and reforms, backed by the threat to BAE's roughly $8 billion in annual federal contracts. The same January 24, 2025 order closed every other pending EO 11246 case, conciliation agreement, investigation and complaint against federal contractors, and the Labor Department's final rule erasing the EO 11246 regulations takes effect October 26, 2026. The accompanying DEI certification demand also threatened Chicago Women in Trades, which drew about 40% of its budget from Labor Department grants.

title: Labor Department Lost 20% of Its Staff to Buyouts While Cutting $577 Million in Anti-Child-Labor and Wage-Enforcement Grants -- Then Warned Remaining Staff They Could Face Criminal Charges for Talking to Reporters
institution: U.S. Department of Labor, including its Bureau of International Labor Affairs (ILAB)
status: As of May 2025 reporting, further reductions-in-force were anticipated following a February 2025 White House order for agencies to draw up 'reorganization' plans; DOL did not confirm departure figures or comment on operational impact when asked by The Guardian.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (ILAB grant cuts) through 2025-05-03 (Guardian report on cumulative workforce departures)
what_changed: By early May 2025, nearly 2,700 Department of Labor employees -- about 20% of the department's workforce -- had left via retirement, early retirement, deferred-resignation buyouts, or the government-wide 'Fork in the Road' program, according to Guardian reporting drawing on department employees. In March 2025, DOL cut **$577 million in international labor grants, eliminating years of ongoing work and research and canceling roughly $237 million in funds not yet disbursed; these grants funded core functions including researching and combating forced and child labor abroad** and enforcing basic labor-rights standards tied to U.S. free trade agreements. The cuts hit DOL's Bureau of International Labor Affairs (ILAB) especially hard: staffing there was cut by more than a third through buyouts and retirement incentives, with one ILAB employee estimating about half the bureau's staff had taken buyout offers following the grant cuts and threats of further terminations. Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer's office separately exempted OSHA and MSHA safety inspectors specifically from the broader federal resignation program, an acknowledgment that cutting those safety-critical roles carried risks the administration wanted to avoid -- a protection not extended to ILAB or other affected offices. Last month before the Guardian's report, Jihun Han, chief of staff to Secretary Chavez-DeRemer, sent a staff-wide email warning employees they could face criminal charges for speaking to journalists about agency business. A Bureau of Labor Statistics employee told the Guardian the cuts were 'catastrophic,' warning that 'all of the core aspects of working life can no longer be assumed' given the department was already 'chronically underfunded for a long time.' A DOL spokesperson said the department could not confirm the number of employees who had taken retirement or resignation offers or were on administrative leave, and did not comment further on operational impact.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Labor
primary_proponent.note: Her office implemented the exemption protecting OSHA/MSHA safety inspectors from the resignation program while other DOL offices, including ILAB, absorbed comparable or larger staffing losses; her chief of staff, Jihun Han, sent the staff-wide email warning of potential criminal charges for talking to journalists.

estimated_impact.summary: The combined ~20% workforce loss and $577 million in canceled international labor grants strips capacity from core DOL functions including wage-and-hour enforcement, safety oversight outside the specifically-exempted OSHA/MSHA inspector corps, and congressionally mandated research and enforcement on forced and child labor tied to U.S. trade agreements -- functions a Bureau of Labor Statistics employee described as underpinning basic assumptions about working life in the U.S. and abroad. The chief-of-staff warning about criminal liability for speaking to reporters raises a separate press-freedom/whistleblower-chilling concern layered on top of the staffing cuts themselves.

title: DOT Ties Transportation Grants to Birth/Marriage Rates and Immigration-Enforcement Compliance, Rescinds Environmental-Justice Guidance ('Duffy Directive'), Immigration Condition Later Enjoined
institution: U.S. Department of Transportation
status: Immigration condition struck down: a federal judge vacated it and permanently enjoined DOT from imposing it on the 22 plaintiff states (Nov. 2025), and DOT dropped its appeal (Jan. 2026). No court ruling on the birth/marriage-rate preference was found as of Sept. 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-01-29 (birth/marriage-rate order), 2025-03-10 (environmental-justice memo rescission), and 2025-04-24 (immigration-compliance funding threat), with litigation through 2026-01-22 (preliminary injunction 2025-06-19, permanent injunction 2025-11-04, appeal dismissed 2026-01-22)
what_changed: One day after being sworn in, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy issued an order on January 29, 2025 directing that DOT grants, loans, and contracts, including DOT-supported state contracts, 'give preference to communities with marriage and birth rates higher than the national average' -- 'to the extent practicable, relevant, appropriate, and consistent with law' -- effective upon signing. The same order listed 'local compliance or cooperation with Federal immigration enforcement' among the goals DOT funding should prioritize, and companion memos released the same day sought to end support for projects addressing climate change or racial and gender inequality. Duffy formally executed the climate and equity piece on March 10, 2025, rescinding two Biden-era DOT memos (issued in 2021 and 2023) that had directed state agencies to factor 'social justice and environmental agenda' considerations -- including disadvantaged-community representation in project planning, selection, and design -- into how Bipartisan Infrastructure Law funding was spent. DOT's own announcement said the memos 'added meritless and costly burdens related to greenhouse gas emissions and equity initiatives' and had no basis in statute. On April 24, 2025, Duffy sent a letter to all DOT funding recipients -- the 'Duffy Directive' -- warning that **failure to cooperate 'generally with Federal authorities in the enforcement of Federal law,' which it said includes cooperating with ICE, 'will jeopardize your continued receipt of Federal financial assistance from DOT and could lead to a loss of Federal funding' -- threatening infrastructure funding unrelated to immigration as leverage**, and DOT began writing an immigration-enforcement condition into grant agreements. Twenty states sued DOT and Duffy in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island on May 13, 2025 over the immigration-enforcement funding condition, arguing it unlawfully forced states to divert law-enforcement resources to federal civil immigration enforcement or lose transportation funds. On June 19, 2025, Chief Judge John J. McConnell Jr. granted a preliminary injunction barring DOT from implementing or enforcing the immigration-enforcement condition as to the plaintiff states and their governmental subdivisions, finding the states faced losing billions of dollars in federal funding; on July 17 he extended it to the District of Columbia and Kentucky, newly added plaintiffs. DOT did not appeal the preliminary injunction. On November 4, 2025, McConnell granted the states summary judgment, declared the condition unlawful, ordered it vacated from all grant agreements DOT administers, and permanently enjoined DOT from imposing it or otherwise conditioning transportation funding on state cooperation with federal civil immigration enforcement; on November 18 he clarified that the injunction covers all 22 plaintiff states and their local subdivisions and ordered DOT to strip the condition from future grant agreements and notify grant recipients that any such existing conditions are void. DOT appealed on January 2, 2026, then voluntarily dismissed the appeal, which the First Circuit closed on January 22, 2026.

primary_proponent.role: U.S. Secretary of Transportation
primary_proponent.note: Personally signed and announced both the January 29, 2025 birth/marriage-rate funding order and the April 24, 2025 immigration-enforcement funding threat.

estimated_impact.summary: DOT threatened to withhold transportation funding -- money states use to keep roads, bridges, transit and rail safe and running -- from any state that would not cooperate with federal civil immigration enforcement, a condition the court found put billions of dollars in federal funding and ongoing projects at risk and threatened the health and safety of transportation services integral to daily life, until the court vacated it and permanently barred it for the 22 plaintiff states in November 2025. Separately, the January 2025 order directs DOT grants, loans and contracts to favor communities with above-average marriage and birth rates, a criterion unrelated to transportation need, a preference no court has ruled on in reporting reviewed, and DOT rescinded Biden-era guidance that had directed infrastructure spending to consider disadvantaged communities and climate impacts.

title: States Sue Twice Over DOT's Withholding of Billions in EV-Charging Infrastructure Funds
institution: Department of Transportation; Federal Highway Administration
status: Two lawsuits: the first, over the $5B NEVI Formula Program, resulted in a June 24, 2025 preliminary injunction and a January 23, 2026 summary judgment finding DOT/FHWA violated the Administrative Procedure Act, releasing roughly $1 billion to 20 states and D.C. A second lawsuit, filed December 16, 2025, challenges DOT's continued withholding of the separate $1.8B Charging and Fueling Infrastructure Grant program and a ~$350 million companion program.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial DOT funding halt) through 2026-01-23 (summary judgment in the first lawsuit); second lawsuit filed 2025-12-16
what_changed: In February 2025, DOT ordered states to halt spending on EV-charging infrastructure funded by the bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, rescinding prior program guidance and revoking states' approved deployment plans. Seventeen states, led by Washington, Colorado, and California, sued in May 2025 (State of Washington v. U.S. DOT, W.D. Wash., case 2:25-cv-00848) over the freeze of the $5 billion National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program. U.S. District Judge Tana Lin issued a preliminary injunction on June 24, 2025 lifting the freeze, and on January 23, 2026 granted summary judgment for the plaintiffs, ruling DOT and the Federal Highway Administration acted unlawfully and in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act, releasing roughly $1 billion to 20 states and D.C. Separately, on December 16, 2025, 16 states and D.C. -- led again by California and Colorado -- filed a second federal lawsuit in Seattle, this one over DOT's continued withholding of **more than $2 billion across two different EV-charging programs: the $1.8 billion Charging and Fueling Infrastructure (CFI) Grant program and a roughly $350 million companion program**, both also created by the infrastructure law. The Government Accountability Office separately found, in its broader review of administration-wide impoundment practices, that DOT's handling of NEVI funds specifically violated the Impoundment Control Act (see this project's Cabinet-Level entry on Vought and the Impoundment Control Act for that broader pattern, which this entry's litigation-specific detail supplements).

title: Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency Budget Cut Two Years Running, Slashing Recovery Missions for Missing Servicemembers
institution: Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA)
status: Ongoing: FY2026 cuts are already reducing recovery missions, and FY2027's budget is capped even lower still. New Pentagon overseer Anthony Tata (assigned June 2026) has pledged to seek roughly $40 million in restored funding via the FY2027 NDAA, but that bill remains stalled in the Senate after a July 14, 2026 cloture vote failed, with no House-Senate conference yet convened -- restoration is not close to secured. DPAA nonetheless conducted its first China recovery mission in 13 years, July-early September 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Hegseth-era Pentagon-wide cost-cutting first put DPAA's budget at risk) through 2026 (FY2026 cuts implemented; FY2027 funding capped)
what_changed: As part of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's broader Pentagon-wide cost-cutting purge that began in February 2025, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency -- the agency responsible for recovering and identifying America's missing servicemembers from past conflicts -- saw its budget cut across two consecutive fiscal years. The FY2026 budget request was $171.3 million for Operation and Maintenance, an 11% reduction from the previously planned $191.4 million, including the loss of 26 civilian billets; the agency's total budget fell from $185 million in FY2025 to $167 million as enacted for FY2026, with FY2027 projected to be capped at $160 million. The funding shortfall forced DPAA to **cut its recovery and investigative teams operating in Vietnam from 27 to seven and in Laos from 13 to five, and reduced planned field missions from 105 to 66 -- a 59% reduction**. In June 2026, Anthony Tata was assigned Pentagon oversight of DPAA and sought to reassure affected families that he had Trump and Hegseth's full support, pledging to work toward restoring roughly $40 million of the cuts through a bill then pending before Congress. A July 26, 2026 South Texas Public Radio / American Homefront Project report ('Time is passing') adds a Cambodia-specific figure this entry did not previously capture: recovery/investigative teams there were also cut, from three to one, alongside the Vietnam and Laos cuts already documented. As of that report, no restoration funding had been secured -- Sen. Fischer's push (a bill she introduced in the Senate, distinct from the general FY2026/FY2027 NDAA cycle) remained pending, and Tata's outreach to Congress had not yet produced enacted relief. Separately, CRS's DPAA budget primer (updated 2026-03-09) shows the enacted FY2026 NDAA authorized and Congress appropriated DPAA's full agency-wide budget at $171.8 million, matching the administration's original request exactly -- indicating that a $19 million above-request add Sen. Fischer secured at the Senate Armed Services Committee markup stage in July 2025 did not survive to final enactment. (This $171.8 million CRS figure is DPAA's total appropriated budget across all accounts; it is not directly comparable to the $167 million O&M-specific figure already cited in this entry from DPAA's own O&M budget justification, and this entry does not attempt to reconcile the two beyond noting neither reflects the requested restoration.) Fischer's FY2027 NDAA push for the $40 million restoration referenced in this entry was confirmed still pending as of a June 11, 2026 press release, in which she urged 'swift passage through the Senate' -- consistent with this entry's existing framing that the restoration is sought, not secured. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 32): the FY2027 NDAA vehicle carrying Fischer's restoration provision remains unenacted and is now specifically stalled -- the House passed its own version (H.R. 8800) 219-206 on July 22, 2026, but the Senate's companion bill (S. 4784, reported by the Senate Armed Services Committee 18-9 on June 15, 2026) failed a cloture vote on July 14, 2026 after Senate Democrats blocked floor consideration over objections to the Iran war and the bill's overall defense-spending growth, unrelated to the DPAA provision itself. No House-Senate conference has been established as of this update, meaning the $40 million DPAA restoration remains contingent on a broader defense-policy fight that has nothing to do with POW/MIA recovery specifically. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 48): despite the funding squeeze, DPAA recovery teams conducted a previously undocumented mission in China from roughly July through early September 2026, with an investigative team in Hunan province and field recovery operations in Guangxi province -- DPAA's own announcement describes it as the agency's first recovery mission in China in 13 years. The mission is part of renewed U.S.-China cooperation on MIA recovery that resumed in January 2024, which has since covered Hunan, Guangxi, and Liaoning provinces and included the identification of a World War II 'Flying Tiger' pilot; roughly 678 U.S. personnel remain unaccounted for in China across conflicts from World War II through Vietnam. No source reviewed confirms an outcome (a specific identification or recovery) resulted from this China mission specifically, and the Senate's cloture-vote stalemate on the FY2027 NDAA and the $40 million restoration remained unresolved as of this update -- no further procedural movement was identified beyond the July 14, 2026 failed cloture vote and Leader Thune's subsequent motion to reconsider.

title: USAID/CDC Staff Removals Slowed Response to an Unidentified Deadly Illness Cluster in DRC's Equateur Province -- Cause Never Definitively Confirmed
institution: USAID (in dismantlement) / CDC global health security programs
status: Outbreak clusters resolved/contained by spring 2025; underlying cause never definitively confirmed
date_of_action: 2025-01 (USAID/CDC staff removed from DRC posts, CDC ordered to halt WHO collaboration) through 2025-03 (illness clusters investigated and contained)
what_changed: Beginning in January 2025, two clusters of an unidentified illness caused a wave of deaths in the Bolomba and Basankusu health zones of DRC's Equateur province, eventually totaling **roughly 2,969 reported cases and 66 deaths across both clusters**. Wired reported that the USAID and CDC staff who would normally work directly with DRC's health ministry to identify and contain such an outbreak had been removed from their DRC posts as part of the agency's dismantlement, and that a separate January 2025 executive order required CDC to cease collaboration with the WHO -- reducing U.S. visibility into and support for the response. USAID had also supported the physical logistics of outbreak response, including training health workers on proper viral-sample storage/shipment and funding the transport of samples from remote areas to central labs; with that support degraded, identifying the cause took longer than it otherwise would have. Laboratory testing ruled out Ebola and Marburg virus disease. WHO and CDC investigators ultimately could not definitively confirm a single cause; leading hypotheses included bacterial meningitis and chemical or food-borne poisoning, with one thread of the investigation tracing part of the Bolomba cluster to three children who died after eating a bat carcass. The clusters were brought under control by late March 2025 without ever being conclusively attributed to a single pathogen or cause.

title: Trump Officials Paused Mental Health Parity Enforcement Rules While Staffing at the Agency That Enforces Them Collapsed by a Fifth
institution: Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA), Department of Labor
status: Ongoing -- rules remain paused, staffing decline projected to continue through 2026
date_of_action: 2025 (rule pause and staffing decline reported)
what_changed: The Trump administration suspended enforcement of September 2024 regulations that required health plans to collect and report detailed data on mental health claim denials and coverage restrictions, and to explain corrective steps where disparities with physical-healthcare coverage were found. Enforcement of these rules falls to EBSA, a Department of Labor agency overseeing workplace benefits for roughly 150 million Americans, whose own workforce is projected to shrink nearly one-fifth -- from 831 employees in 2024 to 687 or fewer by 2026 -- following the expiration of temporary supplemental funding created by the 2020 No Surprises Act. Within that decline, EBSA's benefit advisers (who handle insurance-denial appeals directly with affected patients) fell 30%, and its investigative staff fell 40%. Former EBSA second-in-command Ali Khawar said 'the expectation was that these rules would be incredibly significant in driving better compliance,' while James Gelfand, president of the ERISA Industry Committee (representing large employers), argued the rules created 'an impossible standard.' EBSA's investigative capacity was already limited before this decline: between February 2021 and July 2024, the agency conducted only 150 investigations into mental health parity, finding 70 violations. ProPublica documented one concrete case of the enforcement mechanism's value: **a Massachusetts family facing $80,000 in bills after their daughter's residential mental-health treatment was denied by insurance had the denial resolved only after EBSA intervened**.

title: Department of Education Dismantled via Interagency Transfers, Without Congressional Approval
institution: U.S. Department of Education
status: Ongoing (Supreme Court allowed dismantling to continue via McMahon v. New York, July 14, 2025, pending lower-court challenges; Congress has not abolished the department and continues funding it); as of an August 24, 2026 White House event, the administration continues to publicly frame the dismantlement as substantially accomplished while using additional devolution mechanisms -- unrestricted state waivers -- alongside the interagency-transfer strategy
date_of_action: 2025-03 (executive order) through 2026-06 (agreements moving much of the special education and civil rights offices' work)
what_changed:
Following a March 2025 Trump executive order directing the department's effective abolition and return of control to the states, Education Secretary Linda McMahon -- following a strategy explicitly drawn from Project 2025, written in part by her now-deputy chief of staff Lindsey Burke -- began signing what would eventually total 14 interagency agreements transferring the department's functions elsewhere, since only Congress can formally eliminate the department itself. K-12, higher education, and workforce training oversight moved to the Department of Labor. On March 21, 2025, Trump separately announced that the Small Business Administration would take over management of the department's $1.6 trillion student loan portfolio; the plan drew immediate legal challenge, and a federal judge blocked the transfer on May 27, 2025, ruling the Higher Education Act assigns that responsibility to the Education Department's Federal Student Aid office and that only Congress could reassign it -- the SBA plan was never carried out, and the portfolio instead began transferring to Treasury in March 2026 as described below.

McMahon sought to lay off roughly 1,400 of the department's 4,200 employees in March 2025 (litigated but largely proceeded), halving the department's staff to roughly 2,000. The layoffs' effects were visible within a day: AP News reported more than 300 Federal Student Aid staff were cut, including two dozen from its technology division -- the entire team responsible for the FAFSA systems -- and StudentAid.gov suffered an hours-long outage on March 12, 2025 that blocked students nationwide from completing the federal financial-aid application; laid-off staff, still technically employed through March 21 but with limited system access, struggled to help diagnose the outage, with roughly 70 employees stuck on an hours-long troubleshooting call. The Washington Post reported April 14, 2025 that the disruption continued past that initial outage: universities nationwide described ongoing delays accessing student records and calculating aid packages, with financial-aid platforms crashing multiple times in the weeks after the layoffs and FSA support lines unresponsive or overwhelmed -- a downstream, university-side view of the same staffing collapse described above from the agency side.

The Guardian reported the FSA cuts also gutted the office's compliance function specifically, eliminating the team responsible for policing for-profit-college fraud and abuse in the $1.6 trillion loan program; consumer advocates drew a direct parallel to the late-1980s student-loan crisis, when weak oversight of for-profit schools helped drive a 41% default rate before Congress tightened compliance requirements. An Education Department Inspector General report found 135 of the department's divisions were left with zero employees after the layoffs, and fewer than 20 retained more than five staff. The March 2025 layoffs eliminated some divisions entirely, including the Office of the Chief Data Officer, the unit responsible for tracking student outcomes and program data; departing staff were given roughly 30 minutes to collect their belongings before colleagues held informal 'clap out' hallway send-offs, per ABC News.

The March 2025 cuts included a reduction-in-force that laid off nearly half of the Office for Civil Rights' staff and shuttered 7 of its 12 regional offices; during the period OCR was short-staffed (March-September 2025), **the office received over 9,000 discrimination complaints and dismissed roughly 90% of them without full review**.

Separately, 65 probationary employees fired in the department's initial rounds were ordered reinstated on March 17, 2025 by a federal judge in Maryland presiding over a companion 18-agency case (distinct from Judge Alsup's six-agency ruling covering VA/Agriculture/Interior/Energy/Defense/Treasury); the department reinstated them on paper but placed them on paid administrative leave rather than restoring their duties, and some were laid off again as their divisions were shuttered outright. Reinstated employees also faced broader benefits chaos: CNN reported in May 2025 that department staff who had been reinstated under since-stayed court orders were left without processed health insurance, pensions, or workers'-compensation claims amid a gutted HR function.

In a May 2, 2025 statement on the administration's FY2026 budget request, McMahon said the request 'reflects funding levels for an agency that is responsibly winding down, shifting some responsibilities to the states.'

The Supreme Court allowed the dismantling to proceed via McMahon v. New York, decided July 14, 2025 -- an unsigned emergency-docket order staying a Massachusetts district court's May 22, 2025 injunction that had ordered the laid-off employees reinstated, with Justice Sotomayor dissenting, joined by Kagan and Jackson -- while litigation continues in lower courts.

During the 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 shutdown, 87% of the department's staff were furloughed -- which McMahon later cited as proof the agency was 'nonessential.' During the same shutdown, the department issued reduction-in-force notices to 465 additional employees on the shutdown's tenth day, concentrated in the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, and the Office of Communications and Outreach; a federal judge called the firings 'likely unlawful' and ordered them paused, and the continuing resolution that ended the shutdown in November nullified the notices outright, barred the department from issuing further RIFs through the end of January 2026, and required back pay for shutdown-affected employees.

Around the same shutdown period, Reuters reported October 14, 2025 that the department had fired almost all 60 staff administering the TRIO college-prep programs -- cutting the Office of Postsecondary Education's Student Services division, which houses TRIO, from about 40 staffers to 2-3 -- a program serving roughly 900,000 low-income and first-generation students nationwide that Republican senators had previously defended; sourcing reviewed did not confirm whether these TRIO-specific cuts were part of the 465-employee RIF wave described above or a related but separate action, since OPE is not among the three offices named for that wave. The cuts left the remaining staff unable to keep up with 1,000-1,200 annual TRIO grant applications or monitor existing grants, and the department separately terminated funding for a number of TRIO grantees outright (per a Council for Opportunity in Education lawsuit) -- distinct from and not undone by the RIF-notice nullification, since grant terminations are a different action than staff RIFs; Inside Higher Ed reported by late October 2025 that 120 TRIO programs nationally had already closed, and a March 2026 Boston Globe follow-up found New Hampshire's program still gone months later.

On November 18, 2025, the department signed interagency agreements outsourcing six additional programs -- including the Department of Labor's assumption of oversight for $28 billion in K-12 grants and $3.1 billion in postsecondary-education grants, effectively outsourcing the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education and Office of Postsecondary Education, two of the department's largest remaining units at the time -- with Indian-education and international-studies programs separately transferred to the Departments of the Interior and State. The November 18 wave also included a Child Care Access Means Parents in School (CCAMPIS) partnership transferring that program to HHS, alongside the Labor and Interior transfers. The Guardian's reporting on this wave described staff being locked out of department accounts without explanation and described collapsing morale as programs were scattered across agencies with little coordination.

That same month, special-education and disability-rights advocates began organizing against a further, not-yet-announced transfer: on December 3, 2025, NPR reported that more than 850 local, state, and national organizations had signed a joint commitment opposing any move to separate special-education oversight from the department, and disability advocacy groups held a National Call-in Day pressuring lawmakers to keep IDEA and Section 504 enforcement at the department; that same month, in a roughly 45-minute meeting described by participants as cordial, McMahon and Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey told disability advocates directly that the Office of Special Education Programs (OSEP) would be moved out of the department -- months ahead of the June 2026 OSERS/OCR agreements described below, and the specific 'listening sessions' referenced there. Concern about specifically the special-education transfer was not limited to Democrats and advocacy groups: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), who chairs the Senate committee overseeing the department, also raised objections, prefiguring the bipartisan Senate HELP Committee vote eight months later (S.5046, July 30, 2026).

The OCR reduction-in-force was rescinded in early January 2026. The FY2026 spending law Trump signed on February 3, 2026 funded the department at about $79 billion, roughly $217 million above FY2025, Higher Ed Dive reported. In February 2026, the department moved additional programs and grants to other federal agencies, including HHS and the State Department, continuing the interagency-transfer dismantlement strategy. A February 2026 GAO report found the March 2025 OCR reduction-in-force had cost taxpayers up to $38 million, since the affected employees were kept on paid administrative leave for nine months while barred from working; GAO concluded the department 'lacks reasonable assurance that its actions achieved the stated goal of reforming the federal workforce' and 'cannot ensure that OCR improved service to the American people.' The Century Foundation found nearly 25% of student-loan borrowers with payments due were delinquent as of February 2026, up from about 9% in 2019 -- roughly 7.9 million borrowers newly entering delinquency -- a sharp rise coinciding with the department's broader administrative disruption. Bloomberg reported in February 2026 that the department was still spending around $200 billion a year in federal funds, not counting the student-loan portfolio.

The $1.7 trillion student loan portfolio and federal financial aid administration began transferring to Treasury in March 2026. In June 2026, the administration announced interagency agreements moving much of the work of the Office for Civil Rights to DOJ and much of the Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services (OSERS), which administers IDEA protections for students with disabilities, to HHS, with HHS doing much of the work of administering IDEA formula grants while the Education Department continues to provide management and leadership, according to the agreements' text obtained by NPR. The agreements went ahead over the objection of disability advocates who participated in months of listening sessions McMahon's own office convened. A former OSERS employee, speaking anonymously, told NPR that department special-education staff had spent decades building expertise that 'HHS does not have,' adding, 'It's medically oriented.'

A live, two-sided congressional fight has also emerged over the interagency-transfer strategy itself. On July 16, 2026, the House Education and Workforce Committee approved 10 Republican-led bills -- described by its own backers as a first step toward 'right sizing' and eventually closing the department -- that would codify several of McMahon's existing interagency agreements, making the transfer of functions (including K-12 academic supports, career and technical education, and federal student loan administration) permanent rather than the current agreement-based arrangement a future administration could unwind by simply declining to renew. Two weeks later, on July 30, 2026, the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee voted 13-9, on a bipartisan basis, to advance S.5046, a bill that would instead block four of the specific IAA transfers -- special education, postsecondary education, elementary/secondary education, and Native American education programs -- and require those functions to remain at the Education Department.

Neither bill had passed its full chamber as of late August 2026, per sourcing reviewed; both still need further House/Senate action, and the House and Senate bills point in opposite directions on the same underlying transfers, reflecting the GOP rift reported by Inside Higher Ed in the same window. This bears directly on the argument Frederick Hess of the American Enterprise Institute made to the Washington Examiner, that a future Democratic president would have to cancel the interagency agreements and 'spend a lot of time and energy unwinding them and moving people back' (see Estimated impact) -- Congress is now the arena where that unwinding-or-codifying fight is actually playing out. A Ninth Circuit ruling in the related Sweet v. McMahon case (July 17, 2026, on student-loan borrower claim deadlines) concerns a distinct piece of litigation over SAVE-plan borrower claims, not the interagency-transfer dismantlement this entry primarily documents, and is not folded in here.

On August 24, 2026, Trump and McMahon held a 'Back to School' event in the White House Rose Garden as students returned to classrooms, using it to publicly tout the dismantlement's progress; ABC News, covering the event, noted McMahon's staff cuts had nearly halved the workforce and that she has called removing federal oversight of education her 'final mission' -- a phrase from the title of her March 3, 2025 first-day message to staff, 'Our Department's Final Mission.' Beyond the interagency-transfer mechanism, the administration disclosed a further devolution-of-authority step: it has distributed more than two dozen unrestricted waivers to states, releasing millions of federal education dollars with fewer federal requirements attached -- a mechanism that advances the same underlying devolve-authority-away-from-the-department pattern as the interagency agreements. (Separately reported at the same event -- a DOJ partnership around parental rights/school-district authority, and a new K-12 scholarship tax credit under the Working Families Tax Cuts Act starting 2027 -- are a distinct school-choice/culture-war policy thread, not the interagency-transfer dismantlement mechanism this entry tracks, and are left out as out-of-scope per this tracker's stay-tight-to-subject convention.)

estimated_impact.summary: The March 2025 layoffs, which largely proceeded despite litigation, targeted about 1,400 of the department's 4,200 employees and left 135 divisions with no staff, with direct effects on students: a StudentAid.gov outage blocked students nationwide from completing the federal financial-aid application, and the short-staffed Office for Civil Rights dismissed roughly 90% of over 9,000 discrimination complaints without full review. A former employee of the department's special education office (OSERS), speaking anonymously to NPR, warned against moving special-education oversight to HHS: 'HHS does not have that [expertise]. It's medically oriented.'

title: Education Department Cuts Over $1 Billion in Contracts and $600 Million in Teacher-Training Grants
institution: U.S. Department of Education
status: Implemented, then partly ruled unlawful -- on Sept. 17, 2026 a federal judge in Massachusetts vacated the February 2025 anti-DEI directive behind the teacher-training grant cancellations; the money is not automatically restored, and no appeal had been announced as of Sept. 21.
date_of_action: 2025-02-19 (cuts reported); 2026-09-17 (directive behind the teacher-training cuts vacated)
what_changed:
The Trump administration **cut more than $1 billion in Department of Education contracts, most of them at the Institute of Education Sciences -- the department's primary education-research arm -- including a round of more than $350 million that ended contracts for several Regional Educational Laboratories and Equity Assistance Centers. The department separately announced $600 million in cuts to teacher-training grants.** The administration justified the cuts as eliminating 'woke' and wasteful spending. This action predates and is distinct from the department's later, formal dismantlement documented separately in this database, which began with a March 2025 executive order directing the department's effective abolition -- this entry documents an earlier wave of targeted contract cancellations rather than the subsequent structural reorganization.

Update 2026-09-29: On September 17, 2026, U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley of the District of Massachusetts sided with eight states (California, Colorado, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York and Wisconsin) and vacated the Education Department's February 5, 2025 internal directive ordering the termination of grants involving DEI-related programming, which the department used to cancel more than 100 Teacher Quality Partnership and Supporting Effective Educator Development (SEED) grants. **She ruled the directive "arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law" under the Administrative Procedure Act**. Explaining why she vacated it outright, she wrote that "the Department's hasty implementation of the Directive over less than two weeks, the magnitude of the effects of the termination, as well as the lack of evidence of reasoned decisionmaking in the Administrative Record leave serious doubts as to the Department's choice to adopt the Directive." The ruling does not restore the terminated grants: the court held in November 2025 that challenges to the individual terminations belong in the Court of Federal Claims, and it declined to issue a permanent injunction. The case had earlier produced a March 2025 temporary restraining order that the Supreme Court stayed in April 2025. A department spokesperson said taxpayer dollars should not support "divisive ideology or racial preferences."

primary_proponent.note: DOGE directed the contract cuts, most of them at the Institute of Education Sciences. The teacher-grant terminations followed a February 5, 2025 internal directive on grant priorities issued by then-Acting Secretary Denise Carter, per Judge Kelley's September 2026 opinion; the termination letters were written by a staff member originally from DOGE. Both predate Linda McMahon's confirmation as Education Secretary (later documented as the lead figure in the department's formal dismantlement).
