title: OMB Froze $6.8 Billion in Appropriated School Funding for Nearly a Month
institution: U.S. Department of Education / Office of Management and Budget
status: Reversed (funds released July 25-28, 2025)
date_of_action: 2025-06-30 (freeze announced) through 2025-07-28 (funds released to states)
what_changed: On June 30, 2025 -- one day before the funds were due to arrive -- the Department of Education notified states it would withhold roughly $6.8 billion in previously appropriated FY2025 formula grants, covering six programs: Title I-C (migrant education), Title II-A (teacher training and class-size reduction), Title III-A (English learner and migrant-student services), Title IV-A (student support and academic enrichment, including after-school and summer programs), and adult-education/WIOA Title II funds. An OMB spokesperson said the money was under review for alignment with administration priorities and suggested, without providing evidence, that some funding had supported 'a left-wing agenda' -- a characterization the affected states and school districts disputed. More than 20 Democratic state attorneys general sued the Department of Education and OMB, arguing the freeze was unconstitutional and 'debilitating' to states weeks before the new school year. **A national survey of over 600 school superintendents found many anticipated having to cut extracurriculars, tutoring, and after-school care if the funds weren't released before classes resumed.** After roughly four weeks, OMB completed its review and directed the release of all formula funds; Education Secretary Linda McMahon announced the unfreezing on July 25, 2025, with states beginning to receive the funds the week of July 28.

title: Education Department Rescinds Disparate-Impact Standard From Title VI Civil Rights Enforcement
institution: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights
status: Final rule, effective July 24, 2026
date_of_action: 2026-07-24 (final rule effective)
what_changed: Citing Executive Order 14281, the Department of Education finalized a rule rescinding disparate-impact provisions from its regulations implementing Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, effective July 24, 2026. Disparate-impact provisions had allowed investigators to find a school policy violated federal civil rights law based on its disproportionate effect on students of a particular race or ethnicity -- demographic outcome data alone -- even without a facially discriminatory policy or proof of discriminatory intent. Under the rescinded standard, federal investigators could challenge practices like discipline policies, tracking/placement decisions, or resource allocation that produced racially disparate outcomes, regardless of intent. The new rule clarifies that Title VI 'prohibit[s] intentional discrimination and do[es] not prohibit conduct or activities that have an unintentional disparate impact,' meaning investigators must now prove a school district specifically intended to discriminate -- a substantially higher evidentiary bar. Roughly 60 civil rights and education organizations publicly condemned the change, **warning it 'will hurt Black, Latino, Asian American, and Native American students, other students of color, and other marginalized students who face higher rates of discrimination.'**

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Education
primary_proponent.note: The Education Department, under McMahon, finalized the rule rescinding disparate-impact enforcement under Title VI, implementing the broader Executive Order 14281 disparate-impact policy across federal civil rights enforcement.

estimated_impact.summary: Federal civil rights investigators can no longer use demographic outcome data alone to challenge school policies with racially disparate effects -- they must now prove intentional discrimination, a substantially harder standard to meet, narrowing the practical reach of Title VI enforcement in education even where the outcomes of a policy remain unequal.

title: SAVE Student-Loan Plan Dismantled Over 18 Months, From Application Freeze to Full Termination for 7.5 Million Borrowers
institution: Department of Education
status: Finalized -- SAVE rule vacated by agreed court judgment (Mar. 10, 2026); staggered 90-day exit windows began July 1, 2026, first deadlines Sept. 29; per Department figures, ~6 million of 7.5 million SAVE borrowers had not switched plans as of mid-Sept. 2026
date_of_action: 2025-02-21 (online IDR/consolidation applications pulled down) through 2026-07-01 onward (staggered 90-day SAVE exit windows; first deadlines 2026-09-29)
what_changed: On February 18, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the Biden-era SAVE (Saving on a Valuable Education) income-driven repayment plan -- which had reduced payments to as little as 5% of a borrower's discretionary income and offered forgiveness after 10 years for borrowers who originally borrowed $12,000 or less -- exceeded the Education Secretary's statutory authority, and directed the lower court to broaden its injunction to block the entire SAVE rule, calling into question the legality of related income-contingent plans (PAYE, REPAYE) as well. On Friday, February 21, 2025, the Education Department responded by pulling down the online applications for all income-driven repayment (IDR) plans and Direct loan consolidation entirely -- not just SAVE -- cutting off enrollment access for borrowers who wanted to switch plans regardless of which IDR plan they were pursuing. By mid-March 2025, the administration had closed applications across every IDR plan (even ones not blocked by courts) and moved to limit who is eligible for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, leaving millions of borrowers unable to access repayment calculators or determine their new payment obligations; some reported being unable to determine whether to take a second job or plan for default. On July 18, 2025, Politico reported the Department would deny roughly 460,000 applicants from its backlog of about 1.5 million IDR applications -- about a third of the total -- because they had requested SAVE or the 'lowest monthly payment' option, which would have defaulted most of them into SAVE; a Department spokesperson said servicers could not process those applications because SAVE was 'no longer an option, as it is illegal.' **Nearly 8 million SAVE borrowers who had been held in forbearance since the summer of 2024 while the litigation proceeded then saw interest begin accruing on their loans again on August 1, 2025**; the forbearance itself continued, but balances began to grow, and Education Secretary Linda McMahon, calling SAVE an 'illegal' plan in a press release, urged borrowers to move to a 'legally compliant repayment plan' even as the Department's application backlog stood at roughly 1.5 million. Bloomberg reported August 11, 2025 that, amid this resumption, millions of the borrowers who collectively owe about $1.6 trillion in federal student loans were skipping their bills -- some citing inability to afford payments after covering housing and groceries, others refusing to pay as a form of protest -- despite the risk of credit damage and wage garnishment. A December 15, 2025 court filing later put the confirmed denial figure at 327,955 IDR applications rejected in August 2025 alone, with the Department citing an 'unforeseen ambiguity' about which plan borrowers who had asked for the lowest monthly payment should be enrolled in, and 802,730 IDR applications still pending as of the end of November 2025. Rather than continue defending SAVE, the administration signed a settlement with the seven Republican-led plaintiff states (Missouri, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, North Dakota, Ohio and Oklahoma) on December 9, 2025, agreeing to enroll no new borrowers, deny pending SAVE applications and move all SAVE borrowers into other plans, and the parties jointly asked the court to enter a final judgment. The district court instead dismissed the case as moot on February 27, 2026; the states appealed, and on March 9, 2026 the Eighth Circuit reversed and directed entry of the agreed judgment, which the district court entered on March 10, 2026, vacating the SAVE rule in full except for one provision on which deferment and forbearance periods count toward income-driven repayment. A group of SAVE borrowers who sought to intervene and challenge that judgment was turned away on July 30, 2026, when the court denied their motion to intervene. On March 27, 2026 the Education Department formally directed the 7.5 million borrowers still enrolled in SAVE to prepare to exit the plan and its forbearance. Starting July 1, 2026, loan servicers began issuing notices, staggered across borrowers, giving each borrower 90 days from notice to select a new repayment plan, with the earliest deadlines falling on September 29, 2026. Options include the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP), a new income-driven plan created by Congress in the July 2025 reconciliation law (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) and launched July 1, 2026, which sets payments at 1% to 10% of income with a $10 monthly minimum, reduces them $50 per dependent and forgives any remaining balance only after 30 years; CBS News reported that the available plans mean higher monthly payments for most former SAVE borrowers. Borrowers who do not choose within their 90 days are placed in the Standard Repayment Plan or the new Tiered Standard Plan, which require fixed payments over a set term (10 to 25 years under the tiered plan, depending on the amount borrowed) regardless of income; student-aid analyst Mark Kantrowitz told CNBC that payments for some borrowers could double or triple. As of mid-September 2026, a Department spokesperson said nearly 1.5 million of the 7.5 million SAVE borrowers had selected a new plan, which Newsweek calculated left about 6 million who had not yet switched as the first deadlines approached.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Education
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency administering student loan repayment programs
primary_proponent.note: Chose to pull down applications for all IDR plans -- not just SAVE -- in February 2025, a broader response than the Eighth Circuit's ruling strictly required; in December 2025 settled the states' lawsuit rather than defend SAVE, agreeing to deny pending applications and move all SAVE borrowers out, and set the staggered 90-day exit timeline with default placement in a fixed-payment standard plan. The Repayment Assistance Plan itself was designed by Congress in the July 2025 reconciliation law, not by the Department.

estimated_impact.summary: About 7.5 million borrowers who had budgeted around SAVE's low, income-based payments -- many during more than two years of forbearance -- are being forced into other plans that mean higher monthly payments for most of them; roughly 6 million had not yet switched as the first 90-day deadlines arrived in late September 2026 and face default placement in fixed-payment standard plans that could double or triple some bills. Along the way, hundreds of thousands of borrowers seeking affordable income-driven plans were denied or left waiting in a backlog while interest accrued on their loans.

title: Education Department Ends $1 Billion in School Mental Health Staffing Grants
institution: U.S. Department of Education
status: Finalized; not restored as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-08-01 (reporting) -- grants had been awarded under the 2022 Bipartisan Safer Communities Act
what_changed: The Trump administration abruptly ended roughly $1 billion in federal grants that funded school-based mental health staffing programs -- counselors, behavior analysts, and social workers -- created under the 2022 Bipartisan Safer Communities Act's School-Based Mental Health Services and Mental Health Service Professional Demonstration grant programs. NPR reported over 200 such programs nationwide lost funding, forcing many participants out of training pipelines mid-program. Oklahoma's PRIME initiative, which trained mental-health staff for rural schools, was cited as a specific case study: the state already faced counselor shortages in all 77 of its counties before the cut, and **advocates said the loss would worsen an already severe shortage of school-based mental health support tied to youth suicide prevention and behavioral outcomes.**

estimated_impact.summary: A federal grant program built in direct response to school-shooting-era bipartisan legislation, funding mental-health staffing pipelines for schools nationwide, was eliminated mid-program, disproportionately affecting rural and already-underserved districts like Oklahoma's.

title: Education Department Announced, Then Reversed, Social Security Benefit Seizures for Defaulted Student Loans -- Now Delayed Again to Mid-2026
institution: U.S. Department of Education (with Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service, via the Treasury Offset Program)
status: Social Security offsets specifically remain paused as of this entry's last verification, delayed to no earlier than July 2026 pending rollout of a new repayment plan (RAP) created by the OBBBA; wage garnishment and tax-refund seizure resumed and continue for defaulted borrowers generally
date_of_action: 2025-04-22 (Education Secretary Linda McMahon announces resumption of collections, including Social Security offsets, effective May 5, 2025) through 2026-01-16 (Education Department further delays involuntary collections pending the new RAP repayment plan)
what_changed: On April 22, 2025, Education Secretary Linda McMahon announced the department would resume collections on defaulted federal student loans effective May 5, 2025, ending a five-year pandemic-era pause -- including wage garnishment, federal tax-refund interception, and, notably, seizure of Social Security retirement and disability benefits through the Treasury Offset Program. The Associated Press reported May 16, 2025 that **more than 450,000 older Americans, many already living on fixed incomes below the poverty line, faced losing a portion of their Social Security checks over decades-old defaulted loans**, some of which borrowers said they had already repaid multiple times over through interest and prior collections. Sens. Booker, Warren, and Rep. Pressley reintroduced legislation in mid-May 2025 to suspend such garnishments. Facing intense public backlash and pressure from borrower advocates, the department reversed course on the Social Security-specific piece within weeks: by early June 2025 it confirmed it had not actually offset any Social Security benefits since the May 5 restart and was pausing any future Social Security offsets, while continuing wage garnishment and tax-refund seizure for defaulted borrowers generally. On January 16, 2026, the department announced a further delay to involuntary collections -- including the Treasury Offset Program mechanism used for Social Security -- citing the need to first roll out the Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP), a new income-driven repayment option created by the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act and set to launch July 1, 2026; borrowers who do not enroll in RAP or otherwise resolve their default status by then could see Social Security offsets resume, capped at 15% of the monthly benefit with a $750 minimum-benefit protection floor. On August 17, 2026, Sen. Bernie Sanders announced he would introduce the Stop Social Security Garnishment Act of 2026, seeking to permanently bar the federal government from seizing Social Security payments to collect defaulted federal student loans.

primary_proponent.name: Linda McMahon, Secretary of Education
primary_proponent.role: Announced the April 2025 resumption of defaulted-loan collections, including the Social Security offset plan later reversed under public pressure
primary_proponent.note: The department itself, not McMahon personally, announced both the June 2025 reversal and the January 2026 further delay; sourcing reviewed did not attribute either reversal to a specific named official's individual decision.

estimated_impact.summary: No Social Security benefits were actually seized before the department reversed course, so the documented harm is the widespread anxiety and hardship-planning burden imposed on 450,000+ mostly older, fixed-income borrowers during the weeks the policy was in effect, plus the borrowers who remain in default and could still face garnishment once the pause lifts in mid-2026.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the sequence of events -- the April 2025 announcement (Washington Post, CBS News), the May 2025 AP reporting on the 450,000-borrower figure, the June 2025 reversal (CNBC, Protect Borrowers), and the January 2026 further delay tied to the RAP rollout (multiple 2026 personal-finance/policy outlets) are all independently corroborated. The Sanders bill is confirmed as announced/introduced, not yet enacted.

title: Trump Administration Explored Selling Parts of the $1.6-1.77 Trillion Federal Student Loan Portfolio to Private Investors, Over Democratic Lawmakers' Legal Objections
institution: Department of Education; Department of the Treasury
status: Sale undecided: ED's Feb. 9, 2026 letter said no final decision had been made on selling any loans. Separately, a March 19, 2026 ED-Treasury agreement set Treasury to take over defaulted-loan collection, then more; a June 2026 CRS report found its schedule unspecified.
date_of_action: 2025-10-07 (Politico first reports talks) through 2026-02-09 (Under Secretary Kent's letter says no final decision on a sale; released by Sen. Warren 2026-02-23)
what_changed: On October 7, 2025, Politico reported that senior Education and Treasury Department officials, under Secretary Linda McMahon and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, had held talks -- including approaching finance-industry executives as potential buyers -- about selling portions of the federal government's student loan portfolio (reported variously as $1.6 trillion face value, against a roughly $1.1 trillion 2024 FSA net-value estimate) to private investors. Under the plan, private buyers would gain ownership and collection rights over the loans while the loans' original federal terms would nominally remain unchanged, though critics disputed whether that protection could survive a change of ownership in practice. In a letter dated November 16, 2025 and released November 17, 44 members of Congress -- Democrats plus independent Sen. Bernie Sanders -- led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Sen. Sanders, and Rep. Ayanna Pressley, and also signed by Sens. Ron Wyden and Richard Blumenthal among others, urged McMahon and Bessent to end any plans for a sale, arguing **it could strip borrowers of legally guaranteed protections -- including income-driven repayment, Public Service Loan Forgiveness, disability and death discharges, and relief for borrowers defrauded by predatory schools** -- and that federal law (Section 459 of the Higher Education Act, added in 1998) permits the Education Secretary to sell Direct Loans only in consultation with Treasury and only if the sale results in no cost to the federal government, a condition the lawmakers argued a sale would likely fail, citing experts who said private investors would not pay more than the loans are worth and a 2019 McKinsey review, from Trump's first term, that found the portfolio "worth far less than government accountants had projected." A November 18, 2025 report in The Hill put the portfolio at $1.77 trillion, while an ED spokesperson described it as "nearly $1.7 trillion." In a February 9, 2026 letter to Sen. Warren, which her office released on February 23, Under Secretary Nicholas Kent wrote that the department had met with a variety of stakeholders 'to discuss ideas to reform the student loan portfolio' since January 2025 and would 'continue to explore all viable options,' but that ED 'has not taken any final actions or made final decisions regarding selling all or part of the student loan portfolio' -- leaving which loans might be sold, to whom, on what timeline, and under what terms all undecided as of that response. Warren's office called the letter ED's first public confirmation that it was weighing a sale. On March 19, 2026, separate from the private-sale question, ED and Treasury entered into an interagency agreement (IAA) under which Treasury is to take over federal student loan servicing and review other student aid functions in three phases, as part of the administration's broader effort to dismantle the Education Department (only Congress can formally abolish it, so officials are relocating its functions via inter-agency agreements instead). Phase 1 has Treasury gradually take over servicing and collection of defaulted loans -- about $179 billion owed by about 7.8 million borrowers, roughly 11% of the $1.7 trillion portfolio -- through its Cross-Servicing Program; Phase 2 has Treasury assume servicing operations for non-defaulted loans 'to the extent practicable'; and Phase 3 has Treasury review student- and school-eligibility functions, including FAFSA administration. The agreement set no schedule: a June 9, 2026 Congressional Research Service report found the timing of Phase 1 unspecified, though under an April 3 memorandum ED was detailing seven employees to Treasury to run a scaled transition of defaulted-loan servicing, and Treasury's Fiscal Service had sought industry input on hiring default-resolution contractors. Sen. Warren followed up with a letter dated April 1, 2026, joined by Sens. Sanders, Wyden, Patty Murray, and Tammy Baldwin, urging the secretaries to rescind the IAA, and, in a May 4, 2026 release, said ED's and Treasury's responses 'cannot articulate a clear purpose or plan' for the IAA and failed to provide implementation details on timing, cost, or Treasury's plans for forced collections on defaulted loans. The IAA moves servicing and collection work, not ownership -- its defaulted-loan attachment states that referrals 'are for collection purposes only and do not transfer ownership of the debt from Education to Treasury' -- but it changes who runs the portfolio that a sale would draw from; no reporting found ties the two tracks together as parts of one announced plan, and they are presented here as related but distinct actions.

Elizabeth Warren (released February 23) said ED had met with stakeholders on ideas to reform the portfolio and was exploring all viable options, while stating no final decision on a sale had been made.

estimated_impact.summary: No sale has occurred, and ED said in February 2026 that none had been decided, so no borrower has yet lost a protection. What is at stake is the legally guaranteed relief of about 45 million federal borrowers -- income-driven repayment, Public Service Loan Forgiveness, disability and death discharges, and relief for borrowers defrauded by predatory schools -- which 44 lawmakers warned a profit-seeking owner would push to cut, plus a taxpayer loss if loans sell for less than they are worth to the government, which the law forbids. Separately, the March 2026 ED-Treasury agreement puts collection of about $179 billion in defaulted loans, owed by about 7.8 million borrowers, on course to move to Treasury, whose earlier pilot collected less successfully than ED's contractors; its schedule was unset as of June 2026.

The defaulted-loan figures describe the Treasury agreement, which moves collection work but not ownership, and had no public schedule as of CRS's June 2026 report; the evidence that Treasury collects less effectively comes from first-year findings of a 2015-2017 pilot that ended early. No health or mortality effect is documented.

title: Education Department Withheld Federal Funding From School Districts Over Transgender-Inclusive Bathroom Policies, Then Lost in Court Twice
institution: Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights
status: Ongoing -- funding withheld, two adverse court rulings, underlying district policies mostly unchanged
date_of_action: 2025-07-25 (Virginia Title IX finding) through 2026-04-09 (NYC ruling)
what_changed: Acting Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Craig Trainor's Office for Civil Rights (OCR) ran a coercive funding campaign against school districts that let transgender students use bathrooms and locker rooms matching their gender identity. On July 25, 2025, OCR found five Northern Virginia districts -- Alexandria, Arlington, Fairfax County, Loudoun County, and Prince William County -- in violation of Title IX over these facilities policies and gave them 10 days to rescind them via a proposed Resolution Agreement. All five refused. OCR responded by placing the districts on 'high risk' status, restricting roughly $50 million in federal funding to reimbursement-only and threatening a full freeze. Arlington and Fairfax counties sued to reverse that status; Judge Rossie D. Alston Jr. dismissed the suit on procedural grounds but ruled on the merits that Fairfax and Arlington's policies actually comply with current legal precedent and are not a Title IX violation -- a direct rebuke of OCR's underlying legal theory even as the case itself was dismissed. Separately, on September 16, 2025, Trainor's office sent letters to New York City, Chicago, and Fairfax County demanding the same policy changes as a condition of Magnet School Assistance Program grants; when the districts missed the deadline, OCR withheld the funding -- $3.4 million from Fairfax, $5.8 million from Chicago, and an amount from NYC that OCR initially reported around $15 million but that grew, once all 19 affected NYC magnet schools were counted, to roughly $47 million. New York City sued in October 2025, and on April 9, 2026, Manhattan federal Judge Arun Subramanian ruled that the administration had skirted procedural steps Title IX itself requires before cutting off federal education funding -- a second court loss for the campaign. As of January 2026, none of the five original Northern Virginia districts had reversed their underlying facilities policies.

title: White House Uses a Pocket Rescission to Let $24.9 Million for Migrant Farmworker Students' GED and College Programs Expire
institution: Department of Education, Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, Office of Migrant Education (High School Equivalency Program and College Assistance Migrant Program, funded in the Education for the Disadvantaged account)
status: The fiscal year ended Sept. 30, 2026 with the money withheld and no congressional vote, after GAO said the law bars withholding the funds past that date. The HEP-CAMP Association sued; Judge Tanya Chutkan set briefing on its motion to keep the funds available, ending Oct. 30. No ruling yet.
date_of_action: 2026-09-25 (special message sent to Congress; funds withheld through the end of fiscal 2026 on Sept. 30, 2026)
what_changed: The High School Equivalency Program (HEP) and the College Assistance Migrant Program (CAMP) are Education Department grant programs, authorized by the Higher Education Act, that pay colleges and nonprofits to help students from migrant and seasonal farmworker families earn a high school equivalency credential such as a GED (HEP) or get through their first year of college (CAMP). The administration's fiscal 2026 budget request asked for no money for them, saying "Elimination of this program is part of the Administration's overall effort to restore fiscal discipline and reduce the Federal role in education," as quoted in the association's complaint. Congress instead appropriated $52,123,000 for them in the appropriations law signed Feb. 3, 2026 (Pub. L. 119-75), the same level as fiscal 2025, and in the same law barred using any appropriated funds to "increase, eliminate, or reduce funding for a program, project, or activity as proposed in the President's budget request" until Congress enacts the change. The department announced fiscal 2026 HEP and CAMP grant competitions on May 18, 2026, with applications due June 12; according to the HEP-CAMP Association's complaint, the competition instructions estimated $24,564,675 for seven to nine new five-year awards, more than 70 of the association's member programs applied, and the department never made any new awards. Education Week reported that OMB never delivered the apportionments for roughly half of the HEP-CAMP money to the department. On September 25, 2026, five days before the end of the fiscal year, President Trump sent House Speaker Mike Johnson a special message under the Impoundment Control Act proposing 11 rescissions totaling $810 million, and the Office of Management and Budget issued a reapportionment letter withholding the proposed amounts. One item, $24,907,509, cuts "$25 million of the $52 million appropriated in FY 2026 for the competitive grants within Special Programs for Migrant Students," which the message said "subsidizes aliens to come to the United States at the expense of American children and workers" and "pays for seasonal immigrant workers' kids to go to school in the United States and transition to college." The message added that the program "has previously funded activities such as an LGBT youth summit for 'migrant students' and 'Therapy for Latinx' workshops," and the White House's public release named a grant recipient, Immigrants Rising. Education Week reported that undocumented immigrants are prohibited from participating, that the students served qualify for federal migrant education funds before finishing high school, and that the federal spending database shows no HEP or CAMP grant to Immigrants Rising; the association's president, Andrew Dalton, said, "We have no idea where that came from." Because the Impoundment Control Act lets the executive withhold funds for 45 days of continuous session while Congress considers a rescission, a request sent this close to the funds' expiration lets them lapse without a vote; this is known as a pocket rescission. On September 29, 2026, GAO's general counsel concluded that all 11 accounts expire at the end of fiscal 2026 and that the President "may not force the expiration of budget authority Congress has already enacted and did not rescind." Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, a Republican, said the White House budget office "intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation." **The HEP-CAMP Association estimates the money being pulled back could have provided services for 1,650 students, Education Week reported.** The programs had already shrunk: in 2025, after the association sued over late funding, the department canceled that year's competitions for new HEP and CAMP awards, made no new awards and, Education Week reported, discontinued more than 40 existing grants. The association dropped its suit on Sept. 30, 2025, the day the department told the court it had obligated all of that year's HEP-CAMP money, partly through advance-funded awards to the remaining grantees. Education Week reported the programs fell from 120 programs serving 5,000 students in 20 states as of 2024 to 45 programs in 12 states serving fewer than 2,000 students a year. On September 30, 2026, the National HEP-CAMP Association, which says it represents more than 80 colleges and nonprofits that run or seek to run the programs, sued President Trump, the Education Department and OMB in federal court in Washington, D.C. (No. 1:26-cv-03427). It alleges the cut violates the First Amendment, as viewpoint discrimination and as retaliation for its 2025 lawsuit, along with the Administrative Procedure Act, the Higher Education Act's requirement that the Secretary "maintain and expand" the programs, the appropriations law's ban on carrying out proposed budget cuts Congress has not enacted, and the separation of powers. "Although HEP and CAMP grant programs are codified in law and funded by Congress, the Administration nevertheless seeks to shut them down," the complaint says. It asks the court to suspend the funds' Sept. 30 expiration under a federal law that lets courts keep budget authority alive while a timely suit is pending, and to order the money obligated. The association also filed a motion for a temporary restraining order "out of an abundance of caution," citing a same-day ruling in a separate challenge to the package's housing-counseling cut. Judge Jia M. Cobb declined to treat the case as related to that housing suit, and on October 1 it was randomly reassigned to Judge Tanya S. Chutkan, who on October 2 adopted the parties' joint schedule: the association's full motion is due October 9, the government's opposition October 23 and the association's reply October 30.

More than 70 member programs that applied for new grants received none, according to the association.

title: Education Department fires entire Impact Aid Program Office staff during the 2025 shutdown, freezing payments to tribal and military-base schools

status: Ongoing as of reporting -- office staffing/payment resumption not confirmed

what_changed: During the fall 2025 government shutdown, the Trump administration fired all staff in the Education Department's Impact Aid Program Office, according to Arizona's congressional delegation (Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego, joined by other Arizona Democrats). Impact Aid is the federal program that compensates school districts for lost local tax revenue in areas with non-taxable federal land -- military bases, Native American reservations held in trust, and other federal property -- providing $1.6 billion a year nationally. Arizona's delegation wrote that 'Impact Aid fulfills an important and distinctive function. title: Education Department Ends Most Minority-Serving College Grants as Race-Based and Moves the Money Elsewhere
institution: Department of Education, Office of Postsecondary Education (Higher Education Act Title III and Title V minority-serving institution grant programs)
status: Ongoing. For a second year, fiscal 2026 MSI grant money went to other programs. No court has ruled on whether the programs are constitutional. Seven states sued Sept. 30, 2026, alleging $132M in MSI money was withheld past fiscal 2025's end.
date_of_action: 2025-09-10 to 2026-09-22 (fiscal 2025 grants ended and money redirected Sept. 2025; fiscal 2026 money redirected by Sept. 2026)
what_changed: In June 2025, the state of Tennessee and Students for Fair Admissions sued the Education Department in federal court in Tennessee, arguing that the Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSI) grant program is unconstitutional because it is open only to colleges whose undergraduate enrollment is at least 25 percent Hispanic. In July, Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to House Speaker Mike Johnson that the requirement "violates the Constitution" and that the Justice Department would not defend it; the Hispanic Association of Colleges and Universities (HACU) intervened to defend the program instead. On September 10, 2025, near the end of the fiscal year, the Education Department announced it would end discretionary grants under seven programs for minority-serving institutions (MSIs), among them Hispanic-serving, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian-serving, predominantly Black, Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-serving, and Native American-serving nontribal institutions. Historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) and tribal colleges were unaffected. Education Secretary Linda McMahon said the department would "no longer award Minority-Serving Institution grants that discriminate by restricting eligibility to institutions that meet government-mandated racial quotas." The department said existing discretionary awards would be discontinued and no new awards made, affecting about $350 million in fiscal 2025 funds, and that it would still disburse about $132 million in mandatory funds that it said "cannot be reprogrammed on a statutory basis." On September 15, it announced it would redirect money to a one-time $495 million supplement for HBCUs and tribal colleges, plus $60 million for charter schools and $137 million for civics education grants; The New York Times, citing anonymous sources, reported that the MSI cuts helped pay for the new spending. **Hispanic-serving institutions, predominantly Black institutions and others scrambled to fund programs and student services supported by the grants, and some were forced to lay off personnel**, Inside Higher Ed reported; Long Beach City College, for example, lost about $3 million in grants for programs serving students facing food and housing insecurity and adult learners. On December 2, 2025, the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel concluded, in an opinion requested by the Education Department, that both the discretionary and the mandatory grants for several MSI programs, and the formula-based grants for predominantly Black institutions, are unconstitutional. When the department released its response on December 19, McMahon said, "I agree with the Office of Legal Counsel opinion," and the department said it was evaluating the opinion's full impact. Congress's fiscal 2026 budget, approved February 3, 2026, again funded the MSI programs and barred the department from shifting their money to HBCUs and tribal colleges, but appeared to allow moving it to the Strengthening Institutions Program, a grant program for under-resourced colleges with no racial or ethnic enrollment test. By September 1, 2026, the Office of Management and Budget had reprogrammed $337 million from six MSI grant programs to the Strengthening Institutions Program, Education Week reported. On September 22, 2026, the department announced a further one-time $174 million for HBCUs and $61 million for tribal colleges, taken from the HSI science and technology program and from the Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian, Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander-serving, and Native American-serving nontribal programs. UNCF said the HBCU money came through the mandatory funding mechanism. On September 30, 2026, seven states suing President Trump and OMB Director Russell Vought over impoundments alleged that the administration had "impounded $132 million in funds for the Minority Serving Institutions program past the end of the 2025 fiscal year," and that the funds Congress appropriated again could once more be impounded, with federal data through August 2026 showing at least $132 million appropriated under the mandatory MSI statute still unobligated. The Tennessee lawsuit remains undecided; the plaintiffs moved for summary judgment on August 31, 2026, and HACU cross-moved for summary judgment on September 29.

primary_proponent.name: Linda McMahon
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Education
primary_proponent.note: Announced the September 2025 decision to stop awarding MSI grants that "discriminate by restricting eligibility to institutions that meet government-mandated racial quotas," announced both rounds of redirected funding to HBCUs and tribal colleges, and said in December 2025 she agreed with the Justice Department opinion calling the programs unconstitutional. The Education Department told Inside Higher Ed it worked with the White House Office of Management and Budget to identify legal options for the fiscal 2026 funds.

estimated_impact.summary: **Colleges that relied on minority-serving institution grants lost hundreds of millions of dollars in fiscal 2025, and some laid off staff**, while the programs' fiscal 2026 money was redirected again. Hispanic-serving colleges alone enroll about 5.6 million students, according to HACU; the grants fund campus-wide services such as tutoring, counseling and STEM programs, not only students of one group. HBCUs and tribal colleges received large one-time increases from the same money.

title: EEOC Loses Quorum for Eight Months After Trump Fires Two Democratic Commissioners
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
status: Resolved as a quorum matter (quorum restored October 7, 2025 with Senate confirmation of a third commissioner); Samuels voluntarily dismissed her challenge to the firings July 6, 2026, saying the Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter ruling left her no viable path forward
date_of_action: 2025-01-27 (firings) through 2025-10-07 (quorum restored); related litigation resolved 2026-07-06
what_changed: **Late on January 27, 2025, President Trump fired EEOC Commissioners Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels, both Democratic appointees, and General Counsel Karla Gilbride confirmed her own firing the next day -- in the agency's 60-year history, no commissioner had ever before been removed before the end of their term.** Burrows's term was not set to expire until 2028, Samuels's not until 2026. Title VII requires three commissioners for the EEOC to have a quorum; without one, the agency could continue routine case processing but could not initiate formal rulemakings or issue, modify, or revoke formal guidance. The agency operated without a quorum for over eight months. In April 2025, Samuels sued Trump, the EEOC, and Chair Andrea Lucas, arguing her termination before the end of her statutory term was unlawful. Quorum was restored October 7, 2025, when the Senate confirmed Brittany Panuccio as a third commissioner, giving the EEOC a 2-Republican (Lucas, Panuccio), 1-Democrat (Kalpana Kotagal) composition, with Lucas subsequently named permanent Chair on November 5, 2025. With quorum restored, the EEOC gained the votes needed to pursue the policy changes documented elsewhere in this dataset, including the EEO-1 data-collection rescission proposal. Samuels's lawsuit remained pending until the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter on June 29, 2026, substantially expanding presidential removal power over independent-agency officials and overturning the 91-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent that had previously insulated such agencies from at-will removal. Concluding the ruling foreclosed her claim, Samuels voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit on July 6, 2026.

title: EEOC Moves to End 60 Years of Mandatory Workplace Demographic Data Collection
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
status: Ongoing (written comment period closed August 24, 2026 as scheduled; EEOC has not yet issued a final rule and must review the full comment record first)
date_of_action: Early 2025 (removal of Democratic commissioners clears the path) through 2026-06-09 (OMB review of the rescission proposal concludes); final rule still pending as of the last-verified date
what_changed: Early in his second term, President Trump removed the EEOC's Democratic commissioners, eliminating what would have been a blocking minority against a reorientation of the agency's civil rights enforcement priorities under Chair Andrea Lucas. On May 14, 2026, the EEOC submitted a proposed rule to the White House's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) titled 'Rescission of EEO-1, EEO-2, EEO-3, EEO-4, EEO-5, and Reporting Requirement Under Title VII, the ADA, GINA, and the PWFA.' **The proposal would eliminate the mandatory annual and biennial workforce demographic data collections that have applied since 1966 to private employers with 100 or more employees, unions, state and local governments, and public school systems, covering employee race, ethnicity, and sex data across job categories.** OIRA concluded its review on June 9, 2026, clearing the way for the proposal to be published in the Federal Register for public comment. As of the last-verified date, the EEOC had not opened its EEO-1 filing portal for 2025 data, leaving employers uncertain whether any further demographic data collection will occur before a final rule is issued. The move follows the EEOC's 2025 decision to rescind the option for employers to report non-binary employees on the form, and a separate, still-pending EEOC proposal to rescind a 1979 regulation permitting voluntary affirmative action plans. Re-verified 2026-07-19: the proposed rule had still not been published in the Federal Register as of this update. The EEOC's own regulatory agenda projects publication in July 2026 with a comment period running into September 2026, and the Commission held a Sunshine Act-noticed meeting on July 17, 2026 that included the draft rescission rule -- both signs publication remains imminent, but no notice-and-comment period had formally opened as of this writing. Update 2026-07-26: On July 21, 2026, the Commission voted 2-1 along party lines to advance the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, authorizing publication in the Federal Register and opening a 30-day public comment period (narrower than the September 2026 window earlier projected in the EEOC's own regulatory agenda); a public hearing on the proposal is scheduled for August 11, 2026. Employers remain subject to EEO-1 filing obligations for the 2026 cycle in the meantime. At the August 11, 2026 public hearing, roughly 22 witnesses testified; per National Law Review and Ogletree Deakins coverage, most urged the Commission to retain or reform the EEO-1 framework rather than eliminate it outright, with both employer-side and employee-side speakers warning that rescinding standardized reporting would not actually reduce employers' data burden, since the same information could still be sought via investigations, subpoenas, and litigation on a case-by-case basis. The EEOC took no formal action at the hearing itself. Nearly 1,500 public comments had been submitted on the NPRM as of the hearing date; the written comment period runs through August 24, 2026, after which the Commission will review comments before any final rule. Correction 2026-08-29: this entry's prior text described the proposal as covering EEO-1 through EEO-5, based on the May 14, 2026 OIRA-submission title -- but the NPRM as formally published in the Federal Register on July 23, 2026 (91 FR 46332, 'Removal of Reporting Requirements') covers EEO-1 through EEO-6. EEO-2 and EEO-6 have not actually been collected since 1981 and 1993 respectively, so their formal rescission is largely a procedural formality rather than a change to real-world data collection -- the practical stakes remain concentrated in EEO-1 (private employers), EEO-3, EEO-4, and EEO-5 as before. Separately, written comments on the NPRM closed August 24, 2026 as scheduled, with roughly 1,500 comments already submitted as of the August 11 hearing; no final rule had been issued as of this update, and the Commission must review the full comment record first.

estimated_impact.summary: The federal government's primary tool for identifying systemic race-, ethnicity-, and sex-based disparities in private-sector employment, in continuous use since 1966 and cited in discrimination settlements worth billions of dollars, is on track for elimination with no comparable federal data source proposed to replace it.

title: EEOC Under Lucas Abandoned Disparate-Impact Enforcement, Rescinded Transgender Protections, and Pivoted to Investigating DEI as 'Reverse Discrimination'
institution: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC)
status: Ongoing and expanding -- active subpoena enforcement litigation (Nike) and investigations (Coca-Cola, others) continue; disparate-impact enforcement and the transgender-harassment guidance rescission remain in effect
date_of_action: 2025-11 (Lucas named chair, 2-1 GOP majority) through 2026-05 (ongoing enforcement expansion)
what_changed: After Trump designated Andrea Lucas as EEOC Chair, giving the commission a 2-1 Republican majority, Lucas redirected the agency's civil rights enforcement priorities in two connected ways. First, EEOC pivoted toward investigating employer diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs as unlawful 'reverse discrimination' against white and male employees: in December 2025, Lucas posted a video calling on white men to report workplace discrimination based on race or sex, and the agency subsequently opened investigations into Coca-Cola (for hosting a women's networking/mentorship event) and Nike (for race-restricted mentorship and leadership programs), among others. Lucas personally filed a Commissioner's Charge against Nike on behalf of a class of white employees alleging systemic race discrimination via its DEI programs; in February 2026, EEOC filed a federal subpoena-enforcement action against Nike after the company resisted document requests. Lucas articulated the standard as: 'It doesn't matter if you call that DEI or belonging or "EO" or anything: If it functions like that, it's illegal.' Second, and simultaneously, EEOC rolled back protections historically used to find discrimination against traditionally protected groups: on January 22, 2026, the commission voted to rescind its 2024 Enforcement Guidance on Harassment in the Workplace, which had addressed harassment against transgender employees (including misgendering and facilities access) alongside other protected categories; EEOC had separately, in 2025, moved to dismiss nearly every discrimination lawsuit it had previously filed on behalf of transgender plaintiffs, prompting a lawsuit from FreeState Justice alleging an unlawful 'Trans Exclusion Policy' denying transgender workers access to EEOC's charge-investigation process. Most significantly, **Lucas announced EEOC will no longer process complaints alleging disparate-impact discrimination -- the legal theory, in place for over 50 years, that facially neutral employment practices producing disproportionate harm to a protected group can constitute unlawful discrimination even without proof of intentional bias -- a legal tool historically used to challenge practices disadvantaging people of color, women, disabled people, and pregnant workers.**

primary_proponent.role: Chair, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
primary_proponent.note: Personally directed both the DEI-as-reverse-discrimination enforcement pivot (including personally filing the Nike Commissioner's Charge and publicly soliciting complaints from white male workers) and the rollback of disparate-impact enforcement and transgender-inclusive harassment guidance. Trump designated her chair in November 2025, giving Republicans a 2-1 commission majority.

estimated_impact.summary: The combined effect is a structural inversion of the agency's historical enforcement focus: EEOC is simultaneously expanding investigative and subpoena power against employers' DEI programs (creating new legal exposure for companies with diversity initiatives) while eliminating the disparate-impact theory and transgender-specific harassment protections that have been primary tools for finding discrimination against traditionally protected groups -- narrowing, not just redirecting, the categories of harm the agency will pursue.

title: U.S. Energy Information Administration Lost More Than 100 of Its ~350 Staff, Canceling Its International Energy Outlook
institution: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), Department of Energy
status: No 2025 International Energy Outlook appeared; as of September 2026 EIA still lists the 2023 edition as latest (next release TBD), and DOE's FY2027 budget proposes folding it into other outlooks. The Annual Energy Outlook 2026 came out April 8, 2026. FY2026 enacted staffing: 246, down from 353.
date_of_action: 2025-04 (buyout departures; International Energy Outlook canceled April 16, 2025)
what_changed: In mid-April 2025, Reuters reported that the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) was **set to lose more than 100 employees after the Trump administration's latest round of deferred-resignation offers**. Two sources put those who had left or accepted buyouts at about 40% of EIA's roughly 350 staff; one source said as many as one-third, and others, including three EIA employees, described the departures as dozens. ProPublica later reported that more than 100 of EIA's 350 staff had left through firings or resignations in the wake of the 'Fork in the Road' buyout offers, and that on April 11, hours before the resignation deadline, EIA's acting administrator read a prepared statement at an all-hands meeting urging employees to take the offer. EIA is the federal government's independent statistical agency for energy data, publishing weekly, monthly, and annual reports on oil and gas output, crude and fuel inventories, and price forecasts that traders and energy companies use to gauge supply and demand -- reports that often move global oil prices. Sources told Reuters the agency was assessing which reports it could keep releasing, and that many research initiatives had been put on indefinite hold. That same week, EIA released its flagship Annual Energy Outlook 2025 in abridged form: data tables and a short introduction, without the usual analytical narrative or release event. Former EIA administrator Joseph DeCarolis wrote that it was published 'under difficult circumstances.' The narrative cut predated the April buyout wave: ProPublica reported that the decision to drop it -- then 53 pages in draft -- was announced to staff in a March 10 internal email after conferring with EIA's front office. EIA employees said they believed it was made to avoid angering the administration; an EIA spokesperson said leadership chose to get the results out quickly rather than wait for a written analysis. EIA listed the next edition's release date as 'TBD.' On April 16, 2025, Angelina LaRose, assistant administrator in EIA's Office of Energy Analysis, told staff in an internal email obtained by ProPublica, 'At this point, you can assume we will not be releasing the IEO this year,' calling it 'a difficult decision based on the loss of key resources,' and ordered an all-hands effort to preserve institutional knowledge about the models before more analysts left. The International Energy Outlook is published every two years; the previous (2023) edition ran 70 pages on global energy trends. Its absence leaves the field to the Paris-based International Energy Agency's equivalent publication, which some conservatives accuse of bending its forecasts toward climate-change goals. EIA told Argus in May 2025 that the 2025 edition might still be published early the next year, and in August 2025 a spokesperson said it might not appear until January 2026. By August 2025, S&P Global reported EIA staffing down about 30%, with the administration's fiscal 2026 budget request seeking 246 full-time employees, down from the 353 allotted for 2025; former EIA administrator Adam Sieminski estimated the agency could fall to about 200 staff by the end of 2025. EIA also canceled a 2025 report on net shell storage capacity, delayed its uranium marketing and biofuels capacity reports, and proposed ending its solar photovoltaic module shipments report. DOE's fiscal 2027 budget justification lists EIA's enacted fiscal 2026 staffing at 246 full-time equivalents, down from 353 in fiscal 2025, with funding flat at $135 million, and proposes folding international analysis into new medium- and long-term outlooks instead of a standalone International Energy Outlook. EIA published its Annual Energy Outlook 2026 on April 8, 2026, with a full narrative and a foreword by Administrator Tristan Abbey. As of September 2026, EIA's website still lists the 2023 edition as the latest International Energy Outlook, with the next release date 'TBD.'

primary_proponent.role: Directed the government-wide 'Fork in the Road' buyout offer that drove the EIA departures
primary_proponent.note: No DOE or EIA official was identified in sourcing reviewed as targeting EIA specifically; the departures came through the government-wide deferred-resignation offers and related firings. ProPublica reported that EIA's own acting administrator urged staff at an April 11, 2025 all-hands meeting to take the offer.

estimated_impact.summary: The government's principal energy-statistics agency lost more than 100 of its roughly 350 staff in 2025 through buyouts and firings, was operating about 30% smaller by August 2025, and its enacted fiscal 2026 staffing is 246 full-time equivalents, down from 353. The loss of key analysts led EIA to cancel its 2025 International Energy Outlook, and no new edition has appeared since 2023, leaving long-term global energy projections to the International Energy Agency. EIA also delayed or dropped several smaller reports. Its flagship Annual Energy Outlook 2025 came out without its analytical narrative, though that cut was decided in March 2025, before the buyout wave, and the 2026 edition restored it. No health or mortality effect is documented; the harm is to independent market data that traders, companies, and policymakers rely on.

title: Eisenhower Presidential Library director forced out after refusing to hand over museum sword for a royal gift
institution: Dwight D. Eisenhower Presidential Library (National Archives and Records Administration)
status: Resigned (forced)
what_changed: **Todd Arrington, director of the Dwight D. Eisenhower Presidential Library in Abilene, Kansas for nearly 30 years of federal service, was told on a Monday in late September 2025 to 'resign or be fired' after refusing to release a historic sword from the museum's collection -- one Queen Wilhelmina of the Netherlands gave to Eisenhower in 1947 -- for President Trump to gift to King Charles III during Trump's September 2025 state visit to the United Kingdom.** The request reportedly came through a State Department liaison using the email address 'giftgirl2025'; neither NARA nor the White House provided an on-record official statement (both sent automated shutdown-related auto-replies when press asked). Arrington maintained the sword was a museum artifact belonging to the American people and could not be given away; Trump ultimately gifted King Charles a replica cadet saber from West Point instead. Arrington said he was told he could no longer be trusted with confidential information. The incident falls within the same October 2025-adjacent window as Secretary of State Marco Rubio's concurrent tenure as acting Archivist of the United States (Feb. 16, 2025-Feb. 4, 2026) -- meaning the same individual headed both the State Department (origin of the gift request) and NARA (Eisenhower Library's parent agency) at the time, though no source establishes Rubio personally directed Arrington's ouster.

title: Household Electricity Prices Rose Under Trump's Energy Policy Despite His Promise to Halve Them, Hitting Coal-Dependent West Virginia Hard
institution: Department of Energy / national electricity ratepayers, concentrated impact in coal-dependent states
status: Promise unmet. Past Trump's 18-month deadline, EIA data showed residential electricity rates up about 18% from January 2025 to April 2026 and still 4.9% above a year earlier in July 2026; AP reported in April 2026 that some West Virginia bills top rents and mortgages.
date_of_action: 2025-01 (Trump's term begins) through 2026-07 (18-month price-halving deadline passes)
what_changed: Trump campaigned on halving energy costs: in a September 2024 Economic Club of New York speech he said 'my plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office,' and at a North Carolina rally he said 'we intend to slash prices by half within 12 months, maximum of 18 months.' Instead, residential electricity prices rose nearly 10% nationally in the first months of his second term, according to Energy Information Administration data cited in August 2025 by Forbes and by The Guardian, which reported it from an analysis by the advocacy group Climate Power: the average residential rate climbed from 15.95 cents per kilowatt-hour in January 2025 to 17.47 cents in May (a January-to-May comparison that includes normal seasonal swings; against May 2024, prices were about 6% higher). Some states saw far steeper increases: EIA data cited by CNN in September 2025 showed residential prices up 26% in Maine and 25% in New Jersey as of June, while the Bureau of Labor Statistics measured electricity prices up 5.5% in the 12 months to July 2025, about twice overall inflation. Reporting attributed the increase to several compounding factors tied to administration policy: tariffs on steel and aluminum raising the cost of building and maintaining transmission lines, substations, and power plants; the administration's encouragement of ratepayer-subsidized buildout of private AI data centers, shifting infrastructure costs onto household bills; and, in the Center for American Progress's April 2025 list of actions likely to raise prices, the freezing of clean-energy investments and grants Congress had already allocated through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and Inflation Reduction Act. Climate think tank Energy Innovation separately estimated the energy provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed July 4, 2025) would raise wholesale electricity prices 25% by 2030 and 74% by 2035 and retail electricity rates 9-18% by 2035, raising household energy costs by $170 a year by 2035. Coal-dependent West Virginia, where coal generates roughly 86-87% of electricity (the highest share of any state), shows the cost of that path, according to a September 29, 2025 New York Times report: over the previous 15 years the state's electricity rates had risen almost twice as fast as the national average, driven largely by coal-fuel price spikes, expensive coal contracts, coal-plant costs and state regulators' insistence on coal, and energy experts told the Times the state could be a harbinger as the Trump administration ordered aging coal plants to stay open and halted or denied renewable projects. American Electric Power told state regulators in 2024 that nearly one in five of its West Virginia customers (about 84,000 households) was typically behind on its bill each month, and its two utilities there, Appalachian Power and Wheeling Power, cut power to 56,000 households for nonpayment in 2023, up from 3,300 in 2020. A companion entry documents the separate PJM 13-state grid capacity-market story, in which Trump blamed wind and solar for record price increases driven primarily by data-center demand. One year into the term, a Guardian analysis of EIA data published January 17, 2026 found the average household electricity bill was 6.7% higher in 2025 than in 2024, nearly $116 more, and household gas prices up 5.2%. Households the Guardian interviewed described the strain: a 76-year-old Baltimore resident who unplugs most of her appliances saw monthly gas and electric bills top $500 throughout 2025, and a Texas woman said she was cutting back on doctor's appointments to pay for electricity. NPR reported on January 20, 2026 that electricity costs were still rising and expected to rise more, with wholesale power prices up more than 60% in New York and New England and 45% in the mid-Atlantic, according to BloombergNEF; gasoline was the partial exception, with pump prices down nearly 10%, far short of the promised 50%+ cut and not the household electricity and heating costs at the center of the promise. In March 2026, Democratic staff of the congressional Joint Economic Committee, using EIA data, calculated that the average U.S. household electric bill rose $110 (6.4%) in 2025, with annual bills at least 10% higher in 12 states and DC. In April 2026, Associated Press reporting (published by PBS News, CBS Pittsburgh and other outlets) found **West Virginia utility bills sometimes surpassing residents' rents and mortgages after an arctic winter, with some families forced to choose between food, medicine and heat**; one disabled, fixed-income resident's February electric bill of $940 exceeded her monthly check. The AP cited Public Service Commission figures showing the state's average household electricity rate up 73% from 2015 to 2025, reported that more than one in three West Virginia households is energy burdened (spending over 6% of income on electricity and other fuel), and noted that Trump has forced unprofitable coal plants to stay open and rolled back their pollution standards. Nationally, the Consumer Price Index showed electricity up 4.8% and piped natural gas up 10.9% year over year in February 2026. By July 20, 2026, the 18-month outer deadline Trump had set, EIA data showed average residential electricity rates up about 18% from January 2025 to April 2026 (to 18.83 cents per kilowatt-hour) and up 7.3% from April 2025, roughly twice inflation, as reported by Reason and Common Dreams. The Cato Institute's Travis Fisher told Reason it was 'an impossible promise to deliver on' because the federal government has little direct control over retail rates, while Reason also noted that the administration's tariffs on grid equipment and its moves against offshore wind added costs. EIA data for July 2026 showed the average residential rate at 18.31 cents per kilowatt-hour, down from April's 18.83 cents but still about 4.9% above July 2025.

The Corporate Deregulation tracker documents the underlying actions this consumer-cost story flows from: the first-term repeal of the Clean Power Plan and its replacement with the Affordable Clean Energy rule, the 2026 repeal of the 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards amendments, federal buyouts of offshore wind leases paired with Energy Department emergency orders keeping aging coal plants online, the Energy Department's cancellation of clean-energy grants, and federal support for aging coal-fired power plants.

Nationally, residential electricity rates rose about 18% from January 2025 to April 2026 and the average household electric bill rose about $110 in 2025, the opposite of Trump's promise to halve prices, and the 2025 tax law's clean-energy repeal is projected to push household energy costs higher through 2035.

title: EPA Moved to Eliminate the 30-Year-Old Energy Star Program; Bipartisan Congressional and Industry Pushback Forced a Transfer to DOE Instead -- Then the Administration Proposed Killing It Again a Year Later
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Office of Atmospheric Protection; later transferred to the Department of Energy (DOE)
status: Program preserved via interagency transfer, not eliminated -- fully moved to DOE by June 2026 with a congressionally mandated funding floor, but the administration's FY2027 budget (April 2026) proposed eliminating the EPA office that had housed it for a second consecutive year
date_of_action: 2025-05 (elimination announced internally) through 2026-06 (full transfer to DOE completed)
what_changed: In May 2025, Paul Gunning, director of EPA's Office of Atmospheric Protection, told staff at an internal meeting that 'the Energy Star program and all the other climate work, outside of what's required by statute, is being de-prioritized and eliminated.' Energy Star, launched in 1992, is a voluntary labeling program that has helped identify energy-efficient appliances, buildings, and electronics for over three decades and is credited by the EPA's own historical figures with saving consumers and businesses more than $500 billion in energy costs over its lifetime; the FY2026 President's Budget proposed zero dollars for the program. More than 1,000 companies and organizations -- including appliance manufacturers, 14 HVAC associations, 19 HVAC manufacturers, and energy-management and real-estate firms -- signed letters to Congress opposing elimination, and more than 20 U.S. senators sent a letter (May 28, 2025) urging EPA to reverse course, arguing elements of the program are protected by statute and cannot be unilaterally terminated. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin subsequently indicated the agency would not fully eliminate the program. Rather than being shut down, Energy Star was moved internally to EPA's Office of Radiation and Indoor Air starting around November 2025, then transferred entirely out of EPA to the Department of Energy under a March 2026 interagency agreement, with the move completed by June 2026. In January 2026, Congress funded Energy Star at $33 million for FY2026 -- a $1 million increase over the prior year -- and for the first time attached a mandatory minimum annual spending level to the program, an explicit legislative check against future unilateral elimination attempts. Despite that outcome, the administration's FY2027 budget request, released in April 2026, again proposed eliminating EPA's Office of Atmospheric Protection -- the second consecutive year it targeted the office, though Energy Star itself was by then housed at DOE rather than EPA.

estimated_impact.summary: A 30-year-old, voluntary energy-efficiency labeling program EPA itself credits with saving consumers and businesses over $500 billion was slated for elimination via a zero-dollar budget request, surviving only after unusually broad industry (1,000+ companies, including groups not typically aligned with environmental advocacy) and bipartisan-leaning congressional pushback forced a transfer to DOE rather than termination -- illustrating both the reach of the administration's climate-program-elimination push and the limits imposed when it collided with organized business-sector opposition.

title: EPA Canceled $2.8 Billion in Environmental Justice Grants -- Including a Flood-Protection Grant to an Alaska Village Devastated by a Typhoon Months Later -- Then a Federal Judge Ruled the Cancellation Unlawful and Ordered the Program Revived, an Order the 4th Circuit Stayed in August 2026
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
status: On hold on appeal -- Judge Gergel ruled EPA's termination of the $2.8B program unlawful (June 11, 2026) and ordered EPA to run it (July 22); the 4th Circuit stayed that order Aug. 20 and denied en banc review Sept. 23, and Gergel declined Sept. 24 to toll the Sept. 30 deadline
date_of_action: 2025-02-25 (EPA official decides to terminate the program) through 2026-09-24 (judge declines to pause the program's Sept. 30 expiration)
what_changed: EPA assistant deputy administrator Travis Voyles decided on February 25, 2025 that the Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant Program should be terminated for 'policy reasons,' according to the later court opinion. The Inflation Reduction Act created the program (Clean Air Act Section 138) with $3 billion -- $2.8 billion for grants and $200 million for technical assistance -- to help low-income and minority communities address pollution and climate risk, and required EPA to award the money by September 30, 2026. Its main vehicle was the roughly $2 billion Community Change Grants competition, run by EPA's Office of Environmental Justice and External Civil Rights, which had selected about 105 projects worth roughly $1.6 billion under the Biden administration. Those grants were frozen first. NPR reported April 14-15, 2025 that more than 22 tribes and nonprofits had around $350 million in funding frozen, often without notice; some found their grants marked 'suspended' in the federal payment system in early March, others saw them disappear from it, and Alaska villages including Tyonek received no notice at all. The Tebughna Foundation's $20 million award to renovate or replace 20 asbestos- and lead-contaminated homes in the Native Village of Tyonek, Alaska, and connect them to solar power, was among the frozen grants. A court filing reported by The Washington Post on April 29, 2025 showed EPA moving to cancel 781 grants awarded under the Biden administration, including all of its environmental justice grants. Data Floodlight obtained through a public-records request showed EPA had canceled more than 600 grants of all kinds since January 20, 2025, totaling more than $2.7 billion through May 15, 2025; environmental justice grants took by far the biggest hit, at more than $2.4 billion. Among the canceled grants was a $20 million Community Change Grant to the Native Village of Kipnuk, Alaska, revoked May 2, 2025, that would have stabilized the eroding bank of the Kugkaktlik River, where the village was losing 10 to 28 feet of land a year, and protected homes, boardwalks and other infrastructure. **Roughly five months later, on October 12, 2025, the remnants of Typhoon Halong produced a record storm surge that devastated Kipnuk, washing away dozens of homes and forcing hundreds of residents to evacuate -- the same infrastructure the canceled grant would have helped protect.** EPA publicly defended the cancellation after the storm, with press secretary Brigit Hirsch saying the $20 million was sitting in the Treasury rather than being swept into the river and noting the project would not have begun construction until 2026. Grantees sued on two tracks. In Washington, a class action filed in June 2025 by 15 nonprofits, the Native Village of Kipnuk and seven local governments (Appalachian Voices v. EPA) was dismissed on August 29, 2025 by U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, who found the claims belonged in the Court of Federal Claims; on July 21, 2026 the D.C. Circuit vacated that dismissal and sent the case back to decide first whether Congress's rescission of the program's unobligated funds had made it moot. In South Carolina, nonprofits and local governments including Baltimore, Nashville and San Diego (The Sustainability Institute v. Trump) sued before U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel; on January 21, 2026 the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals vacated his earlier injunctions reinstating the plaintiffs' frozen or terminated grants, leaving challenges to individual grant terminations to the Court of Federal Claims. On June 11, 2026, Gergel ruled that EPA's internal guidance terminating the program 'was arbitrary and capricious and unlawful' and vacated it. He declined to order EPA to resume running the program, saying that would likely require rehiring the fired staff who had administered the grants, which he called impractical, and he refused to extend the September 30, 2026 deadline; the ruling covered only the program-level termination, not individual grants. On July 22, 2026, on the plaintiffs' motion to enforce, Gergel clarified that EPA 'must comply with its statutory obligations to administer the ECJ Program' and make its funds available through September 30, 2026, again rejecting EPA's argument that Congress's rescission of the unobligated funds in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act mooted the case. EPA appealed, arguing that reviving the program would require 'a tremendous diversion' of its resources since its staff had been fired, and on August 20, 2026 a divided 4th Circuit panel -- Judges Allison Jones Rushing and Paul Niemeyer, with Judge Toby Heytens voting to deny -- stayed the July 22 order pending appeal, leaving the program on hold. In late August 2026 the plaintiffs petitioned the full 4th Circuit to rehear the stay, and in early September they asked Gergel to toll the program's September 30 expiration pending appeal. On September 23, 2026 the 4th Circuit denied rehearing en banc, with no judge requesting a poll, and on September 24 Gergel denied the tolling motion, ruling that he lacked jurisdiction while both of his orders were on appeal.

EPA terminated the whole $2.8 billion Environmental and Climate Justice grant program, including about $1.6 billion in Community Change Grants already selected for roughly 105 projects. A judge ruled the termination unlawful and ordered EPA to run the program, but an appeals court stayed that order in August 2026 and refused rehearing in September, and the judge declined to extend the money's September 30, 2026 award deadline.

title: EPA Issues Reduction-in-Force Notices to 22 Remaining Environmental Justice Staffers, Completing a Two-Year Wind-Down of the Function
institution: Environmental Protection Agency
status: Finalized as to this round -- RIF notices issued; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-02-06 (initial administrative leave) through 2026-02 (RIF notices to the final 22 remaining EJ staffers)
what_changed: EPA's dismantlement of its Environmental Justice function played out as a multi-stage process over roughly a year. On February 6, 2025, EPA placed nearly 170 employees of its Office of Environmental Justice and External Civil Rights (OEJECR) on administrative leave agency-wide. Less than a month later, in early March 2025, EPA recalled some of those employees and reassigned them to other duties, chiefly managing Community Change Grants and maintaining relationships with communities, tribes, and local/state partners. The Washington Post and Inside Climate News put the number at 'dozens'; CBS News later called it 'a handful.' The Post reported that regional staff were emailed on Monday, March 3, and returned to work on Wednesday, March 5, and that not all of those brought back had worked in environmental justice roles. EPA confirmed the move but did not say how many it brought back, saying it was 'considering the guidance from OPM and the President'; one returning employee told the Post their role involved tasks required by law. That reprieve did not hold for the office as a whole, though no reporting reviewed says what became of the recalled staff specifically (Inside Climate News noted in April that EPA 'did not clarify' whether the roughly 170 staff placed on leave in February, including those recalled, were among those given layoff notices): on March 12, 2025 -- the same day Administrator Lee Zeldin announced 31 deregulatory actions, and in conjunction with them -- EPA announced it was terminating its environmental justice arm, implementing a March 11 Zeldin memo eliminating all 10 of OEJECR's regional Environmental Justice Divisions and placing their employees on administrative leave. On April 22, 2025, EPA issued formal Reduction in Force (RIF) notices, with the agency stating that a total of 280 EJ staffers -- both in Washington and across the regional offices -- would be laid off effective July 31, 2025 (E&E News later reported that EPA notified 271 employees in April, with the timetable in flux after a court-ordered pause), while another 175 employees whose roles included statutory functions were reassigned to other EPA offices rather than terminated, undertaken to comply with executive orders eliminating environmental-justice programs across the federal government. Finally, in February 2026, EPA issued RIF notices to the 22 EJ staffers still remaining after the 2025 wave -- among the last people at the agency doing this work in any form -- completing the function's elimination. According to InsideEPA, **many of the 22 employees targeted in this final round were staff with disabilities**. The American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Council 238, which represents EPA employees, publicly condemned the final round; council president Justin Chen said the union was 'outraged by the EPA's decision to issue RIF notices to 22 environmental justice employees whose work ensures that communities disproportionately burdened by environmental hazards receive the protections they are entitled to.'

estimated_impact.summary: EPA has now eliminated essentially its entire dedicated environmental-justice staffing function, after a yearlong process in which it recalled some employees in early March 2025 ('dozens' per The Washington Post, 'a handful' per CBS News), then ordered all regional EJ divisions closed about a week later -- roughly 280 announced layoffs and 175 reassignments in 2025, followed by RIF notices to the last 22 remaining EJ staffers in February 2026 -- removing the agency's capacity to specifically track and address pollution and health risks concentrated in low-income and heavily polluted communities.
