title: EPA Froze $20 Billion in Climate Grants Over Unsubstantiated Fraud Claims and Canceled $7 Billion Solar for All -- Courts Have Ruled Against Both
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF)
status: Solar for All: EPA's termination vacated by a federal judge in Rhode Island on Sept. 18, 2026; EPA is weighing an appeal. NCIF/CCIA: the D.C. Circuit upheld the injunction Aug. 4, 2026, with its payment order stayed while the government seeks Supreme Court review.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Zeldin, FBI, and Treasury order Citibank to freeze the grantee accounts) through 2026-08-04 (D.C. Circuit rules against EPA); Solar for All sub-program: 2025-08-07 (terminated) through 2026-09-18 (termination vacated in Rhode Island)
what_changed:
EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin sought to freeze and then terminate roughly $20 billion in Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund grants -- awarded to eight National Clean Investment Fund and Clean Communities Investment Accelerator nonprofit entities to fund clean-energy financing, including in communities that had lacked access to green financing -- out of a $27 billion program Congress established in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. In February 2025, Zeldin, together with the FBI and Treasury Department, ordered Citibank to freeze the grantee nonprofits' accounts, citing possible fraud, waste, and abuse; EPA's stated justification also relied on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's repeal of the underlying IRA statutory section as separate legal authority to claw the funds back. A federal district judge (Tonya Chutkan) issued an injunction in April 2025 blocking the freeze, ruling that the government's 'vague and unsubstantiated assertions of fraud are insufficient.' EPA appealed; on August 4, 2026, a divided U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (6 of 10 judges) upheld the injunction, ruling EPA lacked authority to reclaim funds already disbursed to grantee accounts. No EPA Inspector General, DOJ, or FBI investigation had produced a substantiated fraud finding as of the ruling, more than 17 months after the initial freeze. Separately, on August 7, 2025, EPA terminated the remaining $7 billion Solar for All sub-program -- the third GGRF pillar alongside NCIF and CCIA, which had made 60 awards to states, tribes, territories, and nonprofits (roughly $5.5 billion to 49 state-level awardees, over $500 million to six tribal awardees, and about $1 billion to five multistate awardees) to fund low-income residential solar access -- citing the same One Big Beautiful Bill Act repeal of GGRF's authorizing statute as its legal basis; only about $53 million of the $7 billion had actually been spent at termination. Added 2026-09-10: one of the six tribal Solar for All awardees was the Hopi Tribe in Arizona, which had been approved for a $25 million grant to install solar panels and battery storage connecting roughly 600 previously unelectrified homes; after the termination, **the tribe was left with a far smaller Tribal Electrification Program grant sufficient to power only about 100 homes, forcing Hopi officials to decide which families would remain without electricity**. Twenty-three states sued EPA in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington in October 2025 to reinstate the Solar for All funding, but on June 2, 2026 Judge Tiffany Cartwright dismissed the suit for lack of jurisdiction, holding the states' claim was effectively a Tucker Act money-damages claim belonging in the Court of Federal Claims rather than a district-court APA challenge -- a markedly different legal outcome from the NCIF/CCIA fight, where Chutkan's injunction was upheld on appeal. Grantee nonprofits separately sued in the Court of Federal Claims to recover their withheld Solar for All funds.

Update 2026-09-29: On September 18, 2026, Judge Mary McElroy of the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island vacated EPA's termination of Solar for All, in a suit brought by the Rhode Island AFL-CIO, the Rhode Island Center for Justice, Solar United Neighbors and others. She held that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act did not convert the program's funding into "a lump-sum amount subject to EPA's discretion" and that Congress intended EPA to keep administering grants it had already obligated. **The ruling restores the $7 billion program meant to make solar power accessible to more than 900,000 lower-income Americans**; EPA said it was reviewing the decision and considering an appeal. The 23 states whose Washington suit was dismissed have appealed. On the NCIF/CCIA track, the government filed an unopposed motion on August 6 to stay the D.C. Circuit's mandate pending a petition for Supreme Court review; the court granted it, keeping the injunction's disbursement requirement on hold through Nov. 9, 2026, and longer if a petition is filed.

glance.what: Froze $20B in climate grants on unproven fraud claims and ended $7B Solar for All; courts ruled against both

what_changed.base: EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin sought to freeze and then terminate roughly $20 billion in Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund grants -- awarded to eight National Clean Investment Fund and Clean Communities Investment Accelerator nonprofit entities to fund clean-energy financing, including in communities that had lacked access to green financing -- out of a $27 billion program Congress established in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. In February 2025, Zeldin, together with the FBI and Treasury Department, ordered Citibank to freeze the grantee nonprofits' accounts, citing possible fraud, waste, and abuse; EPA's stated justification also relied on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's repeal of the underlying IRA statutory section as separate legal authority to claw the funds back. A federal district judge (Tonya Chutkan) issued an injunction in April 2025 blocking the freeze, ruling that the government's 'vague and unsubstantiated assertions of fraud are insufficient.' EPA appealed; on August 4, 2026, a divided U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit (6 of 10 judges) upheld the injunction, ruling EPA lacked authority to reclaim funds already disbursed to grantee accounts. No EPA Inspector General, DOJ, or FBI investigation had produced a substantiated fraud finding as of the ruling, more than 17 months after the initial freeze. Separately, on August 7, 2025, EPA terminated the remaining $7 billion Solar for All sub-program -- the third GGRF pillar alongside NCIF and CCIA, which had made 60 awards to states, tribes, territories, and nonprofits (roughly $5.5 billion to 49 state-level awardees, over $500 million to six tribal awardees, and about $1 billion to five multistate awardees) to fund low-income residential solar access -- citing the same One Big Beautiful Bill Act repeal of GGRF's authorizing statute as its legal basis; only about $53 million of the $7 billion had actually been spent at termination.

updates.label: Added
updates.text: Added 2026-09-10: one of the six tribal Solar for All awardees was the Hopi Tribe in Arizona, which had been approved for a $25 million grant to install solar panels and battery storage connecting roughly 600 previously unelectrified homes; after the termination, **the tribe was left with a far smaller Tribal Electrification Program grant sufficient to power only about 100 homes, forcing Hopi officials to decide which families would remain without electricity**. Twenty-three states sued EPA in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington in October 2025 to reinstate the Solar for All funding, but on June 2, 2026 Judge Tiffany Cartwright dismissed the suit for lack of jurisdiction, holding the states' claim was effectively a Tucker Act money-damages claim belonging in the Court of Federal Claims rather than a district-court APA challenge -- a markedly different legal outcome from the NCIF/CCIA fight, where Chutkan's injunction was upheld on appeal. Grantee nonprofits separately sued in the Court of Federal Claims to recover their withheld Solar for All funds.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-09-29: On September 18, 2026, Judge Mary McElroy of the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island vacated EPA's termination of Solar for All, in a suit brought by the Rhode Island AFL-CIO, the Rhode Island Center for Justice, Solar United Neighbors and others. She held that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act did not convert the program's funding into "a lump-sum amount subject to EPA's discretion" and that Congress intended EPA to keep administering grants it had already obligated. **The ruling restores the $7 billion program meant to make solar power accessible to more than 900,000 lower-income Americans**; EPA said it was reviewing the decision and considering an appeal. The 23 states whose Washington suit was dismissed have appealed. On the NCIF/CCIA track, the government filed an unopposed motion on August 6 to stay the D.C. Circuit's mandate pending a petition for Supreme Court review; the court granted it, keeping the injunction's disbursement requirement on hold through Nov. 9, 2026, and longer if a petition is filed.

confidence_note.base: HIGH confidence on the core sequence (Feb. 2025 freeze, April 2025 district-court injunction, Aug. 4 2026 D.C. Circuit ruling, Zeldin's personal role) -- corroborated across TechCrunch, U.S. News/AP, GV Wire, and WTAQ, all citing the same underlying court ruling. MODERATE confidence on the ultimate outcome, since Supreme Court review is still possible and the case is explicitly not final. HIGH confidence on the Solar for All termination and its jurisdictional dismissal, corroborated across Planet Detroit, CBS News, Colorado Sun, IRA Tracker, and Bloomberg Tax/Mealey's coverage of Judge Cartwright's ruling.

title: EPA Employees Suspect Broken Elevators, Extreme Heat Meant to Drive Them Out
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA headquarters, William Jefferson Clinton Federal Building)
status: Ongoing as of July 2025 reporting -- EPA denies intentional degradation, blaming deferred maintenance; no independent facility-condition investigation or GSA repair timeline identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-06 through 2025-07 (reported conditions persisting roughly three weeks before July 11, 2025 CBS News report)
what_changed: By July 2025, EPA headquarters employees had endured roughly three weeks of degraded working conditions they suspected were being used, or at minimum tolerated, as a tool to pressure them into resigning rather than being formally laid off. Multiple employees reported getting stuck in malfunctioning elevators, and some described elevators suddenly dropping between floors. During a Washington, D.C. heat wave with outdoor temperatures above 100 degrees, indoor air conditioning failed in parts of the building, with employees sharing photos of desk-mounted temperature/CO2 monitors showing indoor readings above 80 degrees. **Some employees were relocated to a basement area adjacent to a firing range used by federal law-enforcement officials for target practice, raising employee concern about elevated indoor lead exposure from ammunition residue**. EPA leadership publicly attributed the conditions to ordinary deferred maintenance, telling CBS News the prior administration had 'didn't invest in buildings that were partially empty, due to work-from-home habits' -- a framing that blames pre-2025 remote-work patterns rather than any current decision. The conditions arrived amid a broader EPA workforce contraction: hundreds of employees had already accepted the government-wide 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation offer, and separately, roughly 140 employees had been placed on administrative leave weeks earlier (in a still-ongoing episode this database documents separately, see zeldin-dissent-letter-retaliation-2025-2026.json) after signing a June 30, 2025 'Declaration of Dissent' letter criticizing the administration's treatment of agency science and staff -- a distinct accountability concern (First Amendment retaliation against named dissenters) from the facility-conditions story documented here, which concerns the general workforce rather than the letter's specific signatories.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.role: Administrator, Environmental Protection Agency
primary_proponent.note: As agency head, Zeldin's EPA publicly attributed the facility conditions to deferred maintenance rather than acknowledging or investigating employee concerns that the disrepair was being used as a pressure tactic; no specific facility-management decision-maker was named in sourcing reviewed.

estimated_impact.summary: No quantified injury, illness, or building-repair-cost figure was identified in sourcing reviewed; the documented impact is elevated occupational-safety risk (heat exposure, potential lead exposure near an indoor firing range, elevator malfunctions) affecting an unspecified but multi-employee share of EPA's Washington headquarters staff, compounding an already-contracting workforce.
estimated_impact.caveat: This entry intentionally carries no fabricated dollar or health-outcome figure: no source reviewed provided a building-specific deferred-maintenance repair-cost estimate, a measured indoor lead level near the relocated basement offices, or a documented injury/illness count tied to the heat or elevator conditions -- the record here is employee-reported working conditions and agency denial, not yet an independently measured harm. A future recheck should look for a GSA facility-condition assessment or an OSHA/inspector-general complaint, either of which could supply a quantified figure this entry currently lacks.

confidence_note: MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the conditions themselves -- multiple named and unnamed EPA employees independently described the same broken elevators, heat, and firing-range relocation to CBS News, corroborated by The Daily Beast's and Raw Story's independent reporting on the same underlying employee accounts. LOW-MODERATE confidence on the central accountability claim (that the conditions are a deliberate attrition tactic rather than genuine deferred maintenance) -- this is explicitly presented in the sourcing as employee suspicion, not a proven agency decision, and EPA's on-the-record deferred-maintenance explanation is a plausible alternative that this entry cannot rule out. The entry documents a pattern of employee concern and agency denial, not a settled finding of intentional sabotage.

title: EPA's Environmental-Justice Screening Tool and NOAA's Billion-Dollar Disaster Database Both Discontinued
institution: Environmental Protection Agency; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
status: Both discontinuations are final as of this entry -- EJScreen taken offline, the NOAA disaster database retired with no updates beyond 2024
date_of_action: 2025-02 (EPA's EJScreen taken offline) through 2026-05 (NOAA announces retirement of its billion-dollar disaster database)
what_changed: **EPA's EJScreen -- a mapping and screening tool combining environmental and demographic indicators to identify communities facing higher combined environmental and socioeconomic burdens -- was taken offline by the Trump administration between February 3 and February 5, 2025; a nonprofit, the Public Environmental Data Project, has since built a replica to keep the underlying data accessible.** Separately, NOAA announced it will retire its 'Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters' database, which had tracked the frequency and cost of major U.S. weather and climate disasters for decades -- the agency will keep historical data through calendar year 2024 available but will not add further updates, as part of a Trump 2026 fiscal year budget proposal cutting NOAA's overall budget by $1.52 billion, concentrated in climate-related research, data, and grant programs. Separately, CDC removed multiple web pages addressing health disparities among LGBTQ+ youth, and USDA (which oversees the Forest Service) removed pages referencing climate change, as part of the same broader wave of federal data and web-content removal reported across agencies in 2025-2026. (Note: the parallel removal of USDA's 30-year Household Food Security Survey is documented separately in this tracker's usda-food-security-survey-cancellation-2025.json entry and is not duplicated here.) Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0686): the Federation of American Scientists and other data scientists published a 'Dearly Departed Datasets' list around late October 2025 cataloguing federal datasets killed off, stripped of variables, or made harder to access under the second Trump administration, sorting them into categories (fully terminated, variables deleted, access tools removed, or preserved by outside groups after federal discontinuation). Specific examples beyond the EPA/NOAA/CDC/USDA items above included: figures on transgender inmates removed from Bureau of Justice Statistics inmate data, three gender-identity questions removed from the National Crime Victimization Survey, a race-and-ethnicity column removed from a federal workforce dataset, and a Census Bureau dataset on the relationship between income inequality and disaster vulnerability. The report found the number of fully-terminated datasets 'in the dozens, out of the hundreds of thousands' the federal government produces, and warned that continued loss of federal staff and expertise (following the year's broader workforce reductions) put additional datasets at ongoing risk. No specific administration official was named or quoted defending the removals catalogued in this report.

primary_proponent.name: Multiple agency heads -- no single named official directs all three actions
primary_proponent.role: EPA, NOAA (Commerce Department), and HHS/CDC leadership each independently discontinued or removed tools/data within their own agencies
primary_proponent.note: Reporting reviewed does not identify one official personally ordering all three actions; each agency's leadership (EPA, NOAA under Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's broader NOAA budget cuts, and CDC under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) is responsible for the removal within its own domain.

estimated_impact.summary: Each tool served a distinct, widely-used public function: EJScreen was used by researchers, journalists, and local governments to identify environmental-justice burdens; the NOAA disaster database was the standard reference for the cost and frequency of major U.S. weather and climate disasters, used by researchers, insurers, and policymakers; the CDC pages provided health-disparity data specific to LGBTQ+ youth. Outside groups have moved to independently preserve the EJScreen and NOAA disaster data specifically because federal versions were discontinued.

title: EPA Eliminated Its Scientific Research Office, Placing the Successor Directly Under the Administrator's Political Control
institution: Office of Research and Development (ORD), Environmental Protection Agency
status: Complete: ORD dissolved; its successor OASES, under the Administrator's office, took effect Oct. 19, 2025; Congress was notified Feb. 13, 2026, and the last 124 ORD staff got reassignment notices in April 2026. The finished PFNA IRIS report was still unpublished as of Sept. 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (plan first reported) through 2026-02-13 (EPA formally notified Congress of ORD's elimination)
what_changed: The plan surfaced in March 2025. The New York Times reported on March 17, 2025 that EPA had presented White House officials with a plan to dissolve its Office of Research and Development (ORD), the agency's largest department, and purge up to 75% of its staff -- as many as 1,155 chemists, biologists, toxicologists and other scientists, according to documents reviewed by Democrats on the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee -- placing the remaining staff elsewhere in EPA 'to provide increased oversight and align with administration priorities.' Administrator Lee Zeldin had said he wanted to cut 65% of the agency's budget; an EPA spokeswoman said at the time that no decisions had been made. Lawsuits delayed the reorganization and layoffs for months, and between January and July 2025 more than 300 ORD staff, including senior scientists, took deferred-resignation offers, Science reported. Specific research began to fall away before any formal announcement. On April 24, 2025, EPA terminated a $549,000, three-year grant (planned to run through August 2026) to CU Boulder environmental engineer Marina Vance, who was studying how wildfire smoke particles infiltrate homes and testing practical interventions such as portable air cleaners to cut residents' exposure; the termination notice said the award's objectives were 'no longer consistent with EPA funding priorities,' the same language used in the separately tracked PFAS-farmland research grant terminations. Vance's team had completed only one field deployment, at Wyoming's Elk Fire in September 2024, and she had to return roughly $360,000, she told the New York Times in a profile published December 27, 2025. Reuters reported on May 1, 2025 that Kolibri, a shoebox-sized EPA-developed sensor that attaches to a drone and flies into wildfire smoke plumes to measure airborne pollution, had effectively been grounded by the looming reorganization, according to three people familiar with the project; EPA said its drone program remained active. University of Idaho wildland-fire scientist Leda Kobziar told Reuters the Kolibri team's tools did 'smoke research that no one else right now can do.' Reuters described the House Science Committee's documents as putting up to 75% of ORD's roughly 1,200 staff at risk of layoff, and reported that research had stalled across 11 ORD offices, including health risk assessments of PFAS. On May 2, 2025, Zeldin announced a reorganization that would split up ORD, shift its scientific expertise into EPA program offices focused on issues such as air and water, and form a new Office of Applied Science and Environmental Solutions (OASES); ORD scientists were told to apply for roughly 500 new positions elsewhere in the agency, Wired reported, citing NPR. Wired reported on May 12, 2025 that the reorganization threatened IRIS (the Integrated Risk Information System), ORD's program for assessing chemicals' health risks and a decades-long target of the chemical industry, and that the program's leader had departed ahead of the announcement. On July 18, 2025, EPA formally announced ORD's elimination and OASES's creation, along with a reduction in force that would take the agency's total staffing to 12,448, down more than 3,700 (nearly 23%) from January 2025; EPA put the savings at $748.8 million. ORD then had 1,540 positions across 10 facilities from Florida and North Carolina to Oregon, and the House Science Democrats' document review indicated that as many as 1,155 of its scientists could be laid off; an EPA spokeswoman said all ORD laboratory functions would continue. Justin Chen, president of AFGE Council 238, called ORD 'the heart and brain of the EPA' and said, 'Its destruction will devastate public health in our country.' In a September 22, 2025 memo to staff, Zeldin formally launched the reorganization, housing OASES within the Office of the Administrator, and EPA said the OASES reorganization was 'finalized and effectuated' on October 19, 2025, despite Senate appropriators' attempts to block the changes. Unlike ORD, which operated as its own division, OASES sits directly under the Administrator -- a structural change critics say subjects research to political oversight rather than insulating it. 'Research' does not appear in the new office's name, which former ORD senior science adviser Andy Miller told C&EN reflects what the reorganization was designed to eliminate: 'the kind of work that points out that there are still problems.' The IRIS staffing collapse produced a concrete example. **IRIS had completed its final assessment of PFNA, a 'forever chemical' it found causes lower birth weights and, based on animal evidence, likely damages the liver and male reproductive system, in mid-April 2025, but EPA had not released it**, ProPublica reported on October 9, 2025; of 55 scientists who had worked on recent IRIS assessments, only 8 remained in the office. PFNA is in drinking water systems serving some 26 million people and has been found in drinking water in 28 states, according to an Environmental Working Group analysis cited by ProPublica, and the assessment's safe-exposure calculation can be used to set limits for Superfund cleanups and drinking water -- a number communities need as they fight polluters over who pays for cleanup. The report was finished shortly before EPA announced in May 2025 that it intended to rescind and reconsider the drinking water limits for PFNA and several other PFAS chemicals (see the separately tracked PFAS drinking-water rollback); Darya Minovi of the Union of Concerned Scientists pointed to that pending rollback as a possible motive for withholding it. EPA told ProPublica only that the report would be published when it was finalized. On October 16, 2025, Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) wrote to Zeldin asking why the report remained unpublished, who directed its delay and when it would be released, calling the delay part of 'a growing pattern of interference with the Agency's scientific work'; EPA's press office did not respond to ProPublica's questions about her letter. As of its February 17, 2026 update, EPA's IRIS 'Recent Additions' page listed no final PFNA assessment, and as of September 2026 EPA's IRIS page for PFNA still listed the assessment at step 6 of 7 (final agency review and interagency science discussion), with no final assessment posted. In a letter dated February 13, 2026, EPA notified the House Science Committee of 'the upcoming elimination' of ORD and the reallocation of its remaining resources, roughly nine months after Zeldin first announced the plan. About 150 employees remained in ORD at that point, according to former ORD employees who spoke to C&EN, and an EPA spokesperson said no further reductions in force or location closures were planned in connection with the closure. As of C&EN's March 3, 2026 report, EPA had not said which offices the remaining ORD staff would move to, and OASES's top two positions had no permanent appointees, with Maureen Gwinn serving as acting associate administrator and agency science adviser. In early April 2026, EPA sent reassignment notices to the last 124 ORD employees, 35 of which required relocating to keep their jobs, E&E News reported; OASES is slated to have roughly 500 staffers, about a third of ORD's workforce at the end of the Biden administration. In the same report, E&E News described interim OASES policies Gwinn had circulated on March 25, 2026, which say research addressing agencies' science needs 'must be supported by appropriate political leadership' so that there are 'no surprises' about OASES's work. EPA scientists published 275 peer-reviewed studies in 2025, about 17% fewer than in 2024, according to data from Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (PEER), which shows the decline began under the Biden administration; an EPA spokesperson said the reorganization added about 500 staff to OASES.

primary_proponent.name: Lee Zeldin
primary_proponent.role: EPA Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced and defended the reorganization, framing the mass layoffs using the government euphemism 'reduction in force' and stating it would ensure the agency could 'better fulfill that mission while being responsible stewards of your hard-earned tax dollars.' An EPA spokesperson separately described the restructuring as reflecting 'an unwavering commitment to gold-standard science' through 'integration of scientific expertise directly into EPA's offices' -- the administration's stated rationale is that embedding scientists in program offices improves rather than diminishes the agency's science capacity, a claim directly disputed by the researchers and former officials quoted below. This is the same EPA Administrator whose actions are covered in several deregulation-tracker entries in this project (endangerment finding rescission, MATS mercury standards, etc.) -- this entry covers the elimination of the scientific research infrastructure underlying those separate regulatory actions, not the regulatory actions themselves.

estimated_impact.summary: The loss falls first on health protection. EPA's chemical-risk program (IRIS) was cut to 8 of the 55 scientists who had worked on recent assessments, and its finished assessment of PFNA -- a forever chemical linked to lower birth weights and, from animal evidence, liver and male reproductive harm, in drinking water systems serving about 26 million people -- was finished in mid-April 2025 but still unpublished as of September 2026, leaving regulators and communities without the exposure limit used to set drinking-water and Superfund cleanup levels. Wildfire-smoke exposure research was cut off: the Kolibri drone sensor was reported grounded, and a $549,000 grant testing ways to protect people from smoke inside their homes was terminated after one field deployment. Outside scientists warned that ORD's widely used toxicology databases and air and water pollution models may no longer be kept current, and that new methods for gauging chemical-mixture risks could be delayed or never developed; Rep. Zoe Lofgren said the closure 'will have generational impacts on Americans' health and safety.' Institutionally, an office of 1,540 positions, up to 1,155 of them identified for possible layoff, dwindled to about 150 remaining staff by February 2026 before its last 124 employees received reassignment notices in April 2026; its successor, OASES, is slated for about 500 staff under the Administrator's direct control. EPA projects $748.8 million in savings from the changes it announced in July 2025.

title: EPA Terminated $15 Million in PFAS Farmland-Contamination Research Grants, Then Quietly Restored Two of the Ten Studies Without Explanation
institution: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Office of Research and Development
status: Mostly terminated -- 8 of 10 studies remained canceled as of sourcing reviewed; 2 were restored with no public explanation for the distinction
date_of_action: 2025-05 (termination notices sent) through 2025-07 (broader reporting on the cuts and their farm-level impact)
what_changed: In May 2025, EPA abruptly terminated a $15 million research program funding 10 university-led studies into how PFAS ('forever chemicals') contaminate U.S. farmland -- soil, crops, livestock, and irrigation water -- after **toxic PFAS-laced sewage sludge used as agricultural fertilizer was found tainting farms nationwide**. The program had been launched in 2024 under the Biden administration in response to public pressure over PFAS contamination. EPA sent termination notices to grant recipients stating the research was 'no longer consistent with EPA funding priorities.' Specific canceled awards included a $1.6 million grant to Texas A&M University to study how plants take up and store PFAS and to develop soil/fertilizer/irrigation-water monitoring tools; a $1.6 million grant to Michigan State University studying PFAS accumulation in crops and livestock; and roughly $5 million awarded jointly to the University of Maine, the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik, and the Mi'kmaq Nation to develop methods helping farmers mitigate PFAS contamination in the food supply chain. Reporting connected the cuts to the same DOGE-driven cost-cutting push documented elsewhere at EPA. Following press coverage, EPA restored funding for 2 of the 10 canceled studies, but neither EPA nor reporting identified why those two were restored while the other 8 remained terminated.

title: EPA's Shutdown Furloughs Were 'Scattershot and Seemingly Random,' While Deregulation and Permitting Work Continued
institution: Environmental Protection Agency
status: Shutdown ended November 12, 2025; no lasting policy change identified, though EPA's redefinition of furlough-'exempt' status during the shutdown was not reported as reversed or explained afterward
date_of_action: 2025-10-01 through 2025-11-12 (43-day shutdown)
what_changed: As the October-November 2025 government shutdown stretched into its fifth week, EPA employees and their union described the agency's furlough process as 'scattershot and seemingly random,' with staff in the same division split between furloughed and working with no discernible pattern, and some employees reporting they learned of their own furlough status only through colleagues' out-of-office auto-replies rather than direct notice. EPA's shutdown contingency plan initially indicated only 1,734 of the agency's employees -- 828 traditionally 'exempt' staff plus 906 meeting statutory or public-safety requirements -- would keep working through the funding lapse; **the union representing EPA staff estimated 6,000-7,000 employees were ultimately sent home**. EPA further muddied the picture by sending a mass email from a generic agency address directing a wide swath of employees to keep working because they 'work on activities which currently have available funds and thus are currently exempted from the shutdown' -- a redefinition of 'exempt' status that AFGE Council 238 President Justin Chen said broke from how the term had traditionally been used in furlough planning ('That's not how the term "exempt" has been used in the past in these situations'), since employees paid from leftover fiscal-2025 carryover funds are not the same category as employees statutorily exempt from a shutdown. Even as this confusion left thousands of employees uncertain of their status, EPA kept staff working on Trump administration priorities -- drafting rule rollbacks and processing permits -- while furloughing others essentially at random; the agency's climate offices, already in the process of being disbanded and having their staff reassigned, were left in particular limbo, uncounted in the contingency plan's own working-staff figures. The pattern paralleled a similar, separately-documented disparity at the Interior Department during the same shutdown, where oil, gas, and coal permitting staff were exempted from furlough while renewable-energy work was halted entirely (see shutdown-fossil-fuel-permitting-renewable-freeze-2025.json) -- both agencies kept fossil-fuel-adjacent priority work staffed through the shutdown while other functions were disrupted, though EPA's disruption was additionally marked by chaotic, inconsistent internal communication that Interior's cleaner permitting-exemption policy did not exhibit to the same degree.

estimated_impact.summary: Thousands of EPA employees experienced an unusually chaotic, inconsistently-communicated furlough process during the shutdown's peak, even as the agency kept deregulatory rulemaking and permit processing staffed -- a disparity in priorities that, combined with poor communication, left affected staff both financially exposed and uncertain of their own employment status for weeks.

title: FAA Froze Aircraft-Mechanic Training Grants Over DEI-Language Stripping Requirements Amid a Projected 10% Mechanic Shortfall
institution: Federal Aviation Administration (Aviation Workforce Development Grants program)
status: A new $26 million Aviation Workforce Development Grants round (split between pilot/drone-operator and aviation-maintenance-technician training) opened May 18, 2026, roughly eight months after the DEI-language freeze was reported, following congressional pressure. No source confirms whether this round represents the same previously-frozen funds or a separate appropriation cycle. date_of_action: 2025-09-17 (Reuters reports the freeze) through 2026-05-18 (FAA opens $26M in new grants)
what_changed: Congress had pledged tens of millions of dollars for FAA's Aviation Workforce Development Grants program to train aircraft mechanics and technicians, at a time the Aviation Technician Education Council projected a 10% shortfall in certified mechanics for 2025 amid surging maintenance and production demand from Boeing and Airbus. Reuters reported September 17, 2025 that the approved grant funds had not been issued: officials from at least one technical college and an education council said the FAA told them to reapply once grant applications were rewritten to remove references to diversity, equity, and inclusion, in line with Trump administration executive orders. Marilyn Strickland, Rick Larsen, and Andre Carson -- sent a letter to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford demanding answers, writing that the delays were 'stalling critical aviation workforce development' and warning further delay could violate the law; the FAA said only that it would respond to lawmakers directly. On May 18, 2026, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced $26 million in new Aviation Workforce Development Grants, split evenly between pilot/drone-operator training and aviation-maintenance-technician training, with a June 22, 2026 application deadline -- resolving the freeze roughly eight months after it was first reported, though no source reviewed confirms whether this $26M round represents the same previously-pledged funds or a separate, later appropriation.

title: GAO Finds FAA's Aviation Meteorologist Staffing at a Critical Low, With Some of the Busiest Air-Traffic Control Centers Down to One or Two
institution: Federal Aviation Administration / National Weather Service (Center Weather Service Units)
status: As of the GAO report's June 2025 data, staffing remained critically low relative to the 2016 interagency target; FAA and the National Weather Service have since amended their 2016 agreement to cap staffing at 81 full-time-equivalent positions for fiscal year 2025 -- a lower formal target than the original 90, not a restoration to it. No source reviewed indicates staffing has been raised to meet even that reduced 81-position cap as of this entry's sourcing.
date_of_action: 2025-08-29 (GAO report GAO-25-108597 published)
what_changed: A Government Accountability Office report (GAO-25-108597, 'Aviation Meteorologists: Urgent Actions Needed to Address Staffing Concerns') found that as of June 2025, only 69 aviation meteorologists were working within FAA air traffic control centers -- specialists embedded via Center Weather Service Units who track storms and other hazardous weather to help controllers route aircraft safely. That is down from an average of 81 full-time-equivalent positions over 2019-2024, and well below the 90-meteorologist staffing level FAA and the National Weather Service agreed to in a 2016 interagency agreement. Full staffing under that standard would place four meteorologists at each control center, but as of June 2025 fewer than half of centers met that level; **control centers serving some of the country's busiest air-travel hubs -- Boston, Washington, D.C., and Houston -- had only two meteorologists each, and the center serving Oakland, California had just one**. GAO reported that the meteorologists who remain described suffering from burnout, fatigue, and low morale from working overtime to maintain operations, with many avoiding taking leave. Separately, FAA and the National Weather Service amended their original 2016 agreement to formally cap meteorologist staffing at 81 full-time-equivalent positions for fiscal year 2025 -- lowering the official staffing target itself rather than working to restore it to the original 90.

title: FAA Air Traffic Controller Shortage — Chronic Structural Crisis, Acutely Worsened by 2025 Shutdown
institution: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation
status: Ongoing, unresolved (FAA released a new workforce plan in 2026; current administrator says full staffing may never be reached under the existing structure; a congressionally funded controller pay raise remains undisbursed months after enactment)
date_of_action: Structural decline since 2013; acute crisis point during the Oct-Nov 2025 government shutdown
what_changed:
IMPORTANT ATTRIBUTION NOTE: unlike most entries in this tracker, this is predominantly a chronic, multi-administration structural problem, not a single action taken by the current administration. GAO's own December 2025 report traces the roots to the 2013 budget sequester (which froze hiring), the 2018-2019 shutdown (35 days, further hiring/training delays), and COVID-19 (FAA Academy training suspended 4 months in 2020, reduced-rate training through 2022). The controller workforce declined about 6% since 2015 even as flight volume rose ~10%; the FAA employed 13,164 controllers at the end of FY2025. GAO also cited a 2023 Department of Transportation Inspector General finding that '20 of 26 critical facilities had staffing levels below 85 percent of FAA's desired level.' In 2025, congressional sponsors of the bipartisan Air Traffic Control Workforce Development Act wrote in their bill background materials that 'near-misses at airports across the country have increased' in recent years and described many controllers as 'overworked and understaffed'; Senator Jeanne Shaheen cited 'increasingly frequent near-misses and close calls' when she introduced the Senate version on March 28, 2025.

What IS specific to the current administration: months before the shutdown, the chronic shortage produced an acute, widely covered crisis at Newark Liberty International Airport in late April-May 2025. On April 28, 2025, controllers handling Newark-area airspace -- relocated from the New York TRACON to the Philadelphia TRACON in July 2024 to address N90's own chronic understaffing -- lost radar and radio contact with 15-20 aircraft after a burnt copper wire severed the radar-data feed from a Long Island FAA facility (the FAA did not say how long the outage lasted; Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, reported it was nearly 90 seconds; Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said contact was lost for 30 seconds, the AP reported, and NPR later described the outage as lasting somewhere between 30 and 90 seconds); at least five controllers subsequently took 45 days of trauma leave, and the resulting staffing shortage, compounded by further outages on May 9 and May 11, contributed to over 1,000 flight disruptions and delays of up to seven hours, with as few as 1 to 3 fully certified controllers on duty against a required 14. United Airlines cut 35 daily Newark flights in response.

One of the controllers handling Newark-area airspace, Jonathan Stewart, 45, went on the record with the Wall Street Journal May 16, 2025, describing averting a May 4, 2025 near-miss between two aircraft -- a business jet out of Morristown and a small jet from Teterboro -- flying nose-to-nose at the same altitude; because the facility's radar had failed days earlier, Stewart said he resorted to manually writing down the aircrafts' callsigns to keep track of them. He told the Journal, 'I don't want to be responsible for killing 400 people.' The Philadelphia TRACON facility handling Newark-area airspace was staffed at just 24 of the 38 controller positions the FAA says it needs (63%) at the time of his account.

The outages were not confined to Newark: on May 12, 2025, the FAA's Denver Air Route Traffic Control Center lost both its main and backup radio transmitters covering a segment of airspace over Colorado and neighboring states; Denver7 reported that as many as 20 pilots couldn't connect with controllers. The FAA said in a statement that the outage lasted 'approximately 90 seconds,' while FAA official Frank McIntosh told the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on May 15 that the backup was down 'for approximately two minutes,' NPR reported. Controllers relayed instructions via the 121.5 MHz emergency frequency, no loss of separation occurred, and the FAA later attributed the outage to overlapping transmitter and circuit failures. Testifying before the Senate Appropriations Committee on May 15, 2025 about the Newark episode, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the FAA resorts to buying replacement parts for its outdated, decades-old equipment on eBay and 3D-printing others when none can be found -- disclosing that a GAO review found 76% of the FAA's 138 air traffic control systems were unsustainable or potentially unsustainable -- and unveiled a modernization plan (fiber/wireless/satellite upgrades, 618 replaced radars, six new control centers) targeting 2028 completion at an estimated $12.5 billion. The outages continued even after that testimony and plan: on May 19, 2025, the Newark-area TRACON (the same relocated Philadelphia facility) lost radio contact with aircraft for about two seconds, again with no loss of separation, underscoring that the announced modernization had not yet reached the equipment actually causing the failures.

A June 2025 National Academies (Transportation Research Board) report found that 19 of the 30 largest air traffic control facilities were staffed at less than 85% of what the FAA's staffing model says they need, according to Federal News Network. The controllers' union NATCA said that month, as Federal News Network also reported, that the FAA was 'about 3,800 controllers short' of adequate staffing and that 'more than 41% of certified professional controllers work 10-hour days, six days a week'; in a September 26, 2025 release, NATCA said the roughly 10,800 certified controllers then working were '3,800 short of where we need to be.' The 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 shutdown further disrupted hiring and training pipelines and forced acute flight reductions. Current FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Congress in December 2025 that towers would 'never' reach full staffing under the agency's existing structure, stating plainly: 'The system is designed to be chronically understaffed.' Separately, a 2025 proposal to build a second controller training academy (to relieve the bottleneck at the single Oklahoma City academy) was blocked in Congress amid cost and oversight objections, despite FAA and safety experts' warnings that one campus cannot produce enough certified controllers quickly enough.

In its final report on the January 29, 2025 midair collision near Reagan National Airport (AIR-26-02, adopted January 27, 2026 and released February 17, 2026), the NTSB found that the tower team's loss of situation awareness and degraded performance 'due to the high workload of the combined helicopter and local control positions' was among the causes of the crash, and named as a contributing factor an arrival rate, traffic volume, and airline scheduling practices that 'regularly strained the DCA air traffic control tower workforce.' The NTSB also found that although the tower was not staffed to its target level, the number of staff on duty that night was adequate, and that the decision to combine the two positions 'was not the result of insufficient staffing.' The FAA's new 2026 workforce plan, released in May 2026, resolved the staffing gap partly by lowering the goal itself: full-staffing target dropped from the 14,633 controllers the agency had forecast needing in 2024 to 12,563, a reduction of more than 2,000 positions from the prior target -- the FAA frames this as a modernization-driven reassessment of actual need, not merely redefining the shortfall away, but the effect is that a large share of the 'gap closing' reflects a lower bar rather than more controllers hired. The FAA said at the time that its total controller workforce losses in fiscal year 2025, including retirements, resignations, promotions, removals, training failures and academy attrition, came to 1,460, against 2,028 trainees hired that year, according to Fox News. As of June 2026, the FAA was roughly 3,000 certified controllers below even its original, higher target (about 10,800 actual against a ~13,800 historical goal). The staffing shortfall had concrete summer-2026 consequences: the FAA capped Chicago O'Hare at 2,708 scheduled daily operations from May 17 through October 24, 2026, a nearly 15% cut from airline-planned schedules, with New York and Southern California TRACONs also cited as most strained. A July 21, 2026 DoD Inspector General report on military air-traffic-controller shortages concerns a separate workforce (military, not FAA/DOT) and is not folded into this entry.

Congress funded an additional 2.8% pay increase for controllers (enacted April 2026, intended to bring 2026 controller compensation in line with the 3.8% raise military personnel received), but as of mid-to-late August 2026 -- roughly four months later -- the raise had still not reached controllers' paychecks. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has tied disbursement to the union agreeing to broader schedule/staffing-utilization reforms, telling reporters 'if we can figure out how we can engage with...the union leadership on the basic watch schedule questions...there's no reason we can't unlock it this year'; the FAA's 2026-28 workforce plan argues controllers' average 'time on position' during 8-hour shifts (currently ~4 hours) could rise past 5 hours through modernized scheduling. A statute reportedly gives the FAA Administrator 'sole discretion' over whether operational improvements justify releasing the retroactive raise -- meaning Bedford is using an already-enacted, congressionally funded pay increase as leverage for a separate policy concession from NATCA, rather than a simple implementation delay. NATCA did not respond to the reporting outlet's requests for comment on the delay or on Bedford's remarks.

title: FAA Cut Flights 10% at 40 Major Airports After Unpaid Controllers Began Missing Work
institution: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Department of Transportation
status: Complete (implemented and later lifted after shutdown ended)
date_of_action: 2025-11-05 (announced); ramped from 4% to 10% between Nov. 7-14, 2025
what_changed: During the 43-day Oct-Nov 2025 government shutdown -- the longest in U.S. history -- air traffic controllers, deemed 'essential' employees required to work without pay, began missing shifts in increasing numbers as the shutdown dragged on, compounding the FAA's already-chronic staffing shortage (see related structural staffing entry). The buildup was visible well before the formal reduction order: as early as Oct. 10, staffing shortages left some control towers unmanned (nearly 6,000 delayed flights nationwide that day); by Oct. 27-31, roughly 13,000 controllers and 50,000 TSA officers were working without pay, and ground delays hit major hubs including New York, Washington, Newark, Houston, Austin, and Dallas-Fort Worth (over 4,200 delays Oct. 23, nearly 7,000 Oct. 31); by Nov. 4, the shutdown's 31st day, nearly half of U.S. air traffic centers were short-staffed and 90% of controllers in the New York region were unavailable. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford then announced a mandatory flight-capacity reduction at 40 'high-volume' airports nationwide, ramping from 4% on Nov. 7 to 10% by Nov. 14, affecting an estimated 3,500-4,000 flights daily. Both officials described the move as unprecedented -- Bedford, with 35 years in aviation, said he 'could not recall a similar situation.' Duffy publicly warned the cuts could escalate to 15-20% if the shutdown continued, and separately said he could 'shut the whole airspace down' if it dragged on further. The order also restricted private jets from high-traffic airports to preserve capacity for commercial aviation. The reduction produced immediate, measurable disruption: over 1,000 flights canceled the first day, more than 2,900 cancellations and 10,000+ delays the following Sunday, nearly 2,200 cancellations in a single day by the second weekend, and over 40 emergency staffing alerts issued nationwide since the order took effect. On Nov. 12, as cancellations continued (over 2,000 Monday alone after nearly 3,000 the prior Sunday, with delays topping 6,400 nationwide), Trump escalated the pressure directly on the workforce: he publicly demanded controllers 'get back to work, NOW!!!,' threatened to dock pay from those who missed shifts, and offered a $10,000 bonus to those who stayed on the job -- prompting controller unions to warn that workers were being used as political pawns in the shutdown fight.

primary_proponent.name: Sean Duffy
primary_proponent.role: U.S. Transportation Secretary
primary_proponent.note: Announced and defended the decision personally in multiple press briefings alongside FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, who made the specific operational call. Duffy explicitly and repeatedly tied the cause to controllers working without pay during the shutdown, not any independent FAA policy decision -- this is a downstream consequence of the broader Oct-Nov 2025 shutdown, not an isolated FAA action.

estimated_impact.summary: This was framed by officials as a safety-preserving measure (reducing controller workload to prevent errors) rather than a punitive action, and aviation safety experts generally agreed with that framing -- a former NTSB/FAA accident investigator called it appropriate risk reduction, while also noting the real economic cost to airlines and 'massive inconvenience' to travelers. The scale of disruption was immediate and large: **over 12,000 American Airlines customers alone had flights canceled on the first day of the reduction**.

title: Nearly a Quarter of All FBI Agents Nationwide Reassigned to Immigration Enforcement, Sidelining Counterterrorism, Espionage, and Cybercrime Work
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), under Director Kash Patel
status: Ongoing as of this entry -- no reversal of the reassignment pattern was identified in sourcing reviewed; oversight letters from Sens. Warner, Warren, and Durbin remained pending as of this entry.
date_of_action: 2025 (reassignments accumulate through the year) through 2025-10-08 (Washington Post/Guardian reporting on Sen. Warner's data)
what_changed: Personnel data obtained by Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) and reported by The Washington Post and The Guardian in early October 2025 showed the Trump administration had reassigned roughly 23% of all FBI agents nationwide -- and nearly 45% of agents in the FBI's 25 largest field offices -- to immigration enforcement work alongside ICE, out of a bureau of roughly 13,000 total agents. Warner warned the diversion was pulling resources away from counterterrorism, espionage, cybercrime, and drug-trafficking investigations -- the FBI's traditional core national-security mission -- to help meet the administration's publicly stated goal (announced by White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller in May 2025) of 3,000 immigration arrests per day, roughly triple the rate in January 2025, a target the administration later denied existed as formal policy when challenged in federal court. **Agents themselves, per the reporting, warned the reassignments put U.S. national security at risk and described a sharp decline in workplace morale and their ability to process complex investigations**. This bureau-wide diversion is substantially larger in scale than the narrower, earlier reassignment this tracker separately documented (roughly 16 agents pulled from the FBI's Domestic Terrorism Operations Section in March 2025, per Reuters) -- that section-level move was an early instance of the same broader pattern this entry now documents at its full, bureau-wide scale. Sen. Elizabeth Warren separately wrote to DOJ and FBI inspectors general in January 2026 specifically flagging the diversion of white-collar and financial-crimes investigators to immigration enforcement duties, extending the pattern beyond national-security roles into corruption and fraud investigations as well.

title: FBI Told to Stop Investigating Confrontations Involving Immigration Agents, Shifting Oversight to ICE's Own Investigative Arm
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation / DHS Homeland Security Investigations
status: Guidance reportedly distributed and in effect per internal emails reviewed by CBS News; DOJ and DHS publicly deny any change. Sens. Blumenthal and Schiff demanded rescission on Aug 11, 2026 (answers due Aug 25); no rescission or public response reported
date_of_action: 2026-07 (guidance distributed to FBI agents)
what_changed: The New York Times reported, and CBS News independently confirmed via internal emails reviewed by its reporters, that FBI agents around the country were told in mid-July 2026 that the FBI would no longer investigate confrontations involving immigration agents -- including assault-on-a-federal-officer cases that can arise from violent encounters between ICE agents and members of the public. Under the change, responsibility for these investigations would shift to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), which is itself a component of ICE -- meaning cases involving potential misconduct by immigration agents would be investigated by an arm of the same agency employing those agents, rather than by the FBI as an independent investigative body. FBI and HSI personnel were advised the FBI would defer on all assault-on-federal-officer inquiries involving DHS agents to HSI, according to the emails CBS reviewed. The Justice Department and DHS both publicly denied that any policy change had occurred, despite the written guidance already having been distributed to FBI and ICE personnel.

primary_proponent.name: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (Acting Attorney General at the time; confirmed August 8, 2026)
primary_proponent.role: Attorney General
primary_proponent.note: The FBI operates under DOJ, and Blanche's department publicly denied the policy change existed even as written guidance implementing it had already been distributed to FBI and ICE agents, per emails reviewed by CBS News.

estimated_impact.summary: Shifting investigative responsibility for confrontations involving immigration agents from the FBI -- an independent investigative body -- to HSI, ICE's own internal investigative arm, **creates a structural conflict of interest in which the agency effectively investigates its own personnel's conduct, at a time of heightened public scrutiny over multiple fatal ICE shootings**.

figures.value: FBI and HSI personnel both received the guidance, per CBS News's review of internal emails
figures.source: CBS News, July 2026

estimated_impact.caveat: DOJ and DHS have both publicly denied that any policy change occurred. CBS News says it independently reviewed internal emails that appear to contradict that denial. No official acknowledgment of the change has been given, so the shift is documented by the emails and the reporting rather than confirmed by the government.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the substance of the reported policy shift, since it originates from The New York Times and was independently corroborated by CBS News's review of actual internal emails (not merely anonymous characterization), with further pickup by The New Republic, Common Dreams, and CNBC (the Philadelphia Inquirer ran the NYT report itself). MODERATE confidence on the shift's final, official status, since DOJ and DHS have publicly denied it and no on-the-record government confirmation exists -- the tension between the documentary evidence and the official denial is itself a notable, sourced fact, not a gap in this entry's sourcing. No news report names who issued the directive; Sens. Blumenthal and Schiff wrote to Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel that they 'apparently' made the decision, so attributing it to Blanche rests on that letter and his role as head of the department that oversees the FBI.
pull_quote: DOJ and DHS both publicly denied any policy change had occurred — despite the written guidance already having been distributed to FBI and ICE personnel.

section_summaries.what_changed: Internal guidance told FBI agents to stop investigating confrontations involving ICE agents, shifting them to ICE's own HSI arm; DOJ and DHS publicly denied any policy change.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: The shift means ICE would effectively investigate its own agents' conduct rather than an independent body, raising oversight concerns amid multiple recent fatal ICE shootings.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Well-corroborated by NYT reporting and CBS News's independent review of internal emails; DOJ/DHS's public denial directly contradicts the documented internal guidance.

title: FBI Scaled Back Staffing and Scrapped a Tracking Tool for Domestic Terrorism Investigations
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation / Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing and escalated. A Senate HSGAC report from Ranking Member Gary Peters (July 30, 2026) found roughly 15,000 positions cut across DOJ/FBI combined and 1,300 DHS counterterrorism personnel cut -- far broader than the original ~16-agent DTOS reassignment. The same report found the administration's domestic-terrorism focus has skewed almost exclusively toward left-wing groups, traceable to AG Bondi's December 2025 'Antifa-aligned extremists' directive. No final decision on formally disbanding DTOS has been confirmed.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (initial reassignments and tool scrapping); 2025-04 (congressional oversight letter)
what_changed: FBI leadership transferred roughly 16 agents and intelligence analysts out of the Bureau's Domestic Terrorism Operations Section (DTOS), which supports domestic-terrorism investigations run out of all 55 FBI field offices and would have hundreds of employees if fully staffed, Reuters reported (citing sources familiar with the matter) on 2025-03-21. The FBI also scrapped a tool used to track domestic terrorism cases. Senior FBI officials discussed disbanding the section entirely, though no final decision had been announced as of the reporting. Agents were being redirected instead to assist the administration's immigration enforcement crackdown, while attacks on Tesla property were newly classified and prioritized as domestic terrorism. Domestic terrorism investigations have in recent years disproportionately involved violence tied to right-wing and anti-government ideologies, and FBI Director Kash Patel has been a public critic of the Bureau's domestic-terrorism investigative effort. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, sent a formal oversight letter to DHS Secretary Kristi Noem and Director Patel on 2025-04-08 documenting a broader institutional pullback beyond the FBI reassignments alone: DHS had also dismantled a national database tracking domestic extremism and hate crimes and cut funding for domestic-terrorism-prevention programs supporting community groups and local law enforcement. Durbin's letter cited FBI's own data showing a 357% increase in domestic terrorism investigations between 2013 and 2021 (from 1,981 to 9,049 cases) as the backdrop against which the cuts were occurring, and urged DHS and the FBI to reverse the resource reallocations. ProPublica reported May 31, 2025 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0366, added 2026-09-10) that the DHS prevention cuts documented above also eliminated hate-crime hotlines and halted extremist-threat tracking specifically, and that states -- Michigan among them -- were attempting to fill the resulting gap with their own programs, though ProPublica found many state efforts were unprepared or inactive given the scale of the federal pullback. NBC News reported June 16, 2025 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0392, added 2026-09-10) that the cuts documented above specifically include **elimination of the $18 million Targeted Violence and Terrorism Prevention (TVTP) Grant Program, which had funded local efforts like school-based threat assessments and mental-health interventions credited by experts with helping identify radicalized individuals before attacks**; the administration's budget submission said the program 'does not align with DHS priorities.' A senior DHS official, speaking anonymously out of fear of being fired, told NBC News: 'That line should be quoted after every future mass casualty event in this country.' Update 2026-08-17: A Senate HSGAC report from Ranking Member Gary Peters, released 2026-07-30 ("Peters Report Finds Trump Administration Has Dismantled Critical Counterterrorism Infrastructure and Weaponized What Remains Against Political Opponents"), documents roughly 15,000 positions cut across DOJ and the FBI combined and 1,300 DHS personnel cut from counterterrorism-related roles, a larger institutional pullback than the ~16-agent DTOS reassignment this entry originally documented. The report also found the administration's domestic-terrorism enforcement focus has shifted almost exclusively to left-wing targets, and that a DOJ study showing far-right extremist attacks have outpaced all other domestic-terrorism categories since 1990 was quietly removed from the department's website. Several outlets covering the report describe DTOS's entire remaining staff as having been reassigned, but that specific claim could not be independently confirmed against the report's own text or another primary source in this recheck; it is not asserted as fact here. Update 2026-08-30 (correction -- a primary source for the report's 'skewed toward left-wing groups' finding, missed until now): Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a domestic-terrorism directive on December 4, 2025, predating the Peters report by nearly eight months, that explicitly prioritizes investigation of 'Antifa-aligned extremists' -- defined in the memo to include those holding 'extreme viewpoints on immigration, radical gender ideology, and anti-American sentiment' -- and directs DOJ to prioritize grant funding to state/local law enforcement for domestic-terrorism programs tied to that focus. The memo also orders Joint Terrorism Task Forces to use 'all available investigative tools' to map suspected networks, requires the FBI to compile and update every 30 days a domestic-terrorist-organization list, establishes a cash-reward tip line, and orders a retrospective five-year review of agency files for Antifa-related intelligence to be transmitted to the FBI for potential new prosecutions. This directive is the concrete administrative mechanism behind the ideological-skew finding this entry already cites from the Peters report, not merely a restatement of it.

primary_proponent.name: Kash Patel
primary_proponent.role: FBI Director
primary_proponent.note: No single official is named in reporting as personally ordering the DTOS reassignments; attributed institutionally to Patel as FBI Director, a role in which he has been a public critic of the Bureau's domestic-terrorism investigative effort, per Reuters. Kristi Noem, then DHS Secretary, bears parallel institutional responsibility for the DHS-side database dismantlement and funding cuts documented in Durbin's letter.

estimated_impact.summary: Federal capacity to prevent domestic terrorism was cut back even as FBI data showed such investigations had grown more than fourfold in less than a decade: DHS eliminated the $18 million grant program that funded local school-based threat assessments and mental-health interventions credited by experts with helping identify radicalized individuals before attacks; DHS prevention cuts also ended hate-crime hotlines and extremist-threat tracking. A Senate HSGAC report from Sen. Gary Peters found roughly 15,000 positions cut across DOJ and the FBI overall and 1,300 DHS personnel cut specifically from counterterrorism-related roles, with the administration's domestic-terrorism enforcement focus shifted almost exclusively to left-wing targets. The FBI also scrapped a tool used to track domestic-terrorism cases and weighed disbanding its Domestic Terrorism Operations Section (DTOS; no final decision had been announced as of March 2025 reporting), and DHS dismantled a national database tracking domestic extremism and hate crimes.

The DHS database dismantlement and the broader prevention-program funding cuts rest on Sen. title: FBI Lowered Agent Training Standards and Diverted Agents From Fraud, Corruption, and Counterintelligence Casework to Street Patrols and Violent-Crime Duty
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation
status: Ongoing as of the reporting reviewed -- the reduced training standards and workforce cuts were implemented; the DC-deployment diversion and broader violent-crime pivot were active as of September 2025, with no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-08 (training-standards and mission-shift reporting) through 2025-09 (DC-deployment casework diversion documented)
what_changed: The New York Times reported August 21, 2025 that the FBI, under Director Kash Patel and Deputy Director Dan Bongino, planned to **cut new-agent training at the Quantico academy from 18 weeks to 8 weeks and eliminate the bachelor's-degree requirement for new recruits**, with the shortened curriculum set to begin with an October 2025 class. The changes came as the bureau anticipated losing more than 5,000 employees -- agents, analysts, and other staff -- by September 2025 through severance and early-retirement packages offered under the administration, and as the FBI's specialized-agent workforce was separately reported to be shrinking from roughly 13,000 to 11,000 over the same period. Retired FBI senior counterterrorism official Chris O'Leary called the changes the latest example of 'generational destruction' at the bureau, warning: 'When you lower the standards, your mission effectiveness goes down with that, because not only does the capability of each individual agent decline, but your reputation, both domestically and globally, takes a hit.' Separately, MSNBC reported August 19, 2025 that the bureau was executing a broader mission shift, with a planned 15% workforce reduction (about 5,800 of roughly 37,000 employees) accompanying a redirection of agents toward violent-crime investigations, immigration enforcement, and nightly anti-crime foot patrols in Washington, D.C. alongside D.C. police -- work outside the bureau's traditional investigative role -- at the expense of terrorism prevention, espionage/counterintelligence, white-collar fraud, public corruption, child sex crimes, and cybersecurity casework. Patel described the goal as letting 'good cops be cops'; retired FBI agent Rob D'Amico said 'This is putting the nation in jeopardy -- they seem to be making national security threats secondary,' and one unnamed senior agent said the changes were 'effectively making the FBI a national police force.' The New York Times reported September 15, 2025 that Trump's deployment of National Guard troops and federal agents in Washington had concretely diverted FBI staff from financial-fraud, corruption, and counterintelligence casework specifically to support the D.C. surge, slowing those investigations and prompting resignations; prosecutors told the Times the diversion left D.C. courts flooded with weak street-crime cases, many of which were thrown out by grand juries. This grand-jury pattern is independently corroborated at the case level: D.C. grand juries refused to indict defendants at least six to seven times over the following weeks, including declining a felony assault indictment against Sean Dunn (the 'sandwich thrower' case, tracked separately in this database's pirro-sandwich-thrower-failed-prosecution-2025.json), Alvin Summers, and Sidney Lori Reid, among others -- a pattern reporting characterized as an unusual judicial check given prosecutors ordinarily control grand jury outcomes.

primary_proponent.role: FBI Director
primary_proponent.note: Directed the training-standards reduction and the broader mission shift toward violent-crime/street-policing duty alongside Deputy Director Dan Bongino, describing the goal as letting 'good cops be cops'; the same period's staffing losses and field-office/analyst purges are tracked separately in this database's patel-fbi-field-office-purge-2025-2026.json (personnel-retaliation focus) and prosecution/cabinet-level's patel-fbi-agent-vetting-reduction-2026.json (a later, narrower internal-candidate vetting change) -- this entry covers the distinct training-standards and casework-diversion actions.

estimated_impact.summary: The FBI shortened new-agent academy training by more than half, dropped its college-degree requirement, and reassigned agents from fraud, corruption, counterintelligence, terrorism-prevention, cybersecurity, and child-exploitation casework to violent-crime duty, immigration enforcement, and nightly street patrols in Washington, D.C. -- a mission pivot a former senior counterterrorism official called 'generational destruction,' concurrent with a workforce reduction of roughly 5,000-5,800 employees and a documented diversion of core investigative capacity that prosecutors say has flooded D.C. courts with cases too weak for grand juries to indict.
