title: Leaked 115-Page Assessment Found FBI 'Internally Paralyzed by Fear' Under Director Kash Patel, Amid a Pattern of Patel Disclosing Sensitive Investigation Details on Social Media
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
status: Ongoing -- FBI public affairs chief Ben Williamson rebutted the report on X (Dec. 1, 2025), and Patel publicly disputed its raid-jacket anecdote and dismissed its sources (Dec. 2, 2025); no corrective action has been reported
date_of_action: 2025-02 through 2025-08 (assessment's coverage period) through 2025-11-30 (report leaked)
what_changed:
New York Post columnist Miranda Devine obtained and described in a November 30, 2025 opinion column a 115-page internal assessment -- compiled by a national alliance of retired and active-duty FBI special agents and analysts, drawing on confidential accounts from 24 FBI sources, and prepared for the Senate and House Judiciary Committees -- covering the first six months of Director Kash Patel's tenure (February 21 through August 21, 2025). The report described the FBI as 'internally paralyzed by fear,' with plummeting morale and a 'rudderless ship' in which managers were afraid to take initiative without Patel's explicit personal approval. It characterized Patel himself as 'in over his head,' leading a 'chronically under-performing' agency, and cited concerns from foreign law enforcement partners that the leadership turmoil could cause long-term damage to international law-enforcement cooperation.

On December 1, 2025, FBI Assistant Director for Public Affairs Ben Williamson rebutted the report on X, criticizing the New York Post for 'elevating a dossier of anonymous complaints from current and ex-FBI personnel as some form of gospel' and arguing that 'the unconventional approach may get criticism, but the data says it's working.' Sen. Dick Durbin issued a public statement responding to the report on December 2, 2025. Patel responded on Fox News's 'The Ingraham Angle' on December 2, 2025, calling the report's account that he had demanded an FBI raid jacket '100% false' and saying of its anonymous sources, 'These anonymous sources were individuals from the Comey-Wray era that weaponized the Department of Justice and cratered the public trust in the FBI ...,' without addressing its broader findings, HuffPost reported. White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson also defended him in a statement reported by The Guardian: 'FBI Director Patel is a critical member of the President's team and he is working tirelessly to restore integrity to the FBI.'

Separately, the same period saw a documented pattern of Patel publicly disclosing sensitive operational details on social media before or during active investigations: in one specific instance, **the Secret Service accused Patel of compromising an active covert investigation into a planned attack on a White House-linked UFC event (which numerous high-ranking officials attended) by publicly announcing the plot had been foiled while the operation, including still-at-large suspects, remained active** -- FBI Deputy Director Matthew Quinn confirmed the operation's active status at the time. Lawfare's own dedicated roundup of the pattern documents three further instances of the same pattern, one chronologically earlier and two later than the Charlie Kirk episode described below. The earliest came on August 22, 2025: during the FBI's search of former National Security Advisor John Bolton's home, Patel tweeted 'NO ONE is above the law...@FBI agents on mission' while the search was still underway; the New York Post reported on the raid within 19 minutes of it beginning.

In another instance of the pattern of premature public disclosure during active investigations, on September 10, 2025 -- roughly two months before the November/December 2025 developments this entry documents -- hours after conservative activist Charlie Kirk was fatally shot at Utah Valley University, Patel publicly announced 'the subject for the horrific shooting... is now in custody' -- then retracted the claim about two hours later, saying authorities had the wrong person, while Utah law enforcement officials were simultaneously holding a news conference stating the gunman remained at large, producing hours of public confusion before the actual suspect, Tyler Robinson, was arrested roughly 33 hours after the shooting. Patel also drew criticism for dining at an exclusive New York restaurant hours after the assassination while continuing to post premature investigative updates; former FBI officials characterized both the dining choice and the social-media conduct as 'grandstanding' that undermined public confidence in the bureau during an active national-security-sensitive investigation.

The second of Lawfare's three instances, chronologically: on October 31, 2025, Patel announced the FBI had 'thwarted a potential terrorist attack and arrested multiple subjects in Michigan' before any criminal charges had been filed. Lawfare reported on December 16, 2025 that the announcement 'reportedly prompted two friends of the alleged terrorists to flee the country,' quoting the Wall Street Journal's report that the two friends, in New Jersey and Washington state, 'caught wind of the arrests and moved up plans to leave the country' -- a reported operational-harm consequence (associates of suspects fleeing before charges were filed) distinct from the reputational/morale harm this entry otherwise documents. Separately, only two of those originally arrested were ultimately charged; no cited source establishes that this narrower charging outcome was itself caused by the premature announcement, so it is presented here as a separate fact about the case's eventual scope, not as a second consequence of the announcement.

In a related development the same season, the FBI launched a new 'Rapid Response' social-media account in November 2025 that took an unusually combative public posture, immediately engaging in public disputes with commentators including Tucker Carlson, amplifying Deputy Director Dan Bongino's own frequently partisan public statements, and defending the Bureau's January 6 pipe-bomb investigation against outside criticism -- a marked departure from the FBI's traditionally reticent public-communications posture. The pipe-bomb episode had a specific, well-documented flashpoint: on November 8, 2025, The Blaze reported a purported 'gait analysis' finding a 94% match between the January 6 pipe bomber and a former Capitol Police officer (since employed in CIA campus security), a story Rep. Thomas Massie and Rep. Barry Loudermilk promoted -- Massie went further, claiming 'Capitol Police turned CIA orchestrated the pipe bombs on January 6th, and the FBI has covered it up.'

Bongino, rather than directly debunking the story, posted on November 13, 2025 that some reporting on 'prior persons of interest is grossly inaccurate and serves only to mislead the public,' without disclosing that the FBI had already investigated and cleared the officer (whose attorney, Steve Bunnell, called the allegations 'recklessly false, absurd, and defamatory') using video evidence placing her elsewhere when the bombs were planted; the FBI separately clarified it had actually been tracking an unrelated person captured via SmartTrip card records near the RNC. The Blaze later retracted its story. The FBI ultimately arrested a different suspect, Virginia bail bondsman Brian Cole Jr., on December 2, 2025, who told investigators he believed the 2020 election was stolen and was a Trump supporter -- vindicating the FBI's original investigation over the MAGA-media conspiracy theory Bongino had allowed to fester rather than immediately and clearly contradicting.

The most recent instance in Lawfare's roundup came after a December 13, 2025 mass shooting at Brown University: Patel tweeted on December 14 that a 'person of interest' had been detained in a Coventry, Rhode Island hotel room; Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha announced that same evening the person had been released for insufficient evidence, and on December 15 Patel tweeted new images of a different suspect without acknowledging the prior person's release.

Bongino announced December 17, 2025 he would step down as Deputy Director in January 2026, citing a desire to return to his media career; reporting also cited friction with Attorney General Bondi and the Epstein-files dispute as contributing factors, without identifying the pipe-bomb episode itself as a stated cause.

The Secret Service accused him of compromising an active covert investigation into a planned attack on a UFC event, and, per the Wall Street Journal as quoted by Lawfare, two friends of alleged Michigan plotters 'caught wind of the arrests and moved up plans to leave the country,' which Lawfare said his announcement 'reportedly prompted'; a false 'in custody' claim after Charlie Kirk's shooting also produced hours of public confusion. title: FDA Suspended a 40-Lab Bird Flu Milk-Testing Exercise After Eliminating Its Food Safety Lab, Then Suspended Grade-A Milk Testing Outright
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Testing suspended as of April 2025; no confirmed restoration identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry's addition
date_of_action: 2025-04-03 (VLIRN exercise suspension notice) through 2025-04-23 (grade-A milk testing program suspension reported)
what_changed: As part of the broader 2025 HHS staffing reductions (which cut roughly 3,500 FDA employees overall), the FDA eliminated its Human Food Program's Moffett Center food-safety laboratory in Illinois, including a key quality-assurance officer. On April 3, 2025, the FDA-backed Veterinary Laboratory Investigation and Response Network (VLIRN) informed its roughly 40 member laboratories -- a mix of federal, state, and private labs across the country -- that a planned nationwide exercise to confirm those labs' ability to detect H5N1 avian influenza in milk had to be suspended because of the Illinois lab's elimination and the loss of the quality-assurance function it provided. Three weeks later, CBS News and other outlets reported the FDA had gone further, **suspending its own testing program for grade 'A' milk and other dairy products -- the routine surveillance testing distinct from the VLIRN inter-laboratory readiness exercise** -- citing the same food-safety-division staffing cuts.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Directed the department-wide staffing reductions that eliminated the Moffett Center lab and food-safety-division staff; no single named official was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally directing the bird-flu-testing suspension specifically.

estimated_impact.summary: The combination of a canceled inter-laboratory readiness exercise and a suspended routine milk-testing program came at a moment the H5N1 avian influenza outbreak was actively spreading through dairy cattle and poultry -- reducing federal capacity to confirm the reliability of the lab network relied on to detect the virus in the milk supply and to conduct the FDA's own routine surveillance testing, at the same time this database's separate entries document a broader, sustained federal bird-flu-surveillance capacity collapse through 2025.

figures.source: Reporting on the April 3, 2025 VLIRN member notice

estimated_impact.caveat: No agency-produced quantified public-health-outcome estimate (e.g., cases or deaths attributable to the testing suspension specifically) was found in sourcing reviewed -- the documented impact is the loss of testing/verification capacity itself, at a time of active outbreak spread, not a measured harm figure. This entry is distinct from this tracker's existing usda-bird-flu-response-staff-accidental-firing-2025 (a February 2025 USDA staffing error, different agency and mechanism) and bird-flu-surveillance-collapse-resurgence-2025 (a November 2025 entry documenting the broader, later poultry-flock resurgence and surveillance-capacity gap) -- this entry documents a third, FDA-specific, April 2025 episode within the same broader pattern.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the Moffett Center elimination, VLIRN exercise suspension, and grade-A milk testing suspension are corroborated across CBS News, Yahoo/AOL wire coverage, and Crooks and Liars' contemporaneous reporting, all citing the same underlying FDA/VLIRN communications and agency officials. No subsequent confirmation of the testing programs' restoration was found in sourcing reviewed as of this entry's addition -- worth a follow-up check in a future batch given this tracker's related bird-flu entries show the broader surveillance gap persisting at least into 2026.

title: FDA vaccine/biologics division leadership purge and COVID vaccine access restriction
institution: FDA — Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER)
status: Ongoing -- after Makary resigned as FDA Commissioner May 12, 2026 and the acting CBER and CDER heads turned over May 15, Trump nominated Dr. Heidi Overton as Commissioner on Aug. 19, 2026, and HHS named Karim Mikhail permanent CBER director and Michael Davis permanent CDER director on Sept. 8, 2026.
date_of_action: March 2025 - September 2026
what_changed:
CBER, the FDA division that regulates vaccines, gene therapies, and blood products, went through six leaders (acting or permanent) between January 2025 and May 2026 by The FDA Group's count, which called Karim Mikhail CBER's 'sixth leader since January 2025,' while its sister division (CDER) also had six. Longtime CBER director Peter Marks resigned in March 2025 amid reported disagreements with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. over vaccine policy. Vinay Prasad was installed as CBER director in May 2025. In July 2025 Prasad was forced out after backlash over his handling of Sarepta Therapeutics' Duchenne muscular dystrophy gene therapy, then reinstated roughly two weeks later after Commissioner Marty Makary intervened. Upon returning, Prasad fired the official in charge of vaccine safety/surveillance and took direct control of that function himself; by STAT News's count as of March 6, 2026, he had pushed at least seven leaders out of their positions.

The May 2025 framework did not emerge without warning -- on April 30, 2025, Makary told CBS News the FDA was reconsidering whether to approve updated COVID-19 boosters for the coming winter at all, citing a "lack" of new clinical-trial data and declining public trust in the vaccines, a month-earlier signal of the risk-stratified approach that followed. In May 2025, Makary and Prasad co-authored a New England Journal of Medicine framework limiting FDA approval of updated COVID-19 vaccines to adults 65+ and people with qualifying risk factors, reversing the prior policy of a universal annual-vaccine recommendation for everyone 6 months and older; manufacturers must now run new randomized trials to get approval for healthy people outside that group. The framework estimated that 100 million to 200 million Americans would remain eligible (The Conversation, PBS NewsHour), and FDA officials pointed to similar recommendations in Canada, Denmark and Australia as validation for the policy change, PBS NewsHour reported.

This framework's public rollout came directly from RFK Jr. himself -- on May 27, 2025, Kennedy posted on X that 'we are now one step closer to realizing @POTUS's promise to Make America Healthy Again,' announcing that the COVID-19 vaccine had been **removed from the CDC's recommended immunization schedule for healthy children and healthy pregnant women, ahead of and without input from the CDC's own Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)**, whose next scheduled meeting was roughly a month away; the American Academy of Pediatrics' Dr. Sean O'Leary said 'no one from HHS had consulted the leading pediatricians' group about Tuesday's announcement,' and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists said 'we have seen firsthand how dangerous COVID infection can be during pregnancy and for newborns.' Because CDC recommendations directly govern insurer free-coverage obligations and the Vaccines for Children Program's payment eligibility, the announcement raised the prospect that private insurers could decline coverage and that Pfizer/Moderna doses (list price up to $150) could become a new out-of-pocket cost for the affected groups.

By early August 2025, as COVID-19 cases were rising across 26 states, the guidance had gone further than an age/risk cutoff alone, also dropping the standing recommendation for children and pregnant people specifically -- groups for whom health authorities had previously recommended vaccination regardless of individual risk factors. In September 2025, RFK Jr. and FDA leadership pursued a related but separate effort: publicizing alleged vaccine-harm data specific to pregnant women, including seeking to waive standard medical-privacy protections in order to release that data.

The risk-based restriction triggered a wave of downstream pharmacy and state reactions. By early September 2025, CVS and Walgreens had pulled back on offering COVID-19 vaccines in more than a dozen states, requiring a prescription or halting walk-in access entirely pending action by a CDC advisory panel. States responded unevenly: Colorado, Maine, and New York passed laws to preserve insurance coverage and access to vaccines regardless of federal guidance; New York, Massachusetts, and California declared public-health emergencies, mandated insurer coverage of state-recommended vaccines, and began forming multi-state alliances to keep COVID shots available, while Illinois moved to stockpile doses and Florida moved in the opposite direction, scrapping vaccine mandates. On September 21, 2025, seven northeastern states plus New York City launched the Northeast Public Health Collaborative to coordinate vaccine policy and emergency preparedness, with a similar coalition forming on the West Coast.

Prasad also repeatedly overruled career staff on individual drug and vaccine decisions (initially refusing to review Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine, reversed only after White House pressure; in July 2025, overruling career staff's recommendation to grant Novavax's and Moderna's COVID-19 vaccines full approval for ages 12 and up, narrowing authorization instead to seniors and high-risk individuals only; rejecting or discouraging gene-therapy applications from uniQure, Ultragenyx, Capricor, and Replimune). In early September 2025, then-FDA vaccine chief Vinay Prasad demanded YouTube delete six videos of himself that had been archived to preserve officials' pandemic-era public statements; YouTube complied by deleting the entire channel hosting them, which held roughly 350 videos featuring Prasad, RFK Jr., and other Trump administration health officials -- not just the six Prasad specifically objected to. Prasad had previously criticized vaccine mandates and defended the agency's research-funding cuts; the takedown drew criticism as an attempt to erase a public record of his own prior statements rather than a narrowly targeted correction.

On October 6, 2025, the CDC approved new COVID-19 vaccine rules requiring individuals to consult a doctor or pharmacist before receiving the shot -- a sharp break from the prior practice of walk-in availability -- championed by RFK Jr.'s reconstituted advisory panel and expected to slow distribution and limit access, part of the same COVID-vaccine-access-restriction pattern as the risk-based framework. By mid-October 2025, Reuters reported that the new guidelines had added confusion and complications for Americans seeking shots, and that COVID immunizations were down about 25% nationally for the four weeks ended Oct. 3, 2025, according to IQVIA data in analysts' research notes -- a window that closed before the CDC adopted the consult rule.

The CDER side of this turnover pattern includes two additional directors. George Tidmarsh, installed as CDER director in July 2025, was placed on administrative leave November 1, 2025 after declining, on stated legal grounds, to sign off on approvals under the FDA's new Commissioner's National Priority Voucher (CNPV) program -- a Makary-created pathway promising drug approval in as little as one to two months for medicines supporting 'U.S. national interests,' which lacks formal federal regulations and drew criticism from Harvard's Dr. Aaron Kesselheim ('the concept of doing a review in one to two months just does not have scientific precedent') and former FDA attorney Paul Kim ('it's extraordinary to have such an opaque application process, one that is obviously susceptible to politicization').

HHS separately stated Tidmarsh's leave and subsequent November 2, 2025 resignation followed a review of 'serious concerns about his personal conduct,' tied to a September 2025 LinkedIn post in which Tidmarsh, while still CDER director, publicly criticized the FDA's own 2021 approval of Aurinia Pharmaceuticals' kidney drug voclosporin -- a post that preceded a roughly 20% drop in Aurinia's stock and a subsequent Aurinia lawsuit accusing Tidmarsh of defamation and misusing his position against the company's chairman, Kevin Tang, with whom Tidmarsh had a prior business dispute. Tidmarsh's own account and HHS's stated rationale for his departure describe different conduct entirely (CNPV legal objections versus the Aurinia matter) and are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

Following Tidmarsh, veteran FDA oncology regulator Richard Pazdur -- who had led the agency's cancer-drug division for over two decades -- was installed as CDER director in November 2025 at Makary's urging, then filed retirement papers roughly three weeks later, departing in early December 2025, after clashing with Makary over a policy reducing the standard clinical-trial requirement for drug approval from two trials to one; Pazdur told the Wall Street Journal, 'All of a sudden, I was given a press release with a quotation by myself written in it, and asked to just agree to it,' and said Makary's approach had breached 'this wall between the commissioner's office and the review staff.' Tracy Beth Hoeg, a vaccine critic and former Makary aide, succeeded Pazdur as acting CDER director on December 3, 2025; Tidmarsh's and Pazdur's tenures are among those counted in CDER's six-director turnover since January 2025. Dr. Sara Brenner separately declined the CNPV oversight role after reviewing its legal implications, leaving Dr. Mallika Mundkur to take on that specific responsibility.

Separately, on the CBER side, Prasad asserted in a Nov. 28, 2025 email to staff that COVID vaccines had caused at least 10 children's deaths; STAT News, which obtained the memo, reported that experts were skeptical of the claim because it was not presented with detailed data. Former FDA commissioner Robert Califf, one of the 12 former commissioners who rebuked Prasad in December 2025, told KFF Health News that if Prasad's proposals advance, 'it won't be a viable business.'

When Prasad's departure was announced in March 2026, CNBC reported that, according to RTW Investments, the FDA had denied or discouraged the approval applications of at least eight drugs in the past year after taking issue with the companies' supporting data, and that all of those companies accused the agency of reversing previous guidance on the evidence they could use to support their applications. Commissioner Makary credited Prasad with four 'long-lasting reforms' -- a 2-to-1 pivotal-trial requirement, national priority reviews, the risk-stratified COVID-vaccine framework and a 'plausible mechanism' pathway for ultra-rare diseases -- and said his center hit a record number of approvals in December (PharmExec, quoting Makary on X).

Prasad departed CBER for a second and final time on April 30, 2026; deputy director Katherine Szarama was elevated to acting director, but departed that role herself after only about three weeks. Dr. Houman Hemmati, an ophthalmologist and COVID-response critic, was reported in April 2026 as the frontrunner candidate for the permanent CBER director role.

Leadership turnover also reached the Commissioner level. Marty Makary resigned as FDA Commissioner on May 12, 2026, reportedly after Trump directed FDA to lift its ban on flavored e-cigarette/vape sales over MAHA-aligned officials' objections; Kyle Diamantas, previously FDA's Deputy Commissioner for Food, became Acting Commissioner the same day. The FDA's top three drug/biologics-review positions -- Commissioner, acting CDER director, and acting CBER director -- all turned over within a single business week: acting CDER director Tracy Beth Hoeg, in the role since December 3, 2025, was fired May 15, 2026 and succeeded by CDER deputy director Michael Davis (the sixth person to lead CDER since January 2025); acting CBER director Katherine Szarama transitioned out the same day, succeeded by Karim Mikhail. Diamantas declined to be considered for the permanent Commissioner role, citing his young children among other personal reservations.

Karim Mikhail was named acting director in mid-May 2026 and remained in that role through at least late July 2026; in July 2026 he told STAT News his goal was simply to 'return' the biologics center 'to normal' after the turmoil of the prior year. Trade-press reporting (Zamann Pharma Support, July 24, 2026) indicated the FDA was expected to name permanent CDER and CBER directors together, with Hemmati still described as a frontrunner candidate for CBER -- a signal of movement, not yet a confirmed change. On August 19, 2026, Trump nominated Dr. Heidi Overton, a deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council with no prior FDA experience, as permanent Commissioner -- a Senate-confirmed post; Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA), the physician who chairs the Senate HELP Committee, publicly voiced "strong concerns" about the pick. On Sept. 8, 2026, HHS named the two acting center heads permanent: Karim Mikhail became full-time CBER director and Michael Davis permanent CDER director (BioPharma Dive), rather than Houman Hemmati, the previously reported CBER frontrunner.

estimated_impact.caveat: FDA leadership frames these as deliberate, evidence-based reforms rather than harmful disruption: Commissioner Makary credited Prasad with four 'long-lasting' reforms (a 2-to-1 pivotal-trial requirement, 'national priority reviews,' the risk-stratified vaccine framework, and a new 'plausible mechanism' pathway for ultra-rare diseases), and said CBER hit a record number of approvals in December 2025. FDA officials also pointed to similar recommendations in Canada, Denmark, and Australia as validation for the May 2025 framework, PBS NewsHour reported. On the other side, former FDA commissioner Robert Califf warned that if Prasad's proposals advance, 'it won't be a viable business' (KFF Health News), and the drugmakers whose applications the FDA denied or discouraged all accused the agency of 'reversing previous guidance on the evidence they could use to support their applications,' CNBC reported. A Nov. 28, 2025 internal Prasad memo claiming COVID vaccines caused at least 10 pediatric deaths was reported by STAT News, which obtained it, and by other outlets, but was not presented with detailed supporting data, leaving that specific claim unverified and contested. NBC News and the Guardian, reporting on the same memo in early December 2025, added that it also proposed sweeping new approval restrictions for flu and pneumonia vaccines and further limits for pregnant women, and that outside experts said Prasad had misused raw, unverified VAERS adverse-event reports to support the death claim while bypassing the FDA's normal advisory-committee and scientific-review process. title: FDA Loses ~3,500 Staff in April 2025 Purge -- Pharma Industry Warns of Delays, Though Drug-Review Deadlines Largely Held
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Implemented -- ~3,500 FDA staff laid off April 1, 2025; some (e.g. public-records staff) rehired May 2025. 2025 drug-review deadlines mostly held, but on-time approvals slipped to 78% in the second half of 2025 (RBC).
date_of_action: 2025-02 (industry SEC filings warn of delays) through 2025-04-01 (HHS lays off ~3,500 FDA employees)
what_changed: In late February 2025, dozens of pharmaceutical companies' annual reports to the SEC warned that Trump-administration budget and staffing cuts at the FDA could keep new drugs from being developed, approved, or commercialized in a timely manner, Wired reported March 3, 2025 -- an early, industry-side signal that followed February's firings of probationary FDA staff and came before the agency's own later, larger staffing action. On March 27, 2025, HHS announced that about 3,500 FDA employees, nearly a fifth of the agency's workforce, would be cut as part of a 10,000-job department-wide reduction. HHS said drug, device and food reviewers and inspectors would not be among those fired; the cuts instead targeted staff working on policy, human resources, information technology, procurement and communications. The same day, Reuters reported that some FDA reviewers of medical devices and tobacco products were already struggling to meet statutory deadlines after the February firings, and an Arnold & Porter lawyer who advises drug and device sponsors said the FDA had already canceled some meetings with companies or switched to written responses only. HHS carried out the reduction in force on April 1, 2025, this time hitting support and policy staff broadly across the agency rather than the narrower food-safety/device/tobacco-specific cuts documented in this tracker's separate February 2025 entry. A Skadden client memo of April 30, 2025 listed who was cut: policy staff who write guidance documents and regulations, project managers who keep companies informed about application reviews and answer regulatory questions, scientists who test products and develop regulatory standards, and communications staff. The memo said industry had noticed a decline in FDA responsiveness to nonessential or routine questions even before April 1, which the layoffs would likely aggravate, and cited reports that the device center's sponsor-meeting program had been sharply reduced, with meetings converted to written responses. One specific named casualty of the April 1 action: **the FDA's Division of Learning and Organizational Development, which trained both agency staff and outside doctors, nurses, and pharmacists on opioid safety, medication-error prevention, and other regulatory-science topics, was gutted, with all 30-plus employees laid off, all planned activities canceled, and its processing of continuing-education credits -- which health professionals in many states must earn to keep their licenses -- halted, CNBC reported April 8, 2025.** The Wall Street Journal reported April 17, 2025 that the FDA was missing deadlines and not responding to biotech companies, forcing some to push back clinical trials. Daré Bioscience, which had targeted mid-2025 to start a Phase 3 trial of its Sildenafil Cream for female sexual arousal disorder, postponed that trial after the FDA twice pushed back the date it would give guidance on the trial's analysis plan, CEO Sabrina Martucci Johnson told the Journal and Fierce Biotech, and turned instead toward selling a compounded version -- a concrete case of a company altering its drug-development plans (a trial start, not an approval decision) because of FDA slowdown. Daré began offering the cream as a compounded product, not FDA-approved, in select states in December 2025. Some cuts were partly reversed: on May 1, 2025, FDA staff who process public-records requests on device and tobacco regulation were told their layoffs were rescinded, KFF Health News reported. Despite the cuts, retirements and leadership departures, an Endpoints News analysis published January 8, 2026 found FDA drug reviewers met nearly all of their user-fee (PDUFA) commitments for new drug reviews in 2025; of 53 novel drugs and biologics approved, only two took longer than 12 months, both because of extended reviews of newly submitted data. Endpoints reporting, as summarized by The FDA Group, also flagged warning signs: an RBC Capital Markets finding that 78% of new and supplemental drug approvals in the second half of 2025 were completed on time, down from a historical 85-90%, and FDA staffing data, reported separately by Endpoints, showing the drug center lost 746 staff and hired six in the last quarter of fiscal 2025.

primary_proponent.role: HHS Secretary; the April 2025 FDA-wide staff reduction was part of his department restructuring
primary_proponent.note: The FDA cuts were part of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s department-wide restructuring (CNBC, April 8, 2025); no official was identified as personally choosing which FDA offices were cut. Distinct from the food-safety/device/tobacco cuts attributed institutionally to HHS in this tracker's separate February 2025 entry.

estimated_impact.summary: HHS laid off about 3,500 FDA employees -- nearly a fifth of the agency -- on April 1, 2025, stripping out the policy writers, project managers, product-testing scientists and communications staff who support drug reviewers. The human-facing losses documented so far are indirect: the FDA division that trained outside doctors, nurses and pharmacists on opioid safety and avoiding medication errors, and awarded continuing-education credits clinicians count toward licensing, was gutted; and at least one company, Daré Bioscience, postponed a planned Phase 3 trial of a women's sexual-health drug after the FDA twice pushed back its guidance, selling an unapproved compounded version instead. Companies also faced slower answers to routine questions and some canceled or written-only meetings. The core drug-approval deadlines mostly held in 2025 -- only two of 53 novel approvals ran past 12 months -- but on-time approvals slipped to 78% in the second half of the year, below the usual 85-90%, a sign the agency is running with little margin.

estimated_impact.caveat: The 3,500 figure is HHS's announced cut; some staff were later rehired, and no public count of reinstatements was found. The review-timeline figures are Endpoints News's analysis and an RBC Capital Markets tally, read here through The FDA Group's summary because the Endpoints article is paywalled; they measure all 2025 departures, not only the April layoffs. No estimate of patient harm or of delayed treatments exists; the Daré case is one company's decision, as its CEO described it to the Wall Street Journal and Fierce Biotech, and the responsiveness decline rests on law-firm and sponsor-lawyer accounts, part of which predate April 1. The entry does not claim that approvals themselves were broadly delayed.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the staffing figure (~3,500) and the general fact of industry concern (multiple companies' SEC filings, a formal disclosure requiring good-faith basis). MODERATE confidence on downstream impact -- the responsiveness decline and canceled or written-only meetings rest on a Skadden client memo and a sponsor lawyer quoted by Reuters (both describing conditions partly before the April 1 layoffs) and on Wall Street Journal reporting, but the more dramatic approval-delay concern that prompted the original industry warnings is largely not borne out by 2025 review data (2 of 53 novel approvals ran past 12 months), though RBC found on-time approvals slipped to 78% in the second half of 2025. Kept deliberately distinct from this tracker's separate FDA food-safety/device/tobacco staff-cuts entry, which documents the earlier (February 2025) firing of about 700 FDA probationary employees, apparently concentrated in the food, device and tobacco centers -- this entry's April 2025 reduction in force is a separate, larger, later action.

title: FDA Fires About 700 Probationary Staff, Many in Food-Safety, Device, and Tobacco Oversight -- Top Food-Safety Official Resigns in Protest
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Implemented -- about 700 FDA probationary staff fired Feb. 15-16, 2025; a court-ordered reinstatement was blocked on appeal in April 2025; the early-April HHS layoffs cut about 3,500 more FDA jobs, with some public-records staff later rehired.
date_of_action: 2025-02-15 (firing notices) through 2025-02-17 (Jones's resignation)
what_changed: On Friday, February 14, 2025, HHS announced plans to fire 5,200 probationary employees across its agencies, including the FDA, NIH and CDC. Probationary employees across the FDA received termination notices the next evening, Saturday, February 15; the Associated Press, in a report carried by The Guardian, said the firings appeared to focus on the agency's centers for food, medical devices and tobacco products (which oversees e-cigarettes), and an FDA staffer said they included employees who review the safety of new food additives and ingredients. The New York Times reported that about 700 people were fired from the FDA that weekend. Jim Jones, director of the FDA's food division, resigned on Monday, February 17, in a letter estimating that 89 of the roughly 2,000 people in his division had been fired, many of them recently hired to do in-depth chemical-safety work; CBS News quoted the letter as saying the cuts included staff with expertise in nutrition, infant formula and food safety response, and 10 chemical safety staff hired to review potentially unsafe ingredients. Jones called the layoffs 'indiscriminate' and warned they would add 'one more roadblock' to the 'Make America Healthy Again' agenda of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and he rebuked Kennedy's public comments 'impugning the integrity of the food staff, asserting they are corrupt based on falsities.' On March 13, 2025, a federal judge in Maryland ordered HHS and 17 other agencies to reinstate the fired probationary employees, either to their jobs or to administrative leave, an order covering more than 2,000 HHS probationary workers that the Fourth Circuit blocked on April 9, 2025. A second, larger round followed: HHS announced on March 27, 2025 a plan to cut 10,000 jobs, about 3,500 of them at the FDA (almost 20% of the agency), with layoffs beginning in early April. HHS said FDA food, drug and device reviewers and inspectors would be spared, but the layoffs decimated the FDA's public-records staff across its centers, KFF Health News reported; the FDA rehired at least some of those workers in early May. NBC News reported May 9, 2025 that no FDA warning letters to U.S. food manufacturers had been publicly posted since the week of Trump's inauguration -- the last one went up January 21, 2025 -- with **more than a dozen issued letters, including ones flagging potential botulism contamination at a seafood company, misleading disease-treatment claims on dietary supplements, and inadequate contamination controls at a fresh-sprouts producer, sitting unpublished**. A current FDA staffer and a former FDA employee, speaking anonymously, said the April layoffs gutted the teams that review records and redact confidential information before release, stalling publication; staffers also said a posting backlog existed even before the layoffs, and two former employees said some public-records staff had since been rehired. The FDA's statement did not address the letters. Consumer Federation of America food-policy director Thomas Gremillion said a warning letter is 'an indication that something has gone wrong.'

title: FDA Cut 170 Inspection-Support Staff, Curtailing Routine Food and Drug Safety Inspections -- Foreign Food Inspections Fell 17% in FY2025
institution: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Implemented, partly reversed -- ~170 inspection-support staff cut April 1, 2025; about two dozen travel staff told in late April their layoffs would be reversed. Foreign food inspections fell 17% in FY2025, to 1,140, nearly 35% below 2019 (AP review of FDA records, Sept 2026).
date_of_action: 2025-04-01 (layoffs) through late 2025-04 (partial reversal); foreign-inspection decline documented through FY2025 (reported 2025-11 and 2026-09)
what_changed: As part of the broader 2025 HHS-wide staffing reduction ordered by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- some 10,000 jobs department-wide, about 3,500 of them at FDA -- the April 1, 2025 layoffs cut roughly 170 staff from FDA's Office of Inspections and Investigations, according to federal health officials cited by CBS News: the administrative and management support staff who coordinate and schedule the agency's food and drug safety inspectors, distinct from the inspectors themselves, who were not directly targeted. HHS said the layoffs would not directly cut FDA's inspections staff ('FDA inspectors were not impacted and this critical work will continue,' a spokesperson said), but FDA officials told CBS News on April 2 that the loss of support staff was causing major delays and disruptions. The office's travel operations division, which booked flights and secured translators for inspections abroad, was eliminated, a pilot program of unannounced foreign inspections was paused, and senior FDA leaders were planning to trim routine 'surveillance inspections' -- proactive, scheduled checks not tied to a specific safety complaint -- in favor of more urgent work such as inspections of firms flagged for a safety risk or follow-up visits confirming prior violations had been fixed. On April 7, inspectors were told by email that they would now book their own travel; NPR reported on April 18 that some inspectors were canceling trips and one was still waiting on reimbursement for thousands of dollars in inspection travel, compounding a pre-existing shortfall: according to the Government Accountability Office, FDA had not met its goals for foreign or domestic food inspections since 2018. Internal emails and draft contracting documents obtained by CBS News on April 11 showed FDA finalizing plans, approved by Commissioner Marty Makary, to replace most of the work of more than 50 laid-off travel-logistics and inspector-spending-oversight staff with contractors -- who would be issued FDA laptops and badges -- despite those employees' layoff notices stating their work was 'unnecessary or virtually identical to duties being performed elsewhere in the agency.' On April 17, CBS News, citing multiple federal health officials, reported a more structural tentative plan: handing most routine food-facility inspections to state and local officials, building on existing FDA contracts with 43 states and Puerto Rico (states already performed about a third of routine food inspections, per GAO), while some higher-risk routine inspections, such as infant-formula plants, and foreign-facility inspections would stay with FDA. The plan was described as not final and possibly requiring congressional action to fund, and an FDA spokesperson said on record that 'the claim that the FDA is suspending routine food safety inspections is false' and that the agency 'remains committed to ensuring critical programs and inspections continue.' Leaked draft White House budget documents reported around the same time proposed a 17% cut to FDA's FY2026 budget (to $6.5 billion) that included shifting all routine food-facility inspections to states; the leaked figures were not confirmed as final. HHS's formal FY2026 request, released May 30, 2025, sought $6.8 billion for FDA, a $271 million decrease from FY2025, including $33 million to expand state partnerships for routine inspections. In late April 2025, FDA began reversing a portion of the layoffs: around two dozen of the nearly 200 inspection-support staff cut by CBS's later count, chiefly those booking travel for foreign inspections, were told their layoffs would be reversed, along with scientists at food-safety labs in Chicago and San Francisco and drug-safety labs in Puerto Rico and Detroit. An HHS spokesperson blamed errors in the layoffs on inaccurate data from the department's 'siloed HR divisions.' At that point, one FDA official told CBS News, fewer than 60% of the agency's planned foreign inspections had been completed in a recent week, sidelined foreign inspectors were being asked to pivot to domestic inspections, and more than $700,000 in inspectors' expenses remained unpaid. In May 2025, Makary announced the agency would expand unannounced foreign inspections. A November 2025 ProPublica analysis of FDA inspection data (republished by the Louisiana Illuminator) found that **foreign food-facility inspections had fallen by almost half in March 2025 and were nearly 30% below the prior two years' pace through July, putting the U.S. on track for the fewest foreign food inspections since 2011 outside the pandemic years.** About two dozen current and former FDA officials blamed the drop on the staffing cuts, which ProPublica said began hitting investigative support staff in March: 65% of the staff in the FDA divisions coordinating travel and budgets had left or been fired, investigators were left to arrange their own flights, visas and diplomatic passports, and a backlog of unpaid inspector reimbursements climbed past $1 million, according to a former staffer. Agency records reviewed by the Associated Press in September 2026 showed foreign food inspections fell 17% in fiscal year 2025, to 1,140, and were down nearly 35% from 2019.

title: FDA Refused to Even Review Moderna's mRNA Flu Vaccine Despite a 40,000-Person Trial Showing Stronger Protection for Older Adults
institution: Food and Drug Administration
status: FDA reversed its Feb. 3, 2026 refusal to review on Feb. 18 and approved the vaccine (mFlusiva) Aug. 5, 2026. As of late Sept. 2026 a court-frozen ACIP had issued no recommendation, so mandatory no-cost insurance coverage has not been triggered; about $171/dose uninsured.
date_of_action: 2026-02-03 (FDA's refusal-to-file letter)
what_changed: Moderna submitted an application in December 2025 for FDA approval of its new mRNA flu vaccine (mRNA-1010) for adults 50 and older, supported by a Phase 3 trial of more than 40,000 people that found the new vaccine somewhat more effective than a standard-dose flu shot. Rather than reviewing the application on its merits, the FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) issued a 'refusal-to-file' letter on February 3, 2026 -- declining to even begin substantive review; Moderna disclosed the letter publicly on February 10, 2026. The letter, signed by CBER director Dr. Vinay Prasad, stated the agency did not consider the trial 'adequate and well-controlled' because Moderna compared its vaccine to a licensed standard-dose flu shot rather than one reflecting the 'best-available standard of care' -- the comparator choice was the sole stated reason, not the vaccine's efficacy or safety data. Moderna disputes this, saying it ran the trial the way regulators had discussed and agreed to; CBER had written in 2024 that a licensed standard-dose comparator would be acceptable. Drug regulators in Canada, Europe, and Australia accepted the same application for substantive review. After a Type A meeting, Moderna announced on February 18, 2026 -- 15 days after the letter and eight days after it became public -- that FDA had reversed course and agreed to review an amended application under an age-stratified pathway Moderna proposed: standard approval for adults 50-64 and accelerated approval, contingent on a postmarketing study against a high-dose or adjuvanted comparator, for adults 65 and older. FDA set a review goal date of August 5, 2026, and on that date approved the vaccine, branded mFlusiva, on those terms for adults 50 and older -- the first mRNA-based flu vaccine approved in the U.S. In the main trial the vaccine showed about 26.6% higher relative efficacy against confirmed flu than a standard-dose shot; side effects such as injection-site pain, fatigue, and headache were more frequent than with the comparator but mostly mild and brief. The outcome was approval, not suppression, but only after FDA's vaccine division first refused substantive review of a well-supported application for a flu-vulnerable population that peer regulators abroad had accepted, and reversed itself after the refusal drew public backlash. STAT News reported that Prasad had overruled career scientists preparing to advance the review; HHS disputed that account. FDA approval does not by itself guarantee no-cost access. U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy's March 16, 2026 preliminary injunction in American Academy of Pediatrics v. Kennedy (D. Mass., No. 1:25-cv-11916) stayed the appointments of the 13 sitting Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) members and effectively barred the committee from meeting, so ACIP has issued no recommendation for mFlusiva. An ACIP recommendation is what triggers mandatory no-cost coverage by private insurers under the ACA, and without one Medicaid coverage is uncertain, though adults 65 and over should be able to get it covered by at least some Medicare plans. **As of late September 2026, mFlusiva was on the market at about $171 a dose without insurance, with no ACIP recommendation and the committee's next meeting scheduled for October.**

estimated_impact.summary: Older adults, the group most at risk from flu, faced a period in which FDA refused even to review a vaccine with about 26.6% higher relative efficacy than a standard flu shot in a 40,000-person trial; that refusal was reversed 15 days later and the vaccine was approved on schedule in August 2026. The remaining harm is access: with the court-frozen ACIP unable to recommend it, insurers are not required to cover mFlusiva at no cost, Medicaid coverage is uncertain, and uninsured adults face about $171 a dose.

title: FDA Blocked Publication of Its Own Studies Finding COVID-19 and Shingles Vaccines Safe
institution: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
status: Documented via reporting first published May 2026; no reversal or republication identified as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-10 (two COVID-19 vaccine studies withdrawn after acceptance) through 2026-02 (Shingrix/shingles vaccine conference-abstract submission blocked)
what_changed: In October 2025, **FDA scientists were directed to withdraw two COVID-19 vaccine safety studies that had already been accepted for publication in medical journals, based on data drawn from millions of patient records and finding serious side effects to be rare**. In February 2026, top FDA officials declined to approve submission of study abstracts on the safety of Shingrix, the recombinant shingles vaccine, to a major drug-safety conference. Andrew Nixon, a spokesman for the Department of Health and Human Services (which oversees FDA), defended both actions: on the COVID-19 studies, he said they 'were withdrawn because the authors drew broad conclusions that were not supported by the underlying data'; on the blocked shingles research, he said 'the design of that study fell outside the agency's purview.' Independent experts who reviewed the withdrawn studies disputed that characterization -- Caleb Alexander, a drug-safety and methodology expert at Johns Hopkins University, said after reviewing the reports that 'there is nothing inherently problematic regarding these reports.'

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services

title: RFK Jr. Cancels FDA's Public Flu-Vaccine Advisory Meeting, Strain Selection Made Behind Closed Doors Instead
institution: Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee (VRBPAC), Food and Drug Administration
status: Implemented -- the March 13, 2025 public meeting was never rescheduled; the FDA's 2025-2026 strain recommendation was issued without it
what_changed: HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ordered the cancellation of VRBPAC's March 13, 2025 public meeting, at which the committee's outside experts were set to recommend which influenza strains should go into the 2025-2026 season's flu vaccines -- the annual, decades-old process manufacturers rely on to begin roughly six months of production lead time. Panel members were notified late on February 26 with no explanation given, and no rescheduled date was ever set; VRBPAC member Dr. Paul Offit told reporters he'd received no reason for the cancellation either. It was the second vaccine-related advisory disruption within the same two weeks, following a postponed CDC vaccine meeting the week before. Rather than reconvene the public committee, Acting FDA Commissioner Dr. Sara Brenner and a closed-door interagency group of FDA, CDC, and Defense Department scientists decided the strain composition internally, aligning with the WHO's own recommendation, and the FDA published its selections without the normal open, externally-reviewed VRBPAC process. The FDA maintained the decision would not delay 2025-2026 season vaccine availability.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Reporting attributes the cancellation order to Kennedy directly, who then had Acting FDA Commissioner Sara Brenner make the strain-composition call without VRBPAC's public input -- consistent with Kennedy's broader pattern (see the related ACIP-purge entry in this database, four months later) of removing independent expert panels from vaccine-policy decisions rather than working through them.

estimated_impact.summary: **Removed independent, public scientific review from a decades-old annual process that determines the composition of that season's flu vaccine for the entire country**, replacing it with an unreviewable closed-door decision by political appointees and government scientists.
estimated_impact.caveat: No reporting reviewed found evidence the 2025-2026 flu vaccine's actual availability or effectiveness was harmed by skipping the meeting -- the concern raised by outside experts was about the loss of transparent, independent review itself, and about setting precedent for future strain-selection decisions, not a documented supply-chain failure in this instance.

confidence_note: HIGH -- corroborated by CIDRAP, CNBC, BioSpace, and the Arizona Public Health Association, with a named committee member (Offit) and named officials (Kennedy, Brenner) on record. Explicitly distinguished from this database's separate ACIP mass-removal entry (June 2025) -- same underlying pattern of bypassing independent vaccine-advisory panels, but a different committee, different vaccine, and four months earlier.

section_summaries.what_changed: RFK Jr. cancelled the FDA's public flu-strain-selection meeting with no explanation and had an acting commissioner decide behind closed doors instead of through the normal open expert-review process.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: No documented vaccine-supply harm from this instance, but it removed independent public review from a process the country relies on annually and set a precedent later repeated with ACIP.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Strongly sourced across multiple health-policy outlets with named officials and a named committee member on record.

title: Trump's Disputed Removal of a Democratic FEC Commissioner, Plus Two Resignations, Left the Election Watchdog Without a Quorum to Enforce Campaign Finance Law
institution: Federal Election Commission (FEC)
status: The FEC has lacked a quorum since May 1, 2025. Trainor's resignation effective Oct. 3, 2025 left two commissioners, both Democrats. Trump nominated Republicans Ashley Stow and Andrew Woodson on Feb. 11, 2026; as of mid-September 2026 the Senate Rules Committee had held no hearing.
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (Cooksey resignation effective) through 2025-04-30 (Dickerson resignation effective, triggering quorum loss)
what_changed:
Republican commissioner Sean Cooksey resigned from the FEC effective January 20, 2025 to become counsel to Vice President JD Vance. Effective January 31, 2025, Trump moved to remove Democratic Commissioner Ellen Weintraub, who had been serving as the commission's chair and had sat on the commission since 2002, long past her original six-year term -- an unusual step for a commission designed to be bipartisan and independent. Weintraub said she had received a letter from Trump "purporting to remove me," and she and Democratic senators called the dismissal illegal; the Congressional Research Service describes her vacancy as disputed and does not analyze its legality. The FEC's website listed her seat as vacant by February 7, 2025, and she did not take part in the commission's open meetings when they resumed on March 27, 2025. When Republican Commissioner Allen Dickerson's term ended and he departed effective April 30, 2025, the FEC was left with only three of its six seats filled, below the four-member quorum the agency's governing statute requires to conduct high-level business -- including voting on enforcement-investigation outcomes, issuing advisory opinions, or approving campaign-finance guidance. With the 2026 election cycle already underway, the agency became unable to formally enforce campaign finance law, investigate complaints to conclusion, or issue new guidance until quorum was restored.

Update 2026-09-29: Republican Commissioner Trey Trainor resigned effective October 3, 2025, to join the Dhillon Law Group and run for Congress, leaving only two commissioners, both Democrats: Chair Shana Broussard and Commissioner Dara Lindenbaum. On February 11, 2026, more than eight months after congressional Republicans had recommended them, Trump nominated two Republicans: Ashley Stow, to Trainor's former seat, and Andrew Woodson, to Dickerson's. The nominations went to the Senate Rules Committee, where "paperwork issues" and committee chair Mitch McConnell's monthslong medical absence delayed a hearing; as of mid-September 2026 none had been scheduled, and Vice Chair Alex Padilla said it was "not clear" there would be one before the election. Trump has not nominated anyone to the two remaining vacancies. Broussard said on September 1, 2026 that the FEC's enforcement backlog had grown to 307 cases. Even if both nominees are confirmed, a four-member commission would need unanimous agreement to act on most matters.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Trump's removal of Weintraub, a Democratic commissioner who called her dismissal illegal (a vacancy the Congressional Research Service describes as disputed), was the specific action that -- combined with Cooksey's and Dickerson's separate departures -- reduced the commission below quorum; reporting does not identify Trump as having taken a comparable removal action against a Republican commissioner.

estimated_impact.summary: **The nation's primary campaign-finance enforcement body lost its ability to formally investigate complaints to conclusion, issue advisory opinions, or approve new guidance and, with Trump's two nominees stalled in the Senate, was on track to sit out the 2026 midterm elections**, opening a window for campaign-finance violations, dark-money coordination, and other abuses to proceed without the FEC's normal enforcement check.

estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar figure or documented count of specific campaign-finance violations that went unenforced as a direct result of the quorum loss was identified in sourcing reviewed -- the harm documented is the agency's structural incapacity itself, not yet a quantified count of violations that escaped enforcement because of it. The 307-case backlog counts pending enforcement matters, not confirmed violations.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- corroborated across CNN, The Hill, Campaign & Elections, NOTUS, and the Election Law Blog, all independently confirming the same three departures and resulting quorum loss; Weintraub's removal specifically (as opposed to a routine term expiration) is well documented as the unusual step among the three. Update 2026-09-29: The Congressional Research Service's FEC membership report (updated March 2, 2026) and The Washington Sun's reporting through September 2026 confirm Trainor's October 2025 departure, the February 2026 nominations and the stalled Senate process; CRS says Trump "reportedly removed" Weintraub and calls her vacancy disputed, so the narrative describes the removal as contested.

title: Trump's Attempt to Fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook Blocked by Supreme Court; Second Removal Attempt Pending
institution: Federal Reserve Board of Governors
status: Supreme Court blocked the first firing on procedural grounds (June 29, 2026). Trump opened a second removal attempt August 5, 2026; Cook's lawyer rebutted it by the August 26 deadline. As of late September 2026 no final decision had been reported and Cook remains a governor.
date_of_action: 2025-08-25 (attempted firing); 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling); 2026-08-05 (second removal notice)
what_changed: In August 2025, President Trump attempted to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook -- the first attempted removal of a sitting Fed governor in the central bank's 111-year history -- citing mortgage-fraud allegations from before she joined the Fed. On August 20, 2025, FHFA Director William Pulte (who by June 2026 was also serving as acting Director of National Intelligence) posted a letter to Attorney General Pamela Bondi accusing Cook of claiming two homes as her principal residence in 2021; Trump posted that 'Cook must resign, now!!!' and on August 25 sent her a letter purporting to fire her for cause. Cook, who denied the allegations and had not been charged, sued, arguing that her removal was not 'for cause' as the Federal Reserve Act requires and that she had not been given notice and a chance to respond. A federal district court blocked the firing with a preliminary injunction, and the D.C. Circuit declined to stay that injunction on September 15, 2025. Cook remained in her seat throughout, participating in the Fed's September 2025 rate-setting meeting. The Supreme Court heard argument in the companion case Trump v. Slaughter, over the firing of an FTC commissioner, on December 8, 2025; the case put at stake the for-cause removal protections of other multimember independent agencies, several of which -- including the NLRB, MSPB, CPSC and EEOC -- had already lost members to Trump firings. The Court, which in October 2025 had deferred the government's stay application in Cook's case, heard argument on January 21, 2026; a week later, then-Fed Chair Jerome Powell called it 'perhaps the most important legal case in the Fed's 113-year history.' On June 29, 2026, the Court ruled 6-3 in Slaughter that Trump could remove FTC Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter, overruling Humphrey's Executor, but ruled 5-4 in Trump v. Cook that Cook could remain in office while her lawsuit proceeds. Chief Justice Roberts, writing for a majority that included conservative Justice Kavanaugh alongside the Court's three liberals, held that accepting the administration's arguments **'would in effect transform the Federal Reserve's for-cause protection into at-will employment'** and stressed that 'not only the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve's design.' The Court treated the Federal Reserve as distinct from the other independent agencies in part because of its unique structure and history. It decided the application on the narrow ground that Cook had not received the notice and opportunity to respond that the statute requires, did not decide whether the mortgage allegations amount to 'cause,' and said the President was not barred from trying again. Trump responded on Truth Social that the case had been sent back 'on a strictly procedural basis' and vowed to 'take appropriate action immediately'; Pulte said he believed Cook 'will be indicted for mortgage fraud.' In a letter dated August 5, 2026, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino, citing the June 29 opinion, told Cook the President was 'considering' removing her over the same pre-Fed mortgage allegations and gave her until August 26 to respond through the Director of Presidential Personnel. On August 26, Cook's attorney Abbe Lowell sent White House counsel David Warrington a five-page letter calling the allegations 'unfounded and untrue,' arguing 'An inadvertent oversight is not fraudulent or criminal,' and noting that Trump himself and other administration officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Attorney General Todd Blanche, had reportedly also listed multiple properties as primary residences. As of late September 2026, no final removal decision had been reported, and Cook remained on the Board of Governors.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Posted that Cook 'must resign, now!!!' after Pulte's mortgage-fraud letter, then on August 25, 2025 sent her a letter purporting to fire her for cause; after the Supreme Court blocked that, the White House reopened removal proceedings in August 2026. The district court found his stated cause likely insufficient; the Supreme Court ruled on procedural grounds and did not decide whether cause exists.

estimated_impact.summary: Trump's attempt to fire a sitting Federal Reserve governor over unproven, pre-Fed mortgage allegations was blocked: the Supreme Court kept Cook in office and refused to let the Fed's for-cause protection become at-will employment, preserving for now the central bank's insulation from presidential removal on the same day it let Trump fire an FTC commissioner. The harm averted is institutional and unquantified. It is not settled: a second removal attempt opened in August 2026 under the Court's own notice-and-response roadmap. Then-Fed Chair Jerome Powell called the case 'perhaps the most important legal case in the Fed's 113-year history.'

estimated_impact.caveat: The stated rationale is the mortgage-fraud allegations Pulte raised, which Cook denies; she had not been charged as of August 2026, though Pulte said he believes she 'will be indicted.' Cook's lawyers call the allegations baseless and an effort to interfere with the Fed's independence; Trump has pressed the Fed to cut rates sharply. The Supreme Court's ruling was interim and procedural: it held Cook was owed notice and a chance to respond, did not decide whether the allegations amount to 'cause,' and left the President free to try again, which he did in August 2026. Whether the Fed's independence holds against that second attempt, and any court challenge to it, is the open question; no dollar or market cost of the fight has been estimated.

title: Federal Return-to-Office Mandate Ordered Remote Workers to Report Hundreds of Miles Away on Days' Notice, Into Offices Without Desks or Wi-Fi
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and federal agencies government-wide
status: In effect: OPM's December 2025 guidance reaffirmed full-time in-person work with telework used sparingly; OPM said about 90% of federal employees were on-site full-time as of January 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (presidential memorandum); 2025-01-22 (OPM implementing memo); rollout problems reported March-April 2025
what_changed: On January 20, 2025, Trump's first-day presidential memorandum directed federal agencies to end remote-work arrangements and require full-time in-person work; in a January 22 memo, OPM recommended agencies target full compliance within 30 days. The rollout hit employees hired or relocated for remote positions especially hard: the Washington Post reported **some workers received just days' notice to report to offices hundreds of miles from where they lived** -- one HHS employee working remotely from the Southwest since 2023 was told via an email titled 'Return to In-Person Work Guidance for March 17, 2025' that she needed to report that Monday. Employees described scrambling to book flights, arrange childcare, or sell homes; one Defense Department employee hired as a remote worker was given until April 30 to start reporting to an office a 12-hour drive away, and another employee expected a new commute of an hour and 45 minutes each way. Some reported for work only to learn a day later that the administration had just canceled the lease on their office building, amid its mass federal-lease cancellations. Separately, CNN (March 4) and NPR (March 26) reported the offices employees were ordered back into often lacked basic infrastructure to receive them -- CNN documented offices without desks, Wi-Fi, or working lights, and NPR shortages of desks, computer monitors, parking, and even toilet paper. NPR reported that a USDA remote employee given a list of possible return-to-office locations found that one of them was, in fact, a storage facility; the Washington Post reported that a government-wide office-matching tool suggested a closed Subway sandwich shop and a self-storage facility to a CDC employee. Reuters reported similar conditions on March 16, 2025, documenting a cockroach infestation at a NASA facility employees were ordered back into, IRS tax assessors in Memphis sharing a training room and unable to discuss sensitive tax matters with clients by phone for fear of breaching privacy laws, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services staff in Chicago temporarily working on boxes in a storage room. Wired's April 7, 2025 report, drawing on more than 30 employees at 17 agencies, described workers traveling long distances to spend their days in the same virtual meetings they had taken from home, shortages of basics such as toilet paper, self-reported productivity losses, and employees who said the conditions were affecting their physical and mental health. Some federal employees and outside observers characterized the mandate's chaotic, under-resourced rollout as a de facto pressure campaign to induce resignations, working in tandem with OPM's January 28, 2025 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation offer to all roughly 2 million federal employees (a separate, related action this database references but does not duplicate in full here). The mandate was not relaxed: OPM's December 2025 telework guidance said federal employees should generally be working full-time in person and that telework should be used sparingly, and OPM Director Scott Kupor said in January 2026 that around 90% of federal employees were working on-site full-time. Pew Research Center calculated federal civilian headcount fell 10.3% in 2025 overall, with 348,219 quits, retirements, layoffs and other departures against only 116,912 new hires -- a figure reflecting the combined effect of the RTO mandate, the deferred-resignation program, and other workforce-reduction actions rather than the RTO mandate in isolation.

primary_proponent.role: OPM directed agencies to comply quickly with the return-to-office mandate and, separately, administered the related deferred-resignation program
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally directing the specific relocation notices or the infrastructure shortfalls; reporting attributes the chaotic rollout to agencies scrambling to meet OPM's compressed compliance timeline without first restoring office capacity (desks, IT, parking) that had been reduced during years of remote work.

estimated_impact.summary: Remote federal employees, including people hired as remote workers, were ordered on days' notice to report to offices hundreds of miles away, forcing rushed moves, home sales, childcare scrambles, and commutes of up to an hour and 45 minutes each way into unready offices (no desks, Wi-Fi, or toilet paper; a cockroach-infested NASA building); some said the conditions were harming their physical and mental health. Services suffered too: IRS assessors in a shared room could not discuss taxpayers' cases by phone, and employees reported lost productivity. The mandate stayed in force, with about 90% of employees on-site by January 2026, in a year when the federal civilian workforce shrank 10.3% from combined cuts.
