title: Survey of 300+ Fired Federal Workers Finds 95% Report Ongoing Mental Health Harm, Months After Court Found Firings Unlawful
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and government-wide probationary workforce
status: Harm remains documented and ongoing. Judge Alsup declined to order reinstatement, citing workers who had 'moved on with their lives and found new jobs' -- but the same survey (fielded Feb.-March 2026, published May 2026) found 21% still unemployed (per Nonprofit Quarterly; Federal News Network reported about 17%), 7% underemployed, and 49% of employed respondents earning significantly less as of Jan. 31, 2026, plus 115 of ~157 reinstated respondents describing inadequate communication about that process. OPM separately proposed (reported July 2026) reducing morale-survey questions and easing agencies' disclosure requirements.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (OPM directive to mass-fire probationary employees) through 2026-05 (survey results published)
what_changed:
In February 2025, the Office of Personnel Management directed federal agencies to mass-terminate probationary employees -- workers typically in their first one to two years in a position or newly promoted role, who have fewer job protections than tenured federal staff. About 25,000 probationary employees were fired government-wide as a result. The roughly 25,000 figure comes from agencies' court-mandated declarations in the lawsuit by 19 states and D.C. over the firings (Maryland v. USDA, D. Md.); Federal News Network reported on March 18, 2025 that the filings, which covered most federal civilian agencies but excluded the Defense Department, OPM and the National Archives, showed 24,583 probationary employees terminated, and FedScoop's count of the same declarations was 24,813.

The mental-health toll was documented almost immediately, not just in the 2026 retrospective survey below: in March 2025, NBC News interviewed 20 federal workers -- many of them military veterans -- who **described panic attacks, weight loss, sleepless nights, and suicidal ideation in the weeks after losing their jobs, with some visiting emergency rooms after breakdowns**; several described being harassed on social media on top of the job loss itself, and suicide-prevention specialists among the fired workers said the firings had left them questioning their own worth.

On September 12, 2025, U.S. District Judge William Alsup ruled in AFGE v. OPM (N.D. Cal.) that OPM had unlawfully directed agencies to carry out these terminations. Between February and March 2026, former fired federal employees surveyed more than 300 people affected by the firings; 27 UNIHTED, an organization of former National Institutes of Health employees, published the results, which Government Executive (May 27) and Federal News Network (May 28) reported in late May 2026 -- more than a year after the initial firings and roughly eight months after the court's unlawfulness finding. About 95% of respondents reported continuing mental health effects, including depression and sleep disruption (Federal News Network; Government Executive also reported 95% with new mental health symptoms, while Nonprofit Quarterly put the share reporting mental health consequences at nearly 90 percent), and more than 50% said they had been experiencing trauma-related symptoms (Federal News Network). Federal News Network's May 28, 2026 coverage of the survey quoted one respondent who wrote, 'I still have nightmares about the firings,' and another who wrote, 'I have tried to turn the page and move on, but this will reverberate through my life for years.'

The Mindful Federal Employee separately described what appears to be the same survey (former probationary employees surveying roughly 300 fired colleagues across 14 agencies) and reported that one in four started a psychiatric medication, a figure that does not appear in Federal News Network, Government Executive or Nonprofit Quarterly coverage; Government Executive quoted a fired Forest Service ranger as saying, 'A lot of people have had to go on new medications.'

The survey's release pushed back specifically against the narrative that affected workers had 'moved on' in the year-plus since being terminated. That pushback was aimed squarely at Alsup's own stated reasoning for declining to order reinstatement: he had written that 'the terminated probationary employees have moved on with their lives and found new jobs.' The survey's employment data (drawn from the same 300+ respondents across 43 states and 14 federal agencies, per Nonprofit Quarterly; Government Executive described 12 federal departments, 43 states, and one territory) contradicts that assumption directly -- as of January 31, 2026, 21% of respondents remained unemployed (Nonprofit Quarterly; Federal News Network reported about 17% still unemployed a year later), another 7% had found only part-time work, and 49% of those who were employed reported earning significantly lower salaries than before their firing. Government Executive reported that 49% of employed respondents were earning significantly lower salaries and another 19% lower salaries, and Federal News Network put the combined share of respondents in new jobs with lower or significantly lower pay at 68%.

Separately, of the survey's ~157 respondents who had been reinstated -- through other legal challenges distinct from Alsup's ruling, which did not itself order reinstatement -- 115 said communication about the reinstatement process had been inadequate, and many described returning without any assurance of job security. About 82% of roughly 300 respondents said they no longer have any trust in the top leadership at their former agency (27 UNIHTED; Nonprofit Quarterly).

As this survey data was drawing attention to the firings' psychological toll, OPM moved in the opposite direction on its own government-wide morale measurement -- a pattern with an earlier antecedent. OPM had already fully canceled the 2025 FEVS in August 2025, after months of postponement, despite a federal statute requiring the survey be conducted annually (Government Executive, Federal News Network, August 2025). OPM's stated rationale was to remove questions on diversity, equity, inclusion, accessibility, and gender identity added under the Biden administration, adding a new question about poor performers instead, and said it would field a revised survey in 2026 -- the same 'reworked' framing that later produced the reduced-question, agency-disclosure-control proposal reported the following July. The Washington Post characterized the cancellation as removing one of the few institutional tools for measuring civil-service morale and accountability at a moment when mass firings and relocations had already depressed it.

Reported July 10, 2026, OPM proposed reducing the number of questions on the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS) -- the government's own annual instrument for measuring federal workforce morale and job satisfaction -- while giving individual agencies more control over whether and how their results are publicly disclosed. The proposal emerged amid a broader context of roughly 317,000 federal employees having left government (through firings or buyouts, including the DOGE-driven departures documented elsewhere in this database) by the time DOGE's operations concluded July 4, 2026.

This 317,000 figure traces back at least as far as Reuters reporting from late November 2025, in which Trump's OPM director confirmed the government would shed 317,000 workers over the course of 2025 alone -- consistent with, not a revision of, the July 2026 cumulative figure above. That same reporting specified only about 68,000 replacement hires against the 317,000 departures, and described OPM as working with the White House budget office to 'institutionalize' DOGE's workforce-reduction approach into standing personnel policy ahead of DOGE's own wind-down -- i.e., making the reduction mechanism durable past DOGE itself, not merely a one-time purge.

estimated_impact.summary: Fired federal workers reported serious psychological harm both within weeks of the firings and about a year later: in March 2025, 20 fired federal workers interviewed by NBC News described panic attacks, sleepless nights, and suicidal ideation, with some visiting emergency rooms after breakdowns. The survey of fired workers (fielded February-March 2026, published in late May 2026) describes lasting harm well beyond the initial job loss -- more than 50% of respondents reported trauma-related symptoms, one respondent wrote of still having nightmares about the firings, and another wrote that the experience 'will reverberate through my life for years.' The survey's employment data also showed economic harm: 21% of respondents remained unemployed as of Jan. 31, 2026, per Nonprofit Quarterly (Federal News Network reported about 17% a year later), and Federal News Network put the share of respondents in new jobs with lower or significantly lower pay at 68%.

estimated_impact.caveat: This is a self-selected survey of fired workers, conducted by former fired federal employees and published by 27 UNIHTED, not an independent, randomly sampled clinical study -- the 95%/trauma-symptom figures likely reflect a population motivated to respond because they experienced significant harm, and should be read as documenting the existence and severity of harm within an affected, engaged subset rather than as a precise government-wide psychological-impact rate. The underlying legal question (whether OPM lawfully directed the mass firing) was decided against OPM by a federal district court; the survey's own employment and reinstatement data (21% unemployed as of Jan. 31, 2026 per Nonprofit Quarterly, about 17% per Federal News Network; 49% of the employed earning significantly less; majority of reinstated respondents reporting poor communication) is the closest available evidence on the remedy question, though it still reflects the same self-selected respondent pool rather than an independent audit of all ~25,000 fired workers or of OPM/agency reinstatement records. The March 2025 NBC News interviews independently corroborate that the harm was present and reported within weeks of the firings, not a delayed or survey-artifact effect, though they are individual accounts, not a measured rate. Separately, OPM canceled the 2025 Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey in August 2025 (a cancellation the Washington Post characterized as removing one of the few institutional tools for measuring civil-service morale) and, per a single outlet reporting in July 2026, proposed reducing the survey's questions and giving agencies more control over disclosing results.

OPM (N.D. title: About 317,000-348,000 Federal Employees Left Government in 2025, a 10% Net Workforce Cut -- Mostly Through Resignations, Buyouts, and Retirements, Not Mass Firings
institution: Office of Personnel Management (government-wide, all civilian agencies)
status: 2025 exits largely complete: OPM data show 348,219 separations and a 10.3% net workforce loss (237,652) in 2025 (Pew, Mar. 2026). GAO (Sept. 15, 2026) put 2025 paid-leave salary costs at $9.5B, $6.7B of it for deferred resignations; OPM agreed to track such leave separately.
date_of_action: 2025-01-28 (OPM's 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation memo) through 2026-09-15 (GAO's paid-administrative-leave cost report)
what_changed:
On January 28, 2025, OPM sent all federal civil-service employees a memo titled 'Fork in the Road,' offering deferred resignation (continued pay and benefits through September 30, 2025 in exchange for leaving) to anyone unwilling to work under the new administration's terms -- the opening move in a year-long, government-wide workforce reduction carried out mainly through voluntary programs (deferred resignation, buyouts, early retirement) rather than the individual reduction-in-force actions this tracker's per-agency entries separately document. By late July 2025, more than 154,000 federal employees -- just over 6% of the civilian workforce -- were being paid under the deferred resignation program despite not working, a figure first reported by the Washington Post and confirmed to ABC News by an administration official. A July report by Senate Democrats projected the program would cost $14.8 billion, assuming about 200,000 participants on full pay for up to eight months; Senate Democrats separately estimated that mistakes and waste across the whole Department of Government Efficiency initiative had cost $21.7 billion, a figure ABC noted might include estimates disputed by the administration. In an August memo, OPM Director Scott Kupor wrote that OPM 'designed the DRP as a practical, humane, and voluntary option to accelerate workforce transitions' and that 'the government will save $20+ billion in costs, annually.' On September 30, 2025, roughly 100,000 deferred-resignation participants were set to formally leave government as their paid-leave period ended, out of a federal workforce Newsweek put at 2.4 million (citing BLS); Newsweek also relayed a New York Times estimate that about 135,000 federal workers had been fired. Next Interior, a group Newsweek described as affiliated with the Interior Department, wrote on LinkedIn that the mass resignation 'represents a massive loss in institutional knowledge and capacity across the federal government,' and Newsweek noted the departures could disrupt services at agencies including the VA and the Social Security Administration. In mid-October 2025, the Washington Post reported that about 154,000 buyout takers had been largely removed from the payroll by the end of September and that nearly 105,000 employees had taken regular retirement in the fiscal year that ended in September, an 18% jump from the year before; the Post noted that some of the buyout takers were among those retirees. OPM's backlog of pending retirement claims, over 24,000 in August, reached 34,587 at the end of October, the highest since March 2022, with average processing time up to 79 days; OPM's retirement processing, which Kupor said is funded outside congressional appropriations, kept running through the concurrent government shutdown but could not keep pace with incoming claims. In November 2025, Kupor wrote in an OPM blog post that approximately 317,000 federal employees had left government that year while 68,000 had joined, surpassing his earlier target of 300,000 departures. On December 30, 2025, the New York Times, citing government data, reported that the civilian federal workforce had shrunk by about 10% that year, leaving about 249,000 fewer people on the government payroll than at the start of the year, as many workers resigned or took early retirement and others were laid off. On January 10, 2026, the Washington Post's own agency-by-agency analysis, using newly available federal workforce data, found roughly 335,000 employees had left between January and November 2025 -- more than OPM's November count -- and that the vast majority had quit or retired rather than being purged. Among the losses the Post highlighted: **more than a third of the Agriculture Department's food inspectors and more than a quarter of the Social Security Administration's IT management staff left**, and the Treasury Department was down about 4,000 tax examiners, or about 26%. In March 2026, a Pew Research Center analysis of OPM data found the federal civilian workforce shrank 10.3% in 2025, from 2,312,301 in December 2024 to 2,074,649 in December 2025, a net loss of 237,652: 348,219 people left federal employment, up 80.8% from 2024, while new hires fell 55.6% to 116,912. Among major agencies, the steepest cuts were at USAID (down 92.4%) and the Education Department (down 42.6%); Treasury fell 23.2%, Agriculture 20.9%, and HHS 19.2%, while Immigration and Customs Enforcement added about 7,500 workers, a 36.1% increase.

On September 15, 2026, GAO reported that the 76 agencies in its review (about 95% of the civilian workforce) spent an estimated $9.5 billion in salary costs on paid administrative leave in calendar year 2025, a sixfold increase from 2023, as leave usage rose 435% to about 21.6 million workdays. GAO attributed about 70% of 2025's paid administrative leave, and more than $6.7 billion of its cost, to the deferred resignation program, which it estimated about 144,312 employees used; because OPM's payroll systems did not track such leave separately, GAO said there was no way to accurately determine whether the government-wide savings goal was being met, and OPM agreed to create a dedicated leave category. Kupor disputed the framing, saying the report failed to highlight the difference between "a one-time expense ($9.5 billion) to reduce the size of the federal government by 270,000 employees and the $40 billion per year savings in taxpayer dollars that this reduction provides."

primary_proponent.note: OPM authored and issued the original January 28, 2025 'Fork in the Road' memo that structured the deferred-resignation program underlying a large share of this entry's cumulative departure figures; OPM also self-reported the November 2025 317,000-departure milestone as exceeding its own 2025 target.

estimated_impact.summary: In 2025 roughly 317,000-348,000 federal civilian employees left government while hiring fell by more than half, a net loss of about 238,000 workers (10.3% of the workforce) -- mostly through the deferred resignation program, buyouts, and retirements rather than mass firings, although the New York Times estimated some 135,000 workers were fired. The losses reached front-line capacity that protects the public: more than a third of USDA's food inspectors and over a quarter of SSA's IT management staff left, USAID lost 92% of its workforce and the Education Department 43%, and OPM's retirement-claims backlog hit 34,587, its highest since 2022, stretching average processing to 79 days for departing workers awaiting annuities. Taxpayers also paid an estimated $9.5 billion in 2025 in salaries for employees on paid administrative leave, more than $6.7 billion of it for deferred-resignation participants who were not working; OPM calls this a one-time cost against claimed annual savings of $20-40 billion that GAO says cannot yet be verified.

estimated_impact.caveat: The departure totals come from different producers, methods, and cutoff dates and are not additive: Pew's 348,219 (full-year OPM data) and OPM's ~317,000 (through November) are gross separations, Pew's 237,652 is a net reduction after hiring, the Washington Post's ~335,000 covers January-November, and the New York Times' ~249,000 (Dec. 30, 2025) is a net payroll decline since the start of the year. The 'mostly voluntary' characterization is the Post's; many exits were induced by the threat of layoffs, and the NYT separately estimated ~135,000 firings. GAO's $9.5 billion covers salary costs only, in 76 agencies (Education, NASA, and several others did not provide data), and GAO flagged data-reliability problems. The earlier Senate Democratic projections ($14.8 billion for the program; $21.7 billion for DOGE-wide waste) are superseded by or broader than GAO's figure. The figures do not measure downstream service effects, such as missed food inspections or benefit delays, beyond those noted.

pull_quote: “A massive loss in institutional knowledge and capacity across the federal government,” Next Interior, a group affiliated with the Interior Department, wrote of the September 30, 2025 mass resignation.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the GAO figures (GAO-26-108477, read directly), OPM's own counts (Kupor's November 2025 blog post via Federal News Network; OPM data via Pew Research Center), and the Washington Post, ABC News, and Newsweek figures as reported. The ~200,000-participant and $14.8 billion figures are a July 2025 Senate Democratic projection, and the ~135,000 firings figure is a New York Times estimate relayed by Newsweek, not official data. The New York Times' ~249,000 figure is a net payroll decline it drew from government data. MODERATE confidence in reconciling the totals against each other: they use different date ranges, gross versus net counts, and methodologies, so this entry presents them side by side rather than resolving them into one number. OPM's $20-40 billion annual-savings figures are administration claims GAO said cannot currently be verified.

section_summaries.what_changed: OPM's Jan. 2025 'Fork in the Road' offer set off a mostly voluntary exodus: about 348,000 federal workers left in 2025 and the workforce shrank 10.3%; GAO put 2025 paid-leave costs at $9.5B.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: About 317,000-348,000 federal workers left in 2025 (net loss ~238,000), including a third of USDA's food inspectors; paid leave cost $9.5B, $6.7B of it for buyout takers not working.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Figures trace to GAO, OPM data (via Pew and Kupor), and WaPo/NYT/Newsweek reporting; the totals use different methods and dates and are not reconcilable into one number.

title: FedRAMP Approved Microsoft's Government Cloud Despite Reviewers Saying They Couldn't Assess Its Security and Calling the Package 'a Pile of Shit,' Citing How Embedded It Already Was Across Government
institution: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP), General Services Administration
status: Authorized Dec. 26, 2024; as of Sept. 28, 2026 the FedRAMP Marketplace still lists GCC High as FedRAMP Certified (High) with 5 agency authorizations. No reversal or re-review found since ProPublica's March 2026 report, which said DOGE cuts had left about two dozen FedRAMP staff.
date_of_action: FedRAMP's review began in April 2020; the first review team ended the engagement in October 2023, and a new team restarted it in summer 2024. GCC High was authorized December 26, 2024. ProPublica's investigation was published March 18, 2026, nearly 15 months after the authorization, not concurrent with it.
what_changed: A ProPublica investigation published March 18, 2026 found that federal cybersecurity reviewers could not verify the security of Microsoft's Government Community Cloud High (GCC High) -- a suite of cloud services that key parts of the government, including the Justice and Energy departments, and the defense sector use to protect highly sensitive information -- yet the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) authorized it anyway. The Justice Department had authorized GCC High through FedRAMP's 'agency path' by early 2020 and soon deployed it, and the package reached FedRAMP for review that April. FedRAMP asked Microsoft for data flow diagrams showing where data is encrypted in transit -- detail that, members of the FedRAMP team said, Amazon and Google routinely provided -- but Microsoft supplied what reviewers considered only partial information, and one former reviewer said they never got past Exchange Online. In an October 2023 email, FedRAMP interim director Brian Conrad wrote that after three years, 480 hours of review time and 18 'technical deep dive' sessions, FedRAMP still lacked visibility into the security gaps; he ended the engagement and told Microsoft it would need to start over. Microsoft and Justice Department officials pushed back, and because agencies were allowed to deploy GCC High during the review, it had spread across the government and to defense contractors. In summer 2024, new FedRAMP director Pete Waterman restarted the review with a new team; working through only Exchange Online and Teams, it found 'issues that are fundamental' to risk management and concluded, 'There is a lack of confidence in assessing the system's overall security posture.' As one member of the team put it: 'The package is a pile of shit.' The team's summary said 'not issuing an authorization would impact multiple agencies that are already using GCC-H' and judged it a 'better value' to issue an authorization with conditions for continued government oversight. **Despite these unresolved concerns, FedRAMP authorized GCC High on December 26, 2024,** appending a cover report that laid out the package's deficiencies and noted it carried unknown risks, according to people familiar with the report. ProPublica documented a remarkable deference to Microsoft in FedRAMP memos, logs, emails and meeting minutes, even though Microsoft products had been central to two major cyberattacks on the government: the Russian intrusion discovered in late 2020 and the 2023 Chinese hack of senior officials' email. The investigation's reporter later wrote that FedRAMP authorized the product 'in part because it lacked the resources to keep going.' After the authorization, the Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) slashed FedRAMP's staff and budget: roughly two dozen employees remain, 'entirely focused on' delivering authorizations at a record pace, according to FedRAMP's director, on an annual budget of $10 million, its lowest in a decade -- leaving few people to check whether Microsoft meets the authorization's oversight conditions. Microsoft says it provided 'comprehensive documentation,' has met the conditions of the agreement and stands by its products; GSA told ProPublica that FedRAMP's role is 'not to determine if a cloud service is secure enough' but 'to ensure agencies have sufficient information to make these risk decisions.'

primary_proponent.name: FedRAMP / General Services Administration
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency responsible for authorizing cloud products for government use
primary_proponent.note: Sourcing reviewed did not identify the individual FedRAMP or GSA official who signed the final authorization; the restarted review ran under FedRAMP director Pete Waterman, hired in summer 2024. ProPublica attributes the outcome to institutional dynamics (GCC High's spread across agencies, pressure from Microsoft and Justice Department officials, and FedRAMP's limited resources at the time) rather than one identified decision-maker.

estimated_impact.summary: Highly sensitive federal data -- at the Justice and Energy departments, among others, and across the defense sector -- sits on a Microsoft cloud suite that the government's own reviewers, after the better part of five years, said they could not verify was secure; the government has said a leak of such data 'could be expected to have a severe or catastrophic adverse effect' on operations, assets and individuals. FedRAMP's approval, which helped Microsoft expand a federal business worth billions of dollars, shifted the unresolved risk onto agencies that often lack the staff to vet it themselves, and DOGE's later cuts left roughly two dozen FedRAMP employees, on a $10 million budget, to oversee the authorization's conditions. No breach or health harm tied to the unverified gaps has been documented.

No breach, exploited vulnerability, dollar loss or health harm has been tied to the unverified gaps, so this is a documented oversight failure and unverified risk, not a confirmed attack. The staffing and budget figures describe FedRAMP after the DOGE cuts, not at the time of the December 2024 authorization.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the review findings, the quotes, the 480-hour/18-session figures, the review summary's 'better value' language and the December 26, 2024 authorization date: all were read directly in ProPublica's March 18, 2026 investigation, which draws on internal FedRAMP memos, logs, emails, meeting minutes and interviews with seven current and former government employees and contractors; the authorization date and GCC High's continuing certified status are confirmed on the FedRAMP Marketplace. Boing Boing's post and Schneier's blog comment on the same investigation; Techdirt's piece is a licensed republication of it, so none is independent corroboration. The cover report is described by people familiar with it, not quoted from the document. MODERATE confidence on the role of resources in the decision: that is the reporter's own later assessment ('in part because it lacked the resources to keep going'), not an on-record FedRAMP admission. The DOGE staffing and budget cuts came after the December 2024 authorization and bear on current oversight, not on the decision itself.

title: FEMA Cancelled $3.6B in Disaster-Resilience Grants, Then Was Ordered by a Federal Court to Restore Them a Year Later
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Reversed by court order and subsequent agency action -- FEMA reinstated the program in March 2026 with $1B in new funding, after a federal judge's December 2025 order
date_of_action: 2025-04 (program termination) through 2026-03 (reinstatement)
what_changed: In April 2025, the Trump administration ended FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program, which funded predisaster projects -- floodwalls, elevated infrastructure, fire-resistant building retrofits, and similar hardening work -- for hundreds of communities nationwide. The termination halted $3.6 billion in funding that had already been awarded to specific, in-progress projects but not yet paid out, and separately refused to award another $882 million in grants that had been planned for the following fiscal year. Twenty states, led by New York Attorney General Letitia James among others, sued the administration, arguing FEMA lacked legal authority to cancel a program funded and directed by Congress, that the cancellation undermined already-underway projects, and **that it left disaster-prone communities more vulnerable to floods, fires, and storms.** In December 2025, a federal judge in Massachusetts sided with the 22 states and D.C. that had joined the suit by that point, ordering FEMA to restore the canceled funding. In March 2026, FEMA announced it would reinstate the program -- rebranded as the 'Building Resilient Communities and Infrastructure' program -- making $1 billion available for states, local governments, territories, and tribes to pursue hardening projects against wildfires, floods, earthquakes, and hurricanes, though at less than a third of the originally canceled $3.6 billion figure.

primary_proponent.name: FEMA leadership (Trump administration)
primary_proponent.role: Directed the April 2025 program termination as part of broader disaster-mitigation funding cuts
primary_proponent.note: This action predates and is distinct from FEMA's separately documented staffing collapse ([[fema-capacity-collapse-texas-floods-trump2]]) and partisan-approval-gap pattern ([[fema-disaster-aid-partisan-approval-gap-trump2]]) already in this tracker -- BRIC's cancellation is a specific funding-program termination, not a staffing or approval-timing issue, though all three reflect the same broader disaster-response degradation under this administration.

estimated_impact.summary: The cancellation directly threatened hundreds of already-planned, partially-underway community resilience projects nationwide for nearly a year, until a federal court intervened; the eventual reinstatement restored the program in principle but at less than a third of the originally terminated funding level.

title: FEMA Capacity Collapse — Staff Exodus and Spending Bottleneck Delayed Texas Flood Response
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing institutional instability. Cameron Hamilton's August 2026 Senate confirmation resolved the top-leadership turnover but not the staffing decline or senior-leadership vacancies, and a GAO audit found FEMA's outside surge workforce for the 2026 hurricane season down roughly 60% (about 240 vs. 600 in 2025), with no updated workforce plan in place. A federal judge ruled September 11, 2026 that DHS's order to cut FEMA's workforce roughly in half was unlawful; remedies remain pending, with briefing due October 9, 2026.
date_of_action: Staff departures throughout 2025; acute failure documented July 4-10, 2025 during Texas floods
what_changed:
Kerr County's own flood-warning infrastructure had been left unfunded for nearly a decade before the July 2025 disaster, compounding the federal capacity failures documented below rather than existing independently of them, since the county's earliest funding requests targeted federal money the state administered. Kerr County first requested roughly $1 million in federal Hazard Mitigation Grant Program funding for a flood warning system in 2017; Texas's state emergency-management department denied it, and a second attempt following 2017's Hurricane Harvey was also denied, with the state directing available federal hazard-mitigation money toward more densely populated areas like Houston instead.

Separately, at the state legislative level, a bill that would have created a $500 million grant program to help rural counties fund emergency alert systems -- spurred by prior wildfires -- failed in the Texas Senate earlier in 2025, months before the flood; Republican state Rep. Wes Virdell, who voted against it, said afterward 'in hindsight, watching what it takes to deal with a disaster like this, my vote would probably be different now,' while maintaining his specific objection had been the bill's lack of transparency rather than opposition to funding warning systems themselves. Texas lawmakers separately passed on other flood-specific protections (siren systems, drainage upgrades, rural support) earlier in 2025, prioritizing tax cuts and drought measures instead.

At the federal level, the elimination rhetoric traces back to January 2025, when Trump said FEMA "should go away" -- even before the hiring-policy overhaul that followed. Starting March 24, 2025, Trump implemented sweeping changes to FEMA's hiring policies, forcing thousands of employees to reapply for their jobs through the Department of Homeland Security; more than 200 probationary workers were let go in the same period. Two days later, on March 26, 2025, Noem told reporters discussing border security that "we're going to eliminate FEMA" -- an offhand remark made without further detail, four months before her more formal July 9, 2025 call (see below) to eliminate the agency 'as it exists today,' showing the elimination framing was already administration rhetoric from the earliest days of the hiring-policy overhaul rather than a position that emerged only after the Texas floods. By May 6, 2025, Noem told lawmakers directly that Trump wanted to abolish FEMA outright and replace it with block grants sent directly to states, a cost-and-control-shifting mechanism that recurred later in the November 2025 FEMA Review Council dispute (see below), where Noem's own counter-proposal likewise sought to shift half of recovery costs onto states. Wired reported that same day, May 6, 2025, that FEMA would stop sending workers door-to-door in disaster zones to help survivors register for aid, shifting instead to fixed assistance centers and coordination with local officials; the change aligned with the broader elimination push already underway at that point.

Internal FEMA memos reviewed by Reuters showed that since February 5, 2025, FEMA staff had been barred from travel unrelated to disaster deployment, and since early March 2025 had been required to get speaking engagements and presentation materials approved by the Office of External Affairs and Office of Chief Counsel; few such requests were approved, forcing the National Hurricane Program to cancel or move online training sessions for emergency managers in storm-prone areas. Organizers of the April 2025 National Hurricane Conference in New Orleans canceled several FEMA-led sessions -- including one aimed at helping emergency managers make evacuation decisions during hurricanes -- after FEMA staff dropped out due to the travel restrictions. Lynn Budd, president of the National Emergency Management Association, said states needed more time and resources to compensate, noting FEMA provides local/state jurisdictions expertise 'that the states simply don't have at this time.'

Youth outreach was cut too -- FEMA emailed the 15 students on its 13-year-old Youth Preparedness Council on January 16, 2025 that their culminating Washington summit that summer was canceled, then, after months of silence, emailed them again on August 1, 2025 that the program itself would be terminated early; FEMA told the students the move was meant 'to ensure FEMA is a lean, deployable disaster force that is ready to support states as they take the lead in preparedness and disaster response.'

The abolish-FEMA rhetoric had a concrete early test case: on April 25, 2025, Trump denied federal disaster relief to Arkansas following March tornadoes and storms that killed over 40 people across Arkansas, Mississippi, and Missouri, rejecting the request despite it coming from Republican Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Arkansas's own congressional delegation. Two more denials followed the same pattern. On May 23, 2025, FEMA Acting Administrator David Richardson denied North Carolina Governor Josh Stein's request to extend the 100% federal cost-share (a Biden-era commitment) for Hurricane Helene debris removal and emergency protective measures, reverting the state to the standard 90% share -- a 10-percentage-point cut on a Category 4 storm that had killed over 230 people; Stein was granted 30 days to appeal. Then, after a stalled monsoon system caused flash flooding in Gila and Mohave Counties, Arizona (including the town of Globe) on September 25-27, 2025 with preliminary damage estimated around $33 million, FEMA denied Arizona's major-disaster-declaration request, finding the damage 'not of such severity and magnitude as to be beyond the capabilities of the state and affected local governments'; Governor Katie Hobbs, who had declared a state of emergency, appealed on January 16, 2026, and FEMA denied that appeal too, on July 2, 2026, reaffirming the same finding.

The denial pattern was not partisan -- Reuters reported June 17, 2025 that Trump had declined hazard-mitigation funding requests from six disaster-hit states, all with Republican governors, including Iowa's Kim Reynolds, Mississippi's Tate Reeves, Missouri's Mike Kehoe, and Oklahoma's Kevin Stitt, following March 2025 disasters in their states; Trump had signed major disaster declarations greenlighting some other funding for these states, but their specific hazard-mitigation requests remained undecided, and Reuters found the administration had not approved a single hazard-mitigation request in over a year at that point. The same reporting profiled Lake Lure, North Carolina, still working to rebuild its dam and tourism economy after Hurricane Helene, where the uncertainty created by Trump's FEMA-shrinking plans -- on top of the cost-share reduction to Helene recovery -- left the town's rebuilding timeline in limbo; one local business owner asked, 'There's got to be some federal help, right?'

Throughout 2025, FEMA underwent a wave of staff departures -- about 18% of the agency's permanent full-time employees had left as of June 2025, including 24 senior-level staffers, per GAO. In May 2025 alone, 16 senior officials departed, taking with them a combined 200+ years of disaster-response expertise. On May 24, 2025, Acting Administrator David Richardson abruptly rescinded FEMA's 2022-2026 strategic plan, calling it disconnected from the agency's core mission, and ended the Office of Resilience Strategy. In early June 2025, Reuters reported that Richardson told staff during a briefing he had not known the U.S. has a hurricane season (which runs June 1-Nov 30); DHS later said the remark was a joke, though some employees called it poorly timed given already-low morale amid the ongoing purges.

Trump gave the FEMA-shrinking push a specific timeline and mechanism at a June 10, 2025 Oval Office briefing, saying 'we want to wean off of FEMA, and we want to bring it down to the state level' and that the administration would begin phasing the agency out after the 2025 hurricane season, with disaster-aid funding distributed directly from the president's own office rather than through FEMA. Noem said at the same briefing that the administration would form a council 'over the next couple of months' to plan the agency's future -- the origin of the FEMA Review Council fight documented later in this entry. Jeremy Greenberg, head of FEMA's National Response Coordination Center, resigned in mid-June 2025, just weeks into hurricane season, joining a wave of senior departures as Trump pushed states to 'wean' off federal disaster aid. A ProPublica investigation published June 30, 2025 found Trump had stalled billions in FEMA grant funding, missed legal disbursement deadlines, and begun dismantling core preparedness programs. DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's new requirement that she personally sign off on any FEMA expenditure over $100,000 -- for an agency whose disaster costs routinely run into the billions, officials described this threshold as effectively 'pennies' -- was already slowing operations agency-wide at that point, even as states rely on FEMA for up to 99% of their emergency budgets in some cases.

This bottleneck had direct, documented consequences during the deadly July 4, 2025 Texas Hill Country floods: **FEMA's disaster survivor call-center contract funding lapsed on July 5, and it took Noem five days -- until July 10 -- to approve renewed funding, during which most survivor calls went unanswered** (an internal memo documented the call-answer rate collapsing from 99.9% to 20%, with survivors waiting over 90 minutes). NPR reported in August 2025 that this documented 10-20% call-answer rate directly contradicted Acting Administrator Richardson's own claim to Congress that most survivor calls had been handled during the crisis. Noem also did not authorize deployment of FEMA's Urban Search and Rescue teams until more than 72 hours after the flooding began; Ken Pagurek, head of FEMA's Urban Search and Rescue branch, resigned on July 23, 2025, citing the delayed deployment caused by Noem's $100,000 sign-off requirement as a direct factor in his decision.

Acting FEMA Administrator David Richardson did not travel to Texas for a full week after the disaster, telling a House committee he had stayed in Washington to 'kick down the doors of bureaucracy' -- and separately acknowledged he had been camping with his sons over the July 4 weekend when the floods hit. Politico reported July 10, 2025 that Richardson had made no public appearances or statements at all since the flooding began, even as Noem personally toured the disaster zone and spoke to the press -- a total public-visibility gap, distinct from his week-long physical absence from Texas, that former FEMA officials told Politico broke with the agency's own precedent for how its administrator engages during a major disaster response. The Washington Post separately reported in September 2025 that FEMA staff could not reach Richardson for nearly 24 hours during the acute phase of the disaster, a communications gap that further delayed critical rescue-deployment decisions on top of the sign-off bottleneck itself. Even as FEMA was actively responding to the ongoing Texas disaster, Noem publicly said on July 9, 2025 that FEMA should be 'eliminated as it exists today,' criticizing the agency's response times and bureaucracy and calling instead for a state-led disaster system -- remarks made during a federal disaster-system reform meeting held while FEMA personnel were still deployed to the flood response. Separately, by July 4, 2025, FEMA officials said they were being blocked from communicating directly with Congress and local agencies, with internal memos requiring all inquiries to go through political appointees as Noem tightened control over the agency's external communications.

In July 2025, as California sought $40 billion in wildfire recovery aid, Trump's feud with Governor Newsom became entangled with proposals to raise disaster-aid eligibility thresholds and cut preparedness grants; separately, internal memos reported by CNN on July 28, 2025 revealed plans to cut nearly $1 billion from FEMA's disaster-preparedness and security grants, including the $500 million Urban Areas Security Initiative, with FEMA officials themselves acknowledging the cuts would leave cities more vulnerable.

The following month, Reuters reported that Trump officials began reassigning FEMA personnel to help ICE hire 10,000 new agents, warning staff they could be terminated if they refused the reassignment -- a redirection of disaster-response staff toward immigration enforcement that came at the height of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season. The Guardian reported August 22, 2025 that FEMA had begun requiring an email address to apply for federal disaster aid, with FEMA framing it as streamlining communication while critics warned it would exclude elderly, disabled, rural, and low-income survivors without reliable internet access -- a barrier compounding the loss of door-to-door outreach three months earlier and the closure of field offices. On the 20th anniversary of Hurricane Katrina, August 31, 2025, 180 FEMA employees wrote to Congress warning that the administration's cuts and inexperienced leadership could cripple the agency in a future crisis; days later, more than 190 employees signed a related letter after Noem ordered FEMA staff to publicly praise Trump's leadership even as the agency reeled from mass resignations, contract delays, and the Texas flood response failures.

On September 2, 2025, Noem announced an IT security breach at FEMA and purged 23 employees, blaming FEMA's IT team for "failure" and "incompetence," while saying no sensitive citizen data had been stolen. Around the same time, a GAO report found that 2,500 FEMA employees -- including 24 senior leaders -- had quit since January 2025, a harder figure than the informal 18% departure estimate cited above, leaving the agency understaffed heading into peak hurricane and wildfire season. An Associated Press analysis of decades of federal disaster-declaration data, published September 9, 2025, quantified the delay pattern this entry documents in individual episodes as a systemic trend: major disaster declarations took under two weeks on average in the 1990s and early 2000s, rose to about three weeks over the past decade under presidents of both parties, and reached nearly 34 days on average during Trump's current term as of the analysis -- up from a 24-day average during his first term and nearly four times George H.W. Bush's average.

The same capacity failures produced a months-long recovery stall in St. Louis, Missouri after a mile-wide EF3 tornado struck the city May 16, 2025, killing 4 people and damaging or destroying more than 10,000 properties; a major disaster declaration followed in June 2025. FEMA rejected St. Louis's request to have the Army Corps of Engineers handle private-property debris removal on September 17, 2025, and later that month permanently closed its disaster recovery centers throughout the city and declined Mayor Cara Spencer's request for a 30-day extension of the aid-application deadline, over four months after the tornado. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) sent FEMA Acting Administrator David Richardson a formal letter demanding answers on the delays, and Ward 10 Alderwoman Shameem Clark Hubbard separately raised concerns about inadequate door-to-door outreach to residents still trying to apply for aid -- the same door-to-door-outreach cutback FEMA made agency-wide in May 2025. FEMA had also not provided disaster case management funding for the tornado, forcing the city to spend more than $3 million of its own Rams Settlement Fund to sustain case management instead. WSJ reporting on the stalled recovery also described FEMA resources being diverted to help ICE hire agents -- the same redirection documented above -- as a contributing factor, with residents forced to organize their own debris-clearing and relief efforts as schools remained shuttered.

That October, FEMA froze $300-320 million in preparedness grants (reported with slightly different figures by CNN on Oct. 2 and ABC News on Oct. 21, likely the same freeze), requiring states to recertify population counts excluding deported migrants before releasing funds -- a requirement that followed a court ruling blocking the administration from redirecting FEMA money away from Democratic-led states. On October 20, 2025 -- over three months after the July 4 Texas floods -- the Texas Tribune reported FEMA had denied or delayed the majority of Kerr County residents' aid requests, approving only 22% of applications, with many rejected over technicalities like missed calls or incomplete paperwork, forcing nonprofits to fill the gap. The following day, FEMA employees and former staffers protested outside agency headquarters, accusing Noem of slashing programs, forcing FEMA to cooperate with ICE, and delaying aid as staffing and funding collapsed. The loss of door-to-door outreach and the new email requirement documented above both predate, and offer a mechanism for, the Kerr County 22% approval rate: fewer outreach channels and an added digital-access requirement for exactly the population -- flood survivors in a rural area -- most likely to be excluded by them.

On November 10, 2025, NPR reported FEMA had pulled $14 million in promised funding for a tsunami-proofing project at Columbia Memorial Hospital on the Washington coast after officials abruptly canceled the BRIC disaster-mitigation program mid-construction, leaving the hospital without resources to survive a Cascadia earthquake and tsunami; a similar case surfaced in Oregon by December 31, 2025 (CBS News), where a coastal hospital scrambled to build a tsunami shelter after the same BRIC cancellation hit its project mid-stream, even as courts had separately ruled the BRIC cuts unlawful. In a separate, longer-running flood-mitigation-grant dispute in Washington state, apart from the BRIC-program tsunami-shelter cancellations at Columbia Memorial Hospital, the administration attempted to cancel roughly $182 million in FEMA hazard-mitigation funding for the state, prompting Attorney General Nick Brown and other states to secure a court order requiring FEMA to take concrete steps toward reversing the cancellation, while a separate $31 million in disaster-prevention grants sat awaiting Secretary Noem's personal approval for months. The stalled funding covered projects to elevate flood-prone homes, relocate residents, and build levees and floodwalls, including specific levee/floodwall construction in Aberdeen and Hoquiam; the dispute intensified after a December 2025 storm forced evacuation orders for more than 100,000 Washington residents and damaged nearly 4,000 homes, after which the administration went on to deny the state's request for future flood-preparedness funding entirely.

Richardson resigned in November 2025 after six months in the role, the second of three different acting administrators to lead FEMA within the year. On November 29, 2025, AP reported new detail on the FEMA Review Council fight: the Trump-appointed council's own draft had concluded FEMA should be elevated and given more independence, but Noem intervened with a competing draft that would keep FEMA under DHS, slash its disaster role, and force states to cover half of recovery costs -- cutting the council's own 160-page proposal down to under 20 pages in the process, a more specific and more adversarial picture than the council's workforce-cut recommendation (below) alone conveys.

In January 2026, FEMA abruptly stopped renewing contracts for its Cadre of On-Call Response/Recovery (CORE) employees -- term-limited hires who can hold senior disaster-response roles -- then paused the cuts in late January as a major winter storm affecting roughly half the country's population approached; FEMA managers confirmed in early February 2026 that the CORE staff reductions would resume once the storm passed, though no specific restart date was given. FEMA supervisors had told staff in mid-January 2026 to prepare for roughly 1,000 disaster-worker dismissals that month, and a coalition of federal employee unions (led by AFGE), nonprofits, and local governments sued FEMA in late January/early February 2026 to block the workforce cuts, arguing they violated the law and would leave the agency unable to meet its statutory disaster-response obligations; U.S. District Judge Susan Illston indicated in February 2026 she would likely deny a preliminary injunction after FEMA offered to rehire some of the affected on-call responders. Around the same period, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, who has overseen FEMA's cuts, received a draft report from the Trump-appointed FEMA Review Council recommending the agency's workforce be cut in half.

During the February 2026 DHS funding lapse, DHS halted nearly all employee travel department-wide, including FEMA disaster-response deployments, according to internal emails The Washington Post obtained -- disrupting FEMA's ability to send personnel to respond to active or anticipated disasters during the lapse; a separate internal FEMA email obtained by The Washington Post warned that national continuity operations were 'significantly constrained' during the same shutdown, limiting the agency's ability to maintain critical continuity-of-government functions. A second documented instance of the same DHS approval bottleneck emerged around the same time: CNN reported FEMA failed to renew a $200,000 contract for a tornado-tracking mapping tool used by rescue teams to identify storm damage paths. The contract expired in February 2026 and remained stuck in the DHS approval process even as deadly tornadoes struck the Midwest and Plains, forcing rescue teams to rely on news reports and manual searches to locate the hardest-hit areas instead of the mapping tool.

By March 2026, FEMA's overall staffing had fallen further, from roughly 26,000 employees in January 2025 to about 21,100 -- an approximately 19% decline -- with 18 of the agency's 38 senior leadership positions vacant, including deputy administrator and chief of staff. A CNN KFile investigation published March 20, 2026 found Gregg Phillips -- installed to lead FEMA's Office of Response and Recovery, a key role directing federal disaster-response operations, despite limited emergency-management experience -- has a documented history of promoting conspiracy theories and using violent rhetoric, including saying in January 2025 he would 'like to punch' then-outgoing President Biden 'in the mouth,' and repeatedly claiming on podcasts to have been involuntarily 'teleported,' including once to a Georgia Waffle House 50 miles away. Rep. Tim Kennedy cited Phillips's 'violent statements' and 'deeply troubling bigoted comments about immigrants' as evidence he was 'wildly unfit for his role'; Phillips defended the teleportation claims in a follow-up CNN report the following month, saying 'haters gonna hate.'

Robert Fenton (FEMA's Region 9 administrator) took over as senior official performing the duties of administrator; Trump nominated Cameron Hamilton as permanent administrator. Facing the 2026 hurricane season, FEMA began a limited hiring campaign: it rehired 14 staff Secretary Noem had fired for signing the 'Katrina Declaration' -- the tail end of a longer twice-suspended, twice-reinstated saga -- and DHS approved roughly 300 near-term new hires with hopes of filling up to 700 vacancies. Fenton told reporters FEMA has about 30-40% of its disaster workforce available at any given time, which he characterized as normal availability rather than a crisis-level shortfall; NOAA's 2026 Atlantic hurricane season outlook predicts a below-normal season (8-14 named storms, 3-6 hurricanes).

Hamilton previously served as acting FEMA administrator from January-May 2025 before being fired for telling Congress he did not believe eliminating FEMA was in the public interest; Reuters reported the firing came one day after that testimony, and that DHS officials had attempted to revoke Hamilton's building access hours before he testified but backed off to avoid public fallout; the ouster followed reported clashes between Hamilton and Trump adviser Corey Lewandowski. At his June 17, 2026 confirmation hearing, Hamilton pledged to be 'fair and reasonable' in assessing disaster-aid requests. His nomination advanced out of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on an 8-4 vote in late July 2026, roughly a month after his confirmation hearing, and the Senate confirmed him as permanent FEMA Administrator on August 7, 2026, by a 51-47 vote as part of an en bloc package confirming more than 70 Trump nominees together -- FEMA's first Senate-confirmed administrator under this administration. His confirmation resolves the top-leadership instability going forward, though it does not reverse the staffing decline (~26,000 to ~21,100 employees, Jan. 2025-March 2026) or the vacancy rate among senior leadership positions.

In a May 14, 2026 letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and FEMA senior official Robert Fenton, House Homeland Security Committee ranking member Bennie Thompson and Rep. Timothy Kennedy wrote that the administration 'has overseen the departure of over 5,000 FEMA employees since January 2025' and that 'On June 1, 2025, FEMA had only 12 percent of its incident management workforce available to respond to disasters'; Government Executive, which reported the letter, said FEMA did not respond to a request for comment.

A Government Accountability Office report (GAO-26-108427, 'FEMA Workforce: Staff Reductions and Lack of Planning May Impact Mission Readiness,' published August 4, 2026) independently confirmed and sharpened the staffing-decline trend with nonpartisan-watchdog figures more current than any previously cited here. GAO found FEMA averaged about 25,134 employees in FY2025, down to about 21,742 by May 2026; more than 4,300 employees separated in FY2025 alone, a 55% increase in departures over FY2024; 58 Senior Executive Service personnel departed between January 2025 and January 2026, versus roughly 13 per year historically; and only 4% of FEMA's incident management workforce was available to deploy in November 2024, cited by GAO as prior context for why concurrent-disaster capacity matters. GAO had reported earlier, in May 2023, that at the start of fiscal year 2022 FEMA had approximately 11,400 disaster employees on board against a staffing goal of 17,670, an overall gap of approximately 6,200 staff (35 percent).

Most directly relevant to the 2026 hurricane season: GAO found FEMA anticipated only about 240 personnel available through the DHS Surge Capacity Force for 2026, down from about 600 in 2025 -- a roughly 60% reduction in the external federal support FEMA can draw on during a large or concurrent disaster. GAO's core finding is that FEMA made its workforce-reduction decisions 'without assessing whether it had the necessary staffing capacity to meet its mission,' and that the agency has continued to lack a documented workforce plan for future incidents, including the 2026 hurricane season, since rescinding its 2022-2026 strategic plan in May 2025 -- a structural gap GAO confirms persisted unaddressed fifteen months later.

On September 11, 2026, U.S. District Judge Susan Illston (N.D. Cal.) ruled in a 32-page decision that DHS acted unlawfully by ordering FEMA to cut its workforce roughly in half, including thousands of disaster-response reservists -- finding DHS "unlawfully usurped the authority" Congress gave FEMA to make its own personnel decisions, in violation of the post-Hurricane-Katrina federal law barring DHS from substantially reducing FEMA's authorities or functions. The ruling also found that FEMA and DHS officials had used the Signal messaging app on personal phones to discuss the staffing cuts and then deleted the messages; Illston held the deleted messages would have been relevant to the case and said she would presume they "would have been unfavorable to Defendants because they would have been further evidence" of unlawful conduct. The ruling did not set remedies or penalties -- the parties have until October 9, 2026 to brief what relief remains outstanding, to be addressed in a separate ruling.

primary_proponent.name: Kristi Noem
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Homeland Security (FEMA's parent department)
primary_proponent.note: Noem personally implemented and enforced the $100,000 spending-approval rule that created the call-center funding bottleneck. A DHS spokesperson publicly defended the change as shifting FEMA from 'bloated, DC-centric dead weight to a lean, deployable disaster force,' attributing the framing directly to Noem's leadership. Acting Administrator David Richardson's own July 10 memo to Noem -- which he signed personally -- directly contradicts a later public FEMA statement claiming the call center 'responded to every caller swiftly and efficiently.'

estimated_impact.summary: During the deadly July 2025 Texas Hill Country floods, FEMA's survivor call-center funding lapsed and it took Secretary Noem five days to approve renewed funding under her $100,000 sign-off rule, while the call-answer rate collapsed from 99.9% to 20% and survivors waited over 90 minutes; months later FEMA had approved only 22% of Kerr County residents' aid applications. Those failures came amid a steep staffing decline that the Government Accountability Office found FEMA carried out 'without assessing whether it had the necessary staffing capacity to meet its mission,' and on September 11, 2026 a federal judge ruled that DHS acted unlawfully by ordering FEMA to cut its workforce roughly in half.

estimated_impact.caveat: GovFacts' broader analysis of whether cuts affected the flood response itself is careful to note that specific FEMA deployment numbers for the July 2025 disaster weren't fully public at time of writing, and frames the staffing-to-outcome link as 'plausible' rather than definitively proven for every aspect of the response -- the call-center funding lapse specifically, however, is documented via internal agency records, not just inference. The Kerr County pre-disaster funding-denial history is presented as compounding context, not as an action by this administration: the 2017 and post-Harvey denials were made by Texas's own state emergency-management department (partly administering federal hazard-mitigation money), and the failed $500 million alert-system bill was a Texas Senate vote -- both predate or are independent of the federal FEMA actions that are this entry's actual subject. The September 11, 2026 ruling found the DHS-ordered workforce cut unlawful but did not decide whether staffing cuts caused specific response failures, and it set no remedies or penalties; the parties have until October 9, 2026 to brief what relief remains outstanding. The judge's statement that the deleted Signal messages would be presumed unfavorable to the government is a legal presumption, not a finding about what the messages said. The two staffing-decline series (Federal News Network/The Hill and GAO) cover overlapping but different measurement windows and are directionally consistent, not contradictory. For balance, FEMA's then-acting leader Robert Fenton said the agency has about 30-40% of its disaster workforce available at any given time, which he characterized as normal availability rather than a crisis-level shortfall.

title: FEMA Disaster Aid Approvals Skewed Toward Republican-Led States
institution: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing pattern -- most recent documented denial episode July 2026, no reversal or independent (GAO/IG) audit announced as of this writing
date_of_action: 2025-2026 (pattern); most recent documented episode 2026-07 (four-state blizzard aid denial)
what_changed:
An E&E News/POLITICO analysis of roughly 2,500 major disaster declaration decisions dating back to the Reagan administration found that **under Trump, Democratic-led states have had disaster aid requests approved at a 23% rate, compared to 89% for Republican-led states -- the lowest approval rate for Democratic-led states of any president since Reagan** (every prior president approved at least 67% of their requests). The same analysis found Democratic-led states waited an average of 80 days for a decision versus 39 days for Republican-led states, and documented at least $250 million in specific state disaster requests blocked or left pending, including $34 million to Washington, $41 million to Colorado, and $46 million and $83 million in separate Illinois storm-damage requests.

The pattern includes a concrete, dated episode in July 2026: Trump denied Major Disaster Declaration requests from New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island -- a combined $227 million sought after a February 2026 blizzard that buried New York City, Long Island, and the Mid-Hudson region, with Rhode Island separately citing record snowfall and cold -- after all four states' damage assessments exceeded FEMA's own threshold for triggering aid. The denials came two days after Trump approved disaster declarations for six Republican-led states; Trump has publicly touted having granted over $846 million in disaster relief to Republican-led states. White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson defended the pattern, saying Trump "provides a more thorough review of disaster declaration requests than any Administration has before him."

A follow-up E&E News/POLITICO investigation, drawing on emails and 150+ pages of documents submitted to FEMA by New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island, found that FEMA's own field offices had verified damage estimates exceeding the threshold for aid before Trump personally overrode those agency-level findings to deny the requests -- a former FEMA official said they could not recall another instance of a declaration being denied for a state that met FEMA and NOAA standards. The same reporting found that in Trump's first term, by contrast, he approved 93% of Democratic-led states' disaster requests versus 89% of Republican-led states' -- no partisan gap -- underscoring that the current pattern is specific to this term.

Separately, an AP analysis of FEMA data (reported by PBS NewsHour and Fortune, July 16, 2026) using a different dataset/methodology found Trump approved 80% of Republican-governor requests versus about 60% of Democratic-governor requests, and more than three-fourths of requests from states that voted for him in 2024 versus less than half from states that didn't -- a real, differently-sized partisan gap from the E&E/POLITICO figures already cited here, not a duplicate of them; both analyses agree a gap exists and that it's unprecedented (the AP piece separately notes no other president has shown a comparable partisan divide), but the specific percentages differ by dataset and shouldn't be merged into one number.

In July 2026, FEMA also denied federal fire-management-assistance grants for two major Oregon wildfires, prompting Oregon's Democratic senators (Wyden and Merkley) to publicly press FEMA for an explanation -- Oregon has separately been denied a hazard-mitigation grant (after atmospheric-river flooding, appealed by the state in April 2026) even after its underlying public-assistance request for the same disaster was approved, consistent with the partisan-adjacent denial pattern recurring across different FEMA grant types (major disaster declarations, fire-management assistance, and hazard mitigation), not just the flagship major-disaster-declaration approvals this entry's headline figures track.

The disaster-declaration approval gap is a distinct mechanism from a separate, later legal fight over FEMA's Homeland Security Grant Program: on July 24, 2026, a coalition of 23 Democratic-led states, two Democratic governors, and DC sued DHS in Rhode Island federal court alleging it illegally conditioned that separate grant program on states adopting specific election policies (hand-marked paper ballots, manual audits, the SAVE program) -- a related pattern of FEMA/DHS funding being used as leverage, but a different funding stream and a different specific demand than the major-disaster-declaration approvals this entry tracks. The July 24, 2026 lawsuit over FEMA grant conditions was filed by the attorneys general of California, Illinois, New Jersey, and Rhode Island, joined by 19 other states, the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania, and DC; DHS/FEMA plan to withhold 20% of the plaintiff states' federal disaster grant funding, at least $148 million, if they don't adopt the demanded election-system changes.

The separate Homeland Security Grant Program election-conditions dispute (tracked here only as related context, not this entry's core subject) has grown a second, distinct legal front: on August 17, 2026, Harris and El Paso Counties (Texas), Nashville/Davidson County (Tennessee), and Columbus (Ohio) filed a new lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia -- separate from the July 24, 2026 lawsuit by 23 Democratic-led states/DC already documented here -- arguing DHS/FEMA cannot use counterterrorism-grant funding as leverage to force local election-administration changes (hand-marked paper ballots, 5%-minimum manual ballot audits, SAVE-system citizenship verification), with up to 20% of an award withholdable for noncompliance and a full award potentially at risk.

title: FEMA Shut Down All National Fire Academy Training for Nearly Three Months Amid DOGE-Driven Budget Review
institution: FEMA -- National Fire Academy
status: Reversed -- classes resumed June 2, 2025, after nearly three months closed
date_of_action: 2025-03-07 (classes cancelled) through 2025-06-02 (classes resume)
what_changed: On March 7, 2025, FEMA abruptly cancelled all in-person classes at the National Fire Academy (NFA) in Emmitsburg, Maryland -- along with the co-located National Disaster and Emergency Management University and the Center for Domestic Preparedness in Anniston, Alabama -- as part of a Department of Government Efficiency-driven review of FEMA's spending intended to align it with administration priorities; instructors were told to cancel all future travel, and the suspension was initially described as indefinite, with FEMA saying it would support only 'mission-critical' functions during the review. The NFA provides free, federally funded training that firefighters, EMS providers, and other first responders nationwide travel to Maryland to attend. Lawmakers from both parties pressed FEMA and DHS leadership for an explanation and received none for weeks; **the Congressional Fire Services Institute and fire-service leaders warned the shutdown 'undermines first responder public safety' and posed 'an equal threat to public safety' given elevated wildfire risk nationally.** FEMA reopened the NFA, NDEMU, and the Center for Domestic Preparedness on June 2, 2025 -- nearly three months after the closure -- following what the agency described as a comprehensive review determining that certain courses 'provide effective training to enhance national readiness for state, local, tribal and territorial emergency managers and first responders.'

title: FHFA Director Pulte Purged Hundreds of Staff and Fannie/Freddie Board Members, Replacing Them With Unqualified Loyalists, While Pushing 50-Year Mortgages and Crypto-Backed Loan Assets
institution: Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac
status: Ongoing -- GAO investigation open, no findings issued as of sourcing reviewed; 50-year mortgage and crypto-asset policies remain proposed/directive, not shown to have caused documented market harm yet
date_of_action: 2025-03 (board purge begins) through 2025-12-19 (Reuters investigation)
what_changed: Within a week of taking office as FHFA Director in March 2025, Bill Pulte fired Freddie Mac's CEO and removed 14 of the two companies' nonpartisan board directors, installing himself as chairman of both boards along with business associates and partisan loyalists. Reuters' December 19, 2025 investigation reported Pulte has since driven out hundreds of employees across FHFA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac -- from executive leadership to rank-and-file staff -- replacing many with people who, per staffers' concerns cited in the reporting, lack mortgage-industry experience. Named replacements include Omeed Malik, a venture-fund founder and Trump donor appointed to Fannie Mae's board in April 2025 -- Donald Trump Jr. is a partner in Malik's 1789 Capital fund, and Malik and Trump Jr. share a financial interest in firearms retailer GrabAGun, in which Pulte's own family office separately invested around the time Malik joined Fannie's board -- and Mark Zarkin, a Michigan restaurateur and Trump fundraiser with no housing-finance experience and a vacated felony sex-offense conviction, hired as a consultant (documented in fuller detail, including a separate pending pardon-bribery lawsuit, in pulte-zarkin-sex-offender-consultant-2025.json). Alongside the personnel changes, Pulte pushed two substantive policy changes critics characterized as risky: he announced 50-year mortgages on X as 'a complete game changer,' drawing criticism from economists and industry experts over increased long-term debt burdens and lender risk exposure (not implemented as of sourcing reviewed); and in June 2025 he ordered Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to begin counting cryptocurrency holdings as an asset in mortgage-loan applications, stating he was 'keeping with President Trump's vision' -- a directive following reporting that the Trump family had earned roughly $800 million from crypto sales in early 2025. Internal watchdogs who scrutinized these moves were themselves removed: FHFA's inspector general was ousted, and Pulte fired internal watchdogs at Fannie Mae as well (the removal of Fannie's chief ethics officer, general counsel, and acting inspector general specifically in connection with their review of Pulte's mortgage-data conduct is documented in fuller detail in pulte-mortgage-data-misuse-2025-2026.json). On December 4, 2025, **the Government Accountability Office confirmed it had opened a formal investigation, requested by eight Senate Democrats led by Elizabeth Warren, into whether Pulte and FHFA employees misused federal authority and resources**; federal prosecutors in Maryland were separately reviewing Pulte's conduct in connection with his criminal referral against Sen. Adam Schiff. Government-ethics attorney Richard Painter told Reuters the appointment pattern reflects 'a buddy system' in which people are 'getting into positions because of their political or personal connections,' calling it 'unprecedented.'

title: Trump Used Rescissions to Cancel Billions in Bipartisan Foreign Aid, Gutting Pacific-China-Countering, Myanmar, and Africa Programs

what_changed: Politico reported that Trump officials are slow-walking visa renewals for foreign-born doctors from countries the administration labels national security risks, leaving many physicians unable to continue working legally as their visa status lapses during the delay. **Hospitals -- particularly in rural and underserved areas that rely heavily on foreign-trained physicians to fill positions U.S. medical graduates often don't take -- are already losing doctors to missed start dates, interrupted fellowships, and lapsed renewal deadlines caused by the processing slowdown**, not by any finding of individual wrongdoing or security risk specific to the affected physicians. The slowdown stems from Presidential Proclamation 10998 (issued December 16, 2025, effective January 1, 2026), which imposed a full entry suspension for nationals of 19 countries and a partial suspension for 20 more (39 total), including Nigeria, Venezuela, and Cuba; USCIS paused visa renewals and status updates for people from those countries even though the underlying travel ban does not apply to visa holders already in the U.S. By early May 2026, USCIS quietly exempted physicians already present in the U.S. from the renewal-processing hold, updating its website and having DHS confirm that medical-physician applications would continue processing -- but the exemption does not extend to physicians from the 39 countries who are currently outside the U.S., who remain blocked from returning, and immigration attorneys have described the exemption's own application procedure as unclear and not made public. Update 2026-08-30: a separate, distinct policy change affecting the same J-1 physician population this entry already tracks (17,000+ visa holders) takes effect September 15, 2026: a DHS final rule, published July 16, 2026, eliminates 'duration of status' admission for J-1 (and F-1/I) visa holders. J-1 physicians will move from open-ended admission tied to their training program's length to a fixed admission period capped at four years, generally matching the residency/fellowship end date in SEVIS; those needing longer than four years to complete training -- mid-residency physicians in longer programs, or those planning a fellowship afterward -- are flagged by immigration counsel as most exposed. Physicians who travel internationally after September 15, 2026 will receive a fixed-end-date I-94 and become subject to new extension-of-status filing requirements, though DHS will allow those already admitted under the prior framework to remain through their program end date (up to four years from the rule's effective date) without filing, and a timely extension filing permits continued work for up to 240 days while pending. This is a new administrative-friction layer distinct from the Proclamation 10998 renewal freeze already documented, but affects an overlapping population and could recreate status-lapse risk for the same physicians the freeze already disrupted.
