title: Forest Service Chief's Own Internal Memo Contradicted Agriculture Secretary's Public 'Fully Staffed' Claims — 5,000 Firefighting Positions Vacant
institution: U.S. Forest Service, Department of Agriculture
status: Ongoing, with a genuine mixed 2026 update -- the Forest Service met its 2026 seasonal wildland-firefighter hiring goal (crediting recent pay raises), even as permanent-staff attrition (~6,000 lost since January 2025) and consolidation continue, and the 2026 fire season itself has been severe
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial layoffs) through 2025-08 (peak fire-season staffing crisis and reorganization announcement)
what_changed:
In February 2025, the Trump administration laid off approximately 700 Forest Service employees who support wildland fire operations -- human resource managers, ecologists, and trail-crew workers who hold 'red card' fire-response certifications even though their primary jobs are not firefighting. Many were subsequently rehired, but the administration then pushed remaining staff toward deferred-resignation and early-retirement offers; ultimately at least 1,800 fire-qualified ('red-carded') employees left the agency, out of 4,800 total Forest Service departures in 2025 (more than 13% of the agency's total workforce).

The layoffs' operational impact was visible within weeks. A ProPublica investigation published April 8, 2025 found the agency's remaining support divisions similarly hollowed out beyond the February layoffs and reinstatements: the IT position overseeing the software firefighters use to request equipment sat unfilled after its posting was removed following the inauguration, legal-department cuts threatened the environmental-review capacity prescribed burns depend on, and hiring slowdowns from insufficient onboarding capacity delayed getting new firefighters into the field, on top of training-program and prescribed-burn cancellations.

By mid-June 2025, a Guardian investigation -- quoting five anonymous federal firefighters, all of whom said their agencies were not ready for the season ahead, and Sen. Patty Murray, who separately cited an estimated 7,500 USFS employees pushed out that year (a larger, contemporaneous Senate estimate that doesn't precisely reconcile with the other departure counts above but points the same direction) -- found crews going without power for weeks after maintenance-worker cuts, paychecks arriving late or halved because HR retained less than a quarter of its prior staffing, and purchase-card access revoked for basic supplies including chainsaw fuel, printer ink, radios, and fire shelters; a USFS squad leader said newly hired firefighters had gone without healthcare for months. Chief Schultz told senators the agency had hired 11,000 firefighters that summer, about 900 fewer than the prior season, with 37 incident management teams, five fewer than the year before.

Separately, Murray said $97 million in congressionally appropriated funding for state, local, tribal, and volunteer wildfire-reduction work went undistributed, and fire ecologist Hugh Safford said the administration's Forest Service research budget request was zero dollars; Schultz told senators the agency's forest-health and mitigation grants were halved to redirect more than $43 million toward the deferred-resignation program, with the grants eliminated entirely in the following year's budget request. The same week, Trump's June 16, 2025 executive order directing Interior and the Forest Service to merge wildland firefighting operations added a further layer of uncertainty firefighters said undercut confidence heading into peak season, even among those who supported consolidation in principle -- agency leaders had reportedly told staff the merger wouldn't happen until the following year.

Internal Forest Service data reviewed by ProPublica, High Country News, and Capital & Main found at least 5,000 firefighting positions vacant as of mid-July 2025 -- directly contradicting the agency's own public claim of having exceeded its 2025 hiring goal (11,364 firefighters on board by end of July). USDA spokesperson Cat McRae disputed the vacancy data as reflecting 'outdated org charts and unfunded positions'; ProPublica confirmed its analysis had already excluded unfunded positions. Beyond the internal agency data, ProPublica's July 22, 2025 report cited a recent survey by Forest Service fire managers in California that found 26% of engine captain positions and 42% of engineer positions vacant, and reported that Robert Kuhn, a former Forest Service official who co-authored a 2009-2011 assessment of the agency's personnel needs, said the practice of selectively counting firefighters dates back years.

The same vacancy dispute drew parallel, independent corroboration and a formal congressional response. A Reuters investigation published July 21, 2025 -- citing more than a dozen active and retired Forest Service employees -- reported that roughly 5,000 employees, about 15% of the agency's workforce, had left in the preceding five months, with retired USFS fire chief Riva Duncan describing firefighters "answering phones at the front desk, or cleaning toilets at campgrounds or mowing the lawn at administrative sites" due to short-staffing elsewhere in the agency. On August 14, 2025, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, sent Secretary Rollins a formal letter demanding "a detailed and comprehensive accounting of current staffing and staffing changes at the Forest Service, including firefighting jobs" since January 2025, citing a follow-up ProPublica report that described as much as 27% of firefighting roles as vacant as of July 17, 2025 -- the same underlying internal data already discussed above, expressed as a percentage rather than a raw count -- as directly contradicting the agency's public "fully staffed" claims.

Days after that public dispute, **a memo Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz sent to agency leadership -- obtained by High Country News -- stated plainly: 'As expected, the 2025 Fire Year is proving to be extremely challenging... we know the demand for resources outpaces their availability,' and directed that all red-carded employees, including IT and HR staff, be made available for fire assignments**. At an internal spring planning meeting, one employee was told directly, 'Help is not on the way' -- a phrase the employee said they had 'never been told before' in their career. The agency subsequently took the unusual step of waiving a statutory 1,039-hour cap on seasonal-employee work hours (raising it to 1,560 hours) and asked 1,400 firefighting-qualified former employees to return; as of August 12, only 100 had accepted. Separately, USDA announced a reorganization eliminating the Forest Service's nine regional offices and consolidating them into five 'hub' locations, with Secretary Brooke Rollins acknowledging up to half of affected staff may not relocate. Capital & Main reported on August 25, 2025 that, with so many positions unfilled, wildland firefighters were being asked to take on duties long handled by non-firefighting personnel; Madi Kraus, a Colorado USFS wildland firefighter and union steward for the National Federation of Federal Employees, said, "What we're doing -- for instance, building trails -- that's never been something I've been asked to do."

NPR later reported that fire-prevention work itself, not just firefighter staffing, declined sharply in 2025 -- prescribed burning fell to about 900,000 acres, roughly half of the 1.6 million-plus acres burned in each of 2023 and 2024, and total vegetation-management work (which reduces the dense underbrush that fuels catastrophic fires) fell to 2.6 million acres in 2025 from more than 4 million acres in 2024, a decline of almost 1.5 million acres. This directly connects the staffing losses documented above to a concrete reduction in the preventive work meant to reduce wildfire severity, distinct from firefighting-response capacity alone.

For the 2026 fire season, the Forest Service set a goal of 11,300 wildland firefighters onboard by mid-July and reported 11,816 onboard as of July 6, 2026 -- 104% of goal, which Chief Tom Schultz attributed to recent pay raises improving seasonal recruitment. This is a genuine, verifiable improvement on that specific metric, distinct from the broader permanent-workforce attrition: the agency has still lost close to 6,000 permanent staff (rangers, timber technicians, and others who also held fire-response 'red card' certifications) to layoffs, buyouts, and early retirement since January 2025, and outside observers (including Washington's public lands commissioner) warn this erodes surge capacity in a severe fire year even with seasonal hiring goals met.

As of mid-July 2026, more than 17,000 personnel were assigned to 46 large, uncontained fires nationwide, with over 3.6 million acres burned for the year. The 2026 fire season's severity escalated further -- on July 18, 2026, the country reached 'Preparedness Level 5,' the highest level on the scale measuring how taxed wildfire resources are nationally, only the third time since 2010 that threshold has been reached this early in the season (after 2021 and 2024). This reinforces, rather than changes, the outside observers' point above: seasonal hiring goals being met doesn't resolve the separate concern about permanent-staff attrition eroding surge capacity in a severe fire year.

By mid-August 2026, the fire season had grown into one of the most severe on record -- more than 100 wildfires were burning across 15 states, with 6.4 million acres burned nationwide through August 12, the most for that date on record, and crews had responded to over 46,500 wildfires for the year. The Forest Service's elite interagency hotshot crews, reserved for the most difficult assignments, were down roughly 15% in available numbers. Frontline strain reached the point that Washington state requested National Guard personnel and 250 active-duty Army soldiers to supplement firefighting capacity, and the season produced 12 firefighter entrapments -- the highest year-to-date total since 2006. The administration's response has been to stand up a new U.S. Wildland Fire Service intended to consolidate operations across agencies, an efficiency bet not yet tested against a season this severe. USDA continues to maintain frontline firefighter numbers exceed prior administrations' levels; the separate, disputed permanent-staff attrition documented above (roughly 5,800-6,000 lost since January 2025 depending on source) remains the underlying strain outside observers point to.

title: Forest Service Plans to Close 57 of 77 Research Stations, Including a Key Pacific Northwest Wildfire Smoke Lab, Ahead of Fire Season
institution: U.S. Forest Service (USDA)
status: Ongoing -- closures announced and reported as proceeding as of June 2026, ahead of the 2026 Western fire season
date_of_action: 2026-03-31 (closure list announced) through 2026-08 (senators demand transparency ahead of an Aug. 19 response deadline)
what_changed: The Forest Service announced plans to close 57 of its 77 research stations across 31 states, merging remaining functions into a single organization headquartered in Fort Collins, Colorado, as part of a broader agencywide restructuring that also moves Forest Service headquarters from Washington, D.C. to Salt Lake City and replaces nine regional offices with 15 state-level offices. **Among the stations slated for closure is the Pacific Wildland Fire Sciences Laboratory in Seattle, which issues wildfire smoke forecasts relied on throughout the Pacific Northwest, along with research centers in Portland and Wenatchee, Washington.** Ongoing research projects at risk include work on the most effective ways to reduce fire hazards in degraded forests and updated maps of fire threats to rural communities, wildlife habitats, and carbon storage. The agency has said scientists will not lose their jobs and that research programs themselves will not be ended, but fire researchers and Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA) have said the closures could hamper firefighting and smoke-forecasting capability as soon as the 2026 fire season. This is distinct from, though related to, this tracker's separate entry on Forest Service fire-operations staffing cuts -- that entry covers personnel reductions among fire-qualified ('red card') staff, while this entry covers the closure of dedicated research infrastructure. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 41, real correction): this entry's prior recheck (2026-08-17) concluded no material developments had occurred beyond the April-June 2026 reporting already documented -- that was incomplete. Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden, joined by colleagues, sent Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz a letter dated August 14, 2026 -- three days before that prior recheck -- pressing for a complete list of the criteria used to evaluate each of the 57 facilities, the local stakeholders being consulted for each closure determination, and a timeline for the decisions, noting the Forest Service had failed to provide Congress a comprehensive accounting despite multiple prior inquiries from both chambers. The letter set a response deadline of no later than August 19, 2026; no confirmation that the Forest Service met that deadline or responded was found as of this recheck. The letter also specifies that 20 of the 57 facilities slated for evaluation conduct wildfire-prevention research specifically, and names a fourth affected facility beyond the three (Seattle, Portland, Wenatchee) already documented here: the Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry in Hawaii. The original closure list was announced March 31, 2026, per the senators' letter -- slightly earlier than this entry's prior date range.

title: Internal Forest Service Report Found Trails Nationwide Being Abandoned, 'Unpassable Trails, Unsafe Bridges' After Staffing Purge
institution: U.S. Forest Service, Department of Agriculture
status: Ongoing -- December 2025 internal report documents 2025 conditions; a further FY2027 budget proposal would deepen the trail-funding cut going forward
date_of_action: 2025-12 (internal report completed) with a 2026-03 congressional follow-up and a 2026-04 forward-looking budget proposal
what_changed: An internal U.S. Forest Service Trail Program Status Report, completed in December 2025 after interviews with nearly 300 district-level staff across every Forest Service region and obtained by The Washington Post, found trails across the National Forest System's roughly 158,000-164,000-mile network being abandoned and rapidly deteriorating as staffing losses compound. Some ranger districts lost up to 100% of their dedicated trail crew staff during 2025, part of the agency's broader loss of nearly 6,000 employees to firings, resignations, and retirements documented separately in forest-service-firefighter-shortage-trump2.json (that entry covers the same staffing purge's impact on fire-response capacity; this entry covers its impact on recreation-trail infrastructure specifically). The report found the Forest Service maintained 22% fewer trail miles in 2025 than the prior year, with the share of trails meeting agency maintenance standards falling to its lowest level in 15 years, and stated plainly that 'lost skills are weakening the agency's ability to implement technical projects and oversee partner, volunteer, and contractor work,' producing 'unpassable trails, unsafe bridges, and negative environmental impacts.' **One concrete documented safety consequence: the Madison Gulf Bridge, which carries the Appalachian Trail across the Peabody River in New Hampshire's Androscoggin Ranger District, was closed to pedestrian traffic after an inspection found it unsafe.** In March 2026, Rep. Kim Schrier (D-WA) and Rep. Andrea Salinas (D-OR), joined by 21 House colleagues, sent a formal letter to Forest Service leadership demanding answers, writing that 'USFS trail maintenance operations have been hamstrung by layoffs, hiring restrictions, budget cuts and other policies that make it harder for staff to do their jobs and meet agency objectives' -- citing, among other local examples, the closure of the Denny Creek Trailhead in Washington's Enchantments area due to staffing shortages. Separately, the administration's April 2026 FY2027 budget request proposed cutting the Forest Service's dedicated trails line item specifically from $22 million to $8 million (a 64% reduction, per Washington Trails Association's analysis of the broader 31% cut to the agency's Recreation, Heritage and Wilderness account) -- a forward-looking proposal distinct from, but compounding, the staffing-driven 2025 maintenance decline this entry's internal report documents.

primary_proponent.name: Tom Schultz
primary_proponent.role: Chief, U.S. Forest Service
primary_proponent.note: Publicly framed the agency's broader 2026 reorganization and facilities consolidation as necessary fiscal stewardship (citing a $3 billion agency-wide deferred-maintenance backlog) while his own agency's internal December 2025 trail report documented the operational consequences of the preceding year's staffing losses in Forest Service districts nationwide; no public statement from Schultz or Secretary Rollins directly addresses the trail-specific findings, distinguishing this from the firefighter-shortage entry's more direct public-vs-internal contradiction.

estimated_impact.summary: A rare internal agency report documents its own operational collapse in a mission area (recreation trail maintenance) distinct from firefighting readiness, while a separate forward-looking budget proposal would cut trail funding further. Safety consequences are documented via at least one concrete bridge closure rather than only general risk language.

title: Pentagon's $1.2B Fort Bliss Migrant-Detention Camp Contract Went to a GOP Megadonor Whose Prior Company Pleaded Guilty to Hiring Undocumented Workers
institution: Department of Defense
status: Contract awarded and active as of this entry's last-verified date; no DOD Inspector General review, congressional inquiry, or named official identified in reporting as having personally approved the award
date_of_action: 2025-07 (contract announced)
what_changed: In July 2025, the Department of Defense announced a $1.2 billion contract to build a 5,000-bed migrant detention facility at Fort Bliss, Texas -- among the largest immigration-detention buildouts of the administration. The prime contractor is Virginia-based Acquisition Logistics, with subcontractors Disaster Management Group and Amentum. **Disaster Management Group, whose portion of the work ProPublica estimated at 'hundreds of millions' of dollars, is co-owned and led as CEO by Nathan Albers, a self-described 'big-time Republican donor' who has contributed more than $150,000 to Republican campaigns in the year before the award, attended election-night 2024 festivities at Mar-a-Lago, and co-chaired a Trump National Golf Club fundraiser with Eric Trump.** Albers previously co-owned TentLogix, a temporary-structures company that pleaded guilty in 2019 to a scheme to hire and conceal undocumented workers -- a 2016 audit had found 96 undocumented employees on its books, co-founder Gary Hendry (Albers's former brother-in-law) served time in prison, and the company forfeited more than $3 million before filing for bankruptcy in 2020. A Disaster Management spokesperson told ProPublica that Albers had been cleared in DHS's investigation of TentLogix and had parted ways with the company as a minority, non-operating owner once he learned of Hendry's conduct. Since 2020, Disaster Management Group has won more than $500 million in federal contracts, primarily for Afghan refugee housing, and only began federal lobbying in late 2024 -- spending $210,000 on immigration-related issues with no prior lobbying history -- shortly before securing the Fort Bliss subcontract. Neither the White House nor DOD identified which official approved or oversaw the award; the White House referred ProPublica's questions to DOD, which did not name a responsible official.

primary_proponent.role: Awarding agency
primary_proponent.note: DOD announced and administers the $1.2B Fort Bliss contract; no individual DOD official was identified by name in reporting as having personally approved or overseen the subcontract award to Disaster Management Group, and neither the White House nor DOD would name one when asked.

estimated_impact.summary: A politically-connected donor whose former company had a documented, criminally-adjudicated history of illegally employing undocumented workers stood to profit from a nine-figure share of a taxpayer-funded contract to detain immigrants, without any disclosed competitive-bidding detail or named approving official -- the kind of opacity that invites, without itself proving, favoritism in the award of a large detention-buildout contract central to the administration's immigration enforcement agenda.

title: FTC deletes AI consumer-protection guidance posts from the Lina Khan era
institution: Federal Trade Commission
status: Ongoing (posts remain removed as of reporting; no restoration identified)
date_of_action: 2025-03 (approx. 300 posts) and 2025-10-20 (3 specific AI posts)
what_changed: In March 2025, the FTC removed approximately 300 blog posts from its website, most authored during Chair Lina Khan's tenure, covering AI, consumer protection, and the agency's lawsuits against tech companies including Amazon and Microsoft. **On October 20, 2025, three additional AI-specific posts were found removed: 'AI and the Risk of Consumer Harm' (Jan. 3, 2025, warning of AI's potential for surveillance, fraud, and discrimination), 'Consumers Are Voicing Concerns About AI' (Oct. 2023), and 'On Open-Weights Foundation Models' (July 10, 2024, addressing open-source AI models).** No FTC official publicly took responsibility for or explained the removals; former FTC public affairs director Douglas Farrar said he was 'shocked' the Ferguson-led FTC appeared to be acting out of step with the administration's own stated AI-innovation messaging. The removals occurred under current Chair Andrew Ferguson, who has separately pursued a broader deregulatory agenda, including recommending the deletion or revision of anticompetitive regulations FTC-wide. Reporting flagged the deletions as raising compliance concerns under the Federal Records Act (which requires agencies to preserve records documenting government activity) and the Open Government Data Act (which requires agencies to publish their data as open data by default).

primary_proponent.role: FTC Chairman
primary_proponent.note: No source identifies who specifically ordered the post removals or why; Ferguson is listed as the accountable office-holder for the agency during this period, not because he is confirmed to have personally directed the deletions. A former FTC official's on-record surprise is the only direct internal reaction found in sourcing.

estimated_impact.summary: Removes public-facing consumer-protection guidance and agency lawsuit documentation from public access, potentially violating federal recordkeeping and open-data law, and eliminating the previous administration's public warnings about AI-related consumer harms (surveillance, fraud, discrimination) from the public record.

title: FTC Cuts Workforce 10%, Loses Bipartisan Independence After Supreme Court Upholds Commissioner Firings
institution: Federal Trade Commission
status: Complete (workforce reduction implemented in 2025; commissioner-firing litigation permanently resolved by the Supreme Court on June 29, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-03-18 (commissioner firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling); staff reduction implemented through 2025
what_changed: On March 18, 2025, President Trump fired the FTC's two Democratic commissioners, Rebecca Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya, without citing any statutory cause, instead stating their continued service was 'inconsistent with my Administration's priorities.' This left the five-seat Commission with only its two sitting Republican members. Slaughter and Bedoya sued; Bedoya later resigned and dropped his claim, but Slaughter's case proceeded, with a district court initially ordering her reinstated. Separately, on May 15, 2025, Chairman Andrew Ferguson testified to Congress that the FTC was implementing a 10% workforce reduction, bringing headcount to approximately 1,100 employees (down from 1,221), the agency's lowest staffing level in a decade. **On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the FTC's for-cause removal protections for commissioners are unconstitutional, permanently allowing the president to remove commissioners at will and explicitly overruling the 1935 precedent Humphrey's Executor v. United States, which had protected the independence of the FTC and similar agencies for 90 years.** Re-verified 2026-07-19: the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Chair Andrew Ferguson and Mark Meador) as of this update, with legal commentary noting little short-term incentive to restore a five-member bipartisan structure -- no material change to the entry's core claims. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no material change -- the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Ferguson and Meador); no new nominations or structural changes identified since the prior update. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change -- the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Ferguson and Meador); no new nominations or structural changes identified since the prior update. Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- the Commission remains at two sitting Republican commissioners (Ferguson and Meador); no new nominations, resignations, or structural changes identified since the prior update. Update 2026-09-23: SCOTUSblog reported that the Trump v. Slaughter ruling gave President Trump 'sweeping new authority over approximately two dozen multi-member agencies that Congress intended to be independent,' and ABC News put the number at more than two dozen; Justice Sotomayor's dissent warned that 'dozens of independent commissions are now likely to become purely executive agencies.' In his May 15, 2025 testimony before the House Appropriations Committee, Chairman Ferguson said '$333.7 million was paid to consumers in FY 2024.'

On the commissioner firings, the administration's position, upheld by the Supreme Court majority, is that the FTC 'unquestionably exercises executive power' and must therefore be fully accountable to the president; Chief Justice Roberts's majority opinion carved out a possible exception for the Federal Reserve. Critics, including Justice Sotomayor's dissent (joined by Kagan and Jackson) and former commissioner Slaughter, argue the ruling eliminates meaningful independence not just at the FTC but across the broader universe of agencies Congress designed to be insulated from single-party control, and that FTC policy will become more responsive to political and campaign considerations going forward. Legal scholars are split on how far the precedent extends beyond the FTC itself.

title: State Department Froze Fulbright/Gilman/Critical Language Funding; Entire Oversight Board Resigned Over Political Vetting of Recipients
institution: State Department -- Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs / Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board
status: Split status: the funding question is resolved -- the FY2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act (P.L. 119-75), signed February 3, 2026, enacted $273.4 million for Fulbright ($667 million for State Department exchange programs overall), rejecting the administration's proposed near-total elimination. The political-vetting dispute and Fulbright board vacancy remain unresolved: no replacement members had been named as of the State Department's board page (checked June 17, 2026), over a year after the June 2025 mass resignation.
date_of_action: 2025-02-13 (ECA funding pause begins) through 2025-06-12 (Fulbright board mass resignation)
what_changed: On February 13, 2025, the State Department's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (ECA) paused disbursements for its exchange programs -- including Fulbright, the Gilman International Scholarship, IDEAS, and the Critical Language Scholarship program -- initially described as a 15-day pause but extended well beyond that window, **leaving over 10,000 students and professionals in active exchanges without stipends for housing, food, and travel, both in the U.S. and abroad**; funding began to be restored in the following months. Separately, State Department officials led by Darren Beattie, Under Secretary for Public Diplomacy and Public Affairs, intervened to reject more than 20% of the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board's selected finalists for the 2025-2026 academic year -- a last-minute override the board called unauthorized -- and subjected an additional roughly 1,200 already-selected foreign recipients to a new, unauthorized ideological review process that could still result in their rejection, spanning fields from architecture and biology to medical science and music. On June 12, 2025, 11 of the board's 12 presidentially-appointed members resigned en masse, writing that the administration had 'injected politics and ideological mandates' into award decisions and that senior administration officials had refused to respond to the board's repeated legal objections, raised both verbally and in writing. Trump's FY2026 budget proposal separately sought to eliminate nearly all Fulbright funding; a July 2025 House committee draft instead included $287.8 million for the program, and the appropriations process ultimately resolved the same way -- Congress passed and Trump signed the FY2026 Consolidated Appropriations Act (P.L. 119-75) on February 3, 2026, enacting $273.4 million for Fulbright specifically (a modest trim from the July draft figure, still a $5 million cut to Title VI/Fulbright-Hays combined year over year) within $667 million for State Department educational/cultural exchange programs overall -- a $74 million (10%) reduction from FY2025 but a large restoration relative to the administration's request to all but eliminate the program. That funding resolution was already six months old by the time this entry was first written (2026-08-10) and drafted around 'draft appropriations bill' language; it is corrected here rather than presented as still-pending. The board vacancy is a separate, still-unresolved question: sourcing reviewed found no indication as of mid-2026 that the administration has nominated replacements for the 11 members who resigned in June 2025.

primary_proponent.role: Under Secretary of State for Public Diplomacy and Public Affairs
primary_proponent.note: Led the State Department intervention rejecting more than 20% of the Fulbright board's selected finalists, the action the board's resignation letter identifies as precipitating its mass resignation. The broader February 2025 ECA funding pause was a department-wide action not attributed to a single named official in sourcing reviewed.

estimated_impact.summary: Disrupted stipends for over 10,000 active exchange participants for months, and triggered the resignation of the entire body legally responsible for insulating Fulbright award decisions from political interference, while a separate budget proposal sought to eliminate the program's funding entirely (a move Congress's own draft appropriations bill resisted).

title: Fish and Wildlife Service Loses Over 1,500 Staff; Zero New Species Listed as Endangered
institution: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
status: Ongoing (staffing and budget cuts continue and a further round is proposed for FY2027; the zero-new-listings streak this entry was built around ended July 21, 2026, when FWS finalized endangered status for three Florida Keys reptiles -- the term's first new listings after roughly 18 months at zero; 400+ species remain in the backlog)
date_of_action: 2025-01 to 2026-02 (staffing reductions); ongoing effects on listing backlog through the last-verified date
what_changed: Between January 2025 and February 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service saw a net reduction of 1,538 employees, according to Office of Personnel Management data compiled by the Congressional Research Service, with independent analyses from the Center for Biological Diversity estimating the cuts included more than 500 biologists specifically. The Interior Department separately proposed a FY2026 budget cutting the agency's Endangered Species Act listing-activity funding by 36% year-over-year, part of an overall reduction in FWS's average annual appropriations from roughly $1.94 billion (2017-2025 average) to approximately $1.6 billion for FY2026; the same budget proposed eliminating funding for the State and Tribal Wildlife Grant program entirely. The Service also discontinued its Refuge System Strategic Growth Policy and, according to conservation groups, has effectively stopped conducting the annual Florida panther population count last performed in 2015. As of reporting in April 2026, the Fish and Wildlife Service had added zero new species to the federal endangered or threatened species list during Trump's second term, compared to 22 species added during the entirety of his first term, a gap the Center for Biological Diversity described as the longest period without a new listing decision since the Endangered Species Act was implemented. **A backlog of more than 400 species remains pending final agency listing decisions.** Recent Federal Register activity through mid-July 2026 continues the zero-new-listings pattern with specific examples: on June 16, 2026, FWS found listing 'not warranted' for two petitioned species (Sangre de Cristo peaclam, black-backed tanager); on July 14, 2026, FWS issued 90-day findings (a preliminary step, not a listing decision) for 10 more petitioned species including the Cascade red fox and plains spotted skunk; and on the same day, FWS rejected -- for the second time -- a petition to list long-tailed macaque monkeys. None of this recent activity constitutes an actual new listing, consistent with the entry's core finding. Separately, in June 2026 FWS announced a partnership with Colossal Biosciences to collect and cryopreserve cell/tissue samples from every species on the endangered list -- a genomic-preservation initiative distinct from, and not a substitute for, the listing process itself. CORRECTION 2026-07-26: on July 21, 2026, FWS finalized endangered-species status for three Florida Keys reptiles -- the Florida Keys mole skink, Key ring-necked snake, and rim rock crowned snake -- effective August 20, 2026. These are the first new species listings of Trump's second term, ending the zero-listings streak that was this entry's central, headline finding; the listing process itself took 14 years from initial proposal to finalization, so this reflects the conclusion of a long-pending case rather than a change in the administration's overall listing pace. Separately, FWS finalized an Endangered Species Act regulatory change in July 2026 removing the 'blanket rule' option that had automatically extended full endangered-level protections to newly listed threatened species by default, a change conservation groups argue weakens protection for future threatened listings even as it doesn't affect already-endangered species like these three. The 400+ species backlog and FY2026 budget/staffing cuts already documented in this entry are unaffected by this correction and remain current. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no new species listings or budget/staffing changes identified beyond the July 21, 2026 Florida Keys listings (effective August 20, 2026) already documented above; the 400+ species backlog remains the entry's current standing figure. CORRECTION 2026-08-30: this entry's FY2026 budget/staffing figures were missing the agency's own forward-looking FY2027 budget request, submitted to Congress in April 2026 (predating this entry's original write-up but never previously incorporated). That request proposes cutting FWS's total discretionary funding a further 20% ($1.65 billion enacted FY2026 to a requested $1.33 billion for FY2027) and its total employee count a further 10% (6,513 to 5,861), on top of the 1,538-employee reduction already documented above, and would zero out discretionary funding entirely for five FWS accounts including the Cooperative Endangered Species Conservation Fund and the State and Tribal Wildlife Grant program (whose FY2026 elimination this entry already noted). Notably, in P.L. 119-74 (the enacted FY2026 Interior appropriations law), Congress directed FWS to maintain staffing levels sufficient to fulfill its statutory responsibilities -- a direct tension with the administration's own FY2027 staffing-cut proposal that CRS's analysis flags explicitly. No FY2027 appropriations had been enacted as of this recheck, and no new species listings were identified beyond the three Florida Keys reptiles already documented.

title: The 43-Day Government Shutdown Left ~1.4 Million Federal Workers Unpaid, While OMB Used It to Attempt Mass Layoffs Later Ruled Illegal
institution: Office of Management and Budget (OMB); multiple federal agencies (Treasury, HHS, Commerce, Education, Energy, EPA, DHS, HUD, Interior)
status: The 43-day shutdown ended Nov. 12, 2025. Congress and a Dec. 17, 2025 court order voided shutdown-era RIFs; all were rescinded, though State separated ~250 diplomats May 5, 2026 under a pre-shutdown RIF. A Sept. 23, 2026 settlement strips shutdown-RIF language from agency plans through 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-09-23 (Trump cancels Schumer/Jeffries meeting, precipitating the shutdown) through 2025-12-17 (federal judge orders reversal of shutdown-era layoffs the administration had not reinstated)
what_changed:
On September 23, 2025, Trump abruptly canceled a planned White House meeting with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries -- scheduled for that Thursday, ahead of the September 30 fiscal year-end -- calling Democrats' demand that any stopgap funding deal extend the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits (due to expire at the end of 2025) 'unserious' and 'ridiculous,' and writing that 'no meeting with their Congressional Leaders could possibly be productive.' Schumer responded that Democrats would discuss health care 'when you're finished ranting.' Republicans separately called Democrats' related demand to reverse Medicaid changes a nonstarter, though they said there was time to address the ACA subsidy question in the months ahead. This negotiation breakdown over ACA subsidies was the immediate precipitating dispute for the shutdown that began the following week; the subsidies ultimately lapsed without an extension.

The government shutdown began October 1, 2025 and lasted 43 days -- the longest full federal shutdown in U.S. history -- ending November 12, 2025 when Congress passed a continuing resolution funding the government through January 30, 2026. During the shutdown, roughly 670,000 federal employees were furloughed and roughly 730,000 'excepted' employees continued working without pay, for a combined total of about 1.4 million federal workers unpaid at the shutdown's peak; by the time funding was restored, nearly 3 million paychecks had been withheld, representing almost $14 billion in missing wages. Reporting throughout the shutdown documented workers relying on credit cards, food banks, and side jobs to get by, **with families skipping meals and delaying medical care while backlogs grew at agencies including TRICARE, FEMA, and HUD**. Specific documented cases included hundreds of furloughed workers and contractors waiting hours at the Capital Area Food Bank's Landover, Maryland distribution site by the shutdown's third week, with turnout roughly doubling, including a 21-year military veteran now a civilian federal employee who told reporters it was his first time ever seeking food assistance.

The unpaid-civilian hardship stood in contrast to the administration's selective payment of other federal workers during the same shutdown: beyond the up to $8 billion in redirected defense research funds covering active-duty military pay (detailed below), the administration, about two weeks into the lapse, also moved other money to pay certain law-enforcement personnel. FBI Director Kash Patel said on October 15, 2025 that the bureau's special agents would be paid. On October 16, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem said more than 70,000 DHS law-enforcement officers -- including CBP, ICE, and Secret Service personnel and federal air marshals -- would be paid for all hours worked, and a DHS spokesperson said the next day that One Big Beautiful Bill Act funds would cover their pay. The officers, who had been working unpaid, were to receive a 'super check' by October 22 covering shutdown days already worked without pay, their overtime, and their next pay period, Federal News Network reported. Most other federal employees -- including other FBI employees -- went unpaid for the shutdown's full 43 days. A further, more direct example of selective treatment emerged within the White House's own Executive Office of the President (EOP) at the shutdown's start -- Politico reported October 2, 2025 that while 554 of the EOP's 1,733 employees were furloughed, all 45 DOGE staffers and 437 of OMB's 530 employees (led by Russell Vought) were kept on the job entirely, exempted from furlough because their compensation is funded through a source other than annual appropriations rather than through the ordinary 'excepted-employee' mechanism that kept FBI and DHS law enforcement working.

The October 10 RIF wave described below did not proceed without warning that it was legally questionable. On October 3, 2025, MSNBC/ms.now opinion coverage citing former OMB official Bobby Kogan and former acting OPM director Rob Shriver detailed the legal argument that mass firings during the shutdown likely violated the Antideficiency Act, which bars federal officials from committing the government to future expenditures (including RIF-related severance and compensation obligations) without congressional appropriations; Kogan said 'it doesn't seem to me that they would really be able to legally do that additional work during a shutdown,' while Shriver called the move 'yet another stunt' using the shutdown to advance the administration's broader workforce-reduction agenda.

The dispute over back pay itself also predated the CR's later, narrower-interpretation fight: Government Executive found that shortly after the shutdown began, OMB deleted from its own guidance any reference to the 2019 Government Employee Fair Treatment Act's back-pay guarantee, and that furlough notices sent by GSA and the Interior Department on October 1 (which had cited the 2019 law's guarantee) were replaced by October 31 renewal notices that dropped that language entirely at both agencies and, per Government Executive's review, 'all others reviewed.'

On October 10, 2025, OMB Director Russell Vought announced on social media that 'the RIFs have begun,' as roughly 4,200 employees across at least seven agencies (Treasury and HHS hit hardest, with 1,100+ each) received reduction-in-force notices; Vought said the total could ultimately exceed 10,000. One specific, especially severe instance of this wave was HHS's Office of Population Affairs (OPA), which administers Title X, the nation's only federal family-planning program -- 49 of OPA's roughly 50 employees were sent RIF notices on October 10, 2025, which would have left essentially no staff to administer a program serving 2.8+ million patients; those notices were later voided under the continuing resolution described below, but a Title X funding disruption followed into 2026.

Federal employee unions sued in California federal court (before Judge Susan Illston) seeking to block the layoffs as illegal use of shutdown authority. Judge Illston granted a temporary restraining order on October 15, 2025, ruling the roughly 4,000 October 10 RIF notices 'illegal and in excess of authority' and blocking most agencies from proceeding; she extended that order into a preliminary injunction on October 28, 2025, prohibiting further shutdown-era RIF notices until the government reopened -- a distinct, earlier court action from the continuing resolution's later statutory invalidation of shutdown-era RIFs described below. Separately, federal workers filed unemployment claims at a scale not seen since the 2018-2019 shutdown: 7,224 initial claims were filed for the week ending October 11, 2025 alone (more than double the prior week), and nearly 20,600 furloughed federal employees had filed for unemployment benefits within the shutdown's first three weeks, with Maryland and Texas each accounting for 3,100+ of those filings.

The shutdown also strained military families specifically, a population distinct from the civilian federal workforce discussed above because active-duty pay is funded through separate defense appropriations. Reporting on October 9, 2025 found food pantry visits by military families had climbed more than 30% since the shutdown began, with the Armed Services YMCA -- which operates 22 food banks near military installations nationwide -- expanding distributions across nine states to meet demand (Killeen, Texas, near Fort Hood, saw about a 34% increase). By late October, with the shutdown entering its fourth week, the Armed Services YMCA reported demand at its bases-area food banks had grown 30-75%, with uniformed service members at Fort Hood and other installations showing up for food assistance as their next paycheck remained uncertain.

The administration avoided an outright missed military payday during the shutdown itself by temporarily reallocating up to $8 billion from weapons research and testing funds to cover troop pay disbursed on October 15 and October 31, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned service members would likely miss their November 15 paycheck -- which would have been the first fully missed payday for all military branches in a shutdown -- had the shutdown continued past November 12; the already-thin finances of junior enlisted families, combined with sustained uncertainty over whether pay would arrive on time, drove the documented surge in food-bank reliance even though troops were ultimately paid on schedule throughout the shutdown.

The underlying pay uncertainty was heightened by a two-sided congressional standoff over standalone troop-pay legislation, not a one-party blockade. On October 10, 2025, House Republicans -- with Rep. Mike Bost gaveling out of a pro forma session before Rep. Sarah Elfreth could seek unanimous consent -- blocked a floor vote on Rep. Emilia Sykes's bipartisan Pay Our Military Act; Speaker Mike Johnson argued the House had already addressed military pay by passing its own broader stopgap funding bill weeks earlier and rejected calls for a standalone vote, prompting a widely-covered exchange in which a military spouse told him on C-SPAN her family could go hungry and her 'kids could die' without a paycheck. Separately, on October 23, 2025, Senate Democrats blocked a Republican-authored 'Shutdown Fairness Act' that would have paid the military alongside Coast Guard, air traffic controllers, Border Patrol, ICE, and other excepted federal employees, with Democrats arguing the bill gave Trump excessive discretion over which categories of workers to prioritize for payment; the measure failed 54-45, short of the 60 votes needed, with only three Democrats crossing party lines to support it.

The shutdown's financial strain also touched U.S. Army personnel overseas. On November 5, 2025, U.S. Army Garrison Bavaria's official 'Shutdown Guidance' webpage included a bottom section headed 'Running list of German support organizations for your kit bags,' listing four German food-aid groups (including Tafel Deutschland and Foodsharing e.V.) and the Too Good To Go app; a U.S. Army Europe and Africa spokesperson said the list, created weeks earlier under the heading 'Germany Specific Resources,' was intended for the roughly 11,000 German local-national employees on U.S. bases (whom the German government separately committed to paying during the lapse) rather than U.S. service members, though it remained unclear whether any U.S. troops sought help from the listed resources. The page was removed November 5, 2025 after press inquiries; coverage (404 Media, Task & Purpose, Stars and Stripes, Euronews) presented both the initial 'soldiers told to use food banks' framing and the Army's subsequent German-employees-only clarification without resolving the tension between the page's kit-bags heading and that stated intent.

In the shutdown's final days, the nonprofit Military Family Advisory Network (MFAN) reported an unprecedented surge in need, logging more than 50,000 requests for emergency food assistance over a single three-day span, as reported November 10, 2025; MFAN CEO Shannon Razsadin said the need was real and urgent, warning that strength alone would not fill a pantry. MFAN began distributing boxes of shelf-stable groceries to families across every service branch and state, identifying National Guard and Reserve families -- whose drill pay had been canceled outright by the shutdown rather than merely delayed -- as facing the most acute financial strain.

The continuing resolution that ended the shutdown explicitly invalidated any RIF 'proposed, noticed, initiated, executed, implemented, or otherwise taken' by an executive agency between October 1 and November 12, 2025, requiring reinstatement with back pay, and barred agencies from using any funds to carry out a RIF through January 30, 2026. By November 21, 2025, Justice Department filings showed that all 3,605 employees who had received shutdown-era RIF notices -- from more than 1,300 at the IRS to 54 at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency -- had been notified their layoffs were rescinded, Federal News Network reported. The administration, however, applied a narrower reading of the law than its text supported, reinstating only employees who received RIF notices between Oct. 1 and Nov. 12 while treating layoffs noticed before the shutdown but carried out during or after it as outside the law -- including, the government argued, 299 Education Department Office for Civil Rights employees notified on Oct. 14 under a RIF the department said it had first issued in March 2025, whose separations Education paused pending the court's clarification. The unions went back to court, and on December 17, 2025, Judge Illston issued a second preliminary injunction ordering the Education and State departments, the Small Business Administration, and the General Services Administration to rescind RIFs carried out between Oct. 1 and Nov. 12, and barring Education and State from taking any further step to carry out a RIF of their employees through January 30, 2026; Federal News Network reported the order affected about 680 employees, including nearly 250 Foreign Service officers whose layoffs a temporary restraining order had already put on hold. The government appealed to the Ninth Circuit on December 22, and on December 23 a three-judge panel temporarily stayed the order's requirement to rescind the RIF notices by that day while leaving the rest of the injunction in force; the government moved to drop the appeal on December 31, and the Ninth Circuit dismissed it on January 2, 2026, ending the stay. Education rescinded its notices, and State, GSA, and SBA reinstated the employees they had separated during the shutdown and paid them back wages.

The path toward the January 30, 2026 deadline itself stalled before Congress recessed for the holidays. On December 19, 2025, Senate Republicans attempted to advance a five-bill spending package funding nine major departments (including Defense, Labor, HHS, and Education), but Colorado Senators John Hickenlooper and Michael Bennet refused to lift a hold they had placed on the measure, objecting to the administration's plan to dismantle NCAR, the National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder; Hickenlooper said 'we need to find some Republican supporters -- all we're trying to do is just protect the budget that was already there,' while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the administration's treatment of Colorado 'disgusting.' With the hold unresolved, lawmakers adjourned for the holidays without a deal, leaving the January 30 deadline -- and the RIF pause tied to it -- unresolved heading into 2026; Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he didn't think either side wanted a shutdown, calling it 'toxic for both parties.'

At a January 9, 2026 hearing, Judge Illston said her December order covered only the State Department's December 2 notice setting the Foreign Service officers' separation date, not their original July 2025 RIF notices; she issued no formal order but suggested State could proceed with its plan once the layoff pause ended. A four-day partial shutdown followed the January 30 deadline; the package that ended it, signed February 3, 2026, gave full-year funding to every remaining agency except the Department of Homeland Security, whose stopgap extended the government-wide RIF pause only through February 13, and DHS itself then went unfunded until April 30. On May 5, 2026, State formally separated nearly 250 Foreign Service employees and about 30 civil service employees who had been on paid administrative leave since receiving RIF notices in July 2025. On September 23, 2026, the unions and the government settled the lawsuit. The government represented that OMB's shutdown RIF memorandum and OPM's related guidance had been rescinded in full, and that every RIF notice issued during the lapse had been rescinded and the affected employees reinstated. The defendant agencies agreed to remove from their shutdown contingency plans, for plans in effect through December 31, 2026, any language providing for RIFs during a funding lapse, with any later change taking effect only 30 days after public notice; the case was to be held in abeyance and dismissed by the end of 2026 or once fiscal 2027 appropriations are enacted, with no admission of wrongdoing by either side.

estimated_impact.summary: The 43-day shutdown left about 1.4 million federal workers unpaid at its peak and withheld almost $14 billion in wages; families skipped meals and delayed medical care, military families' food-bank visits rose 30-75%, and one military-family nonprofit logged more than 50,000 emergency food requests in three days. OMB also deleted the 2019 back-pay guarantee from its shutdown guidance and used the lapse to send 3,605 layoff notices; a judge ruled the first wave illegal, Congress voided them, and a second court order in December 2025 was needed to block or reverse about 680 pre-noticed layoffs. All shutdown-era notices were ultimately rescinded and the affected workers reinstated, but the nearly 250 Foreign Service officers covered by that December order were separated in May 2026 under their original July 2025 notices.

estimated_impact.caveat: The furloughed/excepted counts are Bipartisan Policy Center estimates built on agency shutdown plans, and the paycheck/wage totals are reported estimates rather than TAP's own calculation. The skipped meals and delayed medical care are documented in reporting but not counted, and the food-bank figures are the Armed Services YMCA's and MFAN's own tallies. The 3,605 RIF notices describe an attempted action that was fully rescinded, per the government's own court filings and the September 2026 settlement, so they are not a lasting workforce cut; the State Department separations in May 2026 stem from a July 2025 RIF that predates the shutdown. The settlement's limit on shutdown-RIF language covers agency contingency plans only through December 31, 2026 and does not bind future lapses beyond that; agencies may also restore such language on 30 days' public notice. The troop-pay standoff was two-sided: House Republicans blocked a standalone troop-pay bill on October 10, and Senate Democrats blocked a Republican standalone bill on October 23.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- shutdown duration, furlough/excepted worker counts, and paycheck/wage figures are corroborated across the Bipartisan Policy Center, Wikipedia's sourced shutdown article, CBS, NPR, and CNN. The RIF campaign is corroborated by Vought's own public statements plus NPR, CNN, CNBC, and Government Executive reporting naming the specific agencies and the initial 4,200 estimate; the CR's invalidation of shutdown-era RIFs, the 3,605 rescinded notices, the narrower-interpretation dispute, and the December 17, 2025 injunction are corroborated by Federal News Network (Maryland Matters republishes its reporting, so it is not independent corroboration) and Government Executive, which quote the CR's text and Judge Illston's order. The appeal's dismissal, the rescission of all lapse-era RIF notices, and the September 23, 2026 settlement terms are HIGH confidence, taken from the signed settlement agreement itself; the government's representations there were made without admission of fault. State's May 5, 2026 separations are sourced to Federal News Network, which quotes the department's notice. MODERATE confidence on the Army Garrison Bavaria German-food-bank-list episode -- the page's existence, its 'kit bags' heading, and its Nov. 5, 2025 removal are corroborated across 404 Media, Task & Purpose, Stars and Stripes, and Euronews, but the Army's German-employees-only explanation is not independently verified beyond the Army's own spokesperson, and it is unconfirmed whether any U.S. troops actually used the listed resources. HIGH confidence on the military-family food-bank surge, corroborated by Military.com, ABC News, and the Armed Services YMCA's own reporting of its food-bank demand data; the $8 billion weapons-fund reallocation used to cover troop pay is corroborated by The Hill and Federal News Network. The Capital Area Food Bank/Landover case is corroborated by CNN and NBC News, each independently interviewing furloughed workers on scene; the DHS/FBI selective-payment facts are corroborated by Federal News Network's 'budgetary twister' reporting, its October 17, 2025 report on DHS's 70,000 law-enforcement officers and their 'super check,' and The Washington Post's reporting on the administration opting some federal workers out of the shutdown's pay impact. Reporting reviewed does not establish whether DHS law-enforcement pay after the Oct. 22 super check, or FBI agents' pay beyond the paychecks announced in October, continued on schedule through Nov. 12. The Oct. 15/28, 2025 TRO-then-injunction sequence is HIGH confidence, corroborated across CNBC, Federal News Network, AFGE, PBS News, and Roll Call, all citing Judge Illston's own rulings; the unemployment-claims figures are HIGH confidence, corroborated across Bloomberg News (original source), NBC News, and CNN. The House GOP block of the Pay Our Military Act is corroborated across The Hill, CNN, Fox News, Politico, and Rep. Sykes's own office; the Senate Democratic block of the Shutdown Fairness Act (54-45, Oct. 23) is corroborated across Stars and Stripes, Axios, Bloomberg, and Sen. Cramer's office (the bill's sponsor's own account) -- both sides of this exchange are corroborated by sources across the political spectrum, supporting the two-sided framing. The Sept. 23, 2025 canceled Schumer/Jeffries meeting and Trump's 'unserious'/'ridiculous' characterization of the ACA-subsidy demand are HIGH confidence, corroborated across CNBC, PBS NewsHour, The Hill, Federal News Network, and Fox News, all citing Trump's own Truth Social post and Schumer's public response. The MFAN 50,000-request/three-day figure and CEO Razsadin's statement are HIGH confidence, sourced to Military.com's November 10, 2025 reporting citing MFAN's own tally. The December 19, 2025 failed funding package and the Hickenlooper/Bennet hold over NCAR are HIGH confidence, directly sourced to Fox News's report. The Antideficiency Act legal argument and the Kogan/Shriver quotes are HIGH confidence, directly sourced to MSNBC/ms.now's opinion coverage; the OMB back-pay-guidance deletion and the GSA/Interior notice-language comparison are HIGH confidence, directly sourced to Government Executive's dedicated report. A contemporaneous Trump quote about back pay and a specific NIOSH/National Park Service instance could not be confirmed on any single article and are not included.

title: DOGE Shut Down GSA's 18F Tech Unit; IRS Then Killed the Free Direct File Tax Program It Built
institution: General Services Administration (GSA) / Internal Revenue Service
status: Implemented -- 18F shuttered March 2025; IRS Direct File permanently discontinued, not available for Filing Season 2026
date_of_action: 2025-03 (18F shutdown) through 2025 (Direct File discontinued for the 2026 filing season)
what_changed: In February 2025, Elon Musk announced on social media that he had 'deleted' the team behind IRS Direct File, the free government tax-filing tool. In March 2025, DOGE shut down 18F entirely -- the roughly 90-person General Services Administration digital-services unit that had built or supported Direct File and other federal websites and digital tools for two decades. IRS staff assigned to Direct File were told in mid-March 2025 to stop developing it for the 2026 filing season, even though officials initially indicated the tool would stay operational through the 2025 season. AP reported on April 17, 2025 -- citing two people familiar with the decision -- that the administration planned to end Direct File outright; Republican lawmakers and commercial tax-preparation companies had pushed for the program's elimination, calling it a waste of taxpayer money despite existing free-filing alternatives being difficult to use. Amanda Renteria, CEO of Code for America (which had worked with the IRS on Direct File's state-integration systems), called the move 'a betrayal of public trust at precisely the time government should be demonstrating its ability to deliver basic services effectively.' **Direct File accepted 296,531 tax returns in the 2025 filing season, with 94% of surveyed users rating their experience 'excellent' or 'above average,' and had been offered in 25 states.** On November 3, 2025, IRS product manager Cindy Noe emailed those 25 partner states that 'IRS Direct File will not be available in Filing Season 2026. No launch date has been set for the future.' Treasury cited 'low participation and relatively high costs and burdens on the federal government,' estimating the program cost $41 million to operate for tax year 2024 -- at least $138 per tax return filed.

primary_proponent.name: Elon Musk / Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
primary_proponent.role: Musk publicly announced 18F's elimination and directed DOGE's cuts across GSA; IRS leadership implemented the subsequent Direct File shutdown
primary_proponent.note: Musk's own public statement -- that he had 'deleted' the team -- is the clearest on-the-record attribution for the initial action; the IRS's later, formal decision to end Direct File for 2026 followed directly from 18F's elimination and the staff stand-down order.

estimated_impact.summary: Direct File was the government's only free, IRS-run tax-filing option -- eliminating it pushes the roughly 300,000 users who filed through it in 2025 back toward commercial tax-prep software, which the IRS's own Free File partnership with private companies has historically served only a small fraction of eligible taxpayers.

title: GSA Gutted the Staff Responsible for 26,000 Federally Owned Artworks, Then Listed Buildings Holding Statutorily Protected Murals for Sale -- Prompting a Senate IG-Audit Request
institution: General Services Administration (GSA) -- Fine Arts Program / Art in Architecture Program, Public Buildings Service
status: Partial reprieve for one building only. GSA dropped the Cohen Building from its accelerated-disposal list in July 2026, and a House committee approved a bill on Sept. 15 to let it stay federal, but the 2025 sale law stands until that bill is enacted. No restoration of Fine Arts staff is reported.
date_of_action: 2025-03-11 (staff cuts and regional office closures first reported) through 2026-03-11 (Senate letter requesting GSA Inspector General audit)
what_changed: In March 2025, following Trump's Executive Order 14210 directing a Department of Government Efficiency-driven Reduction in Force, GSA's Fine Arts Program -- the small division responsible for preserving and tracking the federal government's collection of roughly 26,000 artworks, more than 23,000 of them New Deal-era pieces dating to the 1930s-40s -- was hit as at least five GSA regional offices were shuttered and more than half of its roughly three-dozen staff were placed on leave pending termination. By an October 2025 internal GSA briefing cited by U.S. senators, GSA's broader Public Buildings Service had lost 44% of its full-time employees in the reduction in force. Regional impact varied sharply: The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that the Mid-Atlantic Region 3 office alone lost at least 100 workers, including fine arts and preservation officers, project managers, communications specialists and engineers, leaving only about a quarter of its workforce in place. Simultaneously, GSA began listing federal properties for accelerated disposal -- 46 by February 18, 2026 -- some of which house Fine Arts Collection works including textiles, sculptures, and paintings. The clearest flashpoint is the Wilbur J. Cohen Building in Washington, D.C. (former Social Security Administration headquarters), which GSA listed for sale and which **contains statutorily protected New Deal murals by Ben Shahn ('The Meaning of Social Security'), Seymour Fogel, and Philip Guston, chemically bonded to the walls and unable to be removed without major cost and risk**. GSA has said it will seek preservation covenants with any buyer but has not detailed how it would enforce continued access, insurance, or maintenance once the building passes into private ownership. On March 11, 2026 -- exactly one year after the initial cuts were first reported -- Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (ranking member, Environment and Public Works) and Chuck Schumer sent GSA Administrator Ed Forst a formal document and information request, and separately asked GSA's own Inspector General to conduct an updated audit of the Fine Arts Program (the IG's last such audit was in 1994), citing the staffing cuts, the accelerated-disposal list, and the Cohen Building murals specifically as reasons for concern. The senators asked GSA to produce the documents by March 31, 2026; no public GSA response to either request, and no new Inspector General audit of the Fine Arts Program, had been identified as of September 2026. The Cohen Building's sale was itself required by law: Section 2312 of the Thomas R. Carper Water Resources Development Act of 2024, signed by President Biden on January 4, 2025 -- a provision The New Republic attributes to an amendment by Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) -- directs GSA to sell the building for fair market value no later than two years after its existing federal tenants vacate, so GSA alone cannot permanently halt the sale. At a Public Buildings Reform Board meeting on Thursday, June 25, 2026, Rich Butterworth, a senior analyst and adviser in GSA's Office of Real Property Utilization and Disposal, signaled that the agency might pull the Cohen Building from its disposal plans -- not over the murals, but because the building shares underground heating and electrical utilities with the adjacent Mary E. Switzer Memorial Federal Building, making it 'extremely expensive to replicate or sever those utilities'; 'unless we can solve that problem,' he said, 'that might be a building that's better reinvested in.' Mary Okin of the preservation group Living New Deal said the group remained concerned because the building was still on the accelerated-disposal list, but welcomed any public announcement that it would not be sold. On July 14, 2026, Reps. Dina Titus (D-Nev.) and Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas) introduced the PRESERVE Act (Protecting Resources and Ensuring Stewardship of Enduring Records of Visual Expression; H.R. 9689), which would require GSA to determine within 30 days of designating a property for disposal whether it contains protected artwork, notify Congress within another 30 days, convene an expert preservation committee no later than 90 days before any demolition or sale, post a public preservation plan, and certify that the art will stay publicly accessible after disposal; Titus said it would protect 'all of the 26,000 pieces of art in GSA's Fine Arts Collection.' Its cosponsors (Doggett, Chellie Pingree and Chrissy Houlahan) are all Democrats, it does not repeal the 2025 sale mandate, and its latest recorded action is referral to the House Transportation and Infrastructure and Oversight committees. Between July 20 and July 23, 2026, GSA removed the Cohen Building -- along with the Robert C. Weaver Federal Building (HUD headquarters) and the USDA South Building -- from its published accelerated-disposition list. On Tuesday, September 15, 2026, the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee approved without opposition a bill sponsored by Rep. Scott Perry (R-Pa.), the Strengthening Oversight in Public Buildings Act (H.R. 10305), that would let the Cohen Building remain in federal hands as 'swing space' for the sale or major renovation of other federal buildings, with spending on it capped at the savings those other projects produce; it still needs passage by both chambers and the President's signature. No reported step restores the Fine Arts Program staff cut in 2025.

title: GSA Briefly Published a 443-Property Sale List That Included a Sensitive CIA Facility, Then Pulled It the Next Day
institution: General Services Administration (GSA)
status: List retracted within a day; a smaller, scaled-back 'accelerated disposition' list released later without full details on the original larger list's fate
date_of_action: 2025-03-04 (list published) through 2025-03-05 (list removed)
what_changed: On March 4, 2025, GSA published a list of 443 federally owned properties -- comprising nearly 80 million rentable square feet and representing more than $8.3 billion in deferred recapitalization needs -- that the agency identified as 'not core to government operations' and intended to dispose of, as part of DOGE's broader push to shrink the federal government's real-estate footprint. **The list included the Parr-Franconia Warehouse Complex in Springfield, Virginia, a facility long rumored to house a clandestine CIA training site used for surveillance, hacking, and break-in tradecraft instruction, according to Wired.** Local officials and national-security experts immediately raised alarms about the security implications of publicly listing such a facility for sale, even if inadvertently. Facing that backlash -- and broader public and congressional pushback covering other listed sites, including FBI and Red Cross headquarters buildings -- GSA pulled the entire list on March 5, one day after publication, quietly scrubbing more than 120 properties including the Springfield site. An internal GSA email said the list would be republished later 'with adjustments to make it easier for stakeholders to understand the nuances of the assets listed,' citing 'an overwhelming amount of interest.' GSA subsequently released a smaller list of properties identified for an 'accelerated disposition' process, while withholding details about its plans for the larger original list.

estimated_impact.summary: A government agency briefly, publicly disclosed the location and disposal-candidacy of a facility reportedly used for sensitive CIA training activity, before pulling the listing within 24 hours -- an example of the disposal process moving fast enough to bypass the kind of security review that would normally catch this before publication.

title: DOGE-Era Cuts Shrank GSA's Tech Service 67% -- April 2025 Layoff Notices Rescinded After Court Order
institution: General Services Administration (GSA) -- Technology Transformation Services / U.S. Digital Service (USDS)
status: Partly reversed: GSA rescinded its April 2025 TTS layoff notices after a Dec. 17, 2025 court order; the USDS and 18F cuts stand, with TTS staff down 67% per GSA's IG. In Sept. 2026 TTS told some staff to submit resumes for reassignment or take deferred resignation or early retirement.
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (USDS mass firings) through 2025-12 (April TTS layoff notices rescinded after a 2025-12-17 court order)
what_changed: On February 14, 2025, roughly a third of U.S. Digital Service (USDS) staff -- about 50 people, by Wired's count -- were fired via an anonymous mass email as Elon Musk's DOGE took over the office, affecting civil servants who worked on Social Security modernization and on tax-filing, healthcare, student-aid, disaster-relief, and veterans-services technology. Wired reported that the firings took most of a USDS team working with the CDC, whose project lead, who had helped manage the CDC's disease-surveillance system, then resigned, warning that the program was 'probably going to die.' On February 25, 21 remaining USDS technologists resigned in protest, writing to the White House that they would not 'carry out or legitimize' DOGE's actions. On March 1, DOGE eliminated GSA's roughly 90-person 18F digital-services unit via an overnight email -- documented separately in this tracker's [[gsa-18f-shutdown-direct-file-2025]] entry on the resulting shutdown of the IRS's free Direct File tax tool. 18F workers told Wired that the cuts left the State Department's Bureau of Consular Affairs with 'significantly reduced capacity' for a new passport-application processing system 18F had been building, and stopped all development on a redesigned Weather.gov, the National Weather Service's public website. At a March 6 town hall, Technology Transformation Services (TTS) Director Thomas Shedd, a former Tesla engineer, told staff that TTS would shrink by 50% over the coming weeks, keeping only work required by statute, deemed critical, or among the administration's priorities, such as Login.gov, Cloud.gov, and FedRAMP. By March 7, Wired counted **around 200 technologists who had resigned or been fired** from GSA's technology teams and USDS since DOGE took them over. Employee frustration surfaced at acting GSA administrator Stephen Ehikian's first all-hands meeting on March 20, 2025, attended by hundreds in person and thousands more online: while the live event stayed polite, Wired reported, the accompanying chat turned hostile as Ehikian and other GSA leaders demonstrated a new internal generative-AI chatbot (GSAi), with over 100 staffers adding a 'thumbs up' to the comment 'We don't want an AI demo, we want answers to what is going on with [reductions in force]'; employees also cited lost access to critical software and the return-to-office mandate. On April 10, 2025, TTS began issuing reduction-in-force (RIF) notices: GSA sent approximately 130 notices of an intention to RIF to staff in the Office of the Integrated Award Environment (IAE, which runs core federal contracting systems), the Office of Regulatory and Oversight Systems, and parts of the Office of Solutions, while sparing FedRAMP, Login.gov, and Cloud.gov. A source familiar with GSA warned FedScoop that cutting more IAE staff 'could break all of federal contracting.' Ehikian left GSA in September 2025. On October 8, 2025, GSA's inspector general reported that, according to GSA human-resources data, **TTS's overall staff had fallen 67% since January 25, 2025**, and warned that its reduced staff and history of weak controls put TTS at risk of misspent money and degraded services for the agencies it serves; Shedd told the inspector general he believed TTS had made the most aggressive changes to meet workforce optimization mandates, due in part to its small size and political leadership. On December 17, 2025, U.S. District Judge Susan Illston, enforcing the November 2025 spending law that ended the government shutdown, barred the Education and State departments from carrying out any RIF through January 30, 2026, and ordered them, GSA, and the Small Business Administration to rescind RIFs carried out during the shutdown; the spending law itself barred federal agencies from carrying out layoffs through January 30. That week, Shedd told TTS staff that GSA was rescinding, for now, the April intent-to-RIF notices and would reassess workforce needs at the end of January; Nextgov/FCW reported that TTS staff did not appear to have received any communication about the notices during the shutdown, but GSA opted, for now, to rescind them as well. One GSA employee told Nextgov/FCW the notices had left about a hundred people under 'the daily threat of being fired' for eight months. Federal CIO Greg Barbaccia led TTS from February 2026, and by August 2026 Treasury CIO and DOGE alumnus Sam Corcos was acting TTS director. On September 23, 2026, Corcos emailed several TTS employees requiring them to submit resumes for 'potential reassignment' elsewhere in GSA, or to choose deferred resignation or voluntary early retirement by October 19.

estimated_impact.summary: Hollowed out the federal government's in-house digital-services capacity: USDS and 18F firings gutted a USDS team supporting a CDC disease-surveillance system, cut capacity on a State Department passport-processing system, and halted a redesigned Weather.gov, and GSA's Technology Transformation Services, which runs Login.gov, FedRAMP, Cloud.gov, and the contracting systems agencies use to buy goods and services, lost two-thirds of its staff, leaving it at risk of misspent money and degraded services, GSA's inspector general warned. About 130 more TTS staff spent eight months under layoff notices before GSA rescinded them after a December 2025 court order.
