title: RFK Jr.'s HHS Discarded Its Own Advisory Committee's Plant-Forward Recommendations for the 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines, Producing a Food Pyramid Nutrition Scientists Call 'Bizarre and Contradictory'
institution: Department of Health and Human Services / U.S. Department of Agriculture
status: The Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030 were finalized and released in January 2026. The final document kept the existing 10%-of-calories saturated-fat cap on the books while simultaneously promoting foods that make hitting that cap difficult to impossible, a contradiction nutrition scientists have publicly criticized since release; no revision had been announced as of this entry.
date_of_action: 2025-10 (RFK Jr. publicly previews the change) through 2026-01 (final guidelines released)
what_changed: In October 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told the National Governors Association that the upcoming 2025-2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans would take a 'common sense' approach and 'stress the need to eat saturated fats, dairy, good meat,' calling existing guidance favoring low-fat dairy over full-fat versions 'antiquated,' and separately praising fast-food chains that had switched their fryers from vegetable oil to beef tallow. This directly contradicted the statutorily-mandated Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee's own December 2024 scientific report, which had endorsed the existing recommendation to limit saturated fat to less than 10% of daily calories starting at age 2, replacing it with unsaturated (particularly polyunsaturated) fat -- a recommendation nutrition scientist Alison Steiber said rested on 'moderate to high' evidence linking excess saturated fat intake to negative health outcomes, including elevated risk of heart attack, stroke, and other cardiovascular disease. When HHS and USDA released the final 2025-2030 guidelines in January 2026, the document did not remove the 10% saturated-fat cap -- but it discarded the advisory committee's plant-forward food recommendations and instead featured a large ribeye steak prominently in the new food pyramid graphic, listed butter and beef tallow as 'healthy fats' cooking options, and encouraged full-fat dairy and red meat consumption. Nutrition scientists characterized the resulting document as internally contradictory: one told STAT News 'it's almost laughable that they kept the 10% limit for saturated fat while really pushing red meat and dairy,' another called following both recommendations simultaneously 'nearly impossible,' and a third said the guidelines would leave people trying to 'circle that square.'

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Publicly previewed and championed the saturated-fat-friendly framing months before the guidelines' release, explicitly calling the prior low-fat-dairy guidance 'antiquated'; the final document's retention of the numeric 10% cap alongside newly-emphasized high-saturated-fat foods suggests an internal compromise between Kennedy's stated preference and the advisory committee's underlying science, rather than a clean reversal of either.

estimated_impact.summary: The Dietary Guidelines for Americans **directly shape school lunch nutrition standards, federal nutrition-assistance program requirements (SNAP, WIC), and clinical dietary counseling nationwide**; nutrition scientists warn the resulting internally-contradictory guidance -- keeping a saturated-fat limit while promoting foods that make it difficult to meet -- will confuse rather than inform public health practice and clinical guidance built on the guidelines.

title: HHS Moved to Fire Most of Its ~5,200 Probationary Staff, Offered $25,000 Buyouts Agency-Wide, and Eliminated Its Entire HIV/AIDS and Infectious Disease Policy Office
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
status: Completed: the Feb. 2025 probationary purge, buyout offer, OIDP elimination, CDC STD/hepatitis lab closures, and June 2025 HIV-vaccine funding cuts; ProPublica counted 20,500+ departures by August 2025. Unresolved: the FY2026 HIV-funding standoff and PACHA's apparent membership gap.
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (probationary terminations) through 2025-04-01 (HIV/AIDS and infectious-disease office layoffs take effect)
what_changed:
On February 14, 2025 -- the day after Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was sworn in as HHS Secretary -- HHS moved to fire most of its roughly 5,200 probationary employees agency-wide (including nearly 1,300 at the CDC alone), notifying many that morning and placing them on four weeks of paid administrative leave. Asked about the cuts, HHS communications director Andrew Nixon said in a statement to the Associated Press that 'HHS is following the Administration's guidance and taking action to support the President's broader efforts to restructure and streamline the federal government,' neither confirming nor disputing the figures. Mother Jones reported the purge as part of a broader climate of pressured departures inside HHS, warning it was destabilizing the agency's infectious-disease response and public-health research capacity at a moment of active bird flu and measles outbreaks. The following month, HHS under Kennedy's direction offered buyouts of up to $25,000 to most of its roughly 80,000 employees -- the workforce responsible for researching disease, inspecting food, and administering Medicare and Medicaid -- an offer hundreds of employees accepted; PBS reported no immediate comment from HHS on the offer.

Separately, on March 29, 2025, Forbes and CBS News reported Kennedy planned to lay off the entire Office of Infectious Disease and HIV/AIDS Policy (OIDP), the HHS office that led the 'Let's Get Real' childhood-vaccination-hesitancy campaign and coordinated the cross-agency Ending the HIV Epidemic initiative; the office's elimination took effect around April 1, 2025 and was confirmed by the Washington Blade and multiple HIV-policy organizations, with OIDP's Executive Director of the President's Advisory Council on HIV/AIDS (PACHA) among those let go and remaining HIV functions folded into a separate HHS treatment program over the objections of HIV-policy advocates, who noted prevention, surveillance, and treatment are distinct functions. CDC's separate Division of HIV Prevention was eliminated around the same time. The office cuts came bundled inside Kennedy's broader restructuring plan, which HHS itself announced on March 27, 2025: 10,000 job cuts on top of roughly 10,000 earlier departures through buyouts and early retirement, shrinking its workforce from 82,000 to 62,000 (about a quarter), and consolidating its 28 divisions into 15, as NPR and BioPharma Dive reported. This entry documents that reduction's early-2025 phase (the probationary purge, the buyout offer, and the OIDP/HIV office elimination specifically).

The same restructuring wave also eliminated CDC's specialized STD- and hepatitis-testing laboratories effective on or around April 1, 2025 -- CBS News reported all 27 scientists in the nation's only lab performing advanced genetic testing for hepatitis outbreaks were let go, along with the only U.S. lab capable of testing and tracking antibiotic-resistant ('super') gonorrhea; staff were locked out of building and email access before they could safely shut down lab equipment or store hazardous materials, and incoming specimens from state and clinical labs nationwide continued arriving with no remaining staff to process them. The Association of Public Health Laboratories wrote to Kennedy asking that the laid-off employees be reinstated; the Washington Post independently corroborated the lab closures in an April 18, 2025 report.

The Guardian reported April 21, 2025 that the same restructuring eliminated all 28 scientists at CDC's STI reference lab -- which tracked chlamydia, syphilis, and gonorrhea and was the only U.S. lab capable of PCR testing for syphilis -- a figure close to but not identical with CBS's 27-scientist hepatitis-lab count above, likely reflecting overlapping but not fully identical staff counts across the CDC's related infectious-disease laboratories eliminated in the same action. The closure's timing drew particular alarm because it coincided with Wisconsin health officials announcing a 1,450% rise in the state's syphilis cases since 2019.

Additional detail on the scale of the April 2025 restructuring phase: the Guardian reported on April 2, 2025 that the cuts hit programs on black lung disease, infertility research, tobacco control, and entire divisions handling environmental health and climate-related health response -- additional named programs cut within the same restructuring this entry already documents, alongside maternal and child health programs Politico separately reported cut around April 7, 2025. That same week, Kennedy told ABC News some cut programs, including the CDC's childhood lead-poisoning prevention program, had been wrongly eliminated and would be reinstated; Politico separately reported Kennedy's claim that 20% of purged staff would be rehired was not supported by any rehiring plan sources were aware of.

In May 2025, HHS resumed efforts to terminate thousands of probationary employees who had been placed on paid administrative leave following a court-ordered pause earlier in February, restarting a strand of the same early-2025 purge this entry documents rather than representing a new, separate action.

The office-elimination and staffing cuts documented above were followed by cuts to HIV vaccine research itself and a further FY2026 budget fight. CBS News reported around June 3, 2025 that HHS was terminating NIH funding for two major HIV-vaccine research efforts dating to 2012 -- the Duke Human Vaccine Institute and Scripps Research Institute -- and pausing Moderna's HIV vaccine clinical trials conducted through NIH's HIV Vaccine Trials Network. An HHS spokesperson said the department would instead 'go with currently available approaches to eliminate HIV,' citing '27 separate programs that address HIV/AIDS' that had spent a combined $7.5 billion. NIH separately changed how it accounts for multi-year HIV vaccine grants -- counting a grant's full multi-year cost against a single fiscal year rather than spreading it across the grant's life -- making such awards substantially harder to approve going forward. Scripps immunologist Dennis Burton called the timing 'terrible,' saying vaccine research was 'beginning to get close' and that shuttered experiments and displaced researchers could not simply resume once funding returned.

The restructuring's next major phase came via litigation: after a federal judge's May 2025 preliminary injunction had blocked planned RIFs at 22 agencies including HHS, the Supreme Court stayed that injunction on July 8, 2025 in an 8-1 ruling (while explicitly declining to rule on the RIFs' underlying legality), clearing the way for HHS to finalize the separations of employees who had been on paid administrative leave -- HHS notified affected employees they were officially separated effective July 14, 2025. By late August 2025, ProPublica's cumulative analysis found more than 20,500 HHS employees, or roughly 18% of the department's workforce, had left or been pushed out since January 2025 -- an analysis ProPublica itself described as an undercount, since it excluded employees still on administrative leave awaiting separation.

Later, NBC News reported the Trump administration's FY2026 budget request sought to eliminate CDC's HIV-prevention division outright (a budget-level formalization of the division's operational elimination already documented above), while House Republicans proposed nearly $2 billion in combined HIV-related cuts, including $525 million (20%) from the Ryan White Program that provides care and treatment for low-income people with HIV; the Senate's own proposal would keep HIV funding essentially flat, setting up a legislative standoff. An April 2025 analysis in the journal AIDS and Behavior by David R. Holtgrave of the New York State Department of Health projected that eliminating CDC's HIV-prevention efforts specifically would produce **more than 213,300 additional HIV cases and over 10,600 additional HIV-related deaths between 2025 and 2030**, at an estimated $52.4 billion in added lifetime medical costs -- a more specific, differently-sourced estimate than the amfAR 143,000-infection projection (see Estimated impact), which covers broader federal HIV funding cuts rather than the CDC prevention-division elimination specifically.

A further, distinct round of cuts hit CDC specifically in October 2025: amid the federal government shutdown, CDC sent roughly 1,300 layoff notices, then reversed about 740 of them within days after public backlash, attributing the overreach to a 'coding error' -- the reinstated staff included employees responding to active measles and Ebola outbreaks, global-health office personnel, and nearly all staff who compile the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. This October 2025 CDC episode is a separate incident from the coding-error RIF documented in another entry in this database (a different April 2025 NIH/NINDS action).

PACHA's member roster, separate from its HHS staff, was affected too. Its member and staff listings disappeared from HIV.gov around February 1, 2025, and Reuters reported April 9, 2025 that the administration planned to remove all of the council's remaining members with no announced timeline for replacements; HHS told Reuters this was 'common practice' when a new administration takes office. Despite that, individuals still identifying with PACHA remained publicly vocal months later: on December 5, 2025, ABC News reported council members warning that House FY2026 appropriations proposals would eliminate domestic and global HIV funding, cut over $1 billion from CDC, and gut the Ryan White Program, estimating full funding could save up to $100 billion in healthcare costs by 2030 -- a warning the White House dismissed, with spokesman Kush Desai calling PACHA 'a largely symbolic body whose members are engaging in another useless PR exercise.'

The exact membership status of PACHA across 2025 is not fully clear from sourcing reviewed: other reporting (Fierce Healthcare) describes the council as not back in regular business until more than a year after the initial firings, and Executive Order 14354 (September 29, 2025) continued PACHA's charter, with a Federal Register notice soliciting new member nominations as late as June 2026 -- suggesting a prolonged gap in formal membership even as some individuals continued speaking publicly in the council's name.

title: HHS Froze $10 Billion in Childcare/Family-Aid Funding to Five Democratic-Led States, Then Rescinded It
institution: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services / Administration for Children and Families
status: Reversed (HHS rescinded the freeze, July 2026)
date_of_action: 2026-01-06 (freeze announced) through 2026-07-14 (rescinded)
what_changed: On January 6, 2026, HHS announced it was freezing roughly $10 billion in appropriated funding across three programs administered by its Administration for Children and Families: approximately $7.4 billion in Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) cash-assistance funds (including over $1 billion for Illinois alone), approximately $2.4 billion in Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) childcare subsidies, and approximately $840-870 million in Social Services Block Grant (SSBG) funding. The freeze applied only to five states: California, Colorado, Illinois, Minnesota, and New York -- **all Democratic-led, together home to roughly 23.7% of the children nationally who rely on federal child-care subsidies**. HHS cited 'serious concerns about widespread fraud' in state-administered programs without publicly providing supporting evidence; the action followed a high-profile federal fraud probe centered on Minnesota's social-services sector, which HHS extended to the other four states without documenting comparable fraud findings there. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and other state officials characterized the freeze as political retaliation targeting Democratic-led states specifically. The five states sued in the Southern District of New York (State of New York v. Administration for Children and Families); on February 6, 2026, Judge Vernon S. Broderick granted a preliminary injunction blocking HHS from restricting the states' access to CCDF, TANF, and SSBG funding. After roughly six months of litigation, HHS formally rescinded the freeze in a letter sent to the states in July 2026, ending the funding restriction entirely.

title: HHS Reportedly Moves About $12 Million From the Office of Minority Health to Pay for Kennedy's Security as the Office Cancels 16 Grants
institution: Department of Health and Human Services, Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health, Office of Minority Health
status: HHS's quoted response did not address the reported $12 million transfer; it denies the grant cuts were tied to security. The 16 grants remain canceled, none reinstated. A separate $5.1 million minority health rescission was withheld to its Sept. 30 expiry and is challenged in a seven-state suit.
date_of_action: 2026 (transfer reported to congressional appropriators earlier in the year; 16 grant terminations Aug. 25, 2026; transfer reported publicly Sept. 22, 2026)
what_changed: The Department of Health and Human Services told congressional appropriators earlier in 2026 that it was moving about $12 million from its Office of Minority Health to help cover the rising cost of security for Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., The Wall Street Journal reported on September 22, 2026, citing people familiar with the matter and a document it reviewed. According to the Journal's sources, Kennedy's security cost grew from roughly $10 million in fiscal 2025 to $17 million in fiscal 2026, while protection for previous HHS secretaries, provided by agents of the department's inspector general, cost about $5 million a year. Kennedy is instead protected by the U.S. Marshals Service. The Journal's sources said the secretary's office had a large pool of discretionary money it could have used, and that HHS took $12 million from the minority health office, well above the roughly $7 million rise in security costs, partly because the secretary's office had been hit by across-the-board budget cuts. HHS has also asked Congress for an additional $14 million in next year's budget for "enhanced physical security of HHS Headquarters and its staff," according to Word In Black. The Office of Minority Health, established in 1986 after research showed that Black infants were more likely to die than white infants and that Black Americans lived shorter lives, funds research and programs aimed at closing racial and ethnic health gaps; the Journal put its annual budget at about $74 million. The administration tried to eliminate the office in 2025 and proposed cutting its funding by 40%, but Congress kept it funded, and the President's fiscal 2027 budget again proposes slashing it by 40%. On August 25, 2026, the office sent termination letters to 16 county, state and nonprofit grantees, more than half its existing grants, saying the awards no longer advance "current agency priorities" and that future awards should address "the root causes of infertility," including low sperm count, low testosterone and erectile dysfunction, or promote "regular physical activity and exercise." The letters were signed by Eric West, acting chief grants officer at the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Health, and Mahyar Mofidi, deputy assistant secretary for minority health. **The 16 grants, worth $38 million over four years, paid for postpartum home nurse visits for new mothers, work to reduce infant mortality, cancer and chronic-disease screenings, fresh produce deliveries, first-responder suicide prevention and obesity prevention among Native American youth**; the grantees had received two years of funding, and the Journal reported that the programs received about $9 million last year. The University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences said its program to reduce infant and maternal mortality among Black families in the Arkansas Delta will likely end without the grant. Separately, on September 25, 2026, the White House's pocket-rescission package proposed cancelling $5,098,000 of the $625 million appropriated for HHS General Departmental Management in fiscal 2026, of which Congress had directed $75 million to the Office of Minority Health in report language, saying the office "targets funding via grants to specific race and sex-based groups"; that money was withheld through its September 30, 2026 expiration, which GAO said the Impoundment Control Act does not allow, and California and six other states listed it among the impoundments they challenged in a September 30 suit in federal court in San Francisco. HHS spokeswoman Emily Hilliard told the Journal that the grant decisions "reflect HHS priorities and programmatic assessments -- not the Secretary's security needs," and that "Secretary Kennedy faces a security environment that differs significantly from that of previous HHS secretaries. His protection reflects the threats he faces, his extensive travel, and the security required for him to safely carry out his duties nationwide." Members of Congress objected: Rep. title: HHS Clawed Back $11.4 Billion in Public Health Grants and Cut 20,000 Jobs, Shuttering Vaccine Clinics as Measles Surged
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
status: Cuts took effect late March/early April 2025 and were not reversed as of this entry's writing; downstream state and local program terminations (clinic closures, layoffs, data-system suspensions) continued to be reported through mid-2025.
date_of_action: 2025-03-25 (grant terminations announced) through 2025-04-01 (10,000-employee HHS layoffs take effect)
what_changed: In late March 2025, HHS under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. terminated $11.4 billion in COVID-era public health grants that state and local health departments had relied on for infectious-disease surveillance, laboratory upgrades, staff, and information technology; HHS said the money was originally allocated for COVID-19 response (testing, vaccination, and community health worker hiring) and was no longer needed since the pandemic emergency had ended. More than $2 billion of the total specifically targeted Immunization and Vaccines for Children grants, which fund vaccine delivery to uninsured children. On April 1, 2025, the administration separately laid off roughly 10,000 full-time HHS employees as part of a restructuring that, combined with earlier voluntary departures and early retirements, shrank the department's workforce from approximately 82,000 to approximately 62,000 -- a reduction of about 20,000 positions across HHS's constituent agencies including the CDC, FDA, and NIH; former FDA Commissioner Dr. Robert Califf said the agency as Americans knew it was now 'finished,' having lost nearly all of its traditionally nonpolitical scientific experts in food, drugs, vaccines, and medical devices. The grant terminations had immediate, documented local consequences: in Texas -- the state hit hardest by the 2025 measles outbreak -- federal grants for immunization and infectious-disease response were terminated, **halting vaccine clinics used to combat the outbreak**; Jackie Griffith, a 60-year-old registered nurse at Collin County Health Care Clinic, was terminated after the funding disappeared. Dallas County canceled 50 community vaccination events. Minnesota lost more than $220 million in federal funds and laid off 170 employees, while its immunization registry lost funding for planned upgrades, leaving what officials described as one of the most outdated vaccine-tracking systems in the country; Pennsylvania and other states similarly reported being unable to operate or upgrade critical vaccine-tracking systems. Washington state furloughed or laid off 46 workers and suspended its Care-a-Van mobile clinic program, eliminating 104 planned clinic events expected to administer roughly 2,000 vaccines to vulnerable populations. New Hampshire's Kayla Hogan, who had been onboarding clinics onto a state vaccine data system, saw that project put in jeopardy. California reported it could no longer guarantee childhood vaccine access to millions of children, and Indiana eliminated two school-based nursing positions dedicated to vaccinations.

title: HHS reclassifies career civil servants under revived Schedule F, stripping removal protections
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (including CDC science positions)
status: Ongoing -- OPM published its final Schedule Policy/Career rule in February 2026; HHS implementation continues incrementally. The underlying litigation (PEER v. OPM, D. Md., Judge Xinis) remains stalled at the pleading stage on an unresolved motion to amend/dismiss, not proceeding to summary judgment as a prior recheck mistakenly reported. A June 2026 executive order separately converted roughly 8,000 federal positions government-wide into the same status.
date_of_action: 2026-02 (OPM final rule) through 2026-05 (HHS supervisor memo)
what_changed: Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0343): OPM's February 2026 final rule followed a proposed rulemaking published in the Federal Register April 23, 2025 ('Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service'), which drew a record 40,500 public comments during its (twice-extended, through June 7, 2025) comment period, 94% of them opposed. During that comment period, the Guardian reported May 18, 2025 that economists and statisticians at agencies including the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Bureau of Economic Analysis specifically warned the proposed rule could let Trump remove career staff seen as producing data that contradicted his political narrative -- flagging, as a contemporaneous and related concern, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's own public suggestion (first reported in March 2025) that government spending be excluded from official GDP calculations to make the metric 'more transparent,' a framing critics said was designed to obscure the economic impact of DOGE-driven federal spending cuts. This early, statistics-agency-specific warning about the rule predates, and was not folded into, its actual February 2026 implementation via HHS/CDC documented below; sourcing reviewed did not confirm any BLS or BEA positions were in fact reclassified under the final rule specifically. The Office of Personnel Management issued a final rule in February 2026 implementing 'Schedule Policy/Career' (the revived Schedule F framework), estimated to affect roughly 50,000 federal positions government-wide by stripping them of traditional competitive-service protections and making them removable at will, without advance notice or the right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board. A May 2026 memo sent to HHS supervisors announced that over 100 HHS positions were being moved into this category, with CDC separately **reclassifying a number of science-focused roles -- including research biologists, epidemiologists, and other health scientists -- into the same at-will status**. Trump subsequently signed an executive order on June 3, 2026 formally converting roughly 8,000 federal positions government-wide into Schedule Policy/Career. Update 2026-08-17: Implementation continues incrementally rather than in one mass action -- CDC officials have said several hundred GS-15 positions (not thousands) were 'tentatively identified' for the initial reclassification tranche, with additional rounds expected to follow. Separately, the framework faces active litigation: AFGE, AFSCME, the AFL-CIO, PEER, and Democracy Forward filed a Second Amended Complaint on March 4, 2026 expanding their challenge to the entire Schedule Policy/Career framework; as of the most recent reporting reviewed, a motion for a preliminary injunction in that case remained under advisement following an April 30, 2026 hearing, with the case proceeding to summary judgment on the merits regardless of the injunction's outcome. No court has yet ruled on the framework's legality. Update (2026-08-30 recheck): identified the specific underlying litigation as PEER v. OPM, D. Md., before Judge Xinis (an Obama appointee). AFGE re-joined this case (voluntarily dismissing a separate D.D.C. suit) alongside AFSCME, the AFL-CIO, PEER, and Democracy Forward, and the coalition filed a Second Amended Complaint March 4, 2026 expanding the challenge to the entire Schedule Policy/Career framework -- the underlying executive order and OPM's final rule itself, not merely HHS's implementation of it. Judge Xinis paused the government's motion-to-dismiss response deadline March 12, 2026 pending resolution of the amendment motion. Separately, on June 3, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order converting roughly 8,000 federal positions into Schedule Policy/Career status government-wide -- the first confirmed actual conversions since the rule was finalized, corroborated by NPR and Government Executive, and not limited to HHS. CORRECTION (2026-08-31 recheck): this entry's prior update (2026-08-30) stated, at MODERATE confidence, that a summary-judgment motion was due August 18, 2026 ahead of an October 16, 2026 hearing, attributing those dates to a search-engine synthesis of CRS Legal Sidebar LSB11412 that could not be independently fetched at the time. This recheck fetched both the CRS sidebar itself (via its everycrsreport.com mirror, since congress.gov continues to block direct retrieval) and the case's own docket via the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse. Neither source supports the prior claim: the CRS sidebar's text on this case goes no further than noting PEER and four other unions filed the Maryland suit, without any summary-judgment or hearing dates; and the Clearinghouse's docket summary, current through August 31, 2026, shows no summary-judgment briefing schedule ever entered. The docket's actual most recent activity is a March 12, 2026 order pausing the government's motion-to-dismiss response deadline pending resolution of plaintiffs' motion to amend (filed March 4, 2026, the same Second Amended Complaint this entry already documents), followed only by a May 21, 2026 motion to withdraw as counsel for one government attorney, granted June 18, 2026 -- procedural housekeeping, not merits progress. In other words, five months after the coalition's amended complaint, the case remains stalled at the pleading stage: the motion to amend and the paused motion to dismiss are both still unresolved, and no summary-judgment schedule exists yet for a court to have set a hearing against. This corrects the entry's own prior claim rather than reflecting a new development in the litigation.

title: HHS Fired Nearly All Staff Administering Title X, the Nation's Only Federal Family Planning Program, Then Delayed and Trimmed Its Funding
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Office of Population Affairs (OPA)
status: Title X funding was eventually restored around April 2026, near-level with 2025 amounts, but only after a severely compressed application window and delays past the program's normal renewal date; the administration has separately signaled a substantive shift in the program's focus and plans to reduce 2027 funding.
date_of_action: 2025-10-10 (Office of Population Affairs staff RIF'd) through 2026-04-10 (Title X funding restored, delayed and reduced for 2027)
what_changed: On the night of October 10, 2025 -- amid the broader shutdown-era reduction-in-force campaign this database separately tracks in government-shutdown-federal-worker-hardship-rif-2025.json -- nearly the entire staff of HHS's Office of Population Affairs (OPA), the small office that administers Title X, the only domestic federal family planning program, lost access to their government email and laptop accounts simultaneously. Reduction-in-force notices were sent to affected employees via the same government email accounts they could no longer access, leaving them unable to confirm their own termination status; five days later, on October 15, HR confirmed the RIF. Of OPA's approximately 50 employees, only one remained -- a Commissioned Corps officer whose termination required separate processing. As one policy expert put it, 'If there's no one who works at the Office of Population Affairs, there's no one to administer the Title X family planning program,' which **serves more than 2.8 million low-income and uninsured patients annually through thousands of clinic sites nationwide, providing contraception, STI testing, cancer screenings, and other reproductive health care**. Title X grants operate on five-year funding cycles with the then-current cycle extending through March 31, 2026, and OPA staff would normally have spent the fall and winter months reviewing clinics' continuation applications -- a process left without any staff to carry it out. The shutdown-ending continuing resolution in November 2025 invalidated shutdown-era RIFs government-wide (see the sibling entry above for the mechanism), but Title X funding remained in disarray into 2026: HHS delayed the normal fall application-opening timeline, ultimately giving clinics just one week (starting March 13, 2026) to submit continuation applications -- compared to the months clinics normally have -- leaving many grantees uncertain about their budgets past the program's typical April 1 renewal date. Funding was ultimately released only days after that deadline, in early April 2026, at levels roughly comparable to 2025. Separately, NBC News reported the administration was shifting the program's stated focus away from birth control access. Looking forward, HHS has indicated it plans to make up to $257 million available through Title X for fiscal year 2027, down from approximately $286 million in recent years -- a real, if smaller-scale, funding reduction layered on top of the disruption already documented above.

title: Trump Proposed Eliminating the HOME Investment Partnerships Program, a $38B Affordable-Housing Lifeline for Rural Communities
institution: HUD -- HOME Investment Partnerships Program
status: Proposed -- House Republicans' FY2026 budget proposal excluded HOME funding at Trump's request; not yet enacted as of this entry's creation
date_of_action: 2025-08 through 2025-09 (budget proposal reporting)
what_changed: Trump proposed eliminating the HOME Investment Partnerships Program, and House Republicans overseeing federal budget negotiations left it unfunded in their FY2026 budget proposal. HOME is a HUD block-grant program that has spent more than $38 billion nationwide since its creation, filling funding gaps and attracting additional private investment to acquire, build, and repair affordable homes; it has helped build or repair more than 1.3 million affordable homes over three decades, including at least 540,000 in congressional districts that are rural or significantly rural. Housing experts and state housing agencies said eliminating the program **would set back tens of thousands of future affordable-housing developments nationwide, hitting Appalachian towns and rural counties** -- where government aid is comparatively sparse and private investors are few -- especially hard, since HOME often fills financing gaps no other program addresses in those markets. Sen. Sherrod Brown, ranking member of the Senate Banking Committee, publicly criticized the proposal as slashing housing assistance for low-income urban and rural communities alike.

title: House Passes Agriculture Spending Bill Cutting WIC Fruit-and-Vegetable Benefits for 5.4 Million Women and Children
institution: U.S. House of Representatives / USDA Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC)
status: Passed the House 213-210 on June 4, 2026; the Senate has not acted, and its Agriculture markup was postponed twice. A stopgap signed Sept. 2, 2026 funds the government, including WIC, at FY2026 levels through Dec. 11. The House's WIC cut is not law.
date_of_action: 2026-06-04 (House floor vote)
what_changed: On June 4, 2026, the House passed H.R. 8646, the fiscal year 2027 Agriculture-FDA appropriations bill, by a 213-210 vote, with five Republicans voting against and four Democrats (Reps. Don Davis, Adam Gray, Vicente Gonzalez, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez) voting for it, providing the margin of passage. Republicans said the bill would trim about 1.5% from federal agriculture spending. It funds WIC at $8.0 billion, $200 million below the $8.2 billion enacted for fiscal 2026; the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP) warned that could force the program to turn away eligible families for the first time in three decades if food costs or participation rise. It also cuts WIC's Cash Value Benefit for fruits and vegetables, setting it at 267% of the fiscal 2020 amount for children and 428% for women, which the Food Research & Action Center calculated as a 10 percent cut; Newsweek put current monthly amounts at about $26 for children, $48 for pregnant and postpartum women, and $52 for breastfeeding women. CBPP estimated the cut would take **over $141 million a year in fruit and vegetable benefits from nearly 5.4 million toddlers, preschoolers, and pregnant and postpartum WIC participants**. The bill also fails to make WIC's virtual service options, including phone appointments, permanent; CBPP noted the waivers allowing them could expire as soon as September 30, 2026. This is the second year in a row House Republicans sought these cuts: the FY2026 agriculture appropriations, enacted November 12, 2025 as part of the shutdown-ending minibus (P.L. 119-37), fully funded WIC and rejected the fruit-and-vegetable cuts the House had proposed for that year. In the Senate, the Appropriations Committee set a full-committee markup of its FY2027 Agriculture bill for June 4, 2026, marked it "to be rescheduled," then postponed the rescheduled June 25 markup after committee leadership failed to reach a bipartisan agreement on overall spending levels; as of late September 2026 the committee's calendar showed no markup held. Instead, Congress passed a stopgap: the Senate approved a continuing resolution 90-6 on August 8, the House passed it 370-48 on September 1, and the President signed it (H.R. 6500) on September 2, 2026. It funds the government at FY2026 levels through December 11, 2026 and lets WIC spend at the rate needed to maintain participation, so the House-passed WIC cuts have not taken effect and are not law.

primary_proponent.role: House majority controlling the agriculture appropriations process
primary_proponent.note: The bill passed with a narrow, largely party-line House majority; its ultimate fate depends on Senate action, and this entry should be rechecked once the Senate acts or the fiscal year appropriations process concludes.

estimated_impact.summary: If enacted, the House bill would cut by about 10 percent the fruit-and-vegetable benefit that low-income pregnant and postpartum women and young children use to buy fresh produce, taking over $141 million a year in produce purchases from nearly 5.4 million WIC participants during a critical developmental window. It would also fund WIC $200 million below the FY2026 level, which CBPP warns could force the program to turn away eligible families for the first time in three decades if food costs or participation rise, and it lets virtual appointments lapse, pushing families back to in-person clinic visits. None of this has taken effect: a stopgap through December 11, 2026 keeps WIC at FY2026 levels.

estimated_impact.caveat: The $141 million and 5.4 million figures are CBPP's own estimates for 2027, and the 10 percent figure is FRAC's; both groups oppose the cut. The bill is not law: the Senate has not acted, and the September 2026 stopgap keeps WIC at FY2026 levels through December 11, so the Senate or a final bill could drop or change these provisions. The figures do not capture health or developmental effects, the cost of any families turned away, or the effect of losing virtual services. Republicans frame the package as a modest 1.5% agriculture-spending trim, not a targeted cut to nutrition aid, and House agriculture appropriations subcommittee chair Andy Harris said that "with lowered participation estimates and increased carryover funding, $8 billion will fully fund the program."

The $141 million and 5.4 million figures are CBPP estimates (made on the April 2026 subcommittee draft, whose benefit formula the passed bill kept); the 10 percent size of the benefit cut is FRAC's calculation. Per-recipient figures of $52 to $13 a month for breastfeeding mothers and $26 to $10 for children do not match this bill's formula and should not be attached to it. This entry concerns the FY2027 cycle, not the FY2026 cycle resolved in WIC's favor in November 2025; the two years' fights involve similar figures and actors and could be conflated. The Senate markup history comes from the Appropriations Committee's hearings calendar; the stopgap's passage and signing from NACo, the enrolled text of H.R. 6500, and the White House signing notice. title: Trump Administration Cuts Funding for the Nation's 50-Year Acid Rain Monitoring Program at Hubbard Brook
institution: National Science Foundation (funder of the Hubbard Brook Long-Term Ecological Research site)
status: The Likens rainwater-acidity monitoring grant cut reported in March 2025 remains in effect and has not been restored. The separate, larger proposed FY2026 NSF budget cut (55-57%) that once threatened Hubbard Brook and up to 26 LTER sites nationwide was rejected by Congress, which funded NSF at $8.75 billion instead -- about 22.5% above the administration's request. No sourcing reviewed confirms Hubbard Brook's specific LTER line item was preserved beyond that agency-wide topline.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (reported)
what_changed: Dr. Gene Likens, the ecologist who co-discovered acid rain in the U.S. through research launched in 1963 at the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest in New Hampshire, confirmed in March 2025 that the Trump administration had **cut federal funding for his continuous rainwater-acidity monitoring program -- one of the longest unbroken datasets of its kind in the world, running since 1976**. The cut comes as EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin's EPA has targeted dozens of air-quality rules for rollback, including limits on sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, the two pollutants that cause acid rain (several of these rollbacks are tracked separately in this database's Corporate Deregulation tracker). Likens warned that defunding the monitoring itself compounds the risk of the emissions rollbacks: 'If the monitoring is disrupted or discontinued, we won't know what is changing.' Separately, and not conflated with the already-executed monitoring-program cut above, the administration's proposed FY2026 budget requested a 55% reduction to the National Science Foundation (to roughly $4 billion), reporting on which noted the cut could force the closure of up to 26 Long-Term Ecological Research sites nationwide, including Hubbard Brook itself -- a distinct, larger, and as of reporting reviewed still-proposed (not enacted) threat to the site's broader research funding beyond the specific acid-rain monitoring grant already cut. Update 2026-08-17: The proposed FY2026 NSF budget cut described above did not take effect. Congress enacted the FY2026 Commerce-Justice-Science appropriations act (P.L. 119-74, H.R. 6938) on 2026-01-23, providing NSF $8.75 billion -- roughly 22.5% more than the administration's FY2026 budget request and a decline of only about 3.4% from FY2025 levels, rejecting the proposed ~55-57% reduction that had put up to 26 LTER sites at risk. This entry's original, already-executed cut to Likens' specific rainwater-monitoring grant, reported in March 2025, is unaffected by this correction and remains in effect as originally documented.

estimated_impact.caveat: This entry documents the specific, already-executed cut to Likens' rainwater-monitoring program reported in March 2025 -- that cut has not been reversed. It does not include dollar figures for that specific grant, which were not identified in sourcing reviewed. The separate, larger FY2026 NSF budget-reduction proposal this entry previously tracked as a distinct, unresolved risk was rejected by Congress via the enacted FY2026 CJS appropriations act (see status/what_changed above); that risk should no longer be described as pending. No source reviewed confirms the LTER program or Hubbard Brook's specific line item was preserved beyond the agency-wide topline, so avoid asserting the 26-site closure risk is fully and specifically resolved, only that the proposed agency-wide cut that would have driven it did not happen.

The $8.75B enacted NSF total and the 22.5%-above-request figure are corroborated across the American Astronomical Society, Chemistry World, and CRS report R48783 (via congress.gov). Re-verified 2026-08-30: no material change -- no reporting found confirming Likens' March 2025 monitoring-grant cut has been restored. Re-verified 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 49): no material change -- no reporting found on Likens' grant status or a new FY2027 NSF/LTER budget threat.

title: HUD's Proposed $33B Cut and Rental-Aid Block Grant Was Rejected by Congress; Two Separate Court Injunctions Blocked Its Bid to Defund Fair Housing Groups
institution: Department of Housing and Urban Development
status: Budget-restructuring proposal rejected: Congress's final FY2026 THUD appropriations act (signed February 3, 2026) increased HUD rental-assistance funding rather than cutting it and did not adopt the block-grant conversion. Fair Housing Initiatives Program (FHIP) defunding blocked twice by federal courts, most recently by a permanent-structure injunction in August 2026; no further HUD appeal or renewed defunding attempt identified as of this entry's last-verified date.
date_of_action: 2025-02-27 (first FHIP grant terminations) through 2026-08-27 (second federal injunction); FY2026 budget proposal released 2025-05, rejected by Congress by February 2026
what_changed: On February 27, 2025, HUD terminated 78 Fair Housing Initiatives Program grants -- worth roughly $30 million and supporting more than 75 fair housing organizations nationwide -- midstream, citing a DOGE determination that the grants were 'incompatible' with executive orders because they contained language addressing 'DEI.' U.S. District Judge Richard G. Stearns issued a temporary restraining order on March 26, 2025, finding the terminations likely violated the Administrative Procedure Act and ordering HUD to reinstate the funding; the Massachusetts Fair Housing Center alone **had lost $1.3 million, roughly half its annual budget, before the order**. In May 2025, the administration's FY2026 budget request proposed cutting HUD's overall funding by $32.9 billion, including a $26.7 billion (roughly 40%) reduction to federal rental assistance that housing advocates said would effectively end Section 8 and other voucher programs; rather than administering rental aid directly, the proposal would have converted it into a state-run 'State Rental Assistance Program' block grant with a two-year cap on assistance for non-disabled adults. The National Alliance to End Homelessness warned the proposal would eliminate funding for 166,000 permanent supportive housing units even as homelessness had risen 18% the prior year. In July 2025, rather than terminating FHIP grants outright a second time, HUD announced a restructured competition redirecting roughly $56 million in FHIP funding toward organizations whose positions aligned with the administration's views on gender, immigration, and religion -- a shift that would have sharply reduced the number of eligible grantees and effectively eliminated funding for most existing fair housing organizations. On August 27, 2026, U.S. District Judge Myong Joun (D. Mass.) enjoined that restructuring, finding HUD's stated 'modernization' rationale 'falls woefully short' of justifying the departure from a funding structure used for decades, and ordered HUD to distribute FHIP funding using the same structure it had used in fiscal 2024, releasing the disputed roughly $30 million to fair housing organizations. Separately, a coalition of Democratic state attorneys general sued HUD over a parallel effort targeting the Fair Housing Assistance Program, challenging the agency's refusal to fund states, including on sexual-orientation protections, that had adopted broader fair-housing protections than the federal statutory minimum. On the budget side, Congress rejected the administration's proposed cuts and block-grant restructuring in the final FY2026 Transportation-HUD appropriations act, signed into law February 3, 2026 as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026: Tenant-Based Rental Assistance was funded at $38.4 billion (up $2.4 billion from FY2025, including $35.0 billion to renew existing assisted-household contracts) and Project-Based Rental Assistance at $18.5 billion (up $1.7 billion), a combined $7.2 billion increase over FY2025 with no block-grant conversion adopted.

primary_proponent.name: Scott Turner
primary_proponent.role: HUD Secretary
primary_proponent.note: Oversaw both the February 2025 FHIP grant terminations and the July 2025 ideologically-screened FHIP funding restructuring that two separate federal judges found likely unlawful; the underlying FY2026 budget cut and block-grant proposal originated with the Trump administration's OMB budget request.

estimated_impact.summary: The rejected FY2026 budget proposal would have cut federal rental assistance by roughly 40% and converted it into a state block grant, a restructuring housing researchers and advocates said would have ended or sharply curtailed assistance for millions of low-income, elderly, and disabled households; Congress instead increased HUD rental-assistance funding. The FHIP defunding attempts, had they stood, would have eliminated most of the federal government's roughly $30-56 million in annual funding for local fair-housing enforcement and discrimination-testing organizations nationwide -- both attempts were enjoined by federal courts before taking lasting effect.

title: Judge Rules HUD's Rewrite of $75M Homeless-Housing Funding Criteria Unlawful, Calling It a 'Slapdash Imposition of Political Whims'
institution: Department of Housing and Urban Development
status: Blocked -- a federal judge ordered the new policy scrapped
date_of_action: 2025 (new NOFO issued) through 2026-03/04 (court ruling)
what_changed: HUD issued a new Notice of Funding Opportunity for its Continuum of Care Builds program -- a separate $75 million funding stream from the broader $3.9 billion Continuum of Care Program documented separately in this tracker (hud-supportive-housing-shift-2026.json) -- that dramatically changed the criteria nonprofits and local providers must meet to receive funding to build housing for homeless families and individuals. title: HUD's Fair Housing Office Lost a Quarter to Half Its Staff, per OPM Data and Advocates, Amid Whistleblower Allegations
institution: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity
status: Partially reversed -- the states' suit over HUD's fair-housing funding guidance (State of Illinois et al. v. HUD) was dismissed Sept. 2, 2026 after HUD, per California's AG, confirmed the guidance is no longer in effect; FHEO staff cuts stand; no ruling yet in the whistleblowers' Heenan v. HUD suit
date_of_action: 2025-01 onward (staffing reductions; 2025-10-10 layoff notices rescinded 2025-11-13); enforcement policy changes 2025-2026
what_changed:
In February 2025, an internal HUD memo obtained by The Washington Post showed that HUD, working with the Department of Government Efficiency, planned to cut staff at the Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity (FHEO), which investigates housing discrimination complaints nationwide, by nearly 77%, HousingWire reported; in a March 17, 2025 letter to Secretary Turner, congressional Democrats led by Rep. Maxine Waters and Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote that it had been 'widely reported that HUD plans to terminate half of all staff, including 77% of staff within' FHEO. Following the February 5, 2025 confirmation of Secretary Scott Turner, probationary employees were terminated, according to a former HUD civil rights attorney, 'with no real justification.' The earliest concrete evidence of case-stalling predates the September 2025 whistleblower complaint by roughly six months: within weeks of the new administration taking office, **HUD rescinded its own Department of Justice litigation referrals in two Texas civil-rights investigations it had already substantiated -- one finding a Texas state agency steered $1 billion in Hurricane Harvey disaster-mitigation funds away from Houston-area communities of color, the other finding a homeowners association in Providence Village, a mostly-white Dallas suburb, barred Section 8 voucher holders (predominantly Black tenants) starting in 2022, displacing Black families.** HUD offered no public explanation for withdrawing either referral, per ProPublica's March 2025 investigation.

FHEO started 2025 with about 600 employees, the National Fair Housing Alliance's Sasha Samberg-Champion told NOTUS, which reported in October 2025 that a voluntary retirement program had since led about half of the office's staff to depart; NFHA said on October 14, 2025 that earlier in the year the administration had 'reduced HUD's Fair Housing enforcement staff by half.' On October 10, 2025, during the government shutdown, HUD issued reduction-in-force notices to 442 employees, according to its own court declarations -- 114 of them in FHEO, Bloomberg reported, while NOTUS put the FHEO figure at 170. Samberg-Champion told NOTUS that if those layoffs went ahead, FHEO 'will have lost about two-thirds of its personnel,' and NFHA's November 5, 2025 release of its Fair Housing Trends Report said FHEO 'now has a third of the staff it had on January 20, 2025.' But a federal court had blocked the shutdown layoffs, the continuing resolution signed November 12, 2025 gave them 'no force or effect,' and HUD told the court that on November 13, 2025 it rescinded all 442 notices and returned the employees to duty, with back pay. Outside experts estimated total HUD departures, including voluntary and buyout-driven exits, at as many as 2,300 employees since January 2025. Office of Personnel Management data compiled by USAFacts count 468 FHEO employees in May 2026, against 645 in May 2025.

In September 2025, HUD issued a memorandum withdrawing previously issued fair housing enforcement guidance. Days later, four HUD attorneys, including Paul Osadebe, filed a whistleblower complaint with Senator Elizabeth Warren alleging the department was illegally winding down and stalling active fair housing discrimination cases. On September 22, 2025, Osadebe, co-whistleblower Palmer Heenan and three other HUD fair-housing attorneys sued HUD and Secretary Turner in federal court in Washington (Heenan v. HUD, D.D.C. No. 1:25-cv-03343), alleging they had been 'unlawfully targeted by HUD leadership and forced to leave' the Office of Fair Housing 'against their will' through involuntary reassignments. On September 29, 2025, HUD summarily terminated Heenan, who was still in his probationary period, and told Osadebe it was recommending that he be fired, the two men told The Real News Network. Warren's January 12, 2026 advisory described both men as 'fired after coming forward with their concerns'; Whistleblower Aid, which represents them, said the same day that Osadebe had been placed on administrative leave, and Tax Credit Advisor later reported that he was officially terminated on February 9, 2026. On January 13, 2026, Osadebe and Heenan spoke at 'Fair Housing Under Fire,' a Spotlight Forum hosted by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the Senate Banking Committee's ranking member. Whistleblower Aid said beforehand that attorneys had been 'barred from speaking to clients and prohibited from citing any past civil rights case'; at the forum, according to the committee Democrats' account, Osadebe said he and his colleagues were 'banned from talking' to their clients and 'blocked…from investigating or charging cases.' The court docket in the attorneys' reassignment suit shows no amended complaint; HUD moved to dismiss it on February 10, 2026, the judge ordered supplemental briefing in August 2026 on whether the Fair Housing Act provides a private right of action against the United States or its agencies, both sides filed on September 11, 2026, and no ruling had been issued as of late September 2026.

Sixteen attorneys general -- from 15 states and the District of Columbia, co-led by California's Rob Bonta and Illinois's Kwame Raoul -- sued HUD over its September 2025 fair-housing funding guidance on March 16, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (State of Illinois et al. v. HUD); Virginia joined through an amended complaint filed June 24, 2026, bringing the plaintiffs to 17. The suit alleges the guidance violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the Constitution by threatening to decertify state and local fair housing agencies that enforce protections broader than the federal Fair Housing Act (including disparate-impact liability, gender-identity protections, and source-of-income safeguards) while separately imposing unrelated funding conditions tied to abortion, immigration, and 'gender ideology.' The coalition sought declaratory relief, APA vacatur, and a permanent injunction. The complaint says the plaintiffs' agencies received about $10.7 million from HUD's Fair Housing Assistance Program (FHAP) in fiscal 2024 alone, and Bonta said about $3 million in federal funding was at stake for California, the Los Angeles Times reported. On September 2, 2026, after HUD sent the states a letter dated that day, the parties jointly stipulated to dismiss the case without prejudice. California's attorney general said on September 8 that HUD had confirmed it would not seek to impose, implement, or enforce the challenged conditions, that 'the FY 2025 Guidance is no longer in effect,' and that the conditions will not apply to FY 2026 FHAP funding. HUD, for its part, said on June 12, 2026 that FHEO had 'reduced the Biden backlog by 27%,' and on September 24, 2026 that since September 1, 2025 it had 'reduced the Biden backlog of pending Title VIII complaints by 46%.'

(A separate, unrelated HUD lawsuit -- over Continuum of Care homelessness-grant funding restrictions, where Bonta secured a preliminary injunction and the administration dropped its appeal in April 2026 -- concerns different funding conditions and is out of scope for this fair-housing-enforcement-staffing entry.)

The federal office responsible for investigating housing discrimination complaints nationwide lost about half its staff in 2025, per the National Fair Housing Alliance; Office of Personnel Management data count 645 FHEO employees in May 2025 and 468 in May 2026 (a 27% drop); shutdown layoff notices that an NFHA lawyer said would have left it about two-thirds smaller were rescinded in November 2025. title: White House Uses a Pocket Rescission to Try to Cancel $56.1 Million in HUD Housing Counseling Grants
institution: Department of Housing and Urban Development, Housing Programs, Housing Counseling Assistance account (Comprehensive Housing Counseling program)
status: A judge suspended the Sept. 30, 2026 lapse of all $57.5 million in housing counseling funds, including the $56.1 million targeted, until she rules on ten nonprofits' injunction bid; briefing ends Oct. 19. New York sued. GAO said the law bars withholding the funds past Sept. 30. No merits ruling yet.
date_of_action: 2026-09-25 (special message sent to Congress; funds withheld ahead of their Sept. 30, 2026 expiration)
what_changed: On September 25, 2026, five days before the end of the fiscal year, President Trump sent House Speaker Mike Johnson a special message under the Impoundment Control Act proposing 11 rescissions totaling $810 million, and the Office of Management and Budget issued a reapportionment letter withholding the proposed amounts from obligation. One item, rescission proposal R26-10, would cancel $56,100,000 from HUD's Housing Counseling Assistance account, money available only through September 30, 2026. The special message called it "$56 million of the $58 million appropriated in FY 2025 for Housing Counseling"; the nonprofits who later sued put the appropriation at $57.5 million, carried into fiscal 2025 by the full-year continuing resolution Congress enacted in March 2025, and called the cut nearly all of it. The program funds HUD-approved housing counseling agencies, national and regional intermediaries and state housing finance agencies that counsel homebuyers, homeowners facing delinquency or foreclosure, and renters. The special message justified the cut by saying grantees "have included NGOs with divisive and DEI-centric agendas that peddle discrimination based on race" and that "the program has not shown reduced delinquencies for counseled homebuyers." The White House's public release named UnidosUS, the National Urban League ($1.6 million) and Housing Action Illinois ($1.5 million) as examples of "radical groups" that had received the money, criticizing the Urban League's positions on immigration enforcement and Housing Action Illinois's view that "housing is a human right." According to the nonprofits' complaint, HUD did not publish the fiscal 2025 funding notice until March 26, 2026, about five months after the grant period it covered had begun; applications were due May 26 and HUD listed August 3 as the expected award date for about 175 awards, but, the plaintiffs allege, did not make the awards. The complaint says agencies kept counseling clients while waiting and that the delays forced some to draw down reserves, cut services or lay off staff. The notice also dropped one-on-one counseling for prospective homebuyers from eligible expenses and limited federally funded foreclosure counseling to borrowers with HUD, VA or USDA mortgages, restrictions the plaintiffs also challenge. Because a rescission request lets the executive withhold funds for 45 days of continuous session while Congress considers it, and these funds were set to expire September 30, the timing would let the money lapse without a congressional vote; this is known as a pocket rescission. On September 29, 2026, GAO's general counsel concluded that all 11 accounts expire at the end of fiscal 2026 and that the Impoundment Control Act does not let the President withhold the funds past that date, writing that the President "may not force the expiration of budget authority Congress has already enacted and did not rescind." That night, the National Urban League, Housing Action Illinois, the North Carolina Housing Coalition, New Jersey Citizen Action and six other nonprofits, represented by Democracy Defenders Fund and Jacobson Lawyers Group, sued President Trump, HUD, HUD Secretary Scott Turner, HUD fair housing Assistant Secretary Craig Trainor, OMB, OMB Director Russell Vought and the United States in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (National Urban League v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03401). They allege the pocket rescission violates the Impoundment Control Act, the housing counseling statute, the Administrative Procedure Act and the separation of powers, and that it was aimed at grantees' speech and viewpoints in violation of the First Amendment; National Urban League president Marc Morial said the White House "effectively has admitted that this rescission was motivated, at least in part, by criticism of the administration's policies." The groups asked for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction the next day. Late on September 30, U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb suspended the September 30 lapse of the full $57.5 million in housing counseling funds until she rules on the groups' motion for a preliminary injunction, writing that the court was "not presently in a position to grant or deny the preliminary relief" and was "hesitant to allow September 30 to pass such that Plaintiffs would lose out on significant amounts of funding due to allegedly unconstitutional actions." The government, which opposed the suspension, may file a fuller response by October 9, and the plaintiffs may reply by October 19. Also on September 30, New York Attorney General Letitia James sued HUD and Secretary Turner in federal court in Manhattan (State of New York v. HUD, No. 1:26-cv-08639, S.D.N.Y.) over its refusal to award the housing counseling money, arguing it violates the Administrative Procedure Act, the housing counseling statute and appropriations law. Her office said New York's state housing finance agency, which applied May 22 and was told its application was complete, passes up to $1 million a year to 22 counseling organizations, and that **over 7,000 households in New York are at risk of losing access to one-on-one counseling services, and nearly 2,800 households may lose financial assistance to improve their living conditions.** It also said the President's fiscal 2026 budget had proposed eliminating housing counseling funding and Congress instead funded the program in the appropriations law signed February 3, 2026. A HUD spokesperson told Real Estate News that the rescission "enables the President to carry out his constitutional responsibility to ensure the faithful execution of the law" and that "HUD is entrusted to ensure that taxpayer funds be deployed in alignment with the President's policy agenda."

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Director of the Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.note: President Trump signed and transmitted the September 25, 2026 special message; GAO's review identifies the accompanying reapportionment letter withholding the funds, sent to HUD among other departments, as coming from the OMB Director. Vought, HUD and HUD Secretary Scott Turner are defendants in the nonprofits' suit, and a HUD spokesperson defended the rescission as aligning taxpayer funds with "the President's policy agenda."

estimated_impact.summary: **Nearly all of the money Congress provided for HUD's housing counseling grants, which pay for foreclosure-prevention, homebuyer and rental counseling, was withheld and targeted for cancellation**; a court has kept it from lapsing for now. New York says over 7,000 of its households could lose one-on-one counseling, and North Carolina's housing coalition says that state would lose $1 million.

title: DOGE Terminated HUD's Contract to Inspect ~6,200 Low-Income Housing Properties for Gas Leaks and Life-Threatening Hazards
institution: Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)
status: Terminated; no reported restoration or replacement oversight identified as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-02 (contract terminated) through 2025-04 (reporting on resulting inspection backlog)
what_changed: In February 2025, the Trump administration terminated a HUD contract with Project Solutions Inc. that had been assigned to inspect roughly 6,200 public housing and other HUD-assisted multifamily properties nationwide over a 12-month period for gas leaks, faulty smoke detectors, and other life-threatening deficiencies. The termination was part of a broader DOGE cost-cutting push that ultimately canceled more than 7,000 federal contracts, each posted to DOGE's public 'Wall of Receipts.' DOGE claimed the cancellation would return $285 million to taxpayers. Robin Miller, a contract manager at Project Solutions, disputed that figure as inflated, saying it was based on an estimated ceiling value that did not reflect the contract's actual likely cost. The abrupt termination **left thousands of legally required inspections undone, including roughly 250 'priority' properties where inspections were already delayed or where prior inspections had found significant deficiencies**.

title: HUD Proposed Optional Two-Year Time Limits and 40-Hour Work Requirements for Section 8 and Public Housing, Risking Aid for Up to 3.7 Million People
institution: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
status: Proposed rule -- comment period closed May 1, 2026; no final rule issued as of this entry's last_verified date
date_of_action: 2025-07 (reporting on the proposal begins) through 2026-03-02 (formal proposed rule published)
what_changed: AP reported on July 22, 2025 that the Trump administration was developing a proposal to cap HUD rental assistance at two years, **citing NYU research projecting the change would push roughly 1.4 million low-income households out of subsidized housing**. On September 30, 2025, ProPublica obtained draft HUD rules confirming plans for work requirements, two-year time limits, and immigration-status checks on federal housing aid, under which a household with even one undocumented member would lose assistance entirely. HUD formalized the plan on March 2, 2026, publishing a proposed rule, 'Establishing Flexibility for Implementation of Work Requirements and Term Limits,' in the Federal Register. The rule would let Public Housing Agencies and owners of Project-Based Rental Assistance housing opt to impose a work requirement of up to 40 hours per adult per week (or require proof of exemption) and a term limit as short as two years for non-elderly, non-disabled households receiving Housing Choice Vouchers, Project-Based Vouchers, Project-Based Rental Assistance, or living in public housing; elderly and disabled households would largely be exempt. Adoption is optional per housing agency or property owner, not mandatory nationwide. The comment period closed May 1, 2026, drawing nearly 2,000 comments, most opposed; as of this entry's last_verified date HUD had not issued a final rule, and no ruling had been identified in any legal challenge.

primary_proponent.name: Scott Turner
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Housing and Urban Development
