title: HUD Proposed Shifting Two-Thirds of Its $3.9B Homeless-Services Program From Permanent Supportive Housing to Short-Term Shelter, Risking Eviction for 170,000 People
institution: Department of Housing and Urban Development
status: A Rhode Island federal court vacated HUD's 2025 NOFOs and its June 1, 2026 FY2026 NOFO, but on Sept 16, 2026 the First Circuit stayed that ruling pending appeal; HUD reopened the FY2026 NOFO Sept 18 (due Sept 30, awards by Dec 1). The 6,689 projects expiring in 2026 were renewed at prior terms.
date_of_action: 2025-11-13 (FY2025 NOFO issued) through 2026-09-18 (HUD reopens FY2026 NOFO after First Circuit stay); appeal ongoing
what_changed: Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0297), the earliest antecedent yet documented: Trump's FY2026 'skinny budget,' released in May 2025, proposed a separate, legislative-track mechanism pursuing the same underlying policy goal the November 2025 NOFO later pursued administratively -- consolidating the Continuum of Care and Housing Opportunities for Persons With AIDS programs into the Emergency Solutions Grant program and capping assistance at two years. The National Alliance to End Homelessness estimated at the time that the residents of roughly 170,000 CoC-funded permanent-supportive-housing units would be at risk of returning to homelessness -- the same figure its executive director, Ann Oliva, later told CNN (March 29, 2026) was at risk under the November 2025 NOFO -- warning it could increase the national homeless population by as much as 36%; all of the residents at risk have a disability, and many were chronically homeless before being housed. Separate cuts of $532 million to Homeless Assistance Grants proposed in the same budget could have additionally affected more than 60,000 Rapid Re-Housing units. Congress did not enact this specific consolidation proposal, and the administration went on to pursue the same underlying goal through the Continuum of Care NOFO mechanism documented below instead. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0491), the direct policy trigger between the May budget proposal and the November NOFO: on July 24, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14321, 'Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets,' which explicitly instructed HUD and HHS to withdraw support for Housing First policy and prioritize federal homelessness grants toward states and localities that expand encampment bans, increase law-enforcement involvement, and use involuntary civil commitment instead. Advocates warned the order also threatened HUD-VASH, the HUD-VA Supportive Housing voucher program that the National Alliance to End Homelessness credits, together with Supportive Services for Veteran Families, for a nearly 50% reduction in veteran homelessness since 2010; Rep. Mark Takano (ranking member, House Veterans' Affairs Committee) publicly criticized the order days after it was signed. HUD's November 2025 Continuum of Care NOFO, documented below, was the administrative implementation of this EO's Housing-First-withdrawal directive, not an independent action. Added 2026-09-09: the November 2025 NOFO change below had an early signal the prior September. AP reported September 28, 2025 that even as California counties made progress reducing homelessness, the Trump administration was moving to condition federal housing funds on alignment with the administration's social agenda -- the same funding-conditionality approach the Continuum of Care NOFO change formalized two months later, reported alongside separate state and local budget cuts also threatening the same programs. In November 2025, HUD released a Notice of Funding Opportunity for its Continuum of Care Program -- which funds shelters, permanent supportive housing, and other homelessness responses -- proposing to shift roughly two-thirds of the program's $3.9 billion budget away from permanent supportive housing and toward transitional housing and other short-term interventions. **Ann Oliva, executive director of the National Alliance to End Homelessness, told CNN that up to about 170,000 formerly homeless people already housed through these programs, including veterans, could be evicted and forced back into homelessness if facilities lost their permanent-housing funding and had to convert to short-term models**. Nonprofits and local governments sued to block the change. On December 23, 2025, U.S. District Judge Mary S. McElroy of the District of Rhode Island, in National Alliance to End Homelessness v. HUD (No. 1:25-cv-00636) and the companion states' case State of Washington v. HUD (No. 1:25-cv-00626), ordered HUD to revert to the original, Biden-era NOFO pending a final ruling, also enjoining a replacement NOFO HUD had published on December 19 after telling the court on December 8 that it had withdrawn the November notice, and HUD reinstated the prior funding notice on January 9, 2026. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, whose state is a plaintiff in the companion states' case, secured the court order there blocking the changes, which he said would also have pressured shelters to discriminate against transgender people and encouraged criminalization of homelessness. Despite the reinstatement, CNN's March 29, 2026 reporting described the eviction risk to formerly homeless people, including veterans, as still live, reflecting that the underlying litigation over HUD's authority to make the shift had not been finally resolved. Litigation continued through mid-2026: on June 29, 2026, the same U.S. District Court (Rhode Island) issued summary judgment vacating HUD's November and December 2025 NOFOs as arbitrary and capricious and exceeding the agency's statutory authority, finding HUD had failed to adequately consider the effects of abandoning its 'Housing First' approach, but denied a permanent injunction, finding vacatur sufficient. HUD had meanwhile issued a new FY2026 NOFO on June 1, 2026 -- a $4.04 billion allocation that again set aside roughly $1.3 billion for new temporary-housing and treatment programs instead of permanent supportive housing. On August 7, 2026, District Judge Mary McElroy blocked that FY2026 NOFO too, ruling HUD had again violated the Administrative Procedure Act by skipping the required public notice-and-comment process. The court again declined to issue a permanent injunction, finding vacatur sufficient. Update 2026-08-29: per KCRHA's tracking of the ruling's practical effect, the entire FY2026 NOFO was set aside, and the competition's original application deadline (KCRHA cites July 3, 2026; other reporting cited August 26, 2026 for a later-extended window) was no longer in force, and HUD could not accept applications under it. HUD had filed a notice of appeal on August 13, 2026. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 50): identified a statutory backstop this entry had not previously documented, running in parallel with the litigation the whole time. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75, signed Feb. 3, 2026) directed HUD to automatically renew any Continuum of Care projects expiring in Q1 2026 at their prior (FY2024/2025 program-competition) terms, with escalating triggers if HUD had not issued awards under a new NOFO by set dates: Q2-expiring projects auto-renew if no awards by April 1, 2026, and ALL remaining (Q3/Q4-expiring) projects auto-renew if no awards by July 1, 2026. HUD complied with the Q1 trigger, announcing on March 31, 2026 $349,205,436 in FY2025 renewal funding for the 622 projects that expired in Q1 2026 (reported by National Network for Youth on April 1). With no awards issued under a new competition, HUD then renewed the Q2 projects after the April 1 trigger and the Q3/Q4 projects ahead of the July 1 trigger: on April 27, 2026 it announced $1,094,870,517 in FY2025 renewal funding for the 1,826 projects that expired in Q2 2026, and on May 21, 2026 it announced $2,402,872,704 for the 4,241 projects expiring in Q3/Q4 2026, both under the Consolidated Appropriations Act -- in all, about $3.85 billion for 6,689 projects expiring in 2026. Critically, NACo's April 1, 2026 reporting confirms the Q1-renewed projects are funded 'based on Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 program competition terms' and 'will not be subject to the planned reductions in PSH or protected renewal funds' -- meaning the specific eviction-risk mechanism this entry documents (projects losing permanent-supportive-housing funding because they couldn't compete under HUD's PSH-cutting NOFO) has been substantially mitigated for the projects covered by these renewals, independent of and prior to the litigation's outcome. This does not resolve the underlying dispute over HUD's authority to shift the program's structure in later competitions, including the FY2026 NOFO, which the auto-renewals do not cover. Update 2026-09-26: On September 16, 2026, the First Circuit (Nos. 26-1922 and 26-1923) stayed the August 7 ruling pending HUD's appeal, finding HUD had 'made a strong showing that it is likely to succeed on the merits' of its argument that the NOFO's $1.3 billion set-aside for transitional housing and 'supportive service only' projects was not a 'bonus or other incentive' requiring notice and comment, and that HUD would suffer irreparable injury without a stay because it must make Continuum of Care awards by December 1, 2026. HUD reopened the FY2026 NOFO on September 18, 2026, essentially unchanged except for a technical correction, with applications due September 30, 2026 (October 14 for CA-600 applications only); HUD describes the competition as offering more than $4 billion. NACo reported that under the NOFO 60 percent of funding would be protected as non-competitive Tier 1 renewals, compared with nearly 90 percent of program funds under the existing framework, and that the NOFO sets no specific cap on permanent supportive housing.

estimated_impact.caveat: The November and December 2025 NOFOs never took effect: a December 23, 2025 preliminary injunction kept HUD on its prior notice, and a June 29, 2026 ruling vacated both. The June 1, 2026 FY2026 NOFO was vacated on August 7, 2026 but is proceeding under the First Circuit's September 16 stay pending appeal; the appeal's outcome, and which projects lose funding in the competition, are not yet known. title: Trump Administration Froze $16B in Committed Funding for the Hudson River Tunnel Project, Threatening Construction Shutdown
institution: U.S. Department of Transportation
status: Resolved in the states' favor -- a federal judge permanently restored the funding on June 29, 2026, ruling the freeze 'flagrantly violate[d] federal law'; the 2nd Circuit had already declined to block a lower-court order requiring interim resumption, and construction has continued since February 13, 2026 without further interruption
date_of_action: 2025-09-30 (DOT announces indefinite funding suspension) through 2026-02-04 (NY/NJ file suit)
what_changed: On September 30, 2025, DOT announced it would indefinitely suspend payment of all previously-committed federal funds for the Gateway Program's Hudson Tunnel Project -- a roughly $16 billion effort to build new rail tunnels under the Hudson River and rehabilitate the existing, more-than-a-century-old crossing between New Jersey and New York City -- pending a newly announced compliance review. The White House budget director stated officials believed the project's spending was based on 'unconstitutional diversity, equity, and inclusion principles,' and DOT said it was reviewing for 'unconstitutional practices.' After roughly four months of the states covering costs with limited operating funds, they warned construction would be forced to shut down entirely by February 6, 2026 without resumed federal funding, **immediately costing an estimated 1,000 workers their jobs**. On February 4, 2026, New York Attorney General Letitia James and New Jersey Acting Attorney General Jennifer Davenport filed suit in the Southern District of New York against the Trump administration, seeking emergency relief to stop the indefinite funding freeze. Update 2026-08-17 (correction -- this entry's original 'litigation ongoing' framing is now outdated): the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to block a lower-court order requiring DOT to resume payments, and funding resumed on an interim basis, with construction restarting February 13, 2026. On June 29, 2026, U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas issued a permanent ruling: the administration's September 2025 funding freeze 'flagrantly violate[d] federal law' because DOT skipped required procedures and never gave the Gateway Development Commission an opportunity to object -- a point the government itself did not dispute. The court rejected DOT's argument that the dispute belonged in the Court of Federal Claims, finding New York and New Jersey could challenge the freeze under the Administrative Procedure Act since the states were not parties to the underlying funding agreements. The Gateway Development Commission said the project -- slated for completion in 2035 -- remained on schedule before the freeze and has made 'significant progress' since funding resumed.

title: Six Months After Promising Body Cameras for All Immigration Agents, DHS Still Hasn't Deployed Them -- Agents in Subsequent Fatal Shootings Had None
institution: Department of Homeland Security / Immigration and Customs Enforcement
status: Ongoing -- reporting is split on the deployment deadline itself (NBC/Venturella said end of August 2026; the same-day AP/PBS account said end of September, with 'more than half' of field officers equipped as of early August), and no independent reporting confirms completion under either deadline as of this recheck; ICE separately disputed AP's characterization of its footage-withholding policy for serious-injury/death cases on August 8-9, 2026, without disputing the underlying policy itself
date_of_action: 2026-01 (body camera pledge made) through 2026-07 (still not fully deployed, additional fatal shootings without cameras)
what_changed: After immigration agents fatally shot two U.S. citizens (Alex Pretti, a VA hospital ICU nurse, and Renee Good) in Minneapolis in January 2026, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem pledged to rapidly expand body camera deployment to immigration agents nationwide. Congress allocated $20 million in FY2026 DHS funding for body camera procurement, deployment, and operations, with plans to purchase more than 5,000 body-worn cameras; as of February 2026, roughly 3,000 of approximately 13,000 ICE agents wore body cameras, with another 6,000 in the deployment pipeline. Nearly six months after the pledge, **none of the officers involved in two subsequent fatal ICE shootings -- of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Duran Guerrero -- were wearing body cameras**, according to NPR reporting; a separate fatal shooting in Houston also involved ICE agents without body cameras despite the DHS funding allocation. Update 2026-08-17: on August 7-8, 2026, ICE Acting Director David J. Venturella said the agency expects to complete nationwide body-camera deployment to every field officer by the end of August 2026 -- a significant acceleration from the ~3,000-of-13,000 partial deployment this entry documents as of February 2026, following the additional fatal shootings without cameras already covered above. Independent confirmation that the rollout was actually completed by the announced deadline was not available as of this update, since the deadline itself had not yet arrived. Separately, ICE's body-camera policy has drawn scrutiny for provisions that let agency leadership withhold or indefinitely delay release of footage following serious injuries or deaths in custody; Venturella defended the restrictions as protecting investigations and privacy and consistent with other federal law enforcement agencies' policies, while reporting noted this means the expanded camera coverage will not automatically translate into public access to the footage. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 32): on August 8-9, 2026, ICE publicly disputed the Associated Press's framing of the footage-release policy, with Venturella issuing a statement saying the AP conflated the narrower expedited-release provision that applies specifically to serious-injury/death-in-custody cases with a claim that ICE would broadly withhold routine footage; ICE maintains the underlying policy -- expedited release when appropriate, withholding when release could compromise investigations or privacy -- is unchanged from what this entry already documents. As of this recheck, which falls on the announced end-of-August 2026 completion deadline itself, no independent reporting confirming (or disputing) that the full nationwide rollout was actually completed was found in sourcing reviewed -- consistent with this entry's existing caveat that the target had not yet been independently verified. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 47): a same-week (Aug 7-8, 2026) PBS/AP account, published within hours of the NBC/Venturella 'end of August' report already documented above, instead described the rollout target as 'the end of September,' with more than half of field officers already equipped and the rest to follow by then -- a discrepancy this entry documents rather than resolves, since sourcing reviewed does not establish which deadline is the agency's operative one. The PBS/AP reporting also added funding and design detail beyond what this entry previously documented: ICE spent $30.9 million in July 2026 to purchase equipment from Axon, on top of the $20 million FY2026 congressional appropriation already documented above; and the deployment plan's actual coverage standard requires only 'at least one member of every arrest team' to wear a camera, not every individual field officer, a materially narrower standard than the 'every officer' framing in HHS's own public statements. The same reporting detailed the footage-release policy more specifically than previously documented: the ICE Director may withhold or indefinitely delay release following 'specific and compelling circumstances,' on a review committee's recommendation, if release is not determined to be in the agency's 'best interests' -- a broader, more discretionary standard than this entry's prior 'expedited release when appropriate' framing suggested. As of this recheck (Sept. 1, 2026), no reporting confirming rollout completion under either the August 31 or end-of-September deadline was found.

title: ICE Quietly Stopped Listing Detainees With Final Deportation Orders in Its Public Locator, Leaving Lawyers and Families Unable to Find Them
institution: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (DHS) -- Online Detainee Locator System
status: Ongoing: ICE has not confirmed, explained or reversed the change. On Sept. 30, 30+ advocacy groups petitioned a UN working group and 45+ House Democrats asked ICE to restore the listings, seeking answers by Oct. 14. No court ruling on the policy itself found.
what_changed: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement stopped listing detainees who are subject to final deportation orders in its public Online Detainee Locator System on Sept. 15, 2026, according to three current and former ICE officials who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity. ICE did not announce the change. AP reported it on Sept. 21, after several lawyers confirmed that their clients had vanished from the system and the American Immigration Lawyers Association had warned its members on Sept. 18. A detainee drops out of the locator once their removal order becomes final, even without being moved, the American Immigration Council wrote. Border Report and the American Immigration Council, citing Washington Post reporting, said ICE staff have also been told not to give these detainees' locations to lawyers and relatives who call to ask. **Lawyers told AP the change leaves families unable to tell whether a relative has been moved or already deported, and can keep attorneys from reaching clients in time to bring last-minute legal challenges before removal.** People with final orders can still seek to reopen their cases or file habeas petitions, and some have protection from deportation to their home countries and face removal to third countries where they have no ties. The Amica Center for Immigrant Rights told AP that every one of its clients with a final order, 17 in all, had disappeared from the locator, and an ACLU attorney said eight Somali men held at the U.S. military base at Guantanamo Bay were among those removed from it. The officials told AP the practice does not cover the Adelanto, California detention facility or temporary holding sites in Minneapolis, New York City and suburban Chicago, where judges in separate litigation have ordered ICE to list detainees promptly. In a statement to AP, ICE neither confirmed nor denied the change, saying detainees with final removal orders were being prioritized for deportation even as the agency faces a "historic number of injunctions" against individual removals. ICE launched the locator in 2010; before it, relatives and lawyers had to call ICE regional offices or individual facilities to find detained people. On Sept. 30, 2026, a coalition of more than 30 advocacy groups, including Amnesty International, Human Rights First and Refugees International, petitioned the UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances to declare the policy a violation of international law. **The petition described a mother and her 7-year-old daughter who lost access to their lawyers while facing deportation to Venezuela; ICE disclosed where they were only about 18 hours after a judge ordered it to, and then released them.** The same day, more than 45 House Democrats led by Reps. Luz Rivas and Veronica Escobar wrote to ICE Acting Director David Venturella asking ICE to restore the listings and to answer questions about the policy by Oct. 14. DHS denied that its practices amount to disappearing people, saying all detainees "have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers" and that "the appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple."

The three are different scopes and should not be added together. title: ICE Detention Deaths: 2025 Was the Deadliest Year in Two Decades, 58+ Since January 2025, Amid Slashed Inspections and Record Overcrowding
institution: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Department of Homeland Security
status: Ongoing and worsening -- after 2025's record 31-33 deaths, deaths continued in 2026: AP counted at least 58 since January 2025 as of a September 18, 2026 death at a Louisiana facility the DHS inspector general had found short of medical-care standards
date_of_action: 2025 (calendar year, cumulative) through 2026-09 (later tracking)
what_changed: The Guardian reported that **31 people died in ICE custody in 2025, the agency's deadliest year in more than two decades**, as the Trump administration detained a record number of people. Nearly 75% of those who died had no criminal convictions. Documented causes included seizure, heart failure, stroke, respiratory failure, tuberculosis, and suicide; families and lawyers alleged some deaths resulted from medical neglect after detainees repeatedly sought and failed to receive care. A KFF health-policy tracker using a slightly different count found 33 deaths in 2025 (versus 11 in 2024 and fewer than 10 in each prior year), breaking down causes as 32 attributable to complications from existing medical conditions, 9 suicides, and 5 other causes including a traffic collision during arrest (the tracker's own totals overlap/double-count across categories in its published breakdown); the same tracker found the cumulative total had reached 46 deaths since January 2025 as of March 18, 2026. The Project On Government Oversight found ICE detention-facility inspections dropped roughly 36% in 2025 even as detention populations surged, and that the number of documented detention-standard violations fell nearly 70% between FY2022 and FY2025 -- a decline POGO's reporting frames as reduced oversight scrutiny rather than genuinely improved conditions, given the simultaneous mortality increase. NPR reported that Public Health Service officers deployed to detention centers described 'moral distress' over conditions, including life-threatening delays in medication and care, chaotic intake screenings, failure to properly monitor detainees at suicide risk, unreported suspected active tuberculosis cases, and insufficient toilet access, in facilities that were simultaneously overcrowded and understaffed. Separately, Members of Congress represented by Democracy Forward Foundation and American Oversight sued after DHS blocked lawmakers' unannounced oversight visits to ICE facilities; a federal court granted a temporary restraining order February 2, 2026 and has since ordered DHS multiple times to restore congressional oversight access, after DHS Secretary Kristi Noem was found to have secretly reinstated a notice requirement via an undisclosed internal memo following an earlier court order blocking that same policy -- the memo surfaced only after Members of Congress were denied entry to a Minnesota ICE facility despite presenting a valid court order, in the same period as the fatal shooting of a U.S. citizen by a federal agent there. DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin denied that detention conditions were declining, stating it is 'a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody.' Update 2026-10-03: The Associated Press reported that Carlos Josue Marchena Marchena, a 36-year-old Costa Rican man with type 1 diabetes, was found unresponsive on September 18, 2026 at Winn Correctional Center in Winnfield, Louisiana, and was later pronounced dead at a hospital; his official cause of death was pending further medical examination. **His sister, his girlfriend and a detainee in the adjacent cell told AP he had complained of missed insulin shots, missed meals and too little water as he was moved between facilities; his family said his condition worsened after he reached Winn, where he died less than a week later.** By AP's own count he was at least the 58th person to die in ICE custody since January 2025, and the third ICE detainee to die at Winn in less than six months. AP also reported that medical examiners and coroners have ruled diabetes a contributing factor in at least six ICE detainee deaths during Trump's second term. The DHS Office of Inspector General's June 2, 2026 report on an unannounced March 2025 inspection found Winn did not fully comply with detention standards for medical care, food service, use of force and other areas: medical staff did not always update medical records or document interpretation of lab test results, perishable food was not stored at required temperatures, and facility staff refused to provide the OIG with copies of all facility video recordings. ICE concurred with all nine of the report's recommendations. In its death notice, ICE said Marchena 'received proper medical care and was seen by medical professionals.'

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Homeland Security (through her March 2026 removal; DHS oversees ICE)
primary_proponent.note: DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin publicly denied any decline in detention medical care on Noem's agency's behalf even as inspections and reported violations both fell sharply during a mortality surge; separately, Noem was found to have secretly reinstated a congressional-oversight-visit notice requirement via an undisclosed internal memo after a court had already blocked that same policy, an action a federal court has since ordered reversed.

estimated_impact.summary: A direct mortality toll -- 31-33 deaths in 2025, the highest in at least two decades, and at least 58 since January 2025 by AP's September 2026 count -- coincides with documented reductions in the oversight mechanisms -- inspections, violation citations, and congressional facility access -- that would otherwise surface and correct the conditions producing those deaths, while the responsible agency denies any decline in care.

No independent dollar-cost estimate applies naturally to this domain (deaths in custody, not a funding action) -- the money side of SCHEMA's figures requirement is not applicable here in the way it is for a funding-cut entry; the entry instead leads with the mortality figures the underlying story is actually about, per SCHEMA's own guidance that money-and-health both apply 'where available' rather than being force-fit. Cumulative counts since January 2025 also differ by tracker: KFF reported 46 as of March 18, 2026; AP counted at least 58 as of September 18, 2026; Detention Watch Network counted at least 56 in a September 23, 2026 release. The AP figure is shown as the most recent, not as a reconciled total.

confidence_note: Very strong, multi-source corroboration across distinct methodologies: The Guardian's original investigative count (re-syndicated via RSN, AOL), KFF's independent health-policy tracker, POGO's inspection/violation-rate investigation, and NPR's PHS-officer interviews all independently converge on the same pattern (record deaths, reduced oversight, understaffed/overcrowded conditions) via different data sources and methods, which is unusually strong triangulation for this tracker. The congressional-oversight-obstruction court fight (Noem's undisclosed memo, the Minnesota facility denial-of-entry incident) is corroborated across multiple House member press releases (Torres, Neguse) and Democracy Forward/American Oversight's own litigation filings, though it is included here as directly relevant context connecting reduced oversight to the mortality trend, not as this entry's central claim. Update 2026-10-03: the Winn death rests on AP's reporting (read via syndicated copies) and ICE's own death notice; the family's and fellow detainee's accounts of missed insulin and food are allegations ICE disputes, and the official cause of death was still pending. The Winn inspection findings come from the DHS inspector general's report itself.

title: ICE Accidentally Exposed a Live Manhunt's Sensitive Data to a Stranger via an Unencrypted Group Text
institution: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)
status: Documented incident, no confirmed corrective action -- 404 Media reported no encryption/access-control fix identified as of publication
date_of_action: 2025-08 (incident reported; the mistaken addition had reportedly occurred weeks earlier)
what_changed: 404 Media reported that a law-enforcement group text called 'Mass Text,' used by ICE and other agencies to coordinate an active manhunt for a convicted attempted murderer slated for deportation, had mistakenly included a random civilian with no law-enforcement role or connection to the case -- added, by the person's own account, weeks before they realized what the messages actually were. **The chat exposed an unredacted ICE 'Field Operations Worksheet' containing detailed information about the manhunt target, along with data pulled from DMV records and automated license-plate readers (LPRs)**. The messages were sent via ordinary MMS text messaging, not an end-to-end encrypted platform like Signal or WhatsApp, meaning the sensitive law-enforcement data traveled with weaker security protections than the encrypted-app practices already documented elsewhere in this database (e.g. the NSC's Signal-based coordination). 404 Media itself characterized the episode as 'a significant data breach and operational security failure for ICE.' No agency statement confirming a fix to the group-messaging or access-control practices that allowed the mistaken addition was identified in sourcing reviewed.

primary_proponent.name: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency (institutional failure; no individual official was named as personally responsible in sourcing reviewed)
primary_proponent.note: The exposure resulted from ICE's and partner agencies' use of unencrypted MMS group messaging to coordinate a sensitive operation, not from a specific named official's individual decision.

estimated_impact.summary: Sensitive, real-time law-enforcement surveillance data -- including DMV records and license-plate-reader tracking data on a manhunt target -- was exposed to an uninvolved civilian for an extended period before discovery, illustrating a broader operational-security gap in how ICE coordinates active operations.
estimated_impact.caveat: This is a single documented incident, not a systemic count of how often ICE uses unencrypted messaging for sensitive operations or how many similar exposures may have gone undiscovered -- no quantified figure beyond the one confirmed incident was identified in sourcing reviewed.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence that the incident occurred as described -- 404 Media's reporting is based on screenshots it obtained and verified directly from the mistakenly added person, and the story was corroborated (without contradiction) by Techdirt, Above the Law, The Daily Beast, Futurism, and wire syndication. No ICE or DHS on-record response confirming or disputing the account was identified in sourcing reviewed, so this entry reflects the reporting outlet's account rather than an agency-confirmed narrative.
pull_quote: 404 Media, which broke the story, called it “a significant data breach and operational security failure for ICE” -- a characterization no agency has disputed.

title: ICE Kept No Miscarriage Count After Oct. 3, 2025, as It Detained More Pregnant Women
institution: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE Health Service Corps; detention medical claims), Department of Homeland Security
status: Unresolved: DHS confirmed to The Guardian it has no ICE miscarriage data for October 2025 through June 2026, then told other outlets ICE tracks miscarriages monthly. The 2021 directive limiting detention of pregnant people remains formally in place.
date_of_action: 2025-10-03 to 2026-06 (miscarriage records end Oct. 3, 2025; DHS confirmed no data through June 2026; reported Sept. 15, 2026)
what_changed:
Records that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement released to The Guardian, after the outlet sued under the Freedom of Information Act together with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, show that **at least 18 women miscarried in ICE custody from January through September 2025**, a count experts told The Guardian is very likely an undercount, but ICE provided no miscarriage data after Oct. 3, 2025. In internal documents, ICE attributed the gap to a change in its medical accounting system: it ended its arrangement with the Veterans Affairs Financial Services Center, which had handled ICE's medical billing, and Acentra Health, a private Virginia-based company, was contracted to replace it starting in October 2025. ICE's medical claims processing has since been delayed for months; Acentra did not say whether it tracks miscarriages for ICE and pointed to government shutdowns for the delays. Immigration attorneys and former DHS officials told The Guardian it was odd that ICE tracked miscarriages only through its billing provider. Asked about the gap, a DHS spokesperson first told The Guardian the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports, then confirmed it has no miscarriage data from October 2025 through June 2026; The Guardian reported that DHS had never before acknowledged the gap, including when senators asked for the data. After The Guardian's Sept. 15, 2026 report, DHS spokespeople told Reason and NPR's Here & Now that ICE tracks and reports miscarriage data monthly under ICE Directive 11032.4; the statement to Here & Now called the report "FALSE."

The same records, which run from October 2024 through mid-January 2026, show ICE holding more pregnant people in detention in fall and winter 2025 than at any time over the previous year: at least 87 pregnant women and adolescents in October 2025 and 101 in November. Directive 11032.4, issued in 2021 and still in place according to DHS, says ICE should not detain pregnant, postpartum or nursing people for civil immigration violations unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist, and requires ICE to monitor the health of any it does detain. In more than a dozen cases The Guardian reviewed, attorneys said ICE gave no clear explanation of how those criteria were met. In a September 2025 letter to then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, 29 Democratic senators wrote that ICE had stopped the semiannual reports to Congress on pregnant, postpartum and nursing women in detention that it had provided until that year, and asked DHS to resume them. DHS's delayed response, signed by Noem on Feb. 23, 2026 and released by Sen. Patty Murray on March 18, 2026, reported 121 pregnant, postpartum and nursing women in detention as of Feb. 16, 2026, 363 removals of pregnant, postpartum or nursing women between Jan. 1, 2025 and Feb. 16, 2026, and 16 miscarriages from Jan. 1 through Sept. 23, 2025, the date DHS received the letter.

Women interviewed by The Guardian, and testimonies shared by their attorneys, describe difficulty getting routine and emergency care. **One woman said she began bleeding heavily about a month after her arrest, was taken to an emergency room a day after her urgent written request for care, and was told there, shackled to a hospital bed, that she was no longer pregnant; she said the detention center has offered no follow-up care despite the ER doctor's instruction.** Another, held at the Dilley facility in Texas in a high-risk pregnancy, stated in a legal declaration that the facility had not approved or scheduled the specialist consultation its own physician said she needed. Deborah Ottenheimer, an obstetrician-gynecologist with Physicians for Human Rights, told The Guardian that detained women "are not getting the prenatal visits that they're supposed to get" and that the care they receive after a miscarriage is "minimal to none." DHS says pregnant detainees receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support and "accommodations aligned with community standards of care," and told MS NOW and NPR's Here & Now that pregnancy in ICE detention is "exceedingly rare," which it put at 0.15% of people in custody as of June 30 in its statement to Here & Now.

primary_proponent.note: Institutional attribution: no reporting reviewed names the official who ended the VA billing arrangement or decided how miscarriages would be tracked afterward. DHS spokesperson Chandler Rebel told The Guardian the 2021 directive "is still in place"; DHS's response to the senators' September 2025 letter came while Noem was Secretary.

estimated_impact.summary: ICE recorded at least 18 miscarriages in custody in the first nine months of 2025 and then, by its own internal documents, had no miscarriage count for the fall and winter months when it held more pregnant detainees than at any time in the prior year. Women describe going without prenatal, specialist and post-miscarriage care. Without the data, neither Congress nor the public can measure pregnancy losses in detention or check ICE's compliance with its own directive.

title: Education Department Cancels $881M in Research Contracts, Then Fires Nearly All Staff at the Agency Behind the 'Nation's Report Card'
institution: Institute of Education Sciences and National Center for Education Statistics (U.S. Department of Education)
status: Complete (contracts terminated February 2025; NCES staff RIF carried out March 2025; no indication of reinstatement as of the last-verified date)
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, the Department of Government Efficiency directed the Department of Education to terminate 89 contracts held by the Institute of Education Sciences (IES), the department's independent research and statistics arm, which DOGE valued at $881 million. The same evening, IES canceled its peer review panels that evaluate the scientific merit of grant applications for its research centers. Canceled work included the National Postsecondary Student Aid Study, a congressionally mandated survey conducted every four years and described by the American Educational Research Association as the 'backbone' of two other longitudinal higher-education studies; the Beginning Postsecondary Students survey; an 11-year study of youths with disabilities that was roughly halfway complete and was meant to serve over 1,000 students in 2025-2026; and U.S. participation in international assessments comparing American student performance with other countries. On February 13, 2025, the Department separately terminated an additional $336-350 million in contracts and grants to Regional Educational Laboratories and Equity Assistance Centers. The Department stated that the National Assessment of Educational Progress, the College Scorecard, and the College Navigator were not affected by the February contract cancellations. That assurance came under direct strain a month later: as part of the Education Department's broader March 11, 2025 reduction-in-force (documented separately in education-department-dismantlement-trump2.json), ABC News reported nearly all of the roughly 130 staff at the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) -- the IES division that has collected and analyzed U.S. education data since the 1860s and administers NAEP, the congressionally mandated 'Nation's Report Card' considered the gold standard of education testing since 1969 -- were fired. One terminated NCES employee told ABC News that producing NAEP without a full staff would be 'the equivalent of manning a 13-person sailboat with a 12-month-old,' and outlets including THE Journal and EdWeek reported **researchers warning the cuts put NAEP's continued administration itself in doubt, a direct complication of the Department's earlier February statement that NAEP would be spared**.

primary_proponent.note: Oversaw the Department of Education as it implemented DOGE's directed contract terminations; the Department issued an official public statement defending the cuts, arguing IES had spent '$14 billion and countless contracts later' without measurable improvement in student outcomes.

estimated_impact.summary: The federal government's primary independent capacity to evaluate its own education programs and collect national statistics on K-12 and higher education students was significantly curtailed in a single week, interrupting data series that researchers say cannot easily resume once broken.

estimated_impact.caveat: The Department's stated rationale, in its own words, is that IES spent '$14 billion and countless contracts later' without evidence that student outcomes improved, and it specifically flagged $101 million in DEI-related contracts and line items such as $4.6 million 'to coordinate Zoom and in-person meetings.' Notably, this is a genuinely mixed-reception story: Mark Schneider, who led IES during Trump's first term, said in a public LinkedIn discussion that the agency needed significant modernization and called the disruption 'an opportunity' rather than a catastrophe, even while acknowledging DOGE had not articulated a modernization plan. Researcher and data organizations, including AERA, the Council of Professional Associations on Federal Statistics, and the Data Quality Campaign, countered that the specific programs cut, especially the National Postsecondary Student Aid Study and international assessment participation, are congressionally mandated, multi-year data series that lose scientific value once interrupted, since gaps cannot be retroactively filled. The Department confirmed core public-facing tools (NAEP, College Scorecard, College Navigator) were not affected by the February contract cuts specifically, indicating those cuts targeted research contracts rather than IES's full range of functions -- but the March 2025 NCES staffing cuts are a separate action that reporting says undermines that same assurance by removing the staff capacity needed to actually produce NAEP, rather than cutting a contract NAEP itself depended on.

title: Indian Health Service Flagged 'Vaccines' and 'Immunizations' as Restricted Buzzwords, Cutting Vaccine Outreach on Navajo Nation During Active Measles Outbreaks
institution: Indian Health Service (IHS), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Ongoing as of the reporting reviewed (through mid-October 2025) -- no reversal of the language-approval policy identified.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (language restrictions implemented) through 2025-10 (reduced vaccine-clinic outreach documented)
what_changed: In March 2025, the Indian Health Service reclassified the words 'vaccines' and 'immunizations' from 'low-risk' to 'medium-risk' terms requiring public-information-officer approval before use in social media posts, presentations, and printed materials. An internal email from Ryan Goldtooth, a public information officer at a Navajo Nation hospital, instructed staff to remove existing social media posts containing those terms. The practical effect was a steep reduction in vaccine-related messaging: through mid-October 2025, IHS published far fewer Facebook posts promoting vaccine clinics than in the same period the prior year, and the surviving posts shifted from actively promoting immunization benefits to framing vaccination as a personal choice, advising patients to consult providers about their 'options regarding vaccines' rather than encouraging specific shots. **During active measles outbreaks in the region, IHS issued only minimal advisories even as independent tribal health facilities not subject to the same restrictions continued actively promoting vaccination.** Dr. Harry Brown, a physician and epidemiologist who spent 26 years with IHS before leaving in 2016, said of the policy, 'it seems to me that they're trying to put up barriers,' adding he had never previously encountered efforts to restrict vaccine messaging during his tenure. An unnamed physician who left IHS in 2025 said, 'I can't keep people safe. I don't have any of the words anymore to say anything I need to say.'

title: International Labour Organization rescinds US deputy director-general appointment over $328 million in unpaid U.S. dues
institution: U.S. participation in the International Labour Organization
status: Ongoing and escalating -- appointment rescinded as of June 1, 2026 reporting, still not restored; the ILO Governing Body formally approved a contingency framework at its June 2026 (357th) session directing the Director-General to identify positions for elimination, and a special session (357th bis) is scheduled for September 7, 2026 specifically to decide on post reductions, with the U.S. arrears still unpaid as of this update
date_of_action: 2026-06-01 (ILO's rescission announcement)
what_changed: The International Labour Organization rescinded the planned July 2026 appointment of U.S. nominee Sheng Li as Deputy Director-General after the United States failed to pay its outstanding contributions -- 257 million Swiss francs (roughly $328 million) in arrears for 2026 and prior years (2024-2025) -- to the agency. The U.S. has historically held the deputy role by virtue of being the ILO's largest financial contributor, paying roughly 22% of the agency's budget. The ILO said the appointment could be restored if the U.S. settles its arrears, but the delay is straining the agency's finances: if member states, including the U.S., have not paid arrears by September 2026, the ILO projects a 27 million-franc liquidity gap that would trigger emergency measures, **with as many as 120 ILO staff positions at risk of elimination by January 2027 as a result.** Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 48): the position-cut risk moved from a projection to a formal Governing Body process. Facing nearly CHF500 million in unpaid dues across all member states against a CHF926 million operating budget (roughly 70 countries paid in full, 14 partially, about 100 -- including the U.S., the largest single defaulter at CHF256 million -- paid nothing, as of an April 2026 Governing Body report), the ILO Governing Body considered two contingency scenarios at its March 2026 (356th) session: a milder option eliminating ~120 posts for CHF82.5 million in savings, and a more severe option cutting 21% of the workforce (~350 jobs) for CHF186 million in savings, 60% of it from staff reductions. At its June 2026 (357th) session, the Governing Body formally approved implementation of a contingency framework, directing the Director-General to identify positions for elimination based on thematic priorities (while protecting critical functions and oversight roles) and suspending replenishment of the Building and Accommodation Fund (US$8.2 million). A special 357th bis session is now scheduled for September 7, 2026 with 'Reduction of posts within the contingency framework' formally on the agenda -- meaning a concrete decision on how many ILO jobs to cut is imminent, six days after this recheck, rather than a still-hypothetical September deadline as this entry's prior text implied.

title: IMLS Dismantlement Permanently Blocked by Federal Court — A Rare Full Reversal
institution: Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS)
status: Reversed -- a Nov. 2025 Rhode Island ruling (appeal withdrawn April 2026) and an April 2026 settlement restored IMLS, its grants and its staff; the White House FY2027 budget (April 2026) still proposes zeroing out IMLS funding.
date_of_action: 2025-03-14 (executive order issued) through 2026-04-09 (binding settlement agreement finalized)
what_changed: On March 14, 2025, Trump issued Executive Order 14238 directing the elimination of IMLS -- the only federal agency dedicated to the nation's libraries and museums. The administration moved quickly: by March 31, all but 12 of the agency's roughly 70-75 employees were placed on administrative leave, with a reduction-in-force notice set for May 4; nearly all IMLS board members were dismissed; and the agency's Acting Director (Keith Sonderling, who stated he would act 'in lockstep' with the administration) began terminating previously-awarded, congressionally-appropriated grants nationwide, in notices that started reaching grantees late on April 2 with an effective date of April 1, including Grants to States, National Leadership Grants, and Laura Bush 21st Century Librarian grants. Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency was directly involved in the dismantlement's early days -- DOGE representatives visited IMLS's Washington offices alongside Sonderling on March 20, 2025, and on April 3, 2025, DOGE publicly congratulated Sonderling for 'cancelling $25M in wasteful DEI grants'. The terminations reached the Grants to States program -- the largest single source of federal library funding, sent to every state by population-based formula at more than $180 million a year -- and in April, California, Connecticut, and Washington were the only states told that the rest of their year's funding was cancelled. The cutoff had immediate on-the-ground effects: **on April 9, 2025, the Maine State Library announced it would close for two weeks and lay off 13 employees -- one-third of its staff -- whose positions IMLS funded (the agency supplied about 30 percent of the library's funding); eight were laid off on May 8, and the closure was extended**; Mississippi libraries suspended the Hoopla e-book and audiobook app in some counties, and South Dakota put its interlibrary loan program on hold. Court filings in the libraries' case described "many hundreds" of terminated grants, with the vast majority of competitive IMLS grants terminated on April 8 and several hundred more cancelled on April 28. A November 11, 2025 American Alliance of Museums survey found IMLS, NEH and NEA were the federal grantmakers most often cited among museums reporting lost federal funding since Trump took office, with two-thirds of affected museums saying the lost funding had not been replaced; the survey's publication predates the same month's court ruling and December reinstatement described below. Unlike most entries in this tracker, this story does not end in unreversed loss: the American Library Association and AFSCME sued (ALA v. Sonderling), and 21 state attorneys general separately sued in Rhode Island v. Trump. On May 1, 2025, the federal court in Washington, D.C., hearing the libraries' case, issued a temporary restraining order barring IMLS from firing staff or placing more on administrative leave, days before the mass layoff was to take effect. In the states' case, the federal court in Rhode Island granted a preliminary injunction on May 6, 2025 (entered May 13), finding the dismantlement likely unlawful. The D.C. order later expired, and that court denied the libraries a preliminary injunction on June 6, 2025. On November 21, 2025, the federal district court in Rhode Island, ruling in the states' case, found the dismantlement actions 'arbitrary and capricious' and 'contrary to law,' set them aside, and permanently barred further steps to carry out the order, and on December 3, 2025, IMLS announced it had reinstated all previously terminated grants. On April 6, 2026, a federal court granted the administration's request to withdraw its appeal of that ruling, and on April 9, 2026, ALA, AFSCME, and the Department of Justice signed a settlement agreement in the libraries' separate case, binding on all parties, that keeps IMLS intact and continuing its congressionally mandated work, confirms that terminated grants were reinstated and staff reductions reversed, and records the administration's representation that it will take no further steps to carry out the executive order against IMLS; the parties filed a stipulation dismissing that case, without prejudice, the same day -- closing the litigation with the agency fully restored, not merely paused.

primary_proponent.name: Keith Sonderling
primary_proponent.role: Acting Director of IMLS (appointed to implement the executive order)
primary_proponent.note: Sonderling stated publicly he would act 'in lockstep' with the administration's directive to eliminate the agency, and personally signed the grant-termination notices sent to states. This is the same official covered in this project's Cabinet-Level Legal Exposure tracker for these IMLS actions.

estimated_impact.summary: During the roughly eight months before grants were reinstated, the shutdown attempt cut library services people used: Mississippi libraries suspended the Hoopla e-book and audiobook app in some counties, South Dakota put its interlibrary loan program on hold, and the Maine State Library closed and laid off eight staff after announcing 13 layoffs (one-third of its staff). In an American Alliance of Museums survey, 24% of museums that lost federal funding in 2025 (most often from IMLS, NEH or NEA) cancelled programming for students, rural communities, people with disabilities, the elderly or veterans, and 67% said the money had not been replaced. Individual grantees were left in limbo: the Science Center of Iowa, which had received a $196,046 IMLS grant, warned that an internship program it hoped to launch would be jeopardized if the agency were dismantled, and the Dubuque Museum of Art's $74,979 award, which it had planned to use to hire and train staff, was frozen until April 2025. IMLS awarded about $266 million in grants to museums and libraries in 2024 (NPR), and its Grants to States program alone distributes more than $180 million a year (EveryLibrary). The attempt was then reversed: all terminated grants were reinstated in December 2025, and the April 2026 settlement confirmed the staff cuts were rescinded.

No health or mortality effect is documented. The White House FY2027 budget, released April 3, 2026, again proposes zeroing out IMLS funding, leaving the agency's FY2027 funding level to Congress even though the dismantlement-by-executive-order question is settled.

title: Immigrant Student Enrollment Collapsed Nationwide Under Trump's Deportation Push, Straining School Budgets and Closing Newcomer Programs
institution: Local public school districts nationwide (Miami-Dade, Denver, Houston ISD, San Diego Unified, and others) -- driven by Department of Homeland Security immigration enforcement policy
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition -- reporting describes a multi-year (2023-2025) decline still in progress, not a single resolved event
date_of_action: 2023-2025 (reporting published November 2025)
what_changed: Public school districts across the U.S. reported sharp, multi-year drops in immigrant student enrollment, driven by deportations, families self-deporting, and a steep decline in new arrivals under the Trump administration's border and immigration-enforcement policies. Miami-Dade County Public Schools enrolled about 2,550 students from another country so far this school year -- down from nearly 14,000 last year and more than 20,000 the year before, per Miami-Dade School Board member Luisa Santos; the collective decline erased roughly $70 million from the district's annual budget. Denver Public Schools enrolled 400 new-to-country students this past summer, compared with 1,500 the previous summer. **Houston Independent School District shuttered its Las Americas Newcomer School, dedicated to children new to the U.S., after its enrollment fell to 21 students from 111 the year before.** At Perkins K-8 in San Diego, Principal Fernando Hernandez had not enrolled a single newcomer student this school year as of the reporting; the school separately serves a student body roughly one-third of whom experience homelessness. Superintendent Bart Reeves (Albertville City Schools) and Daniel Mojica (director of Chelsea's Parent Information Center) were also quoted describing the same pattern in their districts. A companion finding from a separate, independently-conducted survey published the same month (Physicians for Human Rights, Nov. 19, 2025; 691 health care workers across 30 states, surveyed March-August 2025) found 84% of respondents reported significant or moderate decreases in pediatric patient visits since the administration's January 2025 immigration executive orders -- indicating the same fear-driven withdrawal from public institutions documented in schools extends to health care access for immigrant families' children.

title: Surge in Immigration-Detention Habeas Corpus Cases Is Pulling Prosecutors Off Criminal Casework Nationwide
institution: U.S. Attorney's Offices nationwide, Department of Justice
status: Ongoing as of this entry's addition (February 2026 reporting) -- no indication in sourcing reviewed that DOJ has added prosecutorial capacity to offset the habeas caseload surge
date_of_action: 2025-2026 (surge intensifying alongside expanded immigration-detention enforcement)
what_changed: A sharp increase in immigration detentions under the administration's enforcement push has produced a corresponding wave of habeas corpus petitions -- detainees' court challenges to the legality of their detention -- that CBS News's reporting describes as overwhelming U.S. Attorney's offices nationwide. **Prosecutors are being pulled away from criminal casework to respond to the volume of habeas filings, straining offices already reduced by earlier staffing cuts and departures.** The strain compounds separately-documented office-specific staffing collapses this tracker records elsewhere (e.g. the Minnesota U.S. Attorney's Office exodus, prosecution/cabinet-level/bondi-doj-renee-good-widow-investigation-2026.json), applying the same underlying dynamic -- civil/immigration litigation demand outpacing available career prosecutorial staff -- at a national scale rather than a single office. Update 2026-08-17: subsequent reporting has quantified the surge far more precisely than was available when this entry was added. Habeas petitions related to immigration detention rose roughly 36-fold nationally, from about 222 filed in 2024 to approximately 8,000 filed in 2025; one federal district alone received nearly 3,900 immigration habeas petitions in just the first five months of 2026, and the federal court in Minnesota received more than 1,200 such cases in the first half of 2026, up from just 12 two years earlier. DOJ's own Executive Office for United States Attorneys has acknowledged the strain directly: it sent a request to the civil chiefs of all 93 U.S. Attorney's offices asking them to report their pending immigration-habeas caseloads and civil-AUSA staffing levels since the start of fiscal year 2025, as of a January 26, 2026 data pull -- confirming DOJ leadership is tracking the capacity strain this entry documents, even though sourcing reviewed does not show additional prosecutorial capacity has been added to offset it.

primary_proponent.role: Federal agencies whose expanded detention enforcement drove the underlying habeas caseload surge
primary_proponent.note: The strain is a downstream consequence of the administration's detention-enforcement volume rather than a discrete standalone policy decision by DOJ leadership.

title: Trump Ordered U.S. Withdrawal From 66 International Organizations, Including the UN Population Fund and the Climate-Treaty Framework
institution: Executive Office of the President; U.S. Department of State
status: Ordered -- agencies directed to effectuate withdrawal 'as soon as possible'; implementation across 66 distinct bodies ongoing
date_of_action: 2026-01-07 (memorandum signed), following a review mandated by Executive Order 14199 (Feb. 4, 2025)
what_changed: On January 7, 2026, Trump signed a Presidential Memorandum, 'Withdrawing the United States from International Organizations, Conventions, and Treaties that Are Contrary to the Interests of the United States,' directing U.S. withdrawal from 66 international bodies -- 35 non-UN organizations and 31 UN entities -- following a State Department review mandated by Executive Order 14199 (Feb. 4, 2025). The memorandum determined it 'contrary to the interests of the United States to remain a member of, participate in, or otherwise provide support to' the listed organizations and directed all executive departments and agencies to effectuate the withdrawals 'as soon as possible.' The list spans climate, population/health, gender, and multilateral-economic bodies: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC, the treaty underlying the Paris Agreement process) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the International Renewable Energy Agency and International Solar Alliance, the UN Population Fund (UNFPA), UN Women, the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, and multiple UN regional economic commissions, among others. The withdrawal formalizes, at the institutional/treaty level, funding cuts to some of these bodies that had already begun during 2025: **UNFPA -- the main multilateral agency for sexual/reproductive health, maternal health, and gender-based-violence prevention in humanitarian settings -- lost its entire U.S. contribution** (the U.S. was its largest single donor, $286 million in 2024, out of roughly $377 million in total 2025 funding suspended) during 2025, ahead of this formal January 2026 withdrawal. The UNFCCC secretariat, whose 2024-2025 operating budget was about $96.5 million (roughly 22% funded by the U.S., about $7.5 million in 2024), and the IPCC, which the U.S. supplied roughly 30% of historical voluntary contributions to (~$67 million cumulatively, though zero in 2025), both lose their largest historical funder. Philanthropist Michael Bloomberg separately pledged in January 2025 to have Bloomberg Philanthropies cover the UNFCCC's resulting funding gap, an early instance of private philanthropy substituting for withdrawn federal climate-diplomacy funding. Critics, including Nina Schwalbe of the Georgetown Center for Global Health Policy and Politics, called the withdrawal 'a ridiculous and dangerous, thoughtless and malicious action'; commentators argued it cedes U.S. influence over international climate, health, and economic-development norms to other powers as those bodies continue operating without U.S. participation. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0793): the same list also included two counterterrorism/violent-extremism-prevention bodies -- the Global Community Engagement and Resilience Fund (GCERF), which funds community-level extremism-prevention programs across dozens of countries, and the 30-nation Global Counterterrorism Forum (GCTF). Reuters reported GCERF's Geneva-based executive director, Dr. Khalid Koser, said the decision came as a surprise, without explanation, and reflects a deeper ideological shift away from multilateral, prevention-focused counterterrorism programs toward purely security-focused measures. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0811): on January 27, 2026, a separate, dedicated withdrawal process -- the U.S.'s exit from the Paris Agreement itself, distinct from the UNFCCC parent-treaty withdrawal above -- became formally effective, one year after Trump announced it via Executive Order 14162 on his first day in office (Jan. 20, 2025) and the required one-year notice period under the Agreement's own exit clause ran out. Per Harvard's Environmental and Energy Law Program tracker, this made the U.S. the only country to have withdrawn from the Paris Agreement twice (having also done so in Trump's first term before rejoining under Biden), leaving it grouped with Libya, Yemen, and Iran as the treaty's only non-signatories. Amnesty International warned the withdrawal risked triggering a global 'race to the bottom' on climate commitments. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0605): an earlier, narrower instance of the same disengagement pattern -- rejecting a specific UN health text rather than withdrawing from an organization -- came September 26, 2025, when HHS Secretary Kennedy told the UN General Assembly's High-Level Meeting on Non-Communicable Diseases that the U.S. would reject the meeting's draft political declaration on cancer, diabetes, heart disease, and mental health, forcing the text (previously headed for adoption by consensus after five months of formal negotiations) to a full vote instead. Kennedy cited the U.S.'s inability to accept language 'that promotes gender ideology' or 'an international right to abortion' -- but NPR reported the declaration's actual text addresses neither reproductive rights nor gender identity, and HHS did not respond to NPR's request to explain what specific language it objected to. When the declaration finally came to a General Assembly vote in December 2025, it passed 175-2, with only the United States and Argentina voting against and Paraguay abstaining -- leaving the U.S. isolated against near-unanimous global agreement on a framework it had helped negotiate for years.

The memorandum's own stated rationale focuses on organizations being 'wasteful, ineffective, or harmful' and inefficient users of taxpayer funds; it identifies no specific dollar savings figure.

what_changed.base: On January 7, 2026, Trump signed a Presidential Memorandum, 'Withdrawing the United States from International Organizations, Conventions, and Treaties that Are Contrary to the Interests of the United States,' directing U.S. withdrawal from 66 international bodies -- 35 non-UN organizations and 31 UN entities -- following a State Department review mandated by Executive Order 14199 (Feb. 4, 2025). The memorandum determined it 'contrary to the interests of the United States to remain a member of, participate in, or otherwise provide support to' the listed organizations and directed all executive departments and agencies to effectuate the withdrawals 'as soon as possible.' The list spans climate, population/health, gender, and multilateral-economic bodies: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC, the treaty underlying the Paris Agreement process) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the International Renewable Energy Agency and International Solar Alliance, the UN Population Fund (UNFPA), UN Women, the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, and multiple UN regional economic commissions, among others. The withdrawal formalizes, at the institutional/treaty level, funding cuts to some of these bodies that had already begun during 2025: **UNFPA -- the main multilateral agency for sexual/reproductive health, maternal health, and gender-based-violence prevention in humanitarian settings -- lost its entire U.S. contribution** (the U.S. was its largest single donor, $286 million in 2024, out of roughly $377 million in total 2025 funding suspended) during 2025, ahead of this formal January 2026 withdrawal. The UNFCCC secretariat, whose 2024-2025 operating budget was about $96.5 million (roughly 22% funded by the U.S., about $7.5 million in 2024), and the IPCC, which the U.S. supplied roughly 30% of historical voluntary contributions to (~$67 million cumulatively, though zero in 2025), both lose their largest historical funder. Philanthropist Michael Bloomberg separately pledged in January 2025 to have Bloomberg Philanthropies cover the UNFCCC's resulting funding gap, an early instance of private philanthropy substituting for withdrawn federal climate-diplomacy funding. Critics, including Nina Schwalbe of the Georgetown Center for Global Health Policy and Politics, called the withdrawal 'a ridiculous and dangerous, thoughtless and malicious action'; commentators argued it cedes U.S. influence over international climate, health, and economic-development norms to other powers as those bodies continue operating without U.S. participation.

Reuters reported GCERF's Geneva-based executive director, Dr. Khalid Koser, said the decision came as a surprise, without explanation, and reflects a deeper ideological shift away from multilateral, prevention-focused counterterrorism programs toward purely security-focused measures.

updates.text: Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0811): on January 27, 2026, a separate, dedicated withdrawal process -- the U.S.'s exit from the Paris Agreement itself, distinct from the UNFCCC parent-treaty withdrawal above -- became formally effective, one year after Trump announced it via Executive Order 14162 on his first day in office (Jan. 20, 2025) and the required one-year notice period under the Agreement's own exit clause ran out. Per Harvard's Environmental and Energy Law Program tracker, this made the U.S. the only country to have withdrawn from the Paris Agreement twice (having also done so in Trump's first term before rejoining under Biden), leaving it grouped with Libya, Yemen, and Iran as the treaty's only non-signatories. Amnesty International warned the withdrawal risked triggering a global 'race to the bottom' on climate commitments.

updates.text: Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0605): an earlier, narrower instance of the same disengagement pattern -- rejecting a specific UN health text rather than withdrawing from an organization -- came September 26, 2025, when HHS Secretary Kennedy told the UN General Assembly's High-Level Meeting on Non-Communicable Diseases that the U.S. would reject the meeting's draft political declaration on cancer, diabetes, heart disease, and mental health, forcing the text (previously headed for adoption by consensus after five months of formal negotiations) to a full vote instead. Kennedy cited the U.S.'s inability to accept language 'that promotes gender ideology' or 'an international right to abortion' -- but NPR reported the declaration's actual text addresses neither reproductive rights nor gender identity, and HHS did not respond to NPR's request to explain what specific language it objected to. When the declaration finally came to a General Assembly vote in December 2025, it passed 175-2, with only the United States and Argentina voting against and Paraguay abstaining -- leaving the U.S. isolated against near-unanimous global agreement on a framework it had helped negotiate for years.

title: Treasury Watchdog Finds ICE Didn't Meet Data-Safeguarding Standards Before Signing Taxpayer Data-Sharing Deal; Judge Separately Found 47,000 Unlawful Disclosures
institution: Internal Revenue Service (IRS) / Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), under a Treasury-DHS data-sharing agreement
status: Data-sharing agreement remains in effect as of this entry's sourcing; the Treasury Inspector General's findings and the federal court's unlawful-disclosure ruling are both matters of record, with no indication in reporting reviewed that the underlying agreement has been suspended or restructured in response
date_of_action: 2025-04 (ICE-IRS memorandum of understanding signed) through 2026-06 (Treasury IG report released)
what_changed: In April 2025, ICE and the IRS signed a memorandum of understanding allowing ICE to submit names and addresses of immigrants it identified as in the U.S. illegally to the IRS for cross-verification against confidential tax records, supporting the administration's mass-deportation operation. In June 2026, the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) released a partially-redacted report finding that ICE did not meet required data-safeguarding standards before the MOU was signed, and that inconsistent formatting in ICE's submitted data and mismatches with the IRS's own matching criteria produced errors, incomplete records, and improper disclosures of taxpayer information. Separately, **a federal judge ruled in February 2026 that the IRS broke the law by disclosing confidential taxpayer information to ICE, specifically identifying 47,000 unlawful disclosures.**

primary_proponent.name: IRS and DHS/ICE leadership (agreement signed under then-Acting IRS leadership and DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's department)
primary_proponent.role: Agencies party to the April 2025 data-sharing MOU
primary_proponent.note: The watchdog's finding that ICE failed to meet safeguarding standards before the MOU was signed places responsibility on the agencies' own pre-agreement vetting process, not solely on downstream implementation errors.

estimated_impact.summary: The combination of a documented pre-agreement safeguarding failure (per TIGTA) and a court's independent finding of 47,000 unlawful taxpayer-data disclosures (per the February 2026 ruling) establishes both a systemic design flaw and a concrete, quantified harm: confidential taxpayer information -- information millions of Americans, including immigrants who file taxes using ITINs, provide under a decades-old expectation of confidentiality -- was shared through a system that failed basic data-quality and legal-compliance standards.

The 47,000-disclosure court finding and the TIGTA report describe related but distinct failures within the same data-sharing relationship -- a legal violation and a data-quality/safeguarding deficiency, respectively -- and should not be conflated as a single figure.

title: Understaffed IRS's Technical 'Glitch' Left $51 Million in Political Donations Undisclosed, With No Fix Timeline
institution: Internal Revenue Service
status: Unresolved as of this entry's addition -- no fix timeline given
date_of_action: 2025-H2 (donations affected) through 2026-02 (error discovered) and 2026-03 (reported unresolved)
what_changed: The Center for Political Accountability (CPA), a campaign-finance watchdog, found that **a technical error at the IRS left $51 million in political donations undisclosed for the second half of 2025, affecting major state-level election groups from both parties** -- including the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Republican State Leadership Committee, and the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, whose combined missing disclosures totaled $41 million of the $51 million figure. CPA researchers discovered the discrepancy in February 2026, after the standard January 31 deadline for the prior year's donor and spending lists to become public had passed. As of The Guardian's March 2026 reporting, the IRS had given no clear timeline for fixing the error. The IRS began 2025 with about 102,000 employees and finished the year with roughly 74,000 -- a reduction of about 28,000, or 27%, following a series of firings and layoffs driven by DOGE (documented in more detail in this tracker's irs-workforce-collapse-trump2.json entry) -- which The Guardian's reporting connects to the agency's reduced capacity to identify and fix the disclosure error.
