title: IRS Lost 27% of Its Workforce and a Third of Its Auditors — Independent Watchdogs Project $600B in Lost Revenue
institution: Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
status: Ongoing -- the FY2027 request would eliminate roughly 4,800 more positions, nearly all in enforcement; on April 24, 2026, a House committee advanced a bill setting IRS funding at $10.2 billion, not yet enacted. The Tax Year 2023 tax-gap estimate remains unpublished.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial probationary firings) through 2026-04 (most recent GAO/TIGTA reporting)
what_changed:
Beginning February 2025, the IRS workforce was cut by approximately 27%, falling from roughly 102,000 employees in January 2025 to about 74,000 by December 2025 -- a reduction of nearly 28,000 people, primarily via probationary-employee terminations (~7,300), deferred-resignation buyouts (~4,700), and further attrition. The cuts were not evenly distributed: Taxpayer Services (which processes returns, answers phones, and handles correspondence) lost about 21-22% of its staff; the agency's IT function lost 27%; and revenue agents -- the specialists who conduct complex audits of high-income individuals, partnerships, and large corporations -- lost roughly 3,600 people, about 31% of the entire auditing workforce.

A TIGTA report, reported by FedScoop around July 26, 2025, gave an earlier (May 2025) snapshot with division-level breakdowns not otherwise named in this entry: as of May 2025 the IRS had already fallen from ~103,000 to 77,428 staff (a 25% loss), with the Small Business/Self-Employed division down 35%, Human Capital down 28%, and Tax Exempt and Government Entities down 25% -- distinct divisions from the Taxpayer Services, IT, and revenue-agent breakdowns already documented above from the later year-end data. The same report found nearly 300 employees had been separated via formal reduction-in-force actions specifically, as distinct from the far larger numbers who left via deferred resignation or retirement.

Internal IRS emails reveal that senior IRS lawyer Joseph Rillotta warned agency officials in February 2025 that citing 'poor performance' as the justification for the roughly 7,000 probationary terminations that month was false -- no performance assessments had been conducted -- and amounted to fraud; the warning went unheeded, and termination letters citing performance issues went out February 20, 2025. Judge Alsup, ruling on the multi-agency probationary-firings case that also covered Treasury (the IRS's parent department), found in his March 13, 2025 preliminary injunction that the stated justification was 'a lie' and ordered reinstatement; the Supreme Court stayed that reinstatement order on April 8, 2025 on standing grounds, without addressing the merits of the fraud finding, and separate litigation -- including a California case alleging one of the largest employment-fraud schemes in U.S. history -- remained pending as of the reporting reviewed. In the interim, employees who had been reinstated under the since-stayed order were left in administrative limbo: CNN reported in May 2025 that reinstated IRS staff faced lapsed health insurance, unprocessed pension paperwork, and denied workers'-compensation claims amid a decimated HR function, with some describing emergency-room bills and delayed cancer screenings during the gap.

The cuts extended to physical infrastructure as well as headcount: in late February 2025, the General Services Administration sent the IRS a letter proposing to terminate or not renew leases on more than 110 (some reporting says up to 120) Taxpayer Assistance Centers -- the walk-in offices where taxpayers get in-person help with identity theft, audits, and other complex issues -- right at the height of tax-filing season. After pushback from taxpayers, tax professionals, and lawmakers, the IRS agreed to keep TAC offices open through the 2025 filing season, but the closures resumed afterward: by September 2025 the IRS confirmed it would close nine specific centers across six states (Pennsylvania, Iowa, New York, Kentucky, California, and West Virginia), effective November 30, 2025.

The Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) -- the statutorily independent office within the IRS, quoted throughout this entry, that helps individual taxpayers resolve problems and reports directly to Congress -- was itself targeted for a roughly 25% staff cut, losing 430 of its approximately 1,900 employees in an initial phase of reductions reported in March 2025, on top of more than 90 TAS employees who had already left via deferred resignation or earlier layoffs. Former National Taxpayer Advocate Nina Olson (2001-2019) said the cuts 'will have devastating consequences to the taxpayers that are in need of help.' The reduction directly shrank the capacity of the same watchdog office whose independent reporting on IRS-wide staffing and filing-season risk is cited elsewhere in this entry.

Within the IT-function losses, one dramatic episode stands out: on March 31, 2025, roughly 50 senior IT executives -- most at the Senior Executive Service level, largely associate chief information officers with expertise spanning cybersecurity, modernization, applications, contracts, networks, and data-center operations -- were placed on administrative leave and had their system access cut off immediately, in the middle of tax-filing season. The decision was made by Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency and carried out by then-acting IRS Commissioner Melanie Krause; CNN reported the sidelined officials were seen internally as possible 'blockers' to a separate, controversial push to share IRS taxpayer data with immigration enforcement authorities. The IRS's chief information officer, Rajiv Uppal, and chief technology officer, Kaschit Pandya, were not among those dismissed. Of the roughly 50, 26 eventually departed via Treasury's deferred-resignation offer, while the other 22 remained on administrative leave.

Uppal himself resigned two weeks later regardless: on April 14, 2025 -- the eve of the April 15 tax-filing deadline -- he told staff by email he would depart effective April 28, 2025, with Pandya, who had already been working closely with DOGE and assumed many CIO responsibilities, serving as acting CIO. Former IRS officials and governance experts warned the leadership churn and uncertainty, arriving at the height of filing season, risked disrupting tax-revenue collection itself.

One office was singled out early and disproportionately. When the RIF wave began in early April 2025, the IRS's Office of Civil Rights and Compliance -- which investigates discrimination complaints and audits/investigations bias -- was cut far more severely than the agency-wide rate: nearly 80% of its roughly 176 employees received RIF notices (a 75% net reduction), well above the agency-wide 27% rate documented above, with the remaining staff folded into the Office of Chief Counsel. Fox News, Government Executive, and CPA Practice Advisor all reported the office as an early, specific RIF target rather than swept up incidentally in the broader cuts. In August 2025, IRS Commissioner Billy Long told the office's employees the RIF notices were being reversed, with a memo stating the action served as 'cancellation of your prior RIF notice of separation' -- a reversal Federal News Network reported was specific to this office, not the broader workforce reduction documented above.

CNBC reported April 17, 2025 that the staffing losses were already producing concrete, named case-level consequences for wealthy-taxpayer enforcement: one IRS agent described three 'enterprise' cases -- two involving business partnerships and one involving a wealthy sports team owner, together representing millions of dollars in potential additional tax -- that were dropped for lack of staff to continue them when he departed. A subsequent Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) report, covered by CBS News and Yahoo Finance in 2026, confirmed the pattern with agency-wide, post-hoc FY2025 outcome data distinct from the modeled $600B Yale Budget Lab projection (below): after losing about 30% of its auditors, the IRS opened roughly 43,000 examinations of taxpayers earning over $400,000 in FY2025, down 26% from the prior year; the Global High Wealth program (auditing the wealthiest taxpayers) had 27% fewer employees as of January 2026 than before the FY2025 cuts; audits of new business partnerships fell 30%; and audit revenue collected fell 35%, or about $3.5 billion, in FY2025 -- a real, watchdog-confirmed dollar figure of enforcement revenue actually lost, not merely a future projection. The Yale Budget Lab, mapping the National Taxpayer Advocate's breakdown of the 2025 workforce reduction by operating function onto the IRS's four budget-activity categories, projected in April 2026 that the 2025 staffing reductions will reduce IRS revenues by almost $600 billion over the 2026-2035 budget window; it noted that the IRS collects 96 percent of federal revenues and that revenue losses from reduced enforcement capacity compound over time through deteriorating voluntary compliance.

On October 8, 2025, as the Oct-Nov 2025 government shutdown entered its second week, the IRS furloughed more than 34,000 employees, 46% of its remaining staff, leaving about 39,870 employees (53.6%) on the job. The furlough suspended most taxpayer services, including phone assistance and the statutorily independent Taxpayer Advocate Service, while retained staff focused on the 2025 filing season and implementing the administration's tax law; audits and collections activity also halted. The IRS had announced September 29 that furloughs would begin if the shutdown exceeded five business days. During the same shutdown, the IRS rescinded its prior promise to guarantee full back pay to its furloughed workers, citing new guidance from Russell Vought's OMB. The reversal followed an OMB draft legal opinion questioning the legality of automatic back pay for furloughed employees -- despite a 2019 law Trump himself signed into effect requiring it -- and came on the heels of Trump's own public threat, the same month, to withhold pay from federal workers he said 'don't deserve' it.

Heading into the 2026 filing season, the agency had cycled through seven different commissioners or acting commissioners over the course of 2025 alone -- an unprecedented churn rate Brookings separately described as historically unmatched. One of those seven, Gary Shapley -- a Musk- and congressional-Republican-backed IRS Criminal Investigation official -- was installed as acting commissioner April 15, 2025 while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was traveling abroad, then removed just three days later, on April 18, after Bessent objected to not being consulted on the appointment and complained directly to Trump; Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender was named acting commissioner in his place, and Shapley remained at IRS Criminal Investigation. Bessent said 'trust must be brought back to the IRS,' framing Faulkender's installation as a corrective. On January 2, 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Sen. Angus King led 15 senators in a letter to Treasury Secretary/Acting IRS Commissioner Scott Bessent and IRS Chief of Taxpayer Services Ken Corbin warning the agency was not ready for the upcoming filing season given the combination of that leadership churn, the workforce cuts already documented above, and the tax-law changes the agency had to implement simultaneously. National Taxpayer Advocate Erin Collins, who had called the 2025 filing season 'one of the most successful filing seasons in recent memory,' warned in her January 2026 annual report that 'the landscape is markedly different' for 2026, citing a 27% workforce reduction, leadership turnover, and complex tax-law changes from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. At an April 15, 2026 Senate Finance Committee hearing, IRS CEO Frank Bisignano said the agency can have both 'less people and better results'; the IRS reported receiving more than 134 million individual returns by mid-April 2026, with more than 90% of electronic filers refunded within 21 days, and the National Taxpayer Advocate found in June 2026 that the IRS 'performed better than expected in most respects' while taxpayers needing help 'often struggled to get it.'

Congress separately cut the IRS enforcement budget by 8% for FY2026 (the lowest inflation-adjusted level since 1988) and cut $1.1 billion (12%) from the IRS's base budget overall -- what CBPP called the largest-ever cut to IRS base funding -- rescinding most of the remaining Inflation Reduction Act funding that had been allocated to rebuild the agency; the base budget is now about 40% below its 2010 level after inflation. The IRS responded by lowering its own phone-service target from 85% to 70% of calls answered, and an independent analysis by the Center for Taxpayer Rights found call wait times on the main line increased more than 70% between February 2025 and February 2026. A March 2026 GAO audit found the IRS's staffing reductions 'were not targeted or strategic' and that the agency still lacks an updated strategic workforce plan.

Notably, IRS CEO Frank Bisignano simultaneously serves as the Senate-confirmed Commissioner of the Social Security Administration, splitting his attention across both agencies during this period. The IRS's FY2027 budget request, released in 2026, seeks $9.8 billion in discretionary funding, down $1.4 billion from the $11.2 billion Congress enacted for FY2026, and proposes eliminating roughly 4,800 more positions (about 17% of enforcement staff) on top of the 27% already lost in 2025. Nearly all of the proposed staffing reduction falls on enforcement -- examinations and collections -- which would see an 18% budget cut, while taxpayer-service funding would see a small 3% increase. The IRS's own budget documents describe the enforcement-side cuts as yielding roughly $778 million in savings once implemented. Despite Bisignano's 'less people and better results' framing, internal documents reported by NOTUS show the IRS has been rushing to backfill critical staffing gaps, hiring roughly 2,000 employees as of January 2026 -- a partial rehire that still leaves the agency at a net ~28% workforce reduction from its January 2025 level, and that reporting characterizes as evidence of operational strain the agency's public statements had downplayed.

On April 24, 2026, the House Appropriations Committee approved the FY2027 Financial Services and General Government funding bill in a 34-28 vote, setting IRS funding at $10.2 billion -- higher than the administration's own $9.8 billion request but still roughly 8.5% below the $11.2 billion FY2026 enacted level, with close to $1.4 billion of the reduction concentrated in enforcement. An amendment offered by FSGG Subcommittee Ranking Member Steny Hoyer (D-MD) that would have restored $1.8 billion to enforcement funding failed. The bill has not yet passed the full House or been taken up by the Senate as of mid-August 2026, so it remains short of enactment -- but a committee-level vote already exists, which is a materially different posture than the budget request alone.

The New York Times reported in September 2026 that the IRS's Tax Year 2023 "tax gap" estimate -- the amount of taxes owed but not paid on time -- was due last fall and remains unpublished, after the agency's staff shrank by roughly 24% under the current administration. The most recent published estimate, released October 2024, put the Tax Year 2022 gap at roughly $700 billion. Treasury officials told the Times the absence of an updated figure makes it harder for policymakers to see the full extent of the damage from the agency's staffing cuts in real time.

primary_proponent.note: Publicly defended the cuts before the Senate Finance Committee, stating the agency can achieve 'less people and better results,' and that the IRS cut phone-center 'idle time' by nearly 50%. Committee Democrats, led by Ranking Member Ron Wyden, disputed this characterization directly in the same hearing. Bisignano told senators he treats running both SSA and IRS as managing 'two large organizations,' sometimes working 14-hour days across both.

estimated_impact.summary: Taxpayers lost help as the IRS shed about 27% of its staff in 2025: call wait times on the main line rose more than 70%, nine walk-in Taxpayer Assistance Centers were set to close, and a shutdown furlough of more than 34,000 employees suspended most taxpayer services. Separately, CNN reported that reinstated probationary workers faced lapsed health insurance, with some describing emergency-room bills and delayed cancer screenings. Enforcement fell sharply: a TIGTA report confirmed audit revenue fell about $3.5 billion (35%) in FY2025, and the Yale Budget Lab **projected the cuts will reduce federal revenue collection by almost $600 billion over the 2026-2035 window** -- noting that the IRS collects 96% of federal revenue and that revenue losses from reduced enforcement capacity compound over time through deteriorating voluntary compliance.

The $600B revenue projection is a modeled estimate from an academic institution (Yale Budget Lab), which modeled the specific 2025 staffing reductions broken down by IRS operating function using the agency's own budget-activity categories; it is not a government-produced figure and should be cited as such. The full revenue damage is also harder to measure because the IRS has not published its Tax Year 2023 tax-gap estimate; Treasury officials told the Times the absence of an updated figure makes it harder for policymakers to see the full extent of the damage from the agency's staffing cuts in real time.

title: J-1 Visa Interview Suspension and Travel Ban Jeopardized Over 1,000 Foreign Medical Residents Days Before Their July 1 Start Dates
institution: State Department
status: Interview pause lifted mid-June 2025, but recovery was incomplete -- some residents still faced embassy delays and missed start dates
date_of_action: 2025-05 (J-1 interview suspension) through 2025-07-07 (reporting on residual hospital staffing shortages)
what_changed: In late May 2025, the State Department suspended new interview appointments for J-1 exchange-visitor visas -- the visa category used by most international medical residents and fellows -- citing expanded 'enhanced vetting' requirements, just weeks before the July 1 date when most U.S. residency programs begin. On June 4, 2025, the administration compounded the disruption with a new travel ban barring citizens of 12 countries and restricting 7 more. The New York Times reported **at least 1,000 foreign medical residents were blocked or delayed from entering the U.S. as a result, jeopardizing staffing at safety-net hospitals -- particularly in rural and underserved areas -- that rely heavily on international medical graduates to fill residency positions** U.S. graduates often do not take. Roughly 6,600 international doctors had been accepted into U.S. residencies for the 2025 cycle. The State Department lifted the J-1 interview pause in mid-June 2025, but recovery was incomplete: the AP reported in early July that U.S. embassies were slow to reopen interview slots, with some residents still unable to secure appointments, and hospitals bracing for staffing shortages even after the formal pause ended.

primary_proponent.name: Marco Rubio
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of State
primary_proponent.note: The State Department, under Rubio, ordered the J-1 interview suspension and implemented the subsequent enhanced-vetting and travel-ban restrictions affecting medical residents.

estimated_impact.summary: A visa-processing disruption timed just before the annual U.S. residency start date threatened to leave safety-net and rural hospitals -- which depend disproportionately on international medical graduates -- short-staffed for training positions with no readily available domestic substitute, given how many of these positions U.S. medical graduates don't fill.

The interview pause itself was lifted within about three weeks, so the ultimate scale of permanently lost positions (versus delayed starts) was not fully resolved in sourcing reviewed at the time of this entry's creation.

title: Labor Department's Attempt to Shut Down All 99 Job Corps Centers Was Ruled Unlawful; Courts Kept Every Site Open
institution: Department of Labor
status: Blocked -- a federal court found DOL's closure of all 99 centers unlawful under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, and all centers remained open
date_of_action: 2025-05-29 (suspension announced) through 2025-07-29/31 (court orders keeping all 99 centers open)
what_changed: On May 29, 2025, the Department of Labor announced it was suspending operations at all 99 privately-operated Job Corps centers nationwide -- **a residential job-training program for low-income youth, many of them homeless, parents, or caregivers -- with closures to be completed by June 30, 2025, affecting more than 25,000 students**. The National Job Corps Association sued on behalf of private Job Corps operators, arguing the administration lacked authority to unilaterally dismantle a program Congress funds and structures under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA). U.S. District Judge Andrew L. Carter Jr. (S.D.N.Y.) granted a temporary restraining order on June 2025, which was followed by continued litigation over the following two months -- at one point 63 of the 99 centers were allowed to proceed toward closure before a subsequent ruling restored protection to all 99. By late July 2025, the court ruled definitively that DOL had unlawfully 'closed' all 99 privately operated Job Corps centers in violation of WIOA's requirements, and ordered that all centers remain open and continue serving students.

primary_proponent.name: Lori Chavez-DeRemer
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Labor
primary_proponent.note: DOL announced and attempted to execute the suspension of all 99 Job Corps centers; the courts subsequently found this action unlawful.

estimated_impact.summary: An attempted shutdown of a congressionally-funded job-training program serving more than 25,000 low-income youth -- many homeless, parents, or caregivers, some just months from graduation -- was found unlawful and blocked before taking full effect, though the roughly two-month period of legal uncertainty (May 29 to late July 2025) itself caused documented disruption and anxiety for students and staff at the affected centers.

title: LIHEAP Heating Assistance Program Staff Eliminated, Funding Delayed for Millions
institution: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), Administration for Children and Families, HHS
status: About $3.6B released Nov. 28, 2025, after the shutdown; the final ~$421.5M of FY2026 funds was held until Apr. 17, 2026. No public record of the fired staff being restored; in Sept. 2026, 116 House members asked HHS for staffing levels and FY2027 funds by Nov. 1.
date_of_action: 2025-04-01 (entire program staff terminated); 2025-10-01 through 2025-11-28 (funding delayed during shutdown)
what_changed: On April 1, 2025, in the Department of Health and Human Services' department-wide reduction in force, the Trump administration eliminated the entire federal staff that administered LIHEAP -- the ~$4.1 billion program that helps roughly 6 million low-income households pay heating and cooling bills, serving all 50 states, D.C., U.S. territories, and federally recognized tribes. Reported headcounts vary (NBC News counted 10 employees; Utility Dive later put it at about two dozen). Weeks later, Trump's FY2026 budget proposed zero funding for the program. When the October-November 2025 government shutdown (the longest in U.S. history at 43 days) began, LIHEAP's annual allocation -- normally sent to states in early November -- was held up. The Guardian reported that the firings had left no technical staff to apply the funding formula or approve state plans, and that HHS had been relying on outside paid consultants and staff from other programs, some of whom were laid off in October. **Kansas, Pennsylvania, New York, Minnesota, Maine, and Wyoming announced delays or disruptions to their programs as winter set in; Pennsylvania pushed payments for some 300,000 households from November to at least December, while Massachusetts and Alaska stretched leftover funds and Connecticut and Vermont prepared to front costs with state money.** NEADA executive director Mark Wolfe warned that the loss of staff would slow the release even after the shutdown ended: "Once you've fired the staff, things just slow down." The shutdown ended November 12, and about $3.6 billion was finally released to states and tribes on November 28, 2025, over two weeks later and roughly a month past the normal early-November distribution. Full-year FY2026 funding of $4.045 billion was signed into law on February 3, 2026, but the final roughly $421.5 million (10 percent) was not released until April 17, 2026, two days after 35 senators wrote to the White House Office of Management and Budget demanding it. Trump's FY2027 budget, released April 3, 2026, again proposed eliminating all federal LIHEAP funding, even as home heating costs kept rising and the program kept bipartisan congressional support. In September 2026, citing "a history of repeated funding delays by HHS to states," 116 House members asked HHS to release FY2027 funds no later than November 1 and to report how many staff now work on the program.

Advocates warned of heat rationing and of families giving up food, medicine and medical care to pay energy bills, with about 21 million U.S. households already behind on those bills and utility shutoffs projected to reach 4 million in 2025. In Pennsylvania alone, payments for about 300,000 households slipped from November to at least December. About $3.6 billion reached states only on November 28, 2025, and the final ~$421.5 million of FY2026 funds was held until April 2026, while the program ran without the dedicated federal staff fired in April 2025.

title: FDA Commissioner Marty Makary Resigned After Being Pressured to Approve Flavored Vapes and Restrict the Abortion Pill
institution: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
status: Makary resigned May 12, 2026. Kyle Diamantas, deputy commissioner for food, was named acting commissioner and was still acting in a Sept 21, 2026 FDA release; Heidi Overton was nominated as commissioner Sept 14, 2026, pending in Senate committee.
date_of_action: 2026-05-05 (FDA authorizes flavored Glas e-cigarettes under reported White House pressure) through 2026-05-12 (Makary's resignation)
what_changed: The internal turmoil that ultimately led to Makary's departure had a documented earlier flashpoint. The Wall Street Journal reported November 15, 2025 that HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other Trump administration officials had discussed scaling back Makary's role months before his eventual resignation -- floating a plan to install a separate leader to run the FDA's day-to-day operations while leaving Makary as a figurehead, driven by concerns over infighting among Makary's own deputies. Officials paused the plan at the time, giving Makary a chance to fix the agency's leadership issues rather than acting immediately. Days earlier, on November 11, 2025, the FDA had named veteran oncology chief Richard Pazdur director of its Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, which regulates over-the-counter and most prescription drugs, replacing George Tidmarsh, who had resigned earlier that month amid serious concerns about his personal conduct. Within weeks Pazdur filed to retire from the agency; CNN reported on December 2, 2025, citing people familiar with the situation, that his exit came amid frustration with Makary and biologics chief Vinay Prasad and over what Pazdur saw as political interference in his division. FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned on May 12, 2026, amid internal conflicts over two major policy disputes. On flavored vaping products: on May 5, 2026 the FDA authorized four e-cigarette pods from vaping company Glas Inc., two menthol and two in flavors other than tobacco and menthol -- its first such non-tobacco, non-menthol authorization -- for adults 21 and older using a device locked to an ID-verified user's phone -- a move the Wall Street Journal reported came only after **President Trump personally pressured Makary to approve the fruit-flavored vapes, which Makary had been refusing to authorize**; a source told CBS News Makary was leaving over this dispute, having been forced by other members of the administration to approve flavored products he did not want to approve, and a source close to HHS leadership told NBC News the authorization triggered his decision, saying he chose to resign rather than defend it at congressional testimony scheduled for the next day. On the abortion pill: according to NBC's source, some HHS officials were pushing Makary to impose tighter restrictions on mifepristone. Kennedy had asked Makary in June 2025 to review the drug's safety; after December reports that he had slow-walked the study, SBA Pro-Life America and other conservatives called for his firing, and the review had not been released when he resigned. Trump announced on Truth Social that Kyle Diamantas, the FDA's deputy commissioner for food and a lawyer without a medical degree, would serve as acting commissioner, and the Senate Appropriations subcommittee hearing at which Makary had been due to testify was postponed. A senior career FDA official told CBS News that Makary's management of a drug-review voucher program had forced "virtually impossible levels of work on divisions that are significantly understaffed right now" after an exodus of veteran scientists, and former commissioner Scott Gottlieb said on CBS's "Face the Nation" on May 10, two days before the resignation, that "cumulatively, that's taken a toll on the agency," citing departures and political appointees in career leadership posts. Diamantas was still acting commissioner as of a September 21, 2026 FDA announcement. Heidi Overton's nomination to be Commissioner of Food and Drugs was referred to the Senate HELP committee on September 14, 2026, where it was pending as of late September. This resignation is distinct from, but adds to, the extensive leadership churn already documented in this tracker's separate entry on FDA's CBER (vaccine/biologics) division, where Makary had previously intervened as Commissioner during 2025-2026 turmoil -- this entry covers Makary's own departure from the top FDA post over non-vaccine disputes (vaping and the abortion pill).

estimated_impact.summary: The FDA, which regulates products accounting for about one-fifth of U.S. consumer spending, lost its Senate-confirmed commissioner on May 12, 2026 and has since been run by an acting commissioner, a lawyer from the agency's food side, for more than four months; a nominee was sent to the Senate in September 2026. The departure capped a stretch in which the drug center lost two directors within weeks (Tidmarsh resigned; his successor Pazdur filed to retire after about three weeks, reportedly over political interference) and the vaccine chief left for a second time. It followed a flavored-vape authorization the commissioner reportedly opposed but was pressured into, which signals political override of product-review decisions that are supposed to rest on public-health evidence.

The entry does not document measurable effects on drug or tobacco review output, or any health outcome from the Glas authorization, which FDA says it may suspend or withdraw if youth use notably increases.

title: DOGE Moved to Eliminate Nearly All Staff at the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a Bush-Era Foreign Aid Agency
institution: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)
status: Partially reversed -- MCC survived as an agency after congressional/outside pushback, but more than half its programs were slated for cancellation and its workforce was sharply reduced; a leaner, more geopolitically-focused agency emerged rather than the full shutdown DOGE initially ordered
date_of_action: 2025-04-23 (DOGE staff briefing) through 2025-08 (agency confirmed surviving with a reduced portfolio)
what_changed: In late April 2025, Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) informed Millennium Challenge Corporation leadership that the agency's programs would be closed and its staff minimized, with employees told in an internal meeting that the workforce-reduction plan called for eliminating all employees except the agency's acting CEO -- a position MCC is statutorily required to maintain. Staff were told they could be placed on administrative leave as soon as May 5, 2025, roughly a week after DOGE first arrived at the agency. MCC, created by Congress in 2004 under President George W. Bush, provides time-limited grants to developing countries -- including Ukraine, El Salvador, and Nepal -- conditioned on governance and policy reforms, distinguishing it structurally from USAID (tracked separately in this database) even though both are independent foreign-aid agencies targeted by the same DOGE-driven downsizing campaign. Senate Foreign Relations Committee Ranking Member Jeanne Shaheen and House Foreign Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gregory Meeks both issued statements condemning the move. Following that pushback, the shutdown plan did not fully proceed: reporting from August 2025 found MCC would survive as an agency, but **more than half of its existing programs were slated for cancellation, and the agency's own public statements said its 'resulting portfolio will clearly align with the Trump Administration's America First foreign policy.'** MCC's inaugural Trump-era CEO, Sean Cairncross, departed after roughly four months in the role, with coverage describing his brief tenure as focused on executing the downsizing before moving to a different administration post. By FY2026, MCC's own figures show it planning to award $287.3 million in new contracts against an annual budget of $830 million -- a functioning but substantially narrowed agency compared to its pre-2025 scope.

primary_proponent.role: Led the initial staff-elimination directive at MCC
primary_proponent.note: No single named DOGE official was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing the MCC-specific cuts beyond the general DOGE effort; Sean Cairncross served as MCC's CEO during the agency's subsequent downsizing and restructuring before departing after about four months.

estimated_impact.summary: DOGE's initial plan would have eliminated MCC's entire staff outside its statutorily-required CEO position, effectively erasing a 21-year-old bipartisan foreign-aid agency without congressional action. After pushback, the agency survived in sharply reduced form -- with more than half its programs canceled and its remaining portfolio explicitly reoriented around the administration's 'America First' foreign-policy priorities rather than MCC's original development-and-governance-reform mission.

This entry documents the initial DOGE shutdown directive and its partial reversal, not a claim that MCC was permanently destroyed; treat the 'more than half of programs canceled' figure as the best-available August 2025 snapshot, not a final, static outcome.

MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the subsequent partial-reversal outcome, sourced to Devex's ongoing foreign-aid-policy trade coverage and Center for Global Development analysis -- both credible, specialized outlets for this subject area, though not general-interest news outlets with the same broad-audience corroboration as the initial shutdown story.

title: 446 Hospitals Across 44 States Found at High Risk of Closing or Cutting Services Because of Republican Medicaid Cuts
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services / hospitals nationwide reliant on Medicaid funding
status: Ongoing -- a risk assessment based on enacted OBBBA funding cuts and a separate work-requirements rule being implemented. Several named hospitals dispute the methodology as applied to them, while confirmed maternity/OB closures since enactment show some cuts are already happening.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OBBBA Medicaid funding provisions signed into law) through 2026-04 (hospital risk analysis published)
what_changed:
On May 8, 2025 -- while the House/Senate bill was still being negotiated -- NPR/KFF Health News profiled Spencer Hospital in Iowa, one of the few remaining rural hospitals still operating an inpatient psychiatric unit, whose CEO Brenda Tiefenthaler said she intended to keep the 14-bed unit open despite it losing about $2 million a year against the hospital's roughly $120 million total budget; 40% of the unit's patients are covered by Medicaid, versus about 12% of the hospital's inpatients overall, illustrating concretely how disproportionately Medicaid-dependent specialty units like inpatient psychiatric care are exposed to the cuts this entry documents.

On June 13, 2025, before the bill's final text was set, Reuters reported the pending Senate proposal contained an estimated $785 billion in Medicaid cuts over 10 years -- a figure that grew to the roughly $1 trillion decade-scale cut in the law as actually enacted July 4, 2025. Separately, in a concrete state-level example, the Kentucky Hospital Association estimated the state could lose $11-12.3 billion in federal Medicaid funding -- nearly $5 billion more than the next-highest state -- putting 35 hospitals, mostly rural, at risk of closure and threatening coverage for roughly 200,000 Kentucky residents; Gov. Andy Beshear said the law effectively reduces Kentucky's Medicaid reimbursement system to standard Medicare rates, among the lowest in the country, and warned it would force women in affected areas to travel hours for maternity care.

CBS News reported July 1, 2025 -- while the bill was still before Congress -- on six-year-old Kennedy Beaver of North Carolina, who has Noonan syndrome and relies on Medicaid, including the state's CAP/C (Community Alternatives Program for Children) waiver, to access care for medically fragile children; her family said they would have to ration her treatment if the proposed cuts passed. North Carolina officials warned at the time that 600,000 state residents could lose coverage -- a figure in the same range as, but from an earlier and separately-sourced estimate than, the 660,000-North-Carolinian figure NYT reported July 6, 2025; both describe the same state-level exposure rather than two different cuts.

The hospital-closure risk this entry documents was reported in concrete, specific terms within days of OBBBA's July 4, 2025 enactment, well before the November 2025 Harvard analysis below quantified it systematically. The Guardian reported July 4, 2025 that the law's roughly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts **threatened healthcare access for 17 million Americans, with rural areas in Kentucky, Arizona, and Idaho facing hospital shutdowns, job losses, and collapsing health programs** as automatic cuts triggered in states including North Carolina. AP reported the same week that over 300 rural hospitals were at risk of closure, with hospitals in Nebraska and Kentucky warning they might shut down or reduce services despite remaining lifelines in remote areas. The New York Times reported July 6, 2025 that the cuts specifically threatened North Carolina's Medicaid expansion and plans to reopen a rural hospital in Martin County, with over 660,000 low-income North Carolina residents at risk of losing coverage as the law's work requirements and funding cuts took effect.

Separately, NPR reported September 9, 2025 that OBBBA cuts Medicaid by nearly $900 billion over a decade -- a figure in the same order of magnitude as, but sourced independently of, Public Citizen's later ~$1 trillion decade-scale estimate -- and that children's hospitals are among the hardest-hit, with Phoenix Children's Hospital warning it stood to lose hundreds of millions of dollars annually, jeopardizing clinics, mental health staffing, and child-abuse screening programs that rely on supplemental Medicaid payments. NPR noted children make up nearly half of all Medicaid enrollees nationally.

An analysis, published November 17, 2025 by Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health's Healthcare Quality and Outcomes Lab (researchers Jose Figueroa and Thomas Tsai) in collaboration with the New York Times, examined data on more than 4,400 U.S. hospitals from the American Hospital Association, Medicare's Healthcare Cost Report Information System, AHRQ, and the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, and identified 109 hospitals -- those serving 25%+ Medicaid patients, financially distressed, and already caring for vulnerable populations -- as facing the greatest risk from OBBBA's Medicaid cuts. 85% of those 109 highest-risk hospitals are in urban areas, and are therefore ineligible for the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund OBBBA created to cushion rural hospitals from the same cuts; the researchers noted these urban safety-net hospitals disproportionately serve low-income and racial-minority patient populations.

Separately, in the months after OBBBA's enactment (the dated cases before Public Citizen's risk analysis below was published), at least three hospitals have confirmed actual Medicaid-cuts-linked service closures rather than projected risk: St. Mary's Sacred Heart Hospital (Lavonia, GA) closed its labor-and-delivery unit and OB/GYN center in fall 2025; Centra Southside Community Hospital (Farmville, VA) closed labor-and-delivery and OB/GYN surgical services; and Greene County General Hospital (Linton, IN) ended obstetrics services in January 2026. A broader 2026 rural-hospital report (Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform) found 139 rural hospitals have closed labor-and-delivery units since 2020 (a 13% drop nationally), with OBBBA's Medicaid cuts cited as an accelerating pressure on top of pre-existing rural obstetric-unit attrition, not the sole cause -- the report does not attribute the full 139-hospital figure to OBBBA specifically, and this entry does not either.

The Guardian's November 20, 2025 survey of hospital cuts in the four months since OBBBA's enactment documented two further named, confirmed-not-projected cases: East Adams Rural Hospital (Ritzville, WA) laid off 108 employees in November 2025, citing 'severe financial difficulties,' and Providence Health System announced layoffs of 296 people across Washington State and 150 across Oregon, both citing Medicaid cuts.

A new analysis, published by Public Citizen on March 31, 2026 (identified by name via HFMA's follow-up reporting), found that 446 hospitals across 44 states and Washington, D.C. are at high risk of closing or cutting services as a result of Medicaid funding reductions enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Public Citizen's methodology flagged hospitals with a 20%+ Medicaid payer mix and negative net margins over 2022-2024. Many of the at-risk hospitals already operate at a financial loss and rely heavily on Medicaid reimbursement to remain viable; NBC News reported the cuts put jobs, maternity care, mental health services, and general local access to treatment at risk in the affected communities, particularly in rural and underserved areas where Medicaid patients make up an outsized share of hospital revenue.

Public Citizen's own report adds further detail: the 446 at-risk hospitals collectively operate 68,986 beds, served approximately 6.6 million patients in 2024, and employ approximately 275,458 direct patient-care workers; 267 of the 446 (60%) are in urban areas, and five states -- Connecticut (36%), California (31%), New York (31%), Massachusetts, and Washington -- each have more than a quarter of their hospitals on the at-risk list. Public Citizen frames the underlying cause as OBBBA's roughly $1 trillion reduction in federal Medicaid funding over the next decade. Trump himself connected these funding pressures directly to military spending priorities: speaking at a private White House Easter luncheon in April 2026, NBC News reported he said the federal government could not fund Medicaid, Medicare, and child care because military spending had to come first, arguing those responsibilities should shift to the states.

At least four individually-named hospitals on or near the flagged list publicly disputed the risk assessment as applied to them, per HFMA's follow-up reporting: Northwest Mississippi Regional Medical Center's CEO said the analysis's 2022-2024 data window captured a temporary financial disruption from the hospital's May 2023 reacquisition by the county, not its actual trajectory; Minden Medical Center (Louisiana) said flatly it was not at risk of closing; Welch Community Hospital (West Virginia) said the analysis ignored that it is a state-operated facility funded by legislative appropriations rather than exposed to the federal Medicaid cuts the same way; and Metropolitan Hospital Center (NYC Health + Hospitals) pointed to record patient-care revenue and staff expansion as evidence it was securely positioned rather than at risk. None of these four rebuttals were independently adjudicated in sourcing reviewed -- they are hospital self-assessments, not a third-party re-analysis -- but they are documented here for balance given the risk analysis is itself already presented as a projection rather than a confirmed count.

estimated_impact.summary: OBBBA's Medicaid cuts put 446 hospitals across 44 states and D.C. at high risk of closing or cutting services, Public Citizen found. NBC News reported the cuts put jobs, maternity care, mental health services, and local access to treatment at risk in affected communities, and NPR reported children's hospitals are among the hardest-hit. Some of the harm is already real rather than projected: named hospitals have closed labor-and-delivery and OB services, a Washington hospital laid off 108 workers, and Providence Health System announced 296 layoffs in Washington and 150 in Oregon, citing Medicaid cuts.

title: House GOP's Medicaid Provider-Tax Cap Threatened Nursing-Home Funding -- Final OBBBA Carved Out an Exemption, But Broader Cuts Still Risk Long-Term Care Access
institution: U.S. House of Representatives / Congress (OBBBA reconciliation legislation)
status: Enacted (OBBBA signed July 4, 2025) -- nursing-home-specific provider-tax and staffing-mandate carve-outs secured during House-to-Senate negotiation, while the law's broader ~$900B-$1T Medicaid cuts proceed
date_of_action: 2025-05-12 (Washington Post reports the House GOP provider-tax proposal) through 2025-07-04 (OBBBA signed, final provider-tax/staffing-mandate terms confirmed)
what_changed: The Washington Post reported May 12, 2025 that House Republicans were pushing to limit states' Medicaid "provider tax" -- a financing mechanism nearly every state uses to draw down additional federal matching funds, which states then use in part to help pay for long-term care -- warning the change could drastically reduce Medicaid funding for nursing homes, which cover more than 60% of nursing-home stays nationally. The House passed its version of the reconciliation bill May 22, 2025 along party lines, including the provider-tax limits as part of what CNN and Healthcare Dive reported as roughly $700-900 billion in Medicaid cuts over ten years; nursing-home operators publicly said they were bracing for steep losses as the bill moved to the Senate. During Senate negotiation, the nursing-home and long-term-care industry secured two specific carve-outs relative to the original House proposal: the bill's new provider-tax caps -- which phase most providers' allowable rate down from 6% to 3.5% in Medicaid-expansion states by fiscal year 2032 -- exempted nursing homes and intermediate care facilities specifically, freezing their rates at the current safe-harbor level (up to 6%) rather than phasing them down; and **a separate, unrelated Biden-era CMS rule setting federal minimum nursing-home staffing levels was delayed by 10 years**. The Senate-passed version, with these nursing-home-specific provisions intact, cleared the House largely unchanged and was signed into law as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) on July 4, 2025. Despite the industry-specific carve-outs, health-policy analysts (Commonwealth Fund, Penn LDI) warned the law's broader Medicaid reductions -- eligibility/work-requirement changes and other funding cuts documented separately in this tracker's medicaid-work-requirements-cms-rule-2026.json and medicaid-hospital-closure-risk-2026.json entries -- still threaten long-term-care quality and access, since nursing-home Medicaid revenue depends on the overall program's health, not the provider-tax mechanism alone; one nursing-home industry leader was quoted calling the carve-outs "band-aids" that would "soon prove ill-equipped to stop OBBB's damage."

primary_proponent.name: Congressional Republicans / Trump administration
primary_proponent.role: Drafted, passed, and signed the OBBBA's Medicaid provider-tax provisions
primary_proponent.note: The provider-tax cap and staffing-mandate delay were negotiated into the reconciliation bill's Medicaid title between the May 2025 House passage and the Senate's version; Trump signed the final law July 4, 2025. Sourcing reviewed did not identify a single named member of Congress as personally responsible for the nursing-home-specific carve-outs specifically, as distinct from the bill's Medicaid title generally.

estimated_impact.summary: The carve-outs mean nursing homes avoided the more severe, industry-specific funding threat initially proposed in May 2025, but analysts warn the underlying $900 billion-plus, decade-long Medicaid reduction the OBBBA still enacts leaves long-term-care access and quality exposed through other channels (eligibility redeterminations, state budget pressure, and the broader funding cuts documented in this tracker's related entries).

title: CMS Narrows Medical Frailty Exemption Beyond Statute in Medicaid Work-Requirement Rule -- Cancer and HIV Patients Left Unexempted
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services
status: In effect -- interim final rule released June 1, 2026, published June 3; national deadline Jan. 2027; Nebraska and Montana implementing early. Nebraska's Medicaid director estimated ~200 people would lose coverage Aug. 1.
date_of_action: 2026-06-01 (CMS interim final rule released; published in the Federal Register 2026-06-03)
what_changed:
The work-requirement provision that CMS's June 2026 rule ultimately implements has a documented 2025 legislative history directly relevant to this entry's exemption-narrowing question. CBO's first score of a House GOP Medicaid overhaul, in May 2025, estimated 10.3 million people losing coverage by 2034 (7.6 million becoming uninsured), with savings of roughly $625 billion tied to work requirements, citizenship-status restrictions, and eligibility-rule rollbacks (The Hill, May 14, 2025). The House passed its version on May 22, 2025, setting the 80-hours-per-month work/education/training/volunteer-service threshold that CMS's 2026 rule later enforces nationwide for childless adults; CBO estimated 7.6 million people would lose coverage under that House text, with roughly $280 billion in resulting savings redirected toward other tax provisions in the bill (New York Times, May 22, 2025).

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law July 4, 2025, required Medicaid expansion-population adults aged 19-64 to complete at least 80 hours per month of qualifying work, education, job training, or volunteer service to keep coverage, with a statutory exemption for individuals who are 'medically frail.'

Brief context (these describe OBBBA's Medicaid provisions and fiscal impact as a whole rather than the work-requirement/medical-frailty mechanism this entry specifically documents, so are noted briefly as backdrop rather than given full treatment): as the bill moved from the House to a harsher Senate rewrite in June 2025 and on to signature, CBO's estimates of the bill's overall scope grew -- from the House-stage figures above up to roughly $1.1 trillion in Medicaid cuts and 11.8 million people losing coverage under the Senate's June 2025 text (New York Times, June 29, 2025), a claimed $1 trillion-plus in cuts with ACA subsidies also ending that the Washington Post reported could leave at least 17 million Americans without coverage across both programs (July 1, 2025), and a final overall CBO deficit estimate near $3.4 trillion through 2034 with 10 million more people uninsured (Associated Press, July 21, 2025). A separate CBO distributional analysis published in August 2025 found the law would cost the poorest 10% of Americans roughly $1,200/year in net resources while the richest 10% gained roughly $13,600/year, and that about 2.4 million people would lose SNAP food-assistance benefits (NBC News, Aug. 12, 2025). Other coverage flagged risk to home- and community-based Medicaid services relied on by an estimated 4.5 million disabled Americans despite administration assurances those services would not be cut (New York Times, July 21, 2025); David Sacks, the Trump administration's AI and crypto czar, said on his All In podcast that 'This bill cuts $880 billion from Medicaid over a decade,' even as President Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson claimed the bill simply targeted 'waste, fraud, and abuse' (Rolling Stone, May 26, 2025); and the administration's separately proposed FY2026 budget -- a distinct legislative vehicle from the reconciliation bill that became OBBBA -- separately proposed $163 billion in Medicaid cuts and new work requirements, which CBO estimated could leave at least 8.6 million people uninsured by 2034 (ABC News, May 17, 2025).

The drive for further cuts beyond OBBBA's initial Medicaid provisions began almost immediately after the law's passage. On August 14, 2025, the Republican Study Committee -- a caucus of 189 House conservatives -- invited Brian Blase, president of the Paragon Health Institute and a former Trump National Economic Council official, to brief RSC staff as House Republicans quietly began mapping out a possible second party-line reconciliation package; the briefing covered further Medicaid federal-funding-percentage and state-reimbursement changes, the expiring enhanced ACA tax credits, Medicare 'site neutral' payment changes, and other health-policy offsets. Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.), whose 83-member Main Street Caucus had already accepted the first bill's Medicaid/SNAP work-requirement savings, warned of 'severe pushback' to any deeper Medicaid cuts, with GOP leaders themselves acknowledging they were 'scraping the bottom of the barrel for cuts.'

By August 31, 2025, reporting on the enacted law (which cut a reported $911 billion from Medicaid) noted that HHS -- the CMS's parent department, then led by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- had been given broad statutory discretion to define who qualifies as 'medically frail' for exemption purposes (Mother Jones, Aug. 31, 2025); this is the same statutory exemption category CMS's June 2026 interim final rule narrowed with its added functional-capacity threshold, the core subject of this entry.

Reporting the same week the law's work-requirement provision passed also warned that it echoed earlier, smaller-scale state work-requirement pilots in Georgia and Arkansas, where thousands of otherwise-eligible people -- including caregivers, gig workers, and students -- lost coverage due to confusing reporting rules and administrative red tape rather than actual failure to work (NBC News, July 5, 2025), directly foreshadowing the bureaucratic-mechanism critique in this entry's estimated-impact section. A November 2025 New York Times explainer published ahead of the rule's implementation likewise projected the requirement would cut coverage for 'nearly five million people' -- matching the CBO figure cited below -- and specifically noted that most people expected to lose coverage were already working or otherwise exempt, but would be cut off due to reporting/paperwork failures, while states would face costly new compliance and verification systems to administer the requirement (New York Times, Nov. 3, 2025).

On June 1, 2026, CMS -- under Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz -- released an interim final rule implementing the requirement nationwide; the rule, 'Medicaid Program; Community Engagement Requirement for Certain Individuals' (CMS-2454-IFC, 91 FR 33348), was published in the Federal Register on June 3, 2026 and took effect July 31, 2026. Rather than applying the statute's medical-frailty categories as written, CMS added an additional functional-capacity requirement: individuals must affirmatively demonstrate that their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to perform the 80 hours of required activity, a threshold not in the statute's text, which uses 'significantly impairs' only for its disability category, and there for activities of daily living; CMS says it interprets the statute 'to require consideration of the severity of an individual's condition' and that the statute 'expressly delegates definitional authority to the Secretary,' while 48 patient organizations said that redefining the exemption 'to only apply to individuals who can prove they cannot work,' along with limits on self-attestation, 'clearly conflicts with the law.' In practice, advocates and reporting say this leaves out **people with early-stage cancer who are undergoing radiation treatment but are still nominally capable of some work, and people with HIV who are stable on treatment but technically employable -- both groups are not automatically exempted under CMS's narrower reading**, and must instead navigate state reporting/paperwork processes to prove exemption eligibility or ongoing compliance. The rule's preamble says CMS considered naming HIV/AIDS and cancer as automatically qualifying serious or complex conditions but declined; people with HIV/AIDS, for example, are medically frail only if their condition 'significantly impairs the individual's ability to comply with the community engagement requirement.' NPR reported that Carl Schmid, executive director of the HIV + Hepatitis Policy Institute, had lobbied for months, without success, for a blanket exemption for people living with HIV, and a coalition of 48 patient organizations said in a joint statement (June 2, 2026) that the rule 'does not protect people with serious or complex health conditions.'

Under the rule, states must verify compliance at application (covering one to three months before applying) and at each renewal, and they may choose to verify more often; NPR reported that adults aged 19 to 64 in those states 'will have to periodically prove that they are either working, going to school or volunteering at least 80 hours a month.' The rule excludes from the requirement parents and caregivers of children 13 or under or of disabled individuals, pregnant and postpartum individuals, former foster youth under 26, American Indians and Alaska Natives, totally disabled veterans, the medically frail, people complying with TANF work requirements or subject to SNAP work requirements, people in drug or alcohol treatment programs, and inmates of a public institution. The rule's regulatory impact analysis says people 'fraudulently or improperly enrolled in the program' are unlikely to respond to verification requests, but CMS also estimates that 7 percent of applicable individuals who may be working, enrolled in school, or qualify for an exception 'would lose coverage due to administrative or procedural reasons.'

Per CNN's June 6, 2026 reporting on the same rule, the medical-frailty exemption requires more than a diagnosis -- enrollees must submit documentation, such as a signed statement from a medical professional, affirmatively showing their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to meet the 80-hour work standard. A cancer patient in active chemotherapy who remains physically able to sit at a desk part-time may not qualify for the exemption on that documentation standard alone, regardless of diagnosis.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated the work-requirement provisions would cause roughly 5 million people to lose Medicaid coverage, out of a program covering about 68 million low-income Americans, and that the requirements account for roughly a third of the $900 billion in Medicaid savings scored under OBBBA overall (i.e., roughly $300 billion of that total tied to work-requirement-driven disenrollment). Nebraska became the first state to implement the requirement on May 1, 2026; Montana and Arkansas followed by July 1, 2026 (Arkansas delayed enforcement to January 2027), with additional states phasing in through the January 2027 national deadline. Nebraska became the first state to actually remove people from Medicaid coverage under the requirement -- distinct from the May 1 implementation date above, which marked the rule taking effect there, not yet any disenrollment -- with the state's Medicaid director, Drew Gonshorowski, telling Tradeoffs that roughly 200 Nebraskans would lose their coverage on August 1, 2026 (NPR, July 31, 2026).

primary_proponent.name: Dr. Mehmet Oz
primary_proponent.role: CMS Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Oz publicly framed the rule as reducing loneliness and building 'skills and independence through work,' stating: 'This rule helps Americans build skills and independence through work, education, job training, or community service, creating new opportunities for themselves and their families.' CMS's specific choice to add a functional-capacity threshold on top of the statute's medical-frailty categories -- the discretionary regulatory action this entry documents -- was made under his administration of the agency.

estimated_impact.summary: Health-policy advocates and reporting describe the rule's core mechanism as bureaucratic rather than substantive: eligible, low-income people who are already working, studying, or too sick to reliably navigate the requirement's verification paperwork -- proof of compliance or exemption at application and at each renewal, with states allowed to verify more often -- lose coverage not because they fail to meet the underlying policy goal, but because they fail the paperwork. Cancer and HIV are not automatic exemptions: CMS considered listing them as conditions that automatically qualify someone as medically frail but declined, so people such as early-stage cancer patients in radiation treatment who can still work, or people with HIV who can technically work, qualify only if their condition 'significantly impairs' their ability to comply. Carl Schmid of the HIV + Hepatitis Policy Institute had lobbied for months for a blanket HIV exemption, and a coalition of 48 patient organizations said in a joint statement that the rule 'does not protect people with serious or complex health conditions.' Removals were set to begin in Nebraska, where the state's Medicaid director estimated roughly 200 people would lose coverage on August 1, 2026.

estimated_impact.caveat: CMS and the administration argue the requirement is a legitimate work-promotion policy applying only to a defined expansion population. The rule excludes parents and caregivers of a child 13 or under or of a disabled individual, pregnant or postpartum individuals, former foster youth under 26, and American Indians and Alaska Natives, along with other groups such as totally disabled veterans, the medically frail, people complying with TANF work requirements or subject to SNAP work requirements, people in drug or alcohol treatment, and inmates of a public institution. CMS's impact analysis argues that people 'fraudulently or improperly enrolled in the program' are unlikely to respond to verification requests, but it also estimates that 7 percent of applicable individuals who may be working, in school, or qualify for an exception 'would lose coverage due to administrative or procedural reasons.' The specific accountability question this entry documents is narrower: whether CMS's discretionary choice to layer an additional functional-capacity threshold onto the statute's medical-frailty exemption -- rather than applying Congress's own listed categories -- was a reasonable implementation choice or an administrative narrowing of an exemption Congress wrote more broadly. That legal/administrative question was not resolved as of this entry's sourcing.

HIGH confidence on the medical-frailty exemption being narrower than the statutory categories, per the American Medical Association's direct analysis of the rule's functional-capacity add-on. MODERATE confidence on the precise real-world disenrollment numbers for cancer/HIV patients specifically, since implementation is still in its early, staggered, state-by-state phase as of this entry's sourcing. title: Trump Taps the Medicare Improvement Fund for $90 Pre-Election Checks to 20.8 Million Medicare Enrollees, After $500 ACA "Refund" Checks
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (Medicare Improvement Fund; HealthCare.gov federal marketplace user-fee collections), with payments issued through the Social Security Administration and the Treasury Department
status: Under way: $90 Medicare deposits due around Oct. 8, 2026, paper checks later in October, all before the Nov. 3 midterms; $500 ACA checks began going out Sept. 30. Democrats question the legal authority; the White House and HHS did not immediately respond. No court has blocked either payment.
date_of_action: 2026-09-10 to 2026-10-31 ($500 ACA refunds announced Sept. 10 and sent from Sept. 30; $90 Medicare payments announced Oct. 2 and paid in October 2026)
what_changed:
On October 2, 2026, about a month before the November 3 midterm elections, President Trump announced on Truth Social that his administration would "immediately" begin sending "Checks" of nearly $100 to more than 20 million seniors to help pay their Medicare Part B premiums, paid for out of the Medicare Improvement Fund, which he called "a pointless 'Slush Fund' that has only been used by Dumocrats in Congress." A White House fact sheet the same day set the payment at $90 per person. CMS's fact sheet the next day said **20.8 million people in Original Medicare Part B are eligible for one $90 payment**; people whose premiums Medicaid helps pay, higher-income enrollees who pay the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount, everyone in Medicare Advantage, and people living outside the United States are excluded. Most will get a direct deposit from the Social Security Administration on or around October 8, "followed by an email or a letter from the President in mid-October"; others will get a $90 Treasury check later in October marked "Medicare Improvement Fund Payment; $90 Payment to Offset October Premium." Congress created the fund in section 7002 of the Supplemental Appropriations Act of 2008 "to make improvements under the original fee-for-service program under parts A and B," and CNN reported its purpose is improving program operations and raising payments to providers in traditional Medicare. The White House says Congress has given the fund $2 billion and that "no Administration has ever utilized" it; CMS adds that Congress has withdrawn from it around 20 times to offset other spending, including $20.7 billion toward the Affordable Care Act in 2010. Trump's post said he had already reduced Part B premiums "by significant amounts," but the standard premium rose nearly 10% ($17.90) for 2026, to $202.90 a month, the largest increase in four years. The announcement surprised congressional offices in both parties, the Washington Post reported. Democrats questioned the legality of dipping into government accounts to send payments to Americans, and the White House and HHS did not immediately respond to the Post's questions about their legal authority; Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden called the payments "another desperate attempt by a failed president to escape Americans' revulsion with his failed agenda, amounting to one tank of Trump-inflated gas." KFF's Larry Levitt told CNN that "President Trump seems to have hit on a midterm strategy of using little-known pots of money to send checks to people facing increased health care costs."

The Medicare payments followed a similar program for Affordable Care Act enrollees. On September 10, the White House announced "Working Families Obamacare Refunds" of $500 per person to nearly 1 million people in the 30 states that use the federal HealthCare.gov exchange, saying the Biden administration had overcharged them through exchange "user fees" that insurers pay and passed on in premiums, leaving a surplus. The refunds go to people who do not receive premium assistance, mainly those earning more than 400% of the federal poverty line, who lost all premium help when the enhanced ACA subsidies expired at the end of 2025. The Treasury began sending them on September 30 to more than 950,000 people, with a letter from Trump saying "the Biden Administration overcharged you to fund the operation of HealthCare.gov." NBC News reported that the White House made the overcharge claim without evidence, and UNC health policy professor Jonathan Oberlander told CNBC the fees were at times lower under Biden than in Trump's first term and that the refunds are "part of a broader effort by President Trump to buy continued Republican control of the House and Senate via promises of direct government payments to voters." A Reuters analysis cited by CNBC found 71% of the ACA money, $339 million, is going to residents of 13 states with some of the most competitive Senate and governor's races, though eligibility turns on insurance status. Johns Hopkins professor Gerard Anderson told ABC News the checks do not target the people most harmed by the administration's changes, including the end of the tax credits.

In the same October 2 post, Trump called the $90 payments proof that a $5,000 "Trump Dividend" would go to every adult citizen if Republicans keep the House and Senate. It is not enacted, and Trump has not said who would authorize it or where the money would come from; CNBC estimated it would cost roughly $1.2 trillion and need congressional approval.

CMS issued the Medicare fact sheet; no other official was named as approving the use of either fund.

estimated_impact.summary: **A roughly $2 billion fund Congress set aside to improve traditional Medicare is being spent on one-time $90 checks that land just before the midterms**, alongside $500 ACA checks to about 950,000 people. The $90 covers less than half of one month's $202.90 Part B premium.

title: Trump Administration Cut, Then Moved to End, a Federal Subsidy That Had Kept Medicare Part D Drug-Plan Premiums Down
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Ongoing -- the underlying Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration is set to expire after 2026, meaning 2027 premiums will not benefit from the subsidy at all
date_of_action: 2025-08 (reported ~40% cut affecting 2026 premiums) through 2026-07 (announced full end of the demonstration after 2026)
what_changed: The Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration is a temporary CMS program, funded at roughly $9.8 billion, that had reduced the average standalone Medicare Part D prescription-drug-plan premium by about 40% in 2025. In early August 2025, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration had cut the subsidy in a way that would still let 2026 average premiums rise sharply even as CMS negotiated with insurers to limit the increase -- CMS's own later figures put the resulting 2026 subsidy-driven premium reduction at roughly 27%, down from the prior year's 40% offset, meaning the effective subsidy value had already been scaled back for 2026 even before the program's later full termination. In July 2026, CMS announced it would let the demonstration expire entirely after 2026, eliminating the subsidy for 2027 premiums altogether. Reporting on the full expiration indicates it will most affect people enrolled in standalone Part D plans (as opposed to Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage, which have more pricing flexibility to absorb the loss) -- **an estimated 11 million+ Americans face increased premiums, with about half of Part D enrollees seeing some increase and some paying as much as an additional $20 per month**. Officials and reporting describe the change as likely to push more seniors toward Medicare Advantage plans, which the administration has otherwise favored, rather than remaining in traditional Medicare's standalone drug-plan option.

title: Trump's Foreign Aid Freeze Temporarily Stalled a U.S.-Funded Anti-Fentanyl Cargo-Screening Program at Mexico's Busiest Port
institution: U.S. foreign aid programs (State Department/USAID-administered), implemented via UNODC-WCO Container Control Programme
status: Largely reversed: after lawmakers complained, UNODC was notified of a waiver in March 2025; in May 2025 it extended the program to Lazaro Cardenas with U.S. Embassy support, and by September 2025 it was building a U.S.-supported port control unit at Veracruz.
date_of_action: 2025-01-20 (global foreign aid freeze ordered) to 2025-03-16 (Washington Post reports the program's waiver)
what_changed: On his first day back in office, January 20, 2025, Trump ordered a sweeping freeze on foreign aid. Within weeks the freeze stalled U.S. funding for the Container Control Programme, a joint initiative of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the World Customs Organization that trained and equipped Mexico's Navy to screen cargo for fentanyl-precursor chemicals and other contraband at the Port of Manzanillo, Mexico's busiest container port. The U.S. had provided roughly $800,000 to launch the program at Manzanillo in 2023, and **a planned expansion to two additional major ports -- Lazaro Cardenas and Veracruz -- was put on hold by the funding cutoff**. The freeze also paused other U.S.-funded anti-narcotics cooperation with Mexico, including training for Mexican authorities to locate and dismantle clandestine fentanyl labs and U.S. donations of drug-sniffing canines. Reuters, citing eight people familiar with the situation, reported the stall on February 24, 2025; the freeze had also shelved, for now, future training and equipment donations at Manzanillo, including additional cargo scanners and drug-testing equipment, and three sources said the program had not received a waiver. Apart from $7.8 million in waivers for Mexico projects run by the State Department's Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL), most of the bureau's roughly $50 million Mexico budget remained frozen. The same day, a State Department official disputed that the freeze had stalled the program, telling RealClearPolitics that Secretary of State Marco Rubio's foreign-aid review had put only its training portion in temporary limbo, that the Manzanillo project had been two months from completion when the freeze took effect (RealClearPolitics put U.S. launch funding at nearly $1 million), and that already-trained Mexican officials were expected to keep screening containers. In the first week of March, Trump imposed tariffs on Mexico, Canada and China, ostensibly to stem the flow of illicit drugs into the U.S. In a March 8, 2025 report, The Guardian quoted former DEA deputy chief of staff Jim Crotty calling the approach "coercive" and warning that it could backfire, and reported former State Department official Enrique Roig's view that federal funding cuts had stalled the Container Control Programme's implementation in Mexico. In the week before March 16, following complaints from U.S. lawmakers, UNODC received notification of a waiver for the Mexico port program, The Washington Post reported, though the program's long-term continuation remained subject to the administration's 90-day review of foreign aid, and much of UNODC's frozen U.S. funding still had not been released. In May 2025, UNODC and the Mexican government, working with the World Customs Organization and with the support of the U.S. Embassy, extended the program, now called the Passenger and Cargo Control Programme (PCCP), to the port of Lazaro Cardenas, UNODC reported. By September 2025, UNODC, the WCO and the Mexican government were creating a new port control unit at Veracruz, for which 94 Navy and Customs officials had been trained, in work UNODC said was supported by the United States.

estimated_impact.summary: The freeze stalled U.S. support for a UN program that trains and equips Mexico's Navy to screen cargo for fentanyl and methamphetamine precursor chemicals at Manzanillo, Mexico's busiest container port, which a State Department official credited with helping seize more than 110 tons of meth chemicals in 2024. It shelved new cargo scanners and drug-testing equipment for Manzanillo and delayed a planned $1.5-2 million expansion to Lazaro Cardenas and Veracruz, at a time when the administration named fentanyl a top priority. A waiver followed in March 2025, and the expansion went ahead with U.S. support from May 2025. No overdose deaths or drug flows have been tied to the pause.

title: Rollback of Longstanding Military-Family Protections Leads to 50+ Detentions of Spouses and Parents of Active-Duty Troops
institution: Department of Homeland Security; Immigration and Customs Enforcement -- affecting active-duty U.S. service members and their immediate families
status: Ongoing as of August 2026 -- more than 60 members of Congress sent a letter to DHS, the Department of War (Defense), and the VA on August 9, 2026 announcing an investigation into whether the two departments are coordinating to target service members' families; no administration policy reversal or public response was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry's last verification.
date_of_action: Ongoing since early 2025 (start of Trump's second term); publicly reported by the Associated Press in August 2026
what_changed: An Associated Press investigation found the Trump administration has rolled back longstanding, bipartisan-consensus protections that historically shielded immediate family members of active-duty U.S. service members from immigration enforcement. As a result, **more than 50 spouses and parents of active-duty troops have been detained by immigration authorities since the start of Trump's second term, with at least six deported and one self-deported**. Some service members have been forced to take leave from their duties -- including delaying deployments -- to care for children after a spouse was detained. In response, more than 60 members of the U.S. House and Senate sent a letter on the evening of August 9, 2026 to the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of War (Defense), and the Department of Veterans Affairs announcing an investigation into whether DHS and the Pentagon are coordinating to target service members and their families for deportation.
