title: MSPB Loses Quorum for More Than Six Months After Trump Fires Whistleblower Board Chair Cathy Harris
institution: Merit Systems Protection Board
status: Resolved against Harris. The Supreme Court denied her petition on June 30, 2026, a day after Trump v. Slaughter, leaving the D.C. Circuit's December 2025 ruling upholding her firing as final. The Board lacked a quorum April 10-October 27, 2025; a new member's swearing-in restored it.
date_of_action: 2025-02-10 (firing); Board without quorum 2025-04-10 to 2025-10-27; litigation ended 2026-06-30 (cert denied)
what_changed: On February 10, 2025, President Trump fired MSPB Chair Cathy Harris via a one-sentence email without citing any cause, three years before her Senate-confirmed term was set to expire in 2028. Harris sued; a district court granted a temporary restraining order reinstating her on February 18, and on March 4, Judge Rudolph Contreras granted summary judgment finding the firing unlawful. The government appealed, and a three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed her reinstatement on March 28. The full en banc D.C. Circuit voted 7-4 to vacate that stay and reinstate Harris on April 7, but two days later, on April 9, Chief Justice Roberts granted the government an administrative stay, again removing her. With member Raymond Limon's term having ended on February 28, 2025, **the Board was left with a single member, Acting Chairman Henry Kerner, and could not issue final decisions on appeals awaiting Board review from April 10 until October 27, 2025**, although its administrative judges kept issuing initial decisions. On May 22, 2025, the full Supreme Court granted the stay 6-3, saying the government was likely to show that both the NLRB and MSPB 'exercise considerable executive power.' The quorum gap's practical stakes for ordinary civil servants were illustrated in July 2025, when Mary Comans, FEMA's former chief financial officer, sued over her February 11, 2025 termination -- she was fired along with three colleagues after Elon Musk claimed on X that FEMA money sent to New York City to house migrants had gone to 'luxury' hotels (DHS put the payment at $59 million) -- with **her complaint arguing that because the MSPB lacked a quorum, Congress's purpose in enacting the Civil Service Reform Act had been frustrated**. In September 2025, Harris asked the Supreme Court to take up her case before the D.C. Circuit ruled, conditioned on the Court hearing the FTC's Slaughter case; the Court denied that petition on September 22, 2025. On October 7, 2025, the Senate confirmed a new member, James Woodruff, in a party-line en bloc vote, and his swearing-in on October 28 restored the Board's quorum, independent of Harris's litigation. On December 5, 2025, a 2-1 D.C. Circuit panel (Judges Katsas and Walker, both Trump appointees) ruled on the merits that Congress cannot restrict the president's authority to remove NLRB or MSPB members because they 'wield substantial executive power,' with dissenting Judge Florence Pan warning that under the majority's reasoning 'it appears that no independent agencies may lawfully exist in this country.' The D.C. Circuit denied rehearing on January 9, 2026. On March 17, 2026, Harris petitioned the Supreme Court for review, arguing that MSPB is a purely adjudicatory body that sets no policy and is protected by a constitutional tradition for adjudicatory bodies, including Wiener v. United States, that stands apart from the Humphrey's Executor line at issue in Slaughter. Six Senate Democrats led by Chris Van Hollen filed an amicus brief on April 22, 2026 urging the Court to hear her case. On June 29, 2026, the Court decided Trump v. Slaughter 6-3, holding the FTC's for-cause removal protection unconstitutional and overruling whatever remained of Humphrey's Executor. The next day, June 30, 2026, it denied Harris's petition without explanation, leaving the D.C. Circuit's December 2025 ruling as the final word on her removal; the denial did not decide on the merits whether purely adjudicatory bodies like MSPB warrant different treatment than the FTC.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Fired Harris directly via a one-sentence email giving no reason, then had the administration argue through multiple rounds of litigation that MSPB members wield substantial executive power and are therefore removable at will, a position a divided D.C. Circuit panel accepted in December 2025.

estimated_impact.summary: MSPB is where fired or retaliated-against federal employees, including whistleblowers, appeal. After Harris's removal the Board had one member and could issue no final decisions on appeals awaiting Board review for about six and a half months (April 10 to October 27, 2025), stalling those cases, though administrative judges kept issuing initial rulings. MSPB says this gap did not build an excessive backlog, unlike the 2017-2022 quorum loss, which left about 3,800 cases waiting. The lasting loss is structural: the D.C. Circuit ruling the Supreme Court left standing lets the president fire Board members at will, ending the Board's insulation from political pressure.

estimated_impact.caveat: The duration and case counts are MSPB's own figures. MSPB says the 2025 gap was 'relatively brief and did not result in an excessive inventory of petitions for review,' and no public count of appeals delayed by it was found. Whistleblower attorney David Colapinto warned in April 2025 that fired whistleblowers were left with 'no realistic recourse' while the Board lacked a quorum. The figures don't capture the harder-to-measure effect of at-will removal on how independently the Board decides cases against the administration. The Supreme Court's denial left undecided on the merits Harris's argument that a purely adjudicatory body like MSPB differs from the FTC; the Constitutional Accountability Center ties such bodies to a roughly 150-year tradition of multimember independent agencies.

title: National Archives Loses Its Archivist and Digital Access Office Amid Deep Budget Cuts
institution: National Archives and Records Administration
status: Resolved as to leadership -- Senate confirmed Bradford P. Wilson Aug. 7, 2026 (51-47, en bloc); NARA announced him as 12th Archivist Aug. 21. FY2026 enacted: $454.3M (request $414.7M; FY2025 $474.2M), electronic records $30M, Office of Innovation $0. Staff: 2,344 (Aug. 2026).
date_of_action: 2025-02 (Archivist Colleen Shogan fired) through 2026 (ongoing reorganization, office eliminations, and records-center closures)
what_changed:
In February 2025, President Trump fired Archivist of the United States Colleen Shogan without citing cause, an unprecedented removal of the position's confirmed leader. Deputy Archivist William Bosanko briefly became acting archivist; on Feb. 16, 2025, the Washington Post, citing a source familiar with the situation, reported that he had decided to retire and that several other senior officials had resigned. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was then named acting archivist while continuing his separate Cabinet role, a dual appointment later questioned by a U.S. senator given how long Rubio held both positions simultaneously; during Rubio's tenure, the director of the Eisenhower Presidential Library was separately forced to resign in September 2025 after refusing to hand over a museum sword for a royal gift (tracked in its own entry, since no source confirms Rubio personally directed that ouster). Federal News Network reported on Feb. 4, 2026, citing a NARA spokesperson, that Rubio was no longer acting archivist and that, before leaving, he had tapped James (Jim) Byron, senior advisor to the archivist, to perform the archivist's duties. NARA and Rubio's staff told the Boston Globe that Rubio gave up the acting role on Dec. 4, 2025, but NARA and GAO confirmed the vacancy wasn't reported to GAO until Jan. 23, 2026, and Sen. Tammy Duckworth asked GAO to investigate whether Rubio had violated federal law, questioning when he actually left. Byron performed the archivist's functions without being named acting archivist, which only the president can do; a NARA spokesperson told the Globe he would leave on April 3, 2026.

Separately, NARA's FY2026 budget request sought $414.7 million, $59.5 million below the FY2025 enacted level, and cut 136 full-time equivalent positions (FTE), which NARA's Congressional Justification attributed to 'implementation of an organizational realignment to improve program efficiency and operational resilience.' The same document's tables put FY2024 actual budget authority at $507.1 million, including $48.4 million for National Historical Publications and Records Commission (NHPRC) grants and $25.5 million for repairs and restoration; the FY2026 request zeroed out the NHPRC grants and cut repairs to $4.5 million, while operating expenses fell from $427.3 million to $404.3 million. In all, the request was about $92.4 million below FY2024. The request also cut presidential-library staffing from 380 to 357 FTE. The proposal included **full elimination of NARA's 50-person Office of Innovation, which runs the agency's online records catalog, digital access initiatives, and the public 'citizen archivist' transcription project**, with NARA stating those functions would be 'transferred elsewhere' rather than continued directly. In June 2025 statements to Federal News Network, NARA said presidential libraries 'will be fully supported' and, separately, that the Office of Research Services 'will receive more support and personnel through NARA's reorganization.' Jason R. Baron, a University of Maryland professor and former NARA director of litigation, told Federal News Network the reduced request was 'difficult to fathom, given the enormous resource challenges NARA currently faces,' including 'huge FOIA processing backlogs at presidential libraries' and billions of electronic records arriving from other agencies; former Archivist Colleen Shogan called electronic records 'the single biggest challenge facing the National Archives in the next decade'; and the outlet reported that NARA's budget had largely stayed flat over the last three decades, according to the National Security Archive. In June 2025, NARA issued reduction-in-force notices affecting roughly 100 employees (about 3% of staff), which two NARA employees said effectively 'wiped out' the Office of Innovation and the division supporting field offices and presidential libraries; the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library was briefly forced to close in February 2025 after probationary employees were terminated.

The FY2026 proposal also sought to cut NARA's Electronic Records Initiative from $30 million to $20 million (about 33%), even as the agency faces a growing volume of incoming digital records. NARA's FY2027 Congressional Justification, dated April 3, 2026, shows that Congress enacted $454.3 million for NARA in FY2026 -- below the $474.2 million enacted for FY2025 but above the $414.7 million request -- kept the Electronic Records Initiative at $30 million, funded NHPRC grants at $19.3 million, and funded the Office of Innovation at $0 with no staff, as proposed; it lists presidential libraries at 357 FTE for FY2026, and the FY2027 request again seeks $20 million for the initiative within a $419.7 million total. In 2026, NARA also announced it would vacate three federal records centers (Chicago, San Francisco/San Bruno, and Seattle) and sunset its free public History Hub reference forum to save an estimated $370,000 annually.

On March 2, 2026, Trump nominated Bradford P. Wilson to be the permanent Archivist of the United States. In the interim, GSA Administrator Edward Forst was named acting archivist under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (CNN reported on April 3, 2026 that the White House confirmed he was serving), telling GSA staff he would 'dually serve' in both roles -- meaning NARA's day-to-day acting leadership was held by an official whose primary job is running a different agency. Wilson's nomination received a hearing on June 17, 2026, but as one of 11 nominees split across two panels rather than a dedicated AOTUS hearing, with only a few minutes of questioning devoted to him specifically -- notable given the position's usual dedicated-hearing custom, per the Society of American Archivists' own monitoring of the nomination. As of late July 2026, Wilson's confirmation was still pending in the Senate, with Forst serving as acting archivist. The Senate confirmed Bradford P. Wilson as Archivist of the United States on August 7, 2026, as part of an en bloc vote covering 74 nominations together (51-47), per the Senate's own roll call and nominations-confirmed records.

In an Aug. 21, 2026 press release titled 'Bradford P. Wilson Confirmed by U.S. Senate as 12th Archivist of the United States,' NARA quoted Archivist Wilson as saying he was 'deeply honored to lead the National Archives and Records Administration.' NARA now has a Senate-confirmed archivist for the first time since Colleen Shogan's February 2025 firing, ending a sequence of three acting archivists (Bosanko, Rubio, Forst) and an interval in which Byron performed the archivist's functions. The leadership change came after the FY2026 budget was enacted and the Office of Innovation eliminated. As of Aug. 24, 2026, NARA's 'National Archives by the Numbers' page listed 2,344 staff, 13.5 billion pieces of paper in its permanent holdings, and 532,047,895 digitized pages in the National Archives Catalog. Those Catalog pages equal roughly 4% of the paper count. Federal News Network had reported 2,744 NARA staff as of June 16, 2025, based on archived versions of the same page.

Congress funded NARA at $454.3 million for FY2026, more than the $414.7 million requested but below FY2025's $474.2 million.

title: NASA Closed Its Largest Research Library and 100+ Goddard Labs -- Including One Critical to the Roman Space Telescope -- Over Objections From Its Own Union and Congress
institution: NASA, Goddard Space Flight Center
status: Ongoing -- library closed Jan. 2-3, 2026; broader 13-building/100+-lab consolidation targeted for completion by March 2026
date_of_action: 2025-11 (consolidation plan advanced) through 2026-01 (library closure) and 2026-03 (target completion of building closures)
what_changed: NASA closed the Goddard Information and Collaboration Center -- Goddard Space Flight Center's 100,000-volume research library, the largest in the agency -- on January 2-3, 2026, as part of a broader plan to shrink the 1,270-acre Goddard campus (home to Hubble and Webb telescope operations) by roughly 25%, decommissioning 13 buildings and more than 100 laboratories by March 2026. The library's collection included books, journals, and historical documents dating from the early 20th century through the 1950s-60s Space Race with the Soviet Union, much of it copyrighted, out of print, or never digitized. NASA said discarded holdings would undergo a 60-day review, with some materials transferred to other NASA libraries or government warehouses and the rest discarded; the Goddard Engineers, Scientists and Technicians Association (part of IFPTE) said the closure proceeded with 'extreme haste and no transparent strategy.' Administrator Jared Isaacman characterized the closure as a long-planned 'facilities consolidation' dating to a 2022 (Biden-era) master plan, projected to save $10 million per year in operations costs plus $63.8 million in deferred maintenance. IFPTE union leader Matt Biggs disputed both of Isaacman's central claims as 'misguided' and 'misleading': the 2022 master plan actually called for renovating the library building, not eliminating it, and many discarded materials were copyrighted or unique physical items unavailable in any digital form, contradicting Isaacman's assurance that researchers would retain access to needed materials. Biggs said NASA scientists and engineers 'shouldn't have to be dumpster divers to do their work.' Separately, **the building closures include labs used by teams working on the propulsion subsystem for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, one of NASA's flagship missions, raising concern among employees and lawmakers about schedule and technical risk to an active, mission-critical program** rather than only administrative/archival loss. Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), ranking member of the House Science Committee, sent a formal letter to Acting/Administrator Sean Duffy (predating Isaacman's confirmation) demanding NASA immediately halt the closures pending more transparency; the Maryland congressional delegation separately sought information on the closures. This entry is a companion to nasa-science-budget-workforce-collapse-2025.json, which documents the broader FY2026 NASA science-budget cuts and workforce exodus (JPL layoffs, Goddard leadership departures, Earth-science mission cancellations) -- that entry covers people and money; this one covers physical infrastructure, irreplaceable archival materials, and mission-critical lab capacity specifically.

primary_proponent.name: Jared Isaacman
primary_proponent.role: NASA Administrator
primary_proponent.note: Publicly defended the library and building closures as a long-planned, already-approved 'facilities consolidation' that preserves researcher access to needed materials; IFPTE union leader Matt Biggs directly disputed both claims as 'misguided' and 'misleading,' citing the 2022 master plan's actual renovation-not-elimination language and the loss of copyrighted, non-digitized, unique physical materials.

estimated_impact.summary: A named administration official's public defense of the closures is directly disputed by his own agency's union on two specific, checkable factual claims (what the 2022 plan actually said, and whether the discarded materials exist elsewhere), while the closures independently threaten a specific active flagship mission's propulsion-system development, not just archival/administrative capacity.

title: Trump's Proposed NASA Budget Cut Science Funding Nearly in Half, Triggering a 20%+ Workforce Exodus and Dozens of Canceled Missions
institution: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
status: Ongoing -- the FY2026 budget remains a proposal Congress has not finalized, but the workforce reductions and JPL layoffs it triggered have already occurred; satellite decommissioning was planned to begin as soon as October 2025
date_of_action: 2025-04-10 (initial OMB budget draft) through 2025-10-14 (JPL's third layoff round)
what_changed: On April 10, 2025, the White House Office of Management and Budget sent NASA a draft FY2026 budget proposal that would cut the agency's overall funding by roughly 24% and its Science Mission Directorate specifically by nearly half -- from $7.3 billion to $3.9 billion, a 47% reduction. The Planetary Society estimated the cuts would cancel no fewer than 41 active and planned missions, including the Mars Sample Return program (billions of dollars in prior U.S. and international-partner investment already sunk) and a roughly 50% cut to the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, on which NASA had already spent nearly 90% of its projected development cost. Seven former NASA science chiefs publicly condemned the proposal. The budget cuts coincided with, and helped drive, a parallel workforce exodus: NASA opened a second round of its 'deferred resignation' buyout program in mid-2025 after roughly 870 employees took the first round; by late July 2025 nearly 4,000 employees (about 20% of the agency's roughly 18,000-person workforce) had accepted the program, shrinking NASA to about 14,000 employees. The cuts hit NASA's field centers unevenly, with Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland losing the most staff (607), followed by Johnson Space Center (366), Kennedy Space Center (311), and NASA headquarters (307). Leadership departures accompanied the buyouts: Jet Propulsion Laboratory director Laurie Leshin stepped down in June 2025, and Goddard Space Flight Center director Makenzie Lystrup announced her departure July 21, 2025, effective August 1, amid a Goddard staff dissent letter over the cuts. Separately, **the White House's FY2026 budget proposed decommissioning the fully operational Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 and -3 satellites -- which measure atmospheric carbon dioxide and plant health and, per a 2023 senior review, remained in 'excellent condition' with enough fuel to operate until 2040** -- along with other Earth-science missions, with decommissioning planned to begin as soon as October 2025; scientists warned this would create a significant gap in climate-monitoring data. The workforce reductions continued independent of the budget fight: on October 13, 2025, JPL laid off approximately 550 employees (about 11% of its workforce) in what director David Gallagher called an unrelated internal 'realignment' that began in July 2025, not a response to that month's federal government shutdown -- JPL's third layoff round since February 2024.

title: National Cancer Institute Lost Staff and $180 Million in Grants Amid a Proposed 37% Budget Cut and Dismantled Public Communications
institution: National Cancer Institute (NIH)
status: Split status: the already-executed 2025 harms -- staff losses, $180M+ in cancelled active grants, and dismantled public-facing communications infrastructure -- remain in effect. Separately, the proposed FY2026 37.3% NCI budget cut was rejected: the FY2026 Labor-HHS-Education appropriations act (P.L. 119-75, signed 2026-02-03) instead provided NCI $7.4 billion, an increase over FY2025 rather than the proposed cut to ~$4.53 billion.
date_of_action: 2025 (staff purges, grant cancellations, and communications dismantlement, ongoing through at least September 2025); FY2026 budget request proposing a 37% cut submitted 2025
what_changed: Separate from -- but compounding -- a proposed FY2026 budget request that would cut NCI's funding by 37.3% (about $2.69 billion, from roughly $7.22 billion to $4.53 billion), NCI had already lost hundreds of staff and had more than $180 million in active research grants cancelled as of a June 26, 2025 Guardian report, with key prevention, clinical-trial, and community-research programs being dismantled in the process. A May 2025 U.S. Senate Minority Staff report separately found the federal government had cut approximately $2.7 billion in NIH funding overall in the first three months of 2025, including a 31% year-over-year decrease in cancer-research funding through March 2025 compared with the same period in 2024 -- a distinct, already-executed reduction from the proposed FY2026 request. By September 2025, the New York Times Magazine reported NCI's public-facing website and communications functions had been 'devastatingly dismantled,' **leaving patient calls for cancer information unanswered, and that labs studying specific cancers -- including pediatric brain tumors -- were being gutted**, with researchers forced to suspend ongoing studies and lay off their own staff as grant funding lapsed. Analysts and cancer-research organizations warned that if the proposed 37% FY2026 cut were enacted, NCI's grant-approval rate would collapse to roughly 4% of new applications (down from historical norms several times higher), rejecting 96% of new research proposals. Update 2026-08-17: The proposed FY2026 37.3% NCI cut described above did not take effect. Congress enacted the FY2026 Labor-HHS-Education appropriations act (P.L. 119-75, H.R. 7148, Division B) on 2026-02-03, providing NCI $7.4 billion -- an increase over FY2025 funding, not the proposed $2.69 billion/37.3% cut to ~$4.53 billion. This entry's date_added (2026-08-12) came more than six months after that enactment, so the 'proposed, not yet enacted' framing had already gone stale before this entry was first written. The already-executed 2025 harms described above -- the 2025 staff losses, the $180M+ in cancelled grants, and the dismantled communications infrastructure -- are separate, already-completed actions and are unaffected by the FY2026 appropriations increase; they have not been reversed.

title: National Climate Assessment Gutted -- Nearly 400 Authors Dismissed, Reports Pulled Offline, Climate Skeptic Installed to Run the Program
institution: U.S. Global Change Research Program (USGCRP) -- National Climate Assessment
status: Ongoing -- comment period on USGCRP's proposed amendment reclassifying NCA5's high-emissions findings closed September 9, 2026, with four state AGs demanding withdrawal; no final decision or Sixth Assessment plan announced as of September 22, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-04-01 (ICF International coordination contract cancelled) through 2026-08-25 (proposed amendment to the published Fifth Assessment)
what_changed: In early April 2025, NASA cancelled a contract with ICF International, the consulting firm hired to support the U.S. Global Change Research Program's (USGCRP) logistical coordination work across the 15 federal agencies and hundreds of volunteer authors that produce the National Climate Assessment -- a report on climate change's impacts on the United States that has been congressionally mandated every four years since the Global Change Research Act of 1990. On April 28, 2025, nearly 400 scientists and scholars who had already begun volunteer work on the Sixth National Climate Assessment (legally due by the end of 2027 under the four-year mandate; Eos described it as planned for 2028) were told by email from USGCRP that 'we are now releasing all current assessment participants from their roles' while the report's scope was 'reevaluated.' On June 30, 2025, **globalchange.gov -- the USGCRP website that housed the National Climate Assessments, including prior, already-published editions -- went offline without prior notice, taking the reports off federal websites**; days earlier, on June 24, NOAA had redirected its public climate site, climate.gov, to noaa.gov. On July 2, 2025, NASA spokesperson Bethany Stevens said the agency was pursuing a 'technical pathway' to re-host the reports and that 'All preexisting reports will be hosted on the NASA website'; by July 14-15, 2025, NASA reversed that pledge, with Stevens stating 'NASA has no legal obligations to host globalchange.gov's data... We never did and will not host the data' -- relying on the fact that the Global Change Research Act of 1990 only requires the assessments be submitted to Congress every four years, not that they be publicly hosted online, as the legal basis for declining to restore access. The move was consistent with Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation policy blueprint, whose Executive Office of the President chapter, written by Russell Vought (now OMB Director), called for an executive order to 'reshape the U.S. Global Change Research Program,' said the process for producing assessments 'should include diverse viewpoints,' and urged the next president to 'critically analyze and, if required, refuse to accept any USGCRP assessment prepared under the Biden Administration.' The dismissal left the administration able to either skip the congressionally mandated report or pursue an alternative version. Work on the Sixth Assessment did not stop entirely: starting in December 2025, the administration invited a new group of researchers known for climate skepticism to resume work on it. On July 9, 2026, Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced on X, and the White House confirmed to Politico, that Matthew Wielicki, a former University of Alabama geochemist and prominent skeptic of mainstream climate science, would lead USGCRP -- the program responsible for compiling the assessment the administration had gutted fifteen months earlier. That USGCRP role is distinct from a separate Department of Energy effort covering similar ground: Wright convened his own five-scientist 'Climate Working Group' (John Christy, Roy Spencer, Steve Koonin, Judith Curry, and Ross McKitrick) in 2025 to produce a contrarian report critiquing the Fifth National Climate Assessment and the EPA's endangerment finding; Wright dissolved that group in a September 3, 2025 letter after its report drew a rebuttal from 85+ scientists, and on January 30, 2026, Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled that the group had operated in violation of the Federal Advisory Committee Act. That DOE matter is a different agency's action and is tracked separately in the Cabinet-Level tracker. On August 25, 2026, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, on behalf of USGCRP, published a Federal Register notice announcing a proposed amendment to NCA5 -- the existing 2023 Fifth National Climate Assessment, not the still-pending Sixth -- open for public comment through 11:59 p.m. ET on September 9, 2026. The proposed amendment states that RCP8.5, SSP5-8.5, SRES A2, and similar high-emissions pathways should not be used as expected, likely, baseline, business-as-usual, central, or policy-relevant planning futures, and that NCA5 findings substantially dependent on them should be identified as outcomes associated with 'implausible high-end scenario assumptions.' It was the first concrete action under Wielicki's leadership, and it reaches backward to reclassify an already-published, congressionally mandated assessment's findings rather than only shaping the still-pending Sixth Assessment. The amendment's core technical premise is not a fabricated claim: in a May 18, 2026 post on The Climate Brink, climate scientists Zeke Hausfather, Glen Peters, and Piers Forster wrote that RCP8.5 had drawn mounting criticism for about a decade as an implausible worst case -- citing doubts that its coal use was possible given the world's recoverable coal reserves, falling clean-energy costs, and real-world emissions trends -- and that it was being retired from the next generation of climate scenarios. The same post separated that science from its political use: it criticized President Trump's post claiming the United Nations climate committee had 'just admitted that its own projections (RCP8.5) were WRONG! WRONG! WRONG!', and called it ironic for him to criticize past use of high-emissions scenarios while his administration supports rolling back existing climate policy. Criticism of the NCA5 amendment itself also came from a scholar sympathetic to the RCP8.5 objection: in an August 25, 2026 post, Roger Pielke Jr., who has long argued RCP8.5 is overused, wrote that the administration is 'directionally correct in recognizing that RCP8.5 is problematic' but that the amendment 'cannot succeed, because NCA5's problems are systemic and irreparable.' On September 9, 2026, the attorneys general of Massachusetts, California, Connecticut, and New York filed comments opposing the amendment as a 'perfunctory seven-page document' that 'cannot lawfully amend a past National Climate Assessment,' arguing that it lacked the peer review required for highly influential scientific assessments, named no authors, and showed no consultation with NCA5's original authors, and demanding its withdrawal. As of NBC News's September 22, 2026 report, the amendment was still described as a proposal and the administration had not said whether it would produce a Sixth Assessment; 175 independent climate scientists, many formerly involved in the national assessments, had begun publishing their own special research collection in American Geophysical Union and American Meteorological Society journals to fill the gap.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Director, Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.note: Vought, who ran OMB during Trump's first term, wrote Project 2025's Executive Office of the President chapter, which called for an executive order to 'reshape the U.S. Global Change Research Program' and urged the next president to 'critically analyze and, if required, refuse to accept any USGCRP assessment prepared under the Biden Administration'; Rolling Stone reported that the push for a National Climate Assessment written by climate deniers 'is apparently supported by' Vought. No single official's name was confirmed publicly as the signer of the April 28, 2025 dismissal email; Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-CA), ranking member of the House Science Committee, addressed her formal oversight letter on the dismissals to Michael Kratsios, Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, which has institutional oversight of USGCRP.

estimated_impact.summary: The National Climate Assessment is the federal government's congressionally mandated account of how climate change is affecting the United States, which governments, communities and businesses use to prepare for extreme weather, wildfire and sea-level rise. Losing it, one dismissed author said in CNN's coverage, 'makes us less prepared' for those hazards. The administration dismissed the nearly 400 volunteer authors of the Sixth Assessment, cancelled the contract coordinating the 15-agency effort, and took the published assessments off federal websites; NASA then reneged on a pledge to re-host them. The Sixth Assessment, legally due by the end of 2027, has no announced plan beyond a restart with skeptic-aligned authors under a new director who is a prominent skeptic of mainstream climate science. The administration has also proposed an amendment telling federal agencies not to plan around the 2023 edition's high-emissions projections, which would weaken the risk baseline used for planning, regulation and grants.

title: $362 Million in National Park Service Grants Stalled Awaiting Political Review in Burgum's Office
institution: National Park Service / Department of the Interior
status: Ongoing as of Sept. 2026: no reporting reviewed shows the 1,400-grant backlog cleared, the two-appointee review dropped, or a reply to House Democrats' July 28 deadline; in August Interior rejected 130+ funded park agreements worth $25M+.
date_of_action: 2025 ($50,000 political-review threshold set under DOGE); 2026-06 (1,400-grant backlog reported); 2026-08 (130+ funded agreements disapproved)
what_changed: **More than 1,400 active National Park Service grants worth about $362 million were sitting unapproved as of early June 2026, awaiting political review at the Department of the Interior, according to an internal database provided to NOTUS.** An NPS grants employee told NOTUS there had been fewer than 10 active grants backlogged two years earlier. The Department of Government Efficiency set up a $50,000 review threshold for grants and cooperative agreements in 2025, and some version of it stayed in place after DOGE officials left Interior. On May 13, 2026, at a House Natural Resources Committee hearing, Rep. Sarah Elfreth pressed Secretary Doug Burgum on Interior's policy requiring Secretary-level approval of any grant over $50,000, which she said covered 82% of the department's roughly 23,000 FY2025 grants; Burgum answered that such approvals go to staff in the Secretary's office: "It's not me personally on my desk." Under the process NOTUS described in June, every NPS grant or cooperative agreement worth $50,000 or more must, after an internal NPS leadership review, be approved by two political appointees: the assistant secretary for policy, management and budget and the assistant secretary for fish, wildlife and parks. One staffer called the mandatory inclusion of both assistant secretaries "a big step up" from previous policy, and three employees told NOTUS the backlog had worsened in recent months. Interior has also consolidated grants management and other back-end functions from its bureaus into Burgum's office. The stalled projects include nonprofit youth programs to clear trails, groups sent to prevent washouts in parks during persistent rain, and wildlife surveys; Interior employees and grant recipients cautioned that prescribed burns and fuels reduction ahead of wildfire season could also get stuck, and a park service official said organizations that depend on NPS funding had warned of layoffs and possible closure when grants are delayed. Interior is managing the backlog with a much smaller staff: it shed about 13,000 employees (about 20% of its workforce) in 2025, including about 4,000 at NPS. An Interior spokesperson told NOTUS the department's changes would "streamline internal processes" and "reduce unnecessary bureaucracy," adding that "reviewing significant expenditures before funds are obligated is a common-sense stewardship measure that taxpayers expect from their government." On July 22, 2026, House Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Jared Huffman and Rep. Don Beyer led more than 70 House Democrats in a letter to NPS Acting Director Jessica Bowron, calling the two-appointee review a bottleneck that had left more than $360 million in NPS funding behind schedule and asking NPS to adjust it. The letter requested an update on NPS's plans and a full list of all grants and cooperative agreements in the backlog by July 28, 2026; no reporting reviewed shows whether NPS or Interior responded. In August 2026 Interior went beyond delay and "disapproved" more than 130 already-funded NPS partnership agreements worth at least $25 million for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1, according to internal documents reviewed by The Washington Post, which reported them on Sept. 11, 2026. The rejected work included fire preparedness and post-fire recovery at Joshua Tree National Park, removing trees that threaten burial mounds at Effigy Mounds National Monument, raising endangered San Francisco garter snakes, and sled-dog care at Denali. Interior spokesperson Aubrie Spady said the department had disapproved agreements "with groups actively working against the best interests of the American people and the priorities of this administration," without naming them; the Great Basin Institute, which had more than 70 agreements worth at least $12.7 million blocked, said Interior never notified it directly and that it does not know why. Interior approved more than 700 other agreements that year through early August, and projects under $50,000 do not require its review.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of the Interior
primary_proponent.note: Heads the department whose two-political-appointee review of NPS grants of $50,000+ produced the backlog, and which disapproved 130+ funded NPS partnership agreements in August 2026; Interior has also moved grants management into his office

estimated_impact.summary: Park safety and conservation work has been delayed or cancelled. As of early June 2026 about 1,400 NPS grants worth $362 million -- for trail clearing, washout prevention and wildlife surveys, with prescribed burns and wildfire fuels reduction at risk -- were stuck awaiting political review; an NPS grants employee said fewer than 10 grants had been backlogged two years earlier. In August Interior rejected more than 130 already-funded park agreements worth at least $25 million, including Joshua Tree fire preparedness that park documents said the park needed to fight wildfire, protection of Native American burial mounds, and endangered-species recovery. Nonprofit partners have warned of layoffs and possible closure, and the queue is being worked by an Interior workforce down about 13,000 people, with the Park Service down roughly a quarter of its staff.

title: GSA/DOGE Listed 34 National Park Service Buildings for Lease Termination, Including Visitor Centers and Museums Housing Artifacts
institution: National Park Service (NPS); General Services Administration (GSA)
status: Ongoing in phases through 2026; at least two individual sites (Fairbanks, AK and Seattle, WA) reversed or found to have been included in error; the leasing-authority bill Congress introduced in response has since advanced out of committee
date_of_action: 2025-03-06 (list publicly reported) through 2026 (phased terminations continuing)
what_changed: On March 6, 2025, the Washington Post reported that GSA, working with DOGE, had targeted the leases of at least 34 National Park Service buildings for termination as part of the administration's broader federal real-estate cost-cutting push -- including visitor centers, law enforcement offices, park headquarters, and museum/archive space housing millions of cultural artifacts. GSA said terminating the leases could save taxpayers millions of dollars; terminations were structured to arrive in waves stretching from 2025 into 2026, with example dates including a planned September 30, 2025 termination for Seattle's Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park visitor center and a planned end-of-May-2026 termination for a National Park Service building in Fairbanks, Alaska. **Park advocates warned the closures would degrade the visitor experience, particularly during peak summer season, threaten artifact preservation, and disrupt law-enforcement and emergency operations at affected parks.** At least two individual terminations were subsequently reversed or corrected: GSA restored the Fairbanks-area Alaska Public Lands Information Center lease roughly 10 days after terminating it, following pressure from Sen. Dan Sullivan; and the Klondike Gold Rush visitor center lease in Seattle was found to have been placed on the termination list in error -- the lease had actually been extended by Historic Seattle in September 2024 through 2030, with GSA apparently unaware of the extension when it added the site to the list. Members of Congress, including Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith, formally urged GSA not to proceed with terminations affecting other specific NPS buildings; a bill, the National Park System Long-Term Lease Investment Act (S.2498/H.R.4931), was introduced in Congress during this period aimed at giving NPS more stable, long-term leasing authority, though it had not been enacted as of this entry's last verification. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 39): H.R. 4931 advanced out of the House Natural Resources Committee markup on July 22, 2026, alongside several other public-lands bills, moving it a step closer to a House floor vote -- no floor vote had occurred as of this update. The bill's actual mechanism, allowing NPS to extend certain existing leases held 5+ years without competitive rebidding when the Director finds it in the park unit's best interest, drew formal opposition from the National Parks Conservation Association, which argued in December 2025 testimony to the same committee that extending leases without fair-market-rent consideration risks the government failing to secure optimal uses for the 340+ structures NPS currently leases -- a concern in tension with the bill's stated purpose of encouraging private investment in maintaining park assets. No comprehensive updated tally of the original 34 sites' current status was found in sourcing reviewed.

title: National Park Service Lost 24% of Its Permanent Staff — Internal Report Contradicts Interior's Public 'False Narrative' Denial
institution: National Park Service (NPS), Department of the Interior
status: Ongoing -- permanent staffing losses (~24%, ~4,000 people) remain unreversed; 2026 seasonal hiring again fell short of its own target, and approval to refill roughly 600 positions is a small fraction of the loss, not a reversal
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (initial mass layoff, dubbed the 'Valentine's Day Massacre' by affected staff) through 2025-08-27 (internal operational-status report surfaces)
what_changed:
On February 14, 2025, NPS laid off some 1,000 probationary employees just weeks before peak visitor season began across the system's 63 national parks and 370 other managed sites. By March 11, 2025, reporting confirmed the administration was separately pushing for a 30% reduction in NPS's overall payroll -- a budget-driven target distinct from, and layered on top of, the February probationary firings -- expected to further reduce park rangers, custodial staff, and conservation-program capacity. Roll Call reported on March 11, 2025 that, alongside the firings of about 1,000 probationary employees, about 700 other full-time employees had taken buyouts over the previous six weeks, a combined loss Roll Call described as more than 1,700 full-time workers 'forced out' just before the start of the 2025 tourist season. The same report said congressional Republicans overseeing the Park Service were confident that Interior Secretary Doug Burgum could bring on sufficient staff for the 2025 season: Rep. Ryan Zinke (R-Mont.) said Burgum had already announced that seasonal employees were not affected by the hiring freeze and that park superintendents he had spoken to were 'fully prepared for a successful visitor season'; Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.), by email, applauded Burgum for announcing 5,000 seasonal job openings ahead of a busy visitor season; and Rep. Tom Tiffany (R-Wis.) offered what Roll Call called similar assurances by email.

A March 13, 2025 preliminary injunction from Judge William Alsup ordered NPS and five other agencies (Agriculture, Defense, Energy, Interior, Treasury, and VA) to immediately reinstate their terminated probationary employees; NPS and other named agencies complied only nominally, notifying fired staff they were reinstated but then placing them on indefinite paid administrative leave rather than restoring them to duty -- a workaround Alsup explicitly ruled violated the injunction, since it did not restore the services the order intended to restore. The Supreme Court stayed Alsup's reinstatement order on April 8, 2025 on standing grounds, allowing the administration to resume the firings; NPS's ~24% permanent-staff loss documented later in this entry reflects that the initial February terminations were not durably reversed.

In April 2025, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum issued Secretarial Order 3426, mandating that every park remain 'open and accessible' regardless of staffing levels -- meaning parks could not close facilities or reduce services in response to the shortages, only quietly absorb the strain. By July 2025, independent analysis of Interior Department workforce data by the National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA) found NPS had lost 24% of its permanent staff overall (about 4,000 people) since January, while only roughly 4,500 of a promised ~8,000 seasonal positions had been filled.

Per Order 3426's own reporting requirement, every park unit had to submit an updated operational status by July 25, 2025; an internal NPS report compiled from those submissions, first reported by the New York Times, documented widespread, specific impacts: nearly 70 parks reduced visitor center hours, 22 postponed maintenance, and 11 closed or delayed opening facilities. Specific documented examples include **all 13 lifeguard positions vacant at Assateague Island National Seashore (leaving the beach unguarded) -- a shortage CBS News had already reported independently on July 5, 2025, three weeks before Order 3426's own compilation deadline, tying it to the hiring freeze and warning of elevated drowning/injury risk given the beach's millions of annual summer visitors** -- the fire management team reduced to one person at Cumberland Island National Seashore, and Indiana Dunes National Park's ranger-led tours cut from 575 to approximately 100 for the year after 4 of 6 interpretive-division supervisors took deferred resignation, early retirement, or buyout offers. NPCA, which published the park-by-park submissions on August 27, 2025, reported that at times entrance stations at Glacier National Park had gone unstaffed during normal hours, affecting the recreation fee revenue the park relies on to pay staff and visitor services; Glacier's own submission said the Camas Entrance Station may be unstaffed during typical hours of visitor entry, with signs directing visitors to self-pay by QR code on the honor system. Grand Canyon's submission reported no monitoring or prevention of zoonotic diseases (plague, rabies, hantavirus, bedbugs), along with reduced pest-management services in park buildings and lodging.

When this internal report became public, Interior deputy press secretary Aubrie Spady called the reporting a 'false narrative,' stating 'staffing levels and operations at our National Parks this summer are on par with previous years. Full Stop' -- a direct denial of findings drawn from the agency's own internal, Order-3426-mandated data collection.

A Washington Post report published August 27, 2025 documented a concrete, DC-specific consequence of the same custodial-staffing collapse -- NPS's D.C.-area grounds-maintenance staff, which had numbered about 200 people maintaining thousands of acres of trees and gardens in the capital, had fallen to just 20.

With Trump's federal takeover of DC policing deploying more than 2,200 National Guard troops to the city, roughly 110 of those troops were reassigned to a White House-directed 'Safe and Beautiful Task Force,' performing landscaping and sanitation work -- spreading mulch around the Tidal Basin's cherry trees, collecting trash at Lafayette Park, the National Mall, and the Tidal Basin -- that would ordinarily fall to NPS's own gutted maintenance staff. By early October 2025, the Guard had cleared 1,150 bags of trash, spread 1,045 cubic yards of mulch, removed 50 truckloads of plant waste, cleared 7.9 miles of roadway, painted 270 feet of fencing, and pruned 400 trees. The arrangement drew public questions about whether groundskeeping and trash removal are an appropriate use of military personnel trained for security and emergency response, distinct from this entry's own staffing-shortfall thesis but illustrating its practical downstream effect at some of the country's most visible federal sites.

On September 2-3, 2025, nearly 600 employees at Yosemite and Sequoia & Kings Canyon voted overwhelmingly to unionize with the National Federation of Federal Employees, a direct workforce response to the mass purges and budget cuts documented above -- workers cited the strain of being stretched thin (scientists and other specialists covering basic operational duties) as a driving factor.

On April 3, 2026, the White House released its fiscal year 2027 budget proposal, requesting $2.14 billion for NPS operations -- a $736 million, roughly 25% cut from the prior year -- which NPCA and other outlets project would eliminate approximately 2,920 additional full-time positions on top of the ~4,000 permanent positions already lost since January 2025. As with the entry's earlier budget-threat context, this is a proposal, not enacted law: Congress alone controls appropriations, and the FY2027 budget remained under congressional debate, with a final vote not expected before fall 2026 at the earliest. Notably, Congress rejected a comparable roughly $1 billion FY2026 NPS cut proposal in a January 5, 2026 appropriations bill, instead approving $3.267 billion in flat funding and adding a requirement that the administration notify Congress before any future mass firings or reorganizations -- a precedent for congressional pushback, though not a guarantee the FY2027 proposal meets the same fate.

The FY2027 budget fight moved in May 2026: the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Interior, Environment and Related Agencies released its FY2027 bill on May 20, 2026, rejecting the administration's proposed $736 million/~2,920-position cut and instead holding NPS operations funding essentially flat at $2.9 billion (a 1.3%/~$3 million reduction from FY2026), following the same pattern as Congress's FY2026 rejection of a similar cut this entry already documents. The bill still needed full-House passage and Senate reconciliation as of the sourcing reviewed, so this is a subcommittee-level rejection of the administration's ask, not a final enacted FY2027 appropriation.

For the 2026 season, NPS again fell short of its own seasonal-hiring target: roughly 4,500 of a planned 5,000+ seasonal positions were filled heading into peak summer season, with reporting citing paperwork delays, background-check backlogs, and housing shortages as contributing causes -- a smaller absolute gap than 2025's (~4,500 of ~8,000 filled), but the same shortfall pattern for a second consecutive year. The ~24% permanent-staff loss and its downstream effects (documented in this entry's 2025 examples) had not been reversed at last check.

The 2026 peak season brought the staffing crisis to a head -- record crowds collided with reduced capacity at parks including Yosemite, where seasonal employees reportedly went weeks without pay, scientists and hydrologists were reassigned to cleaning restrooms and staffing entrance gates, and some campgrounds closed for lack of staff to run them. NPS also removed timed-entry reservation systems at some of the busiest parks and introduced a new $100-per-person fee for international visitors, both of which affected entrance-line flow during the July 4th weekend's record crowds. On a partial-relief note, NPS was approved to refill roughly 600 staff positions -- a real but small fraction of the several thousand permanent positions lost since January 2025, not a reversal of the underlying staffing loss this entry documents.

The National Parks Conservation Association organized a nationwide 'Day of Action,' running August 22 through September 1, 2026 with roughly 30 events across 20 states and Washington, D.C., calling on President Trump and Interior Secretary Burgum to invest in NPS staffing and address the workforce shortages this entry documents. NPCA -- a 501(c)(3) that states it does not endorse, oppose, or fund political candidates -- organized the events partly in response to Interior Department claims about employee political activity. The campaign's public materials also cited related administration actions not otherwise part of this entry's own documentation: separate pricing for international visitors, placement of Trump's image on the 2026 annual pass, and removal of 'disparaging' content from federal historic sites -- noted here for context but not independently verified by this entry, since they fall outside its core staffing-crisis subject.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) / Doug Burgum
primary_proponent.role: DOGE directed the initial layoffs; Interior Secretary Burgum issued the 'stay open regardless of staffing' order that followed
primary_proponent.note: Burgum's Secretarial Order 3426 is the specific policy mechanism that turned a staffing shortage into a documented service-quality crisis -- by prohibiting parks from closing or scaling back in response to short-staffing, the order effectively required remaining staff to absorb the gap rather than allowing an official acknowledgment of reduced capacity. Interior's own deputy press secretary's 'false narrative' denial is difficult to reconcile with the fact that the cited findings came from data Interior itself required parks to report under Burgum's own order.

estimated_impact.summary: The Park Service's staffing losses and hiring freeze reached into public safety: all 13 lifeguard positions at Assateague Island National Seashore were vacant, leaving a beach with millions of annual summer visitors unguarded, and Cumberland Island's fire management team was cut to one person. Other documented effects include halted disease monitoring (including plague, rabies, and hantavirus surveillance) at Grand Canyon, entrance stations at Glacier that at times went unstaffed during normal hours, and D.C.-area grounds staff falling from about 200 to 20, with National Guard troops reassigned to landscaping and trash work. The shortfall repeated in 2026, when seasonal hiring again missed its target and some Yosemite campgrounds closed for lack of staff.

title: Tribes Lost Over $6 Million in Non-IHS Federal Health Grants and Technical Support Staff Despite RFK Jr.'s Promise to Protect Native American Health Funding
institution: HHS agencies outside the Indian Health Service (CDC, HRSA, and others)
status: Ongoing -- a third, distinct funding threat (ACA enhanced-subsidy expiration hitting tribal marketplace-coverage programs) identified alongside the original non-IHS grant cuts and the FY2026 IHS appropriations fight; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed for any of the three threads
date_of_action: 2025-02 through 2025-06 (cumulative grant cancellations and staffing losses reported)
what_changed: Despite HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s stated commitment to protect Native American health funding by shielding the Indian Health Service (IHS) itself from cuts, tribes reported losing more than $6 million in grants from other HHS agencies -- funding that paid for community health workers, vaccinations, data modernization, and other public health efforts -- according to a May 2025 letter from the National Indian Health Board to Kennedy. The administration canceled funding for programs it classified as violating Trump's ban on diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, including a program supporting Native American youth interested in science and medicine careers and a program helping several tribes increase access to healthy food. Tribal health officials also reported that federal staffing cuts across HHS agencies made it substantially harder to get technical support and administer federally funded health projects, in some cases because specific staffers tribes had worked with directly were fired. Tribal leaders highlighted the contradiction between the administration's stated chronic-disease-prevention priority and its funding cuts, with one official noting it was 'very confusing to say chronic disease prevention is the No. 1 priority and then to eradicate the support needed to address chronic disease prevention in Indian Country.' Update 2026-08-18 (GSR recheck batch 22): the non-IHS pattern documented above continued into 2026 -- CDC's Healthy Tribes program (culturally tailored public health initiatives) was reported terminated, and further reductions were reported at SAMHSA (Tribal Behavioral Health and Opioid Response grants, Native Connections), HRSA, the Administration for Community Living, and NIH, with the administration's FY2026 budget proposal separately seeking to eliminate roughly $128 million in Tribal set-aside mental/behavioral health funding and the Food is Medicine program. On the IHS side specifically -- which RFK Jr.'s promise covered -- Congress rejected the administration's proposed nearly-30%/$900 million FY2026 IHS cut: the enacted FY2026 appropriations package instead increased IHS funding roughly 1.1-1.3% over FY2025 (about $8.05 billion total, plus $5.31 billion in FY2027 advance appropriations), including a $41 million boost to the Special Diabetes Program for Indians (its largest in 22 years) and a $5 million increase for Urban Indian Health. This means the entry's core distinction -- IHS protected, non-IHS agencies cut -- held up and sharpened over the following year: Congress affirmatively reinforced IHS funding while the non-IHS cuts this entry documents continued and expanded. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 39): identified a third, mechanically distinct funding threat missed by the entry's prior two updates -- the December 31, 2025 expiration of enhanced ACA marketplace subsidies has directly strained tribal health organizations' insurance-assistance programs, which help Native Americans access care outside limited IHS facilities. **Tuba City Regional Health Care Corp. (Navajo Nation, Arizona) reported its patient-coverage costs rising roughly 170% to nearly $38,000/month without the enhanced subsidies; Fort Peck Tribes (Montana) said it is now 'limiting who gets help'; and Blackfeet Nation (Montana) paused employer-sponsored coverage for 52 people in January 2026.** National Indian Health Board CEO A.C. Locklear warned that reduced access to general primary care compounds existing health disparities. This is a third, distinct mechanism from the entry's existing two threads (non-IHS HHS grant/staffing cuts, and the IHS budget-appropriations fight) -- it affects tribal organizations' own insurance-navigation and coverage-assistance programs rather than direct federal grants or IHS appropriations, and predates but was not previously captured by this entry's 2026-08-18 update. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 52): identified a fourth, mitigating funding thread not previously in this entry -- the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), a $50 billion, five-year CMS grant program created by HR1 itself (the same law whose Medicaid cuts this tracker's related entries document) and announced Dec. 29, 2025, with awards to all 50 states announced starting late January 2026, includes Tribal-specific set-asides or initiatives in at least 13 states' approved applications (AZ, CA, CO, MN, MT, NE, NM, NY, OK, OR, UT, WA, WI). Oregon's application, developed with its nine federally recognized Tribes, dedicates $21.7 million of the state's 2026 RHTP award specifically to a Tribal Initiative improving healthcare access in rural and remote Tribal communities. This is a distinct, positive-mitigation development running alongside -- not a reversal of -- the entry's existing three threads (non-IHS grant/staffing cuts, the IHS appropriations fight, and the ACA-subsidy marketplace strain); RHTP funds tribal-specific rural-health infrastructure and access initiatives, not the specific non-IHS programs (Healthy Tribes, SAMHSA behavioral-health grants, etc.) this entry documents as cut, so it does not offset those losses directly.

estimated_impact.summary: Tribes lost over $6 million in HHS grants outside the Indian Health Service, plus DEI-flagged program cancellations and technical-support staffing losses, undercutting the administration's own stated promise to protect Native American health funding and directly contradicting its stated chronic-disease-prevention priority. Separately, a new $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program created by the same HR1 law includes Tribal-specific funding set-asides in at least 13 states, including a $21.7 million dedicated Tribal Initiative in Oregon for 2026 -- a mitigating funding stream running alongside, not offsetting, the cuts this entry otherwise documents.

title: Trump Administration Moves to Remove Supercomputers From NCAR, Disrupting Weather and Climate Research for 1,500+ Scientists
institution: National Science Foundation / National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR)
status: Blocked as of June 1, 2026 -- Judge R. Brooke Jackson issued a preliminary injunction halting the transfer of the NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center's stewardship from UCAR to the University of Wyoming, following UCAR's March 2026 lawsuit alleging the plan was retaliation against Colorado. A second, distinct lawsuit filed August 20, 2026 by the Environmental Defense Fund separately challenges the planned closure of NCAR's Mesa Laboratory under the National Historic Preservation Act. Both cases remain pending, with no ruling on the merits.
date_of_action: 2025-12-16 (first reporting of White House plan to 'break up' NCAR) through 2026-02-13 (NSF letter confirming supercomputer removal plan)
what_changed:
Reporting first surfaced in mid-December 2025 that the administration was moving to dismantle the National Science Foundation's National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado -- a 60-plus-year cornerstone of U.S. weather and climate science -- with officials characterizing it as a source of "climate alarmism." That earliest reporting specifically named NCAR's Mesa Laboratory campus as a target for shutdown, described plans to eliminate research programs internally labeled "woke," and indicated only select functions such as weather modeling would be transferred elsewhere rather than preserved intact.

The news broke via a post on X from OMB Director Russell Vought, with no advance warning to NCAR's own funder, NSF, or to the White House's usual channels for announcing agency actions; CNN reported the announcement landed in the middle of the American Geophysical Union's (AGU) annual meeting, where climate scientist Katherine Hayhoe wrote on Bluesky that 'NCAR is quite literally our global mothership... Dismantling NCAR is like taking a sledgehammer to the keystone holding up our scientific understanding of the planet.' AGU convened an emergency town hall of hundreds of scientists at the meeting in response.

Following a January 2026 White House announcement of intent to 'break up' NCAR, an NSF letter released February 13, 2026 confirmed plans to remove NCAR's supercomputing facility and transfer its stewardship to the University of Wyoming, per subsequent reporting identifying the specific recipient. The facility supports weather forecasting models, climate simulations, and extreme-weather prediction research used by approximately 1,500 researchers across more than 500 universities; NOAA itself relies on the facility to run some of its current forecasting models. Former NCAR director James Hurrell and other prominent colleagues in the weather and climate research community warned NSF that 'any path that leads to the fragmentation or dismantling of NSF NCAR is fundamentally not in the nation's interest,' and that the move could further set back NOAA's own weather-modeling capabilities, which the researchers noted have already lagged behind international competitors.

On March 12, 2026, AGU formally submitted comments to NSF opposing the dismantling proposal, arguing NCAR's integrated, interdisciplinary structure is what makes it irreplaceable and that the rushed timeline and limited stakeholder consultation fell short of standard governance practice. On March 16, 2026, the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR) -- the nonprofit consortium of 129 universities that manages NCAR -- sued the federal agencies and officials behind the breakup plan, alleging the effort was retaliation against Colorado: specifically, that the administration was using NCAR's dismantling to pressure the state over Gov. Jared Polis's refusal to grant clemency to Tina Peters, a former county clerk convicted of tampering with voting machines in pursuit of Trump's 2020 election-fraud claims, and over the state's broader resistance to ceding authority over its own elections. OMB Director Russell Vought had publicly framed the plan as 'breaking up' NCAR because it was 'one of the largest sources of climate alarmism in the country,' and a White House spokesperson told CNN that Colorado's treatment depended on having 'a governor who actually wanted to work with President Trump.'

On June 1, 2026, U.S. District Judge R. Brooke Jackson issued a preliminary injunction blocking the administration from taking further steps to dismantle NCAR, a win for the researchers and UCAR that halted the removal plan pending further litigation. DataCenterDynamics, AIP.org, and Courthouse News reporting on Judge R. Brooke Jackson's June 1, 2026 preliminary injunction corroborated that the University of Wyoming, which had offered to take over operations of the Cheyenne facility, was the specific institution NSF planned to transfer the NCAR-Wyoming Supercomputing Center's stewardship to; **the ruling found NSF had announced the transfer more than a month before its own public-comment deadline and that officials' prior statements 'strongly suggest[ed] the outcome was predetermined,' making the reorganization arbitrary and capricious under the APA**. No appeal of that injunction had been identified as of late August 2026.

Separately, a second, distinct lawsuit was filed August 20, 2026 in federal court in Colorado by the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF), unaffiliated with UCAR's suit, specifically challenging the administration's plan to close NCAR's Mesa Laboratory building -- the 1967, I.M. Pei-designed campus the earliest reporting had named as an initial shutdown target. EDF's complaint adds a legal theory UCAR's suit did not raise: that closing the Mesa Laboratory without the environmental and public-consultation review required under the National Historic Preservation Act is unlawful, arguing the building -- while not currently listed on the National Register of Historic Places -- is eligible for listing given its architectural significance and the scientific discoveries made there. EDF seeks to block the closure and compel the required historic-preservation review; corroborated across EDF's own press release, Inside Climate News, E&E News, Boulder Reporting Lab, and BizWest. No ruling on EDF's suit had been identified as of late August 2026.

title: NCUA Board Reduced to a Single Member After Trump Fires Both Democratic Board Members
institution: National Credit Union Administration
status: Ongoing on a fast-track briefing schedule. The D.C. Circuit deferred ruling on Harper and Otsuka's Fed-like-protection argument pending further briefing on how the Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 Slaughter and Cook decisions apply to NCUA, then set a schedule -- administration's brief due September 12, 2026; Harper/Otsuka reply October 3; government reply October 17; oral argument after briefing concludes -- that could produce a ruling by year-end 2026. The two remain off the single-member board.
date_of_action: 2025-04-15 (firings) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court ruling narrowed path to reinstatement)
what_changed: In April 2025, President Trump fired both Democratic members of the National Credit Union Administration's three-person board -- former Chairman Todd Harper and Tanya Otsuka -- by email, without citing cause, leaving Republican Chair Kyle Hauptman as the sole remaining board member. Harper's term was not set to expire until April 2027 and Otsuka's not until August 2029. The Federal Credit Union Act defines the NCUA board as a three-member body with staggered six-year terms, structured (according to a subsequent district court finding) to mirror the Federal Reserve's governance model and insulate credit union regulation from political turnover. With only one board member, the NCUA could continue routine supervision and enforcement but could not vote on new rulemakings or policy changes; a scheduled board meeting was canceled. Harper and Otsuka sued; in July 2025 U.S. District Judge Amir Ali ruled the firings unlawful and ordered reinstatement, finding Congress had deliberately restricted the president's removal power when it added fixed terms to the statute in 1978. The two briefly returned to a board meeting before an appeals court granted the administration an emergency stay, sidelining them again. The case was held in abeyance pending Trump v. Slaughter; when the Supreme Court ruled for the administration on June 29, 2026, credit-union trade groups and legal analysts concluded the ruling 'effectively ends' the Harper/Otsuka challenge, since the Federal Credit Union Act -- unlike the Federal Reserve Act -- contains no explicit 'for cause' removal language for the NCUA to lean on. Harper and Otsuka's attorneys have since asked the D.C. Circuit to let them argue the NCUA deserves Fed-like treatment given its similar market-regulatory structure, but as of this writing they remain off the board, which continues to operate with a single member. Update 2026-07-19: in a filing with the D.C. Circuit in mid-July 2026, Harper and Otsuka's attorneys formally argued NCUA deserves Federal Reserve-like removal protection, leaning on the district court's earlier finding that Congress deliberately modeled NCUA's governance structure on the Fed's -- the same distinction that succeeded for Cook but was rejected for MSPB's Harris. No ruling on this argument had issued as of this update; the appeal remains pending. Re-verified 2026-07-26: no ruling identified yet on Harper and Otsuka's mid-July D.C. Circuit filing arguing for Fed-like removal protection; the appeal remains pending and the board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no ruling identified on Harper and Otsuka's mid-July D.C. Circuit filing arguing for Fed-like removal protection; their reply (due August 5, 2026 per the court's prior order) was not independently located, and no further D.C. Circuit action was found as of this update. The board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member. Update 2026-08-29 (real correction): the D.C. Circuit did not rule on the removal-protection argument directly. Instead, before the August 5 reply deadline, the court deferred consideration of Harper and Otsuka's motion and ordered the administration to explain by July 29 how the case should proceed in light of the Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 Slaughter and Cook decisions, with Harper and Otsuka permitted to respond by August 5. Following that exchange, the D.C. Circuit set a fast-track briefing schedule: the administration's brief is due September 12, 2026; Harper and Otsuka's reply is due October 3; the government's reply is due October 17; oral argument will follow "the first appropriate date following the conclusion of briefing." Legal press described the expedited schedule as one that could produce a ruling by the end of 2026. Harper and Otsuka's central remaining argument is that NCUA falls within the narrow financial-regulator exception the Supreme Court recognized in Cook for the Federal Reserve, rather than the broader removal-power holding in Slaughter. The board continues to operate with Chair Hauptman as its sole member pending this schedule.

title: NDAA FY2026 Permanently Bans Transgender Women From Women's Sports at Military Service Academies, After a Broader House Push to Restrict Gender-Affirming Care and Abortion Access Was Mostly Stripped in Conference
institution: U.S. Congress / Department of Defense (service academies)
status: Passed both chambers and confirmed via the White House's December 9, 2025 Statement of Administration Policy on the final House-Rules-stage bill: the NDAA permanently bars men from women's sports teams at military academies and eliminates DEI offices, programs, and related authorities department-wide, provisions that survived conference. The SAP does not mention any TRICARE or gender-affirming-care coverage restriction, consistent with reporting that the House's original broader healthcare-restriction riders did not survive into the final bill.
date_of_action: 2025-09-10/14 (House passes its version, $892.6B, with the broadest set of riders) through 2025-12 (Senate 77-20 final passage; House-Senate conference resolves differences)
what_changed: On September 10-14, 2025, the House passed its version of the FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act, an $892.6 billion bill, with Republican-added riders restricting gender-affirming care, abortion-related travel funding, and diversity/equity/inclusion programs across the military -- provisions Democrats opposed as partisan 'culture war' additions to a bill traditionally passed on a more bipartisan basis. The Senate passed its own, somewhat narrower version 77-20 in October 2025, which included a ban on transgender participation in women's sports at the military service academies and DEI-related cuts, but had already dropped some of the House's broadest healthcare-restriction language. In House-Senate conference, most of the remaining gender-affirming-care-coverage restrictions were further stripped from the final bill -- reporting on the exact final health-coverage provisions was inconsistent across outlets, and this entry does not assert a specific TRICARE-coverage restriction survived into law given that inconsistency. The White House's own December 9, 2025 Statement of Administration Policy on the final House-Rules-stage bill confirms what did survive: it states the NDAA 'permanently prohibits men from playing on women's sports teams at all military academies' and 'eliminates statutory provisions relating to Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion offices, programs, training, activities, and authorities' department-wide -- the administration's own framing describes the provision as barring men from women's teams rather than specifically naming transgender women, though advocacy groups and other reporting describe its practical effect as a transgender-athlete ban. The SAP itemizes the bill's other notable provisions (a 3.8% troop pay raise, childcare-access improvements, repeal of the 1991/2002 AUMFs, Golden Dome missile-defense funding) without any mention of TRICARE or gender-affirming-care coverage, corroborating that the broader healthcare-restriction riders did not survive into this version. The final bill authorized a record roughly $900 billion in military spending, about $8 billion more than the administration's initial budget request, and the Senate had passed its own version 77-20 in October 2025 before conference.

primary_proponent.name: House Republican leadership
primary_proponent.role: Sponsors of the FY2026 NDAA's original culture-war riders
primary_proponent.note: House Republicans added the broadest set of gender-affirming-care, abortion-travel, and DEI restrictions in the House-passed version; the Trump administration's own Statement of Administration Policy supported the bill's eventual passage, and the transgender-sports-ban provision that survived conference reflects the administration's broader policy priorities on transgender participation in single-sex programs.

estimated_impact.summary: **Transgender women who would otherwise be eligible for service-academy athletics are now permanently barred from competing on women's teams at West Point, Annapolis, the Air Force Academy, and the Coast Guard Academy** -- a small population in absolute numbers, but a permanent, codified exclusion from a specific institutional benefit at federally-run military academies, enacted alongside broader DEI-program cuts across the military the bill also included.
