title: NEA Cancels Hundreds of Open Arts Grants Hours After Budget Plan to Eliminate It
institution: National Endowment for the Arts
status: Terminations took effect May 31, 2025; no ruling restoring them has been found. Congress kept NEA at $207M for FY2026; a stopgap law signed Sept. 2, 2026 extends that rate to Dec. 11, 2026. FY2027 proposals: White House $29M, House bill $135M. Carter confirmed chair Dec. 18, 2025.
date_of_action: 2025-05-02 to 2025-05-12 (termination notices); Carter confirmed as chair December 18, 2025
what_changed: On the evening of May 2, 2025, hours after the administration released a preliminary FY2026 budget proposing to eliminate the NEA entirely, **the agency emailed withdrawal or termination notices to hundreds of arts organizations nationwide**, cutting off support for costs after May 31, 2025. No agency count has been found; a union of NEA employees said more than half of the agency's open awards were being terminated, according to the Washington Post. The cancelled awards, typically $10,000 to $100,000 each, had funded theaters, orchestras, literary organizations and community arts programs. Recipients of the first notices were given seven calendar days, which included a weekend, to appeal; a second round of notices followed on May 12, 2025. Some grantees whose projects appeared to match the NEA's own newly stated priorities were terminated anyway; California Symphony, for example, lost $10,000 supporting a commission written to celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, one of the NEA's own listed new priorities. On May 5, 2025, the NEA's 10 remaining discipline directors, who headed its grant categories, announced they were leaving through the Deferred Resignation Program or retirement by the end of May, and two members of senior leadership also departed. Mary Anne Carter, who had led the NEA during Trump's first term, was serving as senior adviser overseeing the agency when the terminations were issued (the previous Biden-appointed chair, Maria Rosario Jackson, had resigned on Inauguration Day); Trump nominated Carter as chair on May 6, 2025. Separately, on September 19, 2025, Senior U.S. District Judge William Smith in Rhode Island ruled that the NEA's policy of disfavoring grant applications deemed to 'promote gender ideology' violated the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act, enjoining the NEA from applying that standard to the plaintiffs and setting aside its plan to implement the executive order; the government appealed to the First Circuit in November 2025, and the appeal was pending as of September 2026. A November 11, 2025 American Alliance of Museums survey found NEA among the three federal grantmakers (alongside NEH and IMLS) whose grants museums most commonly reported losing since Trump took office. The Senate confirmed Carter as NEA Chair on December 18, 2025. Congress rejected the proposed elimination, appropriating $207 million for the NEA in FY2026, level with the three prior years. The White House's FY2027 budget, released April 3, 2026, again proposed cutting the NEA to $29 million; as of July 15, 2026, a House bill would cut NEA funding 36 percent, from $207 million to $135 million, and the Senate had not acted. On September 2, 2026, a stopgap law (Public Law 119-103) extended FY2026 funding rates, including the NEA's $207 million, through December 11, 2026.

title: Nebraska becomes first state to opt into Trump's uncapped federal private-school tax credit
institution: U.S. Treasury (federal program) / Nebraska Governor's Office (state opt-in)
status: Ongoing (program launches 2027)
what_changed: Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen signed an executive order on September 29, 2025 opting the state into the federal Scholarship Tax Credit program created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, making Nebraska the first state to elect to participate. Under the program, individual taxpayers can direct up to $1,700 to a qualified scholarship-granting organization (SGO) and receive a full, dollar-for-dollar federal income tax credit in return; SGOs may keep up to 10% for administration and distribute the rest to families for K-12 education expenses, including private-school tuition. Families earning up to 300% of area median income qualify (roughly $228,000-$240,000 depending on county). The program is uncapped -- no limit exists on total participation or total federal tax revenue forgone -- and takes effect January 1, 2027; Pillen's order directs state agencies to help compile a list of qualified SGOs for Treasury ahead of that date. **The move comes less than a year after Nebraska voters repealed two similar state-level private-school-scholarship laws (LB 753 and LB 1402) at the ballot box in November 2024**.

title: National Endowment for Democracy Funding Repeatedly Withheld, Released Only Under Litigation, Once by Court Order
institution: National Endowment for Democracy (funded via State Department appropriation)
status: NED's FY2025 funds were released after it sued, a withheld $95M balance after an Aug. 2025 injunction; its $315M FY2026 funds (H.R. 7148) were obligated only in March 2026, after a new injunction bid. A U.S. motion to dismiss as moot was briefed by July 17, 2026; no ruling found by late Sept. 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-01-22 (funding access first denied) through ongoing litigation as of 2026
what_changed:
Since January 22, 2025, the executive branch withheld the National Endowment for Democracy's (NED) access to congressionally appropriated funding, according to NED's federal lawsuit. NED, a nonprofit created by the 1983 National Endowment for Democracy Act, is statutorily directed to receive annual grants through the State Department; it distributes roughly 83% of its funds directly to democracy, free-press, and anti-corruption groups in more than 90 countries. In a February 7, 2025 primer, the Center for Renewing America, a conservative think tank previously run by OMB Director Russell Vought, called NED a 'fully partisan political weapon' and urged Congress to defund it; NPR relayed the characterization when NED sued. NED sued in March 2025, alleging the withholding of nearly $240 million violated the Administrative Procedure Act, the NED Act, and constitutional separation-of-powers and appropriations provisions. The funding halt created what NED officials, as quoted by NPR, called a 'devastating' cash flow crisis **that forced NED to furlough 75% of its staff**. In a March 6, 2025 court declaration, NED President Damon Wilson said 62% of NED staff had been furloughed as of March 1, with 75% to be furloughed by March 15, that NED had suspended all of its active grants in mid-February 2025, and that it had suspended its May and September 2025 grant cycles. Court filings show that on March 10, 2025, five days after NED sued, it received the roughly $97 million in drawdowns it had requested in late January, and that the State Department obligated a further roughly $72 million by March 21; NED later told the court that the government 'released the Endowment's funding in response to these filings.'

NED's FY2025 appropriation was $315 million, the FY2024 level, provided through three continuing resolutions. According to the court's later opinion, as of early June 2025 only about $220 million of it had been apportioned and obligated, and on June 11 government counsel told NED that the executive branch was contemplating reserving the remaining $95 million for FY2026. **The court's opinion noted that this $95 million withholding left NED unable to fund 226 approved grants, 124 grants recommended for approval by its board, and 53 core-institute projects.** On August 11, 2025, U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich -- a Trump appointee -- granted a preliminary injunction, finding NED likely to succeed on its claim that the administration violated the NED Act by subjecting $95 million to 'review for alignment with Administration priorities,' and calling the government's official justification -- preserving NED's funding stability for the coming year -- 'not plausible' given its earlier obstruction of routine drawdowns and other delays. Following the ruling, the government reported on August 13 that all $94,941,000 remaining in NED's FY2025 account was available for obligation, and the State Department obligated it to NED on August 21, 2025; NED later told the court that the government had 'apportioned, obligated, and disbursed the withheld balance' of its FY2025 funding. NED also told the court that on the night of the injunction the State Department announced 'a programmatic and financial audit of NED and each of its four core institutes.' In the FY2026 budget request Vought sent to the Senate on May 2, 2025, the administration had proposed eliminating NED's funding entirely, alleging among other claims that NED funded 'the Ukraine disinformation organization that doxed U.S. journalists' and attacked Vice President Vance and others. The allegation echoed March 2025 reporting, including a March 10 Grayzone article, that a Ukrainian firm called Molfar -- which that article described as USAID-funded -- listed Vance, Rep. Thomas Massie, and Joe Kent as 'foreign propagandists.' NED's fact sheet of May 2, 2025 called the budget request's claim false, saying Molfar, the organization that 'appears to be indirectly referenced,' 'is not a NED partner' and 'has never received funding from NED.' In a counter-signal to OMB's proposed elimination of NED funding, the House Appropriations Committee had recommended $315 million for NED in FY2026 -- the same level as NED's FY2025 appropriation and well above the administration's zero-funding request. The administration appealed the injunction to the D.C. Circuit on October 9, 2025.

Congress provided $105 million for NED in the November 12, 2025 continuing resolution, but by mid-January 2026 the government had not obligated or disbursed any of NED's FY2026 funds, according to NED's court filings. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148, P.L. 119-75), which passed Congress with bipartisan support and was signed into law by President Trump on February 3, 2026, fully funds NED at $315 million in Division F, the National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act ($210,316,000 in the traditional/core-institute manner and $104,684,000 for democracy programs), rejecting the administration's request to eliminate the funding and requiring that the funds be apportioned to NED within 60 days. On February 19, 2026, the government told the court it would either apportion the funds by the April 4 deadline, propose a full or partial rescission to Congress if the President so directed, or consider other lawful options, adding that 'No decision has yet been made.' Judge Friedrich remarked at a February 25 status conference that the government 'seems' to be following a 'similar playbook' in FY2026, as NED quoted her. On March 9, 2026, NED moved for a second preliminary injunction covering its FY2026 funding. On March 13, Under Secretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah B. Rogers wrote to NED that a State Department audit had raised concerns that some NED programming was undermining 'the foreign policy, safety and prosperity of the United States,' and asked NED to confirm by March 25 that it would comply with NED Act requirements before State would work to obligate the funds; NED called the allegations 'not only pretextual; they are false.' OMB apportioned the full $315 million on March 16, the State Department obligated it by March 25, and NED drew down funds into its bank account on March 30. The government told the court it would not terminate NED's grant, claw back funding, or take other adverse action based on the Rogers letter's allegations, and on April 1, 2026 the court granted NED's motion to withdraw its preliminary-injunction request.

Separately, the legal dispute over the withholdings remains open: the D.C. Circuit has held the government's appeal (docket 25-5361) in abeyance since January 15, 2026, pending district-court proceedings. In the district court, a motion-to-dismiss schedule set in January 2026 (motion due March 16, opposition April 13, reply April 27) did not go forward: on March 16 the government asked, with NED's consent, to stay it while NED's second preliminary-injunction motion was pending. After NED withdrew that motion, the parties disagreed over whether the case was moot, and the parties proposed a new schedule on April 14: the government moved on May 29, 2026 to dismiss the case as moot, NED opposed on July 2, and the government replied on July 17, 2026. No ruling on that motion had been found as of late September 2026.

title: National Endowment for the Humanities Grants Terminated, Staff Cut, Funds Redirected
institution: National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH)
status: Partially Reversed (grant terminations ruled unconstitutional and reinstatement process underway as of mid-2026; staff cuts and Council dissolution unaffected by the ruling)
date_of_action: 2025-04-02 (initial grant terminations) through 2025-10-01 (National Council on the Humanities firings)
what_changed: Beginning April 2025, NEH terminated more than 1,000 previously-awarded, congressionally-funded grants covering fiscal years 2021-2025, informing 56 state and jurisdiction humanities councils their funding was being 'repurposed in a new direction in furtherance of President Trump's agenda.' NEH then placed the majority of its staff on immediate administrative leave, followed by formal termination notices to 65% of its ~180 employees (about 117 people) in April 2025 -- letters described the cuts as necessary to comply with a Trump executive order directing DOGE to eliminate 'waste, bloat, and insularity.' NEH Chair Shelly C. Lowe, the first Native American to head the agency, was forced out about a month before the mass layoffs. In October 2025, during the government shutdown, all but 4 of the 26 members of the National Council on the Humanities (the body that advises NEH on funding priorities) were fired by email from the White House Office of Presidential Personnel. Separately, the 2025 tax-and-spending law directed NEH to contribute $40 million toward constructing Trump's proposed 'National Garden of American Heroes' sculpture garden -- redirecting endowment funds toward a specific administration priority rather than the competitive peer-reviewed grants the agency traditionally funds. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0621): after Trump forced Chair Lowe out, he named NEH general counsel Michael McDonald acting chairman, who began issuing non-competitive 'chairman's awards' bypassing the agency's traditional outside peer-review process -- an unprecedented degree to which chairman's awards came to dominate NEH's funding agenda, per reporting. The most prominent example: NEH awarded the Tikvah Fund, a conservative think tank, $10.4 million in September 2025 for a 'Jewish Civilization Project' to combat antisemitism -- the largest single grant in the agency's 60-year history, representing roughly 10% of NEH's total budget alongside one other large grantee. Tikvah's application had originally been rejected by NEH's own advisory council (before its October 2025 dissolution, documented above) over concerns the proposal was vague and too advocacy-focused, and Tikvah was not among the 97 projects in NEH's original August 1, 2025 funding announcement -- the grant was added separately on September 15, 2025, after that rejection. Beyond Tikvah, NEH's chairman's-award pattern directed more than $75 million toward projects reflecting the administration's ideological priorities, including $10 million each to two public universities' new 'civics' schools and to an education network headquartered at a conservative think tank, with funding overwhelmingly favoring Western-civilization, 'great books,' and other conservative-aligned humanities projects. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog cluster c0703): a November 11, 2025 American Alliance of Museums survey found NEH was among the three federal grantmakers (alongside NEA and IMLS) most commonly cited by museums reporting lost federal funding since Trump took office -- see the museum-sector-wide survey findings in aam-survey-museum-funding-cuts-2025.json. Update: On May 7, 2026, U.S. District Judge Colleen McMahon (S.D.N.Y.) ruled in American Council of Learned Societies v. NEH -- brought by ACLS, the American Historical Association, and the Modern Language Association -- that the mass termination of more than 1,400 grants was 'unlawful, unconstitutional, ultra vires, and without legal effect,' violating the First Amendment and the Fifth Amendment's equal-protection component, and undertaken without statutory authority. NEH has since begun a reinstatement process: starting June 30, 2026, the agency began sending affected recipients a 'Reinstatement Assurances Form' asking whether they still want the award, disclosing any personnel changes since termination, confirming continued capacity to complete the project, and specifying whether a restart period or reimbursement is needed. This is not automatic restoration -- it functions closer to a new award action, requiring a fresh institutional review of personnel, budget, subrecipient status, and timeline for each grant. The ruling does not affect the separate staff terminations or the National Council on the Humanities dissolution described above.

primary_proponent.name: White House Office of Presidential Personnel / DOGE
primary_proponent.role: Executed the staff and council terminations
primary_proponent.note: Mary Sprowls of the White House Office of Presidential Personnel personally signed the termination emails to National Council on the Humanities members. The underlying policy direction traces to a Trump executive order tasking DOGE with eliminating 'waste, bloat, and insularity' in federal agencies. No single named individual was identified as personally directing the NEH-specific cuts beyond this White House personnel office role -- flag as a diffuse, White-House-directed action rather than one attributable official.

estimated_impact.summary: NEH is the largest humanities funder in the United States; nearly half its budget flows directly to humanities councils in every state and jurisdiction, supporting museums, libraries, oral history projects, and preservation work nationwide. **Terminated projects cited by name in reporting include an oral history archive of Tulsa Race Massacre survivors (Oklahoma), an initiative digitizing North Carolina Central University's historical records, an oral history project at Kennesaw State University, and a library renovation at the University of Missouri**.

title: HHS Disbanded the Advisory Committee That Recommends Which Rare Genetic Diseases Are Screened for at Birth
institution: Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children (ACHDNC), Health Resources and Services Administration, Department of Health and Human Services
status: Ongoing -- disbanded, no reinstatement identified in sourcing reviewed as of last verification, despite advocacy-organization and congressional requests
what_changed: HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children on April 3, 2025, citing compliance with a Trump executive order to shrink the federal government. The volunteer committee -- composed of medical geneticists, pediatricians, and public health experts -- recommends which rare genetic and metabolic conditions states should add to their newborn-screening panels, the heel-prick blood tests given to virtually every baby born in the U.S. The committee had been scheduled to meet in May 2025 to vote on adding two serious, treatable-if-caught-early conditions to the national Recommended Uniform Screening Panel: metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). The National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD) estimates **roughly 450 babies are born with MLD or DMD combined each year in the U.S.; early detection is clinically significant for both conditions because available treatments are far more effective when started before symptoms appear**. NORD and its network of 40 affiliated Rare Disease Centers of Excellence sent HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. a letter demanding the committee's immediate reinstatement. On August 1, 2025, Rep. Kelly Morrison led a congressional letter to Kennedy pressing for an explanation of the decision and its rare-disease impact. No sourcing reviewed as of this entry's addition indicates the committee has been reinstated or that a replacement process for evaluating new conditions has been established.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: HHS, under Kennedy, terminated the committee April 3, 2025, citing the administration's government-downsizing executive order; the decision was not publicly announced in advance and was first reported by the Boston Globe and NBC News rather than via an HHS press release.

estimated_impact.summary: Eliminating the only federal body that formally recommends new conditions for the national newborn-screening panel stalled the pending addition of two rare genetic diseases affecting an estimated 450 U.S. babies annually, for which early detection materially improves treatment outcomes -- with no replacement review mechanism identified and no reinstatement as of last verification despite advocacy and congressional pressure.

estimated_impact.caveat: No dollar-cost or mortality-rate figure specific to this committee's elimination was found in sourcing reviewed; the ~450-births-per-year figure describes the population potentially affected by delayed screening-panel additions, not a confirmed harm count, since states can still individually adopt MLD/DMD screening on their own regardless of the federal panel's recommendation status.

Morrison's congressional oversight letter independently corroborate the reinstatement-request timeline. No HHS on-record rebuttal or alternative screening-review mechanism was found in sourcing reviewed.

title: NHTSA Cut 4% of Its Staff -- Disproportionately From Its Self-Driving Safety Office -- While Investigating Tesla, Whose CEO Led the Cuts
institution: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)
status: Implemented -- the February 2025 workforce cuts took effect; NHTSA stated it would continue enforcement against all manufacturers despite the reduction
what_changed: As part of DOGE's government-wide purge of probationary federal employees, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration laid off roughly 4% of its staff -- about 32 of its roughly 800 employees -- in late February 2025. Of the employees let go, several came from NHTSA's Office of Vehicle Automation Safety, the unit responsible for regulating self-driving-vehicle software, which was disproportionately affected because it was a newer office (formed in 2023) staffed heavily with probationary hires. The cuts landed while NHTSA had three open investigations into Tesla: **an October 2024 probe into roughly 2.4 million vehicles equipped with Full Self-Driving software after four reported collisions, including one fatal 2023 crash**, and a January 2025 probe into roughly 2.6 million vehicles over a remote-summon feature linked to reported crashes. Tesla CEO Elon Musk was simultaneously serving as the Trump administration's DOGE lead directing the cross-government workforce cuts, including at the agency actively investigating his own company's vehicles. NHTSA said it would continue to enforce the law against all vehicle manufacturers despite the reductions.

title: A Deliberate Biocontainment-Suit Sabotage Shut Down One of the Nation's Few BSL-4 Ebola Research Labs -- Which Remains Closed and Deprioritized Nearly a Year Later
institution: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) / National Institutes of Health (NIH), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Closed since a complete operational halt announced May 7, 2025; as of March 2026, Maryland's congressional delegation continues pressing the administration for answers, and reporting indicates NIAID has restructured the facility under its Division of Intramural Research and is deprioritizing biodefense/pandemic-preparedness research generally, beyond the original safety incident.
date_of_action: 2025-04-29 (initial safety stand-down) through 2026-03 (ongoing congressional pressure over the facility's status and NIAID's broader deprioritization of biodefense research)
what_changed: On April 29, 2025, HHS ordered a 'safety stand-down' halting all experimental work at NIAID's Integrated Research Facility (IRF) at Fort Detrick, Maryland -- one of a small number of biosafety-level-4 labs in the country equipped to study Ebola, Lassa fever, and other lethal high-consequence pathogens. The trigger was a violent altercation between two contract staff: **one allegedly deliberately cut a hole in a co-worker's biocontainment suit during a personal dispute, compromising the suit's protective seal and creating a real risk of pathogen exposure**. On May 7, 2025, newly appointed NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya -- who said he had decided to shut the facility down shortly after taking office in March 2025 -- announced a complete halt to all operations, stating the lab 'will not reopen until I am satisfied it is safe.' Testifying before the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee (reported May 14, 2025), HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. confirmed the FBI had been brought in to investigate, telling Sen. Rand Paul the incident 'appears like it was a deliberate criminal act that was kind of equivalent to attempted murder.' The facility's director was placed on administrative leave. Maryland's full congressional delegation (Sens. Van Hollen and Alsobrooks, Reps. McClain Delaney and Elfreth, among others) sent HHS and NIH multiple letters beginning in June 2025 demanding a detailed accounting of the facility's status, the underlying safety failures, and the national-security implications of the prolonged closure of one of the country's few facilities capable of this research. By March 2026, the delegation was still pressing for answers, and reporting indicated NIAID had restructured the IRF under its Division of Intramural Research and was more broadly deprioritizing biodefense and pandemic-preparedness research -- developments the lawmakers characterized as extending well beyond what the original safety incident alone would require.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.; Dr. Jay Bhattacharya
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services; Director, National Institutes of Health
primary_proponent.note: Bhattacharya made the operational decision to fully halt the facility and has stated it will not reopen until he is personally satisfied it is safe; Kennedy publicly confirmed the FBI investigation and characterized the underlying incident's severity in Senate testimony. This entry's subject is the closure and its prolonged aftermath, not an allegation that either official caused the underlying safety incident -- the alleged sabotage was carried out by contract staff, not administration officials.

estimated_impact.summary: The shutdown removed the United States' operational capacity at one of a small number of BSL-4 facilities equipped to study Ebola, Lassa fever, and other high-consequence pathogens, for nearly a year and counting as of this writing, at a time global health officials were already warning about degraded U.S. disease-surveillance and outbreak-response capacity (see this database's separate entries on USAID's dismantlement and CDC/bird-flu surveillance cuts). The underlying trigger -- an alleged intentional biocontainment-suit sabotage risking real pathogen exposure -- is itself a serious biosafety failure independent of any administration policy; the accountability concern this entry documents is the prolonged, still-unresolved closure and subsequent institutional deprioritization of biodefense research that followed it, which Maryland's congressional delegation says has gone beyond what addressing the safety incident itself would require, with limited public transparency into the facility's remediation timeline or reopening criteria.

estimated_impact.caveat: This entry does not allege the underlying safety incident itself was a politically motivated action by the administration -- available reporting attributes it to a personal dispute between two contract staff, now under FBI investigation as a possible criminal act. The accountability question this entry documents is narrower: the prolonged closure's duration, the limited public transparency into remediation and reopening criteria despite repeated congressional inquiries, and reporting that the facility's mission has been restructured and deprioritized in ways that go beyond addressing the specific safety failure.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the underlying incident, the stand-down and full-halt dates, and RFK Jr.'s and Bhattacharya's public statements -- corroborated across DeepNewz, Just The News (citing the Senate HELP hearing directly), Global Biodefense, and multiple Maryland congressional-delegation press releases and letters. MODERATE confidence on the claim that NIAID is now broadly 'deprioritizing' biodefense/pandemic-preparedness research beyond the specific facility closure, since this characterization currently rests primarily on the congressional delegation's own letters (an interested party pressing the administration, not an independent finding) rather than an HHS/NIH admission or an outside audit; presented here as the delegation's stated concern, not an adjudicated fact. No sourcing reviewed identifies a confirmed reopening date or a public accounting of remediation steps taken.

title: NIH's Research Hospital Saw Patient Numbers Fall to a Fraction of Pre-Pandemic Levels Amid Staff Losses and an Immigration Crackdown
institution: NIH Clinical Center
status: Reported ongoing as of August 2025; no reversal identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-01 (visitor policy change and workforce departures begin) through 2025-07 (most recent reported figures)
what_changed: CBS News reported August 19, 2025 that **patient numbers at the NIH Clinical Center -- the federal government's dedicated research hospital, which treats cancer, rare-disease, bone marrow transplant, and infectious-disease patients, often as their last remaining treatment option -- fell sharply during the first months of the second Trump administration**. The hospital's average daily census ran 60 to 80 patients from February through April 2025, versus roughly 80 in October 2024 and more than 110 daily before the pandemic; April 2025 alone showed a 5.7% year-over-year decline. Cancer clinical-trial enrollment was down approximately 20% by July 2025 compared to the prior year, outpatient visits were down 8.5% year-over-year through April 2025, and new patients overall fell 6.7% to roughly 3,370 people. HHS fired more than 1,200 NIH employees in 2025, with additional departures through early retirement and voluntary exits, including bioethics department leader Christine Grady and former Clinical Center CEO James Gilman, who led the hospital from 2017 until leaving in January 2025 and was succeeded by acting CEO Pius Aiyelawo. Acting CEO Aiyelawo attributed part of the enrollment decline directly to departing investigators no longer recruiting patients into trials, compounding the effect of cancelled grants and delayed research supplies documented elsewhere in this database's NIH-related entries. Separately, a new visitor policy launched in late January 2025 requiring non-citizens to register online, implemented alongside the administration's broader immigration-enforcement operations, coincided with international patients avoiding the hospital; one departing clinician told CBS News 'international patients are terrified to come,' citing fear over 'what will happen to them.'

title: NIH Let Contract-Staff Work Orders Lapse and Was Ordered to Cut $2.6 Billion (35%) in Contracts -- Hitting Nearly Half Its Workforce
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Ongoing as of last verification, with no reported reversal identified; a May 2025 Science/AAAS report puts the actual scale of contract-staff job loss at roughly 2,200 contractors NIH-wide since January 2025, resolving the entry's prior LOWER-confidence anecdotal estimate
date_of_action: 2025-01 (communication freeze begins, contract renewals stall) through 2025-04 (formal 35% contract-cut order and initial implementation)
what_changed: Starting when the Trump administration took office in January 2025, NIH allowed a growing number of contract-staff work orders to lapse without renewal, effectively ending those positions -- NOTUS reported this on March 20, 2025, noting contract staff make up nearly half of NIH's total workforce. The lapses stemmed in part from a since-lifted Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) communications freeze imposed at the start of the administration: contract renewals require NIH to communicate with the outside contracting agencies that formally employ and insure NIH's contract staff, and NOTUS found that communication remained effectively stalled even after the freeze was formally lifted in February. A contract employee at NIH's Vaccine Research Center told NOTUS they personally knew of roughly 10 colleagues whose contracts had recently expired and gone unrenewed -- an early, anecdotal data point NOTUS could not yet size against the full workforce. The lapses were followed by a formal directive: on April 3, 2025, Science reported the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) had ordered NIH to eliminate $2.6 billion in contracts, requiring each of NIH's 27 institutes and centers to cut contract spending by roughly 35% by April 8, 2025 -- part of a broader HHS-wide DOGE directive (reported separately by NOTUS) to cut $13.6 billion in annual contract spending across the department. NIH contracts fund staff scientists, clinical-trial support at universities, biospecimen repositories, and long-term health studies; an NIH official told Science a 35% cut would be 'devastating' given how much of the fiscal year's contract funding had already been committed. By the time of that reporting, a DOGE-linked contract-cut tracking site showed NIH had already cut more than 400 contracts totaling about $780 million, including funding for biospecimen repositories and long-term health-study support. A May 11, 2025 Science/AAAS follow-up, reporting on the Vaccine Research Center specifically, put a number on the scale NOTUS's March 2025 reporting could only estimate anecdotally: data shared with staff at one NIH institute showed **the contractor purge had reached roughly 2,200 contract workers agency-wide since January 2025 -- rivaling the ~2,500 federal staff lost to two rounds of layoffs since mid-February**. At the Vaccine Research Center itself, one immunology lab had lost 40% of its workers and stopped developing antibody tests for some future clinical trials.

title: NIH Strips DEI Requirements From Grant Applications, Then Terminates 1,700+ Active Grants on Disfavored Topics
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Ongoing. The Supreme Court let NIH's grant terminations proceed Aug. 21, 2025, though the directives stay vacated; NIH's director says court-restored grants won't be renewed. Terminations continued into Aug. 2026, and a Sept. 2026 class action alleges NIH screens grants for 235 disfavored terms.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (initial grant terminations begin) through 2026-08 (latest reported terminations)
what_changed:
Starting in late February 2025, NIH began terminating active research grants tied to topics the administration classified as DEI, gender identity, LGBTQ+ health, or vaccine hesitancy, and terminated more than 1,700 grants within a few months, according to the APHA plaintiffs' Supreme Court filing and CBS News and NBC News reporting. In the first days after termination letters began arriving on February 28, 2025, an NIH official told the Boston Globe (in a report STAT republished) of 24 such notices from four NIH institutes and centers, and said there were likely to be hundreds more. Among those terminated in May 2025 was a five-year grant to UC San Diego imaging scientist Uri Manor, who was born with congenital severe-to-profound hearing loss and was studying the cellular mechanisms of hearing loss to develop new treatments; Manor had qualified for the funding through a National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders program supporting researchers with disabilities, and had already spent $1.5 million of the award over two years before **its cancellation forced him to halt long-running experiments and lay off lab staff**.

On March 25, 2025, NIH separately notified staff it was eliminating DEI-related requirements from grant and conference-funding applications going forward: applicants would no longer need to submit 'Plans for Enhancing Diverse Perspectives,' 'Recruitment Plans to Enhance Diversity,' or 'Trainee Diversity Reports,' diversity plans would no longer be evaluated in funding decisions, and training-data tables used in review were revised to drop calculations of the percentage of underrepresented minorities. On April 21, 2025, NIH went further, publishing a notice amending the civil-rights provisions of the NIH Grants Policy Statement to require institutions receiving new, renewal, supplement, or continuation awards to certify they do not operate DEI programs 'in violation of Federal anti-discrimination laws' and are not boycotting Israel, on pain of termination and clawback of funds -- a condition industry commentary (FierceBiotech) characterized as NIH asserting authority to override how recipients interpret their own obligations under the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

In June 2025, U.S. District Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled the terminations violated the Administrative Procedure Act, finding NIH had unlawfully targeted research on 'disfavored' topics and populations -- including training grants meant to diversify the biomedical research pipeline -- without adequately defining what 'DEI' meant or weighing the grants' value, and calling the terminations 'racial discrimination, and discrimination against America's LGBTQ community' on the record; he ordered the funding reinstated. Science put the number of grants covered by that order at about 800 (as reported by Higher Ed Dive); the Minnesota Daily put it at roughly 900.

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to stay that order, telling the Court in July 2025 that it had been compelled to restore $783 million of grant money for the plaintiffs to draw down -- a figure the APHA plaintiffs' opposition said 'appears to be invented out of whole cloth' and is 'nowhere in the proceedings below' -- and on August 21, 2025, the Court allowed the terminations to proceed while the case continued, even as Judge Young's ruling vacating NIH's underlying guidance documents themselves remained in effect below. The Supreme Court's August 2025 ruling in this case is identified in legal commentary (Ogletree, Crowell & Moring, The Arc) as NIH v. APHA; the ruling itself created a jurisdictional split (Justice Jackson dissenting) under which challenges to NIH's underlying guidance continue in district court while claims seeking restoration of terminated grant funding must be filed separately in the Court of Federal Claims, a more burdensome path for affected researchers.

NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya (confirmed by the Senate March 25, 2025 -- the same day as the initial application-requirement change, though sworn in April 1 and not in office for the February terminations) said on December 31, 2025 that DEI-related grants restored to plaintiffs under the court order would not be renewed once their current funding cycles ended. Days earlier, on December 29, 2025, NIH resolved what lawyers described as the 'second phase' of the same Boston litigation, in stipulations with the APHA plaintiffs and with the Democratic state attorneys general: it agreed to review and decide, on set deadlines and without applying its vacated directives, grant applications it had frozen, denied or withdrawn -- which the Boston Globe described as hundreds of stalled applications -- without committing to fund any of them. STAT reported the agreement on December 29, 2025, and a States Newsroom report republished by Government Executive covered it on January 5, 2026; the agreement does not alter the earlier rulings on grants that had already been terminated. The First Circuit heard oral argument on the broader guidance challenge (the appeal of Judge Young's ruling vacating NIH's underlying guidance documents) in January 2026 but had not ruled at last check (a separate First Circuit ruling that same month, upholding the block on NIH's indirect-cost-rate cap, is a related but distinct case and should not be conflated with this still-pending DEI-guidance appeal).

The termination campaign continued into August 2026 -- on August 4, 2026, Bhattacharya notified the University of Pittsburgh that a five-year, $9.6 million grant to social epidemiologist Tamara Dubowitz studying cognitive aging and Alzheimer's risk among African Americans in poor Pittsburgh neighborhoods, with $7 million already spent, would be terminated in full, part of a stated shift toward 'measurable health outcomes' and away from health-disparities framing in NIH's funding priorities.

The summer 2026 wave was broader than the Pittsburgh neighborhood study, which Dubowitz co-led with epidemiologist Andrea Rosso -- Bhattacharya's letters also terminated a second, separate University of Pittsburgh grant to associate professor of psychiatry Ann Cohen, studying social and structural risk factors for Alzheimer's disease, and a National Institute of Mental Health grant to Emory University clinical neuropsychologist Negar Fani, a five-year study (awarded December 2024) examining how racial discrimination affects white-matter brain microstructure in 220 Black volunteers via wearable devices and MRI. Fani's team had been told as recently as June 5, 2026 that its second year of funding was approved, then was notified by the end of July 2026 that the grant was cancelled. NIH's termination notice for the Emory grant stated the research's discrimination measure was 'subjective and problematic' and that studying only Black participants 'seriously limits possible comparisons and controls and does not seem scientifically justified' -- an explicit NIH rationale for why race-specific health-disparities research itself fails its new 'measurable health outcomes' standard, not just a funding-priority reshuffling. Combined, the Emory and Pittsburgh cuts announced in this wave total $15 million, according to The Guardian, as relayed by The Week and TheGrio.

On September 16, 2026, 17 researchers (13 named and four anonymous) filed a proposed class action, Salles v. National Institutes of Health, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California against NIH, Bhattacharya, the Department of Health and Human Services, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the U.S. DOGE Service. The plaintiffs include Rosso and Cohen and Stanford surgeon Arghavan Salles, whose grant on sexual harassment in biomedical research was terminated as 'DEI-related' and, STAT reported, was not reinstated. The complaint alleges that after Judge Young vacated NIH's 2025 directives, NIH replaced them with new ones that continued the same viewpoint-based purge: an August 2025 Bhattacharya directive (revised July 2, 2026), and December 12, 2025 staff guidance requiring NIH's institutes to run every existing and new award through a 'computational text analysis tool' and to renegotiate or terminate flagged grants. According to the complaint, which cites Nature's June 2026 reporting on an internal NIH document, the tool's list held at least 235 disfavored terms by February 2026, among them 'gender,' 'equity,' 'racist,' 'Latinx,' 'queer' and 'climate change.' The complaint alleges the tool was built from words common in the grants NIH terminated in 2025. STAT reported that more than 700 grantees changed their grant titles in 2025 to drop phrases like 'equity,' 'disparity' and 'racism.' The plaintiffs allege that researchers who refuse to scrub flagged words lose their grants or see their applications stalled, and that Rosso's study was terminated in its final year even after she removed the disfavored terms. **The complaint says her team may now be unable to determine whether participants followed for four years have dementia and should follow up with their doctors.** The suit claims First Amendment viewpoint discrimination and violations of the statutes and regulations governing NIH grants. It asks the court to vacate the policies, restore terminated grants and re-review stalled applications. Bhattacharya has publicly denied using banned-word lists, but STAT reported that NIH's head of extramural research acknowledged, in a stipulation filed in University of California researchers' separate case, that NIH 'used search terms, keywords, or phrases to identify and terminate grants.' NIH and HHS said they do not comment on pending litigation.

NIH's own director has stated publicly that grants reinstated by Judge Young's order will not be renewed going forward, meaning the practical effect of the litigation win for affected researchers is temporary continuation, not a reversal of NIH's underlying policy direction.

title: NIH Halted New Foreign Subawards, Then Replaced Them With a New 'Linked Award' Structure -- Threatening Billions in International Research During the Transition
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Department of Health and Human Services
status: New 'linked award' structure required for all new international collaborations as of September 25, 2025 (replacing the halted foreign-subaward mechanism); the underlying international research relationships are not banned, but the roughly five-month transition gap (May 1-September 25, 2025) disrupted ongoing renewals and new international collaborations
date_of_action: 2025-05-01 (foreign-subaward halt takes effect, per NIH notice NOT-OD-25-104) through 2025-09-25 (NIH stops accepting the old subaward structure entirely, forcing all new international work through the replacement mechanism)
what_changed: Effective May 1, 2025, NIH's grants policy office issued notice NOT-OD-25-104 barring any new, renewal, or non-competing continuation award -- to either a domestic or foreign entity -- that includes a subaward to a foreign entity, citing 'a need to maintain national security' alongside tracking and oversight concerns about how U.S. research funds flow to foreign institutions once passed through a domestic prime awardee. STAT News and Science|Business reported the halt threatened roughly $500 million a year in the foreign subawards NIH typically distributes, and 'billions of dollars' cumulatively across ongoing global-health projects, infectious-disease and cancer clinical trials, and university partnerships across Europe and elsewhere. The New York Times reported May 15, 2025 that researchers warned specific projects could be derailed, including breast-cancer research that depends on unique Danish patient-data and tissue-sample registries with no equivalent domestic source. Rather than a permanent ban on international collaboration, NIH announced in September 2025 a replacement award structure -- effective September 25, 2025, ahead of Fiscal Year 2026 -- eliminating the subaward mechanism itself: instead of a domestic principal investigator's subaward flowing on to a foreign partner, NIH now issues separate but coordinated 'linked' awards directly to each domestic and foreign principal investigator under one multi-project funding opportunity, with foreign researchers becoming prime awardees in their own right rather than subcontractors. The policy is prospective, not retroactive -- already-active awards continue unaffected unless and until they come up for renewal or a non-competing continuation -- but **any project needing to renew, add a new foreign component, or start new international collaborative work during the roughly five-month gap between the May halt and the September relaunch faced a genuine funding and administrative disruption**, with institutions' own research offices (UC Santa Cruz, Boston University, University of Utah, Case Western Reserve, Weill Cornell, among others) issuing guidance warning affected researchers of the gap.

estimated_impact.summary: The halt put roughly $500 million a year in ongoing foreign-subaward research funding at risk during the transition, with specific named research areas -- including cancer studies dependent on irreplaceable foreign data registries -- warning of concrete disruption; the eventual replacement structure preserves international collaboration in a different administrative form rather than eliminating it, but the multi-month gap itself produced real, if not fully quantified, harm to time-sensitive renewals and new collaborations.

title: NIH Suspended a Tuberculosis Researcher's Grant Under a 'Dangerous Gain-of-Function' Label She Says Misdescribes Standard Techniques That Make the Bacterium Weaker, Not More Dangerous
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Suspension in effect as of the researcher's account published October 6, 2025; no reversal identified as of this entry's writing.
date_of_action: 2025-05 (executive order on gain-of-function research) through 2025-07-11 (NIH suspension letter to Sarah Stanley)
what_changed: Following a May 2025 executive order targeting 'dangerous gain-of-function research,' NIH conducted an internal review of federally funded pathogen studies and suspended a number of them, including tuberculosis research. On July 11, 2025, Sarah Stanley, an associate professor at UC Berkeley studying Mycobacterium tuberculosis, received an NIH letter ordering her to halt her research, citing the executive order's 'dangerous gain-of-function' definition. Stanley disputed the characterization: her lab's techniques include creating mutations that disable specific bacterial genes -- which she said makes the bacterium 'less virulent, the opposite goal of gain-of-function research' -- and using kanamycin-resistance markers (kanamycin is not used in human medicine) purely as a molecular tool to identify modified strains, with the resulting bacteria 'fully treatable by all clinically used antibiotics' and unable to 'spread drug resistance.' Stanley noted that **tuberculosis 'kills more people than any other infectious disease' globally and pointed to a 2024-25 Kansas City-area outbreak that exceeded 100 cases as evidence the disease remains an active domestic threat that her research was intended to address**. Other outlets (Science/AAAS, Treatment Action Group) reported the suspension affected more than 40 studies government-wide and that NIH Principal Deputy Director Matthew Memoli personally directed the review's implementation, but these broader figures and Memoli's specific role could not be independently confirmed via direct fetch for this entry and are not asserted here as verified fact.

title: NIH Grant Freeze Found to Violate the Impoundment Control Act (GAO)
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH), Department of Health and Human Services
status: GAO Legal Finding Issued Aug 5, 2025 (Impoundment Control Act violation); NIH again spent its full ~$34B external grants budget in FY2026 after a slow start, but funded ~58,000 projects (prelim.) vs. 61,000 in FY2025 (STAT); a Feb 3, 2026 law capped FY2026 multiyear funding at the FY2025 level
date_of_action: 2025-08-05 (GAO report issued); underlying actions Feb 2025 - fall 2025
what_changed:
Following Trump executive orders in early 2025 targeting DEI and 'gender ideology' funding, **NIH terminated more than 1,800 previously-awarded research grants and, separately, obligated roughly $8 billion less in new/continuing grant funding between February and June 2025 than in the same period the prior year -- a drop of more than a third**. NIH also paused grant review meetings entirely from late January to early March 2025, delaying funds to hospitals and universities -- NPR reported on February 22, 2025 that this freeze alone had stalled roughly 16,000 pending grant applications worth about $1.5 billion, as the administration blocked the Federal Register notices required to schedule the review meetings.

Separately, on February 24, 2025, NPR reported the administration's plan to cap NIH's reimbursement rate for research institutions' indirect costs (overhead such as facilities and administrative support) at 15%, down from a historical rate as high as 56% at some institutions -- a change research universities warned would force layoffs and halt projects even where direct grant funding remained intact, since indirect-cost reimbursement funds much of the physical and administrative infrastructure research depends on.

An earlier, larger staffing figure was reported on April 28, 2025: outlets described NIH as having 1,300 staff fired by that point, with $2 billion in research grants cancelled and ongoing clinical trials for Alzheimer's, cancer, and stroke treatments halted -- a snapshot that predates and is not necessarily consistent with (may reflect a different scope or a since-revised count from) the more specifically sourced 250-employee May 6 figure below. NIH's funding contraction had a direct staffing dimension too: CBS News reported NIH issued surprise layoff notices to nearly 250 employees on May 6, 2025, including about 50 from the National Cancer Institute specifically. On June 13, 2025, more than 60 NIH employees signed a public letter, the Bethesda Declaration, condemning the administration's health policies as unethical, politically driven, and dangerous -- accusing leadership of censoring science, cutting billions from NIH's budget, halting over 1,300 grants, and endangering patients in ongoing clinical trials, an internal-dissent episode directly reflecting the funding and grant-termination pattern described above.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan congressional watchdog, concluded on August 5, 2025 that the original 2025 funding actions violated the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which requires the executive branch to spend congressionally appropriated funds unless it follows a specific legal process to formally request a rescission -- a process NIH/HHS did not use. GAO cited the drop in obligations, drawn from USAspending.gov data, as evidence that NIH withheld budget authority in violation of the law; the 1,800+ terminations count was HHS's, as relayed by GAO. GAO also noted that OMB had removed agency apportionment data from its public websites, "contrary to OMB's duty to make such information publicly available." In a July 29, 2025 letter, HHS told GAO that NIH had "scheduled or held 837 peer review meetings" from March 24 through June 30, 186 more than a year earlier, and had "caught up from the pause"; GAO replied that "the reinstatement of grant review meetings alone does not ensure that funds are not being withheld" and that HHS gave no information on NIH's FY2025 obligations. GAO said it had seen public statements that OMB paused NIH grants, research contracts and training around July 29, 2025 and later reversed the pause, but neither HHS nor OMB provided the documents GAO requested. GAO also cited a July 2, 2025 ruling by the federal district court in Massachusetts, in American Public Health Association v. NIH, that NIH's grant cancellations violated the Administrative Procedure Act. House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro said, as reported by Government Executive, that Congress had funded NIH research "to help find cures and treatments for cancer, Alzheimer's disease, ALS, diabetes, mental health issues, and maternal mortality." Senate Appropriations Vice Chair Patty Murray's August 5 release said GAO had found Trump illegally impounded enacted funding "for 5th time in recent weeks"; GAO's earlier 2025 violation findings covered electric vehicle charging funds (B-337137, May 22), the Institute of Museum and Library Services (B-337375, June 16), Head Start (B-337202, July 23) and the Energy Department's Renew America's Schools K-12 energy-efficiency program (B-337208, July 31, in part), before the NIH decision (B-337203). On August 21, 2025, the Supreme Court, 5-4, stayed the Massachusetts judgments (in the APHA case and Massachusetts v. Kennedy) insofar as they vacated NIH's grant terminations, saying the district court lacked jurisdiction over claims based on the grants (Justice Amy Coney Barrett, concurring: they belong in the Court of Federal Claims), and left in place the ruling against NIH's guidance documents.

A peer-reviewed study published in JAMA Internal Medicine and reported by AP News in November 2025 quantified the trial-level disruption this funding contraction caused -- of 11,008 NIH-funded clinical trials the researchers tracked, 383 (about 1 in 30) lost funding between late February and mid-August 2025, affecting more than 74,000 enrolled participants studying cancer, heart disease, brain disease, and infectious diseases including flu, pneumonia, and COVID-19. The disruption took several forms: some trials never began after participants had already enrolled, some participants lost access to medication or were left with an unmonitored device implant, and some completed trials never had their results published.

A concrete instance of this pattern: in fall 2025, the National Cancer Institute told the Pediatric Brain Tumor Consortium -- a network of 16 children's hospitals -- that its roughly $4 million in annual NCI funding would end when the current award expires in March 2026; the consortium responded by halting enrollment in its six active trials, including a CAR T-cell therapy trial for ependymoma and a minimally invasive laser-ablation trial, before that expiration date. NCI's stated plan is to shift pediatric early-phase trials to a broader existing network (the Pediatric Early Phase Clinical Trials Network under the Children's Oncology Group), but the consortium's own chair said the transition would not be seamless and some patients would likely lose access to trials in the interim.

The pattern extended into the funding mechanism itself: a New York Times analysis published December 2, 2025 reported that OMB "in the summer instructed the N.I.H. to spend half of its remaining funds to fully fund research grants," and that NIH, which "managed to spend most of its budget by the end of the fiscal year," made "an unusual number of large lump-sum payments for many years of research" instead of paying one year at a time, so the money went to fewer projects. By the Times' count, NIH awarded 12,588 competitive grants (new grants and competitive renewals) in fiscal 2025, down 22% from its 2015-24 average of 16,099 ("more than 3,500 fewer"); the National Science Foundation, which also paid for nearly all new awards upfront, awarded 25 percent fewer new grants. The Times also cited the website Grant Witness's estimate that the administration canceled or froze 5,415 NIH grants in 2025, roughly half of which had been reinstated; HHS communications director Andrew Nixon said NIH "is no longer directing resources toward science shaped by political or social pressures."

An NPR analysis published September 24, 2026 found that NIH's $47.5 billion budget masked shifts in when and what it funds: NIH ran roughly 44 days behind its 2021-24 average obligation pace in fiscal 2025 and 42 days behind through early July 2026, and grant renewals came 90 or more days late in 3.9% of cases in fiscal 2025 and 2.7% in fiscal 2026, compared with 0.7% in fiscal 2021-24. NPR found more than $1 billion less went to racial- and ethnic-minority health research in 2025 than in 2024 (a 29% drop), while machine learning and AI gained $468 million. Jennifer Troyer, a former director of extramural operations at NIH's National Human Genome Research Institute who resigned at the end of 2025, told NPR that awards she had signed came back stopped at a review step called "Status 19," flagged by HHS, OMB or the White House "as not acceptable." HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard wrote that NIH's August 2025 Unified Funding Strategy "ensures that the NIH embraces transparency, scientific rigor, and unbiased, evidence-driven research," with institute and center directors making final funding decisions. STAT reported on October 2, 2026 that NIH, as in fiscal 2025, spent its entire external grants budget of roughly $34 billion in fiscal 2026 after a slow start, but funded around 58,000 projects, down from 61,000 in fiscal 2025 and well below the roughly 63,700 awarded annually before the second Trump administration; STAT said the drop potentially resulted from the White House's push to fully fund more multiyear grants in advance, and that the count may rise somewhat because of reporting lags.

Section 240 of the Labor-HHS division of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-75, signed February 3, 2026) caps the NIH funds that may be obligated in FY2026 for more than one year of a multiyear award at the amount NIH obligated that way in FY2025. The Association of American Medical Colleges reported on January 23, 2026 that the package, as passed by the House, provided $47.2 billion for NIH's base budget. The Impoundment Control Act (2 U.S.C. 687) lets the Comptroller General sue in federal district court in Washington, D.C., to require withheld budget authority to be made available; as of September 2026, GAO had not filed such a suit over the NIH finding.

title: NIH Terminates 33+ Grants Studying Vaccine Hesitancy Amid a Growing Measles Outbreak
institution: National Institutes of Health (NIH)
status: Ongoing. A court ruled NIH's directives unlawful in June 2025 and ordered ~900 plaintiff grants reinstated; an August 2025 Supreme Court partial stay left the directives vacated but paused reinstatement. No First Circuit ruling as of late September 2026; these 33+ grants' status is unconfirmed.
what_changed:
On March 10, 2025, Science reported that NIH was abruptly terminating at least 33 research grants funding studies of why people are hesitant to receive vaccines and what strategies improve vaccine uptake, with an additional nine grants that "may be modified or cut back"; the Washington Post, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported that an internal NIH email flagged more than 40 grants. The template termination letter Science saw stated: "It is the policy of NIH not to prioritize research activities that focuses on gaining scientific knowledge on why individuals are hesitant to be vaccinated and/or explore ways to improve vaccine interest and commitment." **Affected researchers, including one whose work had identified a genuine vaccine safety signal, were notified their studies were being cut off mid-stream**, an unusual mechanism for ending federally funded research already underway. The terminations came as HHS was newly led by vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and coincided with a Texas-originated measles outbreak; nationally, the Washington Post's March 10 report noted "more than 200 cases of measles in 12 states and two deaths from the disease," and by March 13 the CDC counted 301 confirmed U.S. measles cases in 2025 across 15 jurisdictions, with 1 confirmed death and 1 under investigation, a national count that Forbes contributor Omer Awan cited on March 18. Public health researchers criticized the timing as undercutting exactly the kind of research needed to counter vaccine-preventable disease spread.

On April 2, 2025, the American Public Health Association, Ibis Reproductive Health, the UAW and four researchers, including Center for Science in the Public Interest president Peter Lurie, sued NIH and HHS in American Public Health Association v. NIH (D. Mass. No. 1:25-cv-10787), represented by lawyers including the ACLU, the Protect Democracy Project and CSPI. The complaint said the directives "seek to cancel research deemed related to 'vaccine hesitancy,'" and it cited NIH's prescribed "Vaccine Hesitancy" termination language as one of the directives' "forbidden topics." On June 16, 2025, Judge William Young (D. Mass.) ruled in the case that NIH's directives -- which the court found had terminated roughly $1 billion in grants across categories including vaccine hesitancy, DEI, gender identity, and race-related health research -- were "arbitrary and capricious" and void under the Administrative Procedure Act; Young further found evidence of racial discrimination in the terminations he called, in his 40 years on the bench, among the most "palpable" he had seen. The ruling ordered roughly 900 grants held by the case's named plaintiffs reinstated -- a subset of the estimated 2,300 grants NIH terminated administration-wide, not a reinstatement of every terminated grant nationwide.

The First Circuit denied the government's request to stay Young's order on July 18, 2025. On August 21, 2025, the Supreme Court granted the government's stay application in part, an interim order rather than a ruling on the merits: a 5-4 majority declined to stay the part of the district court's judgments vacating the directives themselves, leaving it in effect pending appeal, while a different 5-4 majority stayed the part vacating the grant terminations, reasoning that the Administrative Procedure Act does not give the district court jurisdiction over claims based on the grants. Justice Barrett, who concurred in the partial grant and wrote that such claims belong in the Court of Federal Claims under the Tucker Act, was the only justice in both majorities. The mixed order left the directives vacated while complicating the remedy for the terminated grants.

The First Circuit separately heard oral argument on the case's appeal on January 6, 2026. Note: a separate First Circuit ruling on January 5, 2026 (one day earlier) in APLU v. NIH unanimously struck down NIH's 15% cap on facilities-and-administrative cost reimbursement -- a different NIH policy dispute with a different plaintiff group; it is not the same case or ruling as the vaccine-hesitancy grant-termination litigation this entry covers, and should not be conflated with it despite the near-identical dates. Separately, under a related stipulation agreement, NIH agreed to evaluate more than 5,000 stalled or previously rejected funding applications in the "ordinary course" of its scientific review process, without applying the challenged directives.

As of late September 2026, no First Circuit ruling had been identified on the January 6, 2026 oral argument in the appeal. The Georgetown Health Care Litigation Tracker's most recent entry for this case was a March 19, 2026 defendants' response to a notice of supplemental authority, with briefing described as ongoing; no ruling was identified between then and late September 2026, and the First Circuit docket showed only attorney-withdrawal motions and orders, in April and June 2026. Whether the specific 33+ vaccine-hesitancy grants named in this entry are among the ~900 plaintiff grants covered by Young's reinstatement order, and whether those grants are currently funded and operating as of late September 2026 or have lapsed again amid the ongoing jurisdictional dispute, were not confirmed in sourcing reviewed.

title: NIH Fired 11 of Its Most Senior Neuroscience Lab Heads -- Including a Breakthrough Prize Winner -- in a Reduction-in-Force Attributed to a 'Coding Error,' Kept Them Terminated for Seven Weeks While RFK Jr. Told Congress No Scientists Had Been Fired
institution: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH/HHS)
status: Reversed -- HHS formally revoked all 30 reduction-in-force notices on May 21, 2025, before the June 2, 2025 termination date took effect
date_of_action: 2025-04-01/02 (RIF notices issued) through 2025-05-21 (formal revocation)
what_changed: On April 1-2, 2025, as part of the Trump administration's broader HHS-wide reduction in force under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., 30 employees at the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) received reduction-in-force (RIF) notices, including 11 of the institute's most senior lab heads and distinguished investigators: Richard Youle, Miguel Holmgren, Steve Jacobson, Dorian McGavern, Joseph Mindell, Katherine Roche, Zu-Hang Sheng, David R. Sibley, Kenton Swartz, Susan Wray, and Ling-Gang Wu, plus senior associate scientist Silvina Horowitz. **Youle, at NIH since 1978 and winner of the $3 million 2021 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for identifying a cellular mechanism behind Parkinson's disease, was among those terminated.** NIH and HHS officials later attributed the firings to a 'coding error' in the RIF process that swept up senior investigators who were not supposed to be included. Despite verbal reassurances from NIH leadership, including Director Jay Bhattacharya, that the layoffs would be rescinded, the RIF notices remained formally in effect for seven weeks. On May 14, 2025, testifying before the Senate health committee, Kennedy stated, 'As far as I know, we have not fired any working scientists... our policy was to make sure none of them were lost and that that research continues' -- a claim contradicted by the NINDS scientists' still-active termination notices at the time he made it. HHS did not formally revoke the RIF notices until May 21, 2025, via email, days before the scheduled June 2 termination date. The 11 affected labs employed roughly 100 total staff, described by reporting as mainly young trainees whose research and career trajectories were disrupted during the seven-week uncertainty. After news of his firing broke, Youle received four outside job offers, three of them from institutions abroad.

title: NIOSH Loses 85-90% of Staff, Gutting Firefighter Cancer Research, the 9/11 World Trade Center Health Program, and Fatality Investigations
institution: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), Department of Health and Human Services (part of CDC)
status: Mixed. The WTC Health Program's separate funding-formula shortfall was permanently fixed by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75, signed Feb. 3, 2026), securing funding through 2040 -- but that does not restore the staff purged in 2025. The underlying staffing crisis this entry documents remains open: roughly 30% of the WTC Health Program's 120 authorized positions were still vacant per 2026 congressional letters, and as of a July 2026 bipartisan letter Dr. John Howard had not been reappointed as NIOSH director.
date_of_action: 2025-02-21 (initial WTC Health Program staffing cut reported) through 2025-06-03 (training-program funding shortfalls reported)
what_changed: On February 21, 2025, the New York Times reported layoffs and buyouts had already cut about 20% of staffing at the World Trade Center Health Program specifically, jeopardizing research grants and delaying certifications critical to treating 9/11 responders and survivors -- a cut initially reinstated after pushback from lawmakers and veterans' groups, though the program's staffing crisis recurred and deepened in the following months as described below. Beginning February 20, 2025, Trump administration cuts began hitting NIOSH more broadly, the CDC institute responsible for occupational safety and health research. Early casualties included Patrick Montague, an investigator for the National Firefighter Registry for Cancer, fired along with colleagues in his program citing probationary status. By April 3, 2025, hundreds of NIOSH staff had been fired, including key personnel from the World Trade Center Health Program -- which provides medical care to 9/11 first responders and survivors -- and the program's longtime director, Dr. John Howard, was also removed. By April 13, the Guardian reported **the WTC Health Program had been plunged into disarray, with cancer treatment, PTSD care, and other services for 9/11 survivors and first responders disrupted with no public transparency about what coverage remained available**. Wired reported April 18, 2025 that the cuts had eliminated roughly two-thirds of the staff at NIOSH's Morgantown, West Virginia lab specifically, leaving thousands of biological specimens -- including human urine samples, rodent brains, and diseased lung tissue used to study black lung disease and other occupational illnesses, some requiring ultra-cold storage to remain viable -- with no clear plan for maintenance or preservation, according to laid-off researchers who warned the samples were at risk of degrading or being lost entirely, along with decades of accumulated exposure and disease data. By April 22, ProPublica reported the purge had eliminated 7 of the 8 members of NIOSH's firefighter fatality investigation team, halting major studies into firefighter cancer risk alongside the WTC-program disruption. On May 12, more than 100 current and former NIOSH employees sent a joint letter to Congress warning that mass purges were putting American workers at risk, stating more than 90% of NIOSH staff had received layoff notices and that critical programs -- the 9/11 Health Program and black lung screening among them -- had already been disrupted. By May 27, the Guardian confirmed an 85% NIOSH staff purge, with only a fraction of positions reinstated after public backlash. By early June, Reuters reported the cuts -- nearly 900 staff purged in April alone -- were forcing shutdowns of occupational-safety training programs specifically serving fishermen, farmers, and loggers, among America's most dangerous occupations, with key training centers warning they would run out of funding by summer or fall 2025. Update, 2026-08-17: two later developments clarify how this crisis evolved. First, the WTC Health Program's separate, longstanding funding-formula shortfall -- which periodically threatened the program's ability to pay for care independent of the 2025 NIOSH staffing purge -- was permanently fixed via a bipartisan provision (led by Rep. Andrew Garbarino, Speaker Mike Johnson, Rep. Brett Guthrie, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, and Sen. Chuck Schumer) in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75), signed by President Trump February 3, 2026, securing funding through 2040. This resolves the funding-formula problem specifically; it does not restore the staff this entry documents being purged in 2025. Second, on the staffing side, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in April 2026 he was 'fixing' the WTC Health Program's problems, but reporting found only four job vacancies had actually been posted against the program's need. A bipartisan, bicameral letter led by Sen. Gillibrand and Rep. Garbarino, sent July 10, 2026 ahead of the September 2026 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, urged Kennedy to reappoint Dr. John Howard to a new six-year term as NIOSH director and WTC Health Program administrator, while acknowledging HHS had taken 'recent steps' on staffing shortages, delayed research grants, and pending petitions for additional covered conditions -- language consistent with the vacancy rate cited above, not with the crisis being over.
