glance.who: DOGE and HHS under Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
glance.what: NIOSH lost 85-90% of its staff, disrupting 9/11 responder care and firefighter cancer research

what_changed.base: On February 21, 2025, the New York Times reported layoffs and buyouts had already cut about 20% of staffing at the World Trade Center Health Program specifically, jeopardizing research grants and delaying certifications critical to treating 9/11 responders and survivors -- a cut initially reinstated after pushback from lawmakers and veterans' groups, though the program's staffing crisis recurred and deepened in the following months as described below. Beginning February 20, 2025, Trump administration cuts began hitting NIOSH more broadly, the CDC institute responsible for occupational safety and health research. Early casualties included Patrick Montague, an investigator for the National Firefighter Registry for Cancer, fired along with colleagues in his program citing probationary status. By April 3, 2025, hundreds of NIOSH staff had been fired, including key personnel from the World Trade Center Health Program -- which provides medical care to 9/11 first responders and survivors -- and the program's longtime director, Dr. John Howard, was also removed. By April 13, the Guardian reported **the WTC Health Program had been plunged into disarray, with cancer treatment, PTSD care, and other services for 9/11 survivors and first responders disrupted with no public transparency about what coverage remained available**. Wired reported April 18, 2025 that the cuts had eliminated roughly two-thirds of the staff at NIOSH's Morgantown, West Virginia lab specifically, leaving thousands of biological specimens -- including human urine samples, rodent brains, and diseased lung tissue used to study black lung disease and other occupational illnesses, some requiring ultra-cold storage to remain viable -- with no clear plan for maintenance or preservation, according to laid-off researchers who warned the samples were at risk of degrading or being lost entirely, along with decades of accumulated exposure and disease data. By April 22, ProPublica reported the purge had eliminated 7 of the 8 members of NIOSH's firefighter fatality investigation team, halting major studies into firefighter cancer risk alongside the WTC-program disruption. On May 12, more than 100 current and former NIOSH employees sent a joint letter to Congress warning that mass purges were putting American workers at risk, stating more than 90% of NIOSH staff had received layoff notices and that critical programs -- the 9/11 Health Program and black lung screening among them -- had already been disrupted. By May 27, the Guardian confirmed an 85% NIOSH staff purge, with only a fraction of positions reinstated after public backlash. By early June, Reuters reported the cuts -- nearly 900 staff purged in April alone -- were forcing shutdowns of occupational-safety training programs specifically serving fishermen, farmers, and loggers, among America's most dangerous occupations, with key training centers warning they would run out of funding by summer or fall 2025.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update, 2026-08-17: two later developments clarify how this crisis evolved. First, the WTC Health Program's separate, longstanding funding-formula shortfall -- which periodically threatened the program's ability to pay for care independent of the 2025 NIOSH staffing purge -- was permanently fixed via a bipartisan provision (led by Rep. Andrew Garbarino, Speaker Mike Johnson, Rep. Brett Guthrie, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, and Sen. Chuck Schumer) in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75), signed by President Trump February 3, 2026, securing funding through 2040. This resolves the funding-formula problem specifically; it does not restore the staff this entry documents being purged in 2025. Second, on the staffing side, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said in April 2026 he was 'fixing' the WTC Health Program's problems, but reporting found only four job vacancies had actually been posted against the program's need. A bipartisan, bicameral letter led by Sen. Gillibrand and Rep. Garbarino, sent July 10, 2026 ahead of the September 2026 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, urged Kennedy to reappoint Dr. John Howard to a new six-year term as NIOSH director and WTC Health Program administrator, while acknowledging HHS had taken 'recent steps' on staffing shortages, delayed research grants, and pending petitions for additional covered conditions -- language consistent with the vacancy rate cited above, not with the crisis being over.

title: NIST workforce reduction and standards/research budget cuts
institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology (Department of Commerce)
status: Ongoing, with a partial reversal on MEP: after issuing RIF notices to the entire MEP staff despite full congressional funding, NIST released a July 2026 NOFO for 14 MEP centers (applications closed Aug. 21, 2026, outcome not yet announced) and separately resolved a funding gap at 12 of 13 other state MEP centers (Colorado still pending). NIST also launched a new $40 million MEP pilot program even as the elimination proposal and RIF notices remain in effect. The Coons oversight letter and Cantwell/Peters GAO request remain unanswered.
date_of_action: 2025-02 to 2026-01 (workforce cuts); FY2026 budget proposal released June 2025
what_changed: NIST, the 125-year-old nonregulatory agency that sets the country's measurement, cybersecurity, and technology standards (including the widely used Cybersecurity Framework, the AI Risk Management Framework, and post-quantum encryption standards), lost more than 700 positions between the start of the Trump administration and January 2026 through resignations, retirements, and voluntary deferments, including roughly 500 recent hires who were let go early in 2025 while still in probationary status. A lab responsible for testing and validating the federal government's encryption implementations lost 89 staff. On March 26, 2025, the administration moved to eliminate NIST's Atomic Spectroscopy Group, which maintains atomic measurement data used as a foundational reference across nuclear fusion, astrophysics, and semiconductor-manufacturing research nationwide -- a specific, named-program elimination distinct from and in addition to the broader probationary and encryption-lab losses already documented in this entry. The administration's FY2026 budget request proposed cutting NIST's $1.2 billion budget by $325 million, eliminating the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership Program entirely (97 positions, $175 million, serving small and mid-size manufacturers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico) and cutting $125 million and 556 positions from NIST's core Scientific and Technical Research and Services program, citing cybersecurity/privacy, health and biological measurements, and physical-infrastructure research as target areas. House appropriators later rejected the steepest of these cuts and restored funding above the administration's request, but the agency has already absorbed the workforce losses and, as of early 2026, is still awaiting a formal Reduction-in-Force and reorganization plan. Congress's final FY2026 appropriation funded NIST's Scientific and Technical Research and Services program at $1.25 billion -- more than $542 million above the administration's request, and higher than even the $980 million House figure already cited in this entry -- and fully funded the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership at $175 million, rejecting the administration's proposal to eliminate it. **Despite that enacted funding, NIST issued Reduction-in-Force and possible-separation notices to every MEP employee, prompting Sen. Chris Coons and colleagues to send a formal letter demanding an explanation for what they characterized as an 'unauthorized dismantling' of a program Congress had just funded.** NIST's Computer Security Division also lost its division head and roughly a dozen subordinates to retirement offers, a specific loss to the cybersecurity-standards function this entry already documents as strained. Update 2026-07-26: NIST released a Notice of Funding Opportunity for 14 Manufacturing Extension Partnership centers (Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, California, Georgia, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Missouri, Montana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, Utah, and Vermont), with an informational webinar scheduled July 28, 2026 and applications due August 21, 2026. Trade press (Advanced Manufacturing) frames this as a real reversal after NIST's earlier funding notice for the program's next tranche of centers was delayed until December 4, 2025 -- itself more than six months behind schedule and a gap that, combined with the RIF notices, had already pushed roughly 90% of MEP centers into layoffs or hiring freezes, with some at risk of closing entirely. This doesn't resolve Sen. Coons's still-unanswered oversight letter about the RIF notices themselves, but is a concrete sign the program is continuing rather than being wound down. Update 2026-08-29: on July 3, 2026, Sens. Maria Cantwell and Gary Peters -- Ranking Members of the Senate Commerce and Homeland Security/Governmental Affairs Committees, respectively -- sent a letter to Acting Comptroller General Orice Williams Brown formally requesting a GAO investigation into whether Commerce, under Secretary Lutnick, followed the law in funding and managing the MEP program. The senators state that Commerce's own Inspector General personally confirmed to Democratic committee staff that the IG findings the Department cited as its stated justification for defunding MEP (concerning executive-compensation limits and overstated economic-impact claims) were not legal or otherwise appropriate grounds for defunding the program -- directly undercutting the administration's own stated rationale for the RIF notices this entry already documents. No GAO findings or response were identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 48): the MEP funding-uncertainty pattern this entry already documents (the 14-center July 2026 NOFO) recurred separately and earlier at a distinct set of 13 existing state MEP centers (Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Indiana, Maryland, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia), which were left operating without renewed federal award obligations into mid-2026; trade press reported 12 of the 13 had received their federal MEP awards by July 6, 2026, with Colorado still delayed over budget revisions. Separately, and in apparent tension with both the RIF notices and the elimination proposal this entry documents, NIST simultaneously launched a new $40 million MEP Pilot Program (Federal Register notice, May 20, 2026; public webinar June 24, 2026) committing roughly $20 million per project over two years to accelerate additive manufacturing for aerospace components and build a domestic critical-minerals supply chain, open only to existing MEP centers. No response to Sen. Coons's original RIF-notice oversight letter, and no findings from the Cantwell/Peters-requested GAO investigation, were identified in sourcing reviewed as of this update.

title: NLRB Loses Statutory Quorum for Nearly a Year After Trump Fires Board Member Wilcox
institution: National Labor Relations Board
status: Complete (Wilcox's removal is now considered constitutionally settled following Trump v. Slaughter, June 29, 2026, though the Supreme Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific case)
date_of_action: 2025-01-27 (firing) through 2026-06-29 (Supreme Court's Slaughter ruling resolves the underlying legal question); board lacked a working quorum for roughly 11 of the intervening months
what_changed: On January 27, 2025, President **Trump fired NLRB Board Member Gwynne Wilcox without citing any of the statutory grounds (neglect of duty or malfeasance) required by the National Labor Relations Act, leaving the five-seat Board with only two active members, below the three-member quorum required to issue decisions.** Wilcox sued on February 5, 2025. U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell ruled the firing unlawful on March 6, 2025, calling it a 'blatant violation of the law' and a 'power grab,' and ordered Wilcox reinstated, which briefly restored the Board's quorum. A three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed that ruling on March 28; the full en banc D.C. Circuit reversed course and reinstated Wilcox again on April 7; Chief Justice Roberts then issued an emergency stay removing her again on April 9. On May 22, 2025, the Supreme Court declined to reinstate Wilcox in a 6-3 emergency-docket order, explicitly not a ruling on the merits. The Board remained below quorum until regaining one in December 2025 through new Trump nominations. On January 28, 2026, the D.C. Circuit declined en banc review of the panel decision upholding Wilcox's termination. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court's decision in the related case Trump v. Slaughter overruled the 90-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent underlying Wilcox's legal theory; legal analysts across firms now consider her removal constitutionally settled even though the Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific still-pending case. Update (GSR recheck batch 2, 2026-09-08): On August 7, 2026, the Senate confirmed James Macy as a new Republican Board member (alongside the renomination of Democratic member David Prouty), giving the NLRB a full 3-1 Republican majority for the first time since Wilcox's firing. A bare quorum had technically been restored in December 2025, but this confirmation is the first point at which the Board has held the three Republican votes needed to formally overturn Biden-era precedent, not just issue decisions.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Fired Wilcox directly via a short email citing loss of confidence in her leadership, then pursued the legal theory that his Article II authority permitted the removal all the way to the Supreme Court, a position the Court substantially validated in the related Slaughter case.

estimated_impact.summary: The National Labor Relations Board, the sole federal agency responsible for enforcing private-sector labor law and adjudicating unfair-labor-practice and union-election disputes, was left without a functioning quorum for nearly all of 2025, halting its ability to issue binding decisions during that period.

glance.what: Fired NLRB member Wilcox, leaving the board without a quorum for ~11 months of 2025

what_changed.base: On January 27, 2025, President **Trump fired NLRB Board Member Gwynne Wilcox without citing any of the statutory grounds (neglect of duty or malfeasance) required by the National Labor Relations Act, leaving the five-seat Board with only two active members, below the three-member quorum required to issue decisions.** Wilcox sued on February 5, 2025. U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell ruled the firing unlawful on March 6, 2025, calling it a 'blatant violation of the law' and a 'power grab,' and ordered Wilcox reinstated, which briefly restored the Board's quorum. A three-judge D.C. Circuit panel stayed that ruling on March 28; the full en banc D.C. Circuit reversed course and reinstated Wilcox again on April 7; Chief Justice Roberts then issued an emergency stay removing her again on April 9. On May 22, 2025, the Supreme Court declined to reinstate Wilcox in a 6-3 emergency-docket order, explicitly not a ruling on the merits. The Board remained below quorum until regaining one in December 2025 through new Trump nominations. On January 28, 2026, the D.C. Circuit declined en banc review of the panel decision upholding Wilcox's termination. On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court's decision in the related case Trump v. Slaughter overruled the 90-year-old Humphrey's Executor precedent underlying Wilcox's legal theory; legal analysts across firms now consider her removal constitutionally settled even though the Court has not yet formally disposed of her specific still-pending case.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update (GSR recheck batch 2, 2026-09-08): On August 7, 2026, the Senate confirmed James Macy as a new Republican Board member (alongside the renomination of Democratic member David Prouty), giving the NLRB a full 3-1 Republican majority for the first time since Wilcox's firing. A bare quorum had technically been restored in December 2025, but this confirmation is the first point at which the Board has held the three Republican votes needed to formally overturn Biden-era precedent, not just issue decisions.

title: NNSA Nuclear-Weapons-Complex Staffing Crisis -- From Accidental Firings to a Shutdown Furlough That Halted Weapons Work for the First Time in History
institution: National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), a semi-autonomous Department of Energy agency responsible for the U.S. nuclear weapons stockpile; related developments at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
status: Ongoing, with escalating severity through the year: initial erroneous firings (Feb 2025) gave way to a documented brain-drain (Mar-May 2025), then a historic shutdown-driven near-total work stoppage (Oct 2025), followed by a policy shift reducing regulatory oversight of new reactor construction (Dec 2025). An April 2026 Stimson Center report quantifies the underlying structural gap: NNSA remains roughly 200 positions short of the ~2,369-person staffing benchmark a 2020 agency study identified as needed by fiscal 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02-17 (initial erroneous firings) through 2025-12-30 (Reactor Pilot Program launch)
what_changed: In February 2025, DOGE-driven federal workforce cuts mistakenly fired NNSA employees -- some working on the nuclear stockpile and on tracking nuclear threats, including in Ukraine -- and the administration then could not contact them about reinstatement because their government email accounts had already been deactivated. ABC News reported on February 21, 2025 that this confusion was not limited to NNSA: hundreds of federal employees initially terminated from agencies including NNSA, the VA, and USDA had their dismissals rescinded, but many remained unclear on their actual employment status even after the reversal, reflecting a broader pattern of chaotic, poorly-tracked terminations across the initial wave of DOGE-directed cuts. By March 2025, the New York Times reported more than 130 senior scientists, engineers, and security experts had been forced out of NNSA, jeopardizing nuclear modernization programs and safety protocols. By May 2025, USA Today reported the cuts had derailed years of hiring progress and raised new safety concerns at weapons facilities including Los Alamos, the Y-12 National Security Complex, and Pantex. The staffing erosion reached the Nuclear Regulatory Commission as well: at a September 4, 2025 Senate hearing, two of the NRC's three remaining commissioners said they feared Trump could purge them too if they resisted his push to fast-track new reactor approvals, part of a stated goal to quadruple U.S. nuclear generating capacity by 2050. The crisis peaked during the October 2025 government shutdown: NNSA warned it would furlough 80% of its workforce as shutdown funding ran out, leaving only 375 'essential' employees and placing facility contractors in 'minimum-safe' status; by October 21, **more than 1,400 employees -- over 75% of staff -- had actually been furloughed, leaving fewer than 400 on duty and suspending nearly all work on the U.S. nuclear weapons program, the first time in the program's history that weapons assembly and modernization work came to a complete stop**. Funding for the Office of Secure Transportation, which physically moves nuclear warheads and materials, was confirmed only through October 27 as the shutdown continued. Then, on December 30, 2025, Trump officials launched a Reactor Pilot Program fast-tracking construction of new, largely untested nuclear reactor designs, with oversight shifted from the traditionally independent Nuclear Regulatory Commission to the Department of Energy itself -- aiming to bring at least three experimental reactors online by July 4, 2026 under an aggressive political deadline and with limited public transparency. In April 2026, the Stimson Center published a report, 'Securing the Future: Building the US Nuclear Security Workforce Pipeline,' putting a structural, longer-horizon number on the staffing gap underlying the year's crisis: a 2020 NNSA study had identified a need for 2,369 personnel by fiscal 2026, but the agency's own FY2026 budget request targeted a workforce of roughly 200 positions below that benchmark. The report attributes the shortfall not just to the year's disruptive events but to durable structural competition -- weak internal career-advancement pathways compared to the private sector, and NNSA's technical talent pool increasingly drawn instead toward AI, quantum computing, and biotechnology roles.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
primary_proponent.role: Directed the initial 2025 workforce cuts across NNSA and related agencies
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing the NNSA-specific cuts; the erroneous-firing episode in particular was reported as a process failure (deactivated emails preventing reinstatement contact) rather than a deliberate targeting decision, though it occurred within DOGE's broader, deliberately aggressive workforce-reduction push. The later Reactor Pilot Program and its shift of oversight from NRC to DOE reflects a distinct, deliberate administration policy choice.

estimated_impact.summary: Substantial, escalating loss of specialized nuclear-weapons-complex staffing capacity, culminating in the first complete halt to U.S. nuclear weapons assembly and modernization work in the program's history, alongside a shift of new-reactor oversight away from the traditionally independent nuclear safety regulator

The Stimson Center's ~200-position shortfall figure describes a structural, years-long gap against a 2020 benchmark, not a fresh cut attributable to 2025-2026 events specifically -- it contextualizes why the year's disruptions land on an agency that was already understaffed, rather than quantifying new losses.

title: NNSA Leak Crackdown Following Real Security Failures at Los Alamos and Kansas City, Amid Internal Opposition to Trump's Push to Resume Live Nuclear Weapons Testing
institution: National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA), Department of Energy
status: Ongoing -- leak-crackdown memo issued; no formal order to resume explosive testing, and no confirmed disciplinary/criminal action under the memo, as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-07 (Kansas City hack) through 2025-11-22 (Williams' leak-crackdown memo)
what_changed: The November 2025 leak crackdown followed two distinct, documented threads. First, real security failures: in July 2025, **foreign hackers breached IT systems at the Kansas City National Security Campus (which manufactures roughly 80% of the non-nuclear components used in U.S. nuclear weapons) by exploiting two unpatched Microsoft SharePoint vulnerabilities (CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-49704)**; Microsoft attributed the broader campaign to three China-linked hacking groups, though a source involved in the incident response told CSO Online a Russian actor, not a Chinese one, carried out this specific intrusion, and the security firm Resecurity suggested a Chinese-developed exploit may have been independently reproduced by Russian, financially-motivated actors. NNSA said only 'a very small number of systems were impacted' and that no classified information was compromised, though unclassified technical requirements documents -- which can reveal the level of precision required for weapons components -- were exposed. Separately, DOE's own security-enforcement records document an unauthorized disclosure of classified information to personnel lacking proper access authorization at the Kansas City campus on September 5, 2025, and recurring incidents of unauthorized controlled articles being introduced into secure areas at Los Alamos National Laboratory. Second, and simultaneously, an internal policy leak: in late October 2025, President Trump posted on social media directing the Department of Defense to begin nuclear weapons testing 'because of other countries testing programs' -- the first public suggestion of a return to explosive nuclear detonation testing since the U.S. moratorium began in 1992. Per CNN's November 14, 2025 exclusive report, NNSA officials prepared an internal memo for Energy Secretary Chris Wright and NNSA Administrator Brandon Williams outlining the agency's existing non-explosive verification methods and the timeline a return to explosive testing would require; Wright, Williams, and National Laboratory officials planned to tell the White House that resuming explosive testing was not 'tenable,' and Nevada's congressional delegation (Reps. Susie Lee and Steven Horsford) sent formal letters in early November 2025 opposing any return to testing. Against that backdrop of both real breaches and a leaked internal policy dispute, Williams sent an agency-wide 'urgent' memo on November 22, 2025: 'It saddens me that this message is necessary,' he wrote, adding that 'past actions by NNSA-affiliated personnel have undermined national leadership's confidence in our ability to safeguard classified and sensitive unclassified information related to our national security work,' and that 'any compromise of information, regardless of its perceived sensitivity, represents a direct threat to our strategic interests.' Williams listed potential consequences as 'severe and far-reaching': administrative penalties, loss of security clearance, civil liability, and criminal prosecution -- without specifying which incident(s) prompted the memo or naming any individuals. The New York Times' coverage of the memo also noted critics' concerns about Williams' own qualifications for the role: he is a former one-term GOP congressman with six years' service as a Navy nuclear submarine officer and an MBA from Wharton, confirmed September 18, 2025 as part of a 48-nominee batch Senate Republicans approved en masse along party lines (51-47) rather than through individualized vetting; Sen. Elizabeth Warren had written to Williams during his nomination warning that 'a leader without strong technical expertise and extensive experience could put our nuclear deterrent at risk and waste billions of dollars.'

The health/mortality stakes are indirect: the nuclear-testing policy dispute the leaks separately concerned carries a well-documented historical health legacy from the prior era of U.S. atmospheric testing, cited as context for why internal experts reportedly opposed a return to testing, not as a quantified harm estimate from this memo itself.

The RECA/downwinder figures describe the historical health legacy of 20th-century atmospheric testing, not a projected impact of a hypothetical new test (which would very likely be underground, not atmospheric) -- included as context for the internal opposition, not as this memo's own harm estimate. title: NOAA Climate Research Zeroed Out in FY2026 Budget Proposal, Princeton Partnership Defunded
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
status: Partially implemented, and repeating -- the Princeton funding cut took effect and the administration proposed eliminating NOAA's climate research office again in its FY2027 budget, for the second year running; Congress rejected the same elimination in FY2026 and House appropriators' initial FY2027 markup signals they are likely to do so again
date_of_action: 2025-04-08 (Princeton funding cut announced) through the FY2026 budget cycle (proposal released July 2025; Congress had not enacted it as of the last-verified date)
what_changed: On April 8, 2025, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced the termination of nearly $4 million in NOAA cooperative research funding to Princeton University, effective June 30, 2025, covering three programs including the Cooperative Institute for Modeling the Earth System, which supports Princeton's partnership with NOAA's Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (GFDL), widely regarded as producing some of the world's most advanced climate modeling. The Commerce Department's official announcement stated the program 'promotes exaggerated and implausible climate threats, contributing to a phenomenon known as climate anxiety.' In July 2025, NOAA's proposed FY2026 budget was reported to contain a literal line reading 'Total, Climate Research: $0,' along with the proposed elimination of the entire Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR), NOAA's research arm, and defunding of all of OAR's climate and weather cooperative institutes nationwide, including CIRES at the University of Colorado Boulder, which houses the National Snow and Ice Data Center. The overall proposal called for cutting NOAA's budget by more than 25% and its ~13,000-person workforce by roughly 17%, along with a 44% reduction in planned investment in next-generation geostationary weather satellites. Congressional spending panels rejected the FY2026 budget request as proposed, but the administration proceeded with some of the changes administratively regardless, including terminating contracts for planned satellite instruments in August 2025 as what agency officials described to staff as a 'down payment' on the broader proposed cuts. The administration's FY2027 budget request, released in 2026, again proposes eliminating the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research (OAR) -- the same office Congress rejected eliminating in the FY2026 cycle -- along with more than $1 billion in additional NOAA program cuts, including defunding the network of global monitoring laboratories and 14 other climate laboratories nationwide. At an April 2026 budget hearing, NOAA officials defended the cuts while members of both parties on the relevant committee pushed back. The House Commerce-Justice-Science Appropriations subcommittee's initial FY2027 markup was reported as favorable to NOAA's weather enterprise, suggesting Congress may again decline to enact the full elimination, consistent with the FY2026 outcome. The administration's separate FY2026 budget request also proposed eliminating all $43.5 million in federal support for NOAA's Integrated Ocean Observing System, a real-time data source used by harbor pilots, weather forecasters, and military operations, according to AP reporting in May 2025. By September 2025, the Washington Post reported the cuts had moved beyond budget proposals into concrete instrument shutdowns: the administration was closing down climate-monitoring satellites, shutting off carbon-tracking instruments, and scrapping sensors used to monitor water contamination and greenhouse gases, with internal budget documents directing NOAA to focus solely on 'weather-only' tools -- consistent with Project 2025's earlier call to dismantle federal climate research capacity. One consequence of NOAA's shrinking disaster-tracking function became visible that fall: NBC News reported in October 2025 that after the administration effectively shut down NOAA's billion-dollar disaster-cost-tracking database, **a group of former NOAA scientists rebuilt an equivalent tracker independently through the nonprofit Climate Central -- their reconstruction found the costliest six-month stretch of U.S. weather disasters on record, with 14 separate events each exceeding $1 billion in damage, led by the Los Angeles wildfires at more than $61 billion**.

Critics, including former NOAA research director Craig McLean, argue the cuts amount to dismantling the scientific basis for hurricane and severe-weather forecasting, and ProPublica reporting noted that Secretary Lutnick's former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, had itself described climate change in prior public materials as 'the defining issue of our time' and warned it would be 'disastrous and life threatening' if unchecked, a contrast critics cite as evidence the funding decision reflects political priorities rather than a reassessment of the science. It is also important to note the FY2026 budget eliminating NOAA's climate research entirely is a proposal, not enacted law: congressional appropriators in both parties have been reported as skeptical of the scale of the cuts and have not approved the request as written, even though the administration has moved ahead with some individual actions, such as satellite contract terminations, independent of congressional approval.

title: DOGE/GSA Listed the Support-Office Lease for NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory -- Home of the Keeling Curve -- for Termination, Then Quietly Resolved It
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Global Monitoring Laboratory -- Mauna Loa Observatory; General Services Administration (GSA)
status: Resolved -- NOAA confirmed in July 2025 the lease matter was settled before the August 31, 2025 expiration, without specifying how; the observatory continued operating and was reported in 2026 to be expanding, not closing
date_of_action: 2025-03-11 (lease publicly reported as targeted) through 2025-07 (NOAA confirms resolution)
what_changed: In March 2025, Reuters and other outlets reported that DOGE/GSA had listed the lease for an eight-person NOAA support office in Hilo, Hawaii (suite 102, Kilauea Financial Plaza) among the federal office leases slated for early termination as part of the administration's real-estate cost-cutting push. The office is the ground-support base for the Mauna Loa Observatory, established in 1956 on the mountain's northern flank, which holds the world's longest continuous record of atmospheric carbon dioxide measurements -- the Keeling Curve -- and was already operating under strain from the loss of its only road access after Mauna Loa's 2022 eruption, making the Hilo office's remote-support role especially load-bearing. The lease was set to expire August 31, 2025. As of a late-August 2025 report, no resolution had been announced and Hawaii's congressional delegation -- Sen. Mazie Hirono and Reps. Jill Tokuda and Ed Case -- introduced a formal resolution expressing concern and reaffirming support for the observatory, with Hirono calling the threatened closure 'yet another attack on science.' NOAA subsequently confirmed to reporters that the lease matter was resolved in July 2025, before the deadline, without detailing the mechanism (renewal, relocation, or reversal of the termination decision). By mid-2026, reporting described the observatory not merely surviving but being rebuilt and expanded, with measurement programs that had been curtailed since the 2022 eruption road closure increasingly restored.

primary_proponent.name: General Services Administration, with DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency)
primary_proponent.role: GSA administered the lease-termination list that included this office; DOGE's broader federal-real-estate cost-cutting push provided the policy driver
primary_proponent.note: No named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally responsible for including this specific office; this is the same GSA/DOGE lease-termination sweep documented separately for the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory's Hilo office, a different agency and mission housed in a different Hilo building, targeted in the same week -- see [[doge-volcano-observatory-lease-terminations-2025]].

estimated_impact.summary: One of the eight-person support offices keeping alive the world's longest-running atmospheric CO2 record was briefly listed for lease termination with no documented contingency plan, at a moment when the observatory's summit instruments were already isolated by 2022 eruption damage and dependent on this office's remote-support role -- an example of a blanket real-estate cost-cutting sweep reaching a scientifically irreplaceable, decades-long dataset without an apparent case-by-case review.

NOAA's own account of the resolution mechanism is vague ('resolved') rather than specific, and no source reviewed states whether the termination decision was formally reversed or the office was relocated on the same footprint.

MODERATE confidence on the precise resolution mechanism, since NOAA's own public statement did not specify how the lease issue was settled. Distinct from, and should not be merged with, [[doge-volcano-observatory-lease-terminations-2025]] -- that entry covers the USGS Hawaiian Volcano Observatory (Ironworks Building, Kilauea volcanic-hazard monitoring) and the Alaska Volcano Observatory; this entry covers NOAA's separate Mauna Loa Observatory support office (Kilauea Financial Plaza, atmospheric CO2 monitoring). Both are in Hilo and were targeted in the same DOGE sweep the same week, which is likely why several outlets -- and an earlier version of the existing tap entry -- conflated the two facilities' reported savings figures; verified independently here against direct wire reporting for each.

title: DOGE Cuts Gutted NOAA's Space Traffic Coordination Office, Then FY2026 Budget Sought to Eliminate Its Core System Entirely
institution: NOAA Office of Space Commerce (Commerce Department)
status: Mixed and recurring. The February 2025 staffing cuts stand, never fully reversed. Congress rejected the FY2026 threat to eliminate TraCSS funding in enacted law (P.L. 119-74, $52.5M against an $11M request), but the fight restarted for FY2027: the administration's April 2026 request again proposed $11M with no dedicated TraCSS funding, and the House again restored funding to $50M (approved May 13, 2026), with the cycle not yet finalized. TraCSS remains operational, with 70 pilot users representing 11,345+ satellites as of August 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02-27 (initial firings) through 2026 budget cycle (proposed elimination of TraCSS funding)
what_changed: On February 27, 2025, DOGE-driven cuts hit NOAA's Office of Space Commerce (OSC), a roughly 25-person office, on a few hours' notice -- about a third of the office's staff, including the chief of the Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS), Dmitry Poisik. TraCSS is the civilian satellite traffic coordination system OSC has been building since 2018 (under Space Policy Directive 3, signed in Trump's first term) to warn commercial and government satellite operators of potential collisions as low Earth orbit becomes increasingly crowded. The cuts also hit OSC's Commercial Remote Sensing Regulatory Affairs Division, which licenses commercial imaging satellite companies; **affected licensees received an email stating 'no senior personnel remain in the office' and warning of 'significant delays' processing licensing actions.** Since the initial layoffs, three staffers in leadership roles were brought back, but congressional Democrats (Reps. Valerie Foushee and Zoe Lofgren among others) continued to warn about the office's reduced capacity. In 2026, the administration's budget request went further, proposing to cut OSC's budget by 85% and eliminate 18 positions, while eliminating federal funding for TraCSS entirely -- a group of space-industry organizations wrote to House and Senate leaders warning the cuts would put both commercial and government satellite operators at risk of collision. Update, 2026-08-17: the FY2026 defunding threat this entry describes as an unenacted budget proposal was resolved -- and rejected -- in enacted law before this entry was even written. The House Appropriations Committee's FY2026 Commerce-Justice-Science bill (approved May 2026) funded the Office of Space Commerce at $50 million against the administration's $11 million request; the Senate Appropriations Committee proposed $60 million; the final enacted figure, signed into law as part of P.L. 119-74 on January 23, 2026, settled at $52.5 million -- preserving TraCSS rather than eliminating it, following sustained pressure from a coalition of 450+ space, satellite, and defense companies. As of July 2026, TraCSS had 68 pilot users representing more than 11,290 satellites in orbit onboarded to the system, though work is reportedly proceeding more slowly than the pre-budget-threat schedule that had targeted full operational capability by January 2026. This funding resolution does not address the February 2025 staffing cuts themselves, which this entry's original reporting describes as only partially reversed (three leadership-role staffers reinstated of the roughly one-third of the office cut). Update, 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 29): the defunding fight recurred for FY2027. The administration's FY2027 budget request, released April 3, 2026, again proposed only $11 million for the Office of Space Commerce with no dedicated TraCSS funding -- industry sources described it to SpaceNews as 'another attempt by the White House Office of Management and Budget to cancel or severely curtail TraCSS,' the same pattern as the FY2026 request a year earlier. The House Appropriations Committee's FY2027 Commerce-Justice-Science bill, approved May 13, 2026, again restored funding, to $50 million, with report language explicitly supporting continued TraCSS work. As of this update the Senate had not yet completed action and no FY2027 appropriations bill had been enacted (the federal fiscal year begins October 1, 2026), so this remains an unresolved, recurring threat rather than a settled one. Separately, TraCSS's pilot-user base grew modestly since the prior update, from 68 to 70 pilot users representing over 11,345 satellites in orbit.

primary_proponent.role: Directed the February 2025 firings; the 2026 budget proposal to eliminate TraCSS funding originated from the administration's Commerce Department budget request
primary_proponent.note: DOGE's cross-agency probationary/short-notice terminations reached OSC directly; the later FY2026 budget proposal to zero out TraCSS funding is a separate, subsequent administration action extending the same disruption to the office's core mission rather than just its staffing.

estimated_impact.summary: Space-industry organizations and congressional Democrats warn the cuts leave commercial and government satellite operators without adequate collision-warning infrastructure at exactly the moment low Earth orbit is becoming most crowded -- and that eliminating TraCSS funding entirely would end the program TraCSS was built to replace (an aging, overloaded Defense Department system never designed for today's commercial satellite volume).

title: NOAA Loses Around a Fifth of Its Workforce in 2025, With a 10% Layoff Planned, Disaster Training Cancelled and Privatization Floated
institution: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), agency-wide (distinct from this database's separate, NWS-specific weather-balloon and staffing-loss entries)
status: Implemented through firings, buyouts and retirements rather than layoffs: OPM data show NOAA's workforce down around 20% and no NOAA reduction-in-force separations in 2025; some fired probationary staff were reinstated with back pay in January 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (probationary firings) through 2025-05-25 (NGS losses reported)
what_changed: In the first months of 2025, NOAA lost staff agency-wide through several overlapping channels, separate from the NWS-specific weather-balloon suspensions and roughly 600-person NWS staffing loss tracked in other entries in this database. In February, NOAA fired its probationary employees -- about 650, according to a spokesman for Sen. Chris Van Hollen (other reports put the figure near 800) -- on top of about 500 employees who had already left under the first deferred-resignation offer. On March 11, the Associated Press reported, citing four people familiar with the matter, that NOAA had begun planning to lay off another 1,000-plus workers, about 10% of its current workforce; three former senior NOAA officials put the planned cut at 1,029 of 10,290 employees. The same day, The Hill reported that **the National Weather Service had cancelled its incident meteorologist training, which prepares forecasters to deploy to wildfires and other disasters, citing 'short staffing' and a severe reduction in travel spending.** An agency source said employee purchase cards had been cut to $1, so staff could not book travel and some had to cancel flights already booked; the weather service had 85 qualified incident meteorologists and 35 trainees at the time. On March 12, ABC News reported that NOAA was preparing to lay off more than 1,000 workers and, citing a person familiar with staffing levels, that the agency was already down about 2,000 people from roughly 12,000 in January (through the first round of cuts, the 'Fork in the Road' deferred-resignation offer and regular retirements), so the planned cuts would leave it down 25% since the start of the year; Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) said NOAA had been asked to eliminate entire functions, not just individual personnel. On March 14, FedScoop reported former officials' warnings that the probationary firings would deepen existing shortfalls across NOAA's missions; Timothy Gallaudet, acting NOAA administrator during the first Trump administration, said the firings would 'exacerbate a problem of not having enough people to do what they need to do.' Court orders in March briefly reinstated the fired probationary employees, placing them on paid administrative leave, but NOAA fired them again in April after an appeals court stayed those orders. On March 25, ABC News examined whether the administration might seek to privatize the National Weather Service, noting that Project 2025 -- whose architects included OMB Director Russell Vought -- said NOAA 'should be broken up and downsized' and that the NWS 'should fully commercialize its forecasting operations'; Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had answered 'No' at his January confirmation hearing when asked whether he agreed with Project 2025's proposals to privatize some NOAA operations. On April 1, The Guardian described chaos at NOAA, with more than 1,000 people already fired or resigning and 1,000 more expected to be removed -- around 20% of the workforce in total. Some firings had already been reversed: five people involved in 'hurricane hunter' flights were fired, and three were then told their jobs would be reinstated. The Guardian also reported that a new, unsecured email server used to relay messages from the Office of Personnel Management had deluged staff with spam in January, a problem NOAA later fixed. On May 25, 2025, Mother Jones republished a WIRED report that the losses had reached the National Geodetic Survey (NGS), the small NOAA office that maintains the nation's official spatial reference system -- the precise measurements of latitude, longitude, elevation, and gravity underlying mapping, infrastructure, and disaster-response work. Former staff said NGS had 174 employees at the start of the year, had lost nearly a quarter of its staff since January 20, and had frozen planned hiring, putting at risk a long-delayed modernization of the national datums scheduled for 2025 and 2026; Tim Burch of the National Society of Professional Surveyors said the office's work 'is kind of like oxygen. You don't know you need it until it's not there.' This entry treats NGS as one more named office within the broader NOAA-wide losses rather than a separate action. By late June, according to Federal News Network, more than 1,000 NOAA employees had also left through the deferred resignation program, early retirement offers and buyouts. In December 2025, NOAA offered reinstatement, with back pay from April 10, 2025, to some of the probationary employees it had fired twice; about 40 had been reinstated by early January 2026, according to one reinstated employee who spoke to Federal News Network. The planned layoff did not materialize as a formal reduction in force: OPM data analyzed by the American Institute of Physics in February 2026 showed NOAA's workforce down around 20% since Trump took office, but no reduction-in-force separations at NOAA in 2025; many of the agency's departures came through voluntary retirements outside the deferred resignation program.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
primary_proponent.role: Spearheaded the administration's federal-workforce-cut campaign under which NOAA's firings, buyouts and planned layoff took place
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing the NOAA-specific cuts described here; attributed to DOGE's broader campaign. The privatization idea discussed here comes from Project 2025's text, as quoted by ABC News, not from a proposal by any current official.

estimated_impact.summary: NOAA's weather, disaster-support, hurricane-reconnaissance and mapping work lost experienced people in early 2025: the National Weather Service cancelled training for the incident meteorologists who support wildfire and disaster crews, five hurricane-hunter flight staff were fired before three were told they would be reinstated, and the National Geodetic Survey lost nearly a quarter of its staff. Agency-wide, NOAA's workforce fell around 20% after Trump took office, according to an American Institute of Physics analysis of OPM data, through roughly 650 to 800 probationary firings, about 500 early deferred resignations, more than 1,000 later buyouts, early retirements and deferred resignations, and many voluntary retirements. A planned 10% layoff of about 1,029 more people was reported but never showed up as a formal reduction in force. The entry documents degraded capacity, not specific deaths or dollar losses.

what_changed: In early May 2025, the Interior Department ordered contractors to stop air-quality monitoring across all 63 U.S. national parks, per an internal email obtained by the Washington Post. The affected program tracked ozone, particulate matter, and other pollutants at monitoring sites in and around park units nationwide -- data used to inform permitting decisions for nearby industrial projects and to track 'regional haze,' the human-caused visibility impairment the EPA has required states to reduce in national parks and wilderness areas since 1999. The pause came shortly after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum granted sweeping administrative authority over the department -- including funding decisions, hiring/firing, and policy-setting across the National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, and Bureau of Indian Affairs -- to Tyler Hassen, a former oil-field-services executive (ex-CEO of Basin Energy) serving as a DOGE-affiliated assistant secretary for policy, management and budget. After the Post's reporting and the leaked stop-work email became public, Park Service spokeswoman Rachel Pawlitz said in an email that the orders would be reversed and 'contractors will be notified immediately'; the agency confirmed monitoring had resumed. Former National Park Service directors and career leaders separately published an open letter and op-ed urging Burgum to reverse course on this and related park policies.

title: NPS Ordered to Strip Climate Science and Native American Mistreatment From Park Signage at 17+ Parks, Including Grand Canyon and Glacier
institution: National Park Service (NPS), Department of the Interior
status: Ongoing -- multiple rounds documented (August/September 2025, January 2026), with no reversal or public accounting identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-03 (executive order signed) through 2026-01-27 (Washington Post's report on the latest round of removals)
what_changed: A March 2025 executive order titled 'Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History' directed federal agencies, including the Department of the Interior, to remove content from federal properties deemed to 'disparage Americans past or living' or reflect 'partisan ideology.' Park Service staff have implemented the directive across multiple rounds -- documented in August and September 2025, and again in a January 2026 round covering at least 17 additional parks across Arizona, Texas, Colorado, Utah, Montana, and Wyoming. At Grand Canyon National Park, exhibit text describing how settlers 'exploited land for mining and grazing' and how federal officials 'pushed tribes off their land' was removed, along with references to cattle ranchers 'carelessly overgrazing,' tourists 'foolishly' leaving trash, and entrepreneurs having 'profited excessively' from tourism. At Glacier National Park, brochures showing glacier retreat linked to human-caused climate change were flagged, **signage stating 'Climate Change Affects National Parks and the Treasures They Protect' was removed, and displays about air pollution and increasing wildfire risk were also removed**. At Big Bend National Park, nearly 20 signs were flagged for removal, including bilingual displays and materials about geology, fossils, and cross-border cooperation with Mexico, without staff being given clear explanations. At Grand Teton, a panel describing an 1870 U.S. Army massacre of Piegan Blackfeet people was removed. At Little Bighorn Battlefield, text describing the United States as 'hungry for gold and land' and describing boarding schools that 'violently erased cultural identities and language' was removed. The Interior Department's own stated justification was that 'all federal agencies are to review interpretive materials to ensure accuracy, honesty, and alignment with shared national values.' Kristen Brengel, senior vice president of the National Parks Conservation Association, said the removals 'should offend every American' and that Park Service staff are 'being forced to select stories because they think the administration will threaten their jobs.' Two retired NPS superintendents directly involved in the affected parks were sharply critical: Jeff Mow, retired Glacier National Park superintendent, called the process 'whitewashing' and compared it to 'taking a torpedo in the bow,' and Bob Krumenaker, former Big Bend superintendent, said the Park Service is simply following orders while expressing hope the removed exhibits will eventually be restored.

title: NRC Commissioner Fired Without Cause, Agency Independence and Staffing Cut Under DOGE Reorganization
institution: Nuclear Regulatory Commission
status: Ongoing (Hanson's firing remains final and unlitigated; the commission remains at its full five members under Chairman Ho Nieh; the DOGE-directed reorganization and regulatory rewrite are continuing on EO 14300's original schedule, with NRC targeting completion of its organizational restructuring by the end of September 2026 and a new rulemaking-procedure rule published August 11, 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-05-23 (executive order) and 2025-06-13 (Hanson firing)
what_changed:
On June 13, 2025, President Trump fired NRC Commissioner Christopher T. Hanson, effective immediately, via a two-line email from the White House Presidential Personnel Office. It was the first removal of an NRC commissioner since the agency's creation in 1974; Hanson's term was not set to expire until 2029, and no cause was cited beyond White House Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly's statement to NPR that 'all organizations are more effective when leaders are rowing in the same direction' and that 'President Trump reserves the right to remove employees within his own Executive Branch who exert his executive authority.' Hanson, originally appointed by Trump in his first term and later designated chairman by President Biden, said he was terminated 'without cause, contrary to existing law and longstanding precedent regarding removal of independent agency appointees.'

The firing left the five-member commission at a 2-2 partisan split with one vacancy, and came three weeks after Trump signed Executive Order 14300, 'Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission' (May 23, 2025), which directs the NRC to reorganize and undertake reductions in force in consultation with its DOGE Team, shrink the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards to the statutory minimum, and issue proposed rules for a 'wholesale revision' of its safety regulations and guidance documents within 9 months and final rules and guidance within 18 months (by Feb. 23 and Nov. 23, 2026, respectively, under the order's sec. 5), with rulemaking routed through OMB Director Russell Vought's office -- a process not previously applied to this traditionally arms-length safety regulator.

EO 14300 grounds the overhaul in its finding that, of the reactors the NRC has authorized since 1978, 'only two reactors have entered into commercial operation,' and sets a policy of expanding U.S. nuclear capacity 'from approximately 100 GW in 2024 to 400 GW by 2050,' citing energy-intensive industries such as artificial intelligence. The order requires the NRC to 'undertake reductions in force' while allowing that 'certain functions may increase in size,' including new-reactor licensing, and to 'create a dedicated team of at least 20 officials' to draft the new regulations. The agency entered this period short-staffed: a December 18, 2024 NRC Inspector General audit (OIG-NRC-25-A-03), reported by Government Executive in May 2025, counted 281 external hires in fiscal 2023, when the NRC 'aimed to hire 400 new employees,' and found the agency ended the year with 2,722 employees against roughly 2,880 budgeted full-time-equivalent positions.

Career staff departures followed; NRC's No. 2 career operations official, a 32-year veteran and self-described two-time Trump voter, retired in May 2025 partly in protest of political operatives being embedded in senior leadership positions with what he called potential to 'significantly influence decision-making.' The Hill named that embedded political operative on July 14, 2025 as Adam Blake, a staffer detailed from the Department of Energy (not NRC itself) placed in charge of implementing EO 14300 at the commission, including overseeing the required reductions in force and structural changes meant to accelerate reactor licensing. Because Blake was detailed from DOE rather than hired by or accountable to NRC, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse called his presence 'a Department of Energy hostile takeover of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.' At a May 2025 meeting, a DOGE representative told the NRC chair and top staff that the agency would be expected to give 'rubber stamp' approval to new reactors already tested by the Energy or Defense Departments -- a directive that would bypass NRC's own independent safety review for those reactors.

On June 16, 2025, the Union of Concerned Scientists' Edwin Lyman called the firing Trump's 'latest outrageous move to undermine the independence and integrity of the agency that protects the U.S. homeland from the types of nuclear power plant disasters that devastated the former Soviet Union and Japan.' Senate Democrats Sheldon Whitehouse, Patty Murray, and Martin Heinrich said 'Trump's lawlessness threatens the Commission's ability to ensure that nuclear power plants and nuclear materials are safe and free from political interference,' and House Energy and Commerce ranking member Frank Pallone called it 'another illegal attempt to undermine independent agencies.' Pro-nuclear groups also objected to Hanson's firing that day: the Nuclear Innovation Alliance's Judi Greenwald said undermining NRC's independence is 'damaging to both long-term U.S. interests and to the ongoing work that is required to ensure that nuclear power can provide reliable and clean energy', and the American Nuclear Society said 'the arbitrary removal of commissioners without due cause creates regulatory uncertainty that threatens to delay America's nuclear energy expansion.' Greenwald had warned in May 2025, when the orders were signed, that NRC's reform progress should 'not be undermined by staffing cuts or upended by conflicting directives,' while Lyman said the administration was 'fatally compromising the independence and integrity of the NRC,' Utility Dive reported.

On June 24, 2025, nearly 30 former NRC officials and staff, organized around former NRC Chairman Stephen Burns, sent a letter of protest over Hanson's firing, warning **it "endangers the independence of the NRC as it raises the specter of political considerations carrying greater weight than public health and safety" and that compromising that independence "can only reduce the effectiveness of nuclear regulation in the United States as well as around the world, increasing the likelihood of a costly accident."** Reuters summarized the letter as saying the action put politics over safety and public health; White House spokesperson Harrison Fields responded that Trump is 'committed to modernizing nuclear regulations, streamlining regulatory barriers, and reforming the Nuclear Regulatory Commission while prioritizing safety and resilience.'

The vacancy left by Hanson's June 2025 removal was filled when Doug Weaver was sworn in December 22, 2025, restoring the commission to its full five-member statutory complement. Separately, on January 8, 2026, Trump designated Commissioner Ho Nieh -- a Republican who previously ran NRC's Office of Nuclear Reactor Regulation from 2018-2021 -- as the NRC's 20th chairman, succeeding David Wright, who continues serving as a commissioner. The commission's current composition includes Republicans Nieh and Wright alongside Democratic commissioners Matthew Marzano and Bradley Crowell. Filling that vacancy did not address the legality of Hanson's firing.

EO 14300 also directed NRC to reconsider its reliance on the decades-old linear no-threshold (LNT) radiation-exposure model in favor of "determinate" limits, and the NRC's resulting February 2026 proposed rulemaking (the "wholesale revision" already documented below) would replace the longstanding As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA) principle -- which requires operators to keep exposures below the legal limit whenever practicable -- with a "graded approach," while raising the allowable radionuclide emissions standard for a hypothetical resident at a plant's property line from 10 to 25 millirem per year. NRC Chairman Ho Nieh said the change removes "ambiguity" and does not alter worker or public exposure limits themselves, but UCS's Edwin Lyman warned some proposals could let actual exposures rise closer to the maximum caps that ALARA's separate, more conservative practice had kept them well below.

The DOGE-directed reorganization required by EO 14300 has proceeded on the order's own timeline: the NRC issued its notices of proposed rulemaking for the 'wholesale revision' of safety regulations by the February 2026 deadline, and in mid-2026 launched a major organizational restructuring -- consolidating around new-reactor, operating-reactor, and materials/waste business lines, and creating two new offices (Office of Advanced Reactors; Office of the Chief Nuclear Reactor Inspector) -- targeted for completion by September 2026, with final rules due under the EO's 18-month deadline (November 2026). Investigative reporting in March 2026 (Sludge) revealed Blake had by then also become Energy Secretary Chris Wright's 'de facto proxy' inside the NRC while simultaneously sitting on the board of KCRise Fund, a venture-capital firm funded by nuclear-industry investors -- a direct financial tie between the DOGE operative directing NRC's deregulatory restructuring and the industry that restructuring benefits, not previously disclosed when Blake's role was first reported in July 2025.

Extending the deregulatory push, the NRC voted in April 2026 to phase out its own agency-led 'force-on-force' security drills at nuclear power plants -- mock attack exercises historically run and evaluated by NRC inspectors to test each plant's defenses -- shifting to a model where plant operators run their own exercises and NRC staff only observe. Reuters reported the change came as Trump pressured the NRC to speed reactor approvals for a major nuclear-capacity expansion tied to AI, data-center, electrification, and crypto-mining electricity demand. The reorganization continued on schedule, with NRC reaffirming a target of implementing its new organization chart by the end of September 2026. On August 11, 2026, NRC published a Federal Register rule, 'NRC Modernization: Rulemaking Procedure, Federal Advisory Committee Act Alignment, Access, and Security,' extending the regulatory rewrite described above into a formal rule governing how the agency itself makes rules and manages its federal advisory committee. No update on Hanson's own removal was identified in sourcing reviewed; it remains final and unlitigated.

It followed the first removal of an NRC commissioner since the agency's 1974 creation and an executive order directing a DOGE-consulted reorganization and reductions in force, alongside an OMB-routed rulemaking process; NRC later voted in April 2026 to phase out NRC-run security drills -- at an agency that, per its Inspector General, had already fallen short of both its FY2023 hiring goal and its budgeted staffing level.

title: Federal Stop-Work Orders and Budget Cuts Forced 114 Layoffs at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, With More Following in 2026
institution: National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), Department of Energy
status: Ongoing -- a second, larger layoff round (130+ employees) followed in February 2026 under the lab's new name, National Lab of the Rockies
date_of_action: 2025-05-05 (layoffs) through 2026-02 (second layoff round)
what_changed: **On May 5, 2025, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory laid off 114 staff -- about 3% of its workforce, spanning both research and operations roles at its Golden, Colorado headquarters and among remote employees -- citing what NREL leadership's internal email described as a need to navigate 'a complex financial and operational landscape shaped by the issuance of stop work orders from federal agencies, new federal directives, and budgetary shifts.'** NREL officially characterized the cuts as 'involuntary separation' intended to redirect resources toward 'critical priorities.' title: NSF Fires 168 Staff Including Antarctic Program Managers, Disrupting U.S. Polar Research Logistics
institution: National Science Foundation
status: Partly reversed, then reorganized: NSF reinstated 84 of about 170 staff fired Feb. 18, 2025 (unreported whether Antarctic managers were among them); it abolished its divisions in Dec. 2025 and by June 2026 moved the Office of Polar Programs under the Office of the Director.
date_of_action: 2025-02-18 (NSF firings); 2025-02-27 (WIRED reports Antarctic Program disruption)
what_changed: On February 18, 2025, following Trump administration and DOGE instructions to agencies to lay off probationary employees, NSF fired 168 people -- roughly 10% of its workforce -- including probationary employees and expert appointments, according to House Science Committee Democrats; an NSF spokesperson put the number at 170. WIRED reported on February 27, 2025 that a number of NSF program managers staffed on U.S. Antarctic Program projects were among those fired. Those program managers maintained communication with NSF's infrastructure and logistics arm and the program's contractors, planned scientist deployments to the continent, and tracked budgets and funding for operations and maintenance at the program's three permanent stations (McMurdo, Palmer, and the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station); the South Pole station alone hosts the South Pole and BICEP telescopes, the IceCube neutrino detector, and NOAA's long-running Atmospheric Research Observatory. One scientist whose NSF project manager was fired told WIRED, 'Without them, everything stops,' adding that they had no idea whom to report to now or what would happen to submitted proposals. Another Antarctic scientist **warned that if the Antarctic program budget were cut, the South Pole station could quickly become impossible to keep open, and that once shut down it would be 'basically nearly impossible to bring it back up.'** A source familiar with McMurdo Station also told WIRED that, under Trump administration directives, gender-inclusive housing-preference language had been removed from Antarctic staffer forms. Scientists and outside experts warned the disruption risked ceding ground at the South Pole: WIRED's sources said Germany, Canada, Spain, and China were already recruiting U.S. Antarctic scientists, and experts raised concern that Russia and China could move to fill any resulting U.S. gap. House Science Committee Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren and Research and Technology Subcommittee Ranking Member Haley Stevens called the firings 'a massive mistake' and said NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan must reverse them, and on February 28 wrote to the National Science Board urging it to stop 'the ongoing destruction' of NSF; the letter said over three dozen program directors had been fired and that reporting had called into question 'the entire future of the U.S. Antarctic Program.' After a federal judge ruled that the administration's directives to fire probationary employees were likely unlawful, NSF reinstated 84 of the fired employees with back pay in early March 2025; the other 86, whom NSF described as intermittent employees rather than full-time staff, were not brought back. Reporting did not say whether the Antarctic program managers were among those reinstated. On May 8, 2025, NSF staff were told that all 37 of the agency's divisions would be abolished, a consolidation Science reported was driven in part by the administration's proposal to cut NSF's budget by 55% for fiscal 2026; Congress rejected that proposal and funded NSF at $8.75 billion for fiscal 2026. The realignment took effect December 15, 2025, and NSF eliminated about three-quarters of its 350 rotator positions as part of it. The administration's fiscal 2027 request, released in early April 2026, proposed moving the Office of Polar Programs out of the Geosciences Directorate and cutting it 13%, to $497 million; by early June 2026 NSF listed the Office of Polar Programs as its own office under the Office of the Director, separate from NSF's new Office of Research Infrastructure. NSF's announcements do not describe staff cuts specific to the Office of Polar Programs; NSF advertised a supervisory program manager post for its Antarctic Infrastructure and Logistics team in August 2025 and new Antarctic and Arctic program director positions in June 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
primary_proponent.role: Pressed agencies, including NSF, to fire probationary employees in February 2025 as part of a broader federal workforce-reduction mandate
primary_proponent.note: The firings followed Trump administration and DOGE instructions to agencies to lay off probationary employees, and NSF leadership carried them out; House Science Committee Democrats said NSF went beyond compliance, firing probationary employees and expert appointees in a way that captured people DOGE had not targeted. Whether the fired Antarctic program managers were probationary employees or expert appointees was not reported.

estimated_impact.summary: The February 2025 firings put about 170 NSF employees out of work and took out an unreported number of the program managers who coordinated logistics, scientist deployments and budgets for the U.S. Antarctic Program, leaving researchers unsure whom to report to or what would happen to pending proposals. Scientists warned that deeper budget cuts could force the South Pole station to close, possibly for good, and that foreign programs were already recruiting U.S. Antarctic researchers. NSF reinstated 84 of the fired employees in March 2025; whether the Antarctic managers were among them was not reported.
