title: DOGE Terminated 1,752 Active NSF Research Grants Worth $1.4 Billion, Bypassing Peer Review
institution: National Science Foundation
status: Ongoing, mixed outcome. NSF reduced external peer review in December 2025. The Ninth Circuit upheld reinstatement only for UC researchers cut over perceived DEI views (Thakur v. Trump); the government sought Supreme Court review in Aug. 2026. Nationwide AAPT v. NSF awaits a summary-judgment ruling.
date_of_action: 2025-04-18 (NSF announces terminations begin) through 2025-05 (bulk of terminations completed)
what_changed: Beginning April 18, 2025, NSF started terminating active research grants that had been flagged in an initial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) review for containing language related to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Between April and May 2025, DOGE terminated 1,752 active NSF grants worth a combined $1.4 billion. The terminations were administrative actions taken at the agency level against grant-abstract language, not decisions run back through the scientific peer-review process or NSF program officers' subject-matter judgment -- the normal mechanism by which NSF grants are awarded and, when necessary, reconsidered. Affected projects spanned a wide range of fields; reporting on individual terminated grants included projects in physics education, computer science mentoring programs for women ("sister circles"), and numerous other social-science and STEM-education projects that referenced diversity or inclusion in their framing, alongside grants in climate and public-health-adjacent research. NSF separately halted new grant awards for a period to conduct a second administrative review of pending awards. Later in 2025, NSF restructured its peer-review process itself, effective December 15, 2025: the minimum number of required external reviewers per grant was cut from three to two (with one of the two now permitted to be an NSF staff reviewer rather than an outside scientist), panel discussions became optional rather than mandatory, and required panel summary write-ups were shortened to three-to-five sentences. Update 2026-08-17: this entry's original write-up (2026-08-12) omitted a material court ruling that predated it by more than two months. Six University of California faculty had sued in Thakur v. Trump (N.D. Cal.), and on June 23, 2025, Judge Rita Lin issued a class-wide preliminary injunction ordering NSF, NEH, and EPA to stop DEI/environmental-justice-based grant terminations and reinstate previously-terminated grants to two provisionally certified UC plaintiff classes (those who received generic form-letter terminations, and those terminated specifically under the DEI executive orders). The Ninth Circuit denied the government's stay request on August 21, 2025, but hours later the Supreme Court decided NIH v. American Public Health Association, and the appeals court then withdrew that order and replaced it with one that stayed the injunction as to the form-letter class. On May 26, 2026, the Ninth Circuit panel affirmed the preliminary injunction in part and reversed it in part. It upheld reinstatement for the DEI Termination Class, finding those researchers likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim: the agencies had selected grants for termination based only on recipients' perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental-justice viewpoints, which likely amounts to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. It reversed as to the Form Termination Class, holding that under the Supreme Court's NIH decision that class's APA claim was likely a contract claim belonging in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, not district court. This was an appeal of a preliminary injunction, not a final judgment, and the reinstatement it upheld covers only UC researchers in the DEI Termination Class -- it does not reopen or resolve the roughly 1,700 other NSF terminations nationwide, which no court has ordered restored. Update 2026-08-29: that separate case is American Association of Physics Teachers v. NSF (1:25-cv-01923, D.D.C.), filed June 18, 2025 by AAPT, AAC&U, WEPAN, AERA, AAUP, and the UAW, and assigned to Judge Jia Cobb. Judge Cobb denied plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion on September 10, 2025 -- the same Tucker Act/jurisdictional theory applied two months earlier in the Vera Institute DOJ-grants case elsewhere in this tracker, which Judge Cobb cited, finding the court lacked jurisdiction to order interim restoration of the funds and that plaintiffs had not shown irreparable harm -- meaning the more than $1 billion in NSF terminations at issue were allowed to stand while the case proceeds, not because a court found the terminations lawful on the merits. The case continued past that point: on March 25, 2026, Judge Cobb granted NSF's motion to dismiss in part and denied it in part. She dismissed plaintiffs' retrospective APA claims challenging the loss of their grant funding for lack of jurisdiction, and separately dismissed their constitutional, ultra vires and unlawful-withholding claims on other grounds, but let their prospective APA claims challenging NSF's 2025 'Change in Priorities Decision' as arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law proceed. Update 2026-08-31 (real correction): this entry's prior text stopped at the partial motion-to-dismiss ruling in AAPT v. NSF. The case has since moved well past that point: per the court's July 9, 2026 amended scheduling order, plaintiffs filed their motion for summary judgment (with supporting memorandum and multiple declarations) on July 23, 2026, plus an errata/additional declaration on July 24; the government responded on August 20, 2026 with a combined memorandum opposing plaintiffs' summary-judgment motion, a cross-motion for its own summary judgment, and a motion to strike certain plaintiff exhibits. Plaintiffs' reply and cross-opposition are due September 3, 2026, the government's reply due September 17, 2026, and a joint appendix due October 1, 2026. This is a substantive procedural advance -- from a motion-to-dismiss stage where only the sufficiency of the pleadings was at issue, to full summary-judgment briefing where the merits of the surviving prospective challenge to NSF's 'Change in Priorities Decision' are now before the court. Contemporaneous reporting fills in the termination wave's own timeline: an early, disinformation-research-specific tranche hit first, on April 22, 2025 -- more than 50 grants worth a combined $9 million, including Vanderbilt researcher Lisa Fazio's work on how false beliefs form and spread, terminated under the banner of Trump's 'free speech' executive order rather than the DEI framing that dominates this entry's later, larger figures. Three days later, on April 25, 2025, NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan resigned, citing an inability to continue advancing the agency's mission under the cuts; by that point, reporting tallied over $230 million in terminated grants, including work on racial equity, DEI in STEM, vaccine information, and disinformation. The termination count continued climbing through the terminations documented above: roughly 700 grants by April 28 (the day after Panchanathan's resignation), and by May 12, 2025, NSF eliminated its Division of Equity for Excellence in STEM entirely, canceled 73 additional grants, and purged approximately 70 staff with another 300 temporary roles marked for elimination -- a staffing reduction distinct from, and later than, the separate February 2025 168-position NSF cut documented in this database's entry on NSF's firing of Antarctic program staff. By May 24, 2025, cumulative reporting put the total at over 1,400 grants worth roughly $1 billion, with **STEM-education projects making up 54% of that total ($773 million) -- disproportionately affecting programs serving underserved students, including Indigenous youth and rural Black students specifically named in reporting.** The same week, separate reporting found NSF's grant-award rate had fallen to its slowest pace in more than 35 years, with new funding down 51% year-over-year, alongside a running tally of 1,600+ canceled awards worth $1.5 billion -- figures that, per this entry's existing caveat, come from contemporaneous press analysis rather than NSF's own later-published $1.4B/1,752-grant figure, and likely reflect an earlier snapshot in the same ongoing termination process rather than a contradiction of it. Separately, on August 1, 2025, U.S. District Judge John Cronan in New York declined to order NSF to restart payments in a different lawsuit brought by 16 Democratic-led states, allowing the agency to keep withholding hundreds of millions of dollars (for halted research on misinformation, DEI, artificial intelligence, PTSD in veterans, and K-12 STEM education) while that case proceeded, in part because the Court of Federal Claims may have jurisdiction over what is essentially a case about money -- reasoning similar to Judge Cobb's September 10, 2025 preliminary-injunction denial in AAPT v. NSF. Update 2026-09-29: the government did not let the Ninth Circuit's Thakur ruling stand. On August 18, 2026, the Solicitor General petitioned the Supreme Court (Trump v. Thakur, No. 26-210), asking whether the First Amendment bars the government from considering the viewpoints furthered by academic research projects when deciding whether to grant or terminate their funding through competitive grant programs; the Court extended the researchers' response deadline to October 19, 2026. The petition says the NSF and NEH grants at issue in the case were awarded approximately $150 million and had approximately $59 million remaining when terminated, and that the researchers have reached a settlement in principle with EPA but not with NSF or NEH. In the district court, the researchers moved for summary judgment and class certification on July 15, 2026, the government cross-moved on August 21, and the researchers replied on September 18. In AAPT v. NSF, the scheduled summary-judgment briefing was completed on time: plaintiffs filed their reply and cross-opposition on September 3, 2026 and the government its reply on September 17, with the joint appendix due October 1, 2026. The court has not yet ruled on the cross-motions.

A federal appeals court has since upheld reinstatement only for University of California researchers whose grants were cut over perceived DEI or environmental-justice viewpoints, a ruling the government has asked the Supreme Court to overturn. The great majority of the 1,752 terminations remain in effect, and the separate nationwide case can no longer restore the lost funds directly: its claims seeking that were dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

glance.what: Terminated 1,752 NSF grants worth $1.4B, bypassing peer review; courts upheld only some UC reinstatements

what_changed.base: Beginning April 18, 2025, NSF started terminating active research grants that had been flagged in an initial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) review for containing language related to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI). Between April and May 2025, DOGE terminated 1,752 active NSF grants worth a combined $1.4 billion. The terminations were administrative actions taken at the agency level against grant-abstract language, not decisions run back through the scientific peer-review process or NSF program officers' subject-matter judgment -- the normal mechanism by which NSF grants are awarded and, when necessary, reconsidered. Affected projects spanned a wide range of fields; reporting on individual terminated grants included projects in physics education, computer science mentoring programs for women ("sister circles"), and numerous other social-science and STEM-education projects that referenced diversity or inclusion in their framing, alongside grants in climate and public-health-adjacent research. NSF separately halted new grant awards for a period to conduct a second administrative review of pending awards. Later in 2025, NSF restructured its peer-review process itself, effective December 15, 2025: the minimum number of required external reviewers per grant was cut from three to two (with one of the two now permitted to be an NSF staff reviewer rather than an outside scientist), panel discussions became optional rather than mandatory, and required panel summary write-ups were shortened to three-to-five sentences.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-17: this entry's original write-up (2026-08-12) omitted a material court ruling that predated it by more than two months. Six University of California faculty had sued in Thakur v. Trump (N.D. Cal.), and on June 23, 2025, Judge Rita Lin issued a class-wide preliminary injunction ordering NSF, NEH, and EPA to stop DEI/environmental-justice-based grant terminations and reinstate previously-terminated grants to two provisionally certified UC plaintiff classes (those who received generic form-letter terminations, and those terminated specifically under the DEI executive orders). The Ninth Circuit denied the government's stay request on August 21, 2025, but hours later the Supreme Court decided NIH v. American Public Health Association, and the appeals court then withdrew that order and replaced it with one that stayed the injunction as to the form-letter class. On May 26, 2026, the Ninth Circuit panel affirmed the preliminary injunction in part and reversed it in part. It upheld reinstatement for the DEI Termination Class, finding those researchers likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim: the agencies had selected grants for termination based only on recipients' perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental-justice viewpoints, which likely amounts to unconstitutional viewpoint discrimination. It reversed as to the Form Termination Class, holding that under the Supreme Court's NIH decision that class's APA claim was likely a contract claim belonging in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, not district court. This was an appeal of a preliminary injunction, not a final judgment, and the reinstatement it upheld covers only UC researchers in the DEI Termination Class -- it does not reopen or resolve the roughly 1,700 other NSF terminations nationwide, which no court has ordered restored.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-29: that separate case is American Association of Physics Teachers v. NSF (1:25-cv-01923, D.D.C.), filed June 18, 2025 by AAPT, AAC&U, WEPAN, AERA, AAUP, and the UAW, and assigned to Judge Jia Cobb. Judge Cobb denied plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion on September 10, 2025 -- the same Tucker Act/jurisdictional theory applied two months earlier in the Vera Institute DOJ-grants case elsewhere in this tracker, which Judge Cobb cited, finding the court lacked jurisdiction to order interim restoration of the funds and that plaintiffs had not shown irreparable harm -- meaning the more than $1 billion in NSF terminations at issue were allowed to stand while the case proceeds, not because a court found the terminations lawful on the merits. The case continued past that point: on March 25, 2026, Judge Cobb granted NSF's motion to dismiss in part and denied it in part. She dismissed plaintiffs' retrospective APA claims challenging the loss of their grant funding for lack of jurisdiction, and separately dismissed their constitutional, ultra vires and unlawful-withholding claims on other grounds, but let their prospective APA claims challenging NSF's 2025 'Change in Priorities Decision' as arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law proceed.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-08-31 (real correction): this entry's prior text stopped at the partial motion-to-dismiss ruling in AAPT v. NSF. The case has since moved well past that point: per the court's July 9, 2026 amended scheduling order, plaintiffs filed their motion for summary judgment (with supporting memorandum and multiple declarations) on July 23, 2026, plus an errata/additional declaration on July 24; the government responded on August 20, 2026 with a combined memorandum opposing plaintiffs' summary-judgment motion, a cross-motion for its own summary judgment, and a motion to strike certain plaintiff exhibits. Plaintiffs' reply and cross-opposition are due September 3, 2026, the government's reply due September 17, 2026, and a joint appendix due October 1, 2026. This is a substantive procedural advance -- from a motion-to-dismiss stage where only the sufficiency of the pleadings was at issue, to full summary-judgment briefing where the merits of the surviving prospective challenge to NSF's 'Change in Priorities Decision' are now before the court. Contemporaneous reporting fills in the termination wave's own timeline: an early, disinformation-research-specific tranche hit first, on April 22, 2025 -- more than 50 grants worth a combined $9 million, including Vanderbilt researcher Lisa Fazio's work on how false beliefs form and spread, terminated under the banner of Trump's 'free speech' executive order rather than the DEI framing that dominates this entry's later, larger figures. Three days later, on April 25, 2025, NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan resigned, citing an inability to continue advancing the agency's mission under the cuts; by that point, reporting tallied over $230 million in terminated grants, including work on racial equity, DEI in STEM, vaccine information, and disinformation. The termination count continued climbing through the terminations documented above: roughly 700 grants by April 28 (the day after Panchanathan's resignation), and by May 12, 2025, NSF eliminated its Division of Equity for Excellence in STEM entirely, canceled 73 additional grants, and purged approximately 70 staff with another 300 temporary roles marked for elimination -- a staffing reduction distinct from, and later than, the separate February 2025 168-position NSF cut documented in this database's entry on NSF's firing of Antarctic program staff. By May 24, 2025, cumulative reporting put the total at over 1,400 grants worth roughly $1 billion, with **STEM-education projects making up 54% of that total ($773 million) -- disproportionately affecting programs serving underserved students, including Indigenous youth and rural Black students specifically named in reporting.** The same week, separate reporting found NSF's grant-award rate had fallen to its slowest pace in more than 35 years, with new funding down 51% year-over-year, alongside a running tally of 1,600+ canceled awards worth $1.5 billion -- figures that, per this entry's existing caveat, come from contemporaneous press analysis rather than NSF's own later-published $1.4B/1,752-grant figure, and likely reflect an earlier snapshot in the same ongoing termination process rather than a contradiction of it. Separately, on August 1, 2025, U.S. District Judge John Cronan in New York declined to order NSF to restart payments in a different lawsuit brought by 16 Democratic-led states, allowing the agency to keep withholding hundreds of millions of dollars (for halted research on misinformation, DEI, artificial intelligence, PTSD in veterans, and K-12 STEM education) while that case proceeded, in part because the Court of Federal Claims may have jurisdiction over what is essentially a case about money -- reasoning similar to Judge Cobb's September 10, 2025 preliminary-injunction denial in AAPT v. NSF.

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-09-29: the government did not let the Ninth Circuit's Thakur ruling stand. On August 18, 2026, the Solicitor General petitioned the Supreme Court (Trump v. Thakur, No. 26-210), asking whether the First Amendment bars the government from considering the viewpoints furthered by academic research projects when deciding whether to grant or terminate their funding through competitive grant programs; the Court extended the researchers' response deadline to October 19, 2026. The petition says the NSF and NEH grants at issue in the case were awarded approximately $150 million and had approximately $59 million remaining when terminated, and that the researchers have reached a settlement in principle with EPA but not with NSF or NEH. In the district court, the researchers moved for summary judgment and class certification on July 15, 2026, the government cross-moved on August 21, and the researchers replied on September 18. In AAPT v. NSF, the scheduled summary-judgment briefing was completed on time: plaintiffs filed their reply and cross-opposition on September 3, 2026 and the government its reply on September 17, with the joint appendix due October 1, 2026. The court has not yet ruled on the cross-motions.

title: DOGE Terminated 1,752 NSF Research Grants Using a Senator's Keyword List, Then NSF Formally Weakened Its Own Peer Review Standards
institution: National Science Foundation (NSF)
status: Largely complete (terminations executed; peer-review rule changes formally in effect since Dec. 15, 2025)
date_of_action: 2025-04-14 (DOGE arrives at NSF) through 2025-12-15 (formal peer-review process change takes effect)
what_changed: On April 14, 2025, three DOGE personnel arrived at NSF headquarters and were given direct access to the agency's internal grant management systems -- an unusual level of access for political appointees into a agency's live award-processing systems, which one NSF program officer told Nature 'raises the hairs on the back of our neck.' DOGE ordered NSF's grants division to pull back all proposals that had already cleared full peer review and internal approval but were awaiting final signoff, instructing career program officers to perform undefined 'mitigation work' to bring the proposals into compliance with Trump executive orders restricting research related to diversity, equity, and inclusion or climate change. NSF ultimately terminated 1,752 active grants worth $1.4 billion. The screening process relied substantially on a list of roughly 3,400 grants compiled by Sen. Ted Cruz's office, which Cruz characterized as funding 'neo-Marxist class warfare propaganda'; independent analysis by the Grant Watch project found the terminated grants' titles and abstracts most frequently contained the words 'Black,' 'climate,' 'student,' 'justice,' 'identity,' and 'teacher' -- and that NSF's STEM Education directorate alone lost 839 grants worth $888 million, nearly half of all dollars terminated agency-wide despite being a small fraction of NSF's total budget. NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan resigned during this period. Separately, effective December 15, 2025, NSF formally revised its own peer review standards (PAPPG 24-1 Supplement 1): the minimum number of required external reviews per proposal dropped from three to two, one of which may now be an NSF staff member rather than an outside expert; panel discussions became optional rather than required; and panel summary write-ups were capped at three to five sentences, down from what had often run several paragraphs. NSF attributed the peer-review changes to a proposal backlog and workforce reductions, not to the DOGE-driven terminations directly. Update 2026-07-28: On April 24, 2026, **all 22 members of the National Science Board (NSF's presidentially-appointed governing/oversight body) received an email notifying them, without explanation, that their positions were 'terminated, effective immediately.'** On May 12, 2026, roughly 1,500 members and supporters of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine -- including 37 Nobel Prize winners -- denounced the dismissal in an open letter calling it 'an alarming attack on the ability of the US to engage in basic and applied research.' Separately, nearly 150 NSF employees sent their own letter of dissent to Congress, warning that the administration's actions -- including steep budget cuts, mass firings, grant terminations, and withholding of billions in appropriated funds -- threaten to dismantle the agency, and calling for congressional intervention.

primary_proponent.name: DOGE personnel Luke Farritor and Zachary Terrell
primary_proponent.role: DOGE staff embedded at NSF with direct grant-system access
primary_proponent.note: Then-NSF Director Sethuraman Panchanathan wrote in an internal priorities update that efforts to broaden research participation 'should not preference some groups at the expense of others' -- the stated policy rationale for the review -- before resigning shortly afterward. Sen. Ted Cruz is the named source of the keyword-flagged grant list that substantially shaped which proposals were targeted, though NSF and the White House have not published an official list or criteria of their own, leaving outside researchers (Grant Watch) to reconstruct the pattern independently from grant titles and abstracts.

estimated_impact.summary: Congress separately and explicitly rejected a much larger cut: the FY2026 appropriations bill (signed January 23, 2026) funded NSF at $8.75 billion, refusing the White House's request to cut the agency to $3.9 billion (roughly 55%), which NSF's own internal projections said would have dropped grant funding rates to approximately 7%. The Senate Commerce Committee described the enacted funding level as preventing 'an existential threat to U.S. science funding.' This creates a notable split: Congress protected NSF's overall budget, while DOGE's targeted, keyword-driven terminations and the subsequent peer-review rule changes altered the agency's internal operations and standards in ways that did not require, and were not subject to, the same congressional appropriations fight.

NSF's own stated reason for the December 2025 peer-review changes (backlog and workforce reductions) is a genuine alternative explanation distinct from the DOGE terminations, and should be presented as the agency's own account rather than dismissed.

title: NSF Announced Dismantling 80% of $368M Ocean Monitoring Network, Then Reversed Course After Bipartisan Congressional Revolt
institution: National Science Foundation (NSF)
status: Reversed -- NSF announced in mid-June 2026 it would terminate the dismantlement plan and reinstall already-removed Pacific Northwest instruments, following bipartisan Senate and House letters demanding the array's preservation
date_of_action: 2026-05 (dismantlement announced) through 2026-06-18 (reversal announced)
what_changed: In May 2026, NSF announced plans to remove roughly 900 deep-sea instruments from the Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI), a $368 million network operating continuously since 2016 that monitors ocean currents, marine heat waves, carbon absorption, coastal flooding risk, fisheries conditions, and broader climate indicators across sites off Oregon, Washington, Alaska, North Carolina, and the Irminger Sea between Greenland and Iceland. **NSF said it would begin removing instruments in June 2026, projecting roughly $48 million in annual operational savings, and had in fact begun removing equipment from Pacific Northwest waters before Congress intervened.** On June 16, 2026, a bipartisan group of senators -- led by Democrat Jeff Merkley and Republican Lisa Murkowski, joined by Sens. Markey, Warren, Baldwin, Murray, Cantwell, Whitehouse, Van Hollen, and Wyden -- sent a letter to NSF directing it to terminate the dismantlement plan and maintain the array; House lawmakers sent a parallel letter the same day. On June 18, 2026, NSF issued an unsigned statement reversing course: it would terminate the plan to disband 80% of OOI and reinstall the equipment already removed from Pacific Northwest waters.

primary_proponent.name: National Science Foundation leadership (unsigned June 18, 2026 reversal statement; original dismantlement announcement made under NSF's Trump-appointed leadership)
primary_proponent.role: Federal agency responsible for basic-science funding and infrastructure, including OOI
primary_proponent.note: NSF's original decision to dismantle 80% of a $368 million active climate-monitoring network -- and its reversal only after direct, bipartisan congressional intervention -- is the accountability record this entry documents; no single named official's public statement defending the original dismantlement decision was identified in reporting reviewed.

estimated_impact.summary: Scientists and lawmakers characterized the initial plan as eliminating one of the only continuous, real-time ocean-climate monitoring systems along U.S. coasts at a moment of accelerating climate risk, warning it would create a lasting data gap for tracking phenomena like Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) slowdown, marine heat waves, and coastal flooding risk. The bipartisan, cross-chamber reversal within roughly five weeks of the announcement is itself notable: an unusually fast congressional check on an agency-level dismantlement decision, in contrast to many other entries in this tracker where similar actions proceeded without reversal.

title: BEAD Broadband Program Director Resigned, Warning Trump Commerce Department Was Rewriting $42.5B Rural Internet Program to Favor Musk's Starlink Over Fiber
institution: National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), U.S. Department of Commerce
status: Program rules under active revision by Commerce/NTIA as of Feinman's March 2025 departure, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick publicly framing the change as removing 'pointless requirements'
date_of_action: 2025-03-14 (Feinman's resignation announced) through 2025-03-15 (last day)
what_changed: Evan Feinman, director of the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program -- a $42.5 billion program created to expand high-speed internet to unserved and underserved rural areas -- resigned effective March 15, 2025, after the program came under review by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who said the review was aimed at eliminating 'pointless requirements' and cutting 'delays and waste.' **In a farewell email to colleagues, Feinman wrote that 'stranding all or part of rural America with worse internet so that we can make the world's richest man even richer is yet another in a long line of betrayals by Washington,'** warning that the administration's review was poised to shift federal broadband funding away from fiber-optic buildout and toward satellite internet service, specifically naming Elon Musk's Starlink as the likely beneficiary. Feinman argued satellite technology is inferior to fiber for the program's purposes and that the shift would leave rural communities with worse service while enriching Musk, who separately led DOGE's federal cost-cutting effort at the time. title: NTSB Vice Chair Alvin Brown Fired Without Cause, in Apparent Violation of the Board's Own Statute
institution: National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB)
status: Litigation ongoing -- Brown's lawsuit, amended to add race-discrimination claims, remained pending in the U.S. District Court for D.C. as of this entry's write date, with no final ruling identified
date_of_action: 2025-05-05 (removal) through 2026 (litigation ongoing)
what_changed: On May 5, 2025, **the Trump White House removed Alvin Brown, the NTSB's Vice Chair, from the board -- a Biden appointee confirmed by the Senate in December 2024 to a term running through December 31, 2026, and the board's only Black member.** The Independent Safety Board Act of 1974, which governs the NTSB, permits a board member's removal only for 'inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office'; the White House did not cite any of those grounds or offer any public justification for the removal. Brown filed a lawsuit challenging the removal as unlawful; on December 4, 2025, he amended the complaint to add race-discrimination claims, arguing the removal was part of a broader pattern of the administration disproportionately firing Black officials from independent multimember agencies -- his attorneys stated roughly 75% of Black officials at such agencies have been removed under this administration, and Brown specifically named the NLRB, EEOC, and Federal Reserve as agencies with comparable patterns. Separately, in December 2025, the Senate Commerce Committee voted to advance a replacement nominee for Brown's seat, prompting Sen. Maria Cantwell to criticize Republicans for proceeding while Brown's removal was still being litigated as unlawful. As of this entry's write date, Brown's case remained pending in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia with no final ruling identified.

primary_proponent.note: The White House directed Brown's removal without citing any of the statute's three permitted for-cause grounds; no more specific individual official was named in sourcing as the one who executed the removal beyond 'the White House.'

title: National Weather Service Lost ~600 Staff, Including a Vacant Position Tied to the Texas Flood Warnings
institution: National Weather Service (NWS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Department of Commerce
status: Partially reversed: in early June 2026 NWS was still 300+ employees below early-2025 levels, though under a 450-hire authorization it had onboarded 300+ staff by late June; a reorganization was underway, and lost senior experience is not replaced by entry-level hiring.
date_of_action: Early-mid 2025 (initial cuts); rehiring and reorganization ongoing through at least June 2026
what_changed: Early in 2025, DOGE-driven early retirement incentives and probationary-employee firings cut roughly 600 employees (about 15% of staff) from the National Weather Service nationwide, part of broader cuts to its parent agency NOAA. Across NOAA, probationary workers who were fired in February 2025, reinstated under court orders in March and fired again in April told NBC News the process was chaotic -- one called it 'intentional chaos' -- and some reported missed paychecks, lapsed health insurance and trouble claiming unemployment benefits. By mid-May 2025, according to the NWS Employees Organization union, 52 of the NWS's 122 weather forecast offices had staffing vacancy rates above 20%, and at least 8 offices, including Sacramento, Goodland (KS), and Jackson (KY), had stopped or were about to stop overnight operations, breaking the service's 24/7 coverage. **Former NWS directors wrote publicly that 'our worst nightmare is that weather forecast offices will be so understaffed that there will be needless loss of life.'** Specifically at the Austin/San Antonio forecast office -- which covers the Texas Hill Country -- the warning coordination meteorologist position (responsible for working directly with emergency managers and the public on what to do when a disaster strikes) had been vacant since the person who held it for decades accepted an early-retirement offer at the end of April 2025, roughly two months before the deadly July 4, 2025 Guadalupe River flash flood that killed more than 100 people. The office's science and operations officer had also left in April, and its meteorology staff had a vacancy rate of about 15% when the flood hit, KUT News reported. On July 7, 2025, three days after the flood began, a White House memorandum extended the government-wide federal hiring freeze through October 15, 2025; the memo exempted positions related to public safety and left existing OPM exemptions in place, but the Center for American Progress read it as barring vacancies from being filled until after the extreme-weather season. In August 2025, President Trump granted the weather service an emergency authorization to hire 450 meteorologists, hydrologists and radar technicians over the following year. On September 27, 2025, the Washington Post reported that nearly 600 workers, about 1 in 7, had left the weather service through firings, resignations or retirements, and that some staffers were working double shifts to keep forecast offices open, others were relying on a 'buddy system' in which adjacent offices monitored severe weather in understaffed regions, and some were dropping services deemed not absolutely necessary, such as presentations to schoolchildren. Hiring under that authorization began in late 2025. In April 2026, as the agency was undergoing a reorganization, an NWS spokesperson said 'There are no staff cuts planned at NWS. In fact, we are hiring,' and that more than 200 positions had been filled since late 2025; Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Congress the same week, 'We do not have staffing issues.' In May 2026 the weather service announced it would recruit another 150 entry-level meteorologists. As of early June 2026, E&E News reported, NWS had hired about 274 people under the authorization but remained more than 300 employees below its staffing at the start of 2025; federal employment data reviewed by CBS News showed NOAA had nearly 300 fewer meteorologists and hydrologists at the end of May 2026 than in January 2025, and the agency said more than 300 new employees had been onboarded by late June. Former NWS meteorologists told CBS News the rebuilt workforce skews inexperienced -- 'because there are no old-timers left,' as one Alaska-based former NWS meteorologist put it -- and two of them said 'upper air' data from weather balloons, which many consider fundamental to forecast models, has noticeably declined or degraded since January 2025; CBS reported that several stations still did not launch balloons twice daily or at consistent morning and evening times. NWS attributed those schedule changes to 'temporary resource and equipment constraints' and said its model performance 'shows no evidence of overall degradation due to variations in balloon launch schedules'; the balloon-launch cuts themselves are tracked in a separate entry in this database.

primary_proponent.name: DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) / NOAA leadership
primary_proponent.role: Executed the early-2025 workforce reductions
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in available reporting as personally directing the NWS-specific cuts -- this was part of the broader, DOGE-driven federal workforce reduction effort. NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs stated during his confirmation hearing that he would 'ensure that staffing the Weather Service offices is a top priority,' an on-the-record commitment worth checking against subsequent NWS staffing trends.

estimated_impact.summary: The cuts thinned the forecasters and coordinators who turn forecasts into public action. By mid-May 2025, 52 of 122 forecast offices had vacancy rates above 20% and at least 8 had stopped or were about to stop overnight operations. The Austin/San Antonio office covering the Texas Hill Country had lost its warning coordination meteorologist, the person who works with emergency managers and the public on what to do in a disaster, and its science and operations officer before the July 4, 2025 flood that killed more than 100 people; that office's forecasts and warnings were timely, and no study has tied specific deaths to the vacancies. By fall 2025 staff were working double shifts, leaning on neighboring offices and dropping non-essential services. Rehiring since late 2025 has brought in 300+ mostly entry-level staff, but in early June 2026 NWS was still more than 300 employees below its early-2025 level, with much of its senior experience gone.

The Texas flood link is about a vacant coordination role, not proven causation: former NWS meteorologists and the Center for American Progress (a progressive advocacy group) credit the Austin/San Antonio office with timely, accurate forecasts, and no study has attributed specific deaths to the vacancies. Effects on forecast quality from lost experience and reduced weather-balloon data are reported by former staff but not measured; NWS says it has found no evidence of overall model degradation from balloon schedule changes.

title: NWS Suspended or Cut Weather Balloon Launches at 11 Sites After Staffing Cuts; Delayed Launches Coincided With Surprise 2026 Tornado Outbreaks
institution: National Weather Service (NOAA, Department of Commerce)
status: Partly restored -- by September 2026 most of the 11 sites again launch twice daily, but six Plains and Western sites fly the morning balloon at midday, after morning model runs, and Green Bay launches once daily; Kotzebue unconfirmed
date_of_action: 2025-02-27 to 2025-03-20 (suspension/reduction notices); partial effect ongoing through 2026
what_changed: On February 26, 2025, OMB Director Russell Vought and then-Acting OPM Director Charles Ezell issued a memo directing federal agencies to prepare for mass layoffs. Separately, acting on OPM's direction to cut probationary staff, NOAA fired several hundred probationary employees on February 27, 2025 -- roughly 650 by the count of Sen. Chris Van Hollen's office and former NOAA Administrator Rick Spinrad -- on top of about 500 employees who had already left under the deferred-resignation offer, and NOAA staff said they had been ordered to identify another 1,029 positions for termination. The National Weather Service, citing 'a lack of Weather Forecast Office (WFO) staffing,' cut twice-daily weather balloon (radiosonde) launches at 11 upper-air sites in four notices on three dates: it indefinitely suspended launches at Kotzebue, Alaska, effective February 27, 2025; on March 7 it began intermittently suspending launches at Albany, New York, and Gray, Maine, saying those offices would 'perform twice daily launches when staffing permits'; and on March 20 it suspended launches at Omaha, Nebraska, and Rapid City, South Dakota, and cut launches to once daily at Aberdeen, South Dakota; Grand Junction, Colorado; Green Bay, Wisconsin; Gaylord, Michigan; North Platte, Nebraska; and Riverton, Wyoming. On April 17, 2025, NWS added a general notice that it may temporarily reduce or suspend scheduled launches at selected sites 'due to staffing limitations or operational priorities.' Some cuts were soon partly reversed: in late April 2025 Rep. Mike Flood said two forecasters on temporary duty were being sent to the Omaha office so it could return to two launches a day. At many sites that kept or resumed two launches a day, the morning flight -- traditionally released at the same time nationwide -- was moved to midday, when day-shift staff are on duty, so its data arrived after the morning forecast-model runs. The disruption continued into the 2026 severe-weather season. In March 2026 no tornado watch was issued for southern Michigan before tornadoes killed four people there, though local offices did issue warnings, and Michigan's two senators asked NWS whether short staffing played a role. NBC News, NPR and KCUR then reported that meteorologists linked missing and delayed morning balloon data to a tornado outbreak that caught forecasters by surprise near Kansas City: **on April 13, 2026, NWS forecast almost no chance of tornadoes in east central Kansas, balloons across a wide swath of the West and Plains went up only around midday or early afternoon, after storms were already brewing, and the tornado watch came about 30 minutes before the first tornado.** Local offices did issue tornado warnings, and no one was seriously hurt. NWS said its model performance had not been affected by the launch-schedule changes and that almost all of its roughly 92 launch sites were functioning normally, with only a few missed launches. The Boston Globe reported that March 2026 saw 202 tornadoes nationally -- more than double the 30-year average for that month -- and April 2026 had 250 by April 28 versus a 180 average for the full month, with forecasters attributing part of the shortfall in advance warning to staffing and resource gaps at NWS offices, of which 122 exist nationwide. By September 2026 most of the 11 sites were again flying two balloons a day, but the restoration was partial: a review of NWS sounding records in Iowa State University's Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive shows that for September 1-26, 2026, Gaylord, Albany and Gray were on the standard morning-and-evening schedule; Omaha, Rapid City, Aberdeen, Grand Junction, North Platte and Riverton were launching twice a day but with the morning flight moved to midday; and Green Bay was launching only once a day, at midday. Kotzebue's current schedule could not be confirmed. Outside the 11 sites, the Salt Lake City office, which had also moved its morning launch to midday, restored its pre-cut launch schedule in August 2026.

primary_proponent.note: Co-signed, with then-Acting OPM Director Charles Ezell, the February 26, 2025 memo directing federal agencies to prepare for mass layoffs, one day before NOAA, acting on OPM's direction, fired roughly 650 probationary employees -- part of the staffing loss behind the 'lack of WFO staffing' NWS cited in its balloon-launch suspensions.

estimated_impact.summary: Staffing losses cut NWS's twice-daily weather balloon launches, a core input to forecast models, at 11 sites in early 2025. Most sites later resumed two launches a day, but in 2026 several Plains and Western sites still flew their morning balloon at midday, after the morning model runs. Meteorologists tie that data gap to a tornado outbreak forecasters did not see coming near Kansas City on April 13, 2026, when the watch came about 30 minutes before the first tornado; reporters note a similar case weeks earlier in southern Michigan, where no tornado watch was issued before tornadoes killed four people. Local warnings were issued in both cases, and NWS says model performance has not degraded.

title: HR1 ("One Big Beautiful Bill") Federal Funding Cuts Strip Essential Plan Coverage From ~450,000 New Yorkers
institution: New York State of Health Essential Plan (federal Basic Health Program, funded through HHS/CMS)
status: Ongoing -- eligibility changes took effect July 1, 2026; the August 30, 2026 gap-free-enrollment deadline has now passed with interim data (as of July 31) showing roughly 44% of the ~450,000 affected still without confirmed replacement coverage; New York State has taken some mitigating action and may seek further restoration funding in the 2027 legislative session, but has not restored coverage to all affected enrollees
date_of_action: 2026-07-01 (eligibility changes take effect, following earlier-2026 enactment of HR1)
what_changed: HR1, the reconciliation law Trump signed in 2026 and that the administration has branded the 'One Big Beautiful Bill,' cut federal funding underlying New York's Essential Plan -- a Basic Health Program that had provided low-cost coverage to low- and middle-income residents who earn too much for Medicaid but still qualify for ACA marketplace subsidy support. **As of July 1, 2026, New Yorkers earning between 200% and 250% of the federal poverty level (a single-person household income of roughly $31,920 to $39,900 per year) lost eligibility for subsidized Essential Plan coverage entirely, and an estimated 450,000 New Yorkers lost coverage as a result.** The law is projected to eliminate $7.5 billion in annual federal funding for the program, which had covered nearly 1.7 million low- and middle-income New Yorkers before the cuts. New York Governor Kathy Hochul's administration used a Basic Health Program waiver mechanism to access billions in a federal trust fund and partially mitigate the impact, preserving coverage for a majority of enrollees, but did not fully offset the loss for the affected income band. title: House Republicans' Reconciliation Megabill Would Strip ACA Cost-Sharing Payments From Insurers Covering Abortion, Clashing With 12 States' Coverage Mandates
institution: House of Representatives / Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
status: Passed the House as part of the broader reconciliation megabill; provision's ultimate Senate/enactment fate tracked as part of the broader bill's status
date_of_action: 2025-06 (reporting on the bill provision) with the exclusion set to take effect in 2027
what_changed: House Republicans' 2025 budget reconciliation megabill (the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act') included a provision that, starting in 2027, would exclude health plans that cover abortion from receiving federal cost-sharing reduction (CSR) payments -- payments that lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs for low-income ACA marketplace enrollees generally, not specifically tied to abortion coverage. **Because losing CSR payments would make an insurer's plans meaningfully less affordable and competitive across their entire enrollee base, the provision creates a strong financial incentive for insurers to drop abortion coverage entirely rather than lose the broader subsidy.** This directly clashes with the 12 states (plus the District of Columbia, per broader coverage-landscape reporting) that require ACA marketplace plans to cover abortion -- states whose own mandates the federal provision would financially penalize insurers for complying with. title: OBBBA's Child Tax Credit Rewrite Softened a Two-Parent SSN Rule Before Passage but Left 17 Million Low-Income Children Without the Full Credit
institution: Internal Revenue Service (IRS), implementing Congress's One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) child tax credit provisions
status: In effect since the 2025 tax year; no legislative change since enactment found in sourcing reviewed. The House-passed two-parent Social Security Number requirement was narrowed by the Senate before final passage, but the credit's continued nonrefundability for the lowest-income families -- a much larger exclusion mechanism -- remains unchanged.
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (OBBBA signed into law); child tax credit provisions effective beginning tax year 2025
what_changed: The Child Tax Credit (CTC) previously required only the qualifying child to have a Social Security Number (SSN); a parent or guardian filing with an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) could still claim the credit for a citizen child. The House-passed version of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, H.R. 1), reported June 4, 2025, would have gone much further, requiring both the filer and, on a joint return, their spouse to have valid SSNs -- a change researchers at the Center for Migration Studies, Columbia University's Center on Poverty and Social Policy, Boston University's Institute for Equity in Child Opportunity, and ITEP estimated would strip roughly 4.5 million U.S. citizen children in mixed-immigration-status households of the credit, concentrated in California, Texas, and Florida. The Senate Finance Committee narrowed this provision before final passage, requiring only the taxpayer (and, for joint filers, at least one spouse) to have an SSN rather than both parents. OBBBA as signed by President Trump on July 4, 2025 adopted the Senate's narrower rule: the qualifying child and at least one filing parent must have an SSN. The Migration Policy Institute estimates this narrower, final rule affects roughly 176,000 U.S. citizen children with undocumented parents -- a real but much smaller population than the House bill's earlier 4.5 million estimate, which did not become law. Separately, and unrelated to immigration status, OBBBA raised the maximum CTC from $2,000 to $2,200 per child and made the credit permanent (avoiding a scheduled reversion toward $1,000 under prior law), but left the credit's core low-income exclusion mechanism untouched: it remains only partially refundable, with a $2,500 minimum-earned-income floor before any refundable credit is available and a $1,700-per-child cap on the refundable ('Additional Child Tax Credit') portion. Because the nonrefundable portion of the credit can't exceed a family's income tax liability, families with little or no federal income tax owed -- disproportionately the lowest-income households -- cannot claim the credit's full higher headline value.

primary_proponent.name: Congress (OBBBA), implemented by the IRS
primary_proponent.role: The child tax credit provisions were written into the reconciliation bill and signed by President Trump; the IRS administers the SSN-verification and nonrefundability rules as written into the tax code
primary_proponent.note: No single named executive-branch official was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally driving this provision beyond Congress's own drafting process -- the House Ways and Means Committee originated the stricter two-parent-SSN version, and the Senate Finance Committee narrowed it before passage -- responsibility here sits primarily with the legislative provision itself, consistent with this tracker's treatment of other OBBBA provisions.

estimated_impact.summary: OBBBA's child tax credit changes had two distinct effects: a narrow, real but much-reduced immigration-status exclusion (about 176,000 citizen children, down from a House-bill proposal that would have affected roughly 4.5 million), and a far larger, structural low-income exclusion built into the credit's continued nonrefundability -- **an estimated 17 million children in low-income families, 30% of all U.S. children nationally, and 99% of children in the poorest fifth of households will not receive the full $2,200-per-child credit in 2026, with Black, Hispanic, and Native American children excluded at roughly double the rate of white children.**

The 176,000, 17 million, 30%, and 99% figures describe the law as actually enacted and in effect for the 2025-2026 tax years. Some advocacy-group coverage of the same underlying analyses cites a higher total (around 19 million) with a previously-ineligible/newly-ineligible breakdown that could not be independently verified here; this entry uses the more conservative, independently cross-corroborated (Brookings + ITEP) 17 million figure and ITEP's own 30%/99% headline percentages rather than that higher total.

title: OBBBA Eliminated Grad PLUS Loans and Capped Federal Borrowing for Medical, Nursing, and Grad Students
institution: U.S. Department of Education / federal student loan program
status: Enacted into law (OBBBA, signed July 2025); new caps take effect for new borrowers starting July 1, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OBBBA signed) through 2026-07-01 (new caps take effect)
what_changed: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), Trump's domestic policy reconciliation bill, eliminated the federal Grad PLUS loan program for new borrowers starting July 1, 2026 and replaced it with fixed annual and lifetime borrowing caps by program type. Early coverage in June 2025, while the bill was still being negotiated, reported a proposed $150,000 lifetime cap on federal loans for graduate students generally -- well below the typical cost of medical school -- prompting warnings from medical and osteopathic schools that the change would deter low- and middle-income students and worsen a projected shortage of nearly 200,000 physicians by 2037. The final enacted law, reported in more granular detail by December 2025, set different caps by program classification: 'professional' programs (medicine and law) received a higher $50,000-per-year / $200,000-lifetime cap, while 'graduate' programs (including nursing and most public-health degrees) were capped at a hard $20,500 per year and $100,000 total including undergraduate borrowing -- both figures well below the actual cost of most medical and advanced-nursing programs. The same law also tightened Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) eligibility rules for health workers, restricting qualification for employees of organizations the Department of Education determined were substantially engaged in activities including immigration-related legal services, gender-affirming care, or actions deemed to 'influence' federal policy -- a distinct, separately controversial PSLF rule change (litigated by a coalition including AFT, AFSCME, NEA, NASW, and 21 state attorneys general) that this entry flags but does not document in full detail; see this database's education-dept-save-plan-termination-2026.json and education-dept-student-loan-portfolio-privatization-2025-2026.json entries for related but distinct PSLF/IDR-access disruptions, and treat the PSLF employer-eligibility rule itself as an open item for a future dedicated entry. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0437): this same OBBBA law also capped Parent PLUS loans, reclassified Pell Grants under a new 'last-dollar' rule, restricted deferment/forbearance for future borrowers, and created a program-level earnings-accountability test -- see the companion entry obbba-parent-plus-pell-accountability-2025.json for those provisions, split out because they affect a distinct population (parent/undergraduate borrowers and every academic program) rather than the graduate/professional borrowers this entry covers.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Signed OBBBA, the reconciliation bill containing the Grad PLUS elimination and new loan-cap structure, into law in July 2025.

estimated_impact.summary: The new caps fall far short of actual program costs -- median medical school cost of attendance runs well above $50,000/year, and many advanced nursing/public-health programs exceed the $20,500/year graduate cap -- meaning **affected students will need to turn to private loans (typically at less favorable terms, with fewer borrower protections like income-driven repayment or PSLF eligibility) or be priced out of these programs entirely, an effect medical and nursing educators specifically warned would fall hardest on low- and middle-income students and worsen existing shortages in primary care and rural/underserved-area practice.**

what_changed.base: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), Trump's domestic policy reconciliation bill, eliminated the federal Grad PLUS loan program for new borrowers starting July 1, 2026 and replaced it with fixed annual and lifetime borrowing caps by program type. Early coverage in June 2025, while the bill was still being negotiated, reported a proposed $150,000 lifetime cap on federal loans for graduate students generally -- well below the typical cost of medical school -- prompting warnings from medical and osteopathic schools that the change would deter low- and middle-income students and worsen a projected shortage of nearly 200,000 physicians by 2037. The final enacted law, reported in more granular detail by December 2025, set different caps by program classification: 'professional' programs (medicine and law) received a higher $50,000-per-year / $200,000-lifetime cap, while 'graduate' programs (including nursing and most public-health degrees) were capped at a hard $20,500 per year and $100,000 total including undergraduate borrowing -- both figures well below the actual cost of most medical and advanced-nursing programs. The same law also tightened Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) eligibility rules for health workers, restricting qualification for employees of organizations the Department of Education determined were substantially engaged in activities including immigration-related legal services, gender-affirming care, or actions deemed to 'influence' federal policy -- a distinct, separately controversial PSLF rule change (litigated by a coalition including AFT, AFSCME, NEA, NASW, and 21 state attorneys general) that this entry flags but does not document in full detail; see this database's education-dept-save-plan-termination-2026.json and education-dept-student-loan-portfolio-privatization-2025-2026.json entries for related but distinct PSLF/IDR-access disruptions, and treat the PSLF employer-eligibility rule itself as an open item for a future dedicated entry.

title: OBBBA's One-Year Medicaid 'Defund' of Abortion Providers Cut Off Planned Parenthood and Independent Clinics, Forcing Real Closures in Maine and Elsewhere
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS); Planned Parenthood affiliates and independent reproductive-health clinics nationwide
status: Resolved -- Section 71113's one-year Medicaid funding cutoff expired July 4, 2026 without congressional renewal or replacement; litigation had already been voluntarily dismissed by March 17, 2026. Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood and other affected providers has resumed. This entry now documents the completed one-year defund episode and its documented harm, not an ongoing cutoff.
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (OBBBA signed into law) through 2026-07-04 (Section 71113's one-year Medicaid cutoff expired without congressional renewal)
what_changed:
Section 71113 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025, cut off Medicaid reimbursement for one year to any tax-exempt 'essential community provider' focused on family planning that both provides abortions beyond the Hyde Amendment's exceptions and received more than $800,000 in combined federal/state Medicaid expenditures in fiscal year 2023 -- a threshold designed to target Planned Parenthood and similarly-sized independent clinics, including Maine Family Planning, while leaving smaller providers unaffected. Nationally, roughly 200 Planned Parenthood health centers across 24 states were identified as being at risk of closure, more than 90% of them in states where abortion remains legal, since over half of Planned Parenthood's patients rely on Medicaid for care unrelated to abortion (contraception, cancer screenings, STI testing, and general primary/reproductive care).

In the immediate aftermath of the July 4, 2025 signing and before any court intervened, at least two regional affiliates -- Planned Parenthood of Metropolitan Washington DC and Planned Parenthood of the Rocky Mountains -- posted notices on their websites telling patients they could no longer accept Medicaid, per July 10, 2025 reporting; because Planned Parenthood Federation of America provides only national oversight while individual affiliates operate and bill independently, the response to the cutoff was inconsistent affiliate-to-affiliate even before litigation began, producing real confusion and coverage gaps in the days before any injunction issued. Planned Parenthood Federation of America and Maine Family Planning separately sued, along with 22 state attorneys general and Pennsylvania challenging the provision as unconstitutional; a federal judge (Talwani) granted Planned Parenthood a preliminary injunction blocking the cutoff nationwide.

A study published August 13, 2025 found Planned Parenthood clinics had logged more than 1.5 million Medicaid-covered patient visits nationally in 2024 -- the baseline population the cutoff threatened -- and cited Texas's earlier, decade-old state-level exclusion of Planned Parenthood from its Medicaid program as a predictive analog: contraceptive implant and IUD placements fell by more than a third in Texas counties that had a Planned Parenthood clinic after that exclusion took effect.

On September 11, 2025, the First Circuit stayed Talwani's injunction on an interim basis, allowing the cutoff to take effect nationwide (blocking an estimated 1.1 million Medicaid patients from using their coverage at Planned Parenthood health centers) while the merits appeal proceeded -- using reasoning similar to its later fuller opinion. On December 12, 2025, the First Circuit issued its full merits ruling on that appeal, holding Section 71113 was not an unconstitutional bill of attainder because it 'looks ahead' and 'imposes no fine or other penalty for past conduct,' instead 'establish[ing] new conditions on the receipt of appropriated funds in service of a new policy goal favored by Congress' -- allowing the funding cutoff to proceed in most states while other litigation continued; the separate Planned Parenthood Federation of America v. Kennedy suit was dismissed January 30, 2026.

In Maine, the funding loss had already produced concrete, documented harm by that point: **effective October 31, 2025, Maine Family Planning discontinued primary care services (not abortion services specifically) at three rural locations -- Houlton, Ellsworth, and Presque Isle -- affecting roughly 800-1,000 patients who had relied on those clinics as their primary-care provider, not just for reproductive health.** Maine Public reported, citing Maine Family Planning nurse practitioner Heather Curran, that the organization was working to connect its 'roughly 800 primary care patients' to other providers while the clinics continued to offer reproductive health services; NPR reported the change affected nearly 1,000 patients, 'including patients on Medicaid and those with private insurance.' Maine Governor Janet Mills proposed $2.25 million in one-time state supplemental funding on January 27, 2026 to offset the federal loss; the state budget signed in April 2026 went further, establishing an ongoing $5 million-per-year state funding stream for reproductive health providers beginning in 2027, alongside Washington State's governor separately announcing the state would cover its own affected providers' funding gap.

Section 71113 was a one-year provision by its own statutory text (July 4, 2025 - July 3, 2026), and Congress missed the deadline to extend or replace it before it expired; all remaining litigation challenging the provision had already been voluntarily dismissed by March 17, 2026, before the expiration mooted the underlying dispute. Medicaid funding to Planned Parenthood and other affected providers resumed after the cutoff lapsed on July 4, 2026. A Planned Parenthood Federation of America report published in the weeks after expiration found that during the one-year cutoff, nearly 30 Planned Parenthood health centers closed nationally (serving roughly 41,000 birth control patients, two-thirds of the closures in rural or medically underserved areas), while Medicaid visits fell by roughly 25% (over 250,000 visits) and specific service categories declined further: birth control pill dispensing down almost 25%, IUD/long-acting contraception visits down 26%, breast exam visits down 20%, and STI testing down 10%.

A renewal push did in fact exist, however, and has since failed to advance. The House Freedom Caucus, in a letter to Speaker Mike Johnson, demanded a 'Reconciliation 3.0' bill extend Section 71113's abortion-provider funding ban; Johnson pursued the idea through July 2026, but the White House-approved Reconciliation 3.0 package that ultimately moved forward -- built around Iran-war spending and voter-ID legislation -- did not include the Planned Parenthood defund extension, and a budget expert cited in coverage noted a 'Reconciliation 4.0' is not procedurally available this Congress since Reconciliation 3.0 exhausts the one reconciliation bill allowed per budget year. Senate Republicans were separately reported as 'cooler' to a third reconciliation bill given reluctance to reopen an abortion fight close to the midterms. Congress did consider renewing the cutoff, but the renewal effort failed to make it into the vehicle that passed, and, per that budget expert's characterization, no further reconciliation opportunity remains this Congress.

primary_proponent.note: No single named executive-branch official was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally driving implementation beyond CMS's routine administration of the statutory provision -- responsibility here sits primarily with the legislative provision itself.

estimated_impact.summary: A one-year Medicaid-funding cutoff aimed at defunding abortion providers produced documented harm to non-abortion care for low-income, often rural patients before expiring on schedule -- the Maine closures specifically ended primary care (not abortion) services for roughly 800-1,000 patients, Medicaid and privately insured alike, who used Maine Family Planning as their primary care provider, and a post-expiration Planned Parenthood report found nearly 30 health centers closed nationally, Medicaid visits down roughly 25%, and drops in birth control, breast exam and STI testing care during the cutoff year. Maine moved to backfill the federal loss with its own money: a proposed $2.25 million in one-time funding, then an ongoing $5 million a year starting in 2027 in its April 2026 budget.

title: OBBBA Tightens Parent PLUS Loans, Reclassifies Pell as 'Last-Dollar' Aid, Cuts Deferment Options, and Ties Loan Eligibility to Graduate Earnings
institution: Federal Student Aid (Department of Education)
status: Enacted into law (OBBBA, signed July 4, 2025); provisions phase in on different timelines -- Parent PLUS caps and Pell reclassification take effect for the 2026-27 academic year (July 2026), while deferment/forbearance restrictions (for loans disbursed or consolidated on or after July 1, 2027) and the earnings-accountability test are the last provisions to take effect, by July 1, 2027.
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (OBBBA signed) through 2027-07-01 (last provisions take effect)
what_changed: Beyond the Grad PLUS elimination and medical/nursing borrowing caps already documented in this database's obbba-grad-plus-medical-loan-caps-2025.json entry, the same law (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025) made several further changes to federal student aid that entry does not cover. Parent PLUS loans -- used by parents to borrow on behalf of undergraduate dependents -- are capped at $20,000 per year per child and $65,000 total per child, replacing a previous structure with no hard borrowing ceiling (Reuters, July 2025; MIT Student Financial Services). Pell Grant eligibility was narrowed by a new 'last-dollar' rule: students whose cost of attendance is already fully covered by other aid (employer sponsorships, state last-dollar grants, third-party payments) become ineligible for Pell for that term, and students with a Student Aid Index at least twice the maximum Pell award also lose eligibility (Citizens Bank, Reuters, July 2025) -- a shift Trump's tax-and-spending law's critics characterized as penalizing students who secure other funding rather than layering federal aid on top. Separately, the law eliminates economic-hardship and unemployment deferment options and caps general forbearance at nine months within any 24-month period, but only for loans first disbursed or consolidated on or after July 1, 2027; borrowers with loans from before that date keep access to the existing deferment options (Edvisors, EdTrust, 2025). **Advocacy group Protect Borrowers and EdTrust warned the change would raise delinquency and default risk during future economic downturns, falling hardest on borrowers of color, veterans, disabled borrowers, and low-income borrowers.** The law also created a new institutional-accountability mechanism -- an earnings test requiring undergraduate program completers' median earnings, measured four years after graduation, to exceed the median earnings of 25-34-year-olds with only a high school diploma in the same field/region (graduate programs use a bachelor's-degree-holder benchmark instead); a program that fails the test twice within three years loses federal Direct Loan eligibility, and repeated failure can cost a program all Title IV federal aid eligibility (NASFAA, American University PEER Center, 2025-2026). This accountability provision applies to every academic program, at every type of institution (public, private, for-profit), regardless of credential level.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Signed OBBBA, the reconciliation bill containing these Parent PLUS, Pell, deferment/forbearance, and earnings-accountability changes, into law on July 4, 2025.

estimated_impact.summary: Parent borrowers lose access to loans beyond a fixed per-child cap well below many private-college costs; some students who secure partial outside funding lose Pell eligibility entirely; future borrowers lose economic-hardship and unemployment deferment options starting mid-2027; and every academic program in the country now faces a two-strikes earnings test that can strip it of federal loan eligibility if its graduates don't out-earn high-school-only workers.

This entry should be re-verified once early-implementation data (available starting July 2026) or actual 2026-27 enrollment/aid data becomes available.

MODERATE confidence on the projected harms (default risk, disparate impact on borrowers of color/veterans/disabled/low-income borrowers) -- these are advocacy-group (Protect Borrowers, EdTrust) projections, not yet realized outcomes, since most provisions have not taken effect as of this entry's creation. This is a companion entry to obbba-grad-plus-medical-loan-caps-2025.json, which covers the same law's Grad PLUS elimination and medical/nursing/graduate borrowing caps -- split into a separate entry because these are a distinct set of provisions (parent borrowers, Pell recipients, and institutional accountability, rather than graduate/professional borrowers) rather than because of any factual disagreement between sources.
