title: Acting DNI Bill Pulte purges Office of the Director of National Intelligence staff
institution: Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI)
status: Concluded for Pulte: Jay Clayton was confirmed as DNI July 28, 2026 and sworn in August 3. A Cato analysis argues Pulte's acts after the confirmation vote were 'legally illegitimate'; no court has ruled, and the FISA 702 standoff remains unresolved. No indication Clayton has reviewed the cuts.
what_changed:
Before he had officially taken office, Bill Pulte showed up at ODNI headquarters a day early, catching staff -- including outgoing DNI Tulsi Gabbard, who was given only a brief heads-up -- off guard. CNN reported Pulte requested a list of every ODNI employee so he could assess whom to fire, repeatedly asked whether he would have access to a government plane, requested a security detail, asked about the status and classification level of his newly issued security clearance, and asked ODNI staff in a briefing whether he could bring the President's Daily Brief to his house. Pulte was the first person to lead ODNI since its creation after September 11, 2001 without any prior intelligence or national-security experience and without having previously held a security clearance.

Beginning Monday, June 22, 2026 -- the first business day after he formally succeeded Tulsi Gabbard on Friday, June 19 -- Acting Director Bill Pulte began firing and reassigning ODNI staff in successive rounds of cuts. An initial round removed 6 career and political intelligence staff and sent 45 others back to their home agencies -- just over 50 people removed from ODNI roles in total. A source told NBC News that Pulte had ordered staff to identify roughly 400 employees for termination at the National Counterterrorism Center, though a source told CNN on June 23 that the Center had not been impacted by the first round of cuts; the National Counterintelligence and Security Center was separately reported as expected to be hit hard, though no later reporting reviewed identified cuts there. Democratic lawmakers objected: in a June 22 letter, Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Jim Himes wrote that 'any large cuts would follow on a substantial downsizing that has already occurred in 2025 and risk jeopardizing the mission of an organization explicitly created after 9/11 to prevent any future such terrorist attack'; Sen. Adam Schiff wrote on X that Pulte 'makes massive cuts to the counter-terrorism workforce'; and Himes said on MS NOW, as The Hill reported, that 'If he just starts willy-nilly firing people, it is going to increase the probability that there is a terrorist attack inside the United States.' Pulte has said publicly that his goal is to reduce the size of ODNI and refocus it on national security.

Separately, Pulte's authority to hold the role at all has been disputed: the DNI has no supervisor other than the president, making it a 'principal officer' under the Constitution's Appointments Clause that legal analysts (Cato Institute, Lawfare) say should require Senate confirmation even in an acting capacity, and federal law arguably required the Senate-confirmed principal deputy DNI to assume the role automatically once it became vacant rather than a new outside appointee. A Project on Government Oversight legal expert said the appointment meets the Vacancies Reform Act's technical requirements but flagged that the Act's eligibility rules are so broad (allowing the president to choose from 350+ federal officials regardless of relevant qualifications) that they may not satisfy the Constitution's stricter requirement for principal officers.

Senate Intelligence Vice Chairman Mark Warner publicly objected to the appointment, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin introduced the MERIT Act on July 16, 2026 to require any acting DNI to have national security experience -- legislative responses that read as a direct rebuke of the Pulte pick. If a court ultimately found the appointment invalid, Pulte's purge decisions and other agency actions taken under his tenure could themselves be legally exposed to challenge.

The Washington Post reported on July 23, 2026 that ODNI had purged approximately 200 employees through firings and reassignments since June 1, 2026 (a window that began before Pulte took office), reducing the office's workforce to roughly 1,300 -- just over half its size when Trump returned to office -- and described the cuts as part of a broader campaign to replace experienced civil servants with political loyalists. Shortly after midnight on Sunday, July 26, 2026, Pulte posted on X that 'we just finished a 4th round of thoughtful, measured layoffs,' Federal News Network reported; he did not say how many employees were affected, and ODNI did not respond to the outlet's request for comment.

On the morning of July 28, 2026, at 7:44 a.m. EDT, Pulte posted on X that ODNI was 'this morning, Executing a 5th and Near Final Round of TERMINATIONS, an approximately 30% Staff Reduction from Weeks Ago' -- a move Senate Democrats had previously warned him against making in an unconfirmed, temporary capacity. At 6:21 p.m. on July 28, more than 10 hours after that post, the Senate confirmed Jay Clayton as DNI (51-47, party-line vote). The New York Times, as quoted by MS NOW on July 29, 2026, reported that 'current and former officials said few people have actually been fired in recent weeks' from ODNI despite Pulte's social media posts, and that those officials said Pulte 'was counting people whose tour of duty at the office was complete and were returning to their home agencies as previously planned' and, per former officials, 'appears to be counting unfilled positions at the National Counterterrorism Center and other parts of the spy office as terminations.' The administration held Clayton's swearing-in until August 3, 2026 -- an unusual delay, since Senate-confirmed nominees are typically sworn in the same day -- while Pulte continued serving as acting DNI for that entire intervening week. Bipartisan senators publicly called for Clayton to be sworn in immediately, and Cato Institute scholar Thomas A. Berry went further, arguing that under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act 'Pulte's time limit as acting DNI expired the moment the Senate confirmed Clayton,' that 'Everything Pulte has done as acting DNI since that moment has been legally illegitimate and is vulnerable to a court challenge,' and that 'Any employees that Pulte purported to fire after Clayton's confirmation would have a strong case in court that they were never lawfully terminated.' Berry's analysis does not address the 5th round, which Pulte announced that morning, before the confirmation vote, and no reporting reviewed establishes whether any firings took effect after the vote.

Separately, the delay had a concrete legislative cost: Senate Democrats, led by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, had conditioned consideration of FISA Section 702 surveillance-authority renewal (lapsed since mid-June 2026) on Pulte's removal from ODNI, so the week-long delay in swearing in Clayton directly prolonged the Section 702 standoff into Congress's limited remaining pre-recess floor time. No source reviewed indicates any court has yet ruled on the Vacancies Act theory, and existing Section 702 certifications continue operating under a statutory grandfather clause through March 2027 even with the underlying authority lapsed, so neither the legal-exposure question nor the surveillance-authority question is resolved. Pulte retained his separate, Senate-confirmed post as FHFA director throughout the ODNI stint and continues to hold it. Sourcing reviewed did not identify any decision by Clayton to reverse, pause, or review the cuts made under Pulte.

title: Office of Government Ethics goes over a year without a permanent or acting director after Trump firing
institution: U.S. Office of Government Ethics
status: Ongoing in practice -- no confirmed or acting director has served since the February 2025 firing. Trump nominated Michael Chamberlain as permanent successor on June 24, 2026; the nomination remains pending in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee as of the most recent reporting reviewed, with no confirmation hearing yet scheduled.
date_of_action: 2025-02 (firing) through 2026-05 (ongoing vacancy)
what_changed: In February 2025, Trump removed David Huitema as Director of the Office of Government Ethics -- the federal agency responsible for monitoring executive-branch financial conflicts of interest and ethics violations -- despite Huitema having been confirmed by the Senate in November 2024 to a five-year term. More than a year later, as of May 2026, no permanent or acting director has been named; a series of acting directors filled the role temporarily before the position went fully vacant, with no one currently serving in an acting capacity and no nominee put forward. Senate Democrats, led by Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Adam Schiff, sent a formal letter pressing the White House on the vacancy. Critics say the leadership gap has curtailed, delayed, or put on hold some of the office's work; the agency had not published its usual annual increase in ethics-violation fines for 2026 as of this reporting. Update 2026-08-17 (correction): this entry previously stated no nominee had been put forward; that is no longer accurate. On June 24, 2026, Trump nominated Michael Chamberlain -- director of Protect the Public's Trust, a conservative-leaning watchdog group he founded in 2021 that frequently targeted Biden-administration officials with ethics complaints, and a first-Trump-administration veteran -- to serve a five-year term as OGE Director. The nomination was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and, as of the most recent reporting reviewed, had not yet received a confirmation hearing date. Watchdog groups (Center for Western Priorities) raised concerns that Chamberlain's own organization misrepresented its IRS nonprofit status in public-records requests and that his selection reflects a partisan rather than independent approach to the office. The underlying vacancy -- no one confirmed or serving in an acting capacity -- continues while the nomination is pending. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 47, moderate): NOTUS reported June 29, 2026 that Protect the Public's Trust, the watchdog group Chamberlain founded and led, filed 'hundreds of actions' against Biden-administration officials during that administration's term, but that 'few' of those actions led to any substantive findings -- a more concrete characterization of the group's track record than this entry's prior general description. No confirmation hearing date has been identified as of this recheck; the nomination remains listed as received and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (June 23, 2026 referral date, per the committee's own nominations page).

title: OMB withholds $324M in appropriated CDFI Fund grants, branding the program 'woke'
institution: OMB / Treasury Department (Community Development Financial Institutions Fund)
status: Ongoing -- bipartisan senators and a lawsuit have both pushed for release; no confirmed disbursement identified
date_of_action: 2025-11 (reported); funds appropriated for FY2025-2026
what_changed: OMB Director Russell Vought withheld $324 million in FY2025-2026 funding Congress appropriated for the CDFI Fund, including $24 million earmarked for Native CDFIs, leaving five CDFI Fund programs without announced awards months after their application periods closed. The White House's own budget document justified broader cuts to the program by claiming past awards 'enabled lender practices in which race was a key determinant in access to loans' and funded services advancing 'immigration, gender and climate radicalism'; Vought separately announced a reduction-in-force at the CDFI Fund itself, stating it was 'necessary to implement the abolishment of the Community Development Financial Institutions [Fund]' based on Treasury's determination the program didn't align with presidential priorities. The administration's FY2026 budget proposed cutting the Fund's appropriation by 63% (from $324M to $119.5M, with $100M of that redirected to a new rural-focused program) -- a similar-scale cut Congress had already rejected the prior year. As of the relevant update, OMB had disbursed only $35 million through seven months of FY2026, all for administrative costs rather than grant awards. A bipartisan group of senators led by Sens. Mark Warner (D-VA), Mike Crapo (R-ID), and John Hickenlooper (D-CO) sent OMB a letter warning the delay 'hinders critical projects in our states and could constrain the flow of capital to businesses and consumers who need it the most,' and requested a spending plan and timeline covering the more than 1,400 certified CDFIs that depend on the funding. A coalition of California nonprofits separately sued the administration, alleging the White House and Treasury are illegally withholding CDFI Fund grants.

title: OMB Proposes Political-Appointee Pre-Issuance Review of Federal Grants, Ending Post-WWII Norm of Apolitical Peer Review
institution: Office of Management and Budget (OMB)
status: Proposed rule, not finalized. Congress's stopgap funding law bars OMB from issuing or finalizing it, or a substantially similar rule, through Dec. 11, 2026. A Sept. 2026 White House push for a commission of political appointees to review NIH grants stalled after bipartisan pushback.
date_of_action: 2026-05-29 (proposed rule published)
what_changed: On May 29, 2026, OMB -- led by Director Russell Vought -- published a proposed rule in the Federal Register (more than 400 pages as filed for public inspection) that would overhaul the federal government's Uniform Grants Guidance, the regulatory framework governing how agencies award more than $1 trillion annually in federal grants to research institutions, state and local governments, nonprofits, and small businesses. **The proposal requires senior political appointees to conduct 'pre-issuance reviews' of grant awards, including assessing whether funded projects 'demonstrably advance the President's policy priorities.'** It also states that 'peer review remains advisory and does not replace agency discretion' -- a direct departure from the practice, standard since the post-World War II establishment of federal science funding, of grant approval being determined primarily by apolitical technical experts assessing scientific and programmatic merit. The proposal additionally grants agencies broad new authority to terminate already-awarded grants at any time and imposes new restrictions on international research collaborations. Public comment closed July 13, 2026, after drawing more than 160,000 submissions, and the rule was proposed to take effect October 1, 2026. Update 2026-09-29: Congress's stopgap funding law for fiscal 2027, signed September 2, 2026, bars OMB from issuing or finalizing this rule, or a substantially similar rule, through December 11, 2026, delaying the planned October start. At what was reported to be a contentious Oval Office meeting on September 18, 2026, Vought pushed for an executive order creating a commission to review all NIH grants, according to the Washington Post as reported by STAT; STAT added that Trump, reportedly angry that NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya had refused to cut funding for Harvard researchers, directed Vought to draft it. Politico reported that Vought and Bhattacharya would sit on the board, which would have to reach unanimous decisions on grants, which STAT described as giving a commission of political appointees veto power over grant awards. **Such a board would add a political sign-off on top of the scientific peer review that Congress requires for every NIH grant.** On September 22, Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) wrote to Vought and Bhattacharya that the plan "appears similar to a provision" of this proposed rule that Congress had blocked in the stopgap law, and urged them not to proceed with a proposal that would undermine the goal of "funding biomedical research projects based on scientific merit and value rather than political ideology." On September 23, STAT reported that the planned order was "looking dead" after bipartisan pushback, citing a person familiar with the decision and Collins; the White House did not respond to STAT and had announced no decision as of late September 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought

title: OPM/MSPB Propose Scrapping the Douglas Factors, the 44-Year-Old Framework Protecting Federal Employees From Arbitrary Discipline
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB)
status: Proposed rule -- published in the Federal Register July 7, 2026, not yet finalized as of this entry
date_of_action: 2026-07-07 (proposed rule published)
what_changed: OPM and the Merit Systems Protection Board jointly proposed eliminating the 'Douglas factors' -- a 12-part framework established by a 1981 MSPB case that agencies have used for over four decades to ensure federal employee discipline is proportionate and considers factors like offense severity, past performance, and rehabilitation potential. The proposed rule, published in the Federal Register on July 7, 2026, would replace the Douglas factors with a vaguer 'totality of the circumstances' standard, which OPM and MSPB argue is more flexible than what they characterized as agencies' 'rigid, mechanistic' application of Douglas. The same proposal includes shortening performance improvement plans to 30 days, banning settlement agreements that remove misconduct documentation from personnel files, and eliminating union officials' paid 'official time' for handling adverse-action appeals.

primary_proponent.name: Office of Personnel Management
primary_proponent.role: Federal civil service's central HR agency, acting jointly with the Merit Systems Protection Board
primary_proponent.note: OPM and MSPB jointly authored and published the proposed rule eliminating the Douglas factors, framing the current framework as overly rigid and an obstacle to agency discipline.

estimated_impact.summary: The proposal would give federal agency managers substantially more discretion to discipline or remove career employees by replacing an established, 12-factor proportionality test with a vaguer standard -- **critics warn this would let agencies remove employees for a single instance of misconduct with no prior discipline, undermining protections designed to prevent politically motivated firings across the career civil service.**

estimated_impact.caveat: OPM and MSPB's stated rationale -- that Douglas has been applied too rigidly, discouraging warranted discipline -- is a genuine policy argument, not merely pretextual, and is presented alongside the critical response. Former MSPB member Raymond Limon disputes the premise, noting the Douglas factors were designed to be 'illustrative' rather than rigid and that agencies already win the large majority of contested discipline cases under the current standard. Federal employment attorney Michael Fallings warns the 'totality of circumstances' language would let agencies ignore factors favoring the employee, enabling removal for a single incident with no disciplinary history.

title: OPM's Musk-Directed 'Five Bullet Points' Email Throws Federal Agencies Into Conflicting-Orders Chaos
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM), government-wide
status: Ended: on August 5, 2025, about six months after the first email, OPM said it would no longer manage or use the weekly 'five things' process. No reporting reviewed documents anyone fired for not responding; OPM's director later said AI was used only lightly on replies, mostly to summarize.
date_of_action: 2025-02-22 through 2025-08-05 (first email to OPM's formal end of the weekly process)
what_changed: The Office of Personnel Management sent an email to federal employees government-wide on February 22, 2025 demanding roughly five bullet points summarizing each employee's accomplishments for the prior week, cc'ing their manager. Elon Musk warned on X that 'Failure to respond will be taken as a resignation,' with responses due by 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Monday, February 24, and separate reporting (NBC News, the Daily Beast) indicated DOGE was building a system to feed the responses into an AI/large-language-model that would help determine whether each employee's role was 'mission-critical' -- a characterization Musk publicly denied ('No LLM needed here'). The directive immediately produced conflicting guidance across agencies: Politico reported that leaders at agencies from the National Institutes of Health to the Justice Department told workers not to respond until they received further guidance, and FBI Director Kash Patel instructed FBI staff to 'please pause any responses'; by Monday, CNN reported, the Justice Department, State Department, Pentagon, FBI, Department of Homeland Security and Department of Energy had all told staff not to respond. Other agencies ordered compliance -- at Treasury, John W. York, a counselor to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and a former Heritage Foundation staffer, emailed employees, including at the IRS, directing them to reply by the Monday night deadline (Bloomberg Tax); he signed without a title from a '*Secretary of the Treasury' address, and Treasury sources told 404 Media they were not sure what his job was. CNN reported one IRS staffer was advised that not responding would be considered insubordination and would result in termination. CNN reported that work was disrupted at some agencies as staff sat in hastily assembled meetings trying to decipher conflicting emails: the Transportation Department ordered compliance, including by the FAA's chronically understaffed air traffic controllers, whose union had called the demand a 'distraction' at a time when the air safety system was 'fragile,' and a NOAA worker said they 'haven't done any of my actual duties due to the email.' Wired reported conflicting guidance at agencies from NOAA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology to NIH. On the afternoon of February 24, President Trump called the demand 'ingenious' and said anyone who didn't respond was 'semi-fired or fired'; a couple of hours later OPM formally notified agencies that responding was voluntary and that not responding would 'not equate to a resignation,' though CNN reported not every agency relayed that before the 11:59 p.m. deadline. HHS took a third distinct posture from Treasury/IRS's compliance order and the FBI's pause: on February 24, **HHS told employees responding was voluntary with no employment consequence for declining, but instructed staff who did respond to 'assume that what you write will be read by malign foreign actors and tailor your response accordingly,' keeping any submission at a high level of generality to protect sensitive data, PII, and applicable privileges.** Forbes reported the ultimatum recurred into a second week (through at least March 2, 2025), with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directing Pentagon employees to respond to that round. Weekly submissions kept arriving at OPM for months, though the effort had quieted down. On August 5, 2025, about six months after the first email, OPM Director Scott Kupor said OPM had told agency HR leads that it 'was no longer going to manage the five things process nor utilize it internally,' pointing managers to other tools and to 'rigorous performance management' instead (FedScoop). A week earlier, Kupor had told FedScoop that AI use on the emails was 'very light,' 'mostly for summarization purposes.'

primary_proponent.name: Elon Musk, former DOGE leader / Special Government Employee
primary_proponent.role: Issued the compliance ultimatum via OPM and publicly on social media
primary_proponent.note: Musk's public warning that non-response would be treated as resignation was the specific trigger for the cross-government confusion documented here; several individual agency heads (e.g. FBI Director Patel, who told staff to 'please pause any responses') are named as having held their own agencies back from complying, while others (Treasury's John W. York, Defense Secretary Hegseth in a second week) ordered compliance.

estimated_impact.summary: The harm documented here is to federal workers and the work they do, not a measured public-health or financial loss. Over February 22-24, 2025, workers across the government were told under threat of dismissal to justify their jobs, then given contradictory orders: some agencies (Justice, State, the Pentagon, FBI, DHS, Energy) said not to respond, others (Treasury, Commerce, Transportation) ordered compliance, and one IRS staffer was told silence meant termination, even as OPM told agencies responding was voluntary. Work was disrupted at some agencies, including ones with safety roles: the Transportation order reached the FAA's understaffed air traffic controllers, whose union had called Musk's demand a distraction for a 'fragile' air safety system, and a NOAA worker said they had done none of their actual duties. The weekly reporting demand then ran about six months until OPM dropped it on August 5, 2025. Reports that DOGE would have an AI system judge the responses were only partly confirmed: OPM's later director said AI was used lightly, mostly to summarize them.

NBC News and the Daily Beast reported DOGE planned to feed responses into a large language model; Musk denied it; in July 2025 OPM Director Scott Kupor told FedScoop AI use was 'very light,' 'mostly for summarization purposes.'

title: OPM Omitted Retirement Services Staff Departures From Oversight Response Amid a Record Retirement-Case Backlog
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM), Retirement Services division
status: Improving on backlog volume; unresolved, and now independently corroborated, on the disclosure/transparency allegation. The pending backlog fell further to 24,784 as of July 31, 2026 -- roughly 62% below February's 65,237 peak -- even as average processing time held near 98-109 days. A separate GAO report (GAO-26-108916, Aug. 14, 2026) found OPM refused to turn over requested documentation or answer written questions during its own review of the same cuts. No OPM correction or fuller accounting was identified in sourcing reviewed.
date_of_action: 2025 (workforce reductions); reported 2026-04
what_changed: House Democrats alleged that OPM, in its initial written response to congressional oversight inquiries about a growing retirement-case backlog, disclosed losing only about 35 customer service representatives but omitted that more than 100 staff in its Retirement Services division had departed -- a figure House Democrats say is drawn from data OPM's own Office of Inspector General cited. Lawmakers attributed the workforce losses to the administration's deferred resignation program, reductions in force, and termination of probationary employees. The pending retirement-case backlog reached 65,237 cases at its February 2026 peak before declining to 55,681 as of March 31, 2026 -- roughly 20,000 cases higher than the prior historical peak of about 36,000 claims reached in 2022, meaning even the post-peak backlog level remains well above any pre-2025 benchmark. Update 2026-08-17: the backlog continued declining after the 55,681 figure already in this entry, falling for a fourth consecutive month to 33,851 in June 2026 (a 12.2% drop from May, and roughly 48% below February's record peak), even as average processing time rose to about 108 days -- a case where the raw case count improved while individual wait times did not. Separately, OPM marked its 'Last Day of Paper' on July 1, 2026, ending paper-based retirement-application processing after more than 65 years for over 95% of applications, moving nearly all filings to its Online Retirement Application system and committing to issue a first pension payment within 7 days of retirement for complete digital applications submitted by the separation date. Sourcing reviewed did not identify any OPM response to House Democrats' original allegation that its disclosure of Retirement Services staff losses (~35 disclosed vs. 100+ alleged) was incomplete. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 39): the backlog fell for a fifth consecutive month, to 24,784 pending cases as of July 31, 2026 -- OPM processed 17,841 claims in July (14,000 digitally) while receiving 10,538 new applications, a net reduction of more than 9,000 cases in a single month and the lowest level since the retirement surge began, though still above OPM's own goal of 13,000 or fewer pending claims. Separately and independently of the House Democrats' allegation, a Government Accountability Office report (GAO-26-108916, dated August 14, 2026) examining OPM's Retirement Services staffing cuts found the office lost 16% of its full-time-equivalent positions (165 people) between fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2026, with 57% of departing staff holding 11+ years of federal service -- and, more directly relevant to this entry's transparency theme, that OPM 'never turned that material over' when GAO requested documentation on the changes it had made to its offices and programs since 2025, and separately declined GAO's requests for a meeting or answers to written questions. This is a second, independent federal oversight body (GAO, distinct from the House Democrats who made the original omission allegation) documenting the same pattern of OPM incompleteness/non-cooperation with oversight into the same underlying staffing cuts.

primary_proponent.role: Federal human-resources agency responsible for processing retirement claims for the federal workforce
primary_proponent.note: Sourcing attributes the underlying workforce reductions to broader 2025 administration-wide deferred-resignation, RIF, and probationary-termination programs rather than a decision specific to Retirement Services; the allegation of an incomplete disclosure to Congress is attributed to OPM institutionally, with no individual official named as responsible for the omission itself.

Separately and independently of the House Democrats' allegation, a Government Accountability Office report (GAO-26-108916, dated August 14, 2026) examining OPM's Retirement Services staffing cuts found the office lost 16% of its full-time-equivalent positions (165 people) between fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2026, with 57% of departing staff holding 11+ years of federal service -- and, more directly relevant to this entry's transparency theme, that OPM 'never turned that material over' when GAO requested documentation on the changes it had made to its offices and programs since 2025, and separately declined GAO's requests for a meeting or answers to written questions. This is a second, independent federal oversight body (GAO, distinct from the House Democrats who made the original omission allegation) documenting the same pattern of OPM incompleteness/non-cooperation with oversight into the same underlying staffing cuts.

title: OPM Cut Its Own Staff by a Third Even as It Processed a Historic Surge of Federal Retirements and Buyouts It Helped Cause
institution: Office of Personnel Management (OPM)
status: Reduction plan announced July 2025, targeted for completion by year-end 2025; NARFE warned of resulting delays in retirement and benefits processing.
date_of_action: 2025-07 (OPM announces its own workforce-reduction plan)
what_changed: In July 2025, **OPM Director Scott Kupor announced that OPM itself -- the federal government's central human-resources agency, responsible for processing retirements, benefits, and onboarding/offboarding for the entire civil service -- would cut its own workforce from roughly 3,110 to about 2,000 employees, a one-third reduction, by the end of 2025.** Of the roughly 1,000 departing OPM employees, 940 left voluntarily through the Deferred Resignation Program, while 129 were separated involuntarily through reduction-in-force actions. OPM separately announced it would halve its contractor workforce, from 1,200 to 600 positions. Kupor said he would use the reduction as an opportunity to 'introduce and prioritize modern technology, including AI, to increase department efficiency.' The cuts came as OPM was simultaneously administering the historic government-wide wave of deferred resignations, buyouts, and retirements documented in this database's separate federal-workforce-cumulative-departures-2025-2026.json entry -- a wave that had already produced a backlog of more than 35,000 pending retirement claims by October 2025. NARFE (the National Active and Retired Federal Employees Association) warned the OPM staffing cuts could cause 'severe delays in processing and response times for retirement, benefits, and onboarding/offboarding' for federal employees and retirees government-wide.

title: HHS/ORR Ends Confidentiality Wall Protecting Unaccompanied Migrant Children and Their Sponsors, Sharing Data With ICE and Cutting Legal Aid
institution: Department of Health and Human Services -- Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), affecting unaccompanied migrant children in federal custody
status: Ongoing -- ICE data-sharing active; the Guardian reported in Sept. that Stephen Miller directs a multi-agency push to speed child removals (almost 200,000 orders for all children since Jan. 2025); Acacia legal-aid contract lapsed July 31, 2026; D.C. Circuit heard the N. v. HHS appeal Sept. 15, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-02-15 (fingerprinting reimposed) through 2026-07-31 (legal-aid contract lapses)
what_changed: Beginning in February 2025, ORR reimposed strict fingerprint-based background-check requirements for every adult in a household sponsoring an unaccompanied migrant child -- a policy first introduced in 2018 and later rolled back after it was found to cause mass detention overcrowding and discourage otherwise-qualified sponsors, many of whom are themselves undocumented, from coming forward for fear of their own deportation. In March 2025, the administration went further, issuing an interim final rule, effective March 25, 2025, that struck a provision of ORR's April 2024 Foundational Rule (45 CFR 410.1201(b)) that had kept sponsors' immigration status information from being shared with immigration enforcement specifically so status alone would not deter family reunification; ORR began providing ICE with sponsor and household immigration-status data on request, and no longer barred denying a child's release based on a sponsor's immigration status. Separately, on March 21, 2025, HHS's Office of Refugee Resettlement terminated its contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, worth more than $200 million a year, which funds legal representation for unaccompanied children in immigration court -- U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin (N.D. Cal.) issued a temporary restraining order on April 1, 2025 blocking the termination, and on April 29, 2025 granted a preliminary injunction ordering the funding restored; NBC News reported in mid-April 2025, citing a filing by the plaintiffs' attorneys, that the administration had not complied with the restraining order. Reuters reported on July 28, 2026, citing internal government data it reviewed exclusively, that ORR had shared more than 460,000 'leads' with ICE about unaccompanied children, sponsors, and other household members since January 2025, that more than 12,000 people had been arrested following ORR tips during Trump's second term, and that **the additional vetting requirements had driven the average time a child spends in ORR custody from about 30 days in fiscal year 2024 to 194 days by June 2026, according to ORR figures.** Update, 2026-08-17: this entry did not previously include ORR's own stated rationale for the policy. At a June 11, 2026 news conference -- before this entry's own 2026-08-08 write date, not a development since last verification, but missing from the original entry -- Acting ORR Director Angie Salazar defended the data-sharing change, saying some children released to unvetted sponsors under the prior policy 'were sexually assaulted, others deceased, and some committing heinous crimes,' and framing the change as closing a child-welfare gap rather than an enforcement expansion: 'when the government lacks reliable contact information or an effective means of tracking children, that is a child welfare failure.' Former Biden-era ORR deputy director Jen Smyers countered that the safeguards were 'completely reversed' and that the program is being 'weaponized... for the purposes of more deportations.' No new policy action beyond continued syndication/discussion of the same July 28, 2026 data was identified since last verification. CORRECTION 2026-08-30: this entry previously covered only the Acacia Center for Justice legal-aid contract case as legal pushback against ORR's policy changes. A second, distinct lawsuit -- N. v. HHS (also captioned Diego N. v. HHS), 1:26-cv-00577 (D.D.C., Judge Carl J. Nichols), filed February 23, 2026 -- directly challenges the re-vetting practice at this entry's core: four unaccompanied minors alleged they were 'suddenly uprooted' from living with previously-approved sponsors and held in federal custody without individualized justification after ORR began forcing sponsors to reapply, raising Fifth Amendment due-process and Administrative Procedure Act claims. The court denied plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion on April 30, 2026, finding them unlikely to succeed on the merits; defendants filed a motion to dismiss May 4, 2026, arguing the case was moot after ORR released three of the four named plaintiffs to a parent; plaintiffs filed an interlocutory appeal to the D.C. Circuit May 8, 2026; and the case was stayed pending settlement negotiations as of May 15, 2026. This case predates the entry's original write date and last recheck but was not previously identified in sourcing reviewed. Update 2026-09-01: the district court's May 15 stay order required the parties to file a joint status report within 90 days; in that report, filed Aug. 6, 2026, the parties said settlement talks had ended without a resolution and asked the court to keep the case stayed pending the plaintiffs' D.C. Circuit appeal (No. 26-5157), which was fully briefed, with the plaintiffs' reply brief filed July 31, 2026, and set for argument on Sept. 15, 2026. Separately, the plaintiffs' own complaint alleges that, 'upon information and belief' and as of January 2026, more than 300 children had been separated from previously-approved sponsors and re-referred to ORR under the challenged re-vetting policy -- a scale figure beyond the four named plaintiffs, but sourced only to the plaintiffs' own pleading (not independently corroborated by a government count or a second source) and not independently adjudicated. Update 2026-09-26: ORR's contract with the Acacia Center for Justice lapsed on July 31, 2026, ending funding for a network of nearly 100 legal service providers that Acacia said had served more than 20,000 unaccompanied children; Acacia said HHS had withheld more than $65 million, with payments stopping around November 2025, and PBS NewsHour, reporting the same day, said Acacia claims the administration stopped making the payments late the previous year. On Aug. 6, 2026, Judge Martinez-Olguin ordered HHS to pay the withheld funds, and CBS News reported the next day that payments were being processed. ORR announced on Aug. 6, 2026 that it intended to award a single-source cooperative agreement of up to $150 million to Burke Law Group, a Houston law firm, to represent children in its care; the firm withdrew from consideration on Aug. 11, and ORR published a withdrawal of the notice on Aug. 17. NPR reported on Aug. 12, 2026 that ORR had awarded a no-bid $158 million contract, running Aug. 7, 2026 to Feb. 6, 2027, to Our Rescue, formerly Operation Underground Railroad, and that ORR had been using the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants to represent children in its care since Aug. 5. The D.C. Circuit (Judges Millett, Pillard and Childs) heard argument in the N. v. HHS appeal on Sept. 15, 2026. Update 2026-10-03: The Guardian reported on Sept. 19, 2026, citing several unnamed sources briefed on the initiatives, that White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller is directing an effort across at least five cabinet-level departments -- HHS, the Department of Homeland Security (including ICE and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services), and the Justice Department, which houses the immigration courts, with the State Department and the Pentagon in more subsidiary roles -- to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children. Sources told the Guardian that ICE officers are present at new in-person appointments in the sponsorship process, that prospective sponsors have been detained shortly before or after a child's scheduled release, that ORR appears to be working with USCIS to rush children's asylum interviews, and that ICE now has access to children's confidential ORR files; these are allegations from unnamed sources, not official findings. The Guardian reported that more than 1,800 children were stuck in ORR custody. Citing an analysis of Justice Department immigration-court data by the advocacy group Mobile Pathways, it reported that **immigration judges have ordered almost 200,000 children removed from the U.S. since January 2025, about 70% of them under the age of 13**, with monthly removal orders for children rising from 7,366 in January 2025 to a peak of 16,750 in July 2026 before easing to 14,744 in August; that count covers all children in immigration court, whether they arrived alone or with family, not only unaccompanied children in ORR care. The White House did not deny that Miller is orchestrating a multi-agency effort but said it was not new; spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the agencies were 'working to locate and rescue these children' and reunite them with their families in their home countries, and an HHS spokesperson said 'ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process.' HHS also told the Guardian it had considered detailing military lawyers to represent children in its care but was no longer pursuing that option.

primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing the 2025 ORR rule and contract changes; attributed institutionally to the HHS Secretary with oversight authority over ORR, per this tracker's standard for department-level actions without a specific named director on the record. The Guardian reported in September 2026, citing unnamed sources, that White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller directs a multi-agency effort to speed the removal of migrant children that includes ORR, and that ORR was pushed to adopt tactics meant to increase deportations of children and their family members; the White House did not deny that Miller leads the effort.

estimated_impact.summary: A 2024 Biden-era rule barring ORR from sharing sponsors' immigration-status information with enforcement agencies was struck in March 2025 and sponsor vetting was tightened, resulting in a large, quantified increase in enforcement actions against sponsors and household members and, from the added vetting, in the time children spend in federal custody. ORR's legal-aid contract for unaccompanied children, terminated in March 2025 and then ordered restored by a court, lapsed in July 2026 after HHS withheld payments. A lawsuit also alleges that the related sponsor re-vetting policy has uprooted children from homes with previously-approved sponsors. The Guardian reported in September 2026 that these changes are part of a wider White House-directed push to remove migrant children, as monthly immigration-court removal orders against children more than doubled between January 2025 and mid-2026.

estimated_impact.caveat: The 460,000-lead and 12,000-arrest figures come from internal government data reviewed exclusively by Reuters, not a formal ORR or ICE public accounting; Reuters dates the leads from January 2025 and the arrests only to Trump's second term. The 194-day custody figure is ORR's own statistic as reported by Reuters. The 300+ separated-children figure comes only from the plaintiffs' own complaint ('upon information and belief'), is not corroborated by a government count or a second source, and has not been adjudicated; the court denied the plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion, finding them unlikely to succeed on the merits. ORR defends the data-sharing change as a child-welfare measure, with its acting director saying some children released to unvetted sponsors under the prior policy 'were sexually assaulted, others deceased, and some committing heinous crimes.' The legal-aid cut was not reversed: after a court ordered the funding restored in April 2025, HHS withheld payments from about November 2025 and let the Acacia contract lapse on July 31, 2026. The $65 million figure is Acacia's; the court ordered $65 million paid in August 2026. Acacia said in July 2026 that its network had provided counsel to more than 20,000 children; that figure is not directly comparable to the roughly 26,000 cited in 2025. The almost-200,000 removal-order figure is an advocacy group's analysis of Justice Department data, counts orders rather than completed deportations, and covers all children in immigration court, not only the unaccompanied children in ORR care that the rest of this entry describes; the Guardian's article also once describes the total as more than 200,000. The Guardian's account of Stephen Miller's role rests on unnamed sources.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the fingerprinting reimposition and the ICE data-sharing policy change, corroborated by the New York Times, Reuters, and the Migration Policy Institute. HIGH confidence on the March 2025 legal-aid contract termination and its judicial blocking, corroborated by AP, NBC News, and Fox News's contemporaneous coverage, and on the contract's July 31, 2026 lapse, reported by PBS NewsHour and the Acacia Center for Justice. MODERATE-HIGH confidence on the cumulative 460,000-lead/12,000-arrest/194-day figures, which come from Reuters' July 28, 2026 report citing government data rather than an official ORR/ICE public report -- worth rechecking against any official accounting if one is published. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change to the underlying policy or figures since last verification; added ORR's own on-record defense (Acting Director Salazar, June 11, 2026) and an outside critic's on-record rebuttal (Smyers) for balance, since the original entry omitted the agency's stated rationale entirely -- these quotes predate this entry's write date and are backfilled context, not a new development. CORRECTION 2026-08-30: added the N. v. HHS / Diego N. v. HHS litigation (1:26-cv-00577, D.D.C.), verified directly against the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse's case-specific docket tracker rather than relying on a search-engine summary alone, per this tracker's standard practice for surprising procedural claims. This is a distinct case from the already-documented Acacia Center for Justice legal-aid contract dispute, and directly challenges the sponsor re-vetting policy itself. Re-verified 2026-09-01: checked the Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse's case-specific docket directly rather than relying on a search-engine summary, per this tracker's standard practice -- the Clearinghouse docket lagged the court record: the Aug. 6, 2026 joint status report (ECF 50) and the D.C. Update 2026-10-03: MODERATE confidence on the Guardian's Sept. 19, 2026 account of Stephen Miller directing a multi-agency effort to speed child removals and of the specific inter-agency practices it describes, which rest on unnamed sources; the White House did not deny that Miller leads the effort. The almost-200,000 removal-order figure and monthly counts are Mobile Pathways' analysis of Justice Department data, not an official count; IBTimes repeated the same figures on Sept. 23, 2026, citing the same Mobile Pathways analysis and the Guardian's reporting; it is not independent corroboration.

title: White House Uses a Pocket Rescission to Let $567 Million in HHS Refugee and Entrant Assistance Funding Expire
institution: Department of Health and Human Services, Administration for Children and Families, Office of Refugee Resettlement (Refugee and Entrant Assistance account)
status: The withheld money expired Sept. 30, 2026 with no congressional vote, after GAO said the law bars withholding the funds past that date. Seven states sued that day in federal court in San Francisco to undo the impoundment and force the funds to be spent; no ruling yet.
date_of_action: 2026-09-25 (special message sent to Congress; funds withheld through their Sept. 30, 2026 expiration)
what_changed: On September 25, 2026, five days before the end of the fiscal year, President Trump sent House Speaker Mike Johnson a special message under the Impoundment Control Act proposing 11 rescissions totaling $810 million, and the Office of Management and Budget issued a reapportionment letter withholding the proposed amounts from obligation. The largest item, $567,401,904, comes from HHS's Refugee and Entrant Assistance account, specifically the fiscal 2024 appropriation that remains available only through September 30, 2026. Congress appropriated $6,327,214,000 to that account for fiscal 2024, of which $6,277,459,000 was made available through September 30, 2026 for refugee resettlement assistance under the Immigration and Nationality Act, entrant assistance under the Refugee Education Assistance Act, and the care of unaccompanied children under the Homeland Security Act and the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act. The special message does not say how the $567 million cut divides between refugee services and the unaccompanied children program. The White House's own justification says the account's programs "provide services to refugees, asylees, and other eligible non-citizens" and "put unaccompanied alien children in harm's way"; **Global Refuge, a resettlement agency named in the White House release, said the package includes money for "programs that protect the most vulnerable unaccompanied children and help refugees find work, learn English, and stand on their own."** The White House called the account "overfunded due to the Administration's successful border policies," citing two executive orders on border security and refugee admissions that it said "have dramatically curtailed arrivals," and said the rescission was consistent with its goal of "ending the use of Federal taxpayer dollars to support non-citizens." Its public release named grants from the account to Global Refuge, Southwest Key Programs and Endeavors Inc. as examples of spending it opposed. Because a rescission request lets the executive withhold funds for 45 days of continuous session while Congress considers it, and these funds expire on September 30, the timing means the money lapses unless it is released before then, even without a congressional vote to cancel it; this is known as a pocket rescission. On September 29, 2026, GAO's general counsel concluded that all 11 accounts expire at the end of fiscal 2026, that the congressional review period will end no earlier than November 9, 2026, and that the Impoundment Control Act does not permit the President to withhold the funds beyond their expiration, writing that the President "may not force the expiration of budget authority Congress has already enacted and did not rescind." Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, a Republican, said the package showed OMB "intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law"; House Appropriations ranking Democrat Rosa DeLauro said the administration "has also clearly been unlawfully impounding funds all year just to get to this point." The House was out of session and not scheduled to return until after the November midterm elections. The rest of the package proposed smaller cuts, including $15 million for a DHS Alternatives to Detention case management pilot and $10 million in USCIS citizenship and integration grants, along with education, housing, health research, minority business, minority health, Justice Department and foreign debt-relief programs. Update 2026-10-03 (funds expired; seven states sue): On September 25, 2026, the day the package was sent, Republicans blocked Sen. Jeff Merkley's attempt on the Senate floor to pass his bill to eliminate pocket rescissions and nullify the new cancellation, according to the Senate Budget Committee's Democratic ranking member's office. The withheld funds expired at the end of the fiscal year on September 30, 2026, without Congress acting on the request, CQ-Roll Call reported. That day California, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico and Oregon sued President Trump, the United States, OMB and Vought in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleging that the impoundments, including the pocket rescission, violate the Constitution's Separation of Powers, Appropriations and Presentment Clauses and the Administrative Procedure Act. They asked the court to declare the impoundments unlawful, set them aside, and order the funds apportioned, obligated and spent. The complaint says HHS budget-execution data through August 2026 showed only about $141 million of the Refugee and Entrant Assistance money still unobligated, and that roughly $426 million backed existing, not-yet-paid obligations, including formula awards to states and an award with $39 million in still-available funds for California. The states argue that a rescission message cannot cancel obligated funds, and that however the administration reaches its target, the money available for refugee programs, and each state's formula share of it, will shrink. The case was reassigned to Judge Edward M. Chen on October 2; no request for emergency relief had been filed by then. Separate suits filed the same week challenge two other items in the package: $56 million in housing counseling grants, where the judge temporarily suspended the Sept. 30 deadline for all $57.5 million in housing counseling funds so they would not lapse, and $24.9 million for the High School Equivalency and College Assistance Migrant programs, according to CQ-Roll Call. GAO issued no further decision on the package after its September 29 opinion.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Director of the Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.note: President Trump signed and transmitted the September 25, 2026 special message; GAO's review identifies the accompanying reapportionment letter withholding the funds as coming from the OMB Director. Sen. Collins said OMB "intentionally withheld these funds for months," and NPR reported that Democrats blamed Vought for the canceled funds, including Sen. Patty Murray, who wrote that "Vought is saying their votes don't count."

estimated_impact.caveat: Apart from the states' split below, dollar figures are the administration's own proposal and the enacted appropriation; the $567 million is a share of a multiyear appropriation, not a single year's program budget. No count of people served by the specific withheld funds was found, and the White House's claim that the account is overfunded because arrivals fell was not independently tested by any source reviewed. The funds expired Sept. 30, 2026, but a pending lawsuit by seven states asks a court to order them obligated and spent, and the states' $141 million / $426 million split is their reading of agency budget data, not an administration figure; how much of the $567 million programs actually lose, and when, is unsettled.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the facts of the cut: the White House's own special message gives the account, amount and justification, the appropriation text is in Pub. L. 118-47, and GAO's Sept. 29, 2026 decision (B-338788) addresses this exact message. CNN, ABC News, Roll Call, NPR and CNBC independently reported the package and the bipartisan criticism. The harm to specific programs is less certain: neither the White House nor any outlet reviewed broke the $567 million down by program or estimated the number of people affected, so frame it as funding for refugee and unaccompanied-children services being cut, not as a counted loss of services. The Supreme Court's September 2025 order letting the 2025 foreign-aid pocket rescission proceed was a stay that the Court said should not be read as a final ruling on the merits, so the legality question remains open in court. Update 2026-10-03 (expiration and lawsuit): The Sept. 30 expiration is reported by CQ-Roll Call, and the seven-state lawsuit is confirmed by the complaint itself, the court docket, the California Attorney General and Reuters. No source reviewed reported the money being released before it expired, and no HHS or Office of Refugee Resettlement statement on which programs lose funds was found. The split between unobligated and already-obligated money comes only from the plaintiff states' complaint.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] This is the administration's second pocket rescission, after the 2025 foreign-aid package, and appropriators of both parties said it capped months of OMB withholding funds. The broader pattern of Office of Management and Budget impoundments is documented in the Cabinet-Level entry on Russell Vought and the Impoundment Control Act. See also: the entry on HHS ending confidentiality protections for unaccompanied migrant children; and, from the same September 25 package, the entry on the HUD housing counseling pocket rescission and the entry on the migrant farmworker students' GED and college programs pocket rescission.

title: FY2027 Budget Proposal Eliminates All U.S. Funding for the Pan American Health Organization
institution: Department of Health and Human Services; Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the WHO's regional body for the Americas
status: Proposed -- part of the discretionary FY2027 budget request released April 3, 2026, not yet enacted by Congress, which writes and passes final appropriations and has historically modified or restored proposed eliminations of this kind.
date_of_action: 2026-04-03 (FY2027 budget request released)
what_changed: The administration's FY2027 discretionary budget request eliminates all U.S. funding for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the WHO's regional body coordinating disease surveillance and public health response across 35 countries in the Americas. The elimination is part of a proposed $4.3 billion cut to the U.S. global health budget overall. The U.S. is PAHO's largest single funder, providing roughly half of all member-state contributions, and already owes PAHO nearly $135 million in overdue payments -- an arrears problem that predates this proposal and followed the administration's earlier withdrawal from the WHO itself and termination of WHO funding (tracked separately in this database's who-withdrawal-surveillance-access-loss entry). PAHO has responded to the funding uncertainty by projecting a 19% cut to its 2026/27 budget and cutting 17% of its staff. More than 100 health, national-security, and business figures signed a July 30, 2026 open letter opposing the elimination, citing PAHO's role in early-warning surveillance for threats including New World screwworm (a livestock parasite eradicated from the U.S. in 1966 that has since reemerged in the region) and H5N1 avian influenza in poultry and dairy herds.

title: FBI Director Kash Patel Runs Successive Purges of Field-Office Leaders and Agents Tied to Trump-Related Investigations
institution: Federal Bureau of Investigation
status: Ongoing -- multiple rounds since 2025, most recently a roughly 25% headcount cut ordered to the FBI's own Office of General Counsel in early August 2026
date_of_action: 2025 (initial rounds of forced exits) through 2026-08 (Office of General Counsel cut)
what_changed:
FBI Director Kash Patel has conducted multiple successive rounds of forced removals, reassignments, and administrative-leave actions against senior FBI leaders and agents, concentrated among personnel connected to investigations touching Trump, the January 6 Capitol attack, or the Mar-a-Lago classified-documents case.

As acting FBI director in early 2025, veteran bureau leader Brian Driscoll refused a Justice Department order to assist in firing agents who worked Jan. 6 cases and resisted then-acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove's demand for a list of those employees; under pressure, the FBI ultimately turned over employee ID numbers rather than names -- details on more than 5,000 employees, according to contemporaneous reporting, while the later lawsuit, as NPR described it, says Driscoll compiled a list of 6,000 people. Driscoll was fired on August 8, 2025, alongside Steven Jensen and Spencer Evans; their later lawsuit recounts the Bove standoff as part of an alleged campaign of retribution and says new conflict arose shortly before the firings, when Driscoll refused to strip FBI pilot Christopher Meyer entirely of his pilot duties after Meyer was falsely linked online to the Mar-a-Lago case. NPR reported Driscoll was fired roughly two years short of pension eligibility, and that two other longtime agents were dismissed that same month with no pension; his removal was legally notable because, as a member of the FBI's Senior Executive Service, he held statutory 'for-cause' removal protections -- misconduct, neglect of duty, malfeasance, or refusal of reassignment, only after written notice and an opportunity to respond -- that his firing did not follow. That month, a group of former FBI, intelligence, diplomatic and national-security officials calling itself The Steady State released a letter, reported by Fox News on August 10, 2025, criticizing the ousters of Driscoll, Michael Feinberg and Walter Giardina and warning that 'the aim, it seems, is to transform the FBI from a respected, constitutionally grounded investigative service into a personal enforcement arm of a political figure.' MSNBC correspondent Ken Dilanian wrote on X the same month that 'the purge that is ongoing is without precedent in the modern history of the bureau,' raising questions about whether the administration was trying to turn the FBI into 'an instrument of presidential whim.'

Driscoll, Jensen, and Evans sued Patel and Attorney General Pam Bondi on September 10, 2025, alleging a White House- and DOJ-directed 'campaign of retribution' and seeking reinstatement; their complaint alleges Patel told Driscoll privately that he knew the firings were 'likely illegal' but was powerless to stop them because 'the FBI tried to put the president in jail and he hasn't forgotten it.' Driscoll's case belongs in the broader pattern of Patel personally directing removals of Trump-investigation-linked personnel.

A second, separate named case from the same period: **FBI Director Kash Patel fired veteran agent Walter Giardina roughly three weeks after Giardina's wife died of cancer, accusing him in the termination letter of 'poor judgment and a lack of impartiality... leading to the political weaponization of the government'; NYT and Ken Dilanian's reporting noted Giardina, a Marine combat veteran who had worked the Mueller investigation and the Peter Navarro arrest, had colleagues describe his conduct as scrupulous and ethical.** Giardina and fellow terminated agent Christopher Meyer sued Patel in September 2025, alleging the firings followed false public claims about their roles in politically sensitive investigations.

In a January 2026 round described as 'renewed,' at least a dozen personnel were removed in a single week, including: Vanessa Tibbits, a 20-year veteran and former senior adviser to ex-FBI Director Christopher Wray, placed on administrative leave from her role as acting assistant director in charge of the New York field office; Lyonel Myrthil, removed from the New Orleans field office after previously overseeing part of the January 6 investigation response in Washington; the Atlanta field office's special agent in charge, forced out; a former Washington office leader who had overseen January 6 investigations, terminated; and multiple Miami agents who had worked the Mar-a-Lago classified-documents case. In several of these cases, the FBI's own Office of Professional Responsibility had recommended lesser discipline (short suspensions), but Patel personally overrode those determinations and removed the employees instead.

The Washington Post's February 26, 2026 report on this same January 2026 purge round detailed that the roughly dozen agents and staff removed included personnel who specialized in Iran and its regional proxies, not only Jan. 6/Mar-a-Lago-linked staff -- and that the firings began just three days before the United States launched a major military strike on Iran.

CNN's follow-up reporting found the purge gutted the FBI's national-security division counterintelligence team specifically tasked with tracking Iranian threats: CNN's March 3, 2026 report on the CI-12 Iran-focused unit (corroborated by four independent re-publications of the same story and by CBS News's parallel coverage) documents roughly a dozen CI-12 agents and staff being fired over Mar-a-Lago-investigation ties. The Post's related reporting characterized this as leaving national-security offices across the FBI and DOJ measurably weakened heading into an active Mideast military conflict, extending this round from a personnel-retaliation concern to one with a direct national-security-capacity dimension. None of CNN's or CBS News's CI-12 reporting names Driscoll, whose firing (described above) came seven months earlier and predates the later Iran-counterintelligence purge round.

In response to the scale of the firings and reassignments, former FBI officials launched the FBI Support Network in June 2026 to provide legal, mental health, and career assistance to current and former employees affected by Patel's purges and by firings the group says were tied to Trump-related investigations and allegations of political bias -- itself evidence of the purges' documented scale and impact on agency personnel.

Also in June 2026, Patel's FBI fired several analysts -- four intelligence analysts and a supervisory analyst -- tied to a 2023 internal memo (the 'Richmond memo') that examined a potential link between 'Radical Traditionalist Catholic' ideology and racially/ethnically motivated violent extremism. FBI leadership had previously condemned the memo's findings once it became public. AP reported that an internal FBI review, described in a 2023 letter to Congress, found that all individuals involved in the creation, review and approval of the memo 'failed to adhere to analytic tradecraft standards'; a 2024 Justice Department inspector general report, summarizing that review, said that despite departures from proper tradecraft, 'no evidence of a malicious intent or an improper purpose' was found. The analysts' attorney, David Laufman, called the firings 'manifestly unjust, completely unsupported by the facts, and subverts standard FBI policy and procedure.' Unlike the Jan. 6/Mar-a-Lago-linked personnel actions detailed above, this round targeted analysts over a substantive intelligence-assessment topic (domestic religious-extremism research) rather than direct involvement in a Trump-related investigation -- and the firings came after a prior internal review had faulted the memo's tradecraft but found no evidence of malicious intent or improper purpose.

The purge continued into mid-2026: AP reported on July 2, 2026 that Douglas DePodesta, head of the FBI's Chicago field office, was leaving after people familiar with the situation said he had been told to retire; he told colleagues his last day would be Monday, July 6, 2026. AP described the departure as part of Patel's effort 'to force out line agents and supervisors alike who are perceived as not supporting the Trump administration agenda.' Patel has denied the removals constitute political retaliation, saying the personnel involved failed to meet bureau standards; the FBI declined further comment on individual personnel actions when asked by reporters.

Patel ordered a roughly 25% headcount cut to the FBI's Office of General Counsel -- the several-hundred-lawyer division that reviews investigations for legality, defends the bureau in lawsuits (including the Driscoll/Jensen/Evans suit described above), and coordinates with DOJ -- in early August 2026, per Bloomberg Law. General Counsel Samuel Ramer, who took the role in February 2025, began implementing the cut through early-retirement offers, with terminations also under consideration; Bloomberg Law separately reported Patel's team had previously directed Ramer to fire one of his attorneys at random 'to send a message,' though that specific instruction was never carried out. The Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 has proposed eliminating the Office of General Counsel entirely and routing legal review through DOJ instead, giving this cut a policy antecedent beyond Patel's own personnel pattern. This extends the entry's documented purge pattern from field-office agents and analysts to the bureau's own internal legal-oversight function -- the office structurally positioned to check the legality of the personnel actions this entry already documents.

Separately, the Driscoll/Jensen/Evans lawsuit against Patel and Bondi (D.D.C., 1:25-cv-03109, Judge Jia Cobb) remains pending: both sides continued briefing through summer 2026 (plaintiffs filed supplemental-authority notices citing related rulings on July 10 and July 23, 2026), and no ruling on the government's motion to dismiss had been identified in sourcing reviewed. A docket entry search-summary claim that the case was 'terminated' on August 21, 2026 was checked directly against the docket and found to be a misread of an unrelated filing -- an attorney's notice of withdrawal from representing the defendants, not a case termination -- so the case's pending status is unchanged.

title: Peace Corps Staff Cut by Roughly 40%
institution: Peace Corps
status: Largely carried out: the agency reported 72% of planned staff cuts done in FY2025, the rest due in FY2026; OMB projects direct staff falling from 926 FTEs (FY2025) to 594 (FY2027). No public answer to lawmakers' Feb. 2026 force-analysis request reported as of Sept. 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-03 to present
what_changed: After the governmentwide 'Fork in the Road' deferred resignation offer began thinning its ranks, Peace Corps supervisors were urged in March 2025, amid mounting DOGE pressure, to compile lists of personnel and programs to cut. On Friday, April 4, 2025, DOGE team members physically arrived at Peace Corps headquarters in Washington, D.C. to review the agency's internal systems, per ABC News; staff were instructed to help the team set up internal accounts and grant system access, told to retain records of all DOGE requests, and informed that 'equivalent datasets' might be substituted for direct access in some cases. A Peace Corps spokesperson confirmed the agency was 'supporting their requests'; staff, aware DOGE had already dismantled USAID, expressed concern the same could happen here. By May 2025, roughly 250 employees took a second deferred-resignation push after being told they faced termination if they declined. **Recruitment and placement were slated for especially steep cuts: The Hill reported in May 2025 a proposed 70% cut to the team of recruiters and placement officers, and Peace Corps Worldwide reported in July 2025 an expected reduction of about two-thirds in the Office of Volunteer Recruitment and Selection, which handles outreach, application review, and volunteer placement across more than 60 countries. The cuts are paired with an agency goal to more than double the volunteer corps, from 3,322 in service at the end of fiscal 2025 to 8,000 by Sept. 30, 2030.** In September 2025, the Peace Corps Union received formal notice of intent to involuntarily separate 26 bargaining-unit and 11 non-bargaining-unit employees, part of a plan to bring headquarters down to 575 full-time-equivalent staff. That RIF notice period was tolled during the Oct. 1-Nov. 12, 2025 government shutdown and then again by a continuing-resolution moratorium on RIFs through Jan. 30, 2026. Meanwhile, in its FY2025 financial report, issued in December 2025, the agency said it had completed 72% of its planned staff reductions in fiscal 2025, with the rest to follow in fiscal 2026, and described the 575 target as U.S. direct-hire staff at headquarters and posts combined. The governmentwide RIF moratorium expired Feb. 13, 2026, clearing the way for the cuts to proceed. On Feb. 19, 2026, 21 Democratic lawmakers led by Rep. James Walkinshaw and Sen. Tim Kaine wrote to Acting Director Richard Swarttz that the agency, which had about 953 headquarters employees at the start of the administration, had lost roughly 40% of its personnel, and asked it to halt further cuts until it completed a force analysis showing it could still meet its statutory duties and keep volunteers safe; the agency told Government Executive it had already reviewed its operational structure. The administration's FY2027 budget, released in April 2026, shows the scale in the government's own numbers: the OMB budget appendix lists Peace Corps direct civilian full-time-equivalent employment falling from 926 in fiscal 2025 to an estimated 703 in fiscal 2026 and 594 in fiscal 2027, and the Peace Corps' FY2027 Congressional Budget Justification shows U.S. direct-hire payroll falling from $166.6 million in fiscal 2025 to $130.0 million in fiscal 2026, with $124.0 million requested for fiscal 2027. On April 21, 2026, President Trump nominated Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes as Peace Corps director; by early May, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau had become Acting Director, and Swarttz is again listed as chief of staff. No public agency response to the lawmakers' force-analysis request had been reported as of September 2026.

primary_proponent.role: Chief of Staff, Peace Corps (since Sept. 2025; Acting Director Jan. 30, 2026 until spring 2026; led the Trump-Vance Agency Review Team for Peace Corps during the presidential transition)
primary_proponent.note: Swarttz led the transition-period review team for the agency, then oversaw implementation as Chief of Staff and, from Jan. 30, 2026, as Acting Director, the position in which 21 members of Congress asked him on Feb. 19, 2026 to justify the reductions before proceeding further. By early May 2026, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau had replaced him as Acting Director, and he is again listed as chief of staff.

estimated_impact.summary: Peace Corps has lost roughly 40% of its personnel since January 2025, according to 21 members of Congress, and the government's own budget data show its direct federal workforce falling from 926 full-time equivalents in fiscal 2025 to a projected 594 in fiscal 2027, with U.S. direct-hire payroll budgeted about $37 million lower in fiscal 2026 than in fiscal 2025. Recruitment and placement, the offices that find, screen and place volunteers, were slated for cuts of about two-thirds or more, even as the agency aims to more than double the volunteer corps to 8,000 by 2030. Lawmakers warned the reductions could leave the agency unable to meet statutory duties such as volunteer health care, safety and sexual-assault response; no source has yet measured harm to volunteers.

title: Government Cancels Funding for PediaFlow, a Nearly-Finished Artificial Heart Pump for Infants, Amid a Broader Cornell Funding Freeze
institution: Department of Defense (Pentagon) and NIH, affecting Cornell University research
status: Implemented -- funding cancelled, research halted as of October 2025 reporting
date_of_action: 2025-05-14 (initial $6.5 million NIH-linked funding pull reported) through 2025-10-13 (Pentagon grant cancellation reported)
what_changed: As part of a roughly $1 billion broader funding freeze affecting Cornell University, the administration pulled $6.5 million in federal funding in May 2025 from a Cornell project developing a life-saving heart pump for infants and children with congenital heart defects. NPR reported in October 2025 that officials had also cancelled a related $6 million Pentagon grant for PediaFlow -- an artificial heart device for infants -- as part of the administration's broader crackdown on universities it characterized as 'woke.' **The cancellation halted Cornell's nearly-finished research on the device, jeopardizing its availability for children who depend on external heart pumps while awaiting a device like PediaFlow, including 4-year-old Caleb Strickland, whose case NPR's reporting used to illustrate the human stakes of the funding cancellation.**

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration
primary_proponent.role: Directed the funding freeze and grant cancellations affecting Cornell, including the PediaFlow project specifically
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed for this entry as personally directing the PediaFlow-specific cancellation; reporting frames it as part of the administration's broader campaign of funding pressure against universities over campus-politics disputes, the same pattern documented in this database's separate Harvard funding-freeze entry.

estimated_impact.summary: Halted a nearly-completed medical device development project with direct, named-patient stakes -- an artificial heart pump for infants with congenital heart defects who currently depend on external devices while a permanent solution remains unavailable
