title: RFK Jr. Diverted CDC Staff to Compile Measles Data, Blocked Briefings, Spread Vaccine Disinformation -- CDC Chief Medical Officer Resigned; in 2026 CDC Left Pennsylvania Measles Deaths Out of Its Count
institution: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
status: Pennsylvania now leads the national surge: 977 cases and five measles-associated deaths by Oct. 2, 2026, after Kennedy suggested its first two might be 'fabricated.' The CDC lists only two U.S. measles deaths this year, among 3,887 cases; elimination status is under review in November.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Corry's resignation) through Houry's resignation in summer 2025, with the broader outbreak-related pattern continuing into 2026
what_changed:
Kennedy's vaccine skepticism predates his HHS tenure -- during a 2015 multi-state measles outbreak he dismissed public concern as 'hysteria,' blamed vaccine manufacturers for pushing legislation to end personal-belief exemptions, and promoted the debunked vaccine-autism link (Mother Jones, reporting in April 2025). Communications turmoil under Kennedy surfaced early: Thomas Corry, HHS's top communications official, resigned without explanation on LinkedIn in early March 2025, just two weeks after taking office and shortly after Kennedy downplayed the severity of the West Texas measles outbreak and misstated the number of deaths -- a resignation The Hill and CBS News both linked to internal frustration over canceled vaccine-advisory meetings, stalled research funding, and Kennedy's mishandling of the unfolding public health crisis, months before the more widely reported resignation of CDC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Debra Houry described below.

Former CDC Chief Medical Officer Dr. Debra Houry said that while CDC staff were actively responding to the largest U.S. measles outbreak in decades -- more than 2,000 cases nationwide in 2025, including two child deaths linked to a West Texas outbreak cluster, with 93% of cases involving people who were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status -- HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his aides requested 15 years of historical data on every individual measles case, including comorbidities among the deceased. Houry said the requests diverted CDC staff time and attention away from active outbreak management and characterized the data requests as 'not based on science or reality, but trying to answer an agenda that was already in place.' Houry said Kennedy separately declined briefings from CDC's top medical officials on the measles epidemic despite CDC's offers to provide 'correct statistics, correct information,' spread false claims about vaccines (including the MMR vaccine) that CDC experts were prevented from countering, and relied on advisers she said lacked medical, scientific, or government background (CBS News). A June 23, 2026 memo from the Senate HELP Committee's minority (Democratic) staff, describing CDC emails Houry provided to the committee, documents one of the requests: in an email with the subject line 'Measles data 2010-present,' CDC political appointee Stuart Burns pushed for a very quick deadline to release that data despite Houry's concerns about staff capacity, and Houry stated, 'The active measles response has to take priority.'

ProPublica reported that in the same March 2025 window, the CDC blocked release of an internal forecast modeling high measles-transmission risk in areas with low vaccination coverage; the agency had originally planned to use the forecast to underscore the importance of vaccination, but instead issued a public statement echoing Kennedy's framing, describing vaccination as 'a personal choice' rather than a public-health recommendation -- a second, earlier instance of HHS leadership overriding a CDC scientific product, predating the 15-year historical-data request Houry later described. The same period produced a documented physical-harm consequence of Kennedy's vaccine-skepticism messaging -- CNN reported Covenant Children's Hospital in Lubbock, Texas treated multiple unvaccinated children for vitamin A toxicity after parents gave them unsupervised high-dose vitamin A supplements, following Kennedy's public promotion of vitamin A as a measles treatment; vitamin A does not prevent or treat measles. ABC News reported the national case count had reached 483 across 19 states as of the same week (most among unvaccinated children, the West Texas outbreak the epicenter), an early data point predating the 2,000+-case 2025 total already documented above.

As noted above, two child deaths were linked to a West Texas outbreak cluster. **The second of the two, 8-year-old Daisy Hildebrand -- unvaccinated, with no known underlying health conditions -- died April 3, 2025 of measles-related pulmonary failure; Kennedy attended her funeral days later.** Separately, CNN reported on April 8, 2025 that the outbreak, which had reached over 600 cases across multiple states (505 in Texas alone) by that point, was raising particular concern among health officials for spreading into urban areas and day cares, as many young children in the affected communities had not yet received their second MMR dose -- an early-April data point in the same case-count climb this entry documents reaching 700 by mid-April and passing 1,000 by mid-May.

During the 2025 outbreak itself, Kennedy made several further specific public claims that contemporaneous reporting showed were false or misleading, beyond the general pattern Houry later described: in April 2025 he asserted on social media that the Texas outbreak's growth curve was 'flattening' thanks to CDC reinforcements and vaccine distribution, a claim ABC News reported was contradicted by Texas's own state data showing infections still rising and spreading into new counties; in a nationally aired Dr. Phil interview on April 29, 2025, he said vaccines are not properly safety-tested and urged parents to 'do your own research' (New York Times); and around May 1, 2025 he revived the long-debunked claim that the MMR vaccine contains 'aborted fetus debris' (Reuters). Case counts climbed steadily through the spring, passing 700 (mid-April, USA Today), 800-900 (late April, ABC News), and topping 1,000 for the first time in five years by mid-May 2025 (Reuters), with Texas's Gaines County the single-county epicenter (405 of the state's 717 cases); the New York Times reported on April 23, 2025 that the CDC had designated the Texas-Oklahoma-New Mexico spread a single unified outbreak, the largest since the 2000 elimination declaration.

Michigan's outbreak first surfaced in this same window -- its first in six years, three cases in Montcalm County and seven statewide (ABC News, April 18, 2025) -- an early data point in the same Michigan story whose 2026 vaccination-rate collapse (69.4% to 66.5%) is documented below via Reuters' March 2026 analysis. Separately, on April 18, 2025, CDC cancelled a planned program to help Texas schools assess and improve ventilation systems to help manage the state's measles outbreak, after notice that the CDC engineer leading the initiative would be terminated by June -- a concrete program loss amid the broader staffing purges affecting outbreak response described throughout this entry. A Stanford Medicine-led modeling study, published in JAMA on April 24, 2025, projected the longer-term consequence of the declining vaccination rates this entry documents: even at 2025's actual vaccination rates, the simulation found measles could become endemic in the U.S. again within two decades, producing more than 850,000 cases, 170,000 hospitalizations, and 2,500 deaths over the next 25 years; a further 50% decline in vaccination coverage would produce an estimated 51.2 million cases over the same period, while a modest 5% increase in coverage would keep the disease safely below endemic thresholds.

By early July 2025 the national total had climbed further to roughly 1,280 cases -- the worst since 2000 -- centered on an unvaccinated Mennonite community in West Texas and spread to 39 states (Newsweek, Guardian, Reuters), with Reuters reporting Kennedy had by then fired CDC vaccine experts and installed anti-vaccine allies to help rewrite immunization policy. Separately released CDC kindergarten-vaccination data in early August 2025 showed national measles coverage had fallen to 92.5% for the 2024-25 school year, with exemptions rising in most states (Reuters) -- a national vaccination-rate data point distinct from, and predating, the Michigan-specific decline documented below.

CDC and HHS employees tied a deadly attack within the period this entry documents to Kennedy's rhetoric. NBC News reported that on August 8, 2025, a gunman, 30-year-old Patrick White of Kennesaw, Georgia, opened fire near CDC's Atlanta headquarters and Emory University; a neighbor said White had told him he believed Covid vaccines had made him sick. A police officer was killed and the shooter also died; ABC News, reporting on a subsequent employee letter, put the toll at two dead including the officer, a figure not fully reconciled with NBC's single-officer-death account in sourcing reviewed here and flagged rather than resolved. Kennedy emailed CDC staff the following day calling the shooting 'deeply unsettling' and visited CDC headquarters the following Monday, meeting with the slain officer's widow; CDC employees were nonetheless outraged, with one telling NBC News 'people feel like this is a natural progression when you spend years denigrating science and public health, spread misinformation about vaccines.'

On August 20, 2025, more than 750 HHS employees signed a letter to Kennedy -- reported by ABC News -- accusing him of endangering the workforce through 'dangerous and deceitful statements and actions,' citing his description of CDC as a 'cesspool of corruption' and his false claims that mRNA vaccines 'failed to protect effectively' against Covid and flu, and characterizing the shooting as driven by 'politicized rhetoric,' not random violence; the letter set a September 2, 2025 deadline for Kennedy to stop spreading inaccurate health information, affirm CDC's scientific integrity, and guarantee HHS workforce safety. Sourcing reviewed did not identify a substantive Kennedy or HHS response to the letter's specific demands by that deadline.

Houry resigned in protest, saying she could no longer protect the agency's scientific integrity and citing measles, whooping cough, and flu deaths she witnessed: 'I couldn't stand behind that.' According to the Senate HELP Committee minority staff's memo, she resigned in response to Kennedy's Aug. 27, 2025 firing of CDC Director Susan Monarez. Her resignation also followed Kennedy's June 9, 2025 removal of all 17 members of CDC's vaccine advisory committee (ACIP), whose replacements included members with ties to lawsuits against vaccine makers -- notable given that Kennedy himself had collected referral fees from such lawsuits before becoming HHS Secretary. A CBS News investigation published August 31, 2025 reported that Trump administration interference with CDC communications and staffing had paralyzed the agency's outbreak response -- internal reports censored, experts sidelined, staff purged -- leaving Texas local health officials feeling 'all alone' as the outbreak spread across six states and into Mexico; the same investigation put the cumulative toll at that point at roughly 4,500 cases and at least 16 deaths, a figure substantially higher than, and not reconcilable with, the 2,000+-case 2025 U.S. national total documented elsewhere in this entry -- this discrepancy is unresolved in sourcing reviewed for this backfill and the 4,500/16 figures are flagged rather than adopted as a corroborated national total; the qualitative claim of CDC communications/staffing paralysis corroborates Houry's account already documented above.

The Utah-Arizona border outbreak documented below (679 cumulative Utah cases as of August 2026) began smaller: NBC News reported 65 confirmed cases across southwestern Utah and Mohave County, Arizona as of September 27, 2025, concentrated among unvaccinated children in communities where some schools reported MMR coverage as low as 7%. A previously undocumented South Carolina outbreak emerged in parallel that autumn and grew into one of the largest legs of the national outbreak: NBC News reported South Carolina and Minnesota outbreaks had quarantined at least 270 unvaccinated students by mid-October 2025; South Carolina's own count reached 16 cases by October 19 (USA Today), traced in part to Global Academy, a charter school with only 17% student immunization that placed over 140 students in quarantine; the national total reached 1,563 cases across 41 states by mid-October, with officials warning the true total could exceed 5,000 (NPR); further NBC News and AP reporting through December 2025 tracked continuing quarantines across South Carolina, Ohio, Utah, and Arizona and a national total approaching 2,000 cases by year's end.

The outbreak's international dimension was reported separately from this domestic case-count tracking: the Guardian reported in October 2025 that measles had resurged across the Americas, with more than 11,000 cases in ten countries -- 4,800 in Mexico alone -- as U.S.-originated anti-vaccine messaging spread through Latin America; and the WHO reported in December 2025 that global measles infections had topped 11 million across 59 countries, warning that collapsing immunization coverage was also priming resurgences of polio, diphtheria, and whooping cough, with the U.S. (over 1,700 cases at the time of that report) among the affected countries. The CDC's own year-end tally for 2025, reported by ABC News on January 5, 2026, put the final total at 2,000+ cases across 43 states and 50 separate outbreaks with roughly 93% of cases among unvaccinated people or those with unknown status -- the same figures already cited above via CBS News' later reporting, now traced to their original CDC source and reporting date.

South Carolina's outbreak then accelerated sharply into 2026: CNN reported it had surpassed 200 cases by January 22, 2026; Reuters put it at 434 cases (up 124 in roughly two weeks) by January 29, concentrated in Greenville and Spartanburg counties and hitting children ages 5-17 hardest; and PBS NewsHour reported nearly 600 additional cases in a single month brought South Carolina's total to 789 by early February 2026, centered in Spartanburg County -- a county-level total that had by then surpassed the entirety of Texas's 2025 outbreak. By the eighth week of 2026, CNN reported measles cases had already surpassed 1,100 nationally -- roughly six times the total typically seen in a full year -- with 96% of infections among unvaccinated people and health officials warning deaths would likely rise, putting the U.S. at risk of losing its measles elimination status -- a designation held since 2000 -- for the first time.

A Reuters analysis of Michigan state data found the state's childhood vaccination series-completion rate fell nearly 3 percentage points, to 66.5%, between January 2025 and January 2026 -- about 13 times the average annual change over the prior 18 years. Reuters found the decline had different drivers across communities: Kennedy's vaccine-skeptic messaging was the primary influence among white families, while the administration's ramped-up immigration enforcement led Latino families to avoid public clinics and other activities outside the home for fear of deportation, after their vaccination rates had partially recovered post-COVID. A related disease is also reappearing: NBC News reported in late March 2026 that doctors were warning that Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) -- a bacterial disease once nearly eradicated in the U.S. through vaccination -- is resurging as childhood vaccination rates decline, with cases still low in absolute terms (8 cases reported nationally as of March 21, 2026) but rising, including severe recent infections and at least one reported death in an unvaccinated infant.

A parallel state-level story, reported the following month, shows the same dynamic playing out through exemption law rather than data or messaging: Informed Consent Action Network (ICAN) -- a private anti-vaccine advocacy group whose founder Del Bigtree is a longtime Kennedy ally -- sued and won a court ruling restoring broad religious exemptions from Mississippi's previously strict school vaccine mandate, celebrating it as 'the right to medical choice for the citizens of Mississippi.' Mississippi Today/The Guardian reported that in the following year, the state's whooping cough (pertussis) cases reached their highest level in at least a decade, and in September an infant died of the disease -- Mississippi's first pertussis death in 13 years. More than one in five kindergarten religious exemptions issued that year came from newly-eligible families, and Kennedy allies were reported to be using the Mississippi outcome to push similar exemption rollbacks in other states. This entry documents ICAN's lawsuit and its allied framing, not a direct HHS or federal action -- distinct from the federally-driven measles-data-diversion and ACIP-panel actions above, though part of the same broader vaccine-skepticism ecosystem this entry tracks.

The Washington Post reports the U.S. recorded 2,295 measles cases in 2026 as of late July -- the highest annual total since 1991 -- with more than five months remaining in the year, which public health experts attribute to declining vaccination rates and sustained outbreaks across multiple states.

Utah's outbreak, part of the sustained 2026 transmission WSJ and CIDRAP report has continued since early 2025, has reached 679 cumulative cases (197 in 2025, 482 in 2026) with measles detected in every health jurisdiction in the state; the CDC has said the U.S. is at risk of losing its measles elimination status -- unbroken since 2000 -- if any transmission chain remains continuous for a full year, a threshold Utah reached in June 2026, though state officials say it is unclear whether its earliest clusters connect to the later Utah-Arizona outbreak (AP). Utah's kindergarten MMR vaccination rate (78.5% in 2023-2024) is well below the ~95% threshold public health officials say is needed to prevent sustained spread.

Pennsylvania then became the center of the national surge, in an outbreak state officials say began in late April 2026. On August 25, 2026 the state health department reported two measles-associated deaths in Lancaster County, the state's first measles-related deaths in 35 years (Al Jazeera). Neither person had been vaccinated; both were infants too young for the vaccine (AP). Gov. Josh Shapiro said he had declined Kennedy's offer of federal staff, telling him that 'his actions and the rhetoric that is coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America.' Kennedy then publicly questioned the deaths, writing on X that the announcement 'appears to have been premature, and the deaths may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor's hopeful staffers' (Al Jazeera). The CDC, which had first extended condolences, said its weekly update would not include the two deaths 'while CDC reviews additional information regarding the circumstances and causes of death' (PolitiFact, published by PBS NewsHour). In early September Kennedy acknowledged the Lancaster County coroner's conclusion that measles caused one of the deaths. **The coroner confirmed that a measles infection killed a 6-week-old girl born with a genetic condition that left her highly vulnerable to infection.** The other infant, a newborn, died of a ruptured spleen. Measles is listed on his death certificate as a contributing factor, though the coroner said it did not contribute to the rupture. Some public health experts have voiced concern, AP reported, about whether the CDC could still be counted on to post data that clashed with Kennedy's worldview. By September 21 the state had confirmed 792 cases across 39 counties and four measles-associated deaths (Pennsylvania Department of Health), with 155 hospitalizations (CBS 21). In a September 16 letter to the CDC asking for an Epi-Aid outbreak investigation, state Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen wrote that 'the CDC's choice not to publicly recognize the deaths undermines our response,' and said the state would withdraw the request if the agency could not communicate accurately about them; HHS called that condition 'political blackmail' and said the CDC had not received the request through normal channels (Al Jazeera). Kennedy countered that Pennsylvania's governor had 'until very recently, refused to cooperate with CDC' (CBS 21). **A fifth measles-associated death, another unvaccinated Lancaster County resident, was reported September 30, and all five people who died had been unvaccinated.** The state's count reached 977 cases by October 2 (Reuters). The CDC's national tally then listed only two measles-related deaths nationwide, without naming the states, and the agency said it was working with state epidemiologists on a standard definition for measles-related deaths (Reuters). The U.S. recorded 3,887 measles cases in 2026 as of October 1 (CDC data, reported by Reuters), and international health officials are to meet in November to decide whether the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status (AP).

estimated_impact.caveat: The 15-year scope of the data request, the declined briefings, and the characterization of Kennedy's motives rest on the on-the-record account of a single named, credible former CDC official (Houry), reported across two separate CBS News pieces. The request itself is documented: a June 23, 2026 Senate HELP Committee minority (Democratic) staff memo on CDC emails Houry provided to the committee describes one with the subject line 'Measles data 2010-present,' in which CDC political appointee Stuart Burns pushed for a very quick deadline to release that data despite Houry's concerns about staff capacity, and Houry stated, 'The active measles response has to take priority.' CBS News stated it sought comment from HHS but no substantive HHS/Kennedy response or denial was available in either article. Treat the characterization of Kennedy's motives as Houry's attributed opinion, not an independently established fact. The broader picture of leadership interference with CDC's outbreak work is separately supported by ProPublica's reporting on the blocked transmission-risk forecast and CBS News' August 2025 investigation, though neither independently confirms the data request itself. That CBS investigation's toll of roughly 4,500 cases and at least 16 deaths conflicts with the CDC's 2,000+-case national total and is flagged rather than adopted here. The Stanford/JAMA figures are a forward-looking projection tied to declining vaccination rates generally, not an observed outcome or one attributed to this specific diversion. title: Trump, RFK Jr., and FDA Promoted an Unproven Tylenol-Autism Link and Fast-Tracked Leucovorin, Drawing Global Regulator Pushback
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (HHS, FDA)
status: Contested and partly walked back -- global regulators and U.S. medical bodies continue to reject the acetaminophen-autism causal claim; the FDA's leucovorin approval was ultimately narrowed to an ultra-rare genetic condition rather than the broad autism indication originally promised
date_of_action: 2025-09-05 (initial report) through 2026-03-11 (FDA's final, narrowed leucovorin approval)
what_changed: News that HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. would link autism to acetaminophen (Tylenol) use during pregnancy first broke on September 5, 2025, ahead of any official announcement, triggering an immediate stock selloff in Kenvue, Tylenol's maker. The report also previewed a related claim: that folinic acid (a folate derivative) could ease autism symptoms. On September 22, 2025, President Trump, Kennedy, and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary held a White House event formalizing both actions. **Trump told pregnant women Tylenol 'is no good' and to 'fight like hell' to avoid it, tying acetaminophen use in pregnancy to autism despite the FDA's own prior conclusions, reached as recently as August 2025, that the evidence does not support a causal link**; the FDA nonetheless began the process of a label change and issued a physician notice. Separately, Makary announced the FDA intended to approve Wellcovorin (leucovorin) -- an existing chemotherapy-support drug -- to treat autism symptoms, predicting 'hundreds of thousands of kids' would benefit, and stating this would proceed based on a systematic review of published literature and case reports rather than a randomized controlled trial. Medical organizations, including the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the American Academy of Pediatrics, and the Autism Science Foundation, immediately rejected the causal claim as unsupported by the evidence and warned that discouraging fever/pain treatment in pregnancy carries its own documented risks. Global regulators followed within a day: on September 23, 2025, the European Medicines Agency, the UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration, and the World Health Organization all publicly stated the evidence does not support an acetaminophen-autism link, with UK Health Secretary Wes Streeting saying he trusted 'British doctors, British scientists... over President Trump.' Physicians reported a surge of anxious patient questions from pregnant women in the announcement's immediate aftermath. On October 17, 2025, Kenvue formally petitioned the FDA to reject a citizen petition (filed by the Informed Consent Action Network) seeking an autism warning on Tylenol's label, calling the request 'unsupported by the scientific evidence and legally and procedurally improper'; the FDA had reaffirmed as recently as August 2025 that the data do not support a causal association. On October 28, 2025, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Kenvue and Johnson & Johnson, alleging the companies deceptively marketed Tylenol as safe in pregnancy while concealing an autism risk -- the first state lawsuit following Trump's September claims, though independent of the FDA/HHS action itself. The next day, October 29, 2025, Kennedy partially walked back the administration's own claim, telling reporters the evidence was 'suggestive' of a link but that a causative association 'is not sufficient to say it definitely causes autism,' calling for further caution rather than certainty. The leucovorin approval itself was ultimately far narrower than promised: FDA's final decision, reported March 11, 2026, cleared Wellcovorin only for cerebral folate transport deficiency in patients confirmed to carry a specific genetic variant -- a condition documented in fewer than 50 people nationwide -- not the broad autism indication Makary had described to 'hundreds of thousands' of children five months earlier; agency officials said they went into the review considering a broader autism approval but could only find sufficient evidence for the ultra-rare genetic condition.

estimated_impact.summary: A federal administration publicly promoted a causal claim its own FDA had repeatedly found unsupported by evidence, triggering a stock rout in a major consumer-health company, a wave of rejection from every major international drug regulator, documented patient anxiety among pregnant women, and a state lawsuit against the drugmaker -- while the accompanying fast-tracked drug approval was ultimately narrowed to a condition affecting a tiny fraction of the population originally promised access.

The underlying scientific question (whether any acetaminophen-autism association survives adjustment for genetic/familial confounding) remains actively studied and is presented here as contested, not resolved in either direction beyond what FDA, ACOG, AAP, and international regulators have themselves concluded.

title: RFK Jr. Directs CDC to Contradict Its Own Vaccine-Autism Guidance and Launches Multi-Agency Reexamination of Debunked Vaccine-Autism Link
institution: Department of Health and Human Services (CDC, FDA, NIH, NIOSH)
status: Ongoing and escalated -- CDC website guidance remains changed and softened; the confirmed CDC director declined to commit to reversing it; and an August 10, 2026 executive order formally directs the reinstated Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines to restructure the federal vaccine schedule within 90 days, a major expansion beyond the reexamination effort this entry originally documented
date_of_action: 2025-05-16 (Reuters first reports NIH autism-research funding cuts) through 2026-07 (CNN reports on the broader dismantling effort)
what_changed:
In March 2025, after reports that the CDC planned to study whether vaccines cause autism, the Infectious Diseases Society of America warned that 'significant federal resources will be diverted from crucial areas of study, including research into the unknown causes of autism.'

On May 2, 2025, HHS announced that all new vaccines would be required to undergo placebo-controlled trials before approval -- a policy an HHS spokesperson called 'a radical departure from past practices,' framed as following the 'Gold Standard of Science.' The spokesperson said 'significant updates to existing vaccines' could be considered 'new products' requiring the additional placebo testing (potentially affecting annual COVID vaccine updates), while suggesting the 80-year-old flu vaccine might be exempt. Medical experts objected that placebo trials are unethical for vaccines already proven safe and effective -- for example, giving trial participants a placebo instead of the established measles vaccine would unnecessarily expose them to a preventable, and at the time actively outbreaking, disease.

Before the CDC webpage changes documented below, Kennedy's HHS had already been cutting the legitimate autism research this reexamination claims to prioritize. A Reuters review of federal spending data published May 16, 2025 found NIH autism-research spending down roughly $31 million (26% below the prior four-year average) for January-April 2025, with grants canceled or held up specifically because they involved diverse populations, studied gender differences in autism, or were based at universities under separate Trump administration scrutiny -- among the eliminated grants Reuters identified by name: a $509,000 study of genetic factors in mental health and gender diversity among 10,000 autistic and non-autistic people, a $211,000 grant on improving mental health outcomes for autistic adults, and a $548,000 study of autism risk among children of women exposed to childhood abuse.

A ProPublica investigation published August 20, 2025 found the cuts extended further: Kennedy eliminated the entire NIOSH division of researcher Erin McCanlies, who had spent nearly two decades studying how parental chemical exposure affects children's autism risk, shutting down her lab just three weeks before she finished her fourth major paper on the subject; ProPublica's own review of federal data found more than $40 million in NIH autism-research grants canceled and more than 50 autism-related studies defunded under Kennedy's tenure -- directly undercutting his own repeated public pledge to find autism's environmental causes.

Separately, on September 11, 2025, the CDC announced a $362,493 sole-source (no-bid) contract to Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute to investigate a vaccine-autism link, a move autism researchers called unnecessary given decades of settled science; Kennedy said in a statement 'families have been left without answers or options as autism rates have soared.'

On October 8, 2025, then-Acting CDC Director Jim O'Neill, backed by RFK Jr., publicly called for splitting the combined measles-mumps-rubella vaccine into separate single-antigen shots -- a position long promoted by anti-vaccine advocates despite no scientific basis, according to Merck (the MMR vaccine's manufacturer) and outside health experts, who warned it risked lower vaccination rates by adding extra required doctor visits. This Oct. 2025 call directly foreshadows EO 14420's single-antigen-MMR directive documented later in this entry.

A separate campaign forms further antecedent context. Beginning Oct. 15, 2025, Trump announced plans to remove aluminum from childhood vaccines after echoing RFK Jr.'s debunked claims linking aluminum adjuvants to autism; scientists warned the move would cripple vaccine production, eliminating roughly half of the nation's polio, whooping cough, and flu shots that rely on aluminum for immune protection (New York Times). By Nov. 4, 2025, Trump officials reportedly ordered a formal review of aluminum additives in vaccines such as flu and tetanus shots, backed by Kennedy and echoing Trump's 'no aluminum in vaccines' call -- this specific report has no identifiable source URL and could not be independently corroborated, so it is included only as consistent with the sourced Oct. 15 and Nov. 22 reporting and should be treated cautiously. By Nov. 22, 2025, Kennedy was suggesting aluminum in vaccines may contribute to rising food-allergy rates while admitting there is no evidence for the claim, reported by Bloomberg -- however the source URL on record for this claim is a Nov. 22, 2025 Bloomberg article about European reaction to a Ukraine peace plan, an evident mismatch to an unrelated story, so this claim is flagged as needing a corrected citation rather than presented as solidly sourced.

On November 19, 2025, the CDC's vaccine-safety webpage was changed from stating 'vaccines do not cause autism' to instead claim that assertion isn't 'evidence-based' -- a change that bypassed the agency's normal scientific-clearance process and was made without the involvement of the CDC office that manages the page, according to NPR and STAT News. Kennedy confirmed on November 21, 2025 that he had personally directed the change. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. personally directed the CDC to update its website to contradict the agency's longtime public guidance that vaccines do not cause autism -- a position supported by decades of scientific consensus and numerous large-scale studies, and one independent researchers across seven countries have tested in more than 40 high-quality studies covering over 5.6 million people.

Kennedy tasked Stefanie Spear, one of his closest advisers, with leading an HHS effort to search for evidence of a vaccine-autism link. HHS separately reinstated the Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, a body disbanded in 1998, to reexamine childhood immunization safety. A broader multi-agency initiative, reported by the New York Times, involves researchers across several federal agencies comparing long-term health outcomes between vaccinated and unvaccinated children and revisiting questions about vaccine ingredients including thimerosal, a mercury-based preservative removed from most childhood vaccines decades ago -- millions of dollars in federal funding have been redirected toward this effort.

In December 2025, federal health officials separately began re-examining RSV vaccines and other preventative infant shots despite no documented safety issues and strong evidence the shots sharply reduce hospitalizations; the FDA confirmed the review after anti-vaccine conspiracists raised concerns (The Guardian, Dec. 10, 2025). NBC News named the two specific products under review -- Beyfortus (Sanofi/AstraZeneca) and Enflonsia (Merck), both preventive RSV monoclonal antibodies for infants, not vaccines in the traditional sense -- and reported HHS spokesperson Andrew Nixon confirmed the review without identifying a specific new safety concern behind it; American Academy of Pediatrics infectious-disease committee chair Dr. Sean O'Leary said 'I certainly hope nothing regulatory comes of this, because there's no basis for it,' characterizing the review as an attempt to 'sow distrust' that would, if it led to restricted access, 'inevitably lead to fewer children receiving the monoclonal antibody and more kids getting hospitalized.' It remained unclear as of that report whether the FDA would change the products' labels or restrict availability.

Contemporaneous NYT reporting from Jan. 5, 2026 described a CDC cut to the childhood schedule from 17 to 11 diseases, a starting count that differs from the White House's later '18 diseases' figure for EO 14420; the discrepancy is flagged rather than reconciled. Around the same time (Jan. 13, 2026), Kennedy suggested it may be 'better' if fewer children received the flu vaccine, following the rollback of routine childhood vaccination recommendations (CBS News).

In early February 2026, Trump administration officials told Gavi, the global vaccine alliance, that future U.S. funding would be withheld unless it phases out vaccines containing thimerosal, a mercury-based preservative widely used in multi-dose vials distributed in low-income countries (Reuters). Days later, Kennedy dismissed the federal autism advisory panel and replaced its membership with vaccine skeptics and figures tied to discredited autism conspiracies; the panel helps steer roughly $2 billion a year in federal autism research funding (Reuters). Sources disagree on the size of the replacement: one account states '21 new members,' while the cited Reuters article's URL/headline states '19 new members' -- a WebFetch attempt on that URL failed (Reuters blocked the fetch), so both figures are preserved here rather than silently resolved in favor of one.

On March 16, 2026, a federal court in Massachusetts stayed the January 2026 schedule cut described above, postponing 'the effective date of the revised 2026 childhood immunization schedule,' and also stayed ACIP votes taken after June 11, 2025 and the appointments of the 13 ACIP members Kennedy named beginning in June 2025, the Congressional Research Service reported; TIME later reported the judge found it unlawful for the CDC to make those changes unilaterally without ACIP's involvement. On May 29, 2026, Executive Order 14407 directed CDC and ACIP to review the January 2026 schedule, among other resources, and 'take steps to update the child and adolescent immunization schedules' (Congressional Research Service).

The scientific basis Kennedy has relied on to justify this reexamination has itself been collapsing under independent scrutiny. At least three studies frequently cited by Kennedy to promote vaccine-safety doubts -- a 2021 Neil Z. Miller paper in Toxicology Reports linking vaccines to SIDS, a 2020 Miller/Brian S. Hooker paper in Sage Open Medicine claiming vaccinated children had higher rates of developmental delays and asthma, and a 2010 Carolyn Gallagher/Melody Goodman paper in the Journal of Toxicology and Environmental Health linking early Hepatitis B vaccination to autism -- have all been removed, retracted, or placed under additional scrutiny by their publishing journals within a roughly two-month span reported in June 2026. Kennedy relied on two of these three studies in a 2023 book he co-wrote arguing unvaccinated children were healthier than vaccinated children. Separately, Kennedy demanded a different vaccine-aluminum study be retracted; the journal declined.

On July 23, 2026, the CDC's vaccine-autism webpage was softened again, this time in the opposite direction -- adding a footnote stating 'Scientists have not identified the root causes of autism. HHS continues to support rigorous scientific research and will update this page as reliable new evidence becomes available.' The change came as a negotiated concession to Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), an HHS critic of Kennedy's vaccine views and chair of the Senate HELP Committee, in exchange for his support of the administration's CDC director nominee, Dr. Erica Schwartz; the Senate HELP Committee voted 13-10 to advance Schwartz's nomination on July 30, 2026.

The page's original 'Vaccines do not cause autism*' header was not removed -- HHS officials told Cassidy it would remain per their agreement -- and the page continued to cite at least one already-retracted study as of late July 2026 reporting, drawing renewed criticism from public-health groups even as the footnote nominally reaffirmed that autism's causes remain scientifically unresolved rather than tied to vaccines. NOTUS reporting (July 24, 2026) identified by name the specific retracted study the page continued citing: a 2010 Gallagher/Goodman paper on hepatitis B vaccination and autism, retracted in May 2026 after an independent statistical reviewer found 'fundamental methodological flaws' and an 'overstated conclusion' -- the CDC page cites it alongside a 2014 HHS review that had deemed it 'reliable,' a characterization the retraction has since undercut.

The full Senate confirmed Schwartz as CDC director on August 5, 2026 by a 51-44, largely party-line vote (Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., crossed over in favor). During her July confirmation hearing, Sen. Bernie Sanders pressed Schwartz on whether she would remove the CDC's vaccine-autism webpage; she acknowledged 'overwhelming evidence' that vaccines don't cause autism but did not commit to removing the page.

On August 10, 2026, Trump signed Executive Order 14420, 'Delivering Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations for Americans,' which directly escalates the reinstated Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines. The order gives the Task Force 90 days to present plans to (a) offer core childhood vaccines, starting with MMR, as single vaccines rather than only in combination form, (b) reassess the timing and sequencing of the full childhood schedule and adjust the federal schedule accordingly, (c) develop alternative adjuvants to aluminum and conduct comparative safety/efficacy studies, and (d) continuously reevaluate vaccine risk/benefit profiles. The order is separately grounded in an HHS scientific assessment claiming the U.S. recommends more childhood vaccines, and more than twice the vaccine doses of some European peer nations, than any peer country -- and per the White House's own fact sheet, reduces the diseases recommended for universal childhood vaccination from 18 (84 doses in 57 shots, by the fact sheet's count) to 11, with the remaining vaccines shifted to 'shared clinical decision-making' between parents and doctors rather than a universal recommendation.

Public-health reporting (KFF) criticized the single-MMR-vaccine directive specifically, noting historical precedent that countries which abandoned combination MMR vaccines saw increased measles, mumps, and rubella outbreaks, and that Trump has separately and inaccurately called MMR 'quite lethal.' The order converts the Task Force from a reexamination body into one with an explicit mandate and deadline to rewrite the federal vaccine schedule, with the process bypassing the CDC's own Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), the body that has historically set U.S. vaccine recommendations. TIME reported on Aug. 12, 2026 that federal vaccine recommendations are developed through a separate legal process, 'never by executive order,' with the CDC determining the childhood immunization schedule following ACIP input.

estimated_impact.summary: **EO 14420 (Aug. 10, 2026) escalates this from a reexamination into a mandated 90-day process to actually rewrite the federal childhood vaccine schedule via the same reinstated task force, cutting the diseases recommended for universal vaccination from 18 to 11 and directing MMR to be offered as single vaccines** -- a directive that echoes an Oct. 2025 MMR-split proposal Merck and outside health experts warned risked lower vaccination rates, and that public-health reporting (KFF) ties to historical outbreak increases in countries that dropped combination MMR vaccines. Earlier moves also threatened children's protection: scientists warned Trump's plan to remove aluminum from childhood vaccines would eliminate roughly half of the nation's polio, whooping cough, and flu shots, and the American Academy of Pediatrics' infectious-disease committee chair warned that restricting infant RSV antibodies under a federal review would lead to more kids getting hospitalized. title: CMS Tied Billions in Rural Health Funding to States Adopting Trump/MAHA-Aligned Policies Unrelated to Rural Health Itself
institution: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services
status: CMS began grading states on policy compliance in 2026, with clawback reductions tied to at least four scheduled grading cycles; several Democratic-led states publicly refused specific conditions (SNAP restrictions, short-term-plan deregulation) even at the cost of forgoing funding, while other states scrambled to pass or pledge the incentivized policies to secure their share
date_of_action: 2025-07 (Rural Health Transformation Fund created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) through 2025-12 (Politico's investigative report on the policy-conditionality structure; state applications and CMS grading continued into 2026)
what_changed: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act created a $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund in July 2025, framed as the largest recent federal investment in rural healthcare and intended in part to offset the same law's Medicaid cuts (see the related medicaid-hospital-closure-risk-2026.json entry). CMS, under Administrator Mehmet Oz, structured the fund's distribution so that 50% is divided equally among applicant states regardless of population, 25% is allocated by rural-population and uncompensated-care factors, and the remaining 25% (roughly $3.75 billion) is awarded based on each state's alignment with a CMS-defined set of policy priorities -- some bipartisan (nutrition education in medical schools, telehealth expansion, expanded scope of practice for nurses and other providers) and some politically divisive and largely unrelated to rural healthcare delivery itself: SNAP restrictions on 'non-nutritious' foods, deregulation of short-term health insurance plans that fall outside Affordable Care Act coverage requirements, and even Presidential Fitness Test implementation in schools (adopted by Tennessee). States receive full credit for policies already enacted and partial credit for pledges to implement them by 2027-2028; CMS said it would grade states at least four times on compliance, with funding subject to 'clawback' reductions if promised policies are not implemented. CMS officials, including Oz, described the clawback threat not as a punishment but as leverage governors could use domestically to push the incentivized policies through their own legislatures. Politico's December 7, 2025 investigation, headlined quoting a state legislator's 'sort of blackmail' characterization, documented the resulting political conflict: Minnesota state Sen. Matt Klein (D), a physician running for Congress, said 'if that rural hospital fund is tied to sort of blackmail policy initiatives that are unacceptable to the people of Minnesota, we'll have to figure out our own pathway to care for our members'; Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer (D) rejected the SNAP-related conditions despite Delaware seeking over $100 million, saying 'we're not going to sell ourselves out to do this for $1 here, $1 there'; and Arizona state Sen. Priya Sundareshan (D) called the food-stamp rules 'paternalistic,' warning the structure penalized states with divided governments that could not easily pass the incentivized legislation. By the December 2025 reporting, 12 Republican-led states had already adopted the SNAP restrictions and 11 more had pledged to, while 14 or more states had already implemented the short-term-plan deregulation; some states with legislatures out of session when November 2025 applications were due, including North Dakota, convened special committees under time pressure to meet CMS deadlines, pushing swift legislative action on policies that in some cases had been debated for over a decade. RFK Jr., whose Make America Healthy Again movement's priorities feature heavily among the incentivized policies (CMS directed policy inquiries to a dedicated MAHARural@cms.hhs.gov address), said in November 2025 that the fund's formula resulted from ordinary legislative negotiation rather than his own direction. KFF Health News's own reporting on the program's enforcement quoted Oz directly: 'We will take the money back if states don't abide by what they wrote, if they don't do a good job,' and described the fitness-test push as giving governors 'extra umph, a little bit of gusto to go after these issues'; CMS deputy director Kate Sapra said federal officers check in with states 'at least twice a month, if not on a weekly basis.' Resistance to the fund's terms was not limited to Democratic states: CBS News reported Republican state lawmakers in Wyoming killed a pre-approved state health-insurance plan ('BearCare'), while GOP legislators in Ohio, Michigan, and North Carolina separately pushed back on funding-allocation and rural-definition disputes; first-year state awards ranged from $147 million (New Jersey) to $281 million (Texas). Nebraska Rural Health Association's Jed Hansen said 'Rural Health Transformation will not save a single hospital in our state,' and Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) called the program 'a complete sham.'

primary_proponent.name: Mehmet Oz
primary_proponent.role: Administrator, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
primary_proponent.note: Oversees the fund's distribution and the CMS-defined policy-alignment scoring criteria; publicly described the clawback threat as leverage for governors rather than a punitive mechanism.

estimated_impact.summary: **A $50 billion program explicitly created to help rural hospitals survive the same law's Medicaid cuts instead conditions roughly $3.75 billion of that funding on states adopting a slate of largely unrelated Trump/MAHA-aligned policies, creating a coercive dynamic in which Democratic-led states with divided or opposition state governments face a choice between forgoing needed rural-health funding or passing politically contested legislation** (SNAP food restrictions, ACA-noncompliant insurance deregulation) they would not otherwise prioritize -- while Republican-led states, largely already aligned with the incentivized policies, capture a disproportionate share of the conditional funding pool with comparatively little friction. The program also drew bipartisan criticism on separate grounds: Republican state lawmakers in several states pushed back on funding-allocation formulas and rural-area definitions, and outside rural-health advocates and at least one senator (Wyden) publicly doubted the fund would meaningfully help rural hospitals at all.

title: SAMHSA Banned Federal Grant Funding for Fentanyl and Xylazine Test Strips, Reversing Harm-Reduction Policy
institution: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Final guidance in effect as of April 24, 2026; no reversal identified as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-07-24 (executive order) / 2025-07-29 (initial SAMHSA Dear Colleague letter, with a test-strip carve-out) through 2026-04-24 (SAMHSA guidance eliminating that carve-out) and 2026-05 (reporting on the resulting funding losses)
what_changed: Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0504: this April 2026 test-strip ban was itself an escalation of a broader harm-reduction defunding policy that began roughly nine months earlier. Following President Trump's July 24, 2025 executive order on 'Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets,' SAMHSA issued a Dear Colleague letter to states on July 29, 2025 stating that federal funds could no longer support activities labeled 'harm reduction,' including technical assistance for syringes, pipes, safer-smoking kits, or syringe exchanges, because such programs 'advocate for policies that are incompatible with federal laws and inconsistent with this administration's policies'; the Washington Post reported August 6, 2025 that this raised the possibility SAMHSA itself could eventually be dissolved into a restructured HHS agency. At that time, SAMHSA explicitly exempted naloxone, drug-checking supplies (including fentanyl test strips), and sharps disposal kits from the funding ban, carving them out as still-eligible lifesaving tools -- the carve-out this entry's April 2026 guidance later eliminated by extending the funding ban to test strips specifically, completing a policy arc from 'harm reduction' broadly to the one tool SAMHSA had initially preserved. On April 24, 2026, SAMHSA issued guidance prohibiting federal grant funds from being used to purchase 'substance test kits, including fentanyl test strips and xylazine test strips,' as well as test strips for medetomidine, a veterinary sedative increasingly found contaminating the illicit drug supply -- reversing the prior (Biden-era) policy that had funded harm-reduction organizations' distribution of these low-cost testing supplies. Test strips cost approximately $1 each and allow drug users to check street drugs for the presence of fentanyl, xylazine, or medetomidine before use, a widely-used harm-reduction measure. The Kentucky Harm Reduction Coalition, one specific organization affected, learned it would lose a $400,000 federal grant that had supported distribution of 48,465 fentanyl test strips in the first quarter of 2026 alone; organizations nationally that relied on SAMHSA grants for this purpose now face cutting services or finding alternative funding.

primary_proponent.name: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration leadership, under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: SAMHSA issued the guidance; HHS Secretary Kennedy oversees SAMHSA as part of his broader restructuring of federal health agencies
primary_proponent.note: Reporting reviewed attributes the guidance to SAMHSA as an agency rather than to a single named individual signer; it fits the broader pattern of harm-reduction and public-health-infrastructure rollbacks documented elsewhere under Kennedy's HHS.

estimated_impact.summary: **The policy arrives as overdose deaths have declined roughly 19% nationally since their August 2023 peak, a reduction public health experts substantially credit to expanded harm-reduction measures including widespread test-strip distribution -- cutting funding for this specific, low-cost tool risks reversing recent progress at a moment overdose deaths, while declining, still number in the tens of thousands annually.**

title: HHS Abruptly Cancelled $2 Billion in Addiction/Mental Health Grants, Then Reversed Within 24 Hours
institution: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Reversed within 24 hours, but the episode itself caused documented real-world disruption before the reversal
date_of_action: 2026-01-14 (termination notices sent) through 2026-01-15 (grants reinstated)
what_changed: On January 14, 2026, SAMHSA sent termination notices to an estimated 2,000-2,900 grantees, immediately cancelling close to $2 billion in federal grants supporting addiction treatment and mental health care nationwide, including funding for overdose prevention, naloxone distribution, and other substance-use-disorder services. The termination letters cited generic, non-specific reasons such as 'adjusting its discretionary award portfolio' or 'non-alignment with SAMHSA priorities,' without program-specific explanations. Providers reported overnight layoffs and service shutdowns as the cuts took effect. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was responsible for the termination. Facing swift bipartisan backlash from behavioral-health advocates and members of Congress -- including Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), ranking member of the Senate's Labor-HHS-Education Appropriations Subcommittee, who said there had been an 'intervention' at the White House to halt the cuts -- the administration reversed the terminations and reinstated the grants within 24 hours, by January 15, 2026. No public explanation was given for either the original decision or the reversal, and no official was identified as personally accountable for the initial termination beyond Kennedy's role as HHS Secretary.

primary_proponent.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: HHS under Kennedy issued the termination notices; no more specific individual official within SAMHSA or HHS was identified in sourcing as personally directing the decision or its reversal.

estimated_impact.summary: **Even though the cuts were reversed within 24 hours, the abrupt termination caused real, documented disruption -- providers reported immediate layoffs and program shutdowns -- illustrating that a policy 'undone' within a day still has real-world consequences for services like overdose prevention and naloxone distribution where even brief interruptions carry acute health risk.**

title: SAMHSA Lost Hundreds of Staff and All Ten Regional Offices Amid Push to Dissolve It Into a New HHS Agency
institution: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), Department of Health and Human Services
status: Ongoing -- spring 2025 staff and regional-office losses not reported reversed (Oct. 2025 layoff notices rescinded by law Nov. 12, 2025); AHA merger plan stalled; HELP Committee vote on SAMHSA nominee Timothy Westlake set for Sept. 30, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-02-14 (probationary firings) through 2025-10-10 (shutdown layoff notices, rescinded 2025-11-12)
what_changed: On February 14, 2025, HHS fired roughly 10% of the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration's workforce of just under 900 -- about 100 probationary employees, including four of SAMHSA's regional directors -- in the first of what senior staff and congressional aides were told could be a cut of up to 50%. CBS News reported that about a quarter of the communications team that raises awareness of the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which SAMHSA administers, was among those let go, and a Chicago recovery coalition told the New York Times in March that the federal advisers from its regional office, who oversaw addiction programs across six Midwestern states and 34 tribes, were gone. In a letter dated March 27, 2025, 13 Senate Democrats led by Sen. Alex Padilla, including Sens. Michael Bennet and Mazie Hirono, told HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that SAMHSA's Region 4 and Region 5 offices had been forced to effectively close for lack of staff, **leaving Americans in 14 states without any access to regional officials to help administer local grants and oversee life-saving substance use and mental health programs**, and warned that further layoffs risked "decimating" the 988 Lifeline, which they said had served more than 14.5 million Americans since July 2022; Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand, Angela Alsobrooks and Andy Kim sent a separate March 26 letter opposing the cuts. On March 27, Kennedy announced an HHS reorganization that would dissolve SAMHSA as an independent agency and fold it, along with HRSA and other units, into a new Administration for a Healthy America (AHA). The April 1, 2025 HHS-wide reduction in force closed all 10 of SAMHSA's regional offices, along with its external management team, Office of Minority Health, Office of Behavioral Health Equity and internal policy lab, and laid off senior staff who had been working on the AHA merger, according to Partnership to End Addiction's roundup of the cuts; NPR later reported that SAMHSA lost about a third of its roughly 900 staff to the spring layoffs. In June 2025, the Washington Post reported that the agency was itself in crisis: hundreds of employees had left, a lawsuit by 20 state attorneys general put the reduction at perhaps as much as half, the agency had stopped updating the Drug Abuse Warning Network and no longer had staff dedicated to the National Survey on Drug Use and Health, and canceled SAMHSA grants had scrapped a suicide- and addiction-prevention summit for Indigenous youth in California and stalled a planned mental health crisis center in Bismarck, North Dakota. The 988 Lifeline's own network was already stretched: the CEO of Los Angeles' Didi Hirsch Mental Health Services told CBS News in April 2025 that 12 million people had contacted 988 since 2022, and a RAND-led national survey of 988 Lifeline center leaders, fielded May through July 2025 and published in JAMA Network Open in May 2026, found 71% of responding centers understaffed and 89% reporting difficulty acquiring resources to hire -- a measure of the state and local call centers' staffing, not of SAMHSA's federal cuts. On August 18, 2025, SAMHSA ended funding for the SSI/SSDI Outreach, Access, and Recovery (SOAR) Technical Assistance Center, which it had funded since 2009. The roughly $2.6 million-a-year program had trained about 3,500 state and local caseworkers a year to help people with serious mental illness who are homeless or at risk of homelessness, including many veterans, apply for SSI and SSDI disability benefits; 65% of SOAR-assisted applicants were approved before any appeal, more than double the national average, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. HHS told Axios the contract never directly funded state-level programs; Axios reported that the work now falls to the states, many of which can't afford to take it on, and the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities warned that ending the training "will mean more people living on the streets." In late August 2025, after a mass shooting at a Minneapolis church, Vice President JD Vance said there was "a mental health crisis in the United States of America," and Kennedy said days later that NIH was evaluating whether some antidepressants and psychiatric medications "might be contributing to violence"; ABC News reported on September 9, 2025 that those remarks followed months of cuts to federal mental health programs, including the Education Department's discontinuation of $1 billion in school mental-health grants, NIH grant cancellations that fell hardest on the National Institute of Mental Health, the SAMHSA layoffs, and a proposed cut of about $1 billion to SAMHSA's budget. On October 6, 2025, NPR reported that two psychiatry organizations -- the Southern California Psychiatry Society, representing more than 1,000 clinicians, and the newly formed grassroots Committee to Protect Public Mental Health -- had issued statements calling for Kennedy to be replaced as HHS Secretary, citing both the SAMHSA firings and dissolution effort and a separate concern: Kennedy's 'Make Our Children Healthy Again' (MAHA) assessment, released May 22, 2025, drew wide expert criticism (including a JAMA Pediatrics viewpoint) for cherry-picking and misrepresenting research on psychiatric medications -- citing only early favorable SSRI trials while omitting nine more recent trials, five of which found no statistically significant benefit -- to support claims that antidepressants are overprescribed, addictive, and hazardous to children. The psychiatrists said Kennedy's actions had increased stigma, instilled fear, and hurt access to mental health and addiction care. On October 10, 2025, during the government shutdown, SAMHSA employees received a new round of reduction-in-force notices; former employees told NPR about 125 people were affected, which NPR said brought the agency down to nearly half its January staffing. On October 30, STAT News, drawing on interviews with more than 30 current and former SAMHSA officials, Capitol Hill aides, lobbyists and behavioral-health leaders, reported that fewer than half of the roughly 900 staff on hand in January remained, including just 5 of the agency's 17 most senior leaders; that more than half of the 130 employees at its Center for Mental Health Services had been let go, including all but one of those responsible for youth mental health programs; and that remaining personnel were demoralized and fearful the 33-year-old agency was on the brink of collapse. The White House had still not nominated an administrator, leaving a low-profile deputy in charge. Roll Call reported on November 6 that SAMHSA's highest-ranking official, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary Arthur Kleinschmidt, now reported to HRSA, that several SAMHSA offices had been transferred, and that Congress had rejected the AHA plan as it drafted fiscal 2026 spending bills. The law that ended the shutdown on November 12, 2025 rescinded the shutdown-era layoff notices, including those for about 125 SAMHSA staff; STAT's and Roll Call's staffing counts predate that reversal and may include staff whose notices were later rescinded. On July 14, 2026, the White House, without a formal announcement, sent the Senate the nomination of Timothy Westlake, a Wisconsin-based emergency-medicine physician serving as SAMHSA's chief of staff, to be assistant secretary for mental health and substance use, the post that heads SAMHSA; the agency had had no Senate-confirmed leader since Trump's January 2025 inauguration. Covering Westlake's September 16, 2026 confirmation hearing before the Senate HELP Committee, NPR reported that Kennedy's restructuring plan, which would have eliminated SAMHSA, was on ice after legal challenges. The committee postponed its planned September 24 vote on the nomination and rescheduled it for September 30, 2026.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
primary_proponent.note: Announced and directed the broader HHS reorganization plan that both cut SAMHSA's staff and moved to dissolve it into the new Administration for a Healthy America; oversaw the agency throughout the reductions.

estimated_impact.summary: The layoffs stripped SAMHSA of the regional officials who helped states, tribes and local groups run addiction and mental-health grants -- first leaving 14 states with no regional SAMHSA officials, then closing all 10 regional offices -- and thinned the staff overseeing grants worth more than $6.9 billion in 2024 and the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. The Washington Post documented canceled SAMHSA grants that scrapped a suicide-prevention summit for Indigenous youth and stalled a crisis center, no dedicated staff left for the national drug-use survey, and a halted emergency-department drug surveillance system. Ending the $2.6 million-a-year SOAR training center removed free national training that helped homeless people with serious mental illness win disability benefits at more than double the usual approval rate, which CBPP warned will put more people on the streets. No estimate of deaths or illness attributable to the cuts exists.

title: Small Business Administration Cuts 43% of Staff
institution: Small Business Administration
status: 2025 reorganization carried out; SBA says it cut headcount by over 50% in 2025 and announced a further reorganization in June 2026; the SBA student-loan plan was dropped for Treasury in March 2026; the proposed 67% FY2027 budget cut is unenacted, with SBA on a CR through Dec. 11, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-03-21 (announced); implemented through 2025
what_changed: On March 21, 2025, the SBA announced it would eliminate approximately 2,700 active positions out of a workforce of nearly 6,500, a 43% reduction, through voluntary resignations, the expiration of COVID-era and other term appointments, and a limited number of formal reductions in force. The agency described the goal as returning to staffing levels from the first Trump administration. The same day, President Trump announced that the SBA would take over the Education Department's federal student loan portfolio (nearly $1.7 trillion), a day after he signed an executive order to begin dismantling the Department of Education. On May 22, 2025, U.S. District Judge Myong Joun in Boston, ruling in a broader challenge to the Education Department's dismantling (New York v. McMahon), preliminarily enjoined the department from carrying out that March 21 directive, along with its March 2025 layoffs and the executive order; the opinion found the directive gave no explanation of how moving congressionally mandated student loan programs to the SBA would make them more efficient. The Supreme Court stayed that injunction on July 14, 2025. At the SBA itself, the reduction included layoffs: the agency sent reduction-in-force notices to 77 employees on September 29, 2025, just before the government shutdown, and in November 2025 told them the notices were rescinded under the shutdown-ending funding law, then reversed itself a day later, saying that law did not apply to its layoffs. The SBA never took over the student loans: in March 2026 the Education Department instead signed an interagency agreement with the Treasury Department, starting with collection of defaulted loans and later extending to servicing much of the rest of the portfolio, and NPR reported it was unclear why the administration had pivoted away from the SBA. In a June 5, 2026 release announcing a further agency-wide reorganization that consolidates its disaster, finance, IT, human resources and legal staff into single offices, the SBA said it had reduced its workforce by over 50% in 2025. Separately, the administration's FY2027 budget request, released April 3, 2026, proposes cutting **SBA's total discretionary budget to $329 million, a $671 million (67%) cut from the FY2026 enacted level of about $1 billion, and eliminating 15 of the SBA's 16 entrepreneurial development programs, which Legis1 reported would affect services to nearly 1 million small businesses annually**; the request also cuts SBA's salaries and expenses account by $170 million, to $260 million. It is a request, not an appropriation: Congress had not enacted FY2027 SBA funding as of late September 2026, and a continuing resolution signed September 2, 2026 (Pub. L. 119-103) funds the agency at fiscal 2026 rates through December 11, 2026.

title: SEC Enforcement Chief Margaret Ryan Resigns After Six Months Amid Clashes Over Pursuing Charges in Trump- and Musk-Linked Cases
institution: Securities and Exchange Commission
status: Ryan resigned March 16, 2026; David Woodcock was named Enforcement Director April 8. Sun's case settled in March ($10M paid by one Sun company); Musk's ended in a $1.5M penalty against his trust, approved July 8, 2026 by a judge citing "red flags."
date_of_action: 2026-03-16 (resignation, after roughly six months in the role)
what_changed: Margaret Ryan, Director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement, abruptly resigned on March 16, 2026 after only about six months in the role, with the SEC's own announcement providing no explanation; Principal Deputy Director Sam Waldon was named acting director. On March 23, Reuters, citing three people familiar with the matter, reported that Ryan had clashed with agency leaders over the direction of the enforcement program, including the handling of cases with ties to President Trump and his family. Two of those people said she wanted to be more aggressive in pursuing fraud and other charges, including in cases touching the president's circle, but faced resistance from SEC Chairman Paul Atkins and other top Republican political appointees; they named two cases that sparked tension, both brought by the SEC's prior leadership: its 2023 fraud suit against crypto entrepreneur Justin Sun, a major backer of the Trump family's World Liberty Financial venture, and its January 2025 suit accusing Tesla/X CEO Elon Musk of disclosing his 2022 Twitter stake too late. An SEC spokesperson said enforcement decisions were based on facts, the law and policy, not politics, and an SEC enforcement official said it was their understanding that Ryan ultimately supported the Sun settlement. **In the Sun settlement disclosed in March 2026, one of Sun's companies paid $10 million to resolve the fraud charges without admitting or denying the SEC's findings, and the SEC dismissed the other related charges. On March 17, the day after Ryan's resignation, the SEC and Musk jointly told the court they were in discussions of a potential resolution; at a March 4 hearing, Musk's lawyer had said the talks were with officials above the SEC staff working on the case.** On April 8, 2026, the SEC named David Woodcock as Enforcement Director. On May 4, the SEC amended its complaint to add the Elon Musk Revocable Trust as a defendant, dropped its request for disgorgement (it had earlier sought roughly $150 million), and jointly moved for a consent judgment under which the trust would pay a $1.5 million civil penalty. On July 8, 2026, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan approved the deal despite what she called "significant misgivings," writing that the SEC's decision-making "raises red flags" but that the settlement did not meet the high bar for rejection; the $1.5 million penalty was about 1% of the roughly $150 million the SEC had alleged was at stake. The SEC dismissed its claim against Musk personally the next day. Ryan's exit and the settlement pattern coincide with a broader enforcement-strategy shift under the current SEC leadership toward traditional fraud/market-manipulation cases and away from several compliance-focused enforcement areas, including certain crypto-related actions, that were more common under the prior administration's SEC leadership. Ryan's departure is one of several factors in the SEC's broader enforcement-capacity decline documented in a separate entry on the agency's staffing losses: two 2025 buyout rounds, about 18% of employees leaving during the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025 (per GAO), and a 47-66% drop in enforcement actions in February-July 2026 compared with the same months of 2024 and 2021.

estimated_impact.summary: The SEC's enforcement division lost its director after about six months amid reported clashes with Chairman Atkins and other political appointees over cases touching the president's circle. Both cases that reportedly caused tension ended in settlements, though securities lawyers told Reuters in March that the SEC had strong cases against both and a good chance of winning tougher penalties in court: Musk's trust paid a $1.5 million penalty with no disgorgement, so Twitter investors the SEC said were underpaid by about $150 million get nothing from this case, and a judge flagged "red flags" in the SEC's handling; one of Sun's companies paid $10 million and the SEC dropped the other charges. The result weakens deterrence and raises questions about enforcement independence for politically connected figures.

title: SEC Lost 18% of Its Workforce in 2025 Amid Repeated Buyout Waves, With Longer-Tenured Staff Most Likely to Leave -- Enforcement Actions Fell Nearly 50%
institution: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
status: Ongoing -- SEC is consolidating functions under its December 2025 staffing plan to cope with reduced headcount. About 18% of staff left in fiscal 2025, and SEC had about 4,000 employees in January 2026, per GAO; Chair Atkins told Congress in February 2026 SEC would fill gaps in some divisions.
date_of_action: 2025-02-28 (initial $50,000 buyout offer made in an all-staff memo, per Reuters) through 2025-09-30 (end of fiscal year 2025, in which ~18% of SEC staff left, per GAO)
what_changed: On February 28, 2025, the SEC's chief operating officer offered staff, in an all-staff memo, a one-time $50,000 lump-sum payment to resign or retire, with a March 21 deadline (Reuters; GAO dates the offer to February 2025), part of the broader Trump administration federal-workforce-reduction push. Roughly 500 staffers accepted the buyout and deferred-resignation offers, with the Division of Enforcement, the Division of Examinations, and the Office of General Counsel among the divisions hit hardest, according to agency data obtained through a public-records request. On September 2, 2025, the SEC's chief operating officer told staff in an internal memo, reported by Reuters, that the agency would offer a second round of incentives specifically to supervisor-graded employees following an 'agencywide review' -- another $50,000 lump-sum buyout option, plus voluntary demotions, aimed at reallocating staff; GAO later reported the September 2025 offer also went to all Office of Information Technology staff, and 42 employees accepted and left by February 2026. A subsequent GAO report (GAO-26-107813, a triennial review mandated by the Dodd-Frank Act, issued in March 2026) reported that SEC's own analysis of the April 2025 departures found longer-tenured employees more likely to have taken the buyouts, with staff of 20 or more years disproportionately represented -- a finding indicating the buyouts disproportionately removed the agency's more experienced personnel rather than being distributed evenly across tenure levels; SEC officials told GAO this was expected because those employees were more likely to be eligible for early retirement. By December 2025, SEC submitted its annual staffing plan to Congress proposing to consolidate business groups and work functions -- including nationwide consolidation of investor-assistance functions under a single office -- to manage operations at the reduced headcount, rather than a plan to restore staffing. In February 2026 Senate testimony, Chairman Paul Atkins said the agency had gaps in different divisions and would fill them (Reuters). SEC's fiscal 2027 budget request sought 4,177 full-time equivalents, up from 4,024 in fiscal 2026, on funding 11% below its fiscal 2026 request, and said SEC would 'begin hiring in areas that support the Administration's agenda as staff attrit the agency' (SEC fiscal 2027 budget justification; CIO, April 7, 2026). GAO found that 871 employees, about 18% of SEC's workforce, left during the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025 -- 599, about 12%, through the voluntary-departure programs between January and April 2025 (more than the roughly 500 first reported), the rest through other attrition -- and SEC's own financial report put the net decline, after hiring, at 17%. That was a steeper drop than the 12% by which the federal civilian workforce shrank over a longer period, September 2024 to January 2026, per Office of Personnel Management data reported by Reuters. The Division of Enforcement -- the SEC's largest division by headcount -- had 1,424 full-time equivalents in fiscal 2024 and 1,302 in fiscal 2025, and 1,114 under fiscal 2026 enacted funding, about 22% below fiscal 2024, per SEC's budget justifications; SEC requested 1,168 for fiscal 2027. GAO found that 18% of the division's staff left during fiscal year 2025. A King & Spalding review found enforcement output fell as staff left: **SEC brought 67 new enforcement actions between February 1 and July 31, 2025, down 47% from 127 in the same period of 2024 and 66% from 198 in the same period of 2021**; the firm named the buyout and early-retirement departures as one likely factor, alongside a shift toward clear-cut fraud cases, leadership changes, and a rush of filings in the prior administration's final months that pulled cases forward.
