The September 2025 second round and the December 2025 consolidation plan came under Atkins; reporting frames the changes as part of Atkins reshaping the SEC's enforcement posture.

estimated_impact.summary: About 18% of the SEC's workforce left in fiscal year 2025, roughly two-thirds of them through buyout and deferred-resignation programs, and the agency's own analysis, reported by a federal watchdog, found the buyouts disproportionately removed longer-tenured, more experienced staff -- as SEC brought 47% fewer new enforcement actions in February-July 2025 than in the same months of 2024, per a King & Spalding review, reducing regulatory scrutiny of the securities markets and public companies at a time the agency's own workload had not correspondingly shrunk.

title: Interior's Shutdown Contingency Plan Exempted Oil, Gas, and Coal Permitting From Furloughs While Halting All Renewable Energy Activity
institution: Department of the Interior (Bureau of Land Management, Bureau of Ocean Energy Management)
status: In effect for the duration of the 43-day October-November 2025 shutdown; the underlying National Energy Emergency declaration (January 2025) that provided the legal basis for the disparate treatment remained in effect after the shutdown ended.
date_of_action: 2025-10-01 (shutdown begins, contingency plans take effect) through 2025-11-12 (shutdown ends)
what_changed: During the 43-day October-November 2025 government shutdown, **the Interior Department's shutdown contingency plans exempted oil, gas, and coal permitting staff from furlough while halting comparable renewable-energy work entirely. The Bureau of Land Management (which oversees roughly 245 million acres of public land) confirmed its staff handling oil and gas drilling and coal mining permits were exempt from furlough, citing President Trump's January 2025 National Energy Emergency declaration -- a declaration whose own definition of 'energy' explicitly excludes renewable sources like solar and wind.** A BLM spokesperson said 'activities related to the National Energy Emergency will continue through the shutdown.' The Interior and Agriculture Departments continued issuing new oil and gas drilling permits throughout the shutdown, with more than 300 issued by late October 2025. The disparity was sharper at the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), which furloughed more than 70% of its staff and declined to use carryover fiscal-year funds to support renewable-energy employees; BOEM's contingency plan directed it to 'cease all renewable energy activities' for the shutdown's duration, halting solar-farm permit issuance entirely and delaying offshore wind project construction as the federal permitting staff needed for urgent matters became unavailable. Kris Ohleth, director of the Special Initiative on Offshore Wind, said the pattern undercut any genuine 'all of the above' energy strategy. The disparity extended beyond routine permitting: on October 2, 2025, during the same shutdown, OMB Director Russell Vought separately announced roughly $8 billion in clean-energy grant terminations targeting the 16 states that had voted for Kamala Harris, calling the funding 'Green New Scam funding to fuel the Left's climate agenda' -- a distinct action documented in full in this tracker's doe-clean-energy-grants-political-cancellation-2026.json entry, but occurring in the same window and reflecting the same underlying fossil-fuel-favoring, renewable-penalizing posture as the shutdown contingency plans described here.

primary_proponent.role: Executive branch decision on which agency functions to designate as shutdown-exempt, executing the January 2025 National Energy Emergency declaration's fossil-fuel priority
primary_proponent.note: The disparate treatment traces directly to the National Energy Emergency declaration's own text, which defines 'energy' to exclude renewable sources -- providing the legal mechanism cited by BLM's own spokesperson for exempting fossil-fuel permitting from furlough while renewable energy activity was halted.

estimated_impact.summary: While more than 700,000 federal workers were furloughed and programs like SNAP and WIC faced funding crises during the same shutdown (documented elsewhere in this tracker), fossil-fuel permitting continued uninterrupted and even advanced (300+ new permits issued), while renewable-energy permitting, including solar-farm approvals, stopped entirely and offshore wind construction was delayed -- a direct, shutdown-specific illustration of the administration's differential energy-sector treatment.

title: White House-directed content review and exhibit alterations at the Smithsonian
institution: Smithsonian Institution (Washington, DC museums, via White House Domestic Policy Council/OMB)
status: Ongoing and escalated: Trump's E.O. 14416 (July 24, 2026) directs agencies to use funding/contract leverage to compel compliance and orders NPS warning signs outside the American History museum. Secretary Lonnie Bunch said Sept. 8 he will retire by year's end. Second-phase museums not yet announced.
date_of_action: 2025-03-27 (executive order) through 2026-07 (findings report)
what_changed:
President Trump's March 27, 2025 executive order 'Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History' directed Vice President JD Vance, who sits on the Smithsonian's Board of Regents, to work to 'remove improper ideology' from Smithsonian museums, and instructed OMB and the Vice President to condition future appropriations on exhibits not 'degrading shared American values' or 'dividing Americans based on race.' The March 2025 executive order had cited the Smithsonian American Art Museum exhibit 'The Shape of Power: Stories of Race and American Sculpture' and said NMAAHC 'has proclaimed that "hard work," "individualism," and "the nuclear family" are aspects of "White culture."' The museum announced in a March 14, 2025 email to staff that NMAAHC director Kevin Young was on indefinite personal leave; Young announced his departure in early April 2025; a Smithsonian spokesperson said the leave was 'totally unrelated' to the March 27 executive order. A Congressional Research Service analysis in April 2025 said the Smithsonian, 'due to its organizational structure outside the three branches, arguably is not subject to policy promulgated by executive order,' and called the order's potential scope and effect on the Smithsonian 'unclear.'

The National Museum of American History removed references to Trump's two first-term impeachments from a display in July 2025 as part of an internal content review the Smithsonian undertook under White House pressure (the Smithsonian said it 'was not asked by any Administration or other government official to remove content' and that the temporary placard 'did not meet the museum's standards in appearance, location, timeline and overall presentation'); the references were restored about a week later after public criticism. National Portrait Gallery director Kim Sajet resigned in mid-2025 after Trump publicly said he was firing her, calling her 'a highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI' (the Smithsonian said only Secretary Bunch could make that personnel decision). In a June 2025 statement, the Smithsonian's Board of Regents affirmed the institution as an 'independent entity' that will continue to be governed by the Board, while directing Secretary Bunch to 'give directors reasonable time to make any needed changes to ensure unbiased content.' Artist Amy Sherald canceled a planned exhibition of her work at the National Portrait Gallery in late July 2025 following a dispute over a painting depicting a transgender Statue-of-Liberty figure. The Smithsonian's Office of Diversity was closed.

In August 2025, White House aide Lindsey Halligan, Domestic Policy Council Director Vince Haley, and OMB Director Russell Vought sent a letter to Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch launching a formal review of eight flagship DC museums (including the National Museum of American History, the National Museum of African American History and Culture, and the National Portrait Gallery), demanding exhibition texts, future exhibition plans, internal curatorial guidelines, staff manuals, and organizational charts, with a 120-day deadline for museums to begin 'content corrections' replacing 'divisive or ideologically driven language.'

The White House's Aug. 12, 2025 letter to Secretary Bunch said the review aimed to 'celebrate American exceptionalism, remove divisive or partisan narratives, and restore confidence in our shared cultural institutions.' It named eight museums for the first phase: the National Museum of American History, the National Museum of Natural History, the National Museum of African American History and Culture, the National Museum of the American Indian, the National Air and Space Museum, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the National Portrait Gallery, and the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. The letter set staged deadlines: exhibition descriptions, America 250 materials, and internal guidelines within 30 days; remaining documentation and curator interview scheduling within 75 days; and 'content corrections' beginning within 120 days.

NPR reported the Smithsonian had submitted some documents in September 2025; in January 2026 it submitted additional records to the review, and ABC News reported that Bunch said the Smithsonian would continue to turn over additional records to the White House 'on a rolling basis.' An April 2026 Yale Law Journal essay said the March 2025 order's legality 'remains uncertain, in part because the Smithsonian's legal status is uncertain,' noting that 'the Supreme Court has never addressed whether the Smithsonian is an executive agency or a trust instrumentality as a distinct entity'; the essay noted that the Smithsonian describes itself, and the U.S. Solicitor General in a 2005 brief described it, as a 'trust instrumentality,' a term its charter does not use (the charter calls it simply a trust), and that courts 'are reticent to define the Smithsonian as a traditional executive agency.'

In July 2026, the White House Domestic Policy Council published a report titled 'Saving America's Story' accusing the National Museum of American History of 'extreme political activism' and faulting it for not having created a dedicated exhibit on the Founding Fathers, the Declaration of Independence, or the Revolutionary War even in the 250th-anniversary year. The White House's July 2026 report -- formally titled 'Saving America's Story: How Ideological Capture at the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History Erases Our Heritage,' issued July 4, 2026 by the Domestic Policy Council -- specifically accused the museum of 'anti-white,' 'illegal alien,' and transgender-related 'activism' in addition to underemphasizing the Founding era. Secretary Bunch responded publicly on July 8-9, 2026, writing that the report 'is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History' and that the institution 'remain[s] focused on what grounds us: a steadfast commitment to scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy and integrity' -- a direct, specific, on-record rebuttal to this particular report, distinct from his earlier general September 2025 independence statement. National Museum of American History director Anthea Hartig testified before a House subcommittee in July 2026 that 'Our work is governed by the Smithsonian standards of scholarship, accuracy, independence, and nonpartisanship.'

On July 24, 2026, President Trump signed Executive Order 14416, 'Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution,' formalizing the July 2026 'Saving America's Story' findings report into a directive. The order instructs the Secretary of the Interior, the OMB Director, the GSA Administrator, and the Domestic Policy Council to 'identify and utilize any and all available authorities' to push compliance, explicitly including funding and contract conditions -- an escalation from review and public criticism to stated administrative/financial leverage. **It also directs the National Park Service to install temporary signage along the public sidewalks/walkways leading to the National Museum of American History warning visitors that the museum reflects 'ideological capture' per the findings report and directing them to alternative sources for 'accurate' history**, and mandates temporary outdoor counter-exhibits focused on the 56 signers of the Declaration of Independence timed to the 250th-anniversary Semiquincentennial.

On August 6, 2026, Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and Jeff Merkley (D-OR) sent a bipartisan letter to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and NPS Director Jessica Bowron questioning the E.O. 14416 signage directive's legal basis, seeking the total number, size, placement, content, and manufacturing/installation cost of the planned signs, the funding source within Interior, the number of DOI/NPS staff assigned, and where visitors would be directed for 'accurate' information and who compiles it; no response from Interior/NPS to the senators' letter had been identified as of late August 2026. No announcement of which museums comprise the review's second phase had been identified as of late August 2026. On Aug. 28, 2026, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and White House domestic policy assistant Vince Haley wrote to the Smithsonian that executive departments and agencies 'cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership by, for example, loaning artifacts for exhibits, enabling procurement processes and making discretionary grants,' and requested an in-person meeting with its board; the Smithsonian declined to comment on the letter, NBC News reported. On Sept. 8, 2026, Secretary Bunch announced his retirement after seven years leading the Smithsonian; ABC News reported it 'comes amid mounting attacks against the Smithsonian from the Trump administration,' and Bunch told ABC News, 'I have fought for as long as I can,' though, ABC noted, his parting statement did not reference the attacks from the White House. NBC News reported that Bunch said he would step down by the end of the year. NBC News also reported, citing a person familiar with the situation, that Bunch told friends after he saw Burgum's Aug. 28 letter that he believed now was the time to step down. The Congressional Research Service reported that Smithsonian museums and the National Zoo received approximately 16.9 million visits in fiscal year 2024.

primary_proponent.note: Co-signed and helped lead the August 2025 letter to Secretary Bunch launching the formal Smithsonian museum review, and, per legal analysis, has 'sought to influence the Smithsonian's decisions, including by instigating a curatorial review of the museum,' despite being a non-Senate-confirmed executive branch appointee with no formal authority over the historically independent institution.

estimated_impact.summary: A White House pressure campaign over Smithsonian content, begun with a March 2025 order to condition future appropriations and widened by an August 2025 review of eight museums, has already coincided with at least one exhibit alteration, the resignation of National Portrait Gallery director Kim Sajet, and an artist's cancellation of a planned exhibition after a dispute over a painting, at an institution that received about 16.9 million visits in fiscal 2024. In July 2026 Trump escalated the campaign with Executive Order 14416, which directs agencies to use 'any and all available authorities,' including funding and contract conditions, to push compliance, and orders National Park Service signs outside the National Museum of American History warning visitors that it reflects 'ideological capture.' In September 2026 Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced his retirement; ABC News reported it came 'amid mounting attacks against the Smithsonian from the Trump administration,' though his parting statement did not mention the White House.

estimated_impact.caveat: The White House frames this as restoring historical accuracy and 'American exceptionalism' rather than suppressing content. Its March 2025 executive order cited specific exhibits as ideological rather than factual, including the Smithsonian American Art Museum's 'The Shape of Power' and NMAAHC material labeling 'hard work,' 'individualism,' and 'the nuclear family' as aspects of 'White culture.' Its July 2026 report, 'Saving America's Story,' accuses the National Museum of American History of 'anti-white,' 'illegal alien,' and transgender-related 'activism.' NMAAHC director Kevin Young's 2025 departure is not counted here: the Smithsonian called his leave 'totally unrelated' to the March 2025 order. The Smithsonian has repeatedly affirmed its independence (a June 2025 Board of Regents statement, Secretary Bunch in July 2026, and American History museum director Anthea Hartig in July 2026 House testimony), though it also turned over records to the White House in September 2025 and January 2026, with more to follow 'on a rolling basis'; it has said it was not directed by the administration to remove the impeachment references (calling that specific placard 'temporary' and not meeting museum standards on its own), and Secretary Bunch responded directly that the July 2026 report 'is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History.' The Smithsonian's unique legal status - a congressionally chartered trust that the Smithsonian itself and the U.S. Solicitor General have called a 'trust instrumentality' (a term its charter does not use), and that federal courts have generally declined to treat as an executive-branch agency - is itself a live, unresolved legal question about whether the White House has authority to compel these changes at all: a Congressional Research Service analysis said the Smithsonian 'arguably is not subject to policy promulgated by executive order,' and a 2026 Yale Law Journal essay said the March 2025 order's legality 'remains uncertain, in part because the Smithsonian's legal status is uncertain'; a bipartisan Senate letter from Sens. Murkowski and Merkley has also questioned the legal basis of E.O. 14416's signage directive, with no Interior or NPS response to that letter identified. Secretary Bunch's retirement, announced Sept. 8, 2026, is counted among the departures because ABC News reported it came amid the administration's attacks and he told ABC 'I have fought for as long as I can'; NBC News, citing a person familiar with the situation, reported he told friends after seeing Interior Secretary Doug Burgum's Aug. 28 letter that now was the time to step down. His parting statement did not mention the White House, so the retirement is not presented as directly caused by the campaign. The full reach of the review is not yet known, since the museums in its second phase had not been announced as of late August 2026.

title: 770,000+ Children Lost SNAP Benefits in the Year After Trump's Domestic Policy Law, Despite Promises Children Would Be Protected
institution: USDA / Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
status: Ongoing and worse than first measured -- ProPublica's original 12-state analysis (776,134 children) was superseded in scope by a 19-state CBPP analysis (1.06M+ children, 44% of all losses) reported July 23, 2026
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed) through 2026-06 (ProPublica analysis published)
what_changed: The child-enrollment losses documented below are the downstream result of a monthslong 2025 legislative process. House Republicans first unveiled SNAP restrictions in May 2025 -- stricter work requirements, limits on aid to citizens and green-card holders, and a proposal to shift 5-25% of SNAP benefit costs onto states starting in 2028, with higher-error states paying more, and to raise states' share of administrative costs to 75% immediately -- as part of a broader tax-and-spending bill (New York Times, May 12, 2025; Washington Post, May 13, 2025). CBO estimated in late May that more than 3 million people could lose SNAP monthly under the House bill's roughly $300 billion in proposed cuts (New York Times, May 22, 2025); by June, a Reuters analysis (June 11, 2025) put the House bill's shift of SNAP benefit and administrative costs to states at about $22 billion and cited a May 22 CBO letter projecting that the state spending requirements would push 1.3 million people off SNAP in an average month; the Wall Street Journal (June 2025) cited a CBO distributional analysis showing the wealthiest 10% would gain an average of $12,000 while the poorest households would lose about $1,600 from the combined Medicaid/SNAP cuts. Late on Friday, June 20, 2025, the Senate parliamentarian advised that the Senate Agriculture Committee's version of the state cost-share -- which made changes to the House approach, whose cost-shift CBO had estimated would save about $128 billion -- violated the Byrd rule; Agriculture Committee Chairman John Boozman said his team was examining options that would comply with Senate rules (AP, June 21, 2025). A state benefit cost-share survived into the final law, tied, as the House plan's had been, to each state's payment error rate (see below and this tracker's separate Arizona SNAP error-rate entry). Through late June and early July 2025, reporting described the reconciliation bill's combined scope as it neared passage: roughly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts alongside the SNAP changes, together projected to strip healthcare from about 11 million people (New York Times, June 26, 2025); one estimate put combined Medicaid/SNAP/ACA-subsidy cuts at $1.4 trillion against $3 trillion in tax cuts, disproportionately benefiting the wealthiest households (Guardian, July 3, 2025); and the expanded work requirements, covering parents of children as young as 7 and adults aged 55-64, were projected pre-passage to threaten aid for up to 8 million people (Guardian, June 28, 2025) -- a figure the CBO later refined, post-passage, to 2.4 million people actually stripped of benefits by the work-requirement expansion alone (Guardian, August 12, 2025). Following the bill's July 4, 2025 signing, Politico (July 6, 2025) reported food banks warning the SNAP cuts could eliminate up to 9 billion meals a year, and the New York Times (July 4, 2025) reported Democratic governors warning that federal emergency funds were inadequate to cover states' new cost burden; the Wall Street Journal (mid-July 2025) reported food banks nearing collapse as pandemic-era aid ended and federal food deliveries were canceled on top of the new work requirements. The state cost-sharing mechanism was enacted with the law on July 4, 2025: beginning in fiscal year 2028 (October 2027; later for the highest-error states), each state pays 0% to 15% of its SNAP benefit costs depending on its payment error rate, and beginning in fiscal year 2027 (October 2026) states' share of SNAP administrative costs rises from 50% to 75% (P.L. 119-21, secs. 10105-10106). The New York Times (September 20, 2025) reported the law requires states to fund a share of SNAP benefits for the first time in roughly 60 years -- a mechanism Arizona (tracked separately in this database) responded to in part by tightening enrollment. On October 1, 2025, the law's elimination of SNAP-Ed -- federal nutrition-education funding that also supported food banks -- took effect; the Guardian (September 30, 2025) called the combined cuts 'the largest SNAP cuts in U.S. history' and warned 4 million people a month would lose benefits amid grocery prices up nearly 18% since 2022, while the law's cancellation of the USDA's hunger survey drew criticism for obscuring the cuts' impact. Separately, the New York Times (September 30, 2025) reported Colorado counties taking on new enforcement costs for the law's expanded Medicaid/SNAP work requirements, part of a $386 billion combined Medicaid/SNAP decade-long cut. A ProPublica analysis published June 17, 2026 found at least 776,134 children stopped receiving SNAP benefits in the 12 states that report participation by age, in the year following Trump's signing of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025 -- legislation that cut roughly $186 billion from SNAP over a decade, the largest cut in the program's history, imposed new work requirements on older adults and parents of teenagers, and shifted billions in administrative and benefit costs onto states. Children made up nearly half of everyone cut from the program across the states studied. The impact was highly uneven: Arizona alone lost 205,223 children from its SNAP rolls since July 2025, a 55% decline (driven in part by the state's own error-rate-penalty response, tracked separately in this database), while Louisiana recorded the second-steepest child decline at 22%. Republicans had promised during the law's passage that children and other vulnerable groups would be shielded from its effects. **A subsequent Center on Budget and Policy Priorities analysis**, reported by Newsweek on July 23, 2026, extended the picture across 19 states (versus the original ProPublica analysis's 12) and found more than 1.06 million children had lost SNAP benefits since the law's enactment, with children accounting for 44% of all enrollment losses in those states -- a materially larger scope than the 776,134/12-state figure this entry was originally built around, though the two analyses use overlapping but not identical state samples. NPR/member-station reporting published August 3, 2026 placed the child losses within the program's wider collapse: national SNAP participation fell from a 2025 monthly average of 42 million recipients to 37 million as of April 2026 (preliminary USDA data); CBPP measured an 11% decline between July 2025 and April 2026, and NPR estimated more than 4 million people lost aid over that span, with over 1 million children losing benefits across the same 19 states CBPP examined. Arizona -- already this entry's steepest-decline example -- lost more than 400,000 total participants and saw enrollment fall to about half its year-earlier size, with more people visiting food banks monthly than remained enrolled in SNAP for the first time on record; Texas separately lost roughly 500,000 participants.

estimated_impact.summary: Hundreds of thousands of children lost federal food assistance as a direct downstream consequence of SNAP funding cuts and administrative changes that Republicans specifically promised would not affect children, with impact concentrated heavily in a handful of states.

estimated_impact.caveat: The 776,134 figure covers only the 12 states that publicly report SNAP participation broken out by age, so it understates the true national child-loss total. Some of the decline reflects state-level administrative-burden responses to the law's error-rate penalties (see this tracker's separate Arizona SNAP entry) rather than direct federal eligibility changes alone -- both mechanisms trace back to the same underlying federal law.

confidence_note: Strong sourcing: this is ProPublica's own original data analysis of state-reported SNAP participation figures, corroborated by independent secondary coverage (Newsweek, IBTimes UK, the Equal Justice Initiative) and citing on-record commentary from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. The state-level breakdowns come from state agencies' own published data, not modeled estimates. A broader 19-state CBPP analysis (reported by Newsweek, July 23, 2026) corroborates and extends the ProPublica finding with a larger child-loss total; both analyze state-reported administrative data, so they are consistent rather than conflicting. NPR/WITF's August 3, 2026 reporting places the child figures inside the program's national decline (42M to 37M recipients), drawing on the same USDA and state data. The legislative history rests on contemporaneous news coverage (NYT, Washington Post, Reuters, WSJ, AP, Guardian, Politico) and the enacted law's text, not on independent data analyses. Two related mechanisms are tracked in separate entries: state income-tax cuts colliding with the new state cost share, and the exposure of roughly 27,000 grocery retailers, disproportionately rural, to the same SNAP cuts.
pull_quote: Republicans had promised during the law's passage that children and other vulnerable groups would be shielded from its effects; Arizona alone lost 205,223 children from its SNAP rolls since July 2025, a 55% decline.

title: SNAP Cuts Threaten 27,000 Small Grocers, Many in Rural Trump-Voting Areas
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture; SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program)
status: Ongoing -- OBBBA's SNAP cuts and eligibility/work-requirement changes were enacted July 4, 2025 and are phasing in; no source reviewed confirmed a national count of actual grocery-store closures attributable to the cuts as of this entry's sourcing
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (OBBBA enactment) through 2025-07-19 (Politico's dedicated reporting on rural-grocer impact)
what_changed: Politico reported July 19, 2025 that OBBBA's deep SNAP cuts -- described by multiple outlets as the largest cuts to the 86-year-old program in its history, affecting more than 42 million recipients nationwide -- were poised to hit independent grocery stores especially hard, including in many rural and small-town communities that voted for Trump. **Small, independent grocers that operate on thin profit margins and depend heavily on SNAP purchases to stay viable are frequently the only full-service supermarket serving a given rural area**; their closure would force residents to travel 30 or more miles for groceries. The Center for American Progress identified roughly 27,000 retailers nationwide, disproportionately in rural areas with large shares of SNAP recipients, as most exposed to the cuts' financial impact. Separately, the Urban Institute projected 22.3 million of the 42 million SNAP-reliant families would lose some or all of their benefits as a result of the law's combined eligibility restrictions and administrative changes -- a demand-side reduction in SNAP purchasing power that directly reduces revenue for the retailers CAP identified as most exposed. This retailer-level economic impact is distinct from, though a direct downstream consequence of, the state-fiscal cost-shift mechanism already documented in snap-state-cost-shift-alec-tax-cuts-collision-2025.json and the child-specific benefit-loss figures documented in snap-770000-children-lost-benefits-2026.json -- together, the three entries document SNAP cuts' effects at the state-budget, individual/family, and local-retail-economy levels respectively.

title: SNAP Benefits Withheld During 2025 Government Shutdown
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Nutrition Service
status: Resolved (shutdown ended, full funding restored through Sept. 2026) but litigation exposed underlying legal violations
date_of_action: 2025-10-31 through 2025-11-13 (peak crisis); shutdown began Oct. 2025, was the longest in U.S. history
what_changed: During the government shutdown, the Trump administration initially announced SNAP benefits (food stamps for ~42 million Americans, about 1 in 8 people in the U.S.) would not be paid in November 2025 at all, breaking from the precedent of prior administrations tapping a contingency fund to keep benefits flowing during shutdowns. After lawsuits, a federal judge in Rhode Island (John McConnell) first ordered partial funding (~65% of normal benefits) from the contingency fund, then found the administration's partial-payment approach itself 'arbitrary and capricious' and ordered full funding by a set deadline. Some Democratic-led states issued full benefits before the Supreme Court intervened with a temporary stay blocking the order, creating a chaotic situation where some recipients got full benefits and others got partial or none, based on which state they lived in and how quickly that state's officials acted. USDA then ordered states to 'immediately undo' full benefit issuances already made. The dispute was ultimately mooted when Congress passed a bill ending the shutdown with SNAP funded through September 2026. Re-verified 2026-07-26: one additional litigation detail worth noting -- the administration itself moved to drop its own First Circuit appeal of the Rhode Island judge's order, rather than the appeal being denied on the merits, consistent with this entry's existing framing that the dispute was ultimately mooted by the funding CR rather than resolved by any appellate ruling. Re-verified 2026-08-17: no material change to this entry's own claims. (A separate, related case -- Rhode Island State Council of Churches v. Rollins, over work-requirement waiver terminations rather than the contingency-fund payment dispute this entry documents -- was dismissed by joint stipulation in early 2026 after the waivers in question expired on their own terms; noted here only to distinguish it from, not as new information about, this entry's tracked dispute.) Added 2026-09-09: earlier in the same crisis, in late October 2025, USDA had told states it could not use the contingency fund because the money was 'not legally available' for regular monthly benefits, per an internal USDA memo reported by AP, and separately directed states not to process November benefits with their own state funds without federal approval -- blocking at least three states (Louisiana, Vermont, Virginia) that had said they would try to keep aid flowing on their own. More than 200 House Democrats sent USDA a letter urging use of the contingency fund; House Speaker Mike Johnson publicly backed the administration's decision not to tap it, while the House remained out of session during the standoff. Two senior USDA Food and Nutrition Service officials -- FNS administrator James Miller and senior adviser Babs Hough -- resigned in late October, days before the November lapse, leaving the agency's SNAP leadership vacant during the crisis. As litigation escalated in early November, Trump publicly said SNAP would resume 'only when the Radical Left Democrats open up government,' appearing to threaten defiance of the court order then in effect, before his press secretary said hours later that partial payments would go out after all; separately, in appealing Judge McConnell's full-funding order, administration lawyers argued they could not 'find $4 billion in the couch cushions.' AP also reported some beneficiaries being turned away at grocery stores during the partial-payment period as merchants grew wary of reimbursement uncertainty tied to the shifting court orders.

primary_proponent.name: Trump administration / USDA leadership
primary_proponent.role: Executive branch decision not to use the SNAP contingency fund
primary_proponent.note: Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly defended the administration's position, calling Judge McConnell's order 'judicial activism at its worst' and arguing a 'single district court in Rhode Island should not be able to seize center stage.' USDA official Patrick Penn signed the memo directing states to reverse full benefit payments already issued. Judge McConnell's own order found the administration's justification for partial-only payment was 'arbitrary and capricious' and suggested the delay may have been for 'political reasons.'

estimated_impact.summary: **Nearly 42 million Americans -- disproportionately children, seniors, and people with disabilities -- had food assistance disrupted or fully withheld for a period during the shutdown, forcing food banks nationwide into 'unprecedented demand' per multiple contemporaneous reports, and leaving benefit amounts dependent on which state a recipient lived in rather than a uniform national standard.**

title: OBBBA's SNAP Cost-Shift Collided With ALEC-Backed State Income-Tax Cuts, Risking Total Program Termination in Some States
institution: State governments (budget offices, human-services agencies) / USDA SNAP program
status: Pending: states' SNAP admin-cost share rises to 75% in Oct. 2026; error-rate-based benefit cost-sharing starts Oct. 2027, with 7 high-error jurisdictions delayed to at least FY2029. As of Sept. 23, 2026, a Senate farm bill delaying the cost shift one year awaited a floor vote.
what_changed: Even before OBBBA's reconciliation bill passed, its scope caught states that had already finalized budgets: the Associated Press reported June 30, 2025 that a new budget year began the next day in 46 states, most of whose legislatures had adjourned and set spending plans without knowing whether, or by how much, federal funding would be cut, including the bill's shift of SNAP benefit and administrative costs onto states. David Adkins (Council of State Governments) described 'great uncertainty and some anxiety in state governments,' Brian Sigritz (National Association of State Budget Officers) said that if cuts were significant, 'states wouldn't be able to fully absorb those,' and Erica MacKellar (National Conference of State Legislatures) said states were 'enacting really cautious budgets'; Medicaid alone accounts for 30% of total state spending nationally, per KFF. Some states had built cushions or triggers: New Mexico created a Medicaid trust fund to be gradually stocked with up to $2 billion; Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin used May 2025 line-item vetoes to create a roughly $900 million cushion; Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe vetoed or froze about $500 million; Hawaii left an extra $200 million as a contingency; Vermont set aside up to $110 million ($50 million usable while the Legislature is out, up to $60 million for later); Montana funded a $50,000 analysis that kicks in if at least $50 million in approved federal funding is canceled or at least $100 million in future revenue is expected to be lost; Maryland requires a report with proposed actions if federal funding falls by at least $1 billion; and North Dakota adjourned its biennial session six days short of its 80-day limit so it could reconvene if needed. Florida lawmakers separately sent voters a proposed constitutional amendment for an emergency reserve of $750 million a year or up to 25% of general revenue, whichever is less, which the AP said was not necessarily tied to federal cuts. The AP noted the Medicaid/SNAP changes came on top of the administration's rollback of transportation and high-speed-internet grants and attempts to withhold funds from sanctuary jurisdictions. The law Trump signed July 4, 2025 (Public Law 119-21) raised states' share of SNAP administrative costs from 50% to 75% starting in fiscal 2027 (October 2026) and, for the first time, requires states with payment error rates of 6% or more to pay 5% to 15% of benefit costs starting in fiscal 2028 (October 2027). Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), a decisive vote, had fought for an exception that delays cost-sharing for the states with the highest error rates, per PBS NewsHour; Alaska's rate was then nearly 25%, the nation's highest. Under the final text, a state whose fiscal 2025 error rate multiplied by 1.5 is at least 20% (a rate of about 13.34% or more) starts in fiscal 2029, and one that crosses that mark in fiscal 2026 starts in fiscal 2030; critics, including Sen. Amy Klobuchar ('They are rewarding errors') and the Food Research and Action Center, said it could encourage states to keep error rates high, the Washington Post reported. The law also lets noncontiguous states such as Alaska seek exemptions from the new SNAP work requirements, and a late change raised a rural-hospital fund from $25 billion to $50 billion over five years to win over holdout GOP senators and House Republicans (Murkowski said the fund and related grants would bring Alaska close to $300 million a year for five years). A ProPublica investigation by Eli Hager published December 9, 2025 identified a deeper structural problem than thin reserves: by ProPublica's own analysis, 26 states had cut income taxes since 2021, 23 of them cutting their top marginal rate and 8 adopting flat taxes, in a post-pandemic wave backed by ALEC (the American Legislative Exchange Council), the Koch brothers-founded Americans for Prosperity and the Tax Foundation, leaving them more reliant on federal money just as OBBBA shifts SNAP and Medicaid costs to them. Most of those states are phasing their cuts in over years, which ProPublica said delayed some of the fiscal fallout and diffused media attention; it reported that proponents were conscious of Kansas's 2012 tax-cut experiment, which a bipartisan supermajority later repealed. North Carolina, which is eliminating its corporate income tax, will likely have to pay an estimated $420 million a year in SNAP benefits based on its relatively high error rate, while recent income-tax cuts will cost it $1 billion in revenue in the coming year alone; it was then the only state heading into 2026 without a full budget, with $535 million for a new children's hospital among the sticking points. West Virginia, where then-Gov. Jim Justice signed the latest of several income-tax cuts in 2024, expects deficits of $400 million and growing; a recent state budget report said vacancies had left economic service workers carrying an average caseload of 947 cases. House of Delegates Deputy Speaker Matt Rohrbach (R) still backs the cuts but told ProPublica that if the state has to take over a significant part of SNAP and Medicaid costs, 'that's really going to put a hurt on a state like ours.' Oklahoma state Sen. Dave Rader (R), who chairs the chamber's revenue and taxation committee, said those programs could have to be 'eliminated' if lawmakers can't pay for them, and that Oklahoma's 'path to zero' income-tax plan would 'put us in an even less fortunate situation because of the decline in revenue.' Missouri is exempting passive income (money made on stocks, real estate and cryptocurrency) from taxation, which ProPublica said will give millionaires an average $43,000 tax break versus $80 for everyone else. On the Medicaid side, ProPublica cited a GAO finding that Georgia spent twice as much on administrative costs as on actual health care when it implemented work requirements. Tax Foundation vice president Jared Walczak defended the cuts, saying revenue remains higher in most states than in the 2010s and that 'everyone's in the same boat'; an Americans for Prosperity spokesperson said the group has also pushed to broaden the tax base and restrain spending; and ALEC's Joshua Meyer wrote in October 2025 that the 'generational effort' to eliminate state income taxes was coming to fruition. Meanwhile, state fiscal-policy researchers Jason Bailey (Kentucky Center for Economic Policy), Wesley Tharpe (Center on Budget and Policy Priorities), Geraldine Miranda (Arizona Center for Economic Progress), and Craig Beck (OpenSky Policy Institute, Nebraska) warned that the tax-cut wave had left budgets strained, cash funds raided and legislatures unwilling to raise revenue. ProPublica's reporting also puts two pieces side by side: in West Virginia, tax cuts contributed to understaffing at the state agencies that must carry out the new SNAP and Medicaid rules, and each state's new benefit share will depend on its payment error rate under OBBBA's formula -- a combination that can compound the fiscal hole. **At a September 2025 congressional hearing, when Rep. Shomari Figures (D-AL) asked whether states that can't afford the new cost share might not have it in their budgets to feed anyone, state and county officials 'from Ohio to Wyoming' answered yes, one by one, ProPublica reported; it also cited the Congressional Budget Office as saying some states could deeply cut or shut down their SNAP programs.** ProPublica called the fall 2025 government shutdown, when the administration refused to fund SNAP for its more than 40 million recipients, 'just a glimpse of what's to come.' Experts told ProPublica that because states must balance their budgets, cutting programs and services was the likeliest response, with state-university tuition increases, canceled road projects and frozen state-worker salaries all on the table. On June 24, 2026, USDA released fiscal 2025 error rates, the first that count: nine states (South Dakota, Nebraska, Idaho, Iowa, Kentucky, Vermont, Utah, Wisconsin and Wyoming) came in under 6% and will owe no benefit share, while Alaska (over 23%), Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, New Mexico, Oregon and D.C. topped 13.34% and won a delay to at least fiscal 2029; the AP estimated that Missouri, at 8.7%, could owe about $150 million a year. In an American Public Human Services Association survey, more than a quarter of responding states said they could consider narrowing eligibility and four unnamed states said they could consider withdrawing from SNAP entirely. As of September 23, 2026, more than 5 million people had lost SNAP nationally since the law's enactment from all of its changes, per Stateline, and the Senate Agriculture Committee had approved on party lines a farm bill that would delay the cost shifts to states by one year, pending a full Senate vote; states' 75% share of administrative costs takes effect in October 2026.

primary_proponent.name: Congressional Republicans / state legislatures pursuing ALEC-backed tax cuts
primary_proponent.role: Enacted OBBBA's state SNAP cost-sharing mechanism; separately, since 2021, enacted the state income-tax cuts (in NC, WV, MO, OK, KY, MS, AZ, and others) that ProPublica's reporting says left states less able to absorb that new cost
primary_proponent.note: This is a two-part causal chain across two levels of government: OBBBA's cost-shift mechanism was a federal congressional action (its legislative history is documented in a companion SNAP enrollment-loss entry); the state income-tax cuts that left many of the same states less able to absorb it were separate state-level actions since 2021, which ProPublica reported moved through legislatures with backing from ALEC, Americans for Prosperity and the Tax Foundation.

estimated_impact.summary: Low-income families in states that cut income taxes since 2021 risk losing food aid if those states narrow SNAP eligibility or leave the program rather than absorb OBBBA's new costs: a 75% share of administrative costs from October 2026 and, from October 2027, 5-15% of benefits for states with error rates of 6% or more. Four states told a recent state-agency survey they could consider withdrawing, and experts expect cuts to other services (tuition, roads, state salaries) to balance budgets. The squeeze is sharpest where tax cuts already shrank revenue: North Carolina faces about $420 million a year in SNAP benefits with recent tax cuts costing it $1 billion in revenue in the coming year alone, and West Virginia faces $400 million-plus deficits with caseworkers already carrying 947 cases each.

title: Trump's Tax and Spending Law Stripped SNAP's Categorical Work-Requirement Exemption for 1.2 Million Veterans
institution: USDA / Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
status: In effect since November 1, 2025 -- veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth up to age 24 are no longer categorically exempt from SNAP's 3-month Able-Bodied Adult Without Dependents (ABAWD) work-requirement time limit; a veteran can still qualify for a different exemption (a disability that limits work, caring for a child under 14, or being 65 or older), but the veteran-specific blanket exemption itself is gone.
date_of_action: 2025-07-04 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed) through 2025-11-01 (nationwide compliance deadline, exemption removal took effect)
what_changed: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025, eliminated the categorical ABAWD work-requirement exemptions that the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act had granted to veterans, people experiencing homelessness, and former foster youth up to age 24 -- populations Congress had specifically carved out of SNAP's work-requirement time limit two years earlier. The same law also raised the ABAWD age ceiling from 54 to 64, sweeping in a larger population of older near-retirees. Effective November 1, 2025, all three previously-exempt groups must now prove at least 80 hours per month of work, job training, or volunteering to keep SNAP benefits beyond three months, unless they qualify for a different exemption (disability, caregiving for a child under 14, or age 65+). Per the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, **an estimated 1.2 million veterans live in households that receive SNAP nationally, with state-level breakdowns including roughly 115,000 in California and nearly 100,000 each in Florida and Texas**; state agencies implemented the change directly -- Pennsylvania's Department of Human Services, for example, explicitly notified recipients that veterans of any branch would lose their exemption as of October 31, 2025. National SNAP enrollment fell sharply in the months surrounding the November 1 compliance deadline, though national data does not break the decline out by exemption category (veteran vs. homeless vs. former-foster-youth vs. newly-covered-by-the-raised-age-cap), and some portion of the drop reflects administrative/paperwork friction during a large, fast-moving rule change -- a caseworker not yet processing a submitted exemption before a deadline passed -- rather than every case being a permanent loss of eligibility.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law July 4, 2025, which eliminated the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act's categorical SNAP work-requirement exemptions for veterans, homeless individuals, and former foster youth, effective November 1, 2025.

estimated_impact.summary: Roughly 1.2 million veterans nationally live in SNAP-participating households and are now subject to proving 80 hours/month of work, training, or volunteering to keep food assistance beyond three months -- a documentation burden advocates say falls hardest on veterans with PTSD, other service-connected conditions that fall short of a qualifying disability exemption, or limited civilian work histories. Food insecurity is independently well-documented among veterans as linked to worse physical and mental health outcomes, including elevated risk of depression and suicidal ideation, particularly among veterans with a history of PTSD or military sexual trauma -- this entry does not attribute any specific health outcome to this policy change directly, since no source reviewed ties a mortality or morbidity figure to this exemption removal specifically, but the general food-insecurity/veteran-mental-health link is independently established research.

National post-deadline enrollment-decline figures reported elsewhere (several hundred thousand to over a million SNAP recipients dropped in the months around November 2025) are not veteran-specific -- they combine veterans with homeless individuals, former foster youth, and the larger newly-covered 55-64 age cohort, and are not included here as a veteran-specific figure for that reason.

title: NIH, CDC, and USAID Cut HIV and TB Research Funding to South Africa, the Largest Non-U.S. Recipient of NIH Grants
institution: National Institutes of Health, CDC, and U.S. Agency for International Development
status: Partially reversed going forward -- NIH lifted its broader 'country of concern' funding ban on South Africa on August 17, 2026, permitting new grant applications to proceed; this does not retroactively restore the ~280 grants terminated in March 2025, new awards are not expected before 2027, and a narrower Fogarty International Center training-grant exclusion remains in place
date_of_action: 2025-02-07 (executive order freezing South Africa aid) through 2025-03-21 and following weekend (mass NIH grant cancellations)
what_changed: On 2025-01-20, Trump signed an executive order pausing nearly all U.S. foreign aid pending review. On 2025-02-07, the administration issued a separate, South-Africa-specific executive order freezing aid to the country, citing what it characterized as 'egregious actions' by the South African government (a land-expropriation law and South Africa's ICJ case against Israel were the cited triggers). Beginning 2025-03-21, NIH started terminating research grants it deemed not aligned with agency priorities under the new administration, including all HIV-prevention research; more than 300 grants funding South African universities' HIV and TB research were cancelled with immediate effect over a single weekend. South Africa was, at the time, the largest recipient of NIH funding outside the United States, receiving an estimated $400 million annually in direct and indirect NIH grants -- funding researchers say supported up to 70% of the country's HIV and TB research. The cuts came alongside separate, parallel reductions to USAID and PEPFAR (the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief) funding flowing to South Africa, and a suspension of CDC grant support to South African health institutions. Public health researchers and rights organizations (including Physicians for Human Rights, which later published a detailed 2026 report on the cuts' downstream effects) warned the combined cuts threatened to reverse two decades of progress against South Africa's HIV epidemic, one of the world's largest, and undermined ongoing tuberculosis research and treatment programs that depend on the same funding streams. Update 2026-08-17: this entry's original write-up (2026-08-12) framed the situation as having no reversal at all, but omitted a narrower, already-public policy change from over a year earlier. On June 30, 2025, NIH announced a workaround for the foreign-subaward funding mechanism it had ended May 1: existing subawards supporting clinical research in South Africa could continue, and about 100 ongoing prime awards to South African researchers 'may proceed,' via conversion into direct supplements to foreign collaborators. Critically, this exception applied only to human-subjects research applications submitted before May 1, 2025, not to lab or animal-study work, and per NIH's own contemporaneous reporting it was unclear even at the time whether the fix would restore awards that had been fully terminated, as opposed to merely frozen mid-process -- an NIH grants official called it 'still a huge administrative lift and unnecessary.' Separately, per South Africa's National Treasury 2026 Budget Review, the South African government committed to reprioritizing R410 million (over the medium term) from the national Department of Health to the South African Medical Research Council specifically to offset the U.S. funding withdrawal -- a domestic mitigation measure, not a reversal of the U.S. cuts themselves. Update 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 43, real correction, major): a much broader reversal than the narrow June 2025 workaround, and one dated the same day as this entry's own 2026-08-17 last-verified date -- NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya signed an internal memo on August 17, 2026 formally lifting the 'country of concern' designation that had blocked essentially all new NIH funding to South Africa since the February 2025 executive order, on the stated legal basis that NIH grants are 'distinct from the objectives traditionally associated' with foreign aid or assistance and so fall outside that order's scope -- the same rationale NIH had used narrowly for the June 2025 workaround, now applied broadly. This is forward-looking, not retroactive: it permits new grant applications and 'meritorious research projects' to proceed, but does not itself restore the ~280 grants terminated in March 2025, and researchers quoted in coverage said the first new grants likely would not be awarded until 2027. The Fogarty International Center exclusion is a new, separate restriction layered on top of the broader lift: as of December 5, 2026, Fogarty will no longer process training/career-development grant applications from South Africa specifically because the country is classified upper-middle-income and a G20 member -- Salim Abdool Karim (director, Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa) called this exclusion 'unfortunate' and a 'self-inflicted wound.' Named South African researchers reacted with relief to the broader lift: Glenda Gray (University of the Witwatersrand, lost HIV/TB grants) said 'It's a huge deal. I am almost crying'; Linda-Gail Bekker (Desmond Tutu Health Foundation) called it 'a lifeline to rebuild.' Coverage citing South African sourcing puts the combined NIH-ban-plus-PEPFAR-cuts loss to South Africa at almost $450 million (R7.4 billion), a broader figure than this entry's existing $400M/year NIH-only estimate since it also incorporates PEPFAR.

The June 2025 NIH workaround did not restore the ~280 terminated grants -- it only let a subset of frozen, not-yet-terminated human-subjects awards continue via a new funding mechanism, and NIH itself was unsure at the time whether it would ever cover terminated awards. Read the R410 million South African government figure as a domestic backfill measure, not evidence the U.S. cuts were reversed. The August 17, 2026 ban lift is likewise forward-looking only -- reporting explicitly frames it as enabling new grants, not restoring the ~280 already-terminated awards, and researchers quoted expect no new awards before 2027; treat 'partially reversed' in this entry's status field as reversal of the funding *ban going forward*, not reversal of the terminations themselves.

The core facts -- the February 2025 South Africa-specific executive order and the March 2025 NIH grant terminations -- are well corroborated; the specific dollar and percentage estimates rest more heavily on South African institutional sourcing than independent U.S. verification. Update 2026-08-17 (GSR recheck batch 20, real correction): the June 30, 2025 NIH policy change is corroborated by Science/AAAS (via EATG's republication) and MedicalBrief; the R410 million South African Treasury commitment is corroborated by the National Treasury's own 2026 Budget Review as reported by SAnews/AllAfrica. The correction adds nuance, not a reversal claim: the underlying terminations remain in effect for the vast majority of the ~280 affected grants. Re-verified 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 43, real correction, major): the August 17, 2026 ban lift -- dated the same day as this entry's own prior last-verified date, so missed by that recheck -- is corroborated across five independent outlets (EWN, SA People, Innovation Village, Sunday Times South Africa, and Science/AAAS), including named on-the-record reactions from South African researchers (Gray, Bekker, Abdool Karim) rather than institutional press-release framing alone. Confidence on the lift itself is HIGH; confidence that it will translate into actually-disbursed new funding is necessarily LOWER, since reporting itself notes no new grants are expected before 2027 and the memo's 'meritorious research projects' language leaves NIH discretion over which specific projects proceed.

title: SSA Drafted, Then Withdrew After Public Backlash, a Rule Change That Would Have Stripped Disability Benefits From 830,000+ Older Blue-Collar Workers
institution: Social Security Administration (SSA); Office of Management and Budget
status: Withdrawn -- SSA scrapped the proposal in November 2025 after public and congressional backlash, before it was ever formally published as a proposed rule
date_of_action: 2025-10 (proposal reported) through 2025-11-20 (withdrawal reported)
what_changed: The Washington Post reported on October 5, 2025 that the Social Security Administration, with prodding from OMB Director Russell Vought, was drafting a rule change to make it significantly harder for older Americans to qualify for Social Security Disability Insurance by removing age as a factor in assessing an applicant's remaining capacity to work -- or, in a less severe version under consideration, raising the age threshold at which age is credited in that assessment from its existing lower cutoffs up to 60. Under SSA's existing 'grid rules,' older applicants, particularly those in physically demanding blue-collar occupations, are more readily found unable to transition to other work given their age, education, and skills; removing or narrowing that age credit would require many of them to be assessed as capable of retraining into different jobs -- including, as the draft reportedly assumed, gig-economy work -- despite often-severe physical limitations from decades of manual labor. ProPublica and the Washington Post reported the change could cut off disability benefits for at least 830,000 people, with other reporting citing an estimate as high as 1.5 million, concentrated among older workers in manual trades such as mining and factory work and disproportionately located in Republican-leaning states, forcing many into reduced early retirement benefits instead. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. John Larson each sent formal letters to SSA Commissioner Frank Bisignano in October 2025 raising objections to the proposal. Following the ProPublica/Washington Post reporting and the resulting public and congressional pressure, the Boston Globe reported on November 20, 2025 that SSA had scrapped the plan entirely; White House officials told disability advocates the rule 'isn't going to be happening.' The proposal was withdrawn before ever being formally published in the Federal Register as a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought, Director, Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.role: Reported by the Washington Post to have prodded SSA to draft the age-factor rule change
primary_proponent.note: SSA itself, under Commissioner Frank Bisignano, was the agency actually drafting and would have formally issued the rule.

estimated_impact.summary: Had it been finalized, the rule would have stripped disability benefits from hundreds of thousands of older, physically-disabled blue-collar workers by assuming they could retrain into new work despite severe physical limitations -- an outcome averted by the proposal's withdrawal, but one that reveals the policy direction under active consideration inside SSA/OMB.

The 830,000 vs. 1.5 million figures reflect different outlets' estimates of the same draft proposal's scope, not two different policies.
