title: Social Security Administration Lost 8,000+ Staff — Lowest Headcount Since 1967 — Then Stopped Publishing Its Own Service Metrics
institution: Social Security Administration (SSA)
status: Ongoing (staffing losses not reversed; some but not all withheld metrics later restored)
date_of_action: 2025-02-24 (earliest documented office closures under Leland Dudek) through 2026-04 (ongoing, per Center on Budget and Policy Priorities' most recent tracking); see also the March 2025 O'Malley warning and April 2025 reclassification push noted below
what_changed:
Since January 2025, the Trump administration drove out more than 8,000 SSA employees in about 15 months (January 2025-April 2026) -- including roughly 7,500 in the first 12 months, the agency's largest one-year staffing reduction on record -- leaving SSA with fewer employees than at any point since 1967, even as it now serves roughly 52 million more beneficiaries than it did then (nearly 75 million total). More than 40 states and D.C. saw staffing cuts greater than 10% between January 2025 and April 2026.

This pattern was already visible within DOGE's first weeks at SSA: ProPublica reported that by February 24, 2025, DOGE operatives working inside the agency under appointee Leland Dudek had already closed at least 10 local field offices and eliminated 41 positions, drawing early alarm from beneficiaries and staff. In March 2025, the Associated Press reported that DOGE's internal, government-wide list of nearly 800 federal real estate leases targeted for cancellation named 47 SSA field offices, 26 of them with lease-termination dates in 2025 -- but SSA publicly disputed the closure framing in a March 27, 2025 agency blog post, stating that since January 1, 2025 it had not permanently closed or announced the permanent closure of any local field office, a direct conflict between DOGE's internal planning documents and the agency's own public position that later reporting in this entry does not resolve.

The website-crash pattern documented below had already begun by then: the Washington Post reported on March 25, 2025 that SSA's website had crashed roughly 10 times over the preceding three weeks due to overloaded servers, that dozens of senior SSA officials -- including its entire cybersecurity leadership -- had resigned or retired amid pressure from Musk's team, and that remaining office managers were personally answering phones because so many receptionist-level staff had been pushed out. Separately, Wired reported in late March 2025 that DOGE -- led by Musk associate Steve Davis, with unvetted operatives embedded in the agency -- was pushing to rewrite SSA's roughly 60-million-line COBOL codebase (which underpins benefit processing for more than 70 million Americans) into Java and other modern languages within a few months, using generative AI to compress a migration SSA had itself previously estimated would take five to ten years; outside engineers quoted in the report warned the accelerated timeline risked exactly the kind of system errors and outages documented below, foreshadowing in specific technical terms the more general IT-overhaul warning Sens. Warren and Wyden issued in June 2025.

The staffing cuts produced concrete technical and administrative failures in the following months: the Washington Post reported the SSA website repeatedly crashed starting around April 8, 2025, disrupting access for millions, with the outages tied directly to Musk-led cuts that slashed IT staff and rushed out undertested software; the next day, CBS News reported SSA mistakenly told some Supplemental Security Income recipients -- including disabled individuals and low-income seniors -- that their benefits had been terminated, with their benefit histories temporarily disappearing from their accounts before the error was corrected roughly a day later. This error pattern had already become individually documented in local and national press starting the same week: on March 21, 2025, the Seattle Times and CNN reported that 82-year-old Ned Johnson of Seattle had been erroneously added to SSA's Death Master File, clawing back his December and January benefits (a combined $5,201) and canceling his Medicare coverage and credit standing until he resolved it in person weeks later; the same week, 9News reported that 90-year-old Denver veteran Tom Kind had likewise been wrongly marked deceased, losing benefits, healthcare coverage, and bank access for more than 10 days.

Newsweek later reported the specific mechanism behind cases like Johnson's: DOGE staffers conducting a self-described 'major cleanup' of SSA's death records -- adding death dates to more than 7 million Social Security numbers that previously lacked one, part of Musk's push to counter his own since-debunked claim that millions of implausibly old people remained on SSA's rolls -- mistakenly moved living people's records onto the Death Master File in the process; SSA's own response to the reporting characterized the affected records only as lacking 'a recorded date of death' rather than acknowledging erroneous death designations outright. A third individual case followed the next month: **on April 12, 2025, KSAT reported SSA had incorrectly declared 40-year-old San Antonio epilepsy patient Joseph Arce deceased, halting his disability payments and terminating his Medicaid and Medicare coverage, cutting off access to his seizure medication**.

The same week, Wired reported SSA planned to cut its regional-office workforce by roughly 90% -- from about 547 employees across nearly a dozen regional offices down to approximately 70 -- while Midwest-West Regional Commissioner Linda Kerr-Davis told staff on a call that the agency would shift to communicating with the press and advocacy groups exclusively through X (formerly Twitter), ending regional offices' press releases and 'Dear Colleague' letters to advocacy groups; SSA publicly disputed the characterization ('This is false. Social Security will continue to communicate through any and all mediums'), while a White House spokesperson framed the regional-office cuts as reassigning staff 'to front-line help.' By May 6, 2025, CBS News reported this had become a further, more consequential error pattern agency-wide: thousands of Americans, disproportionately immigrants and other vulnerable individuals, were being wrongly declared dead or purged from SSA's systems entirely, cutting off Social Security benefits, disability payments, and in some cases banking access tied to a valid Social Security number. SSA has separately noted a baseline error rate of roughly 10,000 wrongly-recorded deaths per year (about 0.3% of the ~3 million deaths it processes) even absent any policy change, and no source found for this entry quantifies whether the 2025 rate rose above that historical baseline -- but Newsweek's and the Center for American Progress's reporting ties the DOGE cleanup effort directly to specific documented cases including Johnson's, distinguishing this from an ordinary-course error.

The on-the-ground effects reached state attorneys general directly. On April 7, 2025, Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes launched a dedicated webpage (azag.gov/socialsecurity) for residents to report Social Security service disruptions, citing constituent concern over changes under DOGE's involvement; her office said it had already received hundreds of reports since March 2025 describing delayed payments, wrongful benefit suspensions, and an inability to reach SSA by phone or in person, a figure that grew to nearly 300 complaints in the following weeks. Mayes separately joined a coalition of 20 state attorneys general supporting a federal injunction against SSA's data-access and operational changes.

In April 2025, SSA briefly eliminated most phone-based benefit applications entirely (reversed after public backlash), while permanently requiring in-person visits or multi-factor online authentication for direct-deposit changes -- a change CBPP notes the agency's own fraud data does not support, since direct-deposit fraud is rare and rarely phone-initiated. As wait times climbed (86 minutes average by April 2025, a 25% increase over the prior year), SSA responded largely by reassigning field-office staff to phone duty rather than hiring -- pulling employees away from processing claims and creating new backlogs elsewhere. In April 2025, the Washington Post also reported the administration was preparing to lay off thousands more SSA workers even after an earlier ~7,000-job elimination, with offices in rural areas losing over half their staff and IT systems already crashing under the strain.

Two named-official developments from this same window are worth noting on their own. First, on March 3, 2025, former SSA Commissioner Martin O'Malley (Biden-era) publicly warned SSA could suffer a full 'collapse of the entire system' and an interruption of benefit payments within 'the next 30 to 90 days' if the DOGE-driven cuts continued -- a high-profile, widely covered warning that did not literally materialize on that timeline (Social Security continued issuing payments past the 90-day mark), though the underlying staffing and service-quality trend O'Malley was warning about is independently documented throughout this entry.

Second, in April 2025 Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek moved to reclassify entire SSA offices -- including mission support, hearings, and communications staff -- under the newly renamed 'Schedule Policy/Career' (formerly Schedule F) excepted-service category, which strips normal civil-service removal protections; roughly 8,000 GS-15-level federal employees government-wide had already been shifted into equivalent categories by that point. This drew bipartisan pushback, and following pressure from Sen. Ron Wyden and colleagues, the administration confirmed by June 27, 2025 that no SSA frontline workers had actually been recategorized under Schedule Policy/Career -- meaning the April reclassification push, as reported, did not fully proceed as originally described, at least for frontline staff, as of that confirmation.

Separately, in May 2025, incoming Commissioner Frank Bisignano told reporters AI would 'soon' handle a significant share of SSA's roughly 400,000 daily phone calls -- an early on-the-record statement of the automation strategy that appears consistent with, and may partly explain the mechanism behind, the dramatically faster call-answer times SSA and its Inspector General later reported for FY2025-2026 (see below), even as field-office staffing and hiring remained sharply reduced.

USA Today reported June 3, 2025 that SSA employees were being directed to prioritize processing roughly 900,000 complex cases created by the Social Security Fairness Act (which repealed the WEP/GPO provisions affecting public-sector retirees) ahead of routine service work -- address updates, direct-deposit changes, Medicaid billing corrections -- against a self-imposed deadline to complete the bulk of retroactive payments by July 1, 2025; employees warned the prioritization risked delaying basic services at an agency already understaffed from the RIFs documented above. SSA disputed that framing. In the event, SSA reported completing over 3.1 million Fairness Act payments (about $17 billion) by July 7, 2025, five months ahead of its own schedule, with roughly 200,000 remaining cases requiring manual processing it said would be finished by November 2025 -- so the specific July 1 completion goal employees warned about was met, though whether routine service quality was in fact degraded in the process, as employees warned, is not resolved by that completion figure alone.

On June 16, 2025, Wired reported Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden formally warned that DOGE's rushed, AI-driven overhaul of SSA's IT systems was jeopardizing the agency's core function, citing the website outages and access failures already documented above as evidence of elevated risk of further benefit disruptions, data loss, or security compromise going forward. In June 2025, amid worsening press coverage, SSA stopped publicly releasing several of its own regular service-performance metrics, including call wait times and appointment-scheduling delays, as the Washington Post reported on June 20, 2025; some measures were later restored, but key ones (hold-time data, appointment-wait data, backlog counts) remain unreported as of CBPP's most recent tracking.

During the federal government shutdown that began October 2025, NPR reported SSA field-office staff said they were unable to issue benefit verification letters -- documents beneficiaries need to access housing assistance, fuel assistance, and other aid -- even as regular benefit payments continued; staff told NPR the letters accounted for an estimated 60-70% of field-office call volume during the shutdown and said they were frustrated the service wasn't classified as essential, while an SSA spokesperson said the agency was operating under its shutdown contingency plan.

By early November 2025, Wired reported the shutdown's toll on staff had reached a breaking point: on a national call, field operations chief Andy Sriubas fielded questions from more than a thousand field-office managers describing employees who could no longer afford gas money to drive to work, some field offices setting up informal food pantries to help unpaid colleagues get by, and staff describing themselves as feeling 'angry and betrayed' while drowning in case backlogs -- with the agency reportedly weighing pausing additional parts of its workload as the shutdown wore on. By early 2026, disability-appeal backlogs had grown by 73,000+ cases in just over a year, and fewer than 850 of SSA's roughly 50,000 remaining employees had less than two years of federal service -- the agency hired fewer than 100 new employees in all of 2025, the lowest annual hiring total on record. The Strategic Organizing Center, a labor-union coalition, reported that in its December 2025-January 2026 online survey of 821 SSA workers, 65% said service quality had worsened and 70% said service had slowed over the prior 12 months.

In June 2026, Commissioner Bisignano told the House Ways and Means Committee and stated in an SSA press release (June 29, 2026) that the agency achieved its 'best all-around performance ever': the National 800 Number's average speed of answer reportedly fell from 34 minutes (2024) to 8 minutes, a 75% reduction; field-office wait times reportedly fell 30%; the initial disability-claims backlog reportedly fell from a high of ~1.3 million (2024) to 853,000, and disability hearing wait times reportedly fell to 266 days, a historic low; the agency also reported 385 million online transactions in FY2026 to date, up 37% from 2024. Government Executive reported that at the June 10, 2026 hearing, Bisignano deflected repeated questions about changes to the methodology behind SSA's improved service metrics; it noted that in 2025 SSA had begun recording callback waits as zero minutes. SSA's workforce continued to shrink over this same period -- roughly 7,000 additional employees left via separation incentives, leaving a workforce of about 50,000, still its lowest headcount in decades.

Independent corroboration of SSA's reported phone-service figures has since emerged. After Sen. Elizabeth Warren raised doubts about SSA's reported phone-service improvements, Commissioner Bisignano agreed to an independent review, and SSA's own Office of Inspector General published an audit in June 2026 confirming the agency's released 800-number performance data was accurate and that service genuinely improved during FY2025: SSA served 68 million callers (a 65% increase over the prior year), with average wait times falling from a January peak of about 30 minutes to roughly 7 minutes by September. This meaningfully corroborates part of Bisignano's disputed 2026 turnaround claim -- specifically the phone-service metrics -- though it does not address or resolve this entry's separate, independently-sourced findings on workforce reduction (8,000+ lost), the disability-appeal backlog, or the 2025 decision to stop publishing certain other service metrics, which remain accurate and unaffected by this audit.

On August 14, 2026 (SSA's 91st-anniversary press release), the agency claimed further improvement beyond the June 2026 figures already documented above -- an average phone wait time of 0.6 minutes in July 2026 (down from the 8-minute figure SSA reported in June and independently corroborated by the OIG audit already cited), a 30% reduction in field-office wait times while serving 25 million visitors, an initial disability-claims backlog of 884,000 (down from the ~1.3 million 2024 high, though nominally higher than the 853,000 SSA itself reported as of the June 29, 2026 release already cited above), and 505 million online transactions in FY2026 to date. These later-2026 figures are presented in the same self-reported, not-independently-audited category as the entry's existing caveat already treats the June 2026 claims -- a continuation of the disputed pattern, not a new resolution of it. Separately, AFGE Council 220 (the union representing SSA employees) continued pressing Congress in August 2026 for $3 billion in additional SSA funding above enacted FY2026 levels and 20,000 new hires, with Council 220 President Jessica LaPointe stating the agency is 'simply bleeding staff and have problems with recruitment and retention as a result' -- consistent with, not a change to, this entry's existing workforce-loss findings.

estimated_impact.caveat: SSA leadership disputes the characterization that more staffing is the answer, and Commissioner Bisignano has publicly staked out a contrary position (efficiency over headcount) -- this is a genuinely disputed policy question, not just a factual one, and should be presented with his stated rationale alongside the outside critique. However, the decision to stop publishing key service metrics amid worsening press coverage is a separately verifiable action, not itself a matter of policy disagreement -- the Washington Post reported it on June 20, 2025, and CBPP later documented the removal of many customer-focused performance metrics SSA had been publishing monthly. A direct, unresolved factual tension has emerged as of mid-2026: SSA's own reported metrics (touted by Commissioner Bisignano in congressional testimony and an official SSA press release) claim dramatic service improvements -- faster phone answer times, shorter backlogs -- achieved with a smaller workforce, which is the opposite of this entry's core framing. The phone-service figures specifically (wait times, call volume) have since been independently corroborated by SSA's own Office of Inspector General in a June 2026 audit prompted by Sen. Warren's concerns -- a genuine confirmation of that piece of the turnaround claim. The April 2025 86-minute average and OIG's FY2025 figure of a ~30-minute January peak are not reconciled in the sourcing and may measure different things. Other claimed improvements (disability-claims backlog, hearing wait times) have not been independently audited as of this update. SSA's August 2026 claims of further gains (a 0.6-minute average phone wait in July 2026, an initial disability-claims backlog of 884,000) are likewise self-reported and not independently audited. Government Executive reported that at a June 10, 2026 House Ways and Means hearing Bisignano deflected repeated questions about changes to the methodology behind SSA's improved service metrics. Present both: the agency's claimed 2026 performance turnaround, sourced explicitly to SSA/Bisignano, alongside the independently-sourced staffing-loss and prior metrics-suppression findings -- don't treat either claim as simply resolving the other. O'Malley's March 2025 '30 to 90 days' collapse warning should be presented as a prediction that did not materialize on its literal timeline, not as a confirmed outcome -- use it as evidence of contemporaneous alarm among former officials, not as proof of an actual system collapse. Similarly, the April 2025 Schedule Policy/Career reclassification push at SSA specifically should be presented as an attempted action that, per the administration's own June 2025 confirmation to Sen. Wyden, had not actually been carried out for frontline SSA workers as of that date -- a genuine attempted-but-contested-and-seemingly-stalled action, not a completed one.

title: More than 100 U.S. ambassador posts left vacant, more than double the rate of Trump's first term
institution: U.S. Department of State / Foreign Service
status: Ongoing -- 98 of 196 ambassador posts vacant as of the American Foreign Service Association's own tracker, last updated August 21, 2026, an improvement from 107 of 195 in late June following the early-August Senate confirmation batch, but still roughly half of all posts
date_of_action: 2026-05 through 2026-07 (reporting period)
what_changed: More than 100 of the United States' 195 ambassador posts remained vacant nearly 18 months into Trump's second term -- 109 of 195 as of mid-May 2026 and 107 of 195 as of late June 2026 -- more than double the vacancy rate at the equivalent point in Trump's first term, when 45 posts were vacant. Vacancies include strategically significant posts: Ukraine, Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Germany, Australia, and South Korea, among others. Of 101 ambassador nominations made during the second term, only 9 have gone to career Foreign Service diplomats, a sharp departure from traditional practice of pairing political and career appointees. In place of confirmed ambassadors, the administration has relied on political allies, megadonors, and informal special envoys to handle diplomacy in many of these countries. Update 2026-08-17: the Senate confirmed a batch of Trump's nominees in early August 2026, including 11 ambassadors and 5 more to ambassador-rank positions -- among them David Brat (Australia) and Michael Kavoukjian (Norway) -- narrowing the vacancy count somewhat. Despite that batch, the underlying pattern this entry documents persists: a Semafor report published August 6, 2026 found Middle East ambassadorships continuing to sit vacant, with the administration relying on special envoys rather than confirmed ambassadors, and broader reporting from earlier in the year found the vacancy pattern extended heavily into Africa (37 of 51 posts without ambassadors as of May 2026) following Secretary Rubio's December 2025 recall of roughly 30 career ambassadors. Update 2026-09-01 (GSR recheck batch 47): the August 7, 2026 confirmation batch (approved 51-47 along party lines, as part of a broader 74-nomination package) named additional confirmed ambassadors beyond the two this entry previously listed -- John Breslow (Cyprus), Joseph Burkhalter (Moldova), Daniel Perez (Brazil), Laurence Socha (The Gambia), John Hurley (OECD, ambassador rank), and Todd Steggerda (UN Geneva, ambassador rank), alongside Brat and Kavoukjian. The American Foreign Service Association's own tracker (afsa.org/list-ambassadorial-appointments, last updated August 21, 2026) puts the current count at 98 of 196 posts vacant -- note the total shifted from the 195 used in this entry's earlier figures to 196 in AFSA's own count, a denominator change not otherwise explained in sourcing reviewed. This is an improvement from the 107-of-195 figure as of late June, consistent with the confirmation batch, and materially better than a since-discarded WebSearch-synthesis claim of 115 vacant 'as of August 26, 2026' that could not be corroborated against AFSA's own primary tracker and is not used here. Despite the improvement, the entry's core throughline -- roughly half of all posts vacant, with a historically low career-diplomat nomination rate -- remains accurate.

title: State Department overhauls diplomat performance reviews into a forced-competition, zero-sum ratings system
institution: U.S. Department of State / Foreign Service
status: Ongoing: the capped-rating EER system was used for the 2026 review cycle; no public outcome of AFSA's announced unfair-labor-practice complaint as of Sept. 2026; an Aug. 20, 2026 DOJ opinion says the Secretary of State, not the Foreign Service Grievance Board, should have the final say.
date_of_action: 2026-01 (new EER form rolled out) through 2026-08 (DOJ opinion curtailing the grievance board's authority)
what_changed: The State Department rolled out a new, numerically scored Employee Evaluation Report (EER) system for Foreign Service officers that makes diplomats compete for a limited number of top ratings rather than being evaluated against an independent standard. On January 15, 2026, the American Foreign Service Association (AFSA), the union representing Foreign Service members, said the new form had been rolled out without negotiation with the union and more than three-quarters of the way through the current evaluation cycle, that it 'risks making career-defining decisions less fair, less transparent, and more vulnerable to bias,' and that AFSA 'will be filing an unfair labor practice against this move by the department.' AFSA tied the lack of negotiation to the administration's elimination of the union's collective bargaining rights. At a House hearing in March 2026, Under Secretary for Management Jason Evans said the department would offer fewer top ratings, that supervisors who gave too many high scores would face consequences, and that it would resume 'low-ranking' officers who miss evaluation criteria, a process that can end in removal; Federal News Network reported the changes could push out more diplomats after the department's 2025 mass layoffs. In a March 31 email, Evans made a 'fully successful' 3 out of 5 the 'standard baseline for performance,' and another department email told raters to 'strictly adhere to an average rating cap of 3.25,' warning that perceived grade inflation 'may lead to a letter in the rater's file.' In May 2026, a performance management reform team in State's human resources office asked managers to 'review and recalibrate' evaluations due later that month, and Federal News Network, citing department emails and four current and former Foreign Service officers, reported that leadership was directing some managers to lower scores on evaluations they had already submitted. One officer said junior employees were asked to accept scores low enough to take them out of promotion contention, keeping higher scores available for senior staff competing for performance pay. The department postponed the evaluation deadline to May 29, 2026. AFSA President John Dinkelman said he was concerned about 'the seemingly intentional creation a zero-sum game among members of a professional corps of diplomats,' while Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau said the change would 'restore accountability and ensure that evaluations reflect actual performance rather than inflated ratings,' according to ABC News. No public record of the filing or outcome of AFSA's announced unfair-labor-practice complaint was found. On August 20, 2026, the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, in an opinion to State's Legal Adviser made public the next day, concluded that the Foreign Service Grievance Board's final decisionmaking authority violates the Appointments Clause and recommended that State decline to enforce the provisions of the Foreign Service Act that make Board decisions binding on the Secretary; under the opinion, the Secretary of State's modification or rejection of a Board decision becomes the final action. AFSA warned on August 24 that the opinion turns the Board from an independent decision-maker into an advisory body and that 'an independent review process cannot provide the same safeguards if the department whose action is being challenged ultimately has the power to overrule the decision.' This narrows the grievance process, the formal route through which diplomats could contest EER scores, low-ranking or separation.

primary_proponent.name: Marco Rubio
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of State
primary_proponent.note: Oversees the State Department's implementation of the new evaluation system, which follows the department's 2025 mass layoffs and which Federal News Network reported could push more diplomats out of the Foreign Service.

estimated_impact.summary: Career Foreign Service officers' promotions, performance pay and continued employment now ride on a rating system that caps each rater's average score and makes colleagues compete for scarce top marks; managers were told to lower already-submitted scores, one officer said juniors were asked to accept scores that took them out of promotion contention while senior staff kept higher scores, and the department plans to low-rank officers toward removal after its 2025 mass layoffs. Their union says the form risks making career-defining decisions less fair, less transparent and more vulnerable to bias, and a DOJ opinion says the Secretary of State, not the independent board that hears diplomats' challenges, should have the final say.

The grievance-board change is a legal opinion; how often the Secretary will overrule the Board is not yet known.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the mechanics of the new evaluation system and AFSA's formal objection, corroborated across multiple independent outlets (Federal News Network in two separate pieces, ABC News, Daily Wire), including department emails directing managers to recalibrate already-submitted scores. AFSA's own January 15, 2026 statement documents its announced unfair-labor-practice filing; no record of the complaint's outcome was found. The grievance-board change rests on the primary source, the Office of Legal Counsel opinion dated August 20, 2026, corroborated by the Washington Examiner and AFSA's August 24 statement. The claim that the overhaul could push out more diplomats is reported analysis and the department's own low-ranking plan, not a measured outcome.

title: State Department Told Americans to 'Depart Now' From 14 Middle East Countries, Then Told Its Own Evacuation Hotline Callers Not to Rely on Government Help
institution: Department of State
status: Ongoing -- the U.S.-Iran ceasefire collapsed in July 2026, hostilities resumed and the U.S. naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz remained in effect as of late August 2026; no new evacuation-capacity reporting for this phase and no resolution of staffing losses were identified in sourcing reviewed.
date_of_action: 2025-06 (June 2025 Israel-Iran war evacuation strain) through 2026 (evacuation gap after the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began 2026-02-28)
what_changed:
After the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran, the State Department issued a 'DEPART NOW' alert urging U.S. citizens to leave 14 Middle Eastern countries plus the West Bank and Gaza -- Bahrain, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, the West Bank, Gaza, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the UAE, and Yemen -- citing serious safety risks. **Americans who called the department's evacuation-assistance hotline were told: 'Please do not rely on the U.S. government for assisted departure or evacuation.'** This walk-back/messaging-gap pattern was not new to the 2026 war: it was already documented during the separate June 2025 Israel-Iran war, about eight months earlier.

On June 18, 2025, Ambassador Mike Huckabee posted that the embassy was "working on evacuation flights & cruise ship departures" for Americans wanting to leave Israel; hours later, the State Department publicly contradicted him, saying there was "no announcement about assisting private U.S. citizens to depart at this time," even as Ben Gurion International Airport and Israeli seaports remained closed on the sixth day of the Israel-Iran war. The following day, June 19, the embassy confirmed it was "planning for contingencies" but clarified any assistance would mean travel to a "nearby, safe country" rather than direct return to the U.S., with evacuees required to sign a promissory note to repay the government -- a financial condition attached to evacuation assistance. By June 23, after U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, AP reported the department had evacuated 79 embassy staff and family members from Israel, that more than 6,400 Americans had sought evacuation information in a single day, and that roughly 200 U.S. citizens and green card holders were still trying to leave Iran itself.

NOTUS reported stranded Americans described receiving little practical help as regional airports closed and commercial travel options rapidly disappeared. The Intercept reported that foreign service officers fired in earlier DOGE-driven State Department workforce cuts had previously and specifically warned the department would be unable to adequately assist Americans stranded in a Middle East crisis -- a warning this episode is reported to have borne out. NBC News separately reported thousands of Americans were left stranded in the war zone amid the department's response gap.

The State Department did publicize a 24/7 emergency hotline, and a State Department official told Fox News on March 3, 2026 that the department had assisted over 130 American citizens in departing Israel over the previous few days, indicating the department was not wholly inactive, but the gap between the 'depart now' directive and the hotline's own explicit disclaimer against relying on government assistance was widely reported as a substantive breakdown in crisis-response capacity. Separately, the State Department's own March 6, 2026 statement put the total picture in fuller context: nearly 24,000 American citizens had returned to the United States from the Middle East since February 28 (a count that excluded Americans who relocated to other countries or were still in transit), and its 24/7 Task Force had directly assisted nearly 13,000 Americans abroad with security guidance and travel assistance -- figures that sit alongside, not in conflict with, the 130+ Israel-specific figure, which covers a narrower slice (Israel only) of the same broader effort.

Additional reporting corroborated and extended the scale of the crisis: CBS News reported on March 3, 2026 that more than a million Americans were believed to be in the region, citing an unnamed source, and The Intercept later said the war put as many as 1 million Americans living in the Middle East at risk. The war began when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Saturday, February 28, 2026, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and the 'DEPART NOW' alert did not go out until Monday, March 2. Asked at a March 3, 2026 Oval Office appearance why there wasn't an evacuation plan, Trump said, 'it happened all very quickly.' CBS News reported Americans arriving back in New York described a 'zero plan for evacuation,' and travelers transiting hubs like Dubai, Doha, and Amman were told for four days not to rely on the U.S. government for assisted departure. The State Department did not open a crisis intake form offering free charter flights until March 4, 2026, with its first chartered evacuation flight arriving in the region and returning to Washington that same week.

Separately, NOTUS reported on March 17, 2026, with Truthout following, that the State Department fired its oil and gas experts in July 2025 as part of President Trump's reduction-in-force initiative. The firings came about seven months before the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28, 2026; NOTUS said 1,300 State Department employees were cut that summer, and The Intercept tied the July 2025 firing of more than 1,300 State Department personnel to Musk's Department of Government Efficiency. The cuts eliminated staff responsible for modeling scenarios in which the Strait of Hormuz was closed, maintaining relationships with Middle East energy companies, and liaising with the International Energy Agency on coordinated strategic-reserve releases; after the cuts, the only Bureau of Energy Resources staff left were those who worked on critical minerals and clean energy, the administration told Congress. Geoffrey Pyatt, a former assistant secretary of state for energy resources, said of the losses once the Strait of Hormuz became effectively closed during the war: 'I'm sure Secretary Rubio wishes he had that expertise available today.'

Sen. Elizabeth Warren publicly criticized the State Department for not tasking U.S. Transportation Command (TRANSCOM) with evacuating non-government-affiliated Americans from the region, contrasting it with the 2006 U.S.-Lebanon war evacuation, in which TRANSCOM partnered with State to evacuate roughly 15,000 Americans -- a specific, named operational-capacity criticism distinct from the staffing-cuts causal argument described above. As of late August 2026, the underlying crisis context remained active rather than resolved: the U.S.-Iran ceasefire/memorandum of understanding collapsed in July 2026 after Iran struck three commercial vessels, hostilities resumed, and a U.S. naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz was reimposed, with no new evacuation-capacity reporting specific to this later phase identified in sourcing reviewed. The naval blockade remained in effect (Trump stated August 18, 2026 that no talks with Iran were underway).

Even during the separate June 2025 Israel-Iran war, the embassy said evacuees receiving any assistance would be required to sign a promissory note to repay the government.

title: State Department Removes All Pre-Trump Public Posts From Its Official X Accounts Department-Wide
institution: U.S. Department of State
status: Finalized -- directive confirmed by the State Department to NPR and applied department-wide as of February 2026
date_of_action: 2026-02 (confirmed to NPR February 7, 2026)
what_changed: The State Department confirmed it will remove all public posts made before January 20, 2025 (when Trump returned to office) from its official X accounts -- a directive applying department-wide, including accounts for U.S. embassies and missions, ambassadors, and department bureaus and programs. The posts are being internally archived but removed from public view; State Department staff were told that anyone wanting to see the older posts would need to file a Freedom of Information Act request -- a departure from how the U.S. government has typically handled preserving the public online record of prior administrations. Internal guidance reviewed by NPR stated the goal was 'to limit confusion on U.S. government policy and to speak with one voice to advance the President, Secretary, and Administration's goals and messaging.'

estimated_impact.summary: **Removing years of official diplomatic communications from public view -- requiring a FOIA request to access material the public and researchers could previously view directly -- reduces real-time public and journalistic access to the historical record of U.S. foreign policy statements, embassy communications, and diplomatic messaging across the department's full range of public-facing accounts.**

title: Rubio Eliminated 132+ State Department Offices and Cut 1,300+ Positions, Including Human Rights and War-Crimes Functions
institution: U.S. Department of State
status: Largely complete: the ~250 foreign service officers laid off in July 2025 had their terminations finalized as of May 2026 after a court fight over a shutdown-deal RIF freeze; a State Department official told House lawmakers there are no plans to reinstate them; a reentry bill is introduced only.
date_of_action: 2025-03-06 (Western Europe consulate-closure plan first reported) through 2025-09-29 (delayed Trafficking in Persons Report finally released)
what_changed:
An earlier, distinct thread preceded the official April 22 announcement below -- in early March 2025, NYT and other outlets reported the State Department was preparing to close nearly a dozen diplomatic missions, mainly consulates in Western Europe (including Dusseldorf, Leipzig, and Hamburg in Germany; Rennes, Lyon, Strasbourg, and Bordeaux in France; and Florence, Italy), plus consulates in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, and Ponta Delgada in Portugal's Azores, with closures reportedly targeted for summer 2025. Reuters, reporting the plan on March 6, noted that it had reported in February that U.S. missions around the world had been asked to look into reducing both American and locally employed staff by at least 10%. A State Department spokesperson at the time denied any closures had been 'announced.' No reporting has confirmed that the Western Europe consulate closures were ever executed -- to the contrary, the U.S. Embassy Germany website shows new Consul Generals assumed duty at both the Leipzig (October 2025) and Hamburg (August 2025) posts, indicating those specific consulates remained open and staffed well past the original summer 2025 closure target. This earlier consulate-closure plan appears to be a distinct, apparently-unexecuted proposal, separate from the domestic office eliminations described below, which did proceed.

Days before the formal reorganization announcement, on April 16, 2025, Rubio shut down the Counter Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference office (R/FIMI, the renamed successor to the Global Engagement Center) -- the department's dedicated office for identifying and countering Russian, Chinese, and Iranian disinformation campaigns -- saying in a press release the office had been used to 'actively silence and censor the voices of Americans.' A federal appeals court had already rejected censorship claims against the office, finding no evidence its officials coerced or pressured social-media platforms to moderate content; other State Department officials called the censorship framing 'fictitious' and said the closure was politically motivated.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a sweeping State Department reorganization in April 2025, describing the existing structure as 'bloated bureaucracy that stifles innovation.' The plan consolidated 734 bureaus and offices down to 602, and specifically eliminated 132 domestic offices, including the entire Undersecretary of State for Civilian Security, Democracy, and Human Rights position, the Office of Global Criminal Justice (which supports international war-crimes prosecutions), the Bureau of Conflict and Stabilization Operations, and the Office of Global Women's Issues. Refugee, religious-freedom, and human-trafficking offices were downgraded and folded under a general foreign-assistance coordination office rather than retained as standalone bureaus. AP reported the plan would reduce U.S.-based staff by 15%, and ABC News, citing officials familiar with the plans, reported it would eventually eliminate roughly 700 Washington-based positions. AP also reported that offices for Africa affairs, migration and refugee issues, and democracy efforts, which had reportedly been targeted in an earlier alleged leaked document, survived at least as bureau names on a chart, and that a week before the announcement the White House Office of Management and Budget had proposed cutting the State Department's budget by almost 50% and eliminating funding for the UN and NATO headquarters, a proposal AP described as highly preliminary. At the April 22 department briefing, spokesperson Tammy Bruce said, 'I would say that DOGE is not in charge of this, but this is the result of what we've learned and the fact that we appreciate results.'

Between the April 22 announcement and the July execution, the internally projected cut count moved sharply upward before settling far lower than the peak estimate -- Government Executive/Defense One/Nextgov reported on May 12, 2025 that the department was now expected to eliminate roughly 3,400 positions, up from an earlier internal estimate of about 2,000, with office eliminations and RIF notices set to begin June 2 and completion by July 1; affected foreign service officers were reportedly told they would not be permitted to apply for other open department roles, though some FSOs at the time argued that briefing conflicted with existing Foreign Affairs Manual provisions. The eventual July RIF (1,353 positions) came in well below this May estimate, consistent with the Bureau of Consular Affairs' passport/visa-processing staff (about half of its roughly 2,400 domestic employees) being exempted from the cuts, removing a large share of the potential RIF pool. On May 29, 2025, responding to the reorganization plan Rubio sent to Congress, Senate Foreign Relations Ranking Member Jeanne Shaheen and House Foreign Affairs Ranking Member Gregory Meeks said in a joint statement, 'When America retreats—as it has under President Trump—China and Russia fill the void.'

The reorganization drew immediate pushback: Reuters reported on July 3, 2025 that more than 130 former U.S. diplomats and officials, including Susan Rice, condemned the planned purge, and the layoffs were temporarily blocked by a federal court order before being cleared to proceed. The Supreme Court ruling that cleared the way was Trump v. AFGE, decided July 8, 2025, which stayed a lower-court injunction blocking Executive Order 14210's agency-wide reorganization/RIF plans nationwide (the Court explicitly declined to rule on the legality of any specific agency's RIF plan, including the State Department's).

Following that ruling, the department executed layoffs affecting more than 1,300 employees (1,107 civil servants and 246 foreign service officers with domestic assignments); affected foreign service officers were placed on 120 days of administrative leave before formal termination, civil servants on a 60-day separation period. The department's own contemporaneous count described the total departures tied to the reorganization as 'nearly 3,000,' a figure that includes staff who took the earlier 'Fork in the Road' voluntary-departure offer in addition to the 1,353 RIF-specific terminations -- both figures are real and consistent, describing overlapping but distinct populations (involuntary RIF vs. total reorganization-linked departures), not a factual conflict. The reorganization is explicitly stated to be 'highly complementary' to the concurrent dismantling of USAID, whose remaining functions were folded into State with reduced independence. Thomas Shannon, a career Foreign Service officer who was Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs from 2016 to 2018 (appointed under President Obama and kept on into President Trump's first term), told NPR on July 11, 2025 that the cuts were not 'just about trimming fat' and pointed to the loss of experts with critical language and cultural skills as a blow to U.S. influence abroad, while the American Academy of Diplomacy, which represents former ambassadors, accused Rubio of gutting the department's institutional knowledge and called the move 'an act of vandalism.'

Among the eliminated offices was the small Office of Casualty Assistance, which supports diplomats and their families following a death or serious injury abroad. **Reuters reported July 17, 2025 that termination notices reached the office's staff while its team leader was actively working to repatriate the remains of Brian Matthew Faughnan, a U.S. Consulate Monterrey officer who died in a car crash in Coahuila, Mexico on July 9, 2025 -- the team leader told other U.S. officials he had just been removed from his job and could no longer assist with the case.** The State Department said the agency remained 'fully equipped' to handle casualty evacuations despite the office's elimination.

The human-trafficking office's downgrading described above proved more severe than 'folded under a general foreign-assistance coordination office' alone conveys -- reporting found the Office to Monitor and Combat Trafficking in Persons lost more than 70% of its staff, leaving fewer than three dozen employees to carry out the office's central anti-trafficking mission. The cuts' effects became concrete in 2025: for the first time in the report's history, the State Department missed the legally required June 30 deadline to deliver its annual Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report to Congress, finally releasing the delayed 2025 report on September 29, 2025 after months of pressure. During the House Foreign Affairs Committee's September 2025 State Department Reauthorization markup, Rep. Sarah McBride passed a bipartisan amendment directing the department to report to Congress on how the reductions-in-force and reorganization affected the office's work, including the TIP Report's timeliness and accuracy, with a detailed analysis due within 180 days.

A December 2025 AFSA (American Foreign Service Association) survey found 98% of U.S. diplomats reported collapsed morale, with roughly a quarter of the foreign service resigning, retiring, or being forced out amid the reorganization and USAID's concurrent dismantlement; diplomats described severe staffing losses, budget cuts, and diminished capacity to conduct U.S. foreign policy, per CNN.

An intervening legal battle preceded the final layoffs of the ~250 foreign service officers from the July 2025 wave. The shutdown-ending continuing resolution Congress passed in November 2025 (signed into law November 12, 2025) included Section 120, barring any federal RIF from being implemented between October 1, 2025 and January 30, 2026, and requiring rescission of any RIF action taken during that window. The State Department proceeded anyway: on December 1 and 2, 2025, foreign service and civil-service employees whose separation dates fell during the shutdown or were approaching in December were emailed that their separations would not be rescinded, some with a new December 5 separation date. AFGE and AFSA sued, and U.S. District Judge Susan Illston issued a preliminary injunction on December 17, 2025 blocking the December terminations and ordering the RIF notices withdrawn -- the administration briefly appealed, an appeals court sided with the government on the narrower question of whether agencies had to fully unwind the layoffs, then the administration voluntarily withdrew its own appeal and told the plaintiffs it would rescind the State RIFs.

On January 9, 2026, Illston clarified her injunction applied only to the updated early-December notice setting a December 5 separation date, not the original July RIF notices, and that the State Department could proceed against the same ~250 officers once the statutory freeze expired January 30, 2026 -- which is what ultimately produced the 'finalized as of May 2026' outcome described below, not a separate, uncontested administrative process.

Federal News Network reported the ~250 foreign service officers laid off in the July 2025 wave had their terminations finalized as of May 2026, with former employees, federal unions (AFGE), and lawmakers continuing to press for reinstatement, warning the reduction has weakened agency expertise and harmed national security. The affected officers are explicitly ineligible to compete for vacant State Department positions even as the department simultaneously runs a new Foreign Service recruitment campaign -- a documented recruit-while-firing contradiction distinct from the original 2025 reorganization announcement.

Separately, Democratic lawmakers introduced the Foreign Service Test-Free Reentry Act in mid-2026, which would let officers separated in the RIF (Jan. 2025-Jan. 2030 window) rejoin without retaking entry exams -- an introduced bill, not enacted, and a State Department official told House lawmakers the department has no plans to reinstate the laid-off officers. Reps. James Walkinshaw (D-VA), Don Beyer (D-VA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), and Dina Titus (D-NV) introduced it July 16, 2026, to authorize the Secretary of State to waive Foreign Service entry exams for officers involuntarily separated by a RIF between January 20, 2025 and January 31, 2030. It remains introduced only, referred to committee, with no hearing or markup identified at last check; a separate, broader Republican-sponsored bill introduced the same period (the Foreign Service Modernization Act, H.R. 9086, Reps. Mast and Lawler, June 2, 2026) reforms Foreign Service personnel rules generally but does not address RIF reentry and is not a competing response to the same laid-off-officer question.

title: State Department Ends 17-Year Global Embassy Air-Quality Monitoring Program, Erasing Historical Data and the Only Independent Pollution Data Many Countries Had
institution: U.S. Department of State
status: Program ended March 4, 2025, and its historical data was later removed from AirNow.gov. A September 2026 PNAS study found satellite-measured pollution rose 24-33% across 46 affected cities; the State Department says it is restoring public reporting but has given no timeframe.
what_changed:
On March 4, 2025, the State Department ended a 17-year-old program that used air-quality sensors at more than 80 U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide to monitor pollution levels, citing 'funding constraints that have caused the Department to turn off the underlying network.' The program had provided real-time, validated air-quality data to the public via AirNow.gov and, for many countries with limited or unreliable government monitoring of their own, was the only independent source of that data. The Beijing embassy's monitor, launched in 2008, was historically credited with embarrassing Chinese officials into greater transparency and stronger air-quality policy -- reporting on the program's shutdown noted this same catalytic effect had extended to other countries over the years. Following the shutdown, roughly 17 years of accumulated historical air-quality data were removed from AirNow.gov, eliminating a public-health and research benchmark, not just halting future collection. The State Department told CBS News the monitors were still running and collecting data, but public transmission and reporting ceased; the State Department said the data "will be made available when there is a secure and reliable way to transmit it."

A peer-reviewed study published in PNAS on September 14, 2026, by researchers led by Zoey Yiyuan Zhou of Columbia University, compared satellite-derived air pollution (aerosol optical depth) before and after the shutdown across 46 cities that had relied on the embassy network, using same-country cities as controls. It found no systematic pollution trend in the 300 days before U.S. reporting ended, then a prompt 24-33% rise in local pollution levels afterward; NPR reported the rise peaked about three to four months after reporting stopped and then eased somewhat. The authors' conservative translation puts the increase at roughly 1.9 micrograms per cubic meter of PM2.5 (about 4%, per NPR), with alternative methods giving 1.5 to 16.3, and the effects were largest and most persistent in cities with poor substitutes for the U.S. data; NPR reported the biggest rises in Southeast Asian cities such as Manila, Rangoon and Vientiane. The study measured pollution, not health outcomes, and cannot say why pollution rose. The State Department declined to comment on the study but, in a statement reported by NPR and Health Policy Watch, said it is working to restore public reporting of the data, without giving a timeframe.

estimated_impact.summary: **People in cities that depended on U.S. embassy monitors lost their only independent, real-time air-quality data, and pollution rose afterward: a peer-reviewed study found satellite-measured pollution up 24-33% across 46 cities, rising most where substitute data was poor.** The program had been credited with pushing China and other governments toward cleaner-air policy, and a 2022 study linked it to lower premature-death risk for more than 300 million people. The shutdown also erased 17 years of historical data from AirNow.gov, a public-health and research benchmark, to save what IQAir reports was only tens of thousands of dollars.

title: State Department Ordered Nonprofit Public Libraries to Stop Processing Passport Applications, Affecting ~1,400 Libraries
institution: U.S. Department of State
status: In effect as of February 13, 2026 -- bipartisan H.R. 6997 (Community Passport Services Access Act) was introduced January 9, 2026 to reverse the change, but had not passed either chamber as of this re-verification; no administrative reversal confirmed in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025 (cease-and-desist letters begin, per reporting) through 2026-02-13 (effective date reported)
what_changed: The State Department began issuing cease-and-desist letters to nonprofit public libraries starting in late fall 2025, informing them they were no longer authorized to participate in the Passport Acceptance Facility program, with the order taking effect February 13, 2026. A State Department spokesperson said the change was required because federal law and regulations 'clearly prohibit non-governmental organizations' from collecting and retaining passport-application fees. The American Library Association estimated approximately 1,400 public libraries nationwide -- about 15% of all public libraries -- could be affected, ending a long-standing, convenient passport-application channel for many communities, particularly ones without a nearby post office or passport agency. A bipartisan group of members of Congress from Connecticut, Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, and Maryland sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio asking him to extend the existing library program until Congress finds a permanent solution. A bipartisan coalition led by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, and including Reps. John Joyce, Madeleine Dean, Mary Gay Scanlon, Chrissy Houlahan, Robert Bresnahan, and Lloyd Smucker, introduced H.R. 6997, the Community Passport Services Access Act, on January 9, 2026, which would amend the Passport Act of 1920 to let qualifying 501(c)(3) nonprofit public libraries continue serving as passport acceptance facilities and retain the execution fee. As of this re-verification the bill had roughly 14 cosponsors but had not received a floor vote in either chamber.

title: State Pledged $410 Million+ for Third-Country Deportation Deals, Paying Some Governments From Refugee-Aid Funds
institution: Department of State, Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration (Migration and Refugee Assistance account; Office of Remigration)
status: Ongoing: as of end of June 2026, State had authorized or pledged $410M+ for deportation deals with 31 countries; at least two of its payments to governments came from refugee-aid funds. On Sept. 28, 2026, Trump nominated the head of the office that negotiates the deals as ambassador to Cameroon.
date_of_action: 2025-05-07 to 2026-06 (MRA determination signed May 7, 2025; $250M transfer to DHS reported June 4, 2025; first refugee-account payment to a government Oct. 29, 2025; $410M+ pledged as of end of June 2026)
what_changed:
The State Department's Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration (PRM) had been, in the words of its top official Andrew Veprek, a "humanitarian assistance" office with a budget of about $4 billion a year that "focused on bringing people to the United States." Under the second Trump administration, money from the bureau's Migration and Refugee Assistance (MRA) account was redirected toward deportation. On May 7, 2025, Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau signed a determination under the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962 that assistance to migrants "without legal basis to remain in the United States to voluntarily return to their country of origin or country of legal status will contribute to the foreign policy interests of the United States" (published in the Federal Register on May 30). On June 4, 2025, a State Department spokesperson told Reuters that the department had moved $250 million to the Department of Homeland Security "to provide a free flight home and an exit bonus to encourage and assist illegal aliens to voluntarily depart the United States" under DHS's Project Homecoming; Reuters reported that the money came from the MRA account. Elizabeth Campbell, a former deputy assistant secretary of state, said those funds had historically been used "to provide protection to vulnerable people" overseas and to resettle refugees in the U.S.

In 2025 the department also created an Office of Remigration, a division of about 15 employees inside PRM led by Christian Ehrhardt, a career Diplomatic Security officer, to negotiate and fund agreements under which other countries accept people deported from the United States who are not their citizens. After the July 2025 State Department layoffs, staff of PRM's office for humanitarian programs in the Caribbean and Latin America were reassigned to it, The Washington Post reported. One of the office's first assignments, in October 2025, was a $7.5 million deal for Equatorial Guinea to accept up to 250 third-country nationals. Federal spending records show a $7.5 million award to Equatorial Guinea dated October 29, 2025, described as for the country's "humanitarian and migration-related needs to be used for 'assistance to or on behalf of refugees,'" and listed under PRM's Overseas Refugee Assistance Programs for Africa. An identically worded $7.5 million award to Palau, dated December 29, 2025, is charged to the Migration and Refugee Assistance account. In a November 10, 2025 letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, wrote that the Equatorial Guinea payment "used funding from the Migration and Refugee Assistance account making this the first ever government-to-government transfer of such funds, which are intended to respond to global refugee and humanitarian crises." She asked how it was a permissible use of an account "meant to assist refugees overseas."

On September 21, 2026, The Washington Post, reporting as part of a consortium of 26 media organizations organized by the Paris-based nonprofit Forbidden Stories, said internal State Department records showed the administration had authorized or pledged at least $410 million to facilitate third-country deportation agreements with 31 countries, mostly in Africa and Latin America, as of the end of June 2026. That total comprised about $81 million in direct payments to 13 foreign governments, $179 million in grants to the International Organization for Migration (IOM), $124 million to the U.N. Refugee Agency (UNHCR), and about $27 million to other organizations. According to the Post, officials determined they could speed up the payments by invoking a provision of the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act that lets the executive branch bypass statutory foreign-aid restrictions to fund crucial programs for refugees; former State Department staffers called this a perversion of Congress's intent to ensure urgent, life-saving humanitarian assistance. One former official said "the whole point was to circumvent [congressional] notification that money was being sent to a government known to be corrupt." The grants to IOM and UNHCR were negotiated by foreign governments in connection with their deportation deals and have largely replaced the voluntary contributions the U.S. traditionally made to the two agencies, the Post reported; a current U.S. official called them "sweeteners." The Central African Republic deal, for example, included $85 million for IOM, $60 million of it for "community stabilization" such as road building. The administration had already cut its regular contributions to IOM and to U.N. refugee programs in its 2025 foreign-aid review, which the Post said left them with budget shortfalls of 30 percent and 24 percent, respectively. "We're not giving funding to UNHCR and IOM as we were in the past ... We're only giving funding for the most part linked to the agreements," a current U.S. official told the Post, Forbidden Stories reported.

Most of the deportation slots the deals pay for remained unfilled, according to the records: only a few people (three, per the Post's text) had been sent to Palau under its $7.5 million agreement to accept up to 75. **Deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea under the first deal the office processed have alleged, through their lawyers, that they were beaten by armed guards, denied food and given inadequate medical care while held in a decommissioned hotel in Malabo.** Equatorial Guinea's government denied the abuse allegations, and PRM officials who visited wrote that claims of refoulement were "hard to substantiate."

The State Department did not answer the Post's detailed questions, saying in a statement that the U.S. would use "all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country," and said the Post had mischaracterized the work of Veprek, Ehrhardt and PRM official Spencer Chretien. Administration officials say third-country deportations are the only way to remove some migrants whose home countries refuse to take them back or who are protected by law from being returned there. "We have changed the orientation of the bureau completely," Veprek said at an April event at the Center for Immigration Studies; "Now, we are focused on implementing the president's immigration agenda." Veprek has since been promoted to oversee all U.S. foreign assistance and humanitarian affairs. On September 28, 2026, President Trump nominated Ehrhardt to be ambassador to Cameroon, which the State Department records list as an operational deportation partner with $30 million pledged to organizations.

These figures differ in scope from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democratic staff's estimate of at least $32.3 million paid to five governments through January 2026: the Post's $81 million covers direct payments to 13 governments as of June 2026, and its $410 million total also counts grants to international organizations.

primary_proponent.name: Andrew Veprek
primary_proponent.role: Top official over the State Department's Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration; since promoted to oversee U.S. foreign assistance and humanitarian affairs
primary_proponent.note: The Washington Post reported that Veprek and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller were the key drivers of the third-country deportation policy, and former officials said Veprek effectively directed PRM from the counselor's office before formally leading it; he said publicly that "we have changed the orientation of the bureau completely." Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau signed the May 2025 MRA determination and, per the Post, has been involved in negotiating the deportation agreements; Christian Ehrhardt runs the Office of Remigration.

estimated_impact.summary: Money Congress appropriated to help refugees and people displaced by war and disaster has gone to deportation: $250 million of Migration and Refugee Assistance funds went to DHS for voluntary-departure flights and exit payments, and $7.5 million payments each to Equatorial Guinea and Palau for accepting deportees were drawn from refugee-assistance funds. Those payments are part of at least $410 million the State Department authorized or pledged for third-country deportation deals as of June 2026; the Post reported that officials determined they could speed payments by invoking a refugee-assistance law provision, but no source says how much of the $410 million came from the refugee account. U.S. grants to IOM and the U.N. Refugee Agency, which have largely replaced the regular contributions the U.S. once made to them, are now tied to those deals, according to current and former officials and people familiar with the deals; earlier, broader U.S. aid cuts had left IOM and U.N. refugee programs with shortfalls of 30% and 24%. No source counts how many refugees lost assistance as a result. Deportees sent under the first deal allege beatings and denial of food in detention in Equatorial Guinea, which its government denies.

title: State Department Paused New Student Visa Interviews for Social-Media Vetting; New International Enrollment Fell 17%
institution: U.S. Department of State, affecting colleges and universities nationwide
status: Online-presence vetting of all F, M, and J applicants remains in force (Sept. 2026). New international enrollment fell 17% in fall 2025 (IIE), and student visas issued fell 23% in 2025 (F-1 down 33%). IIE projected a 9.5% drop in total enrollment for fall 2026.
date_of_action: 2025-05-27 (interview pause announced) through 2025-11-17 (enrollment-decline report published)
what_changed: On May 27, 2025, the State Department instructed all U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide to pause scheduling new interviews for F, M, and J nonimmigrant student and exchange-visitor visas, pending an expansion of social-media and security vetting for applicants. A separate May 30, 2025 cable from Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered enhanced screening that initially focused on Harvard-bound applicants, with the expanded vetting expected to extend to all international students. On June 4, 2025, President Trump signed Proclamation 10949, fully suspending entry for nationals of 12 countries and partially restricting nationals of 7 more, with the partial restrictions covering F, M, and J student and exchange-visitor visas. The Wall Street Journal, in a June 5, 2025 article on the crackdown's threat to the pipeline of immigrant inventors, reported threats to eliminate or drastically limit Optional Practical Training (OPT) and STEM OPT -- post-graduation work authorization used by more than 200,000 international graduates each year (294,253 students were on OPT in 2024-25, according to IIE's Open Doors) -- with a formal OPT-restricting rule anticipated later in 2025. The Journal noted that immigrants had founded or co-founded more than half of America's billion-dollar startups, according to one study, and that many immigrant inventors and founders first came to the U.S. on student visas, citing USB inventor Ajay Bhatt, who left India for graduate study in New York in 1981. On June 18, 2025, the department issued new permanent guidance requiring consular officers to conduct comprehensive vetting, including applicants' online presence, for all F, M, and J visa applicants, and instructing applicants to set all social-media profiles to public so vetting could proceed; interview scheduling then resumed under these expanded rules. Applicants who already held scheduled interviews were largely unaffected, but new applicants faced delays through the pause and the transition to the new vetting regime. The impact was measurable well before the November 2025 national figure: a New York Times analysis of federal arrival data showed international-student arrivals fell 19% in August 2025 alone compared to a year earlier -- the steepest drop outside the pandemic -- with sharply uneven effects by country of origin (India -44%, Iran -86%, Syria -63%, Nigeria -48%, Africa overall -32%, Asia overall -24%, Middle East -17%, Latin America -9%); the arrival data do not distinguish new students from returning ones. Individual institutions reported steep declines: the University at Buffalo's overall international enrollment fell 19% (first-year international graduate students down 58%), and **DePaul University's international enrollment fell 30% (755 fewer students, first-year international graduate enrollment down nearly 62%), which its president attributed to visa difficulties and waning interest in U.S. study. After a hiring freeze and executive pay cuts, DePaul laid off 114 staff (just under 8%) in December 2025 to help close a $12.6 million fiscal 2026 shortfall that also reflected a roughly 300-student drop in continuing undergraduates and about $7 million in unplanned financial aid.** Reuters counted at least 35 other schools that had announced budget cuts in response to Trump administration policies generally; among them, Northwestern (425 positions) and USC (more than 630 laid off) each cited reduced federal funding, an expected drop in international enrollment, and other financial pressures. Johns Hopkins' cut of more than 2,000 jobs, which Reuters listed alongside them, came in March 2025 -- before the interview pause -- after about $800 million in USAID grants were terminated, and is not attributable to the enrollment decline. Small college towns faced a distinct economic risk: Guardian reporting from Oxford, Ohio, home to Miami University, described local restaurants and businesses that depend on international-student spending as threatened by the falloff, though Miami's international intake had already fallen from 2,895 students in fall 2019 to 750 in 2024, well before the pause. On November 17, 2025, the Institute of International Education's Fall 2025 Snapshot, a preliminary survey of 825 institutions, found new international enrollment down 17% from a year earlier -- the largest non-pandemic decline in 11 years -- while total international enrollment fell 1% (graduate -12%, undergraduate +2%); more than half of the surveyed institutions reported fewer new international students, and 96% cited visa-application concerns as an obstacle. A NAFSA analysis released the same day estimated the decline would cost the U.S. economy $1.1 billion; for scale, international students contributed nearly $55 billion to the U.S. economy in 2024, according to the Commerce Department. The decline compounded the separate, institution-specific Harvard SEVP fight, tracked in its own entry, that ran concurrently. State Department figures released in 2026 showed 23% fewer F, M, and J student visas were issued in 2025 than in 2024, with F-1 visas for degree-seeking students down 33.4% and visas for Indian students down 56.6%; an Inside Higher Ed analysis found issuances roughly in line with 2024 until May 2025, the month of the interview pause, and below 2024 levels for the rest of the year. As of September 2026 the online-presence vetting remained in force and had been extended to many other visa categories, and NAFSA projected that a further drop in 2026-27, which IIE's spring 2026 snapshot put at 9.5% of total enrollment, would cost the U.S. economy $3.4 billion. No OPT-restricting rule was issued in 2025; in September 2026 the White House cleared a DHS proposal to set a new OPT fee, after reports that the administration was weighing a $100,000 charge, with the rule's details still unpublished as of September 17, 2026.

estimated_impact.summary: Tens of thousands of prospective international students were kept from or deterred from starting U.S. study: new international enrollment fell 17% in fall 2025, and the State Department issued 23% fewer student visas in 2025 (a third fewer F-1 degree-student visas), with issuances dropping from May 2025, when interviews were paused. Universities lost tuition revenue and cut jobs -- DePaul laid off 114 staff after its international enrollment fell 30% -- and college towns that depend on student spending face losses. NAFSA estimates the fall 2025 decline cost the U.S. economy $1.1 billion and projects a further $3.4 billion loss in 2026-27.

title: HHS Cancels 53 Teen Pregnancy Prevention Grants ($67M), Citing "Normalizing Sexual Activity for Minors"
institution: HHS Office of Population Affairs, Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program
status: Complete for the 53 canceled grants; HHS has opened a new $63M-plus grant round prioritizing abstinence-based programming, with awards expected later in 2026
date_of_action: 2026-06 (grants canceled)
what_changed: In late June 2026, HHS's Office of Population Affairs canceled 53 teen pregnancy prevention grants totaling $67 million, affecting university, community, and public health grantees across more than two dozen states. HHS's termination notices stated the grants were being canceled for 'normalizing sexual activity for minors.' Trump's proposed 2027 budget calls for eliminating the teen pregnancy prevention program entirely, stating the grants have gone to groups that 'promote radical leftist ideology' and asserting there is no evidence the programs contributed to the historic decline in the U.S. teen pregnancy rate, which the administration notes is now at an all-time low. Trump's first-term administration canceled the same grant program's predecessor round as well. Simultaneously with the June 2026 cancellations, the Office of Population Affairs opened a new round of grant applications worth just over $63 million, prioritizing programs that promote abstinence before marriage, reproductive health awareness, and long-term fertility goals, with awards expected later in 2026.
