title: State Paid Five Countries $32 Million-Plus to Take ~300 Migrants They Typically Had No Ties To
institution: Department of Homeland Security / Department of State
status: Practice resumed: on Sept. 29, 2026 the Supreme Court stayed Judge Murphy's Feb. 2026 ruling (largely affirmed by the First Circuit Sept. 18) and agreed to hear the case; argument is set for Dec. 9, 2026. No DHS or State OIG review identified.
date_of_action: 2025-2026 (practice expanded over the prior year per the report)
what_changed:
A Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democratic staff report said the total cost of the Trump administration's third-country deportations -- sending migrants to nations other than their own, where they typically have no prior connection, rather than to their countries of origin -- was unknown but likely upward of $40 million through January 2026, as immigration officials expanded the practice over the prior year. That total comprised at least $32.3 million paid directly to five governments, at least $7.2 million on flights to at least ten third countries, and $307,000 to house deportees on a U.S. military base in Djibouti. The report identified payments ranging from $4.7 million to $7.5 million made to the five countries (Equatorial Guinea, Rwanda, El Salvador, Eswatini, and Palau) in exchange for accepting deportees, which together had received roughly 300 people as of January 2026: El Salvador about 250 Venezuelan nationals, and the other four far fewer (29 to Equatorial Guinea, 15 to Eswatini, 7 to Rwanda, and none to Palau). The report estimated the cost per migrant (payment plus flights) at about $1.1 million for Rwanda ($7.5 million plus an estimated $601,864 in flights, for seven people), $413,333 for Eswatini, $282,126 for Equatorial Guinea and $20,755 for El Salvador, and said the administration 'has paid at least one country more than $1 million per third country national received.' DHS itself had said in a May 5, 2025 release that 'the average cost to arrest, detain, and remove an illegal alien is $17,121.' The report also said that 'in many cases, migrants could have been returned directly to their home countries, avoiding costly third country deportations': as of January 2026, more than 80 percent of the migrants sent to the paid countries had returned to their country of origin or were in the process of doing so, and in some cases the U.S. paid to fly migrants to a third country and later paid again to fly them home. It said the money went to foreign governments 'including those with records of corruption, human rights abuses and human trafficking'; the State Department's own 2023 human rights reports on Rwanda, Equatorial Guinea and Eswatini each cite credible reports of arbitrary or unlawful killings, including extrajudicial killings, and of political prisoners or detainees. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the committee's top Democrat, characterized the practice as 'the epitome' of 'fraud, waste, and abuse.' State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott did not comment directly on the report's figures, saying it 'only underlines much of the unprecedented work that the Trump administration has done to enforce our immigration laws,' ABC News reported.

Eswatini was itself an early, closely watched test case of the practice: **on July 16, 2025, five men (of Vietnamese, Laotian, Yemeni, Cuban, and Jamaican nationality, all convicted of crimes in the U.S.) were flown to Eswatini's capital Mbabane on a U.S. military plane and held in solitary confinement for an undetermined time, under a secretive deal the U.S. and Eswatini governments did not publicly disclose in advance.** The lack of transparency prompted about 150 women, organized by the Eswatini Women's Movement, to protest outside the U.S. embassy, and a coalition of seven women's groups delivered a petition demanding the deportees' return and questioning the deal's legality; Eswatini's largest opposition party, the People's United Democratic Movement (Pudemo), separately called it 'human trafficking disguised as a deportation deal,' The Guardian reported. A later court hearing in Eswatini over four of the men was delayed when the presiding judge failed to appear.

On February 25, 2026, U.S. District Judge Brian E. Murphy (D. Mass.) ruled in D.V.D. v. DHS that the administration's expedited third-country removal practice is unlawful, violating due-process guarantees and the Convention Against Torture's non-refoulement principle, because it gave migrants no meaningful opportunity to contest removal to a country where they feared persecution or torture. The Supreme Court had twice stayed an earlier, broader version of Murphy's injunction in 2025 without ruling on the merits. The Trump administration (DOJ) appealed Murphy's February ruling to the First Circuit, which stayed the district court's decision on March 16, 2026, allowing third-country deportations to continue while the appeal on the merits proceeded.

Separately, on April 7, 2026, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, Rep. Delia Ramirez, and Rep. Troy Carter sent a letter demanding that the DHS and State Department inspectors general investigate the deportation program; DHS's Office of Inspector General responded that a government shutdown at the time prevented it from opening new reviews. The April 7 letter said the administration had entered agreements with 27 countries to receive non-nationals deported from the United States; that as of early March 2026, ICE had over 500 people in its custody slated for third-country deportations; and that DHS had signaled it had its sights on deporting over 8,000 people to third countries. It also cited the Senate report's figure of over $32 million paid to the five countries (El Salvador, Rwanda, Eswatini, Equatorial Guinea, and Palau) -- the direct-payments part of the report's roughly $40 million total, not a separate estimate. Sen. Warren publicized the letter on April 8, 2026, and Rep. Ramirez issued her own press release on the same letter on April 16, 2026.

No further Inspector General action was identified on the Warren/Van Hollen/Ramirez/Carter April 7, 2026 request for a DHS/State Inspector General investigation beyond DHS OIG's shutdown-related response. The DHS-specific government shutdown that IG cited ended April 30, 2026; as of late August 2026, roughly four months later, no third-country-removal review appeared among DHS OIG's listed audits, inspections, or evaluations, nor was any State OIG review of the same subject identified -- the stated blocker has lapsed with no confirmed follow-through.

Merits briefing on the appeal was completed on April 20, 2026, and the First Circuit held oral argument on the merits appeal (case 26-1212) on May 13, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. in the En Banc Courtroom of the Moakley U.S. Courthouse in Boston. On September 18, 2026, a First Circuit panel (Judges Montecalvo, Howard and Aframe, in an opinion by Judge Aframe) largely affirmed Murphy's judgment: the government must give class members effective notice of a planned third-country removal and a meaningful opportunity to contest it on the ground that they reasonably fear persecution or torture there. The panel vacated only, for lack of standing, the declarations that DHS must first try to remove people to countries they designated or of which they are citizens. On September 23, after the plaintiffs told the court that DHS planned to deport class members to Burundi, Rwanda and the Central African Republic the next day, the First Circuit dissolved its March 16 stay, putting Murphy's ruling back into effect. The government asked the Supreme Court for a stay the next day, telling the justices it had already canceled a flight carrying 70 people to three countries. On September 29, 2026, the Supreme Court, in an unsigned order, stayed Murphy's February 25, 2026 order and judgment until it decides the case, treated the government's application as a petition for review and granted it, and set argument for its December 2026 session on whether the district court had jurisdiction, whether it could grant classwide relief, and whether the government's third-country removal guidance is lawful under the removal statute, the Due Process Clause and the law implementing the Convention Against Torture. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson would have denied the stay. The Court then set argument for December 9, 2026, with the government's opening brief due October 23 and the challengers' brief due November 16. The order lets third-country removals proceed without the notice and fear screening the lower courts required; it does not decide the legality question, which remains unresolved rather than settled in the administration's favor, and a decision would likely come by summer 2027, CBS News reported. **The challengers told the Supreme Court that removed class members have faced indefinite detention by foreign governments, onward removal to countries they had fled, disappearance, and beatings and sexual assault in detention**, and, citing a Washington Post estimate, that DHS had deported more than 25,000 people to at least 28 third countries in 2025 and 2026; a tracker run by Refugees International and Human Rights First likewise counts more than 25,000 people sent to at least 29 countries. Those counts cover every third-country removal, far beyond the roughly 300 sent to the five paid countries: the Migration Policy Institute, as reported by NBC News, put 2025 third-country deportations at about 15,000, with Mexico receiving the majority.

primary_proponent.note: The administration's rationale (removing migrants whose home countries refuse repatriation) is a genuine practical constraint this entry does not resolve; the accountability concern documented here is the reported cost-per-deportee and the destination countries' lack of connection to the deportees, not the underlying removal authority itself.

estimated_impact.summary: The practice sends migrants to countries where they typically have no prior connection -- five men deported to Eswatini on July 16, 2025, all convicted of crimes in the U.S., were held in solitary confinement for an undetermined time -- and a federal judge ruled the expedited practice unlawful because it gave migrants no meaningful opportunity to contest removal to a country where they feared persecution or torture, a ruling the First Circuit largely affirmed in September 2026 but the Supreme Court stayed on September 29, 2026 pending December argument, so deportations continue. The challengers, citing a Washington Post estimate, said DHS had deported more than 25,000 people to at least 28 third countries in 2025 and 2026 (most of them to Mexico, per other counts), and that removed class members have faced indefinite detention and abuse in custody abroad. An April 7, 2026 congressional letter said that as of early March 2026 ICE held more than 500 people in custody slated for third-country removal and DHS had signaled intent to deport more than 8,000 people to third countries. On cost, a Senate Democratic staff report put the total through January 2026 at likely upward of $40 million, including more than $32 million paid directly to five countries that had received roughly 300 migrants (the payments figure the April letter cites). The report estimated the cost per migrant at about $1.1 million for Rwanda, $413,333 for Eswatini and $282,126 for Equatorial Guinea, and $20,755 for El Salvador, which took about 250 of the ~300. DHS separately put its own average cost to arrest, detain and remove a person at $17,121 (May 2025), close to the El Salvador figure. The report argued that in many cases migrants 'could have been returned directly to their home countries, avoiding costly third country deportations': more than 80% of those sent to the paid countries had returned or were returning home by January 2026. The payments also went to governments -- Rwanda, Equatorial Guinea and Eswatini among them -- for which the State Department's own 2023 human rights reports cite credible reports of extrajudicial killings.

title: March 2025 Stopgap Bill Stripped Veterans' Toxic-Exposure Fund of Its Guaranteed Advance Funding, Though FY2026 Was Ultimately Fully Funded Anyway
institution: Department of Veterans Affairs -- Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund (TEF)
status: Resolved without an actual funding cut -- the FY2026 advance appropriation was removed as feared, but Congress separately and fully funded TEF for FY2026 through the normal appropriations process at a higher level than the original $22.8 billion figure
date_of_action: 2025-03-08 (House-passed version reported) through 2025-03-15 (H.R. 1968 signed into law)
what_changed: The 2022 PACT Act created the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund (TEF) to cover expanded VA healthcare and benefits for veterans sickened by burn pits, Agent Orange, and other toxic exposures, and specifically included an 'advance appropriation' mechanism -- guaranteeing TEF's funding a full year ahead of when it would be spent -- intended to insulate veterans' toxic-exposure care from being used as leverage in future annual appropriations fights. The Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025 (H.R. 1968), the stopgap spending bill House Republicans advanced and the Senate passed on March 14, 2025 (House 217-213, Senate 54-46; signed into law March 15, 2025), excluded the $22.8 billion FY2026 advance appropriation for TEF that the PACT Act's funding schedule called for -- though it left FY2025 TEF funding itself untouched. The Hill reported House Republicans intended the move to force TEF's future funding under the discretionary spending cap, giving Congress more leverage to cut it in ordinary annual appropriations; VA has never offered gender-affirming or other unrelated services from this fund; opposition Republicans separately criticized TEF's oversight structure, calling it effectively a 'slush fund.' Sen. Bernie Sanders and veterans' groups, including those representing burn-pit-exposed veterans, publicly condemned the removal as a betrayal after Congress had already committed to the funding via the PACT Act. Despite the removed guarantee, Congress ultimately did fund TEF for FY2026 through the ordinary appropriations process rather than the automatic advance mechanism: per VA and congressional budget documents, the FY2026 Continuing Appropriations Act provided $52.68 billion to TEF, reflecting the program's actual growing costs ($20 billion in FY2024, $30.4 billion in FY2025, and the FY2026 figure) -- more than double the originally-scheduled $22.8 billion figure that had been removed.

primary_proponent.role: Drafted and advanced the stopgap bill excluding TEF's FY2026 advance appropriation
primary_proponent.note: No single named individual was identified in sourcing reviewed as personally directing this specific provision; reporting attributes it to House Republican appropriators' stated goal of moving TEF spending under the discretionary cap for closer annual oversight and potential future cuts.

estimated_impact.summary: The removed guarantee created genuine, contemporaneous alarm among veterans' advocates and Democratic lawmakers that toxic-exposure healthcare funding would become a future bargaining chip -- a real structural change to how the PACT Act's funding was protected -- but the feared FY2026 funding shortfall did not materialize: Congress separately appropriated TEF funding at more than double the removed guarantee's dollar figure once actual program costs were known.

estimated_impact.caveat: This entry documents a real, contemporaneously alarming action (removing a specific PACT Act funding safeguard) that did not, in the outcome, produce the feared funding cut -- present both halves honestly: the removal of the guarantee was real and drew bipartisan veteran-advocate criticism at the time, but checking forward to the actual FY2026 appropriation shows TEF was fully funded, and at a higher level than the removed guarantee would have provided. Framing this as a completed 'elimination' of veterans' healthcare funding, as some March 2025 coverage did, is not supported by the eventual outcome.

confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the March 2025 legislative action itself and its contemporaneous reception, corroborated across The Hill, Roll Call, and Military Times, all citing the same bill text and the same March 2025 timeline. HIGH confidence on the FY2026 outcome, corroborated by VA's own FY2026 Budget in Brief and multiple veterans'-benefits trade publications describing the same $52.68 billion figure -- this is the kind of forward-looking outcome check this tracker applies before finalizing an entry describing an older, alarming-sounding action.

title: Trump Administration's TPS and Humanitarian Parole Revocations Trigger Nursing Home Caregiver Staffing Crisis
institution: DHS/USCIS (TPS and humanitarian parole programs) -- downstream effect on nursing homes and long-term-care facilities nationwide
status: Ongoing as of mid-2025 through at least April 2026 reporting -- facilities continue losing staff as TPS/parole terminations take effect in waves by country/program
date_of_action: 2025-01 (TPS/parole terminations begin under the second Trump administration) through 2026-04 (continued reporting of workforce impact)
what_changed: Beginning in 2025, the Trump administration terminated or shortened Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designations and ended humanitarian parole programs for several countries (including Haiti and Venezuela), stripping legal work authorization from hundreds of thousands of immigrants with little advance notice. Nursing homes and other long-term-care facilities, which rely heavily on immigrant labor, began reporting sudden staff losses starting around July 2025 as workers' legal status and work permits lapsed (AP News, Fortune, Haitian Times, July 2025). More than a quarter of the roughly 4 million nursing assistants, home health aides, personal care aides, and other direct-care workers nationally are foreign-born. **One Boca Raton, Florida facility lost 10 workers under humanitarian parole and was slated to lose 30 more once Haitian TPS ended; facilities described being forced to fill shift gaps overnight, raising wages and referral bonuses, but found few American applicants willing to take the vacated positions.** The New York Times reported similar findings (July 2025-2026 coverage), citing one Atlanta-area operator of three nursing homes -- about one-third of whose combined staff came from roughly three dozen countries -- whose CEO said the operator felt 'completely beat up' by the disruption; nationally, immigrants make up roughly three in ten (30%) direct-care workers in long-term-care settings, consistent with AP's >25% figure above. Industry groups and researchers projected steep state-level direct-care-workforce losses if the terminations proceeded as planned: New York (~45%), Massachusetts (~38%), and Texas (~22%) (AP News, July 2025; Skilled Nursing News, April 2026). By April 2026, continued reporting found the disruption still underway, with industry representatives saying facilities were 'not prepared to replace' the departing workforce and warning the instability was undermining care-staffing stability broadly, not just at facilities with the highest concentrations of affected workers (Skilled Nursing News, April 2026).

estimated_impact.summary: Nursing homes and other long-term-care facilities -- which depend on a workforce that is more than 25% foreign-born -- began losing staff en masse as TPS and humanitarian parole protections lapsed, with some facilities losing dozens of workers and states projected to lose more than a third of their direct-care workforce, threatening care quality and access for elderly and disabled residents who depend on these facilities.

The $129,575/year figure is the 2025 baseline national median cost of a private nursing-home room, cited as context for industry warnings that this staffing disruption could push costs higher still -- it is not itself a measured cost increase caused by the TPS/parole terminations. No dedicated health/mortality figure (e.g. a documented increase in resident falls, missed care, or facility closures attributable specifically to this staffing loss) was identified in the sourcing reviewed for this entry -- the harm is currently a workforce-capacity risk to elder/disability care rather than a quantified health outcome.

title: Treasury Moves to Dramatically Shrink the Office of Financial Research, the Post-2008 Systemic-Risk Watchdog, Amid Growing Private-Credit Instability
institution: Department of the Treasury / Office of Financial Research
status: Planned as of this entry's addition -- internal documents describe the plan; implementation status not fully confirmed
date_of_action: 2026-04 (plans reported)
what_changed: Politico reported that the Treasury Department is moving to dramatically shrink the Office of Financial Research (OFR) -- the agency created after the 2008 financial crisis specifically to monitor systemic risks across the broader financial system, independent of any single regulator's jurisdiction. Internal documents reviewed by Politico show plans to slash the office's staffing and cut its budget, even as officials and market analysts raise growing concern about instability in private credit and other lightly regulated corners of the financial system that OFR-style systemic monitoring is specifically designed to catch before it spreads.

title: US Commanders Moved Troops Into Hotels and Civilian Office Spaces After Iranian Strikes Damaged Gulf Bases, Raising Law-of-War Concerns
institution: Department of Defense
status: Relocations into hotels and civilian offices were reported in late March and April 2026; no later reporting found on whether they continue. No official or tribunal law-of-war finding. The war had not ended as of late September 2026; the U.S. rejected Iran's latest ceasefire offer.
date_of_action: March 2026 (relocations under way by the time The New York Times reported them March 25, 2026; law-of-war analysis April 1, 2026)
what_changed: **After Iranian ballistic missile and drone strikes damaged U.S. bases across the Persian Gulf, U.S. commanders moved many troops out of those bases and into hotels and office spaces in civilian areas, some as far away as Europe.** The New York Times reported on March 25, 2026, citing military officials, that many of the 13 U.S. bases near Iran had been rendered 'all but uninhabitable.' Satellite analysis by the BBC and the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed damage at bases including Ali Al Salem in Kuwait, Al Udeid in Qatar and Prince Sultan in Saudi Arabia, and CSIS estimated that Iranian strikes caused about $800 million in damage to bases used by U.S. forces in the war's first two weeks. U.S. defense officials told the Times the troops were moved because the sprawling compounds lacked adequate defenses against Iranian ballistic missiles and drones. Early in the war, an Iranian strike on a hotel in Bahrain had reportedly wounded two Pentagon employees. After the Times report, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote that U.S. soldiers had fled Gulf bases 'to hide in hotels and offices' and accused them of using Gulf citizens as human shields, and Iran's Fars News Agency, citing unnamed sources, reported that Iran had warned hotels in the region, especially in Bahrain and the UAE, that sites housing American soldiers would be treated as legitimate military targets. On April 1, 2026, the Times reported that human rights officials and legal experts said the relocations may amount to violations of international humanitarian law and the U.S. military's own law of war; both the Pentagon's Law of War Manual and the first protocol of the Geneva Conventions call for avoiding placing military forces in or near civilian populations. Brian Castner, a crisis researcher at Amnesty International, said the commanders who ordered the relocations 'should be investigated for violating U.S. laws of war,' and Michael Schmitt, a law-of-war scholar at the University of Reading, said billeting troops in civilian structures still in civilian use 'would be a violation of passive precautions.' The Times noted that Iran had urged people in the Gulf to report the locations of U.S. troops off their bases, and that Iranian strikes had since killed civilians in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait. It added that deliberately using civilians as human shields, a step beyond the relocations, is considered a war crime. Apart from accusations by Iranian officials, including the foreign minister, no source reviewed alleges that the relocations were meant to shield troops. By early April, Pentagon data listed seven U.S. service members killed by enemy fire, among 13 U.S. deaths in the war; the other six were the crew of a KC-135 tanker lost in a non-hostile crash. The war went on. A memorandum of understanding signed in June paused the fighting, but it broke down in July: on July 7 Iran fired on three commercial vessels in Oman's waters near the Strait of Hormuz, according to a U.S. official, and U.S. Central Command struck Iran in response; on July 8 President Trump said the memorandum was 'over'; and on July 13 he said he would reinstate a naval blockade of Iranian ships in the Strait. Pentagon data reported by CNN on July 26 put the toll at 18 U.S. troops killed and 624 wounded since the war began on Feb. 28. The memorandum's 60-day window, which Solace Global described as a truce period and CNN as a deadline for talks on a final deal, lapsed on August 17. Turkish state media, citing Pakistani government sources, had reported on August 12 that the two sides agreed to extend it, but a senior Iranian source said no such talks had taken place, and on August 18 Trump said no talks with Iran were underway or scheduled. Solace Global, a private security-risk firm, assessed on August 14 that the conflict had likely entered a 'lower-intensity phase.' CENTCOM said that as of August 14 it had redirected 62 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two while enforcing the reimposed blockade. By late September the Pentagon's public casualty database listed 19 U.S. troops killed and 861 wounded; The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon had not disclosed four or five more deaths, and the administration rejected an Iranian offer of a new ceasefire deal. No reporting after April was found on whether troops remain housed in hotels or civilian offices, and no official or tribunal law-of-war finding on the practice has been reported.

primary_proponent.name: U.S. Central Command / Department of Defense
primary_proponent.role: Military command responsible for the relocation decisions
primary_proponent.note: Sourcing reviewed attributed the relocation decisions to field commanders responding to base vulnerabilities in real time, rather than to a single named Pentagon official's advance policy decision; the underlying vulnerability itself traces to base air-defense inadequacy against the scale of Iranian strikes.

estimated_impact.summary: Troops were moved out of damaged Gulf bases and into hotels and office buildings among civilians, which human rights officials and law-of-war experts said may violate the rule to keep military forces away from civilian populations. The move put hotel guests, staff and nearby residents at risk in an active war: Iran had urged Gulf residents to report where U.S. troops were staying, and Iranian strikes killed civilians in the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait (the Times did not tie those deaths to the relocations). It also reflected lost military capability, with many of the 13 U.S. bases near Iran described as all but uninhabitable and Iranian strikes estimated to have caused about $800 million in damage to bases used by U.S. forces in the war's first two weeks.

title: Trump Signs Executive Orders Threatening Federal Funding to States/Cities Over Cashless Bail, Asserting Direct Federal Custody Control in D.C.
institution: DOJ / jurisdictions nationwide with cashless-bail policies; D.C.'s local justice system specifically
status: Enacted (executive orders signed Aug. 25, 2025); implementation ongoing -- AG Bondi directed to compile a list of targeted jurisdictions
date_of_action: 2025-08-25 (executive orders signed)
what_changed: On August 25, 2025, during an Oval Office signing ceremony, Trump signed two crime-related executive orders, one specifically targeting Washington, D.C.'s cashless-bail policy and a second targeting cashless-bail policies nationwide. The nationwide order directs the administration to identify federal funds that could be 'suspended or terminated' in jurisdictions -- named examples include California, Illinois, New Jersey, New Mexico, and New York, alongside D.C. -- that rely on risk-assessment tools rather than a defendant's ability to pay for pretrial release, rather than traditional cash bail. It instructs Attorney General Pam Bondi to compile a list of jurisdictions that have 'substantially eliminated cash bail' for offenses posing 'a clear threat to public safety.' **The D.C.-specific order goes further, since D.C.'s local government is subject to direct federal oversight under the Home Rule Act: it directs the administration to pursue 'federal funding decisions, services, or approvals' against the city if it does not change its bail policy, and separately directs federal law enforcement to take people arrested in D.C. into federal custody -- and pursue federal rather than local charges -- 'to the fullest extent permissible under applicable law,' a mechanism that would let the administration route arrests around D.C.'s local bail system entirely rather than changing the underlying policy through normal channels.**

primary_proponent.role: President
primary_proponent.note: Signed both executive orders on August 25, 2025, directing Attorney General Pam Bondi to implement the nationwide funding-threat list and directing federal law enforcement's D.C.-specific custody/charging preference.

estimated_impact.summary: The orders threaten federal funding to at least six named jurisdictions over a specific pretrial-release policy choice, and in D.C. specifically assert a mechanism to bypass the local bail system by routing arrests into federal custody and charges -- critics warn the underlying cashless-bail rollback itself could jail thousands of people who cannot afford cash bail despite posing no flight or safety risk, reversing a reform adopted specifically to reduce wealth-based pretrial detention.
estimated_impact.caveat: No specific dollar figure for threatened/withheld funding, or a count of people who would be newly detained under reversed cashless-bail policies, was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry's creation -- both orders were newly signed and their concrete funding/custody effects had not yet been documented in practice.

The named target jurisdictions (D.C., California, Illinois, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York) and Bondi's compilation directive are consistently reported across these outlets. No sourcing reviewed yet documents whether any specific federal funds have actually been suspended or terminated under this authority, since the orders were newly signed as of this entry's creation.

title: Trump's FY2026 Budget Proposed a $40B HHS Cut, Halving the CDC, and Eliminating CPB, Adult Education, and (Briefly) Head Start
institution: Office of Management and Budget / multiple federal agencies (HHS, HUD, Education Department, CPB)
status: Largely rejected: Head Start's elimination was dropped before the May 2025 release; the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75, Feb. 3, 2026) rejected most other cuts, incl. LIHEAP's elimination; CPB's funding was cancelled by the July 2025 Rescissions Act (P.L. 119-28), not restored.
date_of_action: 2025-04 (initial draft budget reporting) through 2025-05 (formal 'skinny budget' release and FY2026 education-specific budget detail)
what_changed:
The earliest reporting on this draft was USA Today's April 11, 2025 article, which described the same leaked FY2026 draft as proposing to eliminate both Head Start and all federal funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), citing advocacy estimates that eliminating Head Start would force over a million parents out of the workforce and cut services for nearly 800,000 children. **The New York Times reported April 25, 2025 on the same draft of Trump's FY2026 budget proposal, adding that it would cut the Department of Health and Human Services by roughly $40 billion (about 27% of its budget) and cut the CDC's budget roughly in half.** The draft proposed eliminating Head Start entirely (an approximately $12 billion program), cutting rental assistance by $26.7 billion through a two-year voucher cap and block-granting the program to states, cutting Native American housing funding by roughly $479 million, eliminating the Corporation for Public Broadcasting's federal funding ($1.1 billion), and cutting NIH and other federal health-research funding -- framed by OMB Director Russell Vought and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as eliminating 'woke' spending, including support for minority health programs.

When the White House released its formal 'skinny budget' on May 2, 2025, the Head Start elimination proposal had been dropped -- the National Head Start Association and other advocates confirmed the released $1.7 trillion budget document proposed level funding for Head Start instead, following an April wave of public pressure after USA Today and other outlets reported the administration was seriously considering the elimination. LIHEAP's elimination, by contrast, stayed in the May release: OMB's request listed a $4,025 million cut, eliminating the program, and the National Energy Assistance Directors Association said in May 2025 that the request would eliminate $4 billion in assistance to about 6 million very low-income households. The other cuts named in the April draft -- the CDC/HHS cuts, rental-assistance cut, Native housing cut, and CPB defunding -- were not similarly walked back in the May release.

Separately, The Hill reported May 2, 2025 on the administration's FY2026 education budget detail: a proposed $729 million elimination of federal adult-education funding, a $315 million cut to Preschool Development Grants, a 35% cut to the Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights, and a consolidation of 24 K-12 grant programs and seven IDEA (special-education) programs into two funding streams -- alongside a $60 million increase for charter schools, which The Hill described as the only educational institutions to avoid the proposed cuts. OMB's request itself proposed eliminating the whole $315 million Preschool Development Grants program, which it listed in its Health and Human Services section, citing the Minnesota Department of Education's PDG 'guiding principles,' which include 'intersectionality' and 'racial equity'; The Hill also quoted a White House fact sheet saying federal funding through the program had been used to create a guidebook on 'Lessons for Creating Quality Care for Oregon's LGBTQIA+ Families.' Education Secretary Linda McMahon said the budget reflected funding levels for 'an agency that is responsibly winding down.' The adult-ed and OCR cuts and the charter-school increase detailed here are budget-request line items distinct from the department's separate dismantlement, which proceeded by executive order and interagency agreement rather than through the budget process.

A separate report gave the same FY2026 education proposal in macro terms rather than the Hill's line-item breakdown above. The New York Times reported May 2, 2025 that the released budget proposed cutting the Education Department's overall funding by $12 billion, including $4.5 billion specifically from K-12 programs. The figures fit OMB's own May 2 request: its 'Preserve Title I and Streamline K-12 Programs' line cut $4,535 million, consolidating 18 competitive and formula grant programs into 'a new $2 billion formula grant' (The Hill counted 24 K-12 programs, plus seven IDEA programs, in the consolidation), and the same table listed the adult-education (-$729 million), English Language Acquisition (-$890 million), migrant education (-$428 million), Office for Civil Rights (-$49 million) and charter-school (+$60 million) lines. The Congressional Research Service put the Education Department's requested discretionary funding at $66.7 billion, against $78.8 billion in FY2025. Preschool Development Grants sit in the HHS budget, outside the Education Department figure.

CPB's defunding was enacted separately. The Rescissions Act of 2025 (H.R. 4, Public Law 119-28), signed July 24, 2025, rescinded the Corporation for Public Broadcasting's already-enacted appropriations for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027 (provided in Public Laws 118-47 and 119-4). The American Action Forum put those at $535 million in advance for each of the two years. Together, that is about $1.07 billion.

NPR reported (Sept. 26, 2025) on the three competing FY2026 education funding plans then before Congress. Trump's budget request would cut Education Department funding by 15%, eliminate all funding ($1.3 billion) for English-language learners and migrant students, and combine 18 funding streams -- including help for rural schools, civics education, at-risk youth and students experiencing homelessness -- cutting them from roughly $6.5 billion to $2 billion. It left Title I grants to school districts level at about $18.4 billion, the FY2024 and FY2025 amount, per the Congressional Research Service. House Republicans proposed even deeper K-12 cuts, notably a $4.7 billion reduction to Title I, according to NPR; K-12 Dive, on Sept. 2, 2025, described the House plan as a $5.2 billion, or 27%, Title I cut. NPR said the Senate's proposal 'would make minor cuts but largely maintain funding'; K-12 Dive reported that the Senate Appropriations Committee's bipartisan July 2025 bill would fund the Education Department at $79 billion in FY2026, 'a slight increase to current spending.'

After a government shutdown from Oct. 1 to Nov. 12, 2025, a continuing resolution (P.L. 119-37) that ran through Jan. 30, 2026, and a second, brief funding lapse, Congress enacted full-year appropriations on Feb. 3, 2026, in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148, Public Law 119-75), whose Division B covers Labor-HHS-Education and Division D covers HUD. The Congressional Research Service reported that the law 'did not adopt these elimination proposals' for LIHEAP and several other Administration for Children and Families programs, and, of the proposed education eliminations and deep reductions, that 'In general, these proposals were not adopted.' The law provided $4,045,000,000 for LIHEAP, $20 million above FY2025's $4.025 billion, and $12.357 billion for Head Start; CRS reported that it kept $315 million for Preschool Development Grants and $890 million for English Language Acquisition and provided $79.0 billion for the Education Department. Of the two programs in OMB's $428 million 'Migrant Education and Special Programs for Migrant Students' line, the law set aside $52,123,000 for section 418A of the Higher Education Act, which funds the High School Equivalency Program and College Assistance Migrant Program (HEP and CAMP) for students from migrant and seasonal farmworker families; Title I, Part C migrant education is funded within the same $19.13 billion 'education for the disadvantaged' appropriation, but the law sets no separate amount for it. The request's charter-school increase was not adopted as such: OMB had asked for $500 million, 'a $60 million increase,' and the explanatory statement whose 'Final Bill' column the law adopts for its Innovation and Improvement account lists $440 million for Charter Schools Grants, while section 310 of Division B lets the Education Secretary transfer up to $60 million from the department's Nonrecurring Expenses Fund to that account for part C of title IV of the ESEA, the charter-schools program. The American Public Power Association reported in April 2026 that Congress 'ultimately increased funding' for LIHEAP 'over the previous fiscal year.' Senate Appropriations Committee Democrats' summaries of the final bill say it provided $18.4 billion for Title I-A grants, rejecting 'the $4.5 billion cut and proposed consolidations' in the budget request and the House's Title I cut; $729 million for adult education; $9.1 billion for the CDC, 'rejecting the roughly $4 billion—or 50%—cut to CDC programs proposed by the Trump administration'; $48.7 billion for NIH, rejecting 'the catastrophic 40% cut to NIH proposed by President Trump'; $140 million for the Office for Civil Rights, its current level; $38.4 billion for tenant-based Section 8 vouchers, rejecting the proposal to 'slash HUD's rental assistance programs and shift more costs onto states'; and $1.35 billion for Native American housing programs, $467 million more than the request. The law contains no CPB appropriation.

primary_proponent.name: Russell Vought
primary_proponent.role: Director, Office of Management and Budget
primary_proponent.note: OMB is the executive-branch office that drafts and releases the President's annual budget request; the NYT's April 2025 reporting on the draft and the administration's formal May 2025 'skinny budget' release both originate from OMB under Vought's direction. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Education Secretary Linda McMahon are separately named for their agency-specific framing and implementation of the HHS/CDC and education cuts respectively.

estimated_impact.summary: The budget request proposed cutting federal health infrastructure (HHS by roughly 27%, the CDC roughly in half), housing assistance (a rental-voucher cap and a Native housing funding cut), education (eliminating adult-education and English-language-learner/migrant-student funding and the $315 million Preschool Development Grants program), home-energy aid (eliminating LIHEAP) and public broadcasting (eliminating CPB's federal funding). Head Start's proposed elimination, which advocates estimated would cut services for nearly 800,000 children, was dropped before the formal May 2025 release. As a non-binding request, the cuts took effect only where Congress enacted them: CPB's defunding was enacted, via the July 2025 Rescissions Act, and Congress rejected most of the rest in its full-year FY2026 appropriations, signed Feb. 3, 2026, which funded LIHEAP at $4.045 billion, Head Start at $12.357 billion and the Education Department at $79.0 billion.

title: Trump's FY2027 Budget Proposes ~$500B More for Defense While Cutting Non-Defense Discretionary Spending 10%, Including Health, Environment, Agriculture, and Science

what_changed: **Trump proposed a fiscal year 2027 budget that would increase military spending by roughly $500 billion while cutting non-defense discretionary federal programs by 10% overall, including major reductions to health, environmental protection, agriculture, and scientific research funding.** Reuters reported the plan shifts federal resources heavily toward military spending as the U.S. remained engaged in the Iran conflict. title: DHS Suspended, Then Reversed, TSA PreCheck and Global Entry During a Funding Lapse
institution: Transportation Security Administration / Customs and Border Protection, DHS
status: Reversed. PreCheck was restored within a day (Feb. 22, 2026) and Global Entry on March 11 while the DHS shutdown went on. TSA then hit record waits (4.5+ hours) and 480+ officer departures; Trump ordered TSA pay March 27 and signed DHS funding April 30, 2026.
date_of_action: 2026-02-21 (suspension announced) through 2026-02-22 (PreCheck reversal); Global Entry restored 2026-03-11
what_changed: On Saturday, February 21, 2026, DHS announced it would suspend TSA PreCheck and CBP's Global Entry expedited-traveler programs effective 6 a.m. Eastern the next morning, citing the funding lapse from the partial DHS shutdown that began February 14. In a statement released early Sunday, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem said TSA and CBP were "prioritizing the general traveling population." Several airports briefly closed PreCheck lanes on Sunday morning, February 22, but less than a day after the suspension was announced, TSA said PreCheck "remains operational with no change for the traveling public"; airline and travel-industry groups had raised alarm with DHS, though DHS did not say what prompted the change. Global Entry, however, was suspended at airports that night. Airlines for America president and CEO Chris Sununu criticized the suspension, saying the traveling public was 'once again... used as a political football amid another government shutdown.' On February 24, Sen. Mark Warner noted that, according to the administration's own data, more than 18 million travelers used Global Entry in 2025, saving over 300,000 CBP officer-hours across 79 ports of entry, and that both programs had remained operational throughout the 43-day government shutdown the prior fall; he said the administration's funding-lapse claims "don't pass the smell test." On February 25, Noem told CNN that PreCheck could again be suspended if unpaid officers' call-outs rose, while denying the department had reversed its decision ("We never reversed the decision. We just talked about it."). DHS reactivated Global Entry as of 5 a.m. on March 11, 2026, after a pause of about two and a half weeks, even though the DHS shutdown continued. The underlying staffing strain continued to escalate: by mid-March 2026, Reuters reported TSA officers were working without pay as the funding standoff continued, with absentee rates spiking above 30% at some major hubs. Officials warned some airports could be forced to shut down entirely if the standoff persisted, with smaller airports with limited checkpoints described as especially at risk. The shutdown dragged into a second month, and **ABC News reported that roughly 60,000 TSA officers, after more than a month of partial pay, had begun receiving $0 paychecks while still required to report for duty; employees described taking second jobs, leaving the agency, and struggling to meet basic expenses.** The prolonged standoff also had an explicit political dimension: on March 22, Trump rejected a proposed off-ramp -- funding all of DHS except ICE enforcement operations -- and posted that there should be no deal with Democrats "unless, and until, they Vote with Republicans to pass 'THE SAVE AMERICA ACT,'" a federal elections overhaul bill with voter-ID and proof-of-citizenship provisions, even as TSA workers went unpaid and airport disruptions worsened (CNN; the New York Times also reported the demand). Senate Majority Leader John Thune publicly called tying the bill to DHS funding unrealistic. By March 24, a White House official said a Republican plan to fund most of DHS, with a version of the SAVE America Act moved to a separate party-line bill, "seems to be acceptable" (CNBC). On March 23, the administration deployed ICE and other DHS agents to 14 airports to help move passengers through understaffed checkpoints; the NYT reported TSA union leaders said the agents were not trained for screening work and did little to reduce lines. CBS News reported waits of up to six hours at Houston's Bush Intercontinental Airport and that more than 3,400 TSA officers -- nearly 12% of those scheduled -- called out on March 22, the most of the shutdown to that point. At a March 25 House Homeland Security Committee hearing, acting TSA Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill testified that the shutdown had produced "the highest wait times in TSA history, with some wait times greater than 4.5 hours," that TSA had lost more than 480 officers, and that as many as 40% to 50% of officers had called out on certain days at some major airports, with Atlanta, Houston and New York hit hard (Bloomberg); she warned TSA was "being forced to consolidate lanes and may have to close smaller airports if we do not have enough officers" (CBS News). On March 27, Trump signed a memorandum directing DHS to pay TSA employees from funds with a "reasonable and logical nexus" to TSA operations, citing more than 60,000 unpaid TSA employees and nearly 500 departed officers. The same day, the Senate passed by voice vote a bill funding most of DHS except ICE and Border Patrol, but House Republicans rejected it and passed a stopgap instead (NPR). After Thune and House Speaker Mike Johnson announced a two-track plan on April 1 -- the Senate bill plus a separate budget-reconciliation bill for ICE and Border Patrol -- the Senate advanced the bill again on April 2, but the House did not pass it until April 30, when Trump signed it, ending the shutdown for TSA and most of DHS after more than 70 days (CNBC). Trump's FY2027 budget, released earlier, on April 3, 2026, while the shutdown was still under way, and documented in more detail in a separate entry, proposed cutting roughly 8,400 of TSA's 61,000 positions and requiring small airports to enroll in TSA's Screening Partnership Program, replacing federal screening officers with TSA-paid private screeners, a move the administration said would save $52 million (Federal News Network; CNN). CNN noted the idea had gained traction as TSA-staffed airports saw hours-long lines during the shutdown while privately screened airports largely avoided mass absences.

estimated_impact.summary: The shutdown the suspension was pinned on left roughly 60,000 TSA employees, about 50,000 of them screening officers, working without pay for weeks, many on $0 paychecks, taking second jobs or relying on airport food pantries, and more than 480 officers quit. The resulting call-outs produced the longest security waits in TSA history (over 4.5 hours, up to six hours in Houston) before Trump ordered TSA pay on March 27; he signed DHS funding on April 30, 2026. The trusted-traveler suspension itself was short: PreCheck came back within a day, and Global Entry, used by more than 18 million travelers in 2025, was paused for about 17 days (Feb. 22 to March 11), removing a program that saved CBP over 300,000 officer-hours a year even though both programs had run through the 43-day fall 2025 shutdown.

title: TSA's Acting Chief Told Congress 'Nothing Is Off the Table' on Privatizing Airport Screening as White House Proposed Cutting ~$250M From Its Budget
institution: Transportation Security Administration (TSA), Department of Homeland Security
status: Proposal stage as of May 2025; a similar privatization push recurred in the administration's FY2027 budget cycle in April 2026
date_of_action: 2025-05-20 (congressional testimony)
what_changed: At a May 20, 2025 House Appropriations homeland security subcommittee hearing, **TSA Acting Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill testified that 'nothing is off the table' regarding potential privatization of TSA airport screening functions, telling appropriators the agency was 'happy to have that discussion' if a new privatization scheme made sense. The White House's budget request proposed cutting nearly $250 million from TSA's budget, which McNeill said would reduce TSA's total screening workforce by approximately 2% -- even as air travel remained at record-high volumes.** The budget proposal specifically sought to expand privatized screening by requiring smaller airports to enroll in TSA's existing Screening Partnership Program, projecting roughly $52 million in savings from that piece alone. Some Republican lawmakers pushed for full agency privatization. The privatization push recurred in the administration's FY2027 budget cycle, with an April 2026 proposal again pairing TSA funding cuts with pressure on smaller airports to adopt private security screeners, following the same basic template as the May 2025 proposal (documented in this database's broader FY2027 budget entry, trump-fy2027-budget-defense-tradeoff-2026.json).

title: Hundreds of U.S. Scientists Sought "Scientific Asylum" in Europe as France and the EU Launched Dedicated Recruitment Programs
institution: N/A -- documents a researcher-emigration trend attributed by affected scientists and European officials to the federal research-funding and policy environment, not one specific federal action
status: Ongoing and grown -- both the Aix-Marseille and EU-wide recruitment programs continued accepting applicants and expanded funding into 2026, with no reporting of the underlying U.S. funding cuts being reversed
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Aix-Marseille program launched) through 2025-07 (first wave of researchers relocated; EU 2025-27 funding pledge announced May 2025)
what_changed: In March 2025, Aix-Marseille University in France launched 'Safe Place for Science,' a dedicated program offering three-year positions and $16.3 million in combined grant funding to American researchers whose work the university said was 'threatened or hindered' by the Trump administration's research cuts. The Guardian reported June 21, 2025 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0397, added 2026-09-10) that the drivers pushing young academics and international scholars to seek positions abroad extended beyond research-funding cuts alone to include visa suspensions, grant revocations, ICE targeting of international scholars, and a broader climate of political repression on campuses -- documenting the demand-side push factors behind the same emigration wave this entry's supply-side program data (Aix-Marseille, the EU's Choose Europe for Science) was designed to capture. By July 2025, nearly 300 applicants -- from institutions including Stanford, Yale, NASA, NIH, George Washington University, and more than a dozen others -- had applied; the university selected an initial cohort of roughly 20 researchers, with the first several arriving in France by late June 2025 and the full initial group expected by September. Separately, on May 5, 2025, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen launched a continent-wide 'Choose Europe for Science' campaign at a Sorbonne conference in Paris, pledging EUR 500 million in new EU funding for 2025-2027 specifically to attract researchers, including a new seven-year European Research Council 'supergrant' for top scientists and a doubling of ERC relocation grants (from EUR 1 million to EUR 2 million) to cover the cost of moving to Europe and establishing a new lab. French President Emmanuel Macron announced France would separately commit EUR 100 million of its existing EUR 54 billion 'France 2030' investment plan to the same goal. The EU's 'Choose Europe for Science'/'Choose France for Science' online portal drew 30,000 visitors from 157 countries in its first month, 34% of them from the United States, with several hundred formal applications filed. Outlets covering the trend (Rolling Stone, NBC News, Mother Jones, the New York Times) tied the outflow to the cumulative effect of federal actions tracked elsewhere in this database -- NIH's 380+ canceled research grants and broader funding freeze (see nih-impoundment-gao-finding-trump2), NSF and USAID cuts, and attacks on climate-science research -- rather than any single action; European officials and departing researchers cited funding instability, canceled grants, and fears of political interference in research as their stated reasons for leaving. Both programs continued growing into 2026: Aix-Marseille's 'Safe Place for Science' selected an initial cohort of 39 researchers (in fields including health, astrophysics, the humanities, and climate science), with a second group of roughly 20 more being finalized as of mid-2026 for relocation starting that September -- bringing the total selected to roughly 60, still drawn from the ~300 July 2025 applicant pool -- backed by a EUR 15 million, three-year funding commitment. Separately, the European Commission's January 30, 2026 update reported the EU's 'Choose Europe for Science' initiative had grown to over 100 national and regional participating programs, with total committed funding expanding from the original EUR 500 million pledge to nearly EUR 900 million, including a new EUR 240 million European Research Area Chairs call under Horizon Europe for 2026-27 and a EUR 51 million Marie Sklodowska-Curie Actions 'Choose Europe for Science' call for 2027.

title: African Development Foundation Reduced to Near-Nothing Before Courts Fully Reverse Takeover
institution: U.S. African Development Foundation and Inter-American Foundation
status: Reversed (final federal court orders in 2025-2026 fully vacated the takeovers at both agencies)
date_of_action: 2025-02-19 (executive order) through 2026-03 (final court order restoring USADF)
what_changed: On February 19, 2025, President Trump issued an executive order directing USADF, the Inter-American Foundation (IAF), the U.S. Institute of Peace, and the Presidio Trust to be reduced to 'the minimum presence and function required by law.' Peter Marocco, a State Department official who also oversaw the dismantling of USAID, moved to take control of both USADF and IAF within days. At IAF, Marocco held a one-person 'board meeting' outside the agency's locked headquarters on February 28, 2025, after being unable to gain entry, and declared himself acting CEO and president in a notice entered into the Federal Register. At USADF, staff denied DOGE personnel direct access to internal systems, citing privacy and security requirements, while Marocco announced by email that he would chair the agency's board. On March 11, 2025, District Judge Richard Leon initially found that a large reduction in USADF's staff and funding could itself be legal, declining at that stage to block leadership changes, while ordering DOGE staff to explain how they would maintain the agency's minimum required functions. By early April 2025, the government acknowledged in court that IAF had been reduced to a single employee and a single active grant. On April 4, 2025, Judge Loren AliKhan ordered the indefinite reinstatement of ousted IAF president Sara Aviel and blocked Marocco from serving on IAF's board, unwinding his actions including frozen grants. On July 1, 2025, Judge Leon ruled that Trump had violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act by installing Marocco at USADF without Senate confirmation, voiding the staff terminations and grant cancellations Marocco had directed. A final order in Rural Development Innovations Ltd. v. Marocco fully blocked the USADF dismantlement, and by March 2026, USADF staff were allowed back into their offices for the first time in months.

estimated_impact.caveat: The administration's stated legal position, articulated in a Justice Department Office of Legal Counsel memo, was that the president's Article II duty to 'take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed' grants inherent authority to designate acting officers to supervise organizations Congress created to perform executive functions, without requiring Senate confirmation. Court rulings distinguished between two separate legal questions along the way: Judge Leon's initial March 2025 ruling found that a large reduction in USADF's staff and funding could itself be legal, meaning the scale of cuts was not automatically unlawful, while his later July 2025 ruling found the specific mechanism used, installing Marocco without Senate confirmation, violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, voiding the actions taken under his leadership. This is a genuine reversal story: both USADF and IAF ultimately had their takeovers fully undone by final court orders, with USADF staff physically returning to their offices in March 2026, though Devex reporting notes the agency's reentry into the foreign-aid sector 'seems to be just beginning' after a year of program cancellations and funding freezes, and separately references newer, unrelated corruption charges connected to the agency as of that report.

title: USAID DRC mission closure and CDC global-health staffing cuts hampered detection and response to 2026 Ebola outbreak
institution: USAID (dissolved into State Department) / CDC global health security programs
status: Ongoing -- outbreak remains the deadliest DRC Ebola outbreak on record as of late August 2026 reporting (5,794 cases/2,786 deaths as of Aug. 27); a vaccination campaign began Aug. 27, 2026, but UN officials warn response funding will run out within weeks against a ~$679M humanitarian funding gap; USAID's DRC mission and broader global-health staffing cuts remain in effect, unreversed
date_of_action: 2025 (USAID DRC mission closure, CDC global-health staffing cuts) -- outbreak detected April 2026, still growing as of July 2026
what_changed: A Bundibugyo-strain Ebola outbreak, first detected in April 2026 in DRC's Ituri province, grew into the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, reaching 3,442 confirmed cases and 1,521 deaths in the DRC by late July 2026, with additional cases and deaths in neighboring Uganda; WHO and Africa CDC declared it a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. USAID's DRC mission had been shuttered in 2025 as part of the agency's broader 83% program-termination and dissolution into the State Department (see this tracker's usaid-dismantlement entry); **the International Rescue Committee said the resulting reduction in country-level surveillance capacity contributed to delayed detection, and Bloomberg's public-health commentary and multiple outlets identified reduced CDC staffing and USAID/WHO funding cuts as having limited the surveillance, laboratory, and response-team capacity available to catch and contain the outbreak early.** The disease is reported to have spread undetected for several weeks before health authorities officially confirmed it on May 15, 2026. Update 2026-08-17: the outbreak has continued to accelerate sharply. By August 15-16, 2026, DRC's public health institute reported 4,945 confirmed cases and 2,325 deaths, surpassing the 2,299-death toll of the 2018-2020 DRC outbreak to become the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country's history, and the second-largest and fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record globally. The single deadliest week so far (August 3-9) saw 579 new cases and 304 deaths. The outbreak has spread from Ituri into five additional DRC provinces (North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Tshopo, and Bas-Uele) and to Uganda's capital, Kampala. Uganda itself declared its own linked outbreak over on July 28, 2026. Update 2026-08-30: the outbreak has continued accelerating and the international funding response remains critically short. By August 27, 2026, DRC's public health institute reported 5,794 confirmed cases and 2,786 deaths (up from 4,945/2,325 in mid-August). WHO's own August 14, 2026 situation report separately confirmed Uganda's 42-day enhanced-monitoring period tied to its last imported case (discharged July 16) was set to conclude August 27, 2026 -- a formal WHO confirmation distinct from, and following, Uganda's own earlier July 28 declaration that its linked outbreak was over. The DRC's Ministry of Public Health launched the outbreak's first vaccination campaign on August 27, 2026, using the ERVEBO vaccine in Kisangani, targeting the affected Tshopo, Bas-Uele, and Haut-Uele provinces; WHO approved 70,000 doses, with roughly 50,000 for frontline/health workers and 20,000 allocated to a clinical trial testing the vaccine's efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain specifically, since ERVEBO's proven effectiveness is against a different, more common Ebola strain. The UN's senior Ebola coordinator, Julien Harneis, said in late August 2026 that existing response funding 'will run out within weeks' and that the outbreak is spreading 'faster and wider' than previously documented; OCHA's $60 million Central Emergency Response Fund allocation falls well short of a nearly $679 million humanitarian funding gap, and Africa CDC and WHO issued a joint appeal for an additional $518 million. More than 160 healthcare workers have been infected and 43 have died, amid over 260 attacks on health workers in the preceding six months. This funding-shortfall reporting extends this entry's core claim beyond pre-outbreak detection capacity to the ongoing emergency response itself, which independent reporting directly ties to the same underlying USAID/CDC/WHO funding and staffing cuts already documented in this entry.
