title: USAID Dismantled and Absorbed Into the State Department, Despite Being a Congressionally-Independent Agency
institution: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)
status: Operationally dissolved (July 1, 2025) but legally unresolved -- Congress made USAID independent in 1998 and only Congress can formally abolish it, which hasn't happened. Since mid-2026 the State Department has resumed ~$4 billion in humanitarian/health funding via two tranches -- ~$2B through multilateral organizations (Gavi, WFP, UNICEF, Global Fund) and ~$2B through faith-based/community organizations, the latter of which officials say doesn't restore previously cut programs -- rather than rebuilding USAID itself.
date_of_action: 2025-01-24 (foreign aid freeze ordered) through 2025-07-01 (official dissolution and merger into State Department)
what_changed:
On his first days in office, Trump ordered a near-total freeze on foreign aid, and within weeks the administration placed most USAID employees on administrative leave. By March 10, 2025, Secretary of State Rubio announced 83% of USAID's programs (roughly 5,200 contracts) had been terminated following an internal review; on March 28 he formally notified Congress that USAID would be dissolved and its remaining functions absorbed into the State Department -- ABC News reported the dissolution notice came just hours after a federal appeals court lifted a lower-court ruling that had been blocking the shutdown, meaning the announcement followed directly on the litigation clearing rather than preceding it. USAID officially ceased independent operations on July 1, 2025, after 63 years. On that final day, former Presidents Obama and Bush both publicly condemned the dismantlement -- a rare bipartisan former-presidential rebuke -- calling it a 'tragedy' and 'colossal mistake,' per CNN. Staffing was reduced from over 10,000 employees to fewer than 300.

USAID's own Inspector General issued a report warning the spending pause and staff furloughs limited the agency's ability to ensure funds didn't reach terrorist-linked recipients, and separately warned that $489 million in humanitarian food aid risked spoiling due to the furloughs; the White House Office of Presidential Personnel fired that Inspector General less than 30 minutes after the report's publication -- despite a federal law requiring 30 days' advance notice to Congress before removing an inspector general.

A significant, largely unresolved legal question underlies the entire action: USAID was reorganized by Congress as an independent agency in 1998 specifically to give it statutory protection, and per that same statute can only be formally abolished by an act of Congress -- which has not happened. USAID therefore legally still exists even though it has been operationally dissolved.

The cuts reached deep into the U.S. workforce. Johns Hopkins University's own March 2025 announcement put its layoffs at 2,222 positions and $800 million in lost contracts, figures independently corroborated across CNN, Higher Ed Dive, The Daily Record, and CBS News. CBS News reported April 23, 2025 that the domestic fallout extended well beyond Johns Hopkins and EnCompass -- an estimated 19,187 American jobs had been lost across 46 states as of that reporting, with FHI 360 terminating 480 U.S. employees (140 at its North Carolina headquarters) and Georgia alone losing 44 USAID-funded programs worth an estimated $257.9 million. Most remaining USAID employees were slated to lose their jobs on July 1 or September 2, 2025, per that same reporting.

FedScoop reported that on April 24, 2025 USAID's IT office told departing employees -- an agency source said the decision could affect roughly 10,000 people -- that their government-issued iPhones, iPads, and laptops would be remotely wiped and marked disposed from IT asset inventories around each employee's reduction-in-force date, rather than returned; staff could then simply discard the hardware themselves. The agency framed this as reducing burden on departing employees, but it departs from federal agencies' standard practice of auctioning or reassigning surplus equipment rather than wiping and discarding it.

The New York Times reported in early March 2025 that the freeze had already crippled global disease-prevention programs on the ground -- leaving dangerous pathogens unsecured, halting inspections for Ebola and mpox, and stopping screenings at international checkpoints -- with scientists warning that outbreaks once contained by U.S.-funded efforts now posed a greater risk of spreading worldwide, including to the U.S. This is an early, contemporaneous data point on the same disease-surveillance capacity loss later linked to the 2026 DRC/Uganda Ebola outbreak.

Former USAID Administrator Samantha Power said in a Bloomberg interview that she does not believe the Ebola outbreak spreading across the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda -- which has killed more than 400 people -- would be spiraling as it has if USAID had not been dismantled, citing the loss of the agency's early-warning disease-surveillance systems and cold-chain infrastructure (whose degradation contributed to delayed detection, since transported swab samples were no longer reliably preserved). The administration's separate withdrawal from the World Health Organization compounded the effect by removing another layer of international outbreak-response coordination.

The foreign-aid freeze also abruptly halted a $300 million, 10-year USAID commitment to clean up dioxin contamination from Agent Orange at Vietnam's Bien Hoa air base -- the largest remaining Agent Orange hotspot in the country. Work on the site, underway since 2019, stopped in March 2025, leaving exposed pits of contaminated soil at risk of washing into nearby communities during the rainy season; the same freeze also halted a related USAID-funded program clearing unexploded American munitions and landmines, a rehabilitation program for Vietnamese war victims, and work on a museum exhibit documenting U.S. remediation efforts. Following USAID's July 2025 dissolution, funding responsibility for the Bien Hoa cleanup shifted to the State Department, but U.S. diplomats and outside experts have warned that halting a dioxin remediation project mid-cleanup is more dangerous than never having started one, and that the suspension has strained relations with Vietnam, a strategic U.S. partner in the region.

The freeze's on-the-ground consequences extended to disaster response. When a 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Myanmar on March 28, 2025 -- killing more than 1,700 people initially, a toll that continued climbing past 3,300 by early April and eventually surpassed 3,700, and displacing millions amid an ongoing civil war -- a three-person USAID assessment team that had just arrived in the disaster zone received termination notices on April 4, 2025 as part of the broader agency-wide cuts; CNN and BBC reported the notices arrived within days of the team's arrival, and that the three were advisers, not rescuers. NBC News independently corroborated the same terminations, reporting the laid-off workers were left sleeping on the streets alongside earthquake survivors while China and Russia expanded their own aid presence.

The United States' overall response was limited to roughly $2 million in aid channeled through humanitarian groups already operating in Myanmar, a fraction of the scale China and Russia rapidly deployed; CNN, BBC, CSIS, and CFR all reported both the team's termination notices and that roughly $2 million figure. CSIS characterized the episode as the first real-world test of the administration's emergency-aid cuts; sweeping USAID reductions had already left the agency with over $2 billion in unpaid debt to humanitarian organizations, contractors, and international partners operating in Myanmar and elsewhere, forcing partner organizations to scale back operations independent of the earthquake itself.

Rubio's 'no one has died' claim was not the only official denial contradicted by the record -- Mother Jones reported in June 2025 that internal State Department cables reviewed by the outlet documented lifesaving HIV treatment programs in Lesotho and food-aid programs in Malawi being cut as a direct result of the dismantlement, with diplomats warning of resulting deaths, hunger, and trafficking risk. That reporting directly contradicts Elon Musk's own public claim, made while leading the DOGE effort that drove the cuts, that 'zero people have died' as a result.

A Reuters investigation published July 19, 2025 -- based on interviews with 17 sources -- identified 21 unfinished water and sanitation infrastructure projects across 16 countries left half-built after funding was canceled, with hundreds of millions of dollars in cancellations since January 2025; workers abandoned holes half-dug and building supplies unguarded. Documented examples included an abandoned irrigation canal under construction in Kamleza, Kenya, and defunct USAID water kiosks in eastern Congo now used by children as play areas rather than functioning water infrastructure.

Litigation has run on two D.C. Circuit tracks. The earlier one, over the funding freeze itself, reached the D.C. Circuit first: a coalition of international aid organizations sued over the funding freeze on February 10, 2025, and U.S. District Judge Amir Ali issued a preliminary injunction in March 2025 ordering the administration to resume disbursing billions in already-appropriated foreign assistance funds. On August 13, 2025, a divided D.C. Circuit panel reversed that injunction 2-1 (Judges Karen Henderson and Gregory Katsas in the majority, Judge Florence Pan dissenting), holding that only the Government Accountability Office's Comptroller General -- not private grant recipients -- has standing to sue under the Impoundment Control Act; the panel did not reach the underlying constitutional question of whether withholding congressionally appropriated funds was itself lawful. Judge Pan's dissent said the majority's standing ruling ignored the funding cuts' threat to 'the rule of law and the very structure of our government.' The Supreme Court later built on this standing theory, ruling 6-3 on September 26, 2025 to let the administration withhold roughly $4 billion in foreign aid via a 'pocket rescission' -- letting a rescission request expire unacted-upon at the fiscal year's end so the funds lapse without an up-or-down congressional vote -- a separate but related mechanism for withholding the same category of appropriated foreign-assistance funds this entry documents being frozen and terminated administratively.

On the core USAID dismantlement case, AFGE v. Trump (No. 25-5290), the D.C. Circuit held oral argument on April 23, 2026 before Judges Srinivasan, Pillard, and Pan; no ruling had been identified as of August 30, 2026. In a related case, briefing was scheduled to run into summer 2026, with the government's reply brief due July 31, 2026.

Separately, in a class-action suit over USAID's shutdown (Does 1-26 v. Musk, D. Md.), a federal court in Maryland on February 4, 2026 denied efforts to block depositions of Elon Musk and other DOGE-linked officials, but the Fourth Circuit reversed that order on March 4, 2026, blocking Musk from being compelled to sit for a deposition, at least for now (whether the reversal is final or merely delays the deposition question depends on how the broader suit progresses). The underlying constitutional claims (Appointments Clause, separation of powers) remain unresolved and the case continues in the district court, with a related preliminary-injunction appeal still in abeyance at the Fourth Circuit since June 2025.

The multilateral-funding restructuring that followed the dismantlement began on December 29, 2025, when the State Department and the U.N.'s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA, led by Tom Fletcher) signed a first-of-its-kind Humanitarian Reset agreement in Geneva, anchored by a U.S. pledge of $2 billion to 18 country-based and crisis-level pooled funds -- a pledge administration officials themselves said was down from $8-10 billion in annual U.S. voluntary humanitarian funding in recent years (other reporting cited a $17 billion 2022 peak). A State Department statement accompanying the announcement warned that individual U.N. agencies would need to adapt, shrink, or accept elimination, tying the reduced funding to consolidation demands, efficiency/accountability standards, and tighter U.S. control over how the money is spent.

Since June 2026 the State Department has resumed nearly $2 billion in humanitarian and global-health funding, routed not through a rebuilt USAID but through multilateral organizations directly -- $600 million to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance; $800 million to the World Food Programme for malnutrition response in Ethiopia, Myanmar, and Ukraine; $218 million to UNICEF for child health, nutrition, water, and sanitation programs; $661 million to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria; $203 million to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies for disaster response; $100 million to the public-private Operation End Starvation initiative; and $50 million to an Ebola vaccine/pandemic-preparedness coalition, alongside separate DRC-focused Ebola response funding. The funding carries explicit political conditions: reporting describes prohibitions on directing funds to Afghanistan and Yemen, reduced assistance to Sudan, and a ban on climate-change-related humanitarian programming. This does not reverse USAID's dismantlement or restore the agency itself -- it is the administration routing a substantial, but conditioned and narrower, share of prior USAID-level funding through international intermediaries instead.

A second, distinct ~$2 billion funding tranche was announced August 10, 2026, this one routed to faith-based and community organizations under what the State Department calls the 'America First Global Health Strategy' -- a different mechanism from the multilateral-organization funding (Gavi, WFP, UNICEF, etc.) above (see this entry's estimated-impact figures for the breakdown). A State Department official told reporters the funding does not restore any previously cut program: 'there are not programs we cut that are now going to be funded again.'

Boston University researcher Brooke Nichols' 'Impact Counter' -- a running, modeled estimate distinct from the Lancet's forward-looking 2030 projections -- put actual deaths in the year since the cuts began at over 700,000, including more than 500,000 children, a figure NPR reported July 17, 2026 alongside three additional named child-death cases beyond the Nigeria case documented elsewhere in this entry.

On PEPFAR specifically, reporting reviewed found roughly $3 billion of a $6.045 billion FY appropriation remained withheld as of mid-2025, and Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) said July 22, 2026 he had received administration assurances that $1.3 billion of the frozen PEPFAR funds would be released; a July 2026 IAS conference presentation found 1,700 PEPFAR-supported sites closed and 77,000 fewer children receiving PEPFAR-supported treatment as a result of the disruption.

primary_proponent.name: Marco Rubio
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of State
primary_proponent.note: Personally announced the program terminations, the dissolution notice to Congress, and USAID's final closure, writing on Substack: 'As of July 1st, USAID will officially cease to implement foreign assistance... This era of government-sanctioned inefficiency has officially come to an end.' Rubio told a congressional hearing in May 2025 that 'no one has died because of USAID [cuts]' -- a claim directly contradicted by subsequent peer-reviewed research (see below) and by on-the-ground reporting, including one documented case of a child in Nigeria who died after the USAID-funded clinic he depended on for urgent care was closed. This action is closely related to, but categorically distinct from, the separately-tracked State Department reorganization entry in this database -- USAID's elimination is the dismantling of an entire congressionally-independent agency, not an internal State Department restructuring.

estimated_impact.summary: **A peer-reviewed study published in The Lancet (one of the world's most established medical journals) estimated USAID funding prevented more than 91 million deaths globally between 2001 and 2021, including a 65% reduction in HIV/AIDS mortality and 51% reduction in malaria mortality in the countries it funded.** The same study projected that, absent a reversal, the 2025 cuts could contribute to more than 14 million additional preventable deaths by 2030, nearly a third of them children under 5 -- a scale the study's authors explicitly compared to 'a global pandemic or a major armed conflict,' while noting this crisis would stem from 'a conscious and avoidable policy choice.' A follow-up Lancet study one year later, incorporating a full year of real data rather than projections, estimated a somewhat lower but still severe 9.4 million-death figure by 2030 if funding trends continue -- researchers who reviewed the modeling told CNN the precise numbers should be treated with some caution but that the overall conclusion (large-scale, avoidable death) is likely correct. Domestically, the closure eliminated an estimated 19,187 American jobs across 46 states as of April 2025 reporting, spanning USAID staff and its contractor/NGO ecosystem -- one contractor, EnCompass, lost over 400 jobs in under a month, and FHI 360 terminated 480 U.S. employees. The largest single documented example was Johns Hopkins University, the country's top university recipient of federal contracts: after losing $800 million in USAID-funded contracts, Johns Hopkins announced in March 2025 what a university spokesperson called the largest layoff in its history -- 2,222 positions cut (1,975 international staff across 44 countries plus 247 U.S.-based positions), spanning its Bloomberg School of Public Health, Center for Communication Programs, and affiliated nonprofit Jhpiego, with roughly 100 additional workers furloughed to reduced schedules.

estimated_impact.caveat: The State Department disputes the Lancet methodology directly and sharply -- a senior official called it a 'failed journal' and said such studies reflect 'outdated thinking.' This is a genuinely disputed empirical question about mortality modeling, not merely a political disagreement, and modelers themselves (including ones unaffiliated with the study) caution the precise death-toll numbers carry real uncertainty even while endorsing the general conclusion. Separately, the administration's own stated justification (that USAID had significant oversight and accountability failures) has some independent support -- USAID itself failed to conduct legally-required financial reviews for over 70% of the international organizations receiving its funding in 2023, per the agency's own inspector general -- though fact-checkers found most of the administration's specific waste examples cited publicly were false or highly misleading.

confidence_note: Exceptionally strong sourcing across the full political spectrum of outlets (NPR, CNN, ABC News, Newsweek) plus a peer-reviewed medical journal (The Lancet) with two independent studies a year apart, plus USAID's own Inspector General's report before that office was itself eliminated. The legal status question (independent agency status under the 1998 statute) is a matter of public record, not interpretation. Rubio's 'no one has died' claim and the mortality studies represent a genuine, sourced factual conflict -- present both sides with their actual sourcing rather than treating either claim as simply settled. The March 2025 New York Times reporting on halted Ebola/mpox screening is contemporaneous, single-outlet coverage of an immediate operational consequence of the freeze, consistent with and predating the later Power/Bloomberg Ebola-outbreak linkage already documented above. Re-verified 2026-08-30 (GSR recheck batch 29), real correction: the ~$2 billion multilateral funding resumption is HIGH confidence, corroborated across the State Department's own June 2026 press release plus independent reporting from Devex, Washington Examiner, and Geneva Solutions on the individual pledges (Gavi, WFP, UNICEF, Global Fund, IFRC); the specific Afghanistan/Yemen/Sudan/climate-program conditions are sourced to a single outlet (Kathmandu Post) not independently corroborated in sourcing reviewed here, so that detail is MODERATE confidence and flagged accordingly. This is presented as a distinct, narrower, conditioned funding mechanism running alongside the dismantlement already documented, not a reversal of it -- USAID itself remains operationally dissolved and legally unresolved. section_summaries.what_changed: USAID's staff fell from over 10,000 to under 300, and the aid freeze crippled disease-screening and outbreak-prevention programs within weeks; only Congress can legally abolish it, and it hasn't.
section_summaries.estimated_impact: A peer-reviewed Lancet study credited this funding with preventing tens of millions of deaths and projected millions more by 2030 if the cuts hold, calling the toll avoidable, not inevitable; a running BU model estimates 700,000+ actual deaths in the year since the cuts began. A 2026 Ebola outbreak (400+ deaths) and a PEPFAR disruption (1,700 sites closed, 77,000 fewer children treated) are cited as concrete real-world instances of that lost capacity. A combined ~$4B in resumed funding since mid-2026 -- ~$2B via multilateral organizations and a second, distinct ~$2B via faith-based/community organizations -- is a partial, conditioned offset, not a restoration of USAID's own infrastructure; officials themselves say it does not fund previously cut programs.
section_summaries.confidence_note: Exceptionally strong sourcing, including two independent peer-reviewed medical studies and the agency's own Inspector General; official statements and the death-toll research genuinely disagree -- present both. The Ebola link is attributed expert opinion, well-corroborated but not an adjudicated causal finding. The 2026 multilateral funding resumption is well-corroborated on dollar figures; its specific political conditions rest on single-outlet sourcing. The BU Impact Counter's 700,000-death figure is a running model estimate, not a peer-reviewed final count.

title: USCIS sharply increases withholding and redaction of immigrants' own immigration records
institution: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (DHS)
status: New as of this entry -- no reversal or on-record USCIS response to the underlying whistleblower complaint identified in sourcing reviewed
date_of_action: 2025-05 (USCIS staff allegedly ordered to withhold specified document categories) through 2026-09-14 (New York Times reporting published)
what_changed: Immigrants seeking their own government records to prove they are in the country legally are being refused outright or given documents so heavily redacted they cannot use them, according to dozens of immigration lawyers cited by the New York Times. **U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services redacted or withheld more than 80% of the documents requested by one lawyer's clients since April 17, 2025, compared with an average of about 10% between May 2024 and April 2025** -- roughly an eightfold increase. A former USCIS records official, in a whistleblower complaint, alleged the agency improperly enacted policies early in the second Trump administration making it harder for immigrants to obtain documents they are legally entitled to, including a May 2025 order to staff to withhold tax returns, court transcripts, joint bank records, marriage certificates, and any document not written in English. Lawyers say the practice prevents noncitizens from reconstructing their own immigration histories and from making their strongest case for status or against deportation -- directly increasing wrongful-deportation risk for people who are in fact legally present.

primary_proponent.role: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security

title: USDA Moved to Shutter Its 116-Year-Old Flagship Research Campus Over Congress's Own Objection, Scattering Pollinator and Food-Safety Science Nationwide
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Research Service
status: USDA announced April 23, 2026 that it would begin decommissioning the facility, with a reported internal target of vacating by September 30, 2026 (end of fiscal year); Maryland's congressional delegation says the move violates an FY2026 appropriations-bill provision requiring Appropriations Committee approval, and no court ruling or congressional resolution of that dispute was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry
date_of_action: 2025-07 (Secretary Rollins announces reorganization plan to close BARC) through 2026-04-23 (USDA announces start of decommissioning despite the disputed congressional restriction)
what_changed: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced in July 2025, as part of a broader department reorganization, a plan to close the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center (BARC) -- a 6,500-acre, 400-plus-building complex in Prince George's County, Maryland operating continuously since 1910 and widely described as the world's largest agricultural research facility -- and disperse its programs among roughly two dozen other USDA sites nationwide. USDA cited high maintenance costs (an estimated $500 million in one-time modernization costs plus $40 million a year ongoing) and unsafe building conditions, noting a 2023 whistleblower complaint had found mold, water damage, and buildings without running water, and that more than 60% of BARC's buildings sat unused. Maryland's congressional delegation reportedly pushed back publicly starting in August 2025 (per Maryland Matters, a source blocked to direct fetch and relied on here only via search-engine synthesis rather than a directly-read page), and by November 2025 the New York Times reported scientists and farm groups warning that scattering BARC's programs -- which include core research on pollinators, plant diseases, food safety, and crop resilience -- risked losing rare collections and setting research back years; entomologists specifically flagged BARC's bee research lab, whose location supports extensive winter-colony-loss studies difficult to replicate at USDA's other bee labs (mostly in more temperate climates) and whose closure would leave a research gap for Northeast pollination-dependent crops like cranberries, squash, and blueberries. Congress subsequently inserted language into the FY2026 appropriations bill explicitly barring USDA from closing or consolidating research facilities without approval from the House and Senate Appropriations Committees. **USDA nonetheless announced on April 23, 2026 that it would proceed, formally beginning to "decommission" BARC; Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-MD) said the administration was "trying to move forward in violation of what Congress has expressly stated," and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) said USDA was "blatantly violating the law."** USDA framed the move as modernization, saying it would "modernize its research footprint, improve safety, and better connect researchers with the producers they serve." USDA identified 27 potential relocation sites across the country in its restructuring plan, including sending BARC's bee lab to Fargo, North Dakota, and shifting some staff to the Meat Animal Research Center in Clay Center, Nebraska, though as of a June 2026 Greenbelt News Review report the specific destination for each individual lab remained undetermined. At an all-hands meeting, Acting Area Director Joe Rich reportedly told staff the facility must be vacated by September 30, 2026. AFGE Local 3403, the union representing BARC employees, reported that 76% of its members said they did not plan to relocate with their positions -- on top of significant staff losses BARC had already sustained over the preceding 18 months through retirements, resignations, and broader federal workforce reductions.

primary_proponent.name: Brooke Rollins
primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Agriculture
primary_proponent.note: Announced and has continued to defend the BARC closure/reorganization plan, including the April 2026 decision to begin decommissioning despite the disputed congressional appropriations restriction.

estimated_impact.summary: USDA's flagship, 116-year-old agricultural research campus -- supporting roughly 1,000 jobs and decades of pollinator, plant-disease, food-safety, and crop-resilience research -- is being dismantled and its programs dispersed to as many as 27 other sites nationwide, with USDA's own employee union reporting that three-quarters of remaining staff do not plan to relocate, threatening a substantial loss of institutional research capacity and expertise regardless of whether the underlying programs are formally continued elsewhere.

The true cost of lost, hard-to-replicate long-term research (e.g., multi-decade winter-colony-loss data series) is inherently difficult to quantify in dollar terms and is not attempted here.

title: Bird Flu Response Hampered by USDA's Accidental Firing of Response Staff, Plus Broader Funding Freezes and a Federal Communication Blackout
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA); Department of Health and Human Services / CDC
status: USDA said Feb. 18, 2025 it was rescinding the mistaken bird-flu-staff firings; Reuters reported four fired NAHLN lab-network staff were brought back. No reversal was reported for the later losses (about 140 FDA veterinary-center staff fired April 1, 2025; three NAHLN staff leaving April 30).
what_changed: Over the weekend of February 15-16, 2025, USDA fired several employees whose work supported the federal response to the ongoing H5N1 bird flu (avian influenza) outbreak. On February 18, USDA told NBC News the firings were a mistake: "Although several positions supporting [bird flu efforts] were notified of their terminations over the weekend, we are working to swiftly rectify the situation and rescind those letters," a spokesperson said. NBC placed the error within the administration's mass firings of federal workers, carried out with Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency, which in those days included probationary employees across the government. Politico reported on February 16 that a quarter of the 14-person staff of USDA's National Animal Health Laboratory Network (NAHLN) program office, which coordinates the labs that test animal samples for bird flu, had been fired, and that labs were told bird-flu testing would be slower; Keith Poulsen, director of the Wisconsin Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory, said the firing of three NAHLN employees would hurt efforts to combat the virus, and Republican lawmakers privately warned the administration that such cuts could hamper the bird-flu response, NBC reported. Four NAHLN employees fired in the February layoffs were brought back soon after, Reuters later reported. Politico reported on February 27 that USDA was struggling to rehire key bird-flu employees and that the dismissals had helped trigger a partial shutdown at one of its research facilities, according to two USDA employees. Separately, The Hill reported on February 20 that mass firings, funding freezes and an external communications blackout across health agencies were hampering the wider public-health response: as egg prices rose, state and local health departments were only beginning to hear from the CDC nearly a month after the inauguration, a person familiar with the situation said critical updates were still being slow-walked, and a federal funding freeze left virus researchers unsure whether their work would continue. The staffing losses continued after the February episode. **On April 1, 2025, about 140 staff at the FDA's Center for Veterinary Medicine, including its leadership, were fired in the Department of Health and Human Services' reduction in force**; the center had helped link bird flu cases in cats to raw pet food, and **the HHS cuts led the FDA to suspend an effort to improve bird-flu testing of pet food and dairy products**, NBC News and Reuters reported. HHS said the cuts were limited to administrative staff. On April 9, 2025, Reuters reported, citing a source familiar with the situation, that three of the 13 NAHLN employees had accepted USDA's financial incentive to quit and would leave on April 30; they worked on keeping bird flu testing consistent across the network, managing its funding and providing administrative support, and the source said their departures would likely disrupt bird-flu monitoring in livestock during what NBC News called the worst bird flu outbreak in U.S. history.

USDA's February firings of bird-flu staff were a mistake it moved to reverse, and at least four lab-network staff were brought back, but state and local health officials meanwhile went nearly a month with little CDC communication.

title: USDA Canceled the $3.1B Climate-Smart Commodities Program, Rebranding It Without the Climate Focus
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)
status: Implemented -- PCSC canceled April 14, 2025 and folded into the non-climate AMP initiative with no new money; USDA said in April 2026, per E&E News, that around 90 former projects had been awarded new AMP contracts.
what_changed: **Internal emails made public in court filings and reviewed by NOTUS show that in February 2025, Gavin Kliger -- a 25-year-old DOGE staffer on unpaid leave from AI firm Databricks -- pushed USDA officials to write agency-wide guidance for reviewing climate-related awards and to finish $120 million in cuts within days, ahead of the program's public cancellation.** On February 19, 2025, USDA Deputy CFO Lynn Moaney sent Kliger, for his approval, draft agency-wide guidance directing officials to find grants that 'fund climate-related activities which do not demonstrably directly or indirectly benefit farmers or producers,' telling him her team 'thought Monday is not doable' for the $120 million target and asking for an extension on the larger climate review. Kliger approved the guidance and the extension but asked whether mission areas could review all climate grants in that window '(and hopefully therefore exceed our 120m goal significantly)'; he later told Moaney that Secretary Rollins supported the $120 million goal and the climate-grant review, and that he was 'working on getting a memo formalized for her signature.' A USDA spokesperson told NOTUS that everyone on the USDA Efficiency Team is a USDA employee working at Rollins' direction. On April 14, 2025, Rollins announced the cancellation of the Biden-era Partnerships for Climate-Smart Commodities (PCSC), a $3.1 billion initiative spanning 135 projects that paid for carbon-reducing farming practices (about 14,000 farms had enrolled, on 3.2 million acres, as of June 2024), after nearly three months of frozen payments, according to Civil Eats. USDA said a line-by-line review found the majority of the projects had 'sky-high administration fees' that in many instances passed less than half of the federal funding directly to farmers; Rollins has separately made clear she does not support climate-change-focused programs. Rather than simply terminating the program, USDA said existing grant recipients could continue under a new initiative, Advancing Markets for Producers (AMP), which drops the climate framing and requires that at least 65% of each grant's federal dollars go directly to farmers; USDA said it would honor expenses incurred before April 13, 2025, and that the AMP transition uses only existing program funding, with no new funding made available. St. Louis Public Radio reported that more than $1.2 billion had gone to 36 projects involving Missouri, though the University of Missouri's $25 million Conservation Crop and Livestock project was expected to continue under AMP. A year later, Agri-Pulse reported (April 8, 2026) that only about 10% of the 135 original projects had met the 65% farmer-payment threshold, leaving the rest to amend their projects while USDA buyouts thinned NRCS field staff, and that USDA did not respond to its questions, including how many AMP projects had been approved; on April 16, 2026, E&E News reported USDA's count that around 90 former projects had been awarded new contracts meeting the administration's non-climate guidelines.

estimated_impact.summary: Farmers and the organizations paying them bore the disruption: a $3.1 billion, 135-project program that paid for carbon-reducing practices (about 14,000 farms enrolled as of June 2024) went through nearly three months of frozen payments, was canceled, and was rebuilt around a rule that at least 65% of funds reach producers. Only about 10% of projects met that rule at first, so the rest had to amend their work; a year later USDA said around 90 of the 135 had new contracts, all stripped of their climate-mitigation purpose. The money was redirected, not newly cut, and the entry documents no direct health harm.

what_changed: **USDA canceled all existing grants under its Food for Progress program, which sends American-grown commodities -- including milled rice, soybean meal, wheat, and yellow soybeans -- abroad to support agricultural development and food security in developing countries, according to an internal email reviewed by Reuters. title: USDA Terminated Its Two Long-Standing Scientific Food-Safety Advisory Committees, Halting In-Progress Listeria Review
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) -- Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS)
status: Terminated; no reinstatement found as of last verification despite lawmaker and stakeholder calls to restore them
date_of_action: 2025-02-20 (formal termination) / 2025-03-06 (members notified, publicly reported)
what_changed: On March 6, 2025, USDA notified members that it had terminated the National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods (NACMCF, established 1988) and the National Advisory Committee on Meat and Poultry Inspection (NACMPI, established 1971), consistent with a February 20, 2025 termination date reported by trade press, as part of the administration's broader elimination of federal advisory committees under Executive Order 14217. Richard Blumenthal specifically flagged that NACMCF had been actively tasked, as of December 2024, with reviewing FSIS's regulatory approach to Listeria monocytogenes to inform policy improvements and facility oversight -- work that was halted by the termination, coming just months after a 2024 Listeria outbreak linked to Boar's Head deli meat killed 10 people and sickened dozens nationwide. Blumenthal separately urged Secretary Brooke Rollins to reinstate both committees, noting their combined annual budgets ($225,000 for NACMCF, $75,000 for NACMPI) were minimal relative to the scientific oversight they provided. As of this entry's last verification, no source reviewed reported either committee being reinstated.

title: USDA Cancels 30-Year Household Food Security Survey as 4.7 Million Lose SNAP Benefits
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture
status: Complete -- survey terminated; Democratic members of Congress have introduced bills to reinstate it, not yet enacted
date_of_action: 2025-09-20 (survey termination announced)
what_changed: In September 2025, USDA terminated its annual Household Food Security Survey, which for 30 years had been the government's primary tool for measuring whether American households have reliable access to enough food, and which researchers and policymakers widely regarded as the 'gold standard' for understanding food access nationally. USDA's own press release described the survey as 'redundant, costly, politicized, and extraneous.' The cancellation followed passage of Trump's tax and spending law (HR1/OBBBA) in July 2025, which shifted significant SNAP funding responsibility to states and expanded work requirements; since then, roughly 4.7 million people -- about 11% of prior participants -- have lost SNAP benefits, with further losses expected as states continue implementing the changes. Food-security researchers said the survey's elimination will make it substantially harder to measure whether hunger is increasing as a result of the SNAP changes, since no comparable federal data source currently exists. Democratic members of Congress have introduced legislation to reinstate the survey; it has not been enacted as of this entry. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0593): days after the September 20, 2025 cancellation announcement, USDA placed about a dozen Economic Research Service staff behind the survey -- including Acting Administrator Kelly Maguire, her chief of staff, and the food economics division head -- on indefinite leave, citing an investigation into 'unauthorized disclosure' of non-public information; the affected employees had all attended the internal meeting announcing the report's cancellation. They were escorted from their offices and had their laptops seized, though USDA said the leave was not disciplinary. The agency did not specify what was disclosed or to whom, and AFGE, the employees' union, said USDA offered no further clarification; critics characterized the move as retaliation against researchers who had resisted burying the survey's data. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0590): despite the September 2025 termination announcement, USDA released one final edition of the report on December 31, 2025/early January 2026, covering 2024 data already in the survey pipeline -- finding 13.7% of U.S. households (18.3 million) were food insecure in 2024, the highest prevalence in nearly a decade. CSIS noted the series' end eliminates over 25 years of consistent national tracking, with no comparable replacement: the Census Bureau's alternative food-sufficiency survey draws only a 1-10% response rate and asks a single question, versus the USDA survey's 74% response rate and 18-question module.

title: Litigation Revealed USDA Used an Automated Banned-Word Search to Flag ~600 Grants Worth $3B+ for Cancellation
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture; DOGE
status: Ongoing litigation (USDN v. USDA, D.D.C.) -- a preliminary injunction has already restored some canceled grants, and the court has ordered DOGE/USDA to produce administrative records; more plaintiffs joined in 2026 seeking further restoration
date_of_action: 2025-06 (USDN v. USDA filed) through 2026-05 (24 additional plaintiffs join, seeking ~$127M in restorations); documents revealing the search methodology reported 2025-11-13
what_changed: Documents obtained by legal advocacy group FarmSTAND and reported by Reuters on November 13, 2025 revealed that **USDA, complying with 2025 Trump executive orders targeting DEI and climate programs, systematically searched its own grant records for banned terms and topics** -- including 'climate modeling,' 'climate and emission analysis,' 'climate smart agriculture and land use that does not directly benefit farmers,' 'carbon pricing and market mechanics,' 'renewable energy modernization that does not directly benefit farmers,' 'climate adaptation and resilience planning,' and 'biodiversity and ecosystem resilience related to climate change' -- to flag grants for termination. Per DOGE's own website, USDA ultimately terminated approximately 600 grants worth more than $3 billion using this method, spanning USDA's full portfolio from food stamps to farm subsidies to conservation programs. The keyword-search methodology was disclosed through USDN v. USDA, a lawsuit originally filed in June 2025 by Agroecology Commons, the Institute on Agriculture and Trade Policy, Oakville Bluegrass Cooperative, Providence Farm Collective, and the Urban Sustainability Directors Network (USDN), after the administration froze funding, withheld required approvals, and ultimately terminated 49 of 50 projects under USDA's Increasing Land, Capital, and Market Access (LCM) Program. In August 2025, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia granted a preliminary injunction restoring six grants held by the original plaintiffs and ordered DOGE and USDA to produce the administrative records that ultimately revealed the keyword-search method -- the court's order noted that many more grants canceled the same way could be eligible for the same relief. By May 2026, 24 additional organizations and local governments joined the suit, filing their own motion for a preliminary injunction seeking to restore roughly $127 million in canceled grants and compel USDA to honor the underlying grant agreements.

primary_proponent.role: Implementing entity, in coordination with USDA leadership

estimated_impact.summary: An automated keyword search, rather than individualized programmatic review, was used to flag roughly $3 billion across 600 grants for termination across USDA's entire portfolio -- including conservation, climate-resilience, and land-access programs unrelated to DEI in any conventional sense -- with litigation subsequently finding at least some terminations improper enough to warrant court-ordered restoration.

title: USDA Cancels $1 Billion in Local Food Purchasing Programs for Schools and Food Banks
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)
status: Terminated in spring 2025; not restored as of Sept. 27, 2026. Pennsylvania's suit over its $13M LFPA award was dismissed in Dec. 2025; its Third Circuit appeal is set for argument Nov. 17, 2026. Harvest to Hallways (Aug. 2026) funds equipment and grants, not replacement food buying.
date_of_action: 2025-03-07 (USDA notified states; publicly reported 2025-03-10)
what_changed: **USDA canceled the fiscal 2025 rounds of two Biden-era programs that funded states to buy fresh food directly from local farmers for schools, child care sites and food banks: the $660 million Local Food for Schools (LFS) Cooperative Agreement Program, expanded in this round to child care, and the Local Food Purchase Assistance (LFPA) Cooperative Agreement Program, reported at roughly $420 million to $500 million. USDA had announced $1.13 billion for the two programs in late 2024; the LFS round opened on December 10, 2024, and many states had already signed new agreements when USDA's Agricultural Marketing Service notified states on March 7, 2025, that the funding was no longer available and the agreements would be terminated after 60 days' notice**, as part of the administration's broader effort to shrink federal spending. A USDA spokesperson said the pandemic-era programs "no longer effectuate the goals of the agency"; first-round agreements already in place were not affected. The LFS round was to be spent over three years, with about $472 million for K-12 schools and $189 million for child care sites in the Child and Adult Care Food Program. The School Nutrition Association said the lost LFS money would no longer be available to help schools and child care facilities expand fresh, local menus. By late May 2025, CBS News reporting from North Carolina documented on-the-ground effects: the Durham Public Schools nutrition director losing the funds used to buy local produce, a farm that had sold $150,000 of produce to schools the previous year warning it would have to lay off workers, and the Food Bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina putting its share of lost aid at about $2 million amid what its CEO called one of the worst hunger crises in decades. Pennsylvania, whose roughly $13 million LFPA award was cut, sued USDA in June 2025; a federal judge in the Middle District of Pennsylvania dismissed the suit on December 3, 2025, ruling the court lacked jurisdiction over its Administrative Procedure Act claims, and the state appealed to the Third Circuit, which set argument for November 17, 2026. In late August 2026 USDA and HHS announced a "Harvest to Hallways" initiative with up to $70 million for school cafeteria equipment, up to $25 million more for Patrick Leahy Farm to School grants and guidance on spending existing meal reimbursements on local food; it did not restore the canceled purchasing money, and in late September 2026 a Tennessee school nutrition director and local-food nonprofit leaders told the Tennessee Lookout they still felt its loss. This cut is distinct from USDA's separate cancellation of $500 million in supplemental TEFAP funding through the Commodity Credit Corporation around the same time, which is tracked in its own entry; both hit food banks in the same period and region, and some contemporaneous reporting described their compounding effects together, but they are different programs.

primary_proponent.role: Executive action canceling previously awarded cooperative-agreement funding
primary_proponent.note: No single named USDA official was identified in sourcing as personally directing the cancellation; both programs were ended as part of the administration's stated cost-cutting agenda shortly after a new funding round had already opened and states had begun signing agreements.

estimated_impact.summary: USDA withdrew over $1 billion that states were set to spend buying fresh, locally grown food for schools, child care sites and food banks, so less fresh produce and meat reaches students and food-bank clients at a time when food prices and food-bank demand were high. Small farms lost a buyer after agreements were signed; a North Carolina farm that sold $150,000 of produce to schools in a year warned of layoffs, and a North Carolina food bank put its lost aid at about $2 million. USDA's August 2026 Harvest to Hallways initiative funds equipment and grants, not replacement food purchasing.

title: USDA Mass Firings Gutted Food-Safety and Import-Inspection Staff, With a Reinstatement Order Not Immediately Followed
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) -- Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) and Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS)
status: Complete (initial probationary firings reversed under court order, USDA confirmed compliance May 2025; second, larger resignation wave was not reversed)
date_of_action: 2025-02 (probationary firings begin) through 2025-12 (USDA OIG report confirms 20,000+ final H1-2025 tally)
what_changed: Beginning in February 2025, USDA terminated at least 5,692 probationary employees as part of the government-wide firing wave, including roughly 200 inspectors in APHIS's Plant Protection and Quarantine (PPQ) program -- the unit that screens agricultural imports at ports of entry and detects invasive pests and diseases before they can spread domestically. (A separate, narrower incident the same month -- USDA's accidental firing of bird-flu-response staff, later reversed -- is tracked in its own entry in this database.) On March 13, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California issued a preliminary injunction ordering the immediate reinstatement of the terminated probationary employees; the Ninth Circuit denied USDA's request for a stay and upheld the injunction on March 17. Reinstatement did not happen immediately: **on March 25, Rep. Jill Tokuda and 32 House colleagues sent USDA a letter urging urgent rehiring of the terminated agricultural inspectors, warning the delay heightened the risk that unscreened imports could introduce invasive pests and diseases into U.S. agriculture.** USDA did not confirm compliance with the reinstatement order until May 2025, when it sent formal written notices to the affected probationary employees. By then a second, much larger wave of departures was already underway: more than 15,000 USDA employees -- over 15% of the department's workforce -- accepted deferred-resignation buyouts across two rounds (roughly 3,900 in the first round, 11,300 more confirmed by May 5, 2025), including hundreds of food-safety inspectors and technical experts. A subsequent analysis of USDA's own workforce data found FSIS (which inspects meat, poultry, and egg products) lost about 8% of its staff and APHIS (import and pest inspection) lost about 20% of its staff between January and March 2025 alone, with departing staff averaging 16-21 years of experience and 63% of FSIS separations specifically inspectors. Facing internal warnings that the departing employees' work was 'essential to securing the safety of the American food and agriculture system,' USDA reversed course on the ongoing buyout campaign in an April 23, 2025 email urging employees who had already accepted resignation offers to 'reconsider,' calling the work 'vital, mission critical' -- but the reconsideration window applied only to the second round of departures still in progress, not to employees who had already left the agency. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0776): a USDA Office of Inspector General report, released December 2025, provided the first official confirmed final tally covering the full January-June 2025 window -- USDA lost more than 20,000 employees, nearly one-fifth of its entire workforce, roughly three-quarters of them (15,114) via the Deferred Resignation Program already documented above. The OIG's per-agency breakdown showed losses concentrated well beyond the food-safety/import-inspection units already detailed here: the U.S. Forest Service lost 5,860 employees (16% of its workforce), Rural Development -- which administers housing, utilities, and economic-development programs in small towns -- lost 36% of its staff, the Natural Resources Conservation Service lost 2,673 employees (22%), and APHIS's losses (already documented above at 20% for January-March alone) reached 25% by the report's full-period tally, with ARS (Agricultural Research Service) at 23%. Because the OIG report's window ends in June 2025, actual cumulative attrition is understood to be higher still.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Agriculture
primary_proponent.note: Oversaw both the probationary firings and the deferred-resignation buyout programs, while publicly stating 'If you are FSA or frontline or with the farmers, you are not eligible to take early retirement' -- a claim in tension with the hundreds of frontline food-safety and import-inspection staff who did depart through the programs she ran, and with the department's own April 2025 email urging 'vital, mission critical' staff to reconsider resigning.

estimated_impact.summary: The cuts hit the specific functions responsible for stopping unsafe food and invasive pests before they reach the public: import screening at ports of entry, meat/poultry/egg plant inspection, and pest/disease detection. USDA's own workforce data, reviewed by an agricultural-policy nonprofit, documented double-digit staffing losses at the agencies responsible for import and pest inspection within the cuts' first two months, and advocacy groups warned of growing inspection gaps at small and mid-sized processing plants.

title: USDA Shuts Down $420 Million Nationwide Program That Aided Small Farms and Food Businesses
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Agricultural Marketing Service
status: Terminated -- USDA stated it would continue honoring existing commitments on more than 450 already-awarded grants, but the program itself, including its 12 regional centers' broader technical-assistance and coordination work, was shut down
what_changed: Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced the termination of the Regional Food Business Centers (RFBC) program on July 15, 2025. USDA had launched the program in 2022-2023 with $420 million in American Rescue Plan Act funding, establishing 12 regional centers -- covering all 50 states, plus a dedicated national tribal center and centers targeting Colonias (U.S./Mexico border counties) and persistent-poverty areas -- to provide small and mid-sized farms and food businesses with technical assistance, grants, and help navigating federal, state, and local resources to access new markets. Rollins criticized the program's structure directly: 'The Biden Administration created multiple, massive programs without any long-term way to finance them. This is not sustainable for farmers who rely on these programs, and it flies in the face of Congressional intent.' USDA said it would continue honoring more than 450 already-awarded grants to farmers and food businesses so in-progress planning decisions on the farm could proceed, but ended the centers' broader ongoing technical-assistance and coordination role. Local reporting through mid-2025 and into 2026 documented concrete downstream effects: Civil Eats reported the program had already been caught in the administration's earlier funding freeze months before its formal termination, and **KCUR reported in August 2025 on a Midwest small grower who said losing the program's support put her farm's continued operation at risk**; This Is Reno reported small Nevada farms and food businesses stood to lose roughly $3 million in USDA support tied to the program specifically in that state.

title: USDA's SNAP Recipient-Data Demands and a Threatened Mass Reapplication, Backed by Unreleased 'Massive Fraud' Claims, Drew a 21-State Lawsuit and Two Federal Court Losses
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Nutrition Service
status: Ongoing litigation. USDA's proposed mass-reapplication requirement for all SNAP recipients was walked back in December 2025 in favor of existing state recertification procedures, but the underlying fight over USDA's demand for recipients' personal data continues: a federal court blocked USDA from withholding SNAP funding over states' data refusal (Feb. 2026), and USDA/DOJ escalated in June 2026 by directly suing four non-compliant states to compel them to turn over data.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (executive order directing 'unfettered access' to state program data) through 2026-06-26 (DOJ sues four non-compliant states)
what_changed: In March 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to obtain 'unfettered access' to state-held program data. USDA subsequently demanded that all states turn over comprehensive SNAP applicant and recipient records -- names, Social Security numbers, addresses, and financial information -- threatening to withhold SNAP funding from states that refused. In July 2025, California Attorney General Rob Bonta led a coalition of 21 states and the District of Columbia in suing USDA (State of California et al. v. Rollins), arguing the data demand violated the SNAP Act's data-security-protocol requirements and the Administrative Procedure Act; a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction in October 2025 blocking USDA from withholding funding or pursuing noncompliance proceedings against the plaintiff states. USDA responded by sending a new data-demand letter to the same 21 governors in November 2025, characterizing it as a separate action not covered by the injunction and again threatening to withhold benefits from non-compliant states. On November 19-20, 2025, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced that all of the program's roughly 41.7 million recipients nationwide would be required to reapply for benefits, citing what she called 'massive fraud' -- without USDA releasing the underlying data publicly. In subsequent media appearances (including a NewsNation interview), Rollins cited specific figures -- 186,000 dead people receiving benefits, 500,000 Americans receiving benefits twice, and more than 120 arrests for SNAP fraud -- as evidence, though USDA did not make the underlying data available for independent verification. By December 1-5, 2025, facing criticism that ordinary payment-error rates were being mischaracterized as fraud, USDA walked back the universal-reapplication plan, with a spokesperson saying the agency would instead rely on states' 'standard recertification processes' -- the periodic (typically six-to-twelve-month) eligibility updates already required under existing law. Rollins simultaneously previewed broader plans to 'completely deconstruct' SNAP, including new work requirements, continuing to cite the unreleased fraud data as justification. On February 2026, **Judge Maxine Chesney of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California again ruled for the plaintiff states, permanently blocking USDA from withholding SNAP funding over the data-sharing dispute -- finding the relevant statute requires data disclosure 'subject to data and security protocols agreed to by the State agency and Secretary' (a negotiation requirement USDA had bypassed) and that USDA's proposed data-sharing protocols would likely violate separate statutory privacy safeguards**; the judge also rejected USDA's request to stay the ruling pending appeal. By mid-2026, 28 states and Guam had turned over data voluntarily; USDA cited that data as showing 'billions of dollars per year' in overpayments and fraud, again without releasing it for independent review. On June 26, 2026, the Justice Department escalated by directly suing four states that had refused to comply -- Kentucky, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Minnesota -- seeking a court order compelling them to turn over five years of SNAP applicant data, with Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and Secretary Rollins accusing the states of 'shamelessly' defying federal law.

primary_proponent.role: Secretary of Agriculture
primary_proponent.note: Publicly announced the universal-reapplication plan and cited the unreleased fraud statistics in multiple media appearances; later announced the plan's walk-back and previewed the broader 'deconstruct SNAP' initiative. USDA's data demands trace to President Trump's March 2025 executive order on interagency data access.

estimated_impact.summary: No SNAP household is confirmed to have lost benefits specifically from this episode -- the universal-reapplication plan was walked back before implementation -- but the fight put all ~41.7 million SNAP recipients' benefits under a public threat for several weeks based on fraud figures USDA never released for independent verification, and the underlying data-privacy dispute (recipients' Social Security numbers, addresses, and financial records) remains an active federal court fight into mid-2026, with USDA/DOJ shifting from defending against a states' lawsuit to affirmatively suing states to compel data turnover.

title: USDA Canceled $500 Million in Supplemental Emergency Food Assistance Funding, Scrapping 94 Million Pounds of Food Deliveries to Food Banks Nationwide
institution: U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Food and Nutrition Service / Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC)
status: Rescinded and not restored as of last verification. The $500 million was supplemental funding on top of TEFAP's regular annual appropriation, which remains in place; this entry covers only the canceled supplemental tranche.
date_of_action: 2025-03 (cuts begin) through 2025-11-19 (NPR reporting on continued post-shutdown food-bank demand)
what_changed: In October 2024, the Biden administration's USDA announced $500 million in supplemental funding for The Emergency Food Assistance Program (TEFAP), drawn from the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC) -- on top of TEFAP's regular annual appropriation -- adding to nearly $1 billion in similar CCC-funded supplemental commitments announced in September 2022. Beginning in March 2025, the Trump administration's USDA canceled this supplemental funding, halting roughly 4,300 planned deliveries of USDA-purchased meat, dairy, eggs, and produce -- about 94 million pounds of food -- before they reached food banks nationwide, per a ProPublica investigation that tracked the cancellations 'down to the number of eggs.' USDA characterized the canceled funding as a 'Biden-era slush fund,' telling reporters: 'The Biden Administration inflated statutory programs with Commodity Credit Corporation dollars without any plans for long-term solutions.' National-scope reporting emerged first: **The New York Times reported April 28, 2025 that food banks nationwide were already serving diminished, less-nutritious meals as a result of the cuts -- including one West Virginia food bank forced to substitute crackers, dried cranberries, and vegetable soup for previously USDA-supplied ingredients while preparing meals for 40 seniors** -- citing Feeding America's estimate that the Trump administration's combined food-aid cuts (spanning both this TEFAP/CCC rescission and the separately tracked LFS/LFPA program cuts) totaled roughly $1 billion. Early, regional effects were documented by the Washington Post in May 2025: food banks in Virginia, Washington D.C., and Maryland reported losing more than 1.4 million meals combined, compounded by separate USDA cuts to local-food-purchasing programs (see the related, separately tracked usda-local-food-schools-food-banks-cut-2025 entry) and senior nutrition programs -- with rural areas such as Virginia's Blue Ridge region reporting record need even as national unemployment remained low. By September 2025, the strain was also squeezing hunger-relief networks that depend on unpaid labor: NPR and The Maine Monitor reported that Maine's food pantries -- more than 75% of which run entirely on volunteers, many in their 70s and 80s -- had seen their supply from Good Shepherd Food Bank, the state's only food bank, cut by half or more since March. Good Shepherd began allowing pantries running low on food to turn away visitors who didn't live nearby, reversing its longstanding "food for all" policy (one pantry director, Phylis Allen of Neighbor's Cupboard in Winterport, refused to comply); Minnesota's Second Harvest Heartland, the country's second-largest food bank, had to turn away thousands of pounds of donated food in early September for lack of volunteers to sort it. The same reporting noted charitable food networks were separately bracing for $186 billion in SNAP cuts enacted via OBBBA that summer. By the time of ProPublica's October 2025 investigation, the national scope was clear: food banks across the country reported empty warehouses and were forced to cut rations, with state-level examples including Louisiana food banks losing more than $400,000 in aid and Louisiana recipients going months without meat in their food distributions. The cuts landed during a period of food insecurity at its highest level since the Great Recession, and coincided with the largest food-stamp (SNAP) funding reduction in the program's history, enacted via OBBBA the same summer. Demand kept climbing into November 2025: NPR reported the Greater Boston Food Bank, the San Antonio Food Bank, and West Virginia's Facing Hunger Food Bank all describing record strain -- inventories running at less than half of normal, staff working weeks without a day off, and one West Virginia mobile pantry reduced to splitting a single bag of potatoes between two families -- as a spike in need from the government shutdown's SNAP disruption (see the separately tracked snap-shutdown-funding-freeze-trump2 entry) had not abated even after most SNAP payments resumed, compounding with the OBBBA SNAP cuts and expected reductions to Medicaid, housing assistance, and health-insurance subsidies. Feeding America president Linda Nageotte and Harvard public-health researcher Sara Bleich both likened the mounting pressure to a slow-building crisis, with Bleich predicting a "tsunami" effect with "a generational impact." A USDA spokesperson said the SNAP cuts were meant to curb "proven cases of waste, fraud and abuse" and make the program "sustainable for future generations."

title: DOGE Ordered Lease Terminations at 25 USGS Water Science Centers That Support Flood Warnings and Drinking-Water Safety
institution: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), Department of the Interior
status: Partially reversed -- GSA renewed 2 of the 25 leases (New England and South Atlantic Water Science Centers) in June 2025; the remaining terminations stood as of last verification
date_of_action: 2025-04-29 (reporting on the lease terminations) through 2025-06 (partial reversal)
what_changed: DOGE, then led by Elon Musk, ordered the termination of leases at 25 USGS Water Science Centers nationwide, with 16 of the leases set to expire by August 31, 2025. **These centers collect the streamflow, groundwater, and water-quality data that the National Weather Service and FEMA use to issue flood warnings, that states use for drought declarations and water-rights enforcement, and that regulators use to detect aquifer contamination from pollutants including PFAS ('forever chemicals').** The decision to terminate the leases was reported to be based on lease-expiration timing rather than any scientific review of the centers' value. In June 2025, facing criticism from scientists, state water managers, and advocacy groups, the General Services Administration partially reversed course, renewing the leases for the New England Water Science Center and the South Atlantic Water Science Center; the remaining terminated leases were not reported as reversed as of this entry's creation.

title: DOGE Takes Over U.S. Institute of Peace by Force; Building Later Renamed for Trump
institution: United States Institute of Peace
status: Ongoing (a federal district court ruled the takeover unlawful, but a stay pending appeal keeps the administration in control as of late August 2026; USIP moved July 2, 2026 to lift the case's abeyance and schedule oral argument now that Trump v. Slaughter has been decided, the government opposed that motion July 8, 2026, and the D.C. Circuit had not yet ruled on it as of late August 2026)
date_of_action: 2025-02-19 (executive order) through ongoing appeal; headquarters renamed December 3, 2025
what_changed:
On February 19, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing USIP, a congressionally chartered independent nonprofit created under President Reagan in 1984, to be eliminated 'to the maximum extent consistent with applicable law,' incorrectly characterizing it as a government entity. On March 14, 2025, Trump fired most of USIP's 15-member bipartisan board without stating a reason, leaving only Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and National Defense University President Peter Garvin, who then removed acting president George Moose and installed DOGE-affiliated Kenneth Jackson.

**After being turned away once, DOGE staff forced entry into USIP's headquarters on March 17, 2025 using a physical key taken from a former security contractor, with help from D.C. police, following a standoff in which USIP staff had locked the building. Court filings alleged DOGE personnel accessed and disposed of financial records marked 'SHRED' and enlisted a former USIP IT employee to help bypass the institute's cybersecurity to gain full system control.**

On the evening of Friday, March 28, 2025, starting around 9 p.m., USIP's new, DOGE-affiliated leadership sent termination letters, effective immediately, to more than 200 remaining USIP employees, nearly all of its U.S.-based staff; the letters arrived in personal email inboxes and even by WhatsApp because employees had been locked out of work systems since DOGE took over. CBS News reported that the letters told employees, 'Effective March 28, 2025, your employment with us will conclude,' and CNN reported, citing a source, that they said health care would end March 31; NPR reported that the institute was drawing up plans to fire its remaining overseas employees. Around the end of March, the headquarters building was transferred to the General Services Administration. The Associated Press reported in a story carried by NPR on December 4, 2025 that USIP was operating in 26 conflict zones, including Pakistan, Afghanistan, Mali and Burkina Faso, when DOGE shut the operation down.

On May 19, 2025, U.S. District Judge Beryl Howell ruled the board removal was unlawful and declared all subsequent actions, including the staff firings and building transfer, 'null and void,' ordering reinstatement. Her opinion recounted that Amb. Moose and USIP's counsel had explained that USIP is an 'independent nonprofit organization outside of the executive branch of the federal government.' USIP retook physical control of its headquarters on May 22, 2025; acting president George Moose said the building had been 'essentially...abandoned for many weeks,' protected only by a 'woefully insufficient' security and cleaning presence, and staff found extensive damage from the roughly two-month DOGE occupation: water leaks and water damage throughout, missing ceiling tiles in multiple locations, a damaged garage door, non-operational vehicle security barriers, weeds growing in the rooftop cooling tower, and an infestation of rats and roaches. TechCrunch's coverage, corroborated by the security chief's own account, described the building's interior as resembling 'a zombie movie.'

On June 27, 2025, the D.C. Circuit granted the government a stay pending appeal, citing related Supreme Court precedent allowing presidents to remove independent-agency leaders while litigation proceeds and finding USIP 'exercises substantial executive power,' which returned practical control to the administration; DOGE personnel then fired USIP's staff a second time beginning July 11, 2025, including a 'landing team' brought back to rebuild operations after the first firings; CNN reported on July 12, 2025 that, according to former employee Liz Callihan, DOGE personnel installed at USIP notified staff of the firings, with a 'few remaining employees retained to conduct close-out activities and wind down USIP.' The D.C. Circuit denied USIP's motion to partially lift that stay on November 26, 2025, and held the case in abeyance pending the Supreme Court's Trump v. Slaughter ruling, issued June 29, 2026.

On December 3, 2025, the State Department renamed the institute's headquarters the 'Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace,' while the administration's FY2026 budget request proposed eliminating federal funding for the organization. When the headquarters was renamed, CNN reported that White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said USIP 'was once a bloated, useless entity that blew $50 million per year while delivering no peace' and that the renamed institute is 'both beautifully and aptly named after a President who ended eight wars in less than a year,' while George Foote, counsel for former USIP leadership and staff, said 'a federal judge has already ruled that the government's armed takeover was illegal' and that the stay pending appeal 'is the only reason the government continues to control the building.' The Associated Press reported at the time that USIP has maintained it is an independent creation of Congress and outside the president's executive authority, while the administration has argued it is an executive branch organization.

A Senate Appropriations Committee report (S. Rept. 118-71) lists USIP's FY2023 appropriation as $55 million. USIP's own FY2026 Budget in Brief sought a total of $65 million, including $4 million to reestablish the institute's full functionality after the two-month suspension of its activities in early 2025. The President's FY2026 budget request, released by the Office of Management and Budget, listed USIP among small agencies whose federal funding it would eliminate, with remaining funds covering the costs of orderly shutdowns. Congress did not adopt that proposal: the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148) provides $20,000,000 for USIP, to remain available until September 30, 2027, which shall not be used for construction activities.

With Trump v. Slaughter now decided, USIP filed a motion on July 2, 2026 to lift the D.C. Circuit's abeyance and schedule oral argument on the merits of whether USIP 'exercises substantial executive power'; the government filed an opposition on July 8, 2026. As of late August 2026, no ruling had been identified on USIP's July 2, 2026 motion to lift the D.C. Circuit's abeyance and schedule oral argument, which the government opposed on July 8, 2026; the case remained in abeyance and the administration remained in operational control under the existing stay.

estimated_impact.summary: A congressionally chartered independent institute running active peace-building and conflict-resolution programs in 26 conflict zones was forcibly seized and shuttered, nearly all its U.S. staff terminated, effective immediately, by letters sent the night of Friday, March 28, 2025, and its headquarters left damaged after a roughly two-month DOGE occupation. A federal court ruled the takeover and firings unlawful, but a June 2025 stay pending appeal returned operational control to the administration, which it still held as of late August 2026; the administration fired USIP's staff a second time beginning July 11, 2025.

title: Trump Repeatedly Floats Merging USPS Into Commerce Department; New Postmaster General Pledges to Preserve Independence
institution: U.S. Postal Service
status: Ongoing -- as of the most recent reporting reviewed (Feb-March 2026), the merger remains 'under consideration' but has not been formally implemented; new Postmaster General David Steiner has publicly pledged to preserve USPS's independence
date_of_action: 2025-03 (Trump first floats the merger) through 2025-07 (Steiner appointed, pledges independence)
what_changed: **Starting around March 2025, Trump repeatedly said he was considering merging USPS into the Commerce Department, describing it as 'a form of a merger' (NPR, Supply Chain Dive, March 2025). Under a 1970 postal reorganization law, USPS is an independent executive-branch agency governed by an 11-member Board of Governors (nine presidentially nominated) and overseen for postage rates by an independent regulator, insulated from direct day-to-day political control. Democratic senators, including Gary Peters, said an attempt by Trump to seize control of USPS or fire its Board of Governors outright would be illegal under that statute.** Around the same time, longtime Postmaster General Louis DeJoy -- Trump's own favored pick during his first administration -- announced he would step down and asked the Board to identify a successor; the Board named David Steiner, a former FedEx board member, as his replacement. On July 17, 2025, Steiner publicly pledged to keep USPS operating as an independent agency despite the merger talk, a stance drawing skepticism from postal unions given his FedEx background and the administration's continued interest in the merger idea (Reuters, July 2025). As financial context for why the merger idea has traction, USPS has lost more than $100 billion cumulatively since 2007, and the agency has separately been in talks with UPS and other private carriers about better leveraging its delivery network -- a strategy Steiner's team pursued as an alternative to a Commerce takeover.

primary_proponent.name: Donald Trump
